YANGON, Oct. 25 (Xinhua) -- Six people were killed and 12 others injured in a road accident in Myanmar's Mandalay region on Saturday, according to the Myanmar Fire Services Department.
The accident occurred at around 6:05 p.m. local time on a downhill section of the Pyin Oo Lwin-Mandalay road in Pyin Oo Lwin township, when an express bus traveling from Pyin Oo Lwin to Mandalay had brake failure and collided head-on with a van traveling in the opposite direction, the department said.
Following the collision, the bus plunged into a roadside ravine about 50 feet deep and overturned, it said.
Local firefighters and rescue personnel were dispatched to the scene to carry out rescue operations, the department said.
The van's driver was killed in the accident. Among the 29 people aboard the bus, five were reported dead and 12 injured. The injured passengers were taken to hospitals for medical treatment, the department said.
Rescue teams were searching for 12 people who remained missing, it added. ■

Sanctioned Russian energy giant secretly funded US gas project, NYT reports
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
00:29:15 UTC
09:29:15 KST

The Russian company Novatek has been secretly funding a multibillion-dollar U.S. gas project that has been discussed in negotiations between the White House and the Kremlin over ending the war in Ukraine, the New York Times (NYT) first reported on Oct. 23.
Novatek is Russia's second-largest producer of liquefied natural gas (LNG) and has been subject to U.S. sanctions since the full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.
Polar LNG, an American company aiming to liquefy and export natural gas from Alaska, received secret funding from Novatek in potential violation of sanctions, the NYT reported, citing the company's former CEO and two other sources familiar with the matter.
John Riddle, former CEO of Polar LNG, resigned from the company in September after learning about the hidden ties to Novatek. Riddle said he had been told the funding came from a company in the United Arab Emirates.
"It's not only unlawful, but it's not in the U.S. interest to have Russian technology controlling the commercialization of Arctic gas in the North Slope," Riddle told the NYT.
Riddle said he notified officials in the Trump administration about the secret Russian financing and urged them to investigate the situation.
Novatek was not only channeling funds to Polar LNG — it was negotiating a deal to sell technology to the U.S. company as part of a business agreement between Washington and Moscow. U.S. peace envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner discussed the proposal with Russian President Vladimir Putin during their visit in September, sources told the NYT.
It is not clear whether Witkoff or Kushner were aware of the financial relationship between Novatek and Polar LNG, as the deal was only broadly discussed, sources said.
read also
The Novatek-Polar LNG proposal is reportedly one of several energy deals that U.S. President Donald Trump is looking to strike with Russia as he attempts to broker an end to the war against Ukraine. Another involves selling off parts of the Russian energy giant Lukoil to the U.S. government and other investors — including some with ties to Kushner and Wiktoff.
In a statement to the NYT, Novatek confirmed that it was looking to acquire "minority shareholder" status in the Polar LNG project.
The reported backdoor energy deals between the Kremlin and the White House have taken place against the backdrop of intensified Russian attacks on Ukraine — and a marked withdrawal of U.S. support from Kyiv.
Trump made his indifference to Russian sanctions clear when he announced a surprise deal with Putin to purchase diesel from Moscow to offset U.S. fuel prices. The first tanker of Russian diesel is reportedly now bound for the U.S.
The White House has also issued another sanctions waiver to Russia. In the last week, Witkoff has praised Putin as a "humanitarian" and U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio has claimed that the war in Ukraine is a narrow regional dispute that only concerns "11 percent of one part of that country."

Australia's Alexander Volkanovski earns record ninth UFC featherweight title win against Movsar Evloev
In short:
Australia's Alexander Volkanovski was too strong as he wrapped up another UFC featherweight title win.
He defeated previously unbeaten Russian Movsar Evloev by TKO in the second round of their fight at UFC 333 in Abu Dhabi.
The 38-year-old Volkanovski brushed off questions about retirement, saying "maybe we keep going".
Australian Alexander Volkanovski has underlined his greatness with a stunning second-round TKO of previously unbeaten Russian Movsar Evloev in a record-extending ninth UFC featherweight title fight win.
Headlining the UFC 333 card in Abu Dhabi, Volkanovski was considered the underdog in some quarters, but the 38-year-old proved too good for his younger opponent, the number one contender.
He got Evloev down to the ground with some precise, hurtful punching and landed some brutal ground and pound to force referee Marc Goddard to stop the fight with six seconds of the second round remaining.
Volkanovski, from Windang on the NSW South Coast, landed with some good kicks and punches in the first couple of minutes.
Elite wrestler Evloev (20-1) took Volkanovski down three times in the last couple of minutes of the first round, but the Australian quickly bounced back to his feet each time.
The champion had a cut on his face in the second round, but in the last few seconds he bloodied Evloev's face, as his crisp, accurate punches found their mark.
It was his first stoppage win in six fights stretching back to 2023.
"It feels good to get a finish," said Volkanovski, who improved his MMA record to 29-4.
"I actually promised the missus, it was our wedding anniversary on Wednesday, I promised her a quick one (win) so she wasn't stressing on the sidelines."
It was a second successful defence of his second reign and Volkanovski indicated he wasn't ready to retire yet.
"I said if I didn't take too much damage, we'll probably keep going, so maybe we keep going," Volkanovski said.
Evloev landed some good strikes but couldn't maintain the pressure on the wily champion.
"He's like good wine; older, stronger, better, he's truly a legend," Evloev said.
In a thrilling co-main event, Russia's Petr Yan retained the bantamweight world title with a unanimous points decision over Georgia's Merab Dvalishvili, beating him for the second time in three fights.
In the prelims, Australians recorded a win and two losses against Russian opponents.
Volkanovski's stablemate, bantamweight Colby Thicknesse, scored a third straight win and a big upset with a split-decision victory over previously unbeaten Asaf Chopurov.
Middleweight Cam Rowston's run of seven straight wins ended with a first-round guillotine-choke-submission loss to 12th-ranked Abus Magomedov of Russia, and middleweight Jacob Malkoun's three-fight win streak was snapped by a unanimous-points loss to Abubakar Vagaev.

Survivors of clergy sexual abuse have agreed to an $800 million settlement with the Archdiocese of New York, lawyers said on Saturday, to resolve claims brought by approximately 1,300 people.
The Catholic Archdiocese of New York agreed to the payment in May, one of the largest payouts in a wave of lawsuits over clergy sex abuse in the US.
Jeff Anderson & Associates, which represents 300 abuse survivors, called it "a powerful moment in the pursuit of justice."
The settlement is second only to an $880 million deal reached by the Archdiocese of Los Angeles in 2024.
The Catholic Church has paid billions of dollars in settlements across the US in the past several years, after New York and other states enacted laws that temporarily enabled victims of child sexual abuse to file lawsuits over decades-old crimes.
Documents to be released surrounding sexual abuse in the Church
In addition to the $800 million settlement, the archdiocese agreed to release documents pertaining to sexual offenders in the Church.
The settlement also allows survivors to litigate against the Church's insurers for additional payouts, but avoids a bankruptcy by the archdiocese.

Camille Cottin elevates French family drama 'Out of Love' as it opens in Israeli theaters - review
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
00:23:31 UTC
09:23:31 KST

Out of Love, directed by Nathan Ambrosioni, which opened in theaters throughout Israel on Thursday, is a well-made if somewhat bland French drama about a single woman forced through circumstances to care for her sister’s children.
It joins a long list of European movies that play briefly in theaters and tackle the kinds of issues that used to be a staple of American TV movies. Many people enjoy these relatable dramas, and this one features an element that nudges it a little above the usual standard for these films: the always watchable Camille Cottin in the lead.
She is one of France’s most popular actresses, and deservedly so. She is terrific in both comedy and drama, and she has real screen presence. When she’s there, you can’t take your eyes off of her.
Even if you don’t recognize her name, you have likely seen her in recent movies, such as Just an Illusion and In the Land of Arto, or the television series Call My Agent! and the recent movie based on it, where she played an intensely narcissistic character who nonetheless became a fan favorite. She also played Golda Meir’s secretary opposite Helen Mirren in the 2023 movie, Golda.
Jeanne, the character she portrays in Out of Love, is a tense, successful insurance claims adjuster who broke up with her longtime girlfriend because the girlfriend wanted children and she didn’t. So she isn’t exactly delighted when her younger sister, Suzanne (Juliette Armanet), after years of silence, shows up out of the blue with her two children (Manoa Varvet and Nina Birman), asks to stay over, and then leaves during the night.
Movie opens with a powerful scene
Jeanne has no idea where her sister is or why she has done this. The movie opens with what turns out to be one of its most effective scenes, told from the point of view of the children, who are waiting for their mother, who has gone into the store at a gas station and left them in the car.
They are anxious because she seems to them to have been gone a long time, and we soon learn how much her behavior has made them afraid in general lately.
At first Jeanne, understandably, thinks that her sister may be experiencing a momentary crisis and will soon return for the extremely sweet children.
But when she can’t get in touch with Suzanne after a day or so, she contacts the police, who say that they cannot do anything to find a woman who has left her children with a relative and gone away. If she will not care for them, the youngsters will be put into the foster care system and likely sent to different homes.
Scenes are well filmed, well acted
Jeanne reluctantly steps up, and the movie details her journey of trying to tap into her softer side to become a maternal figure to the children. She also copes with a troubled heritage from her very dysfunctional parents, which has harmed her sister deeply and which she has tried to push from her mind.
Each scene is well filmed and well acted. Thanks to Cottin’s performance, we are instantly in Jeanne’s head, and we feel for her. But it’s evident from the beginning that once she is called to take care of these children, it’s only a matter of time until she is transformed into the stable parental figure they need.
Although she has anxiety attacks and chain-smokes nervously, it’s clear that she has a core of inner strength, and the tone of the movie is generally upbeat. Her coworkers are understanding and helpful; even a police officer contacts her to apologize.
Out of Love presents a soothing universe where things fall into place in the end, perhaps a little more neatly than they do anywhere but in a TV-style movie.

Thousands rally in Tel Aviv against Netanyahu ahead of vote
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
00:10:00 UTC
09:10:00 KST

Thousands rally in Tel Aviv against Netanyahu ahead of vote
- Thousands rallied in Tel Aviv against Benjamin Netanyahu before Israel’s election, led by the October Council and families of Oct 7 victims and hostages demanding accountability.
- Polls showed no clear majority for either bloc, while opposition figures Gadi Eisenkot and Naftali Bennett drew support and vowed to challenge Netanyahu’s rule.
- The protest also pushed for an independent inquiry into the Oct 7 failures, as Netanyahu faced criticism over isolation, sanctions, and his talk of a possible alternate digital economy.
AI generated
TEL AVIV – Thousands gathered in Tel Aviv on Oct 24 for a large anti-government demonstration, three days ahead of a general election widely viewed as a referendum on Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.
The protest was organised by the October Council, a group founded by the families of victims and hostages taken by Palestinian militants on Oct 7, 2023, to demand accountability for the failure to prevent the Hamas attack that sparked the Gaza war.
According to Israeli media, the gathering saw the participation of the leaders of the four main opposition parties, including Gadi Eisenkot, the former military chief of staff who is neck and neck with Netanyahu and who received a warm reception from the crowd.
“Three days before the election, we will hold the culminating event marking three years of struggle to uncover the truth, demand accountability, and establish a state commission of inquiry,” the October Council wrote on X ahead of the rally.
The latest polls published before a gag period entered into force on the night of Oct 23 showed that neither bloc would obtain a majority of seats in Israel’s Parliament.
A poll published by public broadcaster KAN found that out of 120 seats in the Israeli Parliament, 52 would go to Eisenkot’s bloc and 50 to Netanyahu’s, with the rest going to non-aligned parties, including Arab ones.
An AFP reporter said thousands were marching from the central Rabin Square towards Hostages Square, a focal point for past anti-government protests to demand the release of those held captive in Gaza.
“Whoever has been leading us for the past four years (since Netanyahu’s government took office in late 2022) has done such a terrible job,” Hadas Feuershtein, 68, told AFP shortly before the start of the rally.
“Israel has never been in a situation as it is now,” she added.
Ahead of the rally, the October Council had alerted law enforcement of possible “provocations” from pro-government agitators.
The Israeli police said on the evening of Oct 24 that it “arrested a suspect for assaulting the security team of a public figure” in Tel Aviv, with the Israeli press identifying the target as former Prime Minister and opposition party leader Naftali Bennett.
The rally came after years of campaigning by Israeli civil society and opposition parties to establish an independent commission of inquiry on the security failures that led to the attack on Oct 7, 2023.
Netanyahu’s government has refused to establish such an independent body, the likes of which Israel has commonly set up in the past to investigate major state-level failings.
It has instead offered to create a “political” commission, half of whose members would be appointed by the ruling coalition and half by opposition lawmakers.
Opposition leaders, however, said they would boycott a commission appointed by politicians.
As the campaign draws to an end, Eisenkot and Bennett are expected to hold separate last meetings with voters in Tel Aviv on the evening of Oct 25.
No ‘bbCoin’
First-time voter Naama Bitterman, 18, said at the rally on Oct 24 that she was confident the anti-Netanyahu bloc she supports would have the upper hand in the vote and improve Israel’s international standing, tarnished by three years of war in Gaza, Lebanon and Iran and surging violence in the occupied West Bank.
“I think that if we win – and we are going to win – we can change how other people in the entire world see us,” she told AFP.
Britain and several other countries imposed sanctions targeting goods from Israeli settlements in the West Bank in response to a wave of settler attacks on Palestinians and settlement construction approved by Netanyahu’s right-wing government.
To circumvent Israel’s growing international isolation, Netanyahu suggested on Oct 23 that Israel may need to develop an alternate digital economy.
Netanyahu, who has previously called for Israel to become self-sufficient militarily, also said that multibillion-dollar weapons packages from key ally Washington “won’t keep coming”.
Opposition leaders on Oct 24 lambasted the premier’s suggestion.
Eisenkot sarcastically referred to the proposed parallel digital currency as “bbCoin”, using a common nickname for the premier, Bibi.
“Netanyahu says that if he is elected again, Israel will disconnect from the global economy. No online shopping, no investments in high-tech, no security. We must not let bbCoin destroy Israel,” he wrote on X.
Yair Lapid, a former prime minister and current leader of the opposition, accused Netanyahu of “promising Israeli citizens before the elections that they will stand in line for an hour and a half for bread like in Russia or Iran”.
“If he wins the elections, that’s what will happen: There will be sanctions, there will be no security agreement with the United States... and there will be no Israeli economy,” he said in an interview with Israel’s Channel 12. AFP

Bulgaria votes for president in wake of deadly Black Sea drone strikes

Bulgaria votes for president in wake of deadly Black Sea drone strikes
SOFIA, Oct 25 - Bulgarians vote in presidential elections on Sunday as Russia's war in Ukraine spreads to the waters off Bulgaria's Black Sea coast.
Polls place acting President Iliana Iotova, 61, and ex-caretaker prime minister Andrey Gyurov, 50, as leaders in a race of 27 candidates.
While the presidency is largely ceremonial, Sunday's vote has taken on added significance after a series of drone attacks on merchant ships off Bulgaria's Black Sea coast that likely killed some two-dozen international seafarers.
The strikes, which sparked international condemnation and concerns about the growing reach of the war in Ukraine, prompted the government to seek allied assistance to bolster maritime security.
Bulgaria has stopped short of directly accusing Russia of carrying out the attacks, but Prime Minister Rumen Radev said their outcome "benefits the Russian Federation".
Both leading presidential candidates condemned the strikes, but they differ over the broader war.
Gyurov, who served as caretaker prime minister this year, is supported by pro-Western, reformist parties and has long expressed support for Ukraine. He signed a security cooperation agreement with Kyiv during his time as premier.
"I want Bulgaria to have a voice of its own in Europe. A reliable NATO ally that defends its interests through preparedness, strong diplomacy and a clear position," he said at a rally on Thursday.
Iotova, formerly vice president, became acting president in January after Radev resigned to enter the parliamentary race, which he won on what many political analysts considered a Kremlin-friendly ticket. Radev supports Iotova and they both call for a diplomatic end to the war.
A victory for Iotova would make her Bulgaria's first elected female president.
"My opponents argue that there must be a war of attrition." she told a rally on Thursday. "The truth is, we are all the ones who are most exhausted."
Polls by Alpha Research give Iotova 41% of the vote and Gyurov 28%. If no candidate wins a majority, a runoff vote will be held on November 1.
Voting starts at 7 a.m. (0500 GMT) and polls close at 8 p.m. REUTERS

New Delhi reiterated that Jammu and Kashmir remains an integral and inalienable part of India.
NEW DELHI: India tore into Pakistan at the United Nations for exploiting the international forum to spread propaganda while failing to protect its own citizens. New Delhi reiterated that Jammu and Kashmir remains an integral and inalienable part of India and demanded that Pakistan vacate all territories under its illegal occupation.Speaking at an interactive dialogue with the Special Rapporteur on Minority Issues at the UN General Assembly's Third Committee, India's First Secretary at the Permanent Mission to the UN, Raghoo Puri, called out Pakistan's conduct and said its representatives should focus on the welfare of their own people instead of taking directions from the military."Pakistan predictably misused the forum for propaganda. Jammu & Kashmir is an integral and inalienable part of India. Pakistan must vacate the territory under its illegal occupation," Puri said.He further said Pakistani representatives would do well to look inwards and address the concerns of their own citizens rather than act on military directives.
India slams Pakistan over minority rights
Puri underlined that protecting minority rights was primarily the sovereign responsibility of individual states, guided by the principle of sovereign equality.He said India's civilisational tradition of diversity was reflected in its constitutional safeguards for religious and linguistic minorities.
He also highlighted the substantial contributions made by minorities to India's national development, including at the highest levels of government and key institutions.
The latest confrontation followed India's strong rebuke to Pakistan at the UN on October 23 over its treatment of religious minorities. New Delhi accused Islamabad of failing to protect vulnerable communities while attempting to lecture India on religious freedom, burial rights and minority protections.During an interactive dialogue with the Special Rapporteur on Freedom of Religion or Belief, India's First Secretary at the UN mission, Bhavika Mangalanandan, challenged the report's approach to religious discrimination during the Covid-19 pandemic and its advocacy concerning funeral rights for terrorists.Mangalanandan argued that the report appeared to place disproportionate emphasis on discriminatory practices and shortcomings in countries in the Global South while overlooking similar tragedies in developed nations.
India asserts climate justice and judicial independence
Separately, India also defended its approach to climate change at the UN General Assembly, stressing the importance of equity, climate justice and sustainable development.Deputy secretary Barkha Tamrakar delivered India's statement before the Third Committee on the report of the Special Rapporteur on the independence of judges and lawyers, titled “An urgent and existential threat: the role of justice systems in addressing the climate crisis.”Tamrakar described climate change as a serious global challenge with consequences for development, livelihoods and human rights. She said India's response was guided by equity, climate justice, sustainable development and the principle of Common But Differentiated Responsibilities and Respective Capabilities (CBDR-RC).
She highlighted the Constitution, environmental legislation, the National Green Tribunal and an independent judiciary as key safeguards supporting environmental protection in India.Tamrakar also noted that the Supreme Court had recognised the fundamental rights to life and equality as essential protections against the adverse effects of climate change.On judicial independence, she pointed to transparent, institutionally supervised training programmes, including those conducted by the National Judicial Academy, as measures to strengthen impartiality and safeguard the independence of the judiciary.

Bodies of ambushed Salvadoran soldiers found in Haiti, New York Times reports
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
02:01:23 CEST
09:01:23 KST

PORT-AU-PRINCE, Oct 24 (Reuters) - Bodies believed to be those of four Salvadoran soldiers missing since an ambush by armed gangs in Haiti have been found outside the capital, Port-au-Prince, the New York Times reported on Saturday, citing two people close to the security mission.
The newspaper said the remains were recovered on Saturday and were badly burned, meaning autopsies would be needed to confirm their identities. It said the bodies were handed over at the international airport to a Salvadoran military team that had flown into Haiti on Friday.
The international security mission declined to comment. Reuters could not immediately confirm the report.
The four Salvadorans went missing on Sunday after they jumped from a burning armored vehicle that came under attack on the outskirts of Port-au-Prince while they were returning from a market to their base, Salvadoran officials said earlier this week. The ambush was the first major attack on the Gang Suppression Force, a United Nations-authorized multinational mission, since it began operations in Haiti this year.
President Nayib Bukele said on Wednesday that gangs were holding the four men and that El Salvador had launched a military operation to bring them back unharmed. Additional Salvadoran troops were later deployed to support search and security operations.
No group has publicly claimed responsibility for the attack. Local media have linked the ambush to gangs operating in the area, including powerful armed groups Chen Mechan and 400 Mawozo.
A year into its mandate, the GSF has about 2,000 troops on the ground, well below its authorized ceiling of 5,500. An earlier Kenyan-led security effort struggled with chronic shortages of money, equipment and personnel.
Haiti’s gangs have expanded sharply since the 2021 assassination of President Jovenel Moise, taking control of large parts of Port-au-Prince and displacing 1.4 million to 1.5 million people.
(Reporting by Kylie Madry and Harold Isaac; Writing by Sarah Morland; Editing by Alistair Bell and Rod Nickel)

Yemen's Houthis renew warning against using Riyadh airport
Oct 25 - Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthis on Sunday renewed their warning against using Riyadh's King Khalid International Airport, hours after the airport announced it will designate two terminals for flights following a suspension earlier this month.
Houthi military spokesperson Yahya Saree said the airport remained a "military target" and operations targeting the airport will continue, warning all airlines, airport staffers and travellers against using it.
Late on Saturday, King Khalid Airport said Terminal 1 would be designated for domestic flights and Terminal 2 for international flights operated by national carriers starting Sunday.
Operations in the airport were halted on October 10, following an attack on the airport, claimed by the Houthis, that killed 13 people and wounded more than 300 others, the deadliest in the kingdom in more than a decade. The suspension of operations was extended two days later.
The Houthis have been firing ballistic missiles and drones at Saudi airports, ports and oil installations, turning US ally Saudi Arabia into a pressure point in the wider war.
Saudi Arabia has recently stepped up its military involvement in Yemen, launching strikes against the Houthis and backing a government counteroffensive after the Houthis seized strategic territory along the Red Sea coast last month. REUTERS

Singapore embraces AI for cyber defence, with one caveat: breach transparency
The city state will take a ‘pragmatic’ approach to AI adoption as it seeks to bolster protection for its critical infrastructure
4-MIN READ4-MIN
 Listen
Kolette Limin Singapore
Singapore is turning to major technology firms to strengthen its cyber defences, even as it presses them for greater transparency over security breaches – a balancing act facing regional governments as they seek to harness artificial intelligence while guarding against the risks it introduces.
Those risks were highlighted by an AI agent linked to OpenAI that gained unauthorised access to files on an Australian government website earlier this year, raising questions over how quickly companies disclose security incidents as AI systems become more capable and autonomous.
At a summit earlier this month, Singapore launched a refreshed cybersecurity strategy that would see it progressively deploy AI across its cyber defence operations and work with industry partners to accelerate adoption, as it seeks to bolster protection for its critical infrastructure.
The city state would take a “pragmatic” approach to AI adoption, allowing it to choose between the “best available” models, K. Shanmugam, coordinating minister for national security, said during a speech at Singapore International Cyber Week on October 13.
“We will not need to develop our own AI models for every use case. What we really need is the capability to evaluate the best available models and to adapt them to our own needs.”

Barack Obama rallies Michigan crowd for El-Sayed, saying he’s ‘fighting for real change’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
23:50:30 UTC
08:50:30 KST

Barack Obama told a Detroit crowd on Saturday that Abdul El-Sayed was “fighting for change, real change, that will get money out of politics and put money in your pocket”, as he threw his weight behind the Democratic Senate candidate and the rest of the ticket on the first day of early voting in Michigan.
Obama said in front of thousands of onlookers at Cass technical high school in Detroit that El-Sayed would “finish the job we started with the Affordable Care Act and guarantee quality, affordable healthcare to every single American”.
The former president headlined the rally for El-Sayed, the Democratic nominee for US Senate, and secretary of state Jocelyn Benson, the party’s candidate for governor, at an evening event to “get out the vote”.
He accused Donald Trump of “enriching himself and his family”, and said the administration had set a “culture … at the top” of taking favors. “Never seen a president so intent on selling favors like this,” he said.
The rally came on the first day of Michigan’s early voting period, with the general election on 3 November. It was also Obama’s first weekend of in-person campaigning during the midterms, which started in Cleveland, Ohio, earlier in the day to stump for the former Ohio senator Sherrod Brown and Democratic nominee for governor Amy Acton earlier in the weekend. He issued similarly scathing remarks aimed at the White House and the GOP.
The Detroit stop is Obama’s first public show of support for El-Sayed, who emerged from a bitter August primary in which the former president stayed on the sidelines. El-Sayed, a doctor and former Wayne county health official, beat the moderate congresswoman Haley Stevens who was riding on the backing of the Democratic establishment and pro-Israel organizations.
Obama was on the offensive against the administration, mocking the defense secretary, Pete Hegseth, as “laser-focused” on the “jawline and testosterone levels of our troops”, asking: “How much time do you think this man spends in front of the mirror every day?”
On tariffs, Obama said Trump was toughest on “that well-known evil empire”, referring to Canada, a few minutes’ drive from Detroit across the bridge. “These are the people who gave us Martin Short and maple syrup,” he said.
He even took a jab at Trump’s attempts to renovate the White House. “He should be on HGTV,” Obama said of the many renovations in Washington, including the White House ballroom and the Rose Garden. “He’s got the White House looking like Saddam Hussein opened a Cheesecake Factory.”
Questions had hung over whether Obama would back El-Sayed at all. El-Sayed, a champion of Medicare for All, had at one point called the Affordable Care Act, Obama’s signature domestic achievement, an incremental fix. The two men spoke by phone after the primary, and El-Sayed has since called Obama a mentor figure.
El-Sayed has the most ground to make up in Wayne county, where Detroit is the county seat, after Stevens beat him there by about 51% to 45% in the August primaries. Obama last campaigned in Detroit – which is more than three-quarters Black – in October 2024 for Kamala Harris, and Harris herself appeared with El-Sayed in Detroit last month.
Republicans have not held a Michigan Senate seat in 25 years, but the party sees the seat as one of its better pickup chances nationwide. El-Sayed faces Mike Rogers, a former congressman endorsed by Donald Trump who lost a 2024 Senate matchup against Democratic senator Elissa Slotkin by less than half a percentage point. The Cook Political Report rates this race a toss-up.
Slotkin, a featured speaker at the rally, told the crowd that “Michigan believes in electing fighters”. And when it came to any disagreements she may have with El-Sayed, she said: “It’s OK because we agree on so much more.”
“We’re putting a check and balance on Donald Trump in the White House,” she said.
A Marist poll of likely voters statewide conducted in mid-October put El-Sayed at 50% and Rogers at 48%, within the margin of error. RealClearPolitics’s average had El-Sayed ahead by about 2.6 points in a similar timeframe.
Trump has attacked El-Sayed throughout the campaign, calling him a “jihadist”, pointing to his middle name and alleging that he had ties to the Muslim Brotherhood, which El-Sayed strongly denies, and has created one of the most viral moments of the year. El-Sayed has also faced a barrage of criticism from the establishment wing of the Democratic party over his appearances with leftwing streamer Hasan Piker.
Trump is due in the state himself on Sunday, when he will hold a rally for Michigan Republicans in Port Huron, on the Canadian border. The city said it will be the first presidential visit to St Clair county.
If elected, El-Sayed would be the first Muslim and first Egyptian American in the US Senate. Benson faces the Republican congressman John James; a James win would make him Michigan’s first Black governor.
Turning to the disagreements between them, Obama acknowledged that some people had pointed out that El-Sayed “didn’t like some things you did as president”. “We are not going to agree on every detail of every issue,” he said. “You know who else doesn’t agree with everything I do? Michelle Obama.”
“We share those values of making sure everybody gets a fair shot in this society,” Obama said, “and that the system’s not just run for those at the top.”

Nigeria: Tinubu launches reelection bid amid economic woes
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24

Nigeria: Tinubu launches reelection bid amid economic woes
October 25, 2026
Nigeria's President Bola Tinubu on Saturday formally launched his campaign for a second term.
"We have prosperity, consistency, growth, recovery and opportunity," Tinubu said at a rally in the northwestern state of Kaduna.
"You grant me the privilege to promise you once again, there is that promise of a better tomorrow," he added.
Africa's most populous country will hold its next presidential election in January 2027. The campaign is expected to focus on Nigeria's economy and security challenges.
Nigeria's worsening cost of living
After taking power in 2023, Tinubu sparked anger by scrapping decades-long fuel subsidies — a move that has fueled Nigeria's inflation.
On Saturday, the incumbent president dismissed criticisms about his economic policies.
"I hear my opponents talking about hunger and poverty. Who created it? They did," Tinubu said at the crowded rally. "They created the hunger, they created the poverty. We are trying to eradicate it."
Earlier this month, the 74-year-old acknowledged Nigeria's economic issues. In his Independence Day address, he argued that his administration's reform "did not create the weaknesses in our economy," but actually "confronted them."
Tinubu's government announced potential price caps on fuel soon after.
Security threats to play big role in Nigeria's election
Apart from grappling with a cost-of-living crisis, Nigeria continues to struggle with armed bandits and kidnappers.
On Friday, gunmen killed at least 20 people in an attack on a village in the country's northeast.
The nation has also been fighting a long-running jihadist insurgency, sparked by Boko Haram's 2009 uprising.
Another three-man race
Tinubu's main challengers are expected to be former Vice President Atiku Abubakar and former state governor Peter Obi.
In the 2023 presidential election,Tinubu only managed to secure less than 36.6% of the valid votes cast, with Abubakar at 29% and Obi at 25.4%.

Speleologist and traveler Borys Hora killed in action
His daughter Alina reported this on Facebook, according to Ukrinform.
"On October 19, our father Borys Hora, the father of both me and Liubko Hora, was killed. We are awaiting the results of DNA testing," she said.
Borys Hora was born in Ternopil on March 10, 1969. In the 1990s, he founded the Krystal tourism club within the Plast scouting organization. He later settled in a village near Mlynky Cave, where he established a speleology base and worked as a guide. Among other activities, he organized rafting trips on the Dniester and Chornyi Cheremosh rivers, hiking trips in the Carpathians, and climbs in the Caucasus Mountains. He also volunteered and cared for animals.
After Russia launched its full-scale invasion, Hora volunteered to join the Ukrainian Armed Forces.

Massive Ukrainian drone attack hits shopping center in Russia's Belgorod Oblast, locals say
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
23:27:09 UTC
08:27:09 KST

Massive Ukrainian drone attack hits shopping center in Russia's Belgorod Oblast, locals say
Editor's Note: This is a developing story and is being updated.
A massive swarm of Ukrainian drones attacked the Russian border region of Belgorod overnight on Oct. 25, according to local officials and eyewitness footage posted to social media.
The bulk of the drones have concentrated on one area in the Belgorod city center, locals report. According to the monitoring channel Exilenova-Plus, the target was the MegaGRINN shopping complex, Belgorod's largest retail and entertainment center.
MegaGRINN covers an area of more than 163,000 square meters and houses over 200 stores, as well as a supermarket, cinema, and restaurants. The facility was closed and empty of visitors during the overnight attack.
Local residents also reported a fire in the courtyard of a residential complex in the area.
The Belgorod Oblast Operational Headquarters confirmed a "massive UAV attack" against the city and said emergency services had been dispatched to the impacted areas, though they did not name any specific targets.
The attack killed one civilian and injured 10 others, authorities said.
Russian officials have not yet provided details regarding damage or casualties from the strike.
Videos published on social media by eyewitnesses show explosions, fires, and air defense operations over the city of Belgorod. The Operational Headquarters has warned residents to stay indoors as attacks are ongoing in the region.
The Kyiv Independent could not verify these reports at the time of publication.
The city of Belgorod lies just 34 kilometers (21 miles) from Ukraine's northeastern border with Russia and approximately 70 kilometers (43 miles) from Kharkiv. Its proximity to the front lines makes it a frequent target of Ukrainian attacks, even as Kyiv's expanding long-range capabilities allow its drones to penetrate deep in the Russian interior.
Previous Ukrainian strikes on Belgorod have targeted energy infrastructure and logistics warehouses, including facilities belonging to the Russian retail giant Ozon.
The reported drone blitz on Belgorod comes shortly after Ukraine confirmed on Oct. 24 that its Starshield system had been restored to full speed, allowing troops to more effectively coordinate drone strikes on Russian targets.
Starshield, the military application of the Starlink satellite internet system, had been operating at drastically reduced speed in Ukraine since Oct. 14. The unexplained restriction disrupted key military missions and Ukraine's ability to shoot down Russian jet-powered drones.

Over 300 Houthis ‘neutralized’ in Yemen in 24 hours: Army
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
23:27:07 UTC
08:27:07 KST

Omer Asur Cuhadar and Tarek Chouiref
25 October 2026•Update: 25 October 2026
The Yemeni army said Saturday that its forces had “neutralized” 307 Houthi fighters and commanders in 736 operations during the last 24 hours, destroying or damaging 68 military vehicles and weapons.
It said the operations targeted command centers, troop concentrations, reinforcements, weapons depots, and supply routes under the “Dawn of Yemen” offensive.
The army did not specify how many Houthis were killed or wounded. There was no immediate comment from the group.
In the southwestern Taiz province, the army said it struck a command center, heavy weapons positions, and arms depots inside an abandoned hotel.
It accused the Houthis of turning the hotel into an observation post and firing position to threaten residential neighborhoods and maintain their siege of the city. Government troops also carried out raids to suppress fire from the area, it added.
Fighting continues in Taiz, where government forces hold the city center, while the Houthis have made recent gains in rural and coastal areas.
Yemen has been engulfed in conflict since the Houthis seized the capital Sanaa and other provinces in 2014, prompting a Saudi-led coalition to intervene in 2015 in support of the internationally recognized government.
The Houthis control much of northern and western Yemen, while government forces and their allies hold Aden and large parts of southern and eastern provinces.

Bodies of ambushed Salvadoran soldiers found in Haiti, New York Times reports
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

08:25:24 KST

Bodies of ambushed Salvadoran soldiers found in Haiti, New York Times reports
PORT-AU-PRINCE, Oct 24 - Bodies believed to be those of four Salvadoran soldiers missing since an ambush by armed gangs in Haiti have been found outside the capital, Port-au-Prince, the New York Times reported on Saturday, citing two people close to the security mission.
The newspaper said the remains were recovered on Saturday and were badly burned, meaning autopsies would be needed to confirm their identities. It said the bodies were handed over at the international airport to a Salvadoran military team that had flown into Haiti on Friday.
The international security mission declined to comment. Reuters could not immediately confirm the report.
The four Salvadorans went missing on Sunday after they jumped from a burning armored vehicle that came under attack on the outskirts of Port-au-Prince while they were returning from a market to their base, Salvadoran officials said earlier this week. The ambush was the first major attack on the Gang Suppression Force, a United Nations-authorized multinational mission, since it began operations in Haiti this year.
President Nayib Bukele said on Wednesday that gangs were holding the four men and that El Salvador had launched a military operation to bring them back unharmed. Additional Salvadoran troops were later deployed to support search and security operations.
No group has publicly claimed responsibility for the attack. Local media have linked the ambush to gangs operating in the area, including powerful armed groups Chen Mechan and 400 Mawozo.
A year into its mandate, the GSF has about 2,000 troops on the ground, well below its authorized ceiling of 5,500. An earlier Kenyan-led security effort struggled with chronic shortages of money, equipment and personnel.
Haiti's gangs have expanded sharply since the 2021 assassination of President Jovenel Moise, taking control of large parts of Port-au-Prince and displacing 1.4 million to 1.5 million people. REUTERS

Typhoon Champi may approach Japan’s Kyushu as heavy rainfall sets records
Typhoon Champi could approach the Kyushu region in southwestern Japan on Monday before transitioning into an extratropical cyclone and moving toward waters off the western coast of Shikoku, the Japan Meteorological Agency said, Qazinform News Agency reports, citing JIJI Press.
The agency has urged caution over the risk of heavy rain, partly due to a lingering weather front stretching across eastern and western Japan.
Champi, the 30th typhoon of the year, was moving over waters north of the Sakishima Islands in Okinawa Prefecture on Saturday afternoon.

As of 3 p.m., the storm was moving north-northeast at 20 kilometers per hour over waters approximately 250 kilometers north of Yonaguni Island, Japan’s westernmost inhabited island. It had a central pressure of 985 hectopascals, with maximum wind speeds of up to 30 meters per second.
On Iriomote Island in Okinawa Prefecture, 48-hour rainfall reached 567 millimeters by 1:40 p.m., setting a new local record. In Owase, Mie Prefecture, rainfall totaled 329 millimeters over 24 hours as of 5 p.m.
Earlier, Qazinform News Agency reported that more than 10,000 households in Chiba Prefecture remained without electricity in September after Typhoon Dujuan brought record rainfall to eastern Japan.

Andy Burnham says he wants ‘honest discussion’ about freedom of movement with EU
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
23:07:12 UTC
08:07:12 KST

Andy Burnham says he wants an “honest discussion” with the British public about the possibility of a return to free movement between the UK and the EU as part of his plans for a new relationship with the bloc.
The prime minister has been open about his desire to revisit the relationship between Britain and Brussels. He has said a new deal could mean the UK goes “all the way” and rejoins the EU.
Other options discussed by Burnham include joining the single market, which would require signing up to free movement, or being part of the customs union. Both would require an element of agreeing to rules set by the EU.
In an interview with the Sunday Times he said: “I think you have to have a very factual, quite evidence-based debate about this.”
The prime minister has previously committed to the red lines in Labour’s 2024 election manifesto, which ruled out the return of free movement, single market membership or a customs union.
It means any fundamental change in the relationship is likely to have to wait until after a general election, expected by 2029.
The prime minister acknowledged freedom of movement “had very significant challenges associated with it”, but suggested that European migration had changed in the past decade.
“It was a type of immigration that perhaps wasn’t as difficult [as now],” he told the Sunday Times.
“Revolving door migration where people would come and then go back is different.
“The balance of migration has changed, hasn’t it, since then? I think we’ve just got to have an honest discussion about those things.”
Burnham will meet EU chiefs at a summit in Brussels on 20 November.
He argued that there had been reciprocal benefits of free movement for Britons, particularly for young members of the population wanting to experience living in Europe.
The issue of migration was one of the dominant debates during the 2016 Brexit referendum campaign.
In the 12 months to June 2016 – the month of the Brexit leave vote – net migration was at a near-record high of 335,000, according to the Office for National Statistics.
Decisions made after the Brexit result would lead to higher levels of migration, however.
Net migration peaked at a record 944,000 in the year to March 2023 due to a surge of foreign workers encouraged to come to the UK by Boris Johnson’s Conservative government as the UK emerged from the Covid pandemic.
It has fallen sharply since then, with net migration dropping to well below pre-Brexit levels. It stood at 171,000 last year, almost half of what it was in 2016.
Burnham has said he will take the opportunity around the summit with EU leaders in November to lay out to the British public different options for the future relationship with the bloc.
But Burnham added that he could not imagine recommending that the UK join the Schengen Area, in which border controls have been abolished, or ditching the pound to adopt the euro.
Nigel Farage said the prime minister’s comments were a “total betrayal” of voters who backed Brexit, including in Burnham’s Makerfield constituency.
The Reform UK leader added: “He is also deluded to say immigration was different when we were members of the EU. We will fight this dishonesty.”
Chris Philp, the Conservative shadow home secretary, said: “Andy Burnham knows full well that a return to EU free movement would mean handing back control of our borders and allowing uncontrolled migration from across Europe.
“The British people voted to end free movement, and there can be no return to it.”

By Cynthia Kim and Joyce Lee
SEOUL, Oct 25 (Reuters) - North Korean leader Kim Jong Un returned to his country by road on Sunday after visiting a historic Korean War memorial in the Chinese border city of Dandong, North Korean state media reported.
Kim visited the city on Saturday and crossed a newly opened bridge that connects the country to its biggest trading partner, China, which was seen as symbolizing a push by Beijing and Pyongyang to expand trade ties.
North Korean state media heavily emphasized the historical weight of the visit, describing the bilateral relationship as an “unbreakable” bond forged during the 1950-1953 conflict.
Kim stated during his tour that the North Korean people would “forever remember the glorious years of fighting alongside the Chinese people” and pass down “generational gratitude to the Chinese people who helped our revolution with blood,” according to the KCNA.
The visit is seen as a renewed push by China and North Korea to bolster their economic relationship ahead of a trip to the region by US President Donald Trump next month. It also highlights a sophisticated diplomatic balancing act by Pyongyang, which has been deepening military ties with Moscow in the past two years.
Kim last visited Beijing in September 2025 for a military parade, and Chinese President Xi Jinping visited North Korea in June.
“Enjoying a bird’s-eye view at the middle point of the newly-inaugurated bridge, Comrade Kim Jong Un expressed expectation that the bridge would undoubtedly and correctly fulfill its historic mission of linking the two countries and firmly joining the minds of the peoples of the two countries,” KCNA reported.
The two Koreas are technically at war after their 1950-53 war ended in an armistice rather than a peace treaty.

Loading Twitter content
In reply, Sam Whiteman plundered 116 from 113 balls to give WA a faint hope of chasing down the mammoth victory target.

As for the first lady, asked whether she might visit Ukraine after helping broker a ceasefire in the city of Oleshky to facilitate humanitarian aid and civilian evacuations, Melania Trump said: "We will see."
Trump has endorsed Republican Rep. Byron Donalds in the race to succeed term-limited Gov. Ron DeSantis. Donalds is facing David Jolly, a former Republican who later became an independent and then a Democrat.

Storm Boelo: Travel disrupted and events cancelled as UK hit by wind and rain
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
22:40:08 UTC
07:40:08 KST

Amber weather warnings have come into force as the worst of Storm Boelo could be set to hit parts of the UK.
Storm Boelo’s winds will peak from Saturday evening, leaving areas in the warning zone, including Scotland, parts of Northern Ireland and the far north of England, braced for gusts of 60-70mph and even 80mph in exposed coastal spots, the Met Office said.
The forecaster’s amber warnings came into force on Saturday at 9pm.
Maximum gust speeds of 75mph have already hit South Uist Range, Western Isles, Highland and Eilean Siar, Scotland on Saturday, according to the Met Office, which has also issued several yellow warnings for rain.
Storm Boelo follows Storm Austen, the first named storm of the season, which brought strong winds to parts of the UK on Friday.
Gusts of 76mph were recorded at St Mary’s airport in the Isles of Scilly, with 74mph at Aberporth in south-west Wales and 71mph at Culdrose in Cornwall.
Heavy downpours since 8am on Saturday have already seen rainfall totals of 72mm in White Barrow, Wiltshire, along with 43mm in both Cwm Dyli, just south of the Snowdon range in North Wales, and Inveruglas on the west shore of Loch Lomond, Scotland.
Hundreds of homes were still without power in south-west England after Storm Austen hit the region on Friday where the National Grid said power had been restored to 131,225 properties by Saturday at 7pm.
An amber wind warning, the Met Office’s second most severe, is active across Scotland, the north of England down to Carlisle from 9pm on Saturday to the same time on Sunday.
A further amber warning runs from 9pm on Saturday to 10am on Sunday in the north-east of Northern Ireland.
Storm Boelo, the second named storm of the season, will bring a danger to life from flying debris and crashing waves and people should stay indoors as much as possible, the forecaster said.
The amber warning sits within wider yellow wind warnings which extend south into parts of England and North Wales and cover the whole of Northern Ireland.
The Environment Agency had issued 58 alerts for spots across England where flooding is possible by 8pm on Saturday, as well as 12 warnings stating that flooding is expected.
Met Office chief forecaster Jason Kelly said: “Storm Boelo will be felt across the UK this weekend, with the strongest winds and greatest potential for disruption in the north.
“Amber warnings are in place across mainland Scotland, parts of Northern Ireland and the far north of England, where gusts of 60-70mph are expected widely, with the potential for 80mph in exposed coastal locations.
“Strong winds will also affect other parts of the UK, with gusts of 50-60mph possible in places. Heavy rain will provide an additional hazard, particularly in the north, bringing the potential for further impacts.
“People should prepare for the potential for disruption, particularly to travel and power supplies.”
People should secure loose items outside, plan ahead if they are travelling and keep an eye on the latest forecast and warnings, he advised.
Storm Boelo has already caused widespread disruption.
Boelo’s strong winds disrupted flights at Dublin airport, where as of 4pm on Saturday, nine outbound and 10 inbound flights had been cancelled by airlines because of weather issues.
It also reported that six inbound flights performed go-arounds – five of which landed on the second attempt, with the other diverting to another airport before returning a short time later.
Network Rail shared images of a trampoline beneath a train and a shed by the tracks, in a call for those living near rail lines to secure their garden furniture firmly.
Visit Liverpool announced that the region’s River of Light event, featuring illuminated artwork, had been cancelled “in the interests of safety”.
London’s annual Diwali on the Square celebrations this Sunday were also cancelled on independent health and safety experts’ recommendations in light of the storm.
Other attractions closed on Sunday include Edinburgh Castle and the Fountains Abbey estate in North Yorkshire, which was due to host its Fountains by Floodlight event.

Gunmen kill at least 10 people in eastern Nigeria, police say

Gunmen have killed at least 10 people in an attack on a village in eastern Nigeria, police said, as the country continues to battle banditry and armed groups in several parts of Nigeria.
Nigerian police said on Saturday that 10 bodies had been recovered as of Friday evening after a large group of gunmen on motorcycles attacked Binnari village in Taraba State.
According to police, the attackers also looted food from shops.
Survivors told the AFP news agency that at least 20 people were killed, while human rights group Amnesty International said in a statement on Saturday that the death toll was 40.
Amnesty International also said that while police had earlier confirmed the killing of 10 people, more bodies were recovered later on Saturday.
The gunmen opened fire just after Friday prayers, residents said.

“They looted shops and took cash, foodstuffs and other provisions. They also took motorcycles abandoned by people fleeing the attack,” Saifullahi said.

Banditry problem

====================================================================================================

Ex-Mossad chief reveals how Israel protected agents in Iran, engineered Hezbollah pager attacks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
22:30:16 UTC
07:30:16 KST

Former Mossad chief David Barnea revealed new details Thursday about Israel’s military operation against Iran and the 2024 explosive pager attacks targeting Hezbollah operatives in Lebanon, describing how Israeli intelligence sought to protect its agents inside Iran, the tense minutes before the pagers detonated and the strategic calculations behind both operations.
Speaking at the Priority Summit conference, Barnea said the Mossad deliberately released an official video showing its operatives conducting missions inside Iran on the opening morning of Operation Rising Lion, Israel’s June 2025 military campaign against Iranian nuclear and military targets.
The video, which prominently displayed the Mossad’s insignia, was intended not merely to publicize the operation but to overwhelm Iranian security services with potential suspects, making it harder to identify actual Israeli agents, he said.
“One of the reasons we immediately released an official video on the morning of Operation Rising Lion, with the Mossad logo, was to protect the agents who were there,” Barnea said. “We wanted to make sure they arrested so many people in Iran that they wouldn’t be able to separate the wheat from the chaff and would eventually release everyone. Incidentally, that is exactly what happened.”
According to Barnea, Iranian authorities arrested 21,000 people on the second day of the fighting.
“You have to imagine that when you arrest 21,000 people, even if you’ve caught an agent or two, eventually you have to release them because everyone’s story will be the same: I was walking down the street, I was driving a car, they arrested me,” he said. “And in the end, they released everyone.”
The figures and the account of the releases could not be independently verified.
Barnea also said some of those arrested or executed in Iran on allegations of working for Israeli intelligence had never been associated with the Mossad.
“Some of the people being hanged in Iran on accusations of being Mossad agents — I have to ask who they are,” he said. “They tell me, ‘Listen, we don’t know either.’”
He described them as innocent people whom Iranian authorities had wrongly identified as Israeli operatives.
“Just unfortunate people whom they decided were our agents, but who never worked for the Mossad, and probably never worked for any other intelligence organization either,” he said.
Barnea claimed that 99.9% of Mossad agents had never been exposed.
He said operatives who participated in the campaign continued to live in Tehran, despite their involvement in the Israeli operation.
“I can’t tell you they’re here with us, but they’re there in Tehran, still living their good lives, knowing in their hearts that they served a noble purpose — not for the State of Israel, but for themselves,” he said.
Agents knew of Iran attack weeks before Israeli pilots
Barnea described the extraordinary secrecy surrounding the preparations for Operation Rising Lion, saying that even Israeli fighter pilots were unaware of their impending missions when they were summoned to their squadrons.
“Nobody in the world knew we were going to attack in Operation Rising Lion,” he said. “And to tell the truth, even our pilots didn’t know they were going to attack when they were called to their squadrons.”
By contrast, he said, dozens of Mossad operatives had been deployed inside Iran weeks before the operation, fully aware of their assignments and the impending military campaign.
“But many dozens of our agents were dispatched knowing they were going to carry out an operation, weeks before it began,” he said. “And they kept that secret entirely to themselves, in their hearts.”
Barnea said he personally approved every operative assigned to the mission, accepting responsibility for their reliability and their ability to maintain secrecy.
“Every one of those agents had to receive the green check mark that I personally had to give each one,” he said. “I meet them, I talk to them, I hug them, I encourage them, and I have to trust them.”
He said the stakes extended far beyond operational success.
“You have to sign off that this secret won’t leak,” he said. “When I say I sign off on each one, I’m staking my head on it.”
‘What happens if it doesn’t work?’ Netanyahu asked before pager attack
Barnea also offered a detailed account of the final minutes before the September 2024 operation in which thousands of pagers used by members of Hezbollah, the Iran-backed Lebanese terrorist group, exploded nearly simultaneously.
The attacks, followed a day later by explosions involving Hezbollah walkie-talkies, killed and wounded people across Lebanon and severely disrupted the organization’s communications network.
Barnea said he was sitting in the underground military command center at 3:20 p.m., alongside Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, the defense minister, the IDF chief of staff and the head of Military Intelligence.
The operation was scheduled to begin at 3:30 p.m.
“The prime minister turns to me and says, ‘Tell me, what happens if it doesn’t work?’” Barnea recalled.
He said it was the first time he had seriously contemplated that possibility, just 10 minutes before the operation was to begin.
“My heart is pounding, and I tell him, ‘There’s no such possibility. Everything is fine,’” Barnea said. “After that, I had 10 whole minutes of thinking, ‘What a stupid thing I just said.’”
When the designated time arrived, everyone in the room turned toward him, expecting immediate confirmation that the devices had detonated.
But Barnea said there was no way to know instantly whether the operation had succeeded.
“What did you expect to hear, a boom? It doesn’t work that way,” he said. “We’ll hear about it in half an hour, maybe, and even then we’ll start hearing about it on the news.”
He said the officials continued demanding updates despite his inability to provide immediate answers.
“They want to know here and now what’s happening, and I have no way to put their minds at ease,” he said.
The first reports eventually arrived through Mossad intelligence sources, followed by news coverage. Only then, Barnea said, did he know the operation had succeeded.
Hundreds of tests and a debate over civilian casualties
Barnea said the Mossad conducted hundreds of experiments before carrying out the pager operation, using mannequins filled with materials designed to simulate the human body.
He described repeatedly demanding reductions in the amount of explosives placed inside the devices to limit the risk of harming people near the intended targets.
“Every time I watched a test, I would say, ‘Reduce the amount of explosives,’” he said.
Barnea said he considered the potential deaths of family members of Hezbollah operatives an unacceptable consequence of the operation.
“I, on behalf of the State of Israel, cannot accept the possibility that the daughter of a Hezbollah terrorist, or his son, or his wife, would be harmed because we want to eliminate him,” he said.
According to Barnea, members of the operation’s planning team repeatedly warned that his restrictions would make the devices less effective.
“They kept telling me I was making the operation ineffective,” he said. “I told them, ‘We have red lines.’”
The former intelligence chief said the resulting large number of injuries, compared with the number of fatalities, was consistent with the operation’s intended effects.
“It’s true that not all of them die, and that has a very significant advantage,” he said.
Barnea claimed that 4,500 people with missing limbs were now living in Dahieh, Hezbollah’s stronghold in Beirut’s southern suburbs, describing their injuries as a continuing warning to the organization.
“There are 4,500 people walking around Dahieh missing limbs, and they are the best reminder I can imagine of what happens to a Hezbollah terrorist who tries to harm the citizens of the State of Israel,” he said.
Barnea identified three principal effects of the operation on Hezbollah.
The first was the direct physical harm inflicted on its operatives. The second was the damage to the organization’s morale and its ability to function as a fighting force.
“Anyone who has commanded people in the military understands that when morale is broken, you have no one to work with,” he said.
The third effect, he said, was fear and uncertainty, intensified when Hezbollah’s walkie-talkies exploded the following day.
Asked whether Israel had prepared a third operation involving compromised devices, Barnea declined to answer, suggesting that uncertainty itself served an important strategic purpose.
“I can’t answer that, but the very question going through your minds right now is still going through theirs,” he said.
He compared the psychological impact to Japan’s uncertainty following the U.S. atomic bombings of Hiroshima and Nagasaki in August 1945.
“After Hiroshima and Nagasaki, the Japanese leadership said, ‘Wait, maybe the Americans have a third bomb, and maybe a fourth and fifth, so perhaps we should surrender,’” Barnea said.
“After the first bomb, you think maybe that was the only one. After the second, you’re not sure whether there’s a third.”
Barnea: Israel was deterred by Iran before 2024 missile attacks
Barnea also acknowledged that Israel had been deterred by Iran’s military capabilities before Tehran launched two major direct attacks against Israel in April and October 2024.
Those attacks marked an escalation in the longstanding confrontation between the two countries, with Iran firing large numbers of missiles and drones toward Israel.
Barnea described the attacks as “two historic strategic mistakes” by Tehran, arguing that they exposed capabilities that Israel had previously regarded with considerable uncertainty.
“We have to tell the truth. Before those attacks, the State of Israel — we — were deterred,” he said.
He explained that Israeli officials had lacked a clear understanding of the effectiveness of Iran’s long-range precision missiles and whether Israeli and American air defense systems could withstand a large-scale attack.
The strikes, he suggested, helped resolve some of those uncertainties, altering Israel’s assessment of the threat posed by Iran.

How have Democrats’ policies shifted since the last major US election?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
22:28:37 UTC
07:28:37 KST

How have Democrats’ policies shifted since the last major US election?
From trans rights to Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza, the party’s candidates have responded to voter shifts on a slew of issues.
Two years after United States voters delivered a stunning rebuke of the country’s Democratic Party by electing Republican President Donald Trump to a second nonconsecutive term, some of the party’s midterm candidates are reassessing stances on a host of hot-button issues.
Whether they have dialled it back on issues like transgender rights or ramped up efforts to oppose Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza, Democrats in some of the toughest midterm battleground races are responding to voter concerns – or even breaking outright with party leadership.
Those shifts have resonated with some voters, while others have been alienated as the party tries to find its footing in Trump’s second term and wrestle away control of both houses of Congress from Republicans.
But in the time since Trump defeated former Vice President Kamala Harris in 2024, Democratic divisions have only grown deeper. Establishment and self-described moderates within the party have struggled to hold back a rising tide of progressive populism as voters increasingly demand stronger, bolder policies.
That movement, powered by groups like the Democratic Socialists of America, has forced a reckoning over what it means to be a Democrat in Trump’s second term, leading to significant differences among candidates on policies that often depend on where they are running.
Here’s how – and why – the party has shifted:
Democrats’ shifting views on Israel
The most notable shift among Democrats has, arguably, been on Israel.
Three years after Israel launched its genocidal war in Gaza and killed more than 74,000 Palestinians following Hamas’s October 7, 2023, attacks, polls have suggested that Americans hold increasingly negative views on Israeli military actions.
A Pew Research Center survey conducted earlier this year suggested that 60 percent of US adults had an unfavourable opinion of Israel. That number is significantly higher – 80 percent – among US Democrats.
In response, some longtime Democratic supporters of Israel – including Senator Chris Coons, who is likely to chair the Senate Foreign Relations Committee if Democrats retake control of the Senate next month – have shifted, as voters, especially younger ones, demand greater accountability from the US ally.
The moderate Delaware Democrat told Politico in an interview this month that he wants a “thorough reexamination” of the US-Israeli relationship and is even willing to impose sanctions on Israel’s prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu.
It is a marked change in tone after Harris rejected calls to feature a Palestinian American speaker at the 2024 Democratic National Convention in Chicago.
Earlier this year, 40 Democratic senators voted in support of a motion that disapproved proposed military sales to Israel. Only seven Democratic senators voted with Republicans to block it.
But as a new Congress may include even more progressive voices demanding the US rethink its relationship with Israel, those calls would likely be met with stiff resistance from some in the Democratic leadership, including Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer.
The New York Democrat, who would likely become majority leader if Democrats retake the Senate, has said that the US “commitment to Israel’s security and defense must be ironclad”.
Have Democrats changed their positions on transgender rights?
Following years of attacks from Republicans, Democrats in tightly contested US House or Senate races have downplayed – or outright dismissed – support for the transgender community, mostly when it comes to the participation of transgender students in school sports.
In Ohio, Democratic Representative Marcy Kaptur ran an advertisement featuring her saying, “Boys should not play in girls’ sports”. And in North Carolina, Representative Don Davis released a television commercial in which the Democrat says there “should always be a safe and fair space for women and girls in sports”.
Next door in South Carolina, Democratic Senate candidate Annie Andrews, a doctor, said in a newly released advertisement that she opposes “biological men playing in women’s sports”.
Trump’s return to the White House was fuelled, in part, by a now-famous advertisement in the 2024 campaign that highlighted Harris’s support for transgender Americans.
“Kamala is for they/them,” a narrator said in the advertisement, referring to gender neutral pronouns used by some in the transgender and nonbinary community. “President Trump is for you.”
But the reassessment of transgender rights after the commercial’s airing is not taking place in every part of the party.
On Thursday at a “Students vs Billionaires” town hall in Portland, Maine, Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez addressed concerns from a transgender college student who told the New York progressive that they felt “abandoned” by Democrats.
“They’re wrong”, Ocasio-Cortez said about some members of her party. “First and foremost, I want to just let you know how shameful and sorry I am that there are people out there that scare so easily after an election”.
The congresswoman added, “The moment you compromise the rights of a trans person in America, you compromise the rights of every citizen.”
What has changed on immigration and border security?
During former US President Joe Biden’s term, Democrats encountered near-daily attacks from Republicans on the country’s immigration system.
US Customs and Border Protection (CBP) recorded more than 8 million encounters at the US-Mexico border between 2021 and 2025, fuelling concerns among some voters that the Biden administration had ignored the issue.
In Texas’s closely watched Senate race, candidate James Talarico has positioned himself as a “border security Democrat”, advocating for stronger border enforcement and comprehensive immigration reform.
Third Way, a US-based organisation that pushes for moderate policies, said stances like Talarico’s resonate better with voters because they have taken a proactive, rather than a reactionary approach.
“I remember very clearly when Harris came out and spoke at the DNC in 2024; she… said we need order at the border and to have a strong immigration system”, Third Way’s senior political adviser, Lucas Holtz, told Al Jazeera.
“The problem is, after that, the Harris campaign really did not stick with that line in the sand… They stopped taking a stand on these issues, and more voters thought that she was too far to the left.”
“[Talarico] is making the case in a lot of his ads that the Biden administration failed on securing the border… It’s putting Republicans on their back foot in some of these races.”
But among progressives, Trump’s response to the nation’s immigration issue has also prompted a strong swing to the left.
After several high-profile incidents earlier this year – including federal immigration agents in Minneapolis, Minnesota, shooting dead US citizens Renee Good and Alex Pretti – calls to abolish, or drastically overhaul, US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) have gained momentum.
Left-leaning political groups and politicians have united behind a message of “abolish ICE”, which would dismantle the federal agency and end its enforcement authority.
Do Democrats support Medicare for All?
As cost-of-living issues remain paramount for voters, Democrats of all stripes have coalesced behind the need for more government intervention in the country’s healthcare system.
But how exactly the party addresses rising medical costs remains up for debate.
Some progressives, including Michigan Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed, have championed policies like Medicare for All, which would expand the nation’s federal health insurance programme for seniors so all US citizens would be guaranteed healthcare.
Others running in more conservative states, like Andrews, have called for the return of Affordable Care Act subsidies that lapsed during Trump’s second term, as well as limits on health insurance companies’ profits.
Polling released by the independent health organisation KFF suggested that 66 percent of US adults now support Medicare for All, a 13-point increase from October 2020.
“Everybody’s going to have their own approach to this, but by and large, all Democrats want to move to a universal healthcare system in the best way possible”, Holtz said.
“We’re in agreement that we need to do better than what the Trump administration has done.”

By Fernando Cardoso, Sebastian Rocandio and Lais Morais
SAO PAULO, Oct 24 (Reuters) - Brazilian President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva and Senator Flavio Bolsonaro wrapped up their campaigns on Saturday ahead of Sunday’s presidential runoff vote, mobilizing supporters and making a final push for undecided voters.
The two candidates have remained neck and neck in polls following a stronger-than-expected performance by the right-wing senator in the first round. On Saturday, a CNT/MDA poll showed the senator with a 1.3-point lead.
Lula, who is seeking a fourth non-consecutive term, kicked off his last day of campaigning with a march along Rio de Janeiro’s iconic Copacabana beach, where thousands of supporters joined the leftist incumbent under a blazing sun.
“We’re going to win the election for one simple reason: it’s true that the people want change, (but) they want to move forward. They don’t want to go backward,” Lula told journalists before the rally.
Later, the president led another march in Sao Paulo, passing along Paulista Avenue, a traditional venue for political demonstrations in Brazil’s largest city.
“It’s so exciting to see everyone here. This is the kind of energy we want for Brazil. Brazil is ours,” said Gisele Passos, a 61-year-old businesswoman at the Sao Paulo rally.
For many Lula supporters, the rallies carried a bittersweet undertone. The 80-year-old president and former union leader is widely expected to be making his final bid for office, lending the campaign’s closing events the feel of a farewell tour.
“He’s one of a kind. He has had an incredible, remarkable, and hard-fought journey. We’re very proud of that,” said Olga Leal, a 62-year-old retiree in Sao Paulo.
BOLSONARO RALLIES IN BATTLEGROUND STATE
Bolsonaro, meanwhile, joined a motorcycle caravan in Belo Horizonte, the capital of Minas Gerais, a key battleground state. No candidate has won the presidency without carrying Minas Gerais since the country’s return to democracy in the 1980s.
The senator led Lula by around 5 percentage points in the state in the first round.
“The time is almost here. There are only a few hours left before we shape the future of our nation for the next 30 or 40 years,” said the lawmaker, the eldest son of former President Jair Bolsonaro, in a social media video.
He later took part in a campaign march in his home state of Rio de Janeiro, which he has represented in the Senate since 2019.
The younger Bolsonaro was first backed by his father to run for the presidency last December. The former president was sentenced to over 27 years in prison for plotting a coup after losing the 2022 presidential election to Lula.
On Friday, Lula and Bolsonaro met for a final debate on TV Globo, the country’s main free-to-air television channel, where they sparred over the cost of living and traded personal attacks.
