Almost 1,000 arrested as clashes follow another day of mass protests across France
- Published
Nearly 1,000 arrests were made as hundreds of thousands of people took part in another day of protests across France which were followed by some clashes late on Saturday, officials have said.
After a day of largely peaceful demonstrations, police fired tear gas and water cannon to disperse protesters in a number of cities including Paris, while barricades were set alight in Marseille and people ripped boards from a shop in Bordeaux.
But officials have so far managed to avoid rioting and looting on the scale seen last weekend, which resulted in some of the worst scenes of disorder in France's modern history.
The interior ministry said an estimated 410,000 people protested on Saturday, while the unions put the number at about 800,000.
Some 70,000 police officers were deployed and restrictions imposed in several cities to prevent the latest protests over the cost of living and poor school conditions from descending into the kind of chaos which saw officers outnumbered, hundreds of businesses looted and buildings torched.
President Emmanuel Macron had decreed earlier this week that only demonstrations organised by a recognised trade unions would be permitted. Hundreds of people have been jailed for vandalism, arson and looting after fast-track court hearings in recent days.
Clashes between protesters and riot police in Paris erupted at the end of a peaceful march from the city's Porte d'Italie towards Porte de Vincennes on Saturday, where the police operation included an elite unit that usually deals with organised crime and counter-terrorism.
Some protesters were seen erecting makeshift barricades and pelting officers with projectiles, while police baton-charged groups of masked youths who were smashing the windows of a car dealership.
French Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez said that "several thousand radical activists gathered at the rear of the march, including around 500 individuals identified as rioters", the AFP news agency reported.
In the southern port of Marseille, rubbish bins were set ablaze and metal sheets used to block streets. A law enforcement vehicle was seen driving through a burning barricade in France's second-largest city.
Meanwhile, some protesters in dark clothing and face coverings were seen taking boards off a building to build a street barricade in the southern city of Bordeaux.
In Lyon, police used tear gas grenades to disperse a crowd which had reportedly gathered in an area deemed off-limits by the local prefecture.
"There were around 150 of us, mostly secondary school and university students. Then the tear gas came almost immediately. You could barely see anything in the street," said one protester in France's third-largest city.
Nuñez said late in the day that nearly 1,000 people had been arrested, a number he said would increase.
The minister also said two people had been "seriously injured": one in the south-western city of Toulouse, and another one in Clermont-Ferrand, central France.
Earlier, a peaceful protester in Paris who gave her name as Zelie told the BBC people had taken to the streets because they were "really frustrated" and had been "suffering a lot" since Macron came to office.
"They keep us quiet. They take our money, they tax us a lot and we can't say anything. Today we are in the streets because it's been too long, it's been too much," the 26-year-old said.
Two masked teenage protesters, who did not want to give their names, also said their generation was in despair and felt abandoned by the government.
"I think looting is really not good," one of the demonstrators said of last Saturday's disorder. "But it's because of poverty and the violence of the police."
He added that the protests would end "when we have a response to our demands. We really want a change in France".
Meanwhile, some 13,000 people joined a rally against the hard-right National Rally party in the north-central city of Orléans which proceeded peacefully.
Mass protests triggered by similar issues as in France also rocked several other European cities on Saturday.
In Albania's capital Tirana, riot police fired tear gas to disperse thousands of anti-government demonstrators, while clashes were also reported in Belgium's capital Brussels.
In Milan, northern Italy, a major security operation including hundreds of soldiers alongside police prevented protesters gathering in the city. Many had feared a repeat of violent scenes last week when some started fires, smashed windows and looted shops.
Around 550,000 people took part in last weekend's demonstrations against rising fuel prices and the cost of living, with frustrations escalating after weeks of student protests. The chaos which followed resulted in more than 2,500 arrests.
Marches were initially largely peaceful but became marred by scenes of violence, looting and destruction, with more than 2,000 shops and other businesses across France said to have been directly impacted. The damage was estimated "at hundreds of millions euros", France's Chambers of Commerce and Industry (CCI) said.
One demonstrator's hand was blown off by a police crowd-control grenade, according to the AFP news agency, while about 1,000 police officers were injured.
The French authorities later said they were forced to impose overnight curfews in Paris and other cities.
The continuing protests come ahead of France's presidential elections in six months' time, and leading contenders have levelled the blame at Macron and his ministers.

The Arctic giant: How Russia dominates the frozen frontier
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
21:08:49 UTC
06:08:49 KST

The Arctic giant: How Russia dominates the frozen frontier
“Russia’s future... lies in the Arctic,” President Vladimir Putin declared last year, portraying the frozen north as a cornerstone of national prosperity for generations to come.
One look at a map shows why: The country accounts for approximately 53% of the Arctic Ocean’s coastline, according to the Arctic Council, making it the world’s largest Arctic power in geographical terms.
However, the stakes go well beyond geography, as Russia’s Arctic territories contain enormous oil, gas, and mineral reserves, host vital elements of its nuclear deterrent, and accommodate multiple military bases.
As climate change and retreating sea ice gradually open new opportunities for maritime navigation, Moscow is also seeking to transform the Northern Sea Route into a lucrative trade artery connecting Europe and Asia.
Meanwhile, both NATO and the EU are increasingly challenging Russia’s traditional presence in the Arctic. On October 20, EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas described the region as the “frontline of global power competition,” accusing Moscow of militarization while setting course on expanding cooperation with NATO, developing military logistics corridors, and catching up with Moscow in its icebreaker capacity.
Russia maintains that it has “never threatened anyone in the Arctic” but vowed to safeguard its sovereign interests while accusing NATO of escalating tensions.
But what exactly makes the Russian Arctic so special, and why is Moscow so determined to stand its ground there?
What defines the Arctic?
Unlike Antarctica, which is a continent surrounded by ocean, the Arctic is an ocean surrounded by the northern reaches of Eurasia and North America, Greenland, and numerous islands. The region’s generally accepted geographical boundary is the Arctic Circle, beyond which the sun can remain above the horizon for 24 hours during summer and disappear entirely for at least one day during winter.
Eight countries have territories in the Arctic: Russia, Canada, the United States, Denmark through Greenland, Norway, Sweden, Finland, and Iceland, with the first five having coastlines directly bordering the Arctic Ocean – which gives them an important role in determining maritime boundaries and access to resources.
The region is characterized by extreme cold, extensive sea ice, permafrost, prolonged polar darkness during winter, and continuous daylight during summer. Temperatures can fall below -40C in continental areas, while thick sea ice, storms, and limited infrastructure make transportation and industrial operations exceptionally challenging.
However, the Arctic is warming nearly four times faster than the global average, creating unprecedented opportunities for maritime trade and resource exploitation, even if thawing permafrost threatens existing infrastructure.
Who owns what in the Arctic?
Russia, Canada, the US, Denmark, and Norway – countries bordering the Arctic Ocean – exercise sovereignty over their established land territories and islands, as well as their territorial waters extending up to 12 nautical miles offshore. Coastal states also enjoy exclusive rights to natural resources within a 200-nautical-mile exclusive economic zone.
However, their rights can extend considerably farther if they establish that the seabed beyond this limit forms part of their continental shelf. This is where high-stakes game begins, as countries with rights over an extended continental shelf can exclusively explore and exploit its oil, gas, and mineral resources.
The Arctic is estimated to hold 90 billion barrels of oil and 1,669 trillion cubic feet of natural gas in undiscovered and recoverable reserves alone, on top of abundant deposits of nickel, copper, palladium, iron ore, zinc, lead, phosphate, and bauxite. To put it into perspective, OPEC estimates Russia’s entire proven reserves at 80 billion barrels of crude oil and approximately 1,483 trillion cubic feet of natural gas.
At the same time, extended continental shelf rights are not equal to territorial sovereignty, with the waters remaining open to international navigation.
Russia was the first country to formally seek recognition of an extended Arctic continental shelf, submitting several claims to a UN commission since 2001. The commission requested additional scientific evidence, prompting Moscow to conduct extensive Arctic expeditions.
Other countries joined the Arctic race: Denmark submitted claims in 2014, followed by Canada in 2019. After Russia significantly expanded its proposed continental shelf in 2021, Canada responded with an enlarged claim in 2022, complaining that Moscow’s move had tripled the area overlapping with its own submission.
However, Moscow has made significant strides in defending its claims. In 2023, the UN Commission on the Limits of the Continental Shelf largely endorsed Russia’s geological arguments, supporting an extended shelf encompassing an estimated 1.8 million sq km.
Yet UN recommendations alone do not settle the dispute. Russia, Canada, and Denmark must still resolve their overlapping entitlements through negotiations or other lawful means. The outcome is not entirely without precedent, as Russia and Norway managed to settle a decades-long disagreement over approximately 175,000 sq km of the Barents Sea in 2010.
What does the Russian Arctic look like?
Russia’s Arctic stretches from the Kola Peninsula near Norway in the west to Chukotka opposite Alaska in the east, with the total coastline spanning more than 24,000 km. Russia’s officially designated Arctic Zone covers approximately 4.8 million sq km, or 28% of the country’s territory, and encompasses entire administrative regions, from Murmansk in the west to northern Yakutia in the east.
The landscape varies from rocky coastlines and tundra plains to frozen wetlands and vast taiga forests. Farther north lie remote archipelagos, including Novaya Zemlya, Franz Josef Land, Severnaya Zemlya, and the New Siberian Islands, some of which are extensively covered by glaciers and permanent ice. Novaya Zemlya also served as a major Soviet nuclear weapons testing ground.
The Russian Arctic is home to nearly 2.5 million people, with the region generating an estimated 7% of national GDP and 11% of its exports as of 2025.
Despite its unforgiving climate, the Russian Arctic is far from an empty wilderness. Its major population and industrial centers include Murmansk – the world’s largest city north of the Arctic Circle with a population of 260,000 which is also a major ice-free port – and Norilsk, a powerhouse of nickel, copper, and palladium production.
Other important Arctic Zone centers include Arkhangelsk and Severodvinsk, known for maritime industries and nuclear submarine construction, as well as Vorkuta, Salekhard, and the gas-producing hub of Novy Urengoy.
Yamalo-Nenets Autonomous District is also the site of Novatek’s Yamal LNG plant, the largest of its kind in Russia, which exports gas through the port of Sabetta. Farther east, Pevek is home to the Akademik Lomonosov, the world’s only floating nuclear power plant.
The unique design is dictated by necessity: Western Chukotka is cut off from Russia’s national power grid, while the NPP was built at a shipyard and transported to the remote location by sea, avoiding major problems associated with construction of an ordinary nuclear facility.
How important is the Arctic to Russia, and vice versa?
Russia’s Arctic Zone is an economic powerhouse, underpinning its energy exports and supplying critical raw materials, hosting more than 80% of national natural gas production, alongside substantial shares of its oil, nickel, and platinum-group metal output. Major industrial complexes, including the Yamal gas fields and Norilsk mining operations, are central not only to Russia’s welfare, but also to global energy and commodity markets.
As for trade, Russia’s ports, major Siberian rivers, and icebreaker fleet – the largest in the world – form an extensive transportation network connecting resource-rich territories with international markets.
In this vein, the Northern Sea Route is now emerging as the most important Arctic itinerary due to climate change, having handled more than 37 million tons of cargo in 2025, including 5.4 million tons transported between Russian and Chinese ports.
Despite tensions with the West over the Ukraine conflict, Russia continues to participate in limited Arctic Council cooperation, including technical work on environmental monitoring and other shared regional challenges.
Why is the Arctic a key military stronghold for Russia?
Beyond its economic importance, the Arctic is a cornerstone of Russia’s national security, hosting crucial elements of its nuclear deterrent and providing strategic access to the Atlantic and Pacific oceans.
The Kola Peninsula, bordering Norway and Finland, anchors the Northern Fleet and its nuclear-armed submarines, while an extensive network of airfields, radar installations, missile defenses, and military bases protects Russia’s northern approaches. Since the early 2010s, Moscow has also been restoring numerous Soviet-era facilities across remote Arctic islands.
The importance of the Arctic only increased after Finland and Sweden acceded to NATO in 2023 and 2024, respectively, leaving Russia as the only non-NATO member among the eight Arctic states.
Moscow subsequently sounded the alarm about the bloc’s expanding presence near its strategic naval bases. This year, NATO launched the so-called Arctic Sentry initiative, aimed at strengthening military coordination and surveillance, with joint drills involving tens of thousands of troops.
The EU, meanwhile, is also looking to interfere in regional affairs, with the bloc’s new Arctic Strategy envisaging the development of military logistics, upgrading ports and airports for military use, expanding icebreaker fleets, and increasing satellite surveillance of the region and tracking of Russian oil tankers.
In light of Western countries’ saber-rattling, Putin accused NATO of increasingly treating the Far North as a “springboard for potential conflicts,” warning that “we will proceed from current realities and will respond to all this.”
Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov went further, accusing NATO of deliberately militarizing the Arctic, stressing that “such military activity in the Far North poses a direct threat to Russia’s security.” He also warned that escalating tensions could trigger an armed clash with “potentially disastrous consequences.”
How powerful is Russia’s icebreaker fleet?
Russia’s icebreaker fleet is in a league of its own, comparable in numbers to the rest of the world combined. The country operates 43 icebreakers, including eight nuclear-powered vessels and 35 diesel-electric ships.
Nuclear icebreakers are particularly formidable as they can operate for extended periods without refueling, maintaining access to remote ports, and escorting commercial ships through heavily ice-covered waters. Russia’s four modern 60-megawatt Project 22220 icebreakers are designed to break through ice up to approximately 2.8 meters thick.
Moscow also continues to press its icebreaker advantage, with plans to commission four additional nuclear icebreakers that are now at various stages of development. These include the behemoth Project 10510 Rossiya, designed to deliver 120 megawatts of propulsion power and support navigation through even thicker Arctic ice. The icebreaker is expected to be ready for operations in late 2029.
Russia’s icebreaker fleet is far ahead of the American one, which only operates three polar icebreakers – a shortcoming several US administrations described as a national security concern.
As for the EU, it collectively operates around ten icebreakers, depending on classification. The bloc’s foreign policy chief, Kaja Kallas, acknowledged the gap, declaring that “in the Arctic, icebreakers are the measure of power,” with plans to explore joint procurement, though these efforts are unlikely to yield results for many years.
How does Russia govern the Arctic?
Given the region’s undeniable importance, Moscow has built an extensive state apparatus dedicated to managing its northern territories.While overall priorities and strategic vision are set by Putin personally, much of the federal coordination falls to Deputy Prime Minister Yury Trutnev, who chairs the State Commission for Arctic Development. Established in 2015, the body brings together senior officials, regional governors and representatives of major companies to coordinate economic, infrastructure and security policies.
The region is also overseen by the designated Ministry for the Development of the Russian Far East and Arctic, headed by Aleksey Chekunkov, which handles Arctic development policy, investment incentives, and socioeconomic programs.
As for the Arctic’s maritime portfolio, it is supervised by former Russian Security Council Secretary Nikolay Patrushev, now a presidential aide, who chairs the Maritime Board, established in 2024 to coordinate maritime strategy and defend Russia’s interests at sea.
Russia’s state nuclear corporation, Rosatom, also plays a significant role in the region while managing the Northern Sea Route infrastructure and nuclear icebreaker fleet. Murmansk Governor Andrey Chibis also chairs a dedicated State Council commission on the Northern Sea Route and the Arctic, helping coordinate regional development proposals.
The Russian government has also for years run several incentivizing special programs in the region, including a preferential business regime offering qualifying companies multi-year tax breaks and reduced social insurance contributions.
Moscow also operates the Arctic Hectare program, allowing eligible citizens to obtain up to one hectare of land for development completely free of charge, with the possibility of subsequently obtaining ownership, and the Arctic Mortgage scheme, offering qualifying borrowers subsidized housing loans at rates of up to 2%.
Some of the Arctic Zone regions boast the highest average salaries nationally. According to Rosstat, average gross monthly salaries in 2025 reached approximately 215,000 rubles ($2,570) in Chukotka and 178,000 rubles ($2,130) in the Yamal-Nenets Autonomous Area – a level exceeding or comparable to Moscow’s and higher than the national average of 100,000 rubles ($1,200). However, the financial advantages are partly offset by higher living costs.
The region also benefits from a dedicated Soviet-inherited Northern Delivery system that coordinates supplies of essential goods to remote settlements.
How did Russia develop its Arctic frontier?
While indigenous peoples inhabited the region for thousands of years, Russian Pomor seafarers first began exploring the White and Barents Seas in the Middle Ages, establishing trading and fishing settlements. However, a full-scale expansion picked up steam only in the 16th century and beyond.
The most dramatic transformation took place in the Soviet era, when Moscow poured major resources into polar exploration, industrialization, and transportation infrastructure. In 1932, the Soviet icebreaking steamer Alexander Sibiryakov became the first vessel to traverse the Northern Sea Route in a single navigation season.
Another landmark achievement came in 1959 when the Soviet Union commissioned the Lenin, the world’s first nuclear-powered icebreaker, allowing ships to operate in the Arctic for extended periods of time. During the Cold War, Moscow also heavily invested in naval and submarine bases in the region.
Following the Soviet collapse in 1991, investment plunged, infrastructure deteriorated, and northern shipping declined. However, Russia began rebuilding its Arctic presence in the 2000s, developing major energy projects, reviving military facilities, and expanding its icebreaker capabilities.
How is Russia investing in the Arctic?
Moscow has made Arctic development a long-term national priority, with the current strategy running through 2035. According to Russian officials, more than 1,000 state-supported projects have been launched in the region since 2020, attracting approximately 2.6 trillion rubles ($32 billion) in investment. Moscow expects total investment over the coming decade to exceed 30 trillion rubles.
Much of the effort is focused on natural resources, as major companies, including Gazprom, Rosneft, Novatek, and Nornickel, are expanding oil, gas, and mining operations, while the government offers preferential tax arrangements and other incentives to attract investors.
Moscow is also modernizing Arctic ports, expanding railway connections, and developing specialized cargo fleets. Apart from building icebreakers, it plans to construct at least ten rescue vessels and launch 12 weather-monitoring and radar satellites by 2035 in a bid to support more reliable navigation along the Northern Sea Route.
The military development remains another priority, with Russia continuing to modernize airfields and bases, strengthening the Northern Fleet and expanding the number of personnel deployed in the region. Last year, Putin also ordered the extension of a military-town renovation program through at least 2030, with a minimum of 10 billion rubles in annual federal funding.
Bottom Line
While the Arctic race has been overshadowed by the Russia-West standoff over Ukraine, the region remains crucial to Russia’s long-term interests. The Arctic’s enormous natural reserves underpin the national economy, and its military bases form an indispensable part of Russia’s nuclear deterrent, while the Northern Sea Route promises lucrative trade opportunities along the country’s vast northern coastline.
As both NATO and the EU hanker after influence in the region, Russia has made clear that it has no intention of surrendering its longstanding position. For the Arctic giant, the frozen frontier is far more than a distant outpost or a peripheral prize – it is a cornerstone of its security, prosperity, and future.

Former Defense Minister adviser Serhii Sternenko stated that the civilian Starlink system did not technically work while in motion. The drone missions were carried out using the military Starshield system.
Former Ukrainian Defense Minister’s adviser Serhii Sternenko denied SpaceX founder Elon Musk’s claim that Ukrainian servicemen violated the terms of use of Starlink satellite communications by using it for drone strikes. This was reported by UNN.
Details
According to Sternenko, so-called "white lists" were introduced in February this year, allowing both military and civilians to register stationary terminals in their own names.
However, for any satellite terminal to operate while on the move, it had to be added to a special list and connected to the military Starshield system. Otherwise, any satellite communication terminals in Ukraine did not work. In other words, it was technically impossible to use civilian Starlink specifically to carry out missions with drones
He clarified that all drone missions requiring satellite communications could be carried out only using Starshield.
Recall
American billionaire Elon Musk stated that Ukrainian servicemen violated the terms of use of Starlink satellite communications by using it for drone strikes.

The great divorce: Why Russia must turn away from Europe
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24

The great divorce: Why Russia must turn away from Europe
In Russia, many people, driven by lingering Europhilia and habits formed during the second half of the 20th century, when Western Europe enjoyed a period of relative peace following its defeat, continue to look for signs of its ‘recovery’ and ways to restore relations.
There are forces within Russia that would advocate overcoming the current hostility and there are decent people in Western Europe, too, even if they are increasingly marginalized. But the causes of this outbreak of desperate Russophobia run deep and cannot easily be remedied and overcoming them may require the complete defeat and dismantling of much of the current European elite. But achieving that goal could come at too high a cost.
I shall attempt to analyze the causes of the almost unprecedented hostility towards Russia among the elites of most European countries and offer recommendations for Russian policy towards Western Europe.
I have written more than once that Peter the Great’s journey towards the rest of Europe, which initially brought many benefits, including helping to create some of the world’s greatest literature and music and modernizing the armed forces, continued for a century and a half longer than was necessary or beneficial.
For many centuries, Europe was the principal source of evil in the world, offering endless wars, including two world wars within a single generation, repeated genocides, colonialism, racism and other calamities.
For Russians who grew up in the shadow of Peter the Great and Catherine the Great, and who internalized a love of Europe, it’s not easy to acknowledge this simple truth and act accordingly.
Russian Europhilia was greatly reinforced when Western Europe, having been overwhelmed by the torrent of evil it had unleashed, became relatively peaceful for a time during the second half of the 20th century. In the USSR, Europhilia was fueled by the everyday hardships of Soviet socialism, contrasted with the far greater material prosperity of the western part of the half-continent.
There are many reasons for the current anti-Russian hysteria. The main one is the all-encompassing, multi-layered crisis that has gripped the western part of Europe and this crisis is particularly painful after decades of relative prosperity and, above all, the euphoria of victory that swept the West following the collapse of the USSR.
That euphoria temporarily obscured the mounting signs of crisis in European economies and societies, which had already become apparent by the end of the 1960s, when a mood of protest was beginning to take hold. And then a miracle happened as the collapse of the Soviet Union and the Eastern Bloc provided hundreds of millions of eager new consumers and millions of cheap workers.
From the 2000s onwards, these problems resurfaced with renewed force. A decade later, most Western European countries had fallen into stagnation as inequality began to worsen once again. Living standards for much of the population began to decline, while competitors started pulling ahead, not only the US and China, but also many countries of the Global South.
Euphoria gave way to a sense of failure and European elites are now trying to drown out that feeling by fueling hostility towards Russia.
At the same time, from the end of the 20th century, the consequences of the anti-colonial revolutions of the 1950s and 1960s began to make themselves felt. The flow of resources that Europe had extracted from the rest of the world since the 16th century, and upon which its prosperity and cultural, military, scientific and technological leadership had largely been built, began to dry up.
An unusually long period of relative peace and prosperity brought to the surface some of the worst traits of the European character and heritage as Western Europe began to turn its back on humanism and the desire to serve the common good.
Decades of development in a climate of peace and formal democracy have led to the degradation of the ruling elites because democratic political systems are anti-meritocratic. The majority elect those who resemble themselves, or even those who are worse, and in the best cases, they elect shrewd manipulators.
One of the most significant causes of Western Europe’s current decline, and to a lesser extent, that of other parts of the collective West, is the rejection of faith.
This began with the Age of Enlightenment, which created the conditions for the decline of people who, consciously or unconsciously, set about rejecting the divine, the best within themselves.
I finally realized that Western Europe had taken a sharp and irreversible downward turn in the early 2000s, when following lengthy debates over the European Union’s proposed constitution, it was decided not to mention Christianity as its spiritual foundation.
Losing its footing and falling behind in economic and spiritual competition, Western Europe is reverting to one of the worst traits of its civilization, which is militarism.
The militarization of the economy is seen as one of the principal ways out of economic decline and militarization requires an enemy. As so often before, that enemy has been identified as Russia as the image of the enemy is being inflated practically out of thin air.
We must tell ourselves firmly, we are not Europeans, but an independent northern Eurasian civilization whose external spiritual roots lie in the south and east.
Our traditional religions came to us from the south, from Byzantium, Palestine, and the Arab and Buddhist worlds. Our political culture stems from the east, from two and a half centuries of interaction and conflict with the Great Mongol Empire, of which the territory of modern-day China was historically a part.
The Mongols plundered, but they didn’t suppress religion, language or culture and we would never have become Great Russia, the world’s largest and one of its most culturally, nationally and religiously open countries, united through a rigid vertical hierarchy of power centered on the Russian people and the Russian language, had it not been for the Mongol political and ideological legacy.
From Western Europe, which, relying on its military superiority, took the lead in education during the 17th and 18th centuries, we sought to adopt the European Bologna system.
Yet that system is increasingly anti-meritocratic as it churns out poorly educated people on a mass scale, many of whom are now coming to power. Let me remind you that some of the earliest institutions of higher learning were established in North Africa and Byzantium.
Some of our more affluent fellow citizens still send their children to study in Europe, ‘abroad’, where as I have seen time and again, they often lose more skills and talents than they acquire.
Our military doctrine contains a clear directive and in circumstances of extreme necessity, provides for the possibility of nuclear strikes against key European countries that are fueling anti-Russian hysteria while simultaneously supporting the war in Ukraine.
Our restraint and peacefulness over recent decades have proved counterproductive. They have contributed to the resurgence of the worst aspects of European political culture so Western Europe must therefore face firm deterrence.
But at the same time, we must remember that we are a country of Pushkin, Tchaikovsky, Dostoevsky, and Tvardovsky, as well as Goethe, Dante, Shakespeare, Mozart and countless others.
Culturally, we must not cut ourselves off from Europe. Rather, we must develop and nurture our Asian roots, of which we have foolishly been ashamed.
The main direction of our internal spiritual, economic and political development must be a shift towards Siberia as there, in the east and north, lies Russia’s future.
We must finally acknowledge that we are not an Eastern European civilization, but a northern Eurasian one, among the most open to the world.
We must also recognize, however difficult it may be, that ‘European-ness’, in the present circumstances, is increasingly becoming a sign of intellectual narrow-mindedness and moral duplicity.
And given the current orientation of European elites, it is simply harmful to us, the representatives of the great multinational, multi-confessional and multicultural Russian people.
Our country-civilization must at last become, for all of us, Russian Yakuts, Russian Buryats, Russian Ossetians, Russian Tatars, Russian Belarusians, Russian Great Russians and others, an independent northern Eurasian civilization.
Europe, in its present and foreseeable future condition, must end at our borders.
This however, is not a call for a new Iron Curtain, but for a rational, modern policy directed towards the future.
This article was first published by Russia in Global Affairs, translated and edited by RT.

'The marches went well' – French government on demonstrations a week after looting and violence
Hundreds of thousands marched across France Saturday protesting the rising cost of living. While demonstrations in Paris started peacefully, they ended with a heavy government security response following escalation. Other cities saw clashes that also contributed to the near-1,000 arrested across the country, meanwhile other countries in Europe rallied over issues with some overlap. Clashes broke out Saturday in Paris and other French cities amid demonstrations held a week after others that degenerated into street violence and prompted a robust security backlash as President Emmanuel Macron seeks to restore order.
Police arrested nearly 1,000 people as officers were confronted with "an extremely elevated level of violence" from black-clad "ultra-left" extremists, Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez said.
Riot police squads fired tear gas at protesters in the capital as well as in Marseille, Lyon, Bordeaux, Lille, Toulouse, Montpellier and Nantes.

Two people were "seriously" injured, Nuñez said: one man in Toulouse, who reportedly had fingers blown off, and another person in Clermont-Ferrand. He did not give details of either case.
Authorities had deployed 70,000 security forces across the country for the new marches, called to protest the cost of living.
The violence came a week after rioting that saw public buildings vandalised, hundreds of shops looted and 2,700 people arrested, casting a pall over a country that goes to the polls in six months to choose a successor to Macron after 10 years.
Nuñez said Saturday's outcome was more "positive" than a week ago, with more police on the streets acting more rapidly, conducting more pre-demonstration checks and better protecting businesses.
There was nevertheless widespread anger at the government over a protest crackdown viewed as an assault on the right to protest.
Police battle 'rioters'
Saturday's demonstrations drew between 410,000 and 800,000 people across the country, according to different estimates by authorities and the organising CGT union.
The main Paris march had between 110,000 and 250,000 attendees, according to those sources.

Will Maga die in red Ohio? Controversial ad tests Trump’s staying power in midterm elections

Will Maga die in red Ohio? Controversial ad tests Trump’s staying power in midterm elections
- Ohio’s governor race has become a test of Trump-style politics, with Vivek Ramaswamy's ad featuring the estranged mother of Democratic rival Amy Acton casting her daughter as untrustworthy and a “liar”.
- The Ramaswamy ad using family trauma sparked anger and sympathy, but Trump defended the ad while JD Vance called critics “whining”.
- Polls are tight in a usually Republican state, with voters split over costs, taxes and character, and the result may show whether Trump’s style still wins.
AI generated
WOODSVILLE, Ohio – The world perhaps doesn’t care too much about who runs an American Rust Belt state, if we are to be painfully honest.
But it is hard to look away when the race to become governor of Ohio morphs into the most crucial stress test for President Donald Trump’s brand of shoot-from-the-hip politics.
Will Trump’s combative style – demonising an opponent and never saying sorry even in the face of certifiable fact and breaching the norms of human decency – survive beyond his term? Can a candidate win by borrowing his methods? What kinds of leaders will American voters elevate after seeing two years of Trump’s second term? What, now, is the political temperament of the world’s most influential democracy?
Ohio will offer an answer to all those questions on Nov 3, when Vivek Ramaswamy, a biotech billionaire, attempts a Trump-like transition from a MAGA celebrity to an elected executive.
For most of 2026, the race favoured the Ohio-born Ramaswamy whose Tamil-speaking parents emigrated from the southern Indian state of Kerala. The 41-year-old, who studied biology at Harvard and law at Yale, had already made a splash on the national stage with his 2024 presidential run.
His gubernatorial run seemed a shoo-in at first, given Ohio’s hospitality to Republicans and an endorsement by Trump, who won the state in all three of his Republican Party presidential campaigns.
Meanwhile, the Democrats, who have won only one of the state’s past nine gubernatorial elections, have thrown in their lot with Amy Acton, 60, a physician who has never worked as a doctor but won notice for her handling of the state’s response to Covid-19 as a former state health director. A New York Times opinion piece in May 2020 called her “the leader we wish we all had”.
Under Acton’s guidance, Ohio became the first state in the US to order a statewide closure of all public schools. Her policies were widely praised by liberals and panned by conservatives who found the lockdown and mask mandates to be too intrusive and alarmist. She resigned soon after, under pressure to roll back the Covid-19 restrictions.
As months went by, the opinion polls began to show Acton catching up with Ramaswamy against a backdrop of inflation and growing dissatisfaction with Trump.
When the contest tightened, the vitriol rose. She called him a con artist, an out-of-touch billionaire surveying the state from a private jet.
He called her tenure as health director a failure. Her “only qualification for this job is a short-lived stint as the health director when she shut down the economy of this state, and then when the legislature forced her to actually follow real data, she quit on the job”, he said.
But all that paled beside a bombshell ad by the Ramaswamy campaign that began airing on Oct 22. From bitterness over public records, it crossed the line to private trauma.
The ad featured Acton’s elderly mother casting her daughter as untrustworthy and a “liar”. What it left out was that the mother lost custody of Acton at the age of 12 after Acton accused her stepfather of sexual assault. He fled the state before he could be tried and Acton’s mother stood by him.
The ad won Acton, who had publicly disclosed the abuse in 2019, a wave of public sympathy.
It also elicited an intervention from Trump, who leaned in to praise the mother’s “courage” and told Ramaswamy to carry on broadcasting the ad. “What she was really doing was saving Ohio from making a truly horrible choice,” he wrote on Truth Social.
“The Press is trying to convince everyone that this ad is bad, because it’s so good! Who wouldn’t use such an Ad? I would, it’s called, ‘hitting pay dirt’,” he wrote.
Vice-President J.D. Vance, seen as a contender in the 2028 presidential election, said he was “disgusted”. Not by the ad but by fellow Republicans who were “whining” about it.
Confidence beneath the rafters
A day before the storm broke, I spoke to Ramaswamy briefly at a campaign stop in Woodsfield, a once prosperous Appalachian town in south-eastern Ohio, its compact historic downtown surrounded by wooded hills and farmlands.
The townhall-style meeting was held in a cosy barn with wooden rafters. Ramaswamy spoke from a small wooden stage, his voice modulating with emphasis, rather like a businessman making a pitch than a politician given to rhetoric.
He told me his voters were missing in the opinion polls.
“Midterm environments are always tough for the party that’s in power. That’s always true, whether it’s Democrat or Republican. I am confident we will win this election because Ohio polls have consistently undercounted Republicans,” Ramaswamy said.
“That’s just a fact. In this room, if I asked how many have been polled, probably no hands would go up. I ask them how many are going to vote, all of them are going to vote.”
He pointed to the elections in 2024, 2022, 2020 and 2018 as evidence. “That has been the pattern in Ohio,” he said. “I am confident we will prevail because of people like those who are in this room.”
Nathaniel Swigger, associate professor at the Ohio State University who studies public opinion, political psychology and campaigns, told The Straits Times that there was no particular reason to think the polls are wrong.
“Many Republicans will use the ‘Republicans don’t answer polls’ line to claim that they are always undercounted, but that’s not really true,” he said.
Response rates across all groups, including independents, are pretty bad and pollsters use weighted sample results to try and make up for that.
“If the polls are wrong – a big if – then they are just as likely to be wrong in ways that overrate voter support for Ramaswamy,” Swigger said.
“For example, social desirability bias may prevent voters from expressing true opinions if they think others will judge those views as racist or sexist.
“Maybe some people say they’ll vote for Acton because they don’t want to admit they would never vote for a woman.
“Or maybe some people say they’ll vote for Ramaswamy because they don’t want to admit they would never vote for an Indian-American or non-Christian candidate.
“Without controlled experiments to specifically test that, it’s hard to say what that bias might be ahead of an election,” he said.
The uncertainty is striking because Ohio’s recent political history has been stable. This has been ruby-red Republican for a decade, having voted for Trump, Trump and Trump again in the last three presidential elections after spurning Hillary Clinton, Joe Biden and Kamala Harris. Of its 88 counties, only six voted for the Democrats in 2024.
Ohio Republicans are trying to hold on to the control over all three branches of the state government they’ve had since 2011.
Of 15 congressmen that Ohio elected to the US House of Representatives, 10 are Republican. Both senators from Ohio are Republican as well. The last time a Democrat won the governor’s race in Ohio was in 2006.
Yet, most polls now paint Ohio as a volatile, purple territory. “Anything could happen” is the response I heard over and over as I travelled.
In Monroe County, county commissioner Mick Schumacher, describing a transformation of what was predominantly Democrat territory until it voted Trump the first time in 2016, said: “And then we broke a national record per capita for people that flip from D to R.”
That flip has not erased practical concerns. Schumacher cautiously welcomed Ramaswamy’s promise to cut property taxes. “Now, I’m a county commissioner and we depend on that property tax to run the emergency services and county government. So I was not in favour of it until we know what there is that’s going to replace it,” he said.
He also said he had heard that the plan was to raise sales tax to make up the difference, but that could devastate a border town like Woodsfield.
“We border West Virginia; a lot of our people can shop there. So it will decimate the border towns. People in Columbus, maybe they won’t be affected,” Schumacher said.
For Jimmy Williams, a Monroe County Republican Party official, polls that showed Acton in the lead were a pressure tactic.
“The Democrats’ playbook is to talk and try to sound like they’re winning and trying to discourage the Republicans from getting out the vote. But they don’t realise, we’re energised,” he said.
What do the candidates stand for?
Away from the campaign events, it was easier to find voters who are firmly opposed to Acton but still needed persuading about Ramaswamy, a Hindu in a state where over 60 per cent of the predominantly white population identify as Christian.
A florist’s assistant in Youngstown, a largely Democratic area, who asked not to be named for fear of hurting the shop’s business, said the Acton campaign is running limp, “kind of like Joe Biden’s campaign”.
“You don’t see her; you just see ads on TV. And if anybody wants to get close to her, she’s got bodyguards that don’t let you get near. She doesn’t answer questions. We don’t even really know what she’s for. She’s just there,” she said.
She was more tentative on Ramaswamy. “Vivek seems smart. I am going to give him a closer look,” she added.
An air force veteran expressed surprise that an Oct 12 Trump rally in Youngstown had pulled in a sizeable crowd.
“This area is very Democratic,” said Chad, who gave only his first name. “So if he got 70 per cent seats filled, he did well,” he said.
He regarded Trump’s defence of the controversial ad featuring Acton’s mother as “marginal”.
“Some things Trump does and says I don’t agree with, but I think he does what he thinks is right for the country. And at least I know where he stands. I’d rather have a politician do that than one that lies in my face, which is what we normally get,” he said.
It was an argument I’ve heard often: an approval of Trump despite reservations about his conduct.
Democrats believe that rising costs and unease about government corruption have cracked the door open.
At the Ohio Democratic Party’s headquarters in state capital Columbus – an inconspicuous building with no boards, banners or signs to mark it – spokeswoman Marisa Nahem maintained that Acton was ahead.
“Ohioans are excited about Dr Acton’s campaign because they know she’s the only candidate in this race who will tackle rising costs, stand up to the corporate special interests and billionaires trying to buy Ohio, and put working families first,” she said.
“We are seeing incredible energy among Ohioans, with raw Democratic vote totals in primaries higher in most counties when compared to 2022,” she said, adding that there was lower Republican primary participation and stronger Democrat early voting.
A promise to lower costs and tackle Republican corruption was a message that crossed party lines, she said.
“It is a mission that isn’t just popular, it’s unifying among Ohioans of all political backgrounds,” she added.
The quiet on the campaign trail
For all the competing claims of loyalty and energy, the race’s intensity was not always apparent on the streets: Along the routes I visited, few yard signs advertised a contest that polling showed was closely fought.
There were the occasional posters for local judges or sheriffs or other county officials. Officials from both parties claimed that the fear of intimidation from the other side had discouraged yard signs this cycle.
When I said I saw only a few Ramaswamy signs and more of Acton’s, Williams in Monroe County brushed it off.
“Was that Acton sign just setting out along the road? When I’m driving around, it doesn’t bother me if they’re along the road. It bothers me if they’re in someone’s truck, but I don’t see that,” he said.
Gathering hard data on yard signs is problematic so it’s hard to say for sure, said Swigger, who teaches at Ohio State University. But he, too, had noticed fewer in his neighbourhood.
“My guess is that it is a combination of conflict avoidance and exhaustion,” he said.
“It’s no secret that American politics, and Ohio politics, has become angrier and many people are probably reluctant to put up signs or put bumper stickers on their cars because they are avoiding a touchy subject.”
But that itself had a message, he said.
“I think the lack of yard signs can be taken as a sign that many, many voters are dissatisfied with the US political system,” he said.
That leaves Ohio with a contest where the currents are hard to read. Is it hidden Republican strength or Democratic opportunity?
Trump’s name will not be on the ballot but this is still his race.

Rs 10 lakh cover for 45 paise: Counter rail ticket buyers get insurance option
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
20:44:19 UTC
05:44:19 KST

At present, the optional travel insurance facility is available only for reserved tickets bought online.
NEW DELHI: From Tuesday (Oct 27), all railway passengers buying reserved tickets from reservation counters can opt for travel insurance. At present, optional travel insurance facility is available only for reserved tickets bought online.The insurance premium is only 45 paise per passenger, including taxes, with coverage of Rs 10 lakh in case of death and permanent total disability in a train accident.The scheme has provision for payment of Rs 7.5 lakh for permanent partial disability and up to Rs 2 lakh for hospitalisation expenses arising from injuries, as well as Rs 10,000 towards transportation of mortal remains of deceased passengers. The Railway Board has directed all its zones to implement the facility.It said, “Where a passenger opts for insurance, the applicable premium shall be collected along with the ticket fare through digital means only. Staff shall ensure that where the person is opting for insurance, payment is done through digital means.”Reservation staff will inform passengers about the availability of the optional insurance facility and facilitate the exercise of their choice.The board said reservation staff will ensure that the mobile number (mandatory) along with other requisite passenger particulars are captured accurately so as to facilitate transmission of relevant details to the insurance firm for issuance of the policy.
Passengers opting for insurance shall be informed that the policy details will be communicated to their registered mobile number.It covers specified railway accidents and untoward incidents, including train collisions, derailments, violent attacks, robbery, arson and accidental falls from trains. Coverage extends to diverted routes and alternative transport arranged by the railways in certain cases of train diversion or short termination.
Normal second class or general class passengers are not covered under the insurance policy. It is also not applicable to children below the age of 5 years for whom tickets are issued without a berth or seat. But it is applicable to children in 5-11 age group who have reservation with berth or without berth.

split ceramic curves cast soft reflected light in dimmable table lamp

split ceramic curves cast soft reflected light in dimmable table lamp
designed by alexey danilin for maytoni, hope is a table lamp featuring a split ceramic body that conceals internal LEDs.
prefer designboom on google
[FEATURED]
ALEXEY DANILIN CONCEIVES ‘hope’ CERAMIC TABLE LAMP for MAYTONI
Designed by Alexey Danilin for German lighting brand Maytoni, Hope is a table lamp composed almost entirely of natural ceramic. Conceived for mass production within technical and budgetary parameters, the design replaces conventional fabric or metal shades with a split ceramic envelope, allowing approximately 90% of the fixture’s mass to remain recyclable at the end of its lifecycle.
LED MODULES PROJECT REFLECTED LIGHT THROUGH SLIT OF SPLIT VOLUMES
For the lamp’s sculptural silhouette, designer Alexey Danilin draws inspiration from classical Roman statuary and traditional pottery forms, pairing curved, arching geometries with contemporary product design. Internally, integrated LED boards are oriented to direct illumination outward through the central gap separating the two ceramic halves, utilizing surface reflection to soften light output. A central vertical stem fastens the two ceramic elements, capped by a small metal sphere at the top. This structural component doubles as a functional touch-sensitive switch and dimmer, offered in various metal finishes to integrate with diverse interior palettes.

Protesters held a march across the capital demanding pensions to remain indexed to inflation and the gender pension gap to be eliminated.
Some 50,000 people, according to the organizers, while the government reported 25,000, chanted slogans in support of the state pension scheme, including "pensions aren’t for sale, pensions are to be defended," "widows and widowers will not be silenced" and "here they are, these are the ones fighting for your pension," according to the El Pais newspaper.
The protesters expressed concern over the state pension scheme, which could be weakened depending on who wins next month’s snap election. Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez has accused the right-wing Popular Party (PP) of planning to weaken inflation-linked pension increases.
The country’s monthly pension bill hit a record high this year of some $16.2 billion. The pressure is driven by several factors such as an ageing population, a low birth rate and wage stagnation.
Protests have lately been seen across many countries in Europe, including Italy, France and Belgium, over a range of issues such as rising costs of living and poor school conditions.

Iraq believes Israel may have struck militia weapons supplied by Iran - report
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
20:10:26 UTC
05:10:26 KST

Iraq believes that Israel was behind recent strikes on two sites where Iran-backed militias had stockpiled “Chinese-made shoulder-fired air defense systems” sourced from Tehran, sources told London-based Arabic international newspaper Asharq Al-Awsat on Saturday.
It was unclear which specific type of system the report referred to. One source told the newspaper that “the armed group that identified this location for storing air defense systems believed it was extremely difficult to access or detect…the suspected attack occurred shortly after the shipments arrived at the two storage sites.”
The report, which said the strikes occurred last week, did not provide evidence for the claims and noted that parts of the claims could not be confirmed.
Asharq Al-Awsat added that the Popular Mobilization Forces (PMF), an umbrella group that contains numerous Iranian-backed militias and is also an Iraqi government paramilitary force, had said one of their bases suffered an explosion on October 17.
However, the PMF claimed at the time that this was an accident, and Iraq’s government vowed to investigate. The explosion had affected a stockpile of obsolete ammunition inside one of their headquarters in Baghdad's East Canal, injuring five people, according to Asharq Al-Awsat.
Not first time Iraq has blamed Israel for strikes
This is not the first time that Iraqis have sought to blame Israel for strikes in the country. Iranian-backed militias also blamed Israel for strikes in 2019 and a strike in Albukamal in Syria on the Iraqi border. In May, The Wall Street Journal reported that Israel set up a secret airstrip in Iraq in the midst of the Iran campaign.
Iran has been supplying Iraqi militias with weapons for many years. This has included missiles and drones capable of threatening Israel. The militias also carried out numerous attacks on Israel, especially after Hamas began its war on Israel on October 7, 2023.
The Asharq Al-Awsat report further cited an anonymous Iraqi government official who said that relevant authorities are still investigating the circumstances surrounding the incident, with the report noting that over a week had passed since the incident without any update.
Other sources said that the explosion in mid-October followed another incident on October 1. In that incident, warehouses belonging to Iran-backed groups in and around Baghdad had apparently been affected, “including warehouses containing drones intended for suicide attacks and reconnaissance.”
The report also reveals that the Iran-backed militias appear to be preparing for escalation. Iran has sought to make Iraq a frontline of the war since the US and Israel began airstrikes in February. For instance, Iran has carried out more than 1,000 strikes on the Kurdistan Region of northern Iraq since February. It has used drones and missiles.
In addition, Iran and the Iranian-backed militias carried out 600 attacks throughout Iraq, some targeting US diplomatic sites. The US withdrew forces from Iraq on September 30, a deadline that had been agreed to with Baghdad over the last years. Also, the US has warned Americans not to travel to Baghdad and noted the terror threats from the militias.
Asharq Al-Awsat appears to try to connect earlier reports about China supplying Iran with weapons to the movement of the same systems to Iraq. However, the report admits that this is “unconfirmed.” It further notes that on July 28, the Chinese Foreign Ministry denied these reports.
At the time, Iran was expected to receive, within weeks, its first shipment of up to 400 Chinese-made shoulder-fired air-defense missile launchers as it rebuilt its defenses after its war with the United States, three sources familiar with the deal told Reuters.
The militias may be preparing for what comes next. It should be noted that an Iran-backed militia targeted Saudi Arabia’s East-West Pipeline in a drone attack. It is believed, according to a report at Al-Hurra and other reports, that the attack was carried out from Iraq’s Maysan province near the Iranian border. That border crossing has now been closed amid US pressure and Iraq’s concerns apparently over trafficking.
Asharq Al-Awsat further noted conflicting reports describing sorties by Israeli fighter jets through Iraqi airspace near the Iranian border, supported by midair refuelers, an operation it said had not been independently confirmed.
A security official told Asharq Al-Awsat that Iraqi authorities have not yet determined the nature of the strikes, but have seen sufficient evidence to believe Israel was behind them.
Strikes suggest the start of a new round of conflict, Asharq Al-Awsat reports
The report concluded that the strikes suggest the start of a new round of conflict. This seems sensational because the alleged incident took place in mid-to-early October. On the other hand, a source within the Shi’ite Coordination Framework told Asharq Al-Awsat that “leaders of ruling parties had been predicting for weeks that the resumption of war between Washington and Tehran would begin with the complete destruction of the capabilities of the Iraqi factions.”
The Shi’ite Coordination Framework includes the Shi’ite parties in Iraq. Many of the parties have armed wings that are part of the PMF. For instance, the Badr Organization has numerous brigades within the PMF. Other groups include Kataib Hezbollah, Asaib Ahl al Haq and Harakat Hezbollah al Nujaba. Most of these groups, except Badr, have been sanctioned by the US as terrorist groups.
Meanwhile, the Islamic Resistance in Iraq, which includes many of the militias and has been responsible for attacks on Israel and the US in the past, published a report claiming Iraq’s airspace was being violated.

Turkish court orders probe into nationals over involvement in Gaza flotilla abuse
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
20:09:41 UTC
05:09:41 KST

An Istanbul court ordered prosecutors to investigate Turkish nationals allegedly involved in the mistreatment of participants in a Gaza-bound aid flotilla while they were held in Israel during the first hearing of a case against 35 defendants, including the Israeli prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu.
The Istanbul 11th High Criminal Court ruled that individuals identified by complainants as Turkish citizens who participated in alleged abuses against them in Israeli custody should be identified and referred to prosecutors for necessary legal action.
The court also ordered that existing arrest warrants and Interpol Red Notice requests against all 35 defendants remain in effect.
The case concerns Israel's armed interception of the Gaza-bound flotilla, which was carrying humanitarian aid to Gaza.
Flotilla participants describe alleged mistreatment
During the hearing, one complainant said he had joined the flotilla as a doctor to deliver medical supplies to Palestinians in Gaza.
He said Israeli soldiers confiscated five or six boxes of medical supplies from their vessel and that participants were subjected to mistreatment at Israel's Ashdod port.
He said he wished to pursue his complaint against the defendants.
Another complainant said she had been subjected to two strip searches and had an altercation with Israeli soldiers after refusing to remove her headscarf.
"They recorded me wearing the clothes they gave me instead of my headscarf and mocked me," she told the court.
She said one of the soldiers who detained her had told her he was from Türkiye's central province of Yozgat.
"They took our personal belongings, and I have not been able to recover any of them. Our privacy was seriously violated. I am filing a complaint," she said.
A Turkish lawmaker also testified, saying she and approximately 80 other participants were held in a poorly ventilated room after being detained.
She said that an Israeli soldier insulted Islam while they were reading the Quran.
Un said detainees were not allowed to sleep and were subjected to verbal abuse and psychological mistreatment.
"We were not even allowed to close our eyes where we were held. Sleeping was forbidden," she said.
She added that police officers who arrived the following day insulted Türkiye and the detainees in Hebrew.
Lawyers call for broader investigation into Gaza
Riza Saka, president of the bar association, described the proceedings as historic and called for further international evidence to be included in the case.
Saka referred to provisional measures ordered by the International Court of Justice (ICJ) in proceedings concerning allegations of genocide in Gaza.
He requested copies of relevant ICJ documents and a UN report concerning allegations of genocide in Gaza.
He also referred to the arrest warrants and Red Notice requests issued against Netanyahu and the other defendants.
Lawyer Yasin Samli argued that the case involved allegations of genocide, crimes against humanity and attacks against civilians.
Samli said lawyers had submitted eight volumes of evidence, including five concerning alleged crimes against women and children in Gaza.
Court seeks separate indictment over alleged crimes against Gaza civilians
In its interim ruling, the court noted that the existing indictment primarily described actions taken against the Gaza-bound aid flotilla, while allegations concerning crimes committed against civilians in Gaza were presented only indirectly and in general terms.
The panel said investigations into genocide and crimes against humanity could be conducted upon a request from Türkiye's justice minister.
Taking into account the principle that courts are bound by the factual allegations set out in an indictment, the panel ordered a formal request to prosecutors concerning a possible new indictment.
The request calls for alleged crimes against civilians in Gaza, separate from the actions involving the flotilla, to be described in concrete terms and linked to supporting evidence.
The court said evidence submitted by legal organisations should be considered in that process.
Court orders asset inquiries, requests ICC documents
The panel also ordered inquiries into whether any of the 35 defendants hold movable or immovable assets in Türkiye.
It directed that a request be sent through the Justice Ministry for documents from proceedings involving the defendants before the International Criminal Court (ICC).
The court additionally ordered that a UN report submitted concerning allegations of genocide in Gaza be requested through the Justice Ministry.
The panel accepted applications to participate in the proceedings from complainants and several legal and human rights organisations.
The hearing was adjourned until 30 March 2027.

Bulgarian businessman and former politician Slavi Binev was shot dead at his home in Sofia’s Pavlovo district on October 24.
The police received a report of the killing shortly before 10:30 a.m.
Three suspects have been detained by the police.
Binev had a notable sporting career in addition to his political activities. He was a multiple Bulgarian taekwondo champion, an overall Balkan champion and a European champion, and served as president of the Bulgarian Taekwondo Federation. In the 1990s, Binev owned some of Sofia’s best-known entertainment venues, and his name was linked to conflicts between criminal groups.
Binev later entered politics. In 2007, he ran in the European Parliament elections and was elected MEP on the ticket of the Ataka party. That same year, he also ran for mayor of Sofia. In 2009, he was re-elected as a Member of the European Parliament. In 2011, he left Ataka party and, a year later, founded the conservative party Movement for Success. It subsequently became part of the political alliance Civic Union for Real Democracy (GORD).
In 2014, Binev left GORD and joined the National Front for the Salvation of Bulgaria (NFSB). In the parliamentary elections held in October that year, he was elected as an MP for the Haskovo constituency on the party’s ticket. He became chair of the parliamentary Committee on Culture, a move that sparked protests from numerous intellectuals and public organisations. Binev subsequently resigned from the post.

Andrew Wasike 
24 October 2026•Update: 24 October 2026
More than 14,000 Ethiopians have fled deadly fighting in southern Ethiopia into neighboring Kenya, humanitarian officials said on Saturday, noting that more than a dozen people have been killed in clashes between rival communities.
"We urgently need more well-wishers to support us with food and water. There is also a need for sanitary supplies and more toilets to avert diarrheal diseases," Malik Adan, Kenya Red Cross head of the Upper Eastern region, told reporters.
The Kenya Red Cross said more than 10,900 displaced people were being accommodated at six temporary camps in the Kenyan border town of Moyale, while another 4,000 were staying with relatives and host families.
The figures mark a sharp increase from Friday, when Marsabit County Commissioner Stanley Kamande said more than 2,000 Ethiopians had crossed into Kenya following the outbreak of violence on Wednesday.
Residents reported on social media that heavy gunfire and shelling continued from both sides of the conflict, leaving Kenya as the only refuge for many civilians fleeing the violence.
The fighting involves Oromo and Somali communities in Ethiopia's southern border region, where a dispute over the display of the Somali Regional State flag in an area administered by Oromia has fueled tensions. Both are federal regions of Ethiopia.
At least nine deaths were reported on Friday, but there are fears that more than a dozen people may have been killed as heavy fighting continues, according to humanitarian officials.
The Kenya Red Cross has distributed tents, blankets, sleeping mats and other essential supplies while providing nutritional assistance to children and breastfeeding mothers.
Local authorities have pledged additional food supplies, including rice and beans, but humanitarian officials warn that available resources may not meet the needs of the growing displaced population.
Moyale, a major crossing between the two East African countries, lies approximately 780 kilometers (485 miles) north of Nairobi, Kenya's capital, and 775 kilometers (482 miles) south of Addis Ababa, Ethiopia's capital, by road.
The continued fighting has disrupted cross-border trade and raised concerns about further displacement.

No EC nod needed for voter to sue candidate over false information: Supreme Court
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
20:03:20 UTC
05:03:20 KST

The Supreme Court said that Section 125-A was inserted in the RoP Act in 2002.
NEW DELHI: A voter can now not only cast a vote in an election but can also drag an election candidate to court and initiate criminal proceedings for lying and furnishing a false declaration as Supreme Court has ruled that a complaint filed by a private person alleging an offence under Section 125-A of Representation of People Act (filing false affidavit) is maintainable and the Election Commission’s nod was not needed.Explaining the interplay between Section 125-A of Representation of People Act and Section 195(1) of the CrPC which says that no court shall take cognisance of any offences punishable under sections 172 to 188, including the offence of furnishing false information to a public servant, the top court held that Section 125A of RoP Act does not come within the ambit of Section 195 of CrPC and a court can take cognisance of a private complaint. The court’s ruling will further empower the electorate against candidates who lied in their affidavits.A bench of Justices Dipankar Datta and Sheel Nagu quashed the Karnataka HC order which had held that “right given to the voter is only to file an election petition, and not to register a private complaint of crime which is the duty of the Election Commission, if it wants to do so”.SC said that Section 125-A was inserted in the RoP Act in 2002, while Section 195 of CrPC was amended in 2006, and that the omission of the legislature to include Section 125-A of the RoP Act in Section 195 of CrPC was deliberate and no court would be barred from taking cognisance of an alleged offence under Section 125-A of the RoP Act, even on the complaint lodged by a private person.
“Should we read into Section 195 of CrPC a prohibition in respect of Section 125-A of the RoP Act also, apart from those expressly included? If indeed it were the intention of the legislature that cognisance of any offence relating to furnishing of false information by a candidate in an affidavit with intent of being elected in an election (referred to in Section 125-A of the RoP Act) could only be taken if the complainant were a public servant, the same could have been provided by an amendment of Section 195, CrPC since Section 125-A of the RoP Act is of fairly recent origin.”SC also refused to give credence to the EC’s press note that it can take cognisance of such complaints and refer such matters to the relevant investigating authorities on a case-to-case basis. “...Even though the ECI is supreme in its own sphere and has, indeed, issued guidelines/press notes based on its understanding of the statutory provisions, interpretation of statutes is primarily the task of the courts and such guidelines/press notes do not bind us,” the court said.
It said that Karnataka HC erred in holding that a private complaint cannot be filed for an offence under Section 125A of RoP Act which is punishable up to six months of jail term. The HC had interpreted the provision solely upon reading the letter issued by the Election Commission of India on the issue which was rejected by the apex court.Allaying the apprehension that allowing the lodging of a criminal complaint by a private person would be misused and frivolous cases would be filed by political rivals, SC said, “If at all a complaint is lodged to harass an elected candidate or frivolous allegations are levelled therein, the laws of the country duly empower the competent magistrates to pass such order(s) as they deem fit and proper commensurate with the facts and circumstances of each case.”

Expecting to lose economic standing hurts well-being more than expecting to gain helps it
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
20:00:56 UTC
05:00:56 KST

Believing that your socioeconomic position could decline in the future may itself reduce well-being by increasing anxiety about social status, according to research published in Personality and Social Psychology Bulletin. Expectations of moving up the ladder, by contrast, had weaker and less consistent effects.
Social mobility describes movement up or down the socioeconomic ladder, which can involve changes in income, employment and social standing. Much of the previous research has focused on the promise of upward mobility. But the prospect of moving in the opposite direction may be especially important at a time when some people in wealthy countries expect to experience lower living standards than previous generations.
The researchers focused on status anxiety, or worry about one’s position in the socioeconomic hierarchy. This can include concerns about losing status, failing to advance or being left behind compared with other people. Because anticipated downward mobility represents the possibility of losing resources and social standing, the researchers proposed that it could increase status anxiety and consequently reduce well-being.
Led by Davide Melita of the University of Granada in Spain, the researchers conducted four studies involving 2,819 people in Spain and the United States. The first two were surveys, while the final two were experiments designed to determine whether changing people’s expectations about their socioeconomic future could actually affect status anxiety.
Study 1 surveyed 216 full-time U.S. workers (average age 39; 49% women) about their beliefs regarding mobility in American society as a whole, such as whether most people now earn less than the previous generation. Those who believed downward mobility was more common reported greater status anxiety, which was in turn associated with lower life satisfaction, poorer perceived health and more depressive symptoms. Beliefs about upward mobility were not linked to status anxiety.
Study 2 surveyed 1,536 people in Spain (51% women), recruited to resemble the national population, using single questions about whether participants expected their own socioeconomic status to improve or worsen. Expecting one’s own status to worsen was associated with greater status anxiety and lower life satisfaction. Unexpectedly, expecting one’s status to improve was also associated with greater status anxiety, although it was directly linked to higher life satisfaction as well. The authors suggest that strong expectations of change in either direction may bring uncertainty about the future.
The researchers then tested the relationship experimentally. In Study 3, 472 Spanish university students (average age 22; 70% women) imagined starting a new life in a fictional society called Bimboola. Everyone began in the middle-income group, but participants were randomly told they had good chances of moving up, staying in the same group or moving down, while the level of inequality in the society was held constant.
Participants told they were likely to move down reported more status anxiety than those told they were likely to stay put, although the difference was small. In exploratory analyses, that increased anxiety in turn predicted lower satisfaction with their imagined life in Bimboola. Being told they were likely to move up, however, did not affect status anxiety.
Study 4 repeated the experiment with 595 employed Americans recruited online, and here the manipulation had much stronger effects on participants’ expectations. Prospects of moving down increased status anxiety, while prospects of moving up reduced it, and these changes in anxiety carried through to life satisfaction in Bimboola in opposite directions. The negative effect of anticipated decline was larger than the positive effect of anticipated advancement.
Across the four studies, the pattern for downward mobility was notably consistent: believing that one’s socioeconomic position could worsen was associated with greater status anxiety and, through that anxiety, lower well-being. By contrast, the results for upward mobility varied between studies, and only the U.S. experiment found that prospects of moving up reduced status anxiety and indirectly increased life satisfaction.
Melita and colleagues summarized, “our findings suggest that both upward and downward beliefs influence well-being through status anxiety, but the effects of downward mobility beliefs are stronger and more consistent.” The authors argue that policies aimed at improving well-being should not only expand opportunities for upward mobility but also protect vulnerable groups from economic downturns, for example by strengthening social safety nets.
Some limitations should be noted. The first two studies were correlational, and Study 2 measured mobility expectations with single questions. The experiments involved an imaginary society rather than actual unemployment, income loss or downward mobility, and they measured satisfaction with life in that imaginary society rather than participants’ real lives.
The researchers also noted that cultural circumstances could influence people’s reactions to the scenarios. The Spanish experiment involved young adults in a country with high youth unemployment, who may be skeptical about upward mobility, while Americans tend to overestimate how much mobility exists.
The study, “Prospects of Downward Mobility Cause Status Anxiety and Life Dissatisfaction,” was authored by Davide Melita, Matthias S. Gobel, Juan Matamoros-Lima, Rosa Rodríguez-Bailón and Guillermo B. Willis.
