Violence flares in Paris after largely peaceful protests across France over living costs, inequality
- France saw huge protests over living costs and inequality, with 410,000 people nationwide, or 110,000 in Paris, according to the Interior Ministry.
- Most marches were peaceful, but clashes broke out in Paris, Marseille and other cities after dark, with tear gas, water cannon and raids on shops.
- The government deployed 70,000 police and gendarmes, while critics accused it of overreacting and warned the unrest could continue each week.
AI generated
PARIS - Hundreds of thousands of demonstrators marched in France on Oct 24, with largely peaceful rallies giving way to clashes in Paris and Marseille as night fell despite a huge security operation aimed at preventing a repeat of last week’s unrest.
The Interior Ministry said 410,000 people took part in protests nationwide, though unions said the true figure was twice as high.
The main demonstration took place in Paris, where around 110,000 people marched on the southeastern fringes of the capital, denouncing rising living costs and growing inequality.
The atmosphere deteriorated sharply after the rally ended. Riot police fired tear gas and water cannon to disperse a group of around 500 hooded youths who hurled stones at officers, a security official said.
In France’s second city, Marseille, youths dragged large metal sheets to block a street, set fire to rubbish bins, and hurled rocks and bottles at riot police.
The confrontations continued after sunset and police said two jewellery shops were raided.
Clashes also flared in Lyon, Bordeaux and Grenoble, while police fired volleys of tear gas at demonstrators in Clermont-Ferrand, Lille, Nantes and Nice.
However, the violence was still less intense than a week ago, when looters and vandals went on the rampage in a number of French cities.
Police carry out pre-emptive searches
Authorities deployed 70,000 police officers and gendarmes, 10,000 more than a week earlier, after conceding they had underestimated the scale of the unrest on Oct 17.
“We have to be ultra, ultra responsive,” Interior Minister Laurent Nunez told reporters on Oct 24, accusing far-left activists and criminal gangs of seeking to foment violence.
Much of central Paris took on the appearance of a city under lockdown, with shopkeepers boarding up storefronts, museums closing their doors and more than 20 metro stations shut.
Business groups urged retailers to remain closed after thousands of shops and businesses were damaged or looted across France last weekend.
“There are hardly any customers, so it’s not really worth staying open,” said Oskar, manager of a Kiton boutique in Paris.
Several of the capital’s best-known cultural institutions, including the Louvre, the Musee d’Orsay and the Paris Opera, closed for the day as a precaution, leaving tourists frustrated.
“Everything’s boarded up and we’re not quite sure where we should be,” said Xavier Dolliole, a tourist from the US city of New Orleans.
Protests ripple across Europe
The nationwide unrest began with small student demonstrations in suburban Paris in September to denounce school conditions.
After it spread into a broader protest against the state of the economy in France, it also prompted demonstrators to take to the streets in neighbouring countries.
On Oct 24, Belgian police used tear gas and pepper spray as they clashed in Brussels with anti-government demonstrators, while protests took place in a number of Italian cities for a second weekend.
Leftist leaders in France denounced a government move to limit the number of authorised marches in many cities, as well as a last-minute decision to shift the Paris event to the southeastern fringes of the capital.
Hard-left leader Jean-Luc Melenchon, who joined the Paris rally, hailed what he called a “magnificent mass display of collective discipline and self-restraint”.
He predicted the protests would continue until President Emmanuel Macron, whose mandate expires in 2027, addressed the social malaise in France, one of the world’s richest nations but with a growing debt mountain that has alarmed investors.
“Given the current situation, I think he will come to understand that this will happen again every week. There is still time for (Macron) to give in. After that, the only thing left to him will be the exit door,” Melenchon told reporters.
Far-right party holds congress
Many demonstrators have accused the government of overreacting, as soldiers were dispatched to patrol the Champs-Elysees, a grand boulevard lined with luxury shops and restaurants.
“We shed tears for shops, not for the people who are being impoverished all year round,” said Clara Lebbadi, a 22-year-old arts student.
“My friend and I almost didn’t come because we were scared, but we came precisely because it’s important not to let repression win,” she added.
The first authorised march on Oct 24 passed off peacefully in Orleans, around 120km south of Paris, where demonstrators rallied against Marine Le Pen’s far-right National Rally, which is holding a party congress in the city.
A shooting west of Paris on Oct 23 heightened tensions. A gunman suspected of acting out of Islamophobic hatred killed one person and wounded four others, including a 12-year-old girl.
“We have come to tell the far right, face-to-face, that we are not afraid,” said Bally Bagayoko, the mayor of Saint-Denis and a member of Melenchon’s France Unbowed party. REUTERS

Trump Thinks Alaskans Could Vote for the Wrong Sullivan. What Can the DOJ Do?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
18:26:54 UTC
03:26:54 KST

The Department of Justice (DOJ) on Thursday filed a lawsuit that intends to weigh in on the results of the Senate race in Alaska. It seeks to block certification of the election results under certain conditions if Republican Sen. Dan S. Sullivan loses.
Experts question whether it has the legal basis to do so—and if this intervention is a preview of how the Trump Administration might respond to unfavorable midterm results across the U.S.
The DOJ, in its filing, expressed concern that there might be “voter confusion” stemming from the fact that two candidates on the ballot are named Dan Sullivan. Republican Sen. Dan S. Sullivan is currently seeking re-election, and one of his challengers is Daniel J. Sullivan (who also registered as a Republican, but will no longer be listed as such, to better discern the candidates).
The GOP first raised concerns in May, prompting a proposal to add “incumbent” beside the sitting senator’s name on the ballot. But the party continued to warn that voters could split their votes between the two Sullivans, opening the door for Democrat Mary Peltola.
Alaska has traditionally been a state that leans Republican: Trump won the state by 13 points in 2024, and the state has not had a Democratic governor since 2002.
But the race is closer than analysts first expected. October polls from The New York Times/Siena, Alaska Survey Research, and Data for Progress show Peltola leading Dan S. Sullivan by between 2 and 7 points.
The DOJ lawsuit claims that the “sole purpose” of Daniel J. Sullivan’s candidacy is to benefit Peltola. Therefore, it seeks to block certification if the incumbent loses but would have won with all of Daniel J. Sullivan’s votes. To determine that, it proposes recalculating the ranked-choice count as though those votes had gone to the incumbent instead.
In a Wednesday Truth Social post, Trump said he was “very concerned” about the race and described the situation as “totally confusing.”
“Even 1, 2, or 3% could make the difference,” he wrote of the potential outcomes.
The DOJ said there would need to be an “investigation” to determine which vote was meant for which Sullivan. There is no indication of how they might distinguish voter intent. Neither the DOJ nor the candidates’ campaigns responded to TIME’s requests for comment.
On Friday, Peltola’s campaign and the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee asked to join the DOJ’s case as defendants, writing: “Alaskans, apparently, must elect Senator Dan S. Sullivan or the President will not let them elect anyone at all.”
Voting rights experts are calling it a “garbage lawsuit” and “an unprecedented intervention by the federal government.”
Lisa Murkowski, Alaska’s other senator and also a Republican, endorsed the incumbent Sullivan in January but on Friday condemned the DOJ’s efforts to intervene.
“Alaskans don’t need any help voting for their preferred candidates,” she wrote in a post on X. “The Department of Justice should never have filed this lawsuit.”
Asked to comment on the DOJ filing Friday, Trump told reporters: "I'm the one that said do it."
Why experts question the DOJ’s Alaska election lawsuit
Prior to the DOJ lawsuit, Republicans sought to remove Daniel J. Sullivan from the ballot in June.
When he decided to run, Republicans sent complaints to Carol Beecher, the director of Alaska’s Division of Elections. She wrote a letter to Sullivan in June saying that election officials had determined that he would be removed, claiming his candidacy was not filed “in good faith for the purpose of genuinely pursuing” leadership.
Sullivan challenged the decision and sued the state. Judge Thomas Matthews of Alaska’s Third District Superior Court ruled in June that he could remain on the ballot beside the other candidates. He wrote in a 32-page decision that elections officials were introducing a “new, previously unstated ‘good faith’ criteria” and said that this requirement is not present in state law or the Constitution.
That decision was upheld by the Alaska Supreme Court on June 29.
It was later determined that a “mitigating remedy” would be to present each candidate’s name with the middle initial and to add “incumbent” to the sitting senator’s name.
The Alaska Supreme Court ruling did not end scrutiny of Daniel J. Sullivan’s candidacy. In August, Reuters reported that the DOJ had issued grand jury subpoenas while investigating whether he entered the race to confuse voters.
The DOJ then filed its new lawsuit amid October polling that showed Peltola ahead.
The department justifies the move using language in the National Voter Registration Act (NVRA) that says its purpose is to “protect the integrity of the electoral process.”
Experts, however, dispute whether that language authorizes the intervention.
Derek Muller, a professor of election law at the University of Notre Dame, wrote in a blog post after the filing that the proposed investigation is “essentially impossible.” But succeeding is not the point, he continues.
“The legal claim is so absurdly thin, there’s essentially no likelihood of success,” he wrote, adding that the real purpose of litigation is to signal to the press and public that the Trump Administration is “ready” if the result goes against the GOP’s interests in Alaska.
The Center for Election Innovation and Research (CEIR), a nonpartisan nonprofit working to inform voters, called the move “unprecedented” in a statement that also said the lawsuit “raises serious concerns about political interference.”
“I cannot recall an administration ever attempting to stop the certification of an election—and certainly not 11 days before polls close,” CEIR Executive Director David Becker said in the statement.
“Furthermore, this issue has already been fully litigated by Alaska’s courts,” he continued. “Alaska election officials are following state law, as the Constitution requires, and the courts will uphold that.”
Richard Hasen, a professor of law at UCLA, called the move a “desperate and unprofessional assault” on the American elections system.
Common Cause, a nonpartisan organization represented by the ACLU, filed a motion on Friday seeking to join the case to oppose the DOJ’s effort. Its president and CEO, Virginia Kase Solomon, said in a statement Saturday: “Politicians don’t dictate election outcomes; the people do.”
Nate Adams, a spokesperson for Dan S. Sullivan’s campaign, expressed confidence in his candidate’s re-election but told local media outlet KFSK on Friday: “We’ll let the DOJ complaint run its course.”
How has the federal government used the National Voter Registration Act?
The National Voter Registration Act was enacted in 1993 to address barriers to voter registration that depressed participation and disproportionately affected racial minorities. It was predicated upon the fundamental right of every eligible citizen to vote, as well as the duty of local and federal governments to protect that participation in the democratic process.
In the past 30-plus years, it has been used to sue states that fail to maintain their voter rolls or enforce registration requirements.
The Biden Administration also reckoned with Alaska in 2022, finding that the state wasn’t consistently letting residents register to vote—or update their voter registration—as part of their routine paperwork at the Department of Motor Vehicles. An agreement reached that June required Alaska to bring those procedures into compliance with the NVRA.
In 2012, the Obama Administration sued the state of Florida over a program intended to identify and remove suspected noncitizens from its voter-registration rolls too close to the elections. The parties agreed to dismiss the case in January 2013.
The George W. Bush Administration also sued several states under the NVRA to enforce requirements for offering voter registration and maintaining accurate voter rolls.
The DOJ’s Alaska lawsuit goes further than those earlier cases. Experts say the NVRA does not expressly authorize blocking election certification over suspected voter confusion.
If courts accept the DOJ’s argument, the consequences could extend beyond Alaska, warns Walter Olson, a senior fellow at the libertarian Cato Institute. It could give the federal government a new basis to challenge how states design ballots, determine which candidates qualify, and certify election results—all in the name of protecting election integrity.
“[The lawsuit] attempts to stretch a federal statute, the National Voter Registration Act (NVRA), beyond recognition by snipping language from the law’s preamble and treating it as if it creates vast and open-ended new duties that the federal government can enforce on states,” Olson said in a statement Friday. “If accepted, it would suddenly federalize many issues of local election administration.”

Thousands of people rallied on Tel Aviv's Hostage Square on Saturday to demand the establishment of a commission of inquiry into the failures committed during the October 7 massacre in 2023, with most of the opposition's leaders present at the event.

Protest opens with addresses from families of victims
Yossi Marshak and Titi Aynaw opened the rally with an address to the bereaved families, the survivors of the massacre and captivity, the families of the hostages, the fighters, and those wounded in body and soul, saying, “To all of you, we want to say: our hearts are with you. At the opening of the rally, Titi Aynaw addressed the families in the square, also mentioning the families who joined the circle of bereavement in recent days.

"We deserve answers. We deserve taking responsibility. And our children deserve a safer future," he added. Mor concluded his remarks with the memory of his son's words that day: "Dad, I don't want to die today."

Out of 41 people who were there, 28 were murdered, including Noa. She described her daughter as a young woman full of joy for life, a social activist who always cared for others.
"On October 7, I lost the dearest thing to me in the world. I lost my little girl, her hug, her voice, her laughter," she said.
"In every such moment, there was also a sharp, deep, and personal pain with the realization that my Noa did not get to return," she said.
Threats to disrupt the rally
Ahead of the rally tonight at Hostages Square in Tel Aviv, the October Council appealed to the Police Commissioner, Inspector General Danny Levy, warning against planned attempts to disrupt the event.
According to the organizers, information they received points to preparations by elements directly or indirectly connected to figures within coalition parties to incite provocations and harm the rally's message.
The concern presented by the families did not stop at disrupting speeches. They warned of an effort to create scenes of clashes, signs, and flags that would be perceived as part of the rally, even though they have no connection to its organizers. More than one million supporters of Brazil’s leftwing president, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, have streamed on to Rio’s most famous beach for a giant protest they hope will propel him towards a historic election fightback against his far-right rival, Flávio Bolsonaro.
Nearly 159m Brazilians will vote in the election’s runoff on Sunday, with the pair tied in the polls after Bolsonaro won the first round on 4 October by 47% to 45%.
On Saturday, under a fierce sun, red-clad crowds packed the 2.5-mile Copacabana beach in an attempt to help Lula clinch a dramatic and unprecedented comeback. Never since the return of democracy to Brazil in the 1980s has the first-round loser managed to bounce back.
Josias Silva, a 61-year-old truck driver, voiced confidence that his 80-year-old president, who was first elected in 2002, would win a fourth non-consecutive term. He carried a homemade sign to the carnival-like procession reading: “Lula re-elected. Tomorrow will be a new day.”
“The people have woken up,” Silva said of the large pro-Lula street protests that have swept Brazil since the leftist’s first-round defeat, many led by students.
“Young people know we need this victory because otherwise we will have dictatorship again – and we don’t want dictatorship. We don’t want hatred. We don’t want guns. We want a country of love,” added Silva, celebrating the large number of people who came to witness one of the final presidential campaign rallies in Lula’s storied 50-year political career.
“There’s never been a demonstration like this one. This is the biggest protest in the history of Brazil. And we are going to win tomorrow with more than 60% of the votes,” Silva claimed.
Polls suggest a far tighter margin and most analysts see Bolsonaro, whose father, Jair Bolsonaro, was president from 2019 to 2022, as the slight favourite, having sold himself to voters as someone who will tackle chronic levels of violent crime with an iron fist.
However, in recent days Lula has appeared to regain the initiative and climb in the polls, amid a succession of scandals involving his rightwing foe. Last week the Brazilian magazine Piauí claimed that at the height of Brazil’s 2020 coronavirus outbreak, Flávio Bolsonaro attended a boat party attended by sex workers and vaccine lobbyists hoping to strike a deal with the government of his father.
Some experts speculate a Lula comeback may be possible. At the Copacabana rally – which Rio’s City Hall said attracted about 1.1 million people – activists unfurled an enormous yellow and green banner declaring: “WE ARE GOING TO TURN THIS AROUND!”
On Saturday afternoon, Lula attended an even larger rally on Paulista Avenue, in the heart of Brazil’s biggest city, São Paulo.
“I’m super excited. Lula’s going to win,” said Marta Moraes, a 59-year-old restaurateur, as she joined Saturday’s demo in Rio.
Moraes said the election was not about left versus right. “We’ve nothing against the right … what we’re against is Bolsonarismo,” she said, tears filling her eyes as she recalled how Flávio Bolsonaro’s father botched the response to Covid during his chaotic 2019-2022 administration.
“I lost four members of my family because of Bolsonaro’s neglect,” Moraes said.
Jair Bolsonaro is serving a 27-year prison sentence for plotting a coup after he lost the 2022 election to Lula. Many Brazilian democrats fear he will be released – and could even return to government – if his son wins. Reports in the Brazilian press suggest several of Bolsonaro’s fellow plotters – who are now in prison or hiding in exile – may be given top military and police jobs in a Bolsonaro administration.
Cammy Marinho, a 49-year-old DJ and activist, said: “I’m here to prevent democracy becoming extinct – which is what the Bolsonaro family wants”.
Marinho said she had spent the past fortnight fighting to persuade people who voted for Bolsonaro, or did not vote in the first round, to back Lula.
“It’s non-stop work: in the bakery, in the supermarket, on the underground – whenever you feel there is an opening to talk to someone and show to them the reality, everything that Lula has done and is doing for the people and everything that this [Bolsonaro] family has done against the people,” she said.
Many marchers were part of the so-called “Lula’s Army” – a 10 million-member WhatsApp group that was created after the first round in the hope of turning the election around.
“Being a soldier in Lula’s army … means fighting for Brazilian democracy. This isn’t a normal election,” said Isabella Gaze, 64, a retired teacher and one of the group’s members.
“They constantly claim Lula is corrupt. But the truth is that they represent the most rotten and worst part of Brazilian politics. This is what we are fighting against now,” Gaze said of the Bolsonaros.
Many of the faces on Copacabana beach were teenagers, including 14-year-old Heitor Lopes da Silva. Silva had come from the city of Duque de Caxias in his wheelchair, with a placard that said: “Lula, I’m a person with a disability and I’m here to support you.”
“My whole life I’ve believed Lula was a good president. [Bolsonaro] represents the destruction of Brazil …. he represents sadness and death,” he said of the Bolsonaro-era Covid catastrophe.
Large crowds of Bolsonaro supporters also hit the streets, including in Belo Horizonte, the capital of Minas Gerais state, which has Brazil’s second-largest electorate after São Paulo, and is a key bellwether. No presidential candidate has ever won the presidency without securing Minas Gerais, where Bolsonaro led by just under 5% in the first round.
Thousands of Bolsonaristas gathered to see their candidate in a palm-lined plaza called Praça da Liberdade. To the booming sound of AI-generated funk carioca tracks praising Bolsonaro, a sea of supporters dressed in Brazil’s yellow football jersey waved Brazilian flags – and many of the United States too.
“The US is a great nation. Who wouldn’t want to be aligned with them?” said 56-year-old cosmetics entrepreneur Marcos Antonio, holding a flag that merged the emblems of both countries.
“I don’t want an alliance with Cuba or Venezuela. I want to move forward,” Antonio added. When reminded that Venezuela was currently aligned with the US after Donald Trump’s January invasion, he said: “True. But for now, a fully right-wing government hasn’t been installed yet. It’s in transition.”
Antonio Carlos Costa Jr, the 59-year-old owner of a shooting club, complained: “Lula did nothing for the country.”
Jair Bolsonaro relaxed gun ownership and buying laws – which security experts agree ended up diverting many firearms to criminal gangs – whereas Lula tightened regulations once again. “Jair Bolsonaro simply gave citizens the right to defend themselves, and his son will do the same,” said Costa Jr.
Lula supporters scoff at the idea that Bolsonaro, who has a history of well-documented ties with members of Rio’s paramilitary “militia” groups, could rid Brazil of criminality.
“If we vote the militias into power, we will be living in a dictatorship,” said Erika Cavalcante, 43, an architect who came to the march with a sign reading: “Don’t let the mobsters win.”

He emphasized that Kazakhstan is launching a new investment cycle and strengthening its role as Eurasia's key transport and logistics hub, leveraging the Trans-Caspian International Transport Route (TITR) and the North–South Corridor.
Talking about foreign policy, the ambassador recalled that 468 nuclear tests were conducted on Kazakhstan territory, reinforcing the country's commitment to global nuclear non-proliferation. He added that this commitment is complemented by Astana's initiative to establish an International Agency for Biological Safety. Turekhanov also underscored that Central Asia remains a central foreign policy priority.
"We are convinced that Central Asia must become a region of cooperation rather than competition, and of connectivity rather than dividing lines," the ambassador said.

Kazakhstan remains one of the major investors in Tajikistan’s economy, with investments exceeding $148 million.
"History made us neighbors, shared values bound us as brothers, economic ties turned us into reliable partners — and mutual trust rendered us allies," the diplomat stressed.
A cultural program highlighted the event, featuring an instrumental ensemble and young artists who showcased traditional Kazakh folk songs, dances, and national cuisine.

Breast reduction surgery is linked to improved sexual function
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
18:00:51 UTC
03:00:51 KST

Women who undergo breast reduction surgery often experience improvements in their sexual function, including enhanced desire, arousal, and satisfaction. A recent systematic review and meta-analysis published in The Journal of Sexual Medicine evaluated previous research to better understand how altering breast size influences sexual well-being. The combined data suggest that both physical relief and psychological shifts contribute to a better sexual experience after the procedure.
Breast reduction, medically known as reduction mammoplasty, is one of the most common aesthetic and therapeutic surgeries performed globally. The procedure involves removing excess skin, fat, and glandular tissue to create smaller, more proportionate breasts. Women often seek the surgery to alleviate the physical burdens of having very large breasts, a condition called macromastia. These physical burdens can include chronic back and shoulder pain, skin irritation, and difficulty exercising.
Beyond physical discomfort, excessively large breasts can impact a person’s mental health and body image. Breasts are closely associated with femininity and sexual identity in many cultures. Deviation from societal standards regarding breast size can sometimes lead to psychological distress, low self-esteem, and sexual health challenges. Women may feel self-conscious during intimacy, an internal distraction that can hinder sexual arousal and satisfaction.
While many patients pursue breast reduction hoping to improve their sexual life, previous research on the topic has produced conflicting results. Some studies have reported positive impacts on sexual desire and body image. Other studies found no measurable changes in sexual satisfaction compared to women who did not undergo the surgery.
To clarify these mixed results, a team of researchers based in Iran led the current investigation. The team included Mahdiye Taheri, Zahra Ghorbani, Fatemeh Alavi-Arjas, Maryam Firouzabadi, and Hamid Alavi Majd. They set out to systematically evaluate and synthesize the existing data on how breast reduction affects postoperative sexual function.
The researchers conducted a comprehensive search of medical databases to identify studies published up to April 2025. They specifically looked for original, English-language articles that quantitatively assessed sexual function in women after breast reduction surgery. They excluded studies focusing on breast surgeries performed for cancer treatment or gender affirmation. This exclusion kept the focus strictly on healthy women with symptomatic macromastia, avoiding the overlapping psychological effects of cancer or gender dysphoria.
Their search yielded 13 eligible studies containing data from 676 participants. The studies took place across several countries, including Brazil, Turkey, the United Kingdom, the United States, Italy, Iran, Poland, and Spain.
The review revealed that nine of the 13 studies documented an improvement in sexual function after surgery. Four of the studies reported no notable changes. Many of the included studies used the Female Sexual Function Index, a standardized questionnaire designed to measure domains such as sexual desire, physiological arousal, lubrication, orgasm, satisfaction, and pain. Across the research, women frequently reported enhancements in almost all of these categories following their operations.
For example, one study included in the review found that the percentage of women experiencing clinical sexual dysfunction dropped from 62.5 percent before the surgery to 21.4 percent afterward. Another prospective study conducted in the United States demonstrated an improvement in sexual function in over 68 percent of the women tracked.
Because eight of the studies used similar standardized instruments, the researchers were able to perform a meta-analysis. A meta-analysis combines the statistical data from multiple independent studies to identify overall trends. This combined analysis demonstrated that breast reduction was associated with a 13.27 percent increase in the mean score of sexual function among patients.
The researchers identified several physiological pathways that might explain these outcomes. On a physical level, reducing the volume of the breast can alleviate chronic pain and physical restrictions. This relief removes persistent physical discomfort that can act as a sensory distraction during sexual arousal.
Some evidence also suggests that removing excess tissue can normalize the distribution of sensory nerves in the breast. The nipple-areola complex is heavily innervated and plays a role in triggering the release of oxytocin, a hormone involved in arousal and emotional bonding. Modern surgical techniques aim to preserve these neural pathways, maintaining the physical triggers required for a full sexual response.
Psychologically, the surgery often leads to a reevaluation of body image. Women with large breasts frequently experience “spectatoring,” a cognitive process where attention is diverted from erotic sensation toward continuous self-monitoring of their appearance. This self-surveillance can induce performance anxiety and diminish sensory engagement.
By alleviating appearance-related anxiety, breast reduction allows individuals to engage more fully in sexual experiences. This psychological shift creates a positive feedback loop. Enhanced body image facilitates sexual satisfaction, and positive sexual experiences then reinforce a more cohesive self-concept and better global self-esteem.
The researchers noted that mental health benefits extend beyond the bedroom. One large database study cited by the researchers in their discussion reported that prescriptions for certain antidepressant and anti-anxiety medications dropped from 46.3 percent to 29.5 percent among patients following breast reduction. This alleviation of psychological distress likely establishes a stronger mental foundation for sexual desire.
Partner reactions also play a role in postoperative sexual well-being. Positive reactions from a partner regarding the physical changes can enhance the sexuality-promoting effects of the surgery. Conversely, criticism or neutral reactions can undermine the potential benefits. One study demonstrated that improvements in female sexual function after the operation were accompanied by an increase in their partners’ own sexual function scores.
While the combined data indicate a positive association between breast reduction and sexual function, the results rely primarily on observational studies. Observational research can identify links between variables but cannot definitively prove that the surgery directly caused the improvements in sexual function.
The individual studies included in the review often featured small sample sizes, typically involving fewer than 50 participants. Most of the research also relied on brief follow-up periods, usually checking in with patients just three to six months after their operations. This short timeframe limits the ability to determine if the sexual and psychological benefits persist over the long term or if delayed complications arise later.
The studies varied widely in their design and the surgical techniques used. The available data did not allow the researchers to measure how specific factors, such as the exact volume of tissue removed or the specific surgical methods employed, influenced the final sexual outcomes. Future research will need to record these surgical parameters to help doctors provide personalized advice to patients regarding nerve preservation and physical sensation.
Future studies would also benefit from evaluating more diverse populations. The current body of literature focuses almost entirely on cisgender, heterosexual women. Expanding this research to include LGBTQ+ individuals and women from a wider variety of cultural and socioeconomic contexts would provide a more comprehensive understanding of how breast reduction affects sexual well-being across different demographics.
The study, “Sexual function following reduction mammoplasty: a systematic review and meta-analysis,” was authored by Mahdiye Taheri, Zahra Ghorbani, Fatemeh Alavi-Arjas, Maryam Firouzabadi, and Hamid Alavi Majd.

Ghosts of past reports linger for NT child protection review
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
18:00:00 UTC
03:00:00 KST

analysis
Ghosts of past reports linger for Northern Territory child protection review
Poring over the 62 pages of the Independent Review into the Conduct of the Department of Children and Families report and its 45 recommendations, a multitude of systemic issues for the Northern Territory are made clear.
Underneath all of these complex challenges remains a key issue: accountability.
It's a question that threads through a growing mountain of reports and their hundreds of recommendations made over many decades, detailing failures in reducing harm for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Australians.
The NT government has committed to acting on all recommendations as a first step.
But the question remains: who has responsibility for making the changes to ensure children are kept safe?
Which leads to a further question.
What are the consequences if change does not happen?
Without an answer to these questions, communities are stuck with the status quo, or worse, having the wrong response applied without adequate means to correct course.
Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Social Justice Commissioner Katie Kiss has acknowledged the NT government's response, emphasising the need for "implementation that delivers lasting change".
Commissioner Kiss also remarked that "the NT government still has not implemented the recommendations of the 2017 Royal Commission into child protection".
Currently, the consequences of inaction and inappropriate responses are evident in the Closing the Gap measures that remain locked in place, or widening on many counts.
Youth crime, child removal, family and domestic violence patterns across Australia point to significant, systemic flaws in the way those with authority exercise their power.
This was made heartbreakingly clear in the alleged murder of Kumanjayi Little Baby.
WARNING: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander readers are advised that this article contains the image of an Indigenous person who has died, used with the permission of her family.
Tackling the problem at the root
The review's co-authors singled out the immediate need for an audit into current safety plans. This will ensure the appropriate people are given safety roles for the protection of children in the NT.
In the case of Kumanjayi Little Baby, the review found that one person in her family's safety network had a "long criminal history of violence, including five counts of threaten to kill".
Media reports and comments made in NT parliament have named this person as the man now charged with Kumanjayi Little Baby's murder.
Information such as this is of critical importance, so that all steps taken by authorised officers are based on relevant and appropriate processes.
But the co-authors were also determined to say that "the review does not suggest that a prior conviction, of itself, necessarily renders a person unsuitable" for a protective role.
Developing a clear mechanism for assessing the risk — the nature of which type of conviction represents a relevant threat — will be essential.
For a community with high rates of interaction with police, the justice system and incarceration, understanding the implications of this step is significant.
As is recognising the highly mobile and overcrowded nature of many households in communities across the NT.
These considerations sit within a broader landscape that presents myriad challenges for the most vulnerable.
We see children born into families facing significant disadvantage and dysfunction, where even the most basic needs, such as finding a home or shelter and having a means of getting there, are hard to access and becoming more so.
This month has seen the 400-bed YiSSA short-stay accommodation centre closed in Darwin, while the Bush Bus service, which operates between remote communities and Alice Springs, has had funding cut.
Dealing with this is hard enough.
But, as the review also revealed, "the current practice places significant responsibility on the non-offending parent to protect the child" — a burden the parent carries while their own safety is in jeopardy.
National Commissioner for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Children and Young People, Sue-Anne Hunter, puts the onus on the Department of Children and Families.
"The question that needed answering was what the department did with what it knew. Responsibility for violence sits with the people who use it. Responsibility for the response sits with the department. It should never sit with a victim."
It's a view echoed by Muriel Bamblett, the chair of SNAICC, the peak body for community-controlled Indigenous children's services. She highlights the work of violence reduction programs in Victoria that tackle the problem at the root.
"You need behaviour change. You need to be able to work with those communities around preventing violence,"
she said.
"In Victoria, we've got violence reduction now […] It has to take a public health approach."
Rushed remedies
There is much to consider around community and child safety and, with lives in the balance, it is worth looking at the record set so far.
One case stands out: the Northern Territory Emergency Response, or NT Intervention.
When the Howard government suspended Australia's Racial Discrimination Act on June 21, 2007, military units were deployed to discrete Aboriginal communities.
The decision came after the release of the Ampe Akelyernemane Meke Mekarle "Little Children Are Sacred" report, led by Pat Anderson and Rex Wild QC.
Tasked with inquiring into the protection of Aboriginal children from sexual abuse, the co-chairs delivered a comprehensive 316-page report with 97 recommendations.
Clear guidance was provided: "In the first recommendation, we have specifically referred to the critical importance of governments committing to genuine consultation with Aboriginal people in designing initiatives for Aboriginal communities, whether these be remote, regional or urban settings."
That never happened. The legislation was rushed through in two months.
Ten years later, Anderson described the NT Intervention response as a "betrayal" that had led to "further abuse of Aboriginal people. That's what the intervention was".
The NT Intervention framework ended in July 2022 but stands as a stark reminder of the long-lasting impacts that can emerge when change is made without proper consideration of the recommendations.
This is something certainly worth remembering as the wheels turn once again on resolving this most enduring set of challenges.

Kiwi expats could prove crucial in New Zealand's 'knife edge' election
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
18:00:00 UTC
03:00:00 KST

New Zealanders living in Australia prepare to vote in 'dead heat' election back home
With the upcoming New Zealand election on a "knife edge", expats like Brisbane woman Mary-Leigh Scheerhoorn could help shape the result.
A permanent resident of Australia, she is one of about 126,000 New Zealanders living overseas who are registered to vote ahead of the general election on November 7.
Kiwi expats account for more than 3 per cent of registered voters at this election, with nearly two-thirds of them in Australia.
Ms Scheerhoorn, a clinical nutritionist who has lived in Australia for 24 years, said she was voting to influence the country she hoped to return to one day.
As a Māori woman, she said she had a strong connection to New Zealand and was "drawn back to be with my people and my culture".
Voting is not compulsory in New Zealand, but at the 2023 election more than 77,000 of the up to 1 million Kiwis living overseas voted.
According to Electoral Commission figures, about 33,000 more overseas voters have registered than for the 2023 election.
Election a 'dead heat'
New Zealand Prime Minister Christopher Luxon, who leads the National Party, is seeking a second term after defeating the Labour Party's Chris Hipkins in 2023.
The incumbent government — a right coalition of the National Party, New Zealand First and ACT Party — is up against a left bloc of the Labour Party, Green Party and Te Pāti Māori (Māori Party).
Tom Jamieson, a senior lecturer in political science at Te Herenga Waka-Victoria University of Wellington, said polling suggested both the major parties, National and Labour, were generally in the high 20s.
However, a 1News-Verian poll released on Tuesday had National pushing ahead by five points.
Nonetheless, Mr Jamieson said there was a "dead heat" between the two blocs and the election looked to be on a "knife edge".
"A 1 per cent or a 2 per cent swing could decide the election," Dr Jamieson told the ABC.
"So I think it's probably in all of their interests to court the overseas vote as much as possible."
He said the non-aligned Opportunity Party could be a "kingmaker" if it won more than 5 per cent of the party vote — the threshold required to enter parliament without winning an electorate seat under the country's electoral system.
However, he said a lot depended on the turnout.
Dr Jamieson said New Zealand expats usually voted for minor parties, in part because they had historically worked harder to secure the votes of Kiwis overseas than the major parties.
He said the expat vote had also tended to "track left", with the Green and Te Pāti Māori parties receiving strong support from overseas voters at the 2023 election.
"The kinds of people who live overseas may relate more to their environmental stewardship and advocacy for Māori," he added.
Expat voting intentions
Ms Scheerhoorn said she was hoping for a new New Zealand government.
She said she was dismayed by the government's handling of issues relating to the Treaty of Waitangi/Te Tiriti o Waitangi, the nation's founding agreement with Māori people, and the removal of Māori language from some books that teach young children to read to avoid "confusion".
"This has felt like an open attack on the culture, which I think is very much the fabric of New Zealand," she said.
She said a future move home had made her consider things like the cost of living, housing and health care.
"If we want to go back and live in New Zealand … are there jobs available? What's the earning capacity? What's the tax situation look like?" she said.
She said she was very strongly drawn to the Green Party at this election and had voted for them previously.
Ron Deane, who moved to Australia from Rotorua three years ago, was also leaning towards voting for a minor party.
The Brisbane-based truck driver came over after struggling to find work in New Zealand and had similar concerns about the treaty, the cost of living and affordable housing.
He was voting because his friends and family in New Zealand were "feeling the pinch", often forced to make decisions about buying food and paying rent.
"Although I live in Australia, New Zealand is still home. I care about its future and believe it's important to have a say in the decisions that affect our people, culture and future generations," he said.
The 44-year-old said he was still deciding who he would vote for.
About 120,000 more New Zealand citizens left in the three years to August 2026 than returned, according to Stats NZ estimates.
Many like Jethro George moved to Australia in that time.
He said Australia's higher wages, cheaper house prices and lower cost of living were significant factors in the move.
"The roles I applied for in Australia paid almost double what I was on in New Zealand, with less responsibilities," he told the ABC from his home in Perth.
"Couple that with lower living costs and a relocation package, it was hard to say no."
Mr George, a 35-year-old mental health worker who also owned his own consultancy business, said he was a swing voter.
He used to work in New Zealand on housing, homelessness and poverty-related issues.
All were key policy concerns for him along with the cost-of-living crisis, which he saw first-hand on a trip to New Zealand earlier this year.
However, he was frustrated by parties that "just attack each other" rather than suggest solutions and was not yet convinced by the policies of any party, major or minor.
"There isn't the strength that you would want to see in leadership," he said.
Parties court overseas voters
Kiwi expat Tracey Lee, a strategist and former sociologist, created the non-partisan campaign Every Kiwi Vote Counts in 2020, which aims to boost the number of overseas voters.
"Those [expat] votes and perspectives can change what goes forward," she told the ABC from her home in London.
Ms Lee helped organise a virtual town hall in early October so party leaders could speak to expat voters around the world.
Jethro George said a big challenge for expats was holding on to their connection to New Zealand and seeing "the value of the vote".
"I think our votes count and they matter … the challenge is just really identifying and understanding where to put that," he said.
He wanted to see "a New Zealand that's thriving" and hoped to return there one day because he missed his family, friends and the culture.
It was difficult to see a return now, though, he said, based on where the country sat politically and economically.
"I want to live in a country where families can do more than just get by, and where contributing to the wellbeing of others doesn't come at the expense of your own family's time and financial security," he said.

The Houthis warned airlines earlier this month against using Saudi airspace, exempting only the airspace over Mecca and Medina, as they intensified attacks on the kingdom.

By Camillus Eboh and Ben Ezeamalu
KADUNA, Oct 24 (Reuters) - President Bola Tinubu formally launched his campaign for a second term on Saturday in the northern city of Kaduna, where he sought to convince voters that painful economic reforms are beginning to pay off despite a lingering cost-of-living crisis.
Tinubu, 74, faces a contest ahead of a January 16 election that is likely to be dominated by the economy and security. His main challengers include former Vice President Atiku Abubakar and Peter Obi, who finished second and third respectively in 2023.
By midday, thousands of supporters of the president’s All Progressives Congress party had filled much of the 10,000-capacity Ranchers Bees Stadium, with more arriving as the rally got underway.
“Thank you for this massive showing up. It is a promise. Come 2027, January 16, you must go out massively and elect me again,” Tinubu told the crowd.
OPPOSITION CREATED PROBLEMS, SAYS TINUBU
Since taking office in 2023, Tinubu has scrapped fuel subsidies, devalued the naira and introduced other reforms credited with improving public finances, foreign reserves and investor sentiment. But the measures have also fuelled Nigeria’s worst cost-of-living crisis in a generation.
Petrol prices rose to about 1,400 naira ($1.05) a litre in Lagos and Abuja in September and as much as 1,500 naira in parts of northern Nigeria, adding to pressure on household budgets.
Tinubu dismissed opposition complaints about hunger and poverty, arguing that his rivals created those problems.
“They created the hunger. They created the poverty. We are trying to eradicate it.”
Phrank Shaibu, a spokesperson for the Atiku campaign, told Reuters the president was attempting to dodge responsibility.
“Mr President, blaming the opposition for hunger is either delusion or a staggering case of political amnesia,” he said.
Security will provide another test. Nigeria continues to battle armed bandits and kidnappers in the northwest and a 17-year Islamist insurgency in the northeast, where militants have stepped up attacks on military positions.
Tinubu nevertheless enters the race with a formidable political machine. His camp says he has the backing of 32 of Nigeria’s 36 state governors, potentially giving him an unprecedented organisational advantage, although past elections have shown governors cannot always deliver their states to presidential candidates.
His toughest electoral test could come in the north, where Atiku, a veteran northern politician with an established support base, will seek to erode the president’s vote.
Tinubu has said he will not attend campaign rallies in all 36 states as he needs to remain focused on governing. The party’s proposed timetable has him personally attending rallies in 12 states, culminating in a major closing rally in his home state of Lagos on January 9.

Normalization of attacks on nuclear sites unacceptable

“Nuclear facilities shall never, under any circumstances, be subjected to attack or threat of attack,” the countries said in a joint statement delivered at the 81st session of the United Nations General Assembly’s First Committee on Friday.
According to Press TV's report, the statement was issued by Belarus, Burkina Faso, China, Cuba, Eritrea, Iran, Nicaragua, Niger, Pakistan, Russia, Tajikistan and Zimbabwe, addressing the prohibition of attacks and threats against nuclear sites dedicated to peaceful purposes.
The countries reaffirmed “the inalienable right of all states to develop research, production, and use of nuclear energy for peaceful purposes without discrimination.”
They underscored that attacks or threats against nuclear facilities violate the principles of the UN Charter, international law and the IAEA Statute, adding that such actions are “profoundly inconsistent with the objects and purposes of the NPT,” referring to the Treaty on the Non-Proliferation of Nuclear Weapons.
The statement also recalled UN Security Council Resolution 487 (1981), which strongly condemned a military attack against nuclear facilities, as well as relevant decisions and resolutions adopted by the IAEA General Conference.
The 12 countries warned that attacks against nuclear facilities have “grave implications for nuclear safety, nuclear security” and pose a serious threat to the credibility and effectiveness of the IAEA safeguards system and the wider global non-proliferation framework.
They also cautioned that such attacks could undermine the peaceful use of nuclear energy and international cooperation, potentially triggering radioactive releases with severe consequences both inside and beyond the affected country.

Hundreds of thousands marched in cities across France on Saturday in largely peaceful protests to support schoolchildren’s demands for more teachers and repairs to dilapidated buildings, as Emmanuel Macron faces a social and political crisis in his final months as president.
In Paris, at least 110,000 people marched along the eastern edge of the city, according to government estimates. They supported high schoolers but also complained of the high cost of living and the government’s heavy policing, saying riot police had been sent to target school protesters over the past month, instead of the government offering political solutions.
The mood in Paris on Saturday afternoon was peaceful and lighthearted, with brass bands playing and children and grandchildren present. Some people carried banners critical of the government’s policing, saying: “Oppression breeds rebellion” and “The right to protest”.
But at the end of the Paris demonstration, at Porte de Vincennes on the city’s eastern edge, different groups of masked men dressed in black emerged who had not appeared to have taken part in the peaceful march. Some groups of masked men threw glass bottles and stones at police, who responded with teargas, water cannon and stun grenades. A bin was set alight and fireworks were set off towards police.
Riot police also charged a larger crowd of protesters at the end of the Paris march, using batons against them.
Police fired teargas to prevent protesters in Lyon, Lille, Montpellier, Nantes and Toulouse from reaching city centres. In Marseille, some bin fires were lit amid clashes with police. At least two people were seriously injured, one in Clermont-Ferrand and another in Toulouse, who reportedly had fingers blown off.
The government estimated that at least 400,000 people had marched across France. Trade unions estimated the number at double that. The interior ministry said there had been almost 1,000 arrests.
Laurent Nuñez, the interior minister, said that at various street marches across France there were what he called “high-risk groups” who “broke away from the main body and sought to commit acts of violence”.
More than 70,000 police were on the streets of French cities, with shops boarded up and many museums closed. The government had feared a repeat of last Saturday, when, despite peaceful protests taking place, France saw one of the most violent days of unrest in years, with public buildings burned, hundreds of shops destroyed and looted and at least 2,700 people arrested in cities across the country.
At Saturday’s protests, there was widespread anger at Macron for banning non-union demonstrations that his government deemed “illegitimate” and for keeping all protesters away from city centres.
At the Paris march, Nadège, a 43-year-old communications worker, said she had been teargassed last weekend at a peaceful demonstration. “I’m out again peacefully today to support everyone who is brave enough to demonstrate. It does take courage. People are afraid now. We have to keep our rights alive … In France, it’s our legal right to protest in the street and I’m here to defend that.”
A 21-year-old student from a Paris science faculty that is now blockaded by demonstrators said: “We feel in France that we are increasingly living in an authoritarian regime that is trying to stop our democratic right to protest in the street.”
The radical left presidential candidate, Jean-Luc Mélenchon, who took part in the Paris rally, said Macron must “give in” and address France’s social malaise or face repeated protests. “Given the current situation, I think he will come to understand that this will happen again every week,” Mélenchon said.
The government has been facing a crisis since the start of high school demonstrations in mid-September, when children aged between 15 and 18 began protesting against staff shortages at their schools, leaking and crumbling buildings, and a lack of chairs in overcrowded classrooms. It grew into the biggest youth movement in years, with trade unions, teachers and parents joining. Police investigations are under way after some children and protesters were maimed and injured by explosive police weaponry.
At Saturday’s march there were some people dressed in yellow vests who had taken part in the gilets jaunes anti-government protests of 2018 and 2019. Standing amid demonstrators, Jérôme Rodrigues, a key figure from the gilets jaunes protest, said: “Today the government is afraid; that is why they are pushing demonstrators to the edge of the city, away from places of power. It’s not police shields that will provide an answer to French people struggling and unable to make ends meet.” He said it was likely that demonstrations would continue.
Pierre, 60, a retired banking consultant, said he was demonstrating in support of school students. “I have an eight-year-old granddaughter. I want her to have a brighter future than the sombre times we are facing today. There is a complete refusal by the government to listen to people’s demands.”
Jesse, 40, a charity worker from the north of Paris, carrying a sign saying “Free Hugs”, said: “I’m so angry. I’m here to support schoolchildren’s demands for better conditions. I’m so proud of them, and we have to stand together.”
She said: “I know I’m not going to war by coming out to demonstrate peacefully. But at times it really does feel like a war … This is the first time I’ve prepared so carefully for a peaceful march, wearing old clothes in case they are gassed or torn.”
In Orléans, thousands shouting anti-fascist slogans marched against a congress held by Marine Le Pen’s far-right anti-immigration National Rally party. Protesters criticised Le Pen, a frontrunner in next year’s presidential election, as well as Macron, who steps down from power next year. “Macron, resign. Le Pen in prison,” the crowd shouted.

Lula against Flavio - both candidates in the second-round presidential election in Brazil hold rallies in major cities on the last day of campaigning. With around 20% of the electorate having abstained in the first round, the result is wide open and opinion polls show them neck and neck.
Brazilian President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva and right-wing senator Flavio Bolsonaro rally their supporters one last time on Saturday, converging on the beaches of Rio de Janeiro and closing a fraught election campaign one day after a combative final live television debate.
In the first round of voting Bolsonaro won 47% over Lula's 45%. But in the intervening 3 weeks of intense and acrimonious campaigning the left-wing incumbent seems to have made up some ground.
80-year-old Lula aims for historic 4th non-consecutive term
Lula, who got his start as a union worker and became the country's first working class president, inspired a cult-like devotion during his first and second terms in office, as Brazil's economy expanded with the help of a commodities boom and social programmes, including direct cash assistance, that lifted millions of Brazilians out of poverty.
He later spent more than a year in prison on corruption convictions that were eventually annulled before winning a third term in 2022.
Former U.S. President Barack Obama once called Lula “the world’s most popular politician,” but his approval rating have at times fallen as low as 24% this term as voters raise concerns about crimes and the cost of living.
Former lawyer Bolsonaro hopes to continue his father's politics
Senator Bolsonaro began his political career at 21, when he became Rio’s youngest elected state lawmaker.
When his father, former President Jair Bolsonaro, barred from running as he serves a 27-year sentence under house detention for staging an attempted coup after losing to Lula in 2022, his eldest son took on the challenge to continue the right-wing agenda. He has largely embraced his father’s ultra-conservative politics, while trying to moderate his communication style to attract centrist voters.
His hard-line security policies have been a pillar of his campaign, and polls show these proposals are popular.
Sunday's runoff will determine whether Brazil remains one of the few leftist nations in the region or joins the ranks of right-wing governments friendly with US President Donald Trump.
In their final debate on Friday night, the rivals struck a calmer tone than their first showdown, which descended into insults and was empty of policy proposals.
Lula attacked the senator's lack of experience while Bolsonaro accused the president of leaving behind a "broken country."
"He doesn't know what hunger is," Brazil's first working-class president said of Bolsonaro, who asked the incumbent: "Why are things so expensive?"
He has promised to resolve Brazil's crime woes, create 500,000 more spots in prisons and slash government spending.
International repercussions for the future
Brazil plays a vital role in mitigating global warming by protecting the Amazon rainforest, but deforestation a record high during Jair Bolsonaro's presidency, and his son has likewise denied human-caused climate change, committing only to stopping illegal deforestation. This was followed by a record low in new clearances in recent years, as Lula's government increased satellite monitoring and targeted law enforcement.
Sen. Bolsonaro’s admission that he accepted millions of dollars from disgraced banker Daniel Vorcaro to produce a film on his father’s life has cast a shadow over his campaign. He is under investigation for corrution, money-laundering and tax evasion in connection with the case.
Lula has repeatedly warned the US not to meddle in Brazil’s elections and has made defending Brazil's sovereignty and interference by foreign social media a key campaign issue.
Trump announced 50% tariffs on Brazilian goods last year, citing — among other reasons — the trial of Jair Bolsonaro. This year, he imposed a new round of US tarrifs, citing unfair trade practices despite running a U.S. surplus. Trump also classified Brazil’s biggest drug-trafficking groups as foreign terrorist organisations, shortly after receiving Sen. Bolsonaro at the White House — a move Lula's administration opposed as a pretext for intervention.
A victory by Bolsonaro would add Brazil to a list of Latin American countries — including Argentina, Chile, Costa Rica and Peru — that have elected Trump-friendly governments in recent years.

“The service Netanyahu has rendered to the Islamic Republic of Iran and the Palestinian cause is something that even the greatest reformers and revolutionaries who support Palestine could not have accomplished,” he said. “He has played a major role in advancing the Palestinian revolution and the Islamic Revolution.”
Global public opinion turning against Israel
Naqdi also pointed to what he described as a significant shift in global public opinion toward Israel.
Several years ago, he said, Iran had pursued diplomatic efforts to persuade nearly 100 foreign delegations to walk out of the UN General Assembly, make noise, and boo the Israeli prime minister during his address.
“I asked artificial intelligence about this,” Naqdi said, recounting that the response was that even years of diplomatic work would not have achieved such an outcome. Instead, he said, the change had resulted from the Israeli regime’s own conduct and actions.
Naqdi said he had posed another question about how many years of publicity and campaigning would have been needed to persuade millions — or even hundreds of millions — of people across the five continents to raise the Palestinian flag and support the Palestinian cause, despite the difficulties they faced.
“Again, the answer was the same,” he said. “The nature of Netanyahu’s operations, the conduct of his government toward the Palestinian people, and the events they brought about have all worked in our favor.”
Naqdi points to changing US attitudes toward Israel
Naqdi also cited what he described as a shift in American public opinion toward Israel.
“Could we have brought American public opinion to the point where a US serviceman set himself on fire in front of the Israeli Embassy, shouting ‘Free Palestine’?” he asked, referring to an act of self-immolation that he said had taken place in protest against Israel.
He also pointed out that five US service members had set themselves on fire in Atlanta, Boston, and Washington in protest against Israel.
“Could we have brought American public opinion, which was entirely pro-Israel, to such a point? We could not have done that ourselves,” Naqdi said. “Who did it? This is the result of Netanyahu’s actions. God can even make your enemy serve your cause.”

In France, police used tear gas against protesters in five cities

In France, clashes with police occurred during protests against the high cost of living. Law enforcement used tear gas in Paris, Marseille, Lyon, Lille, Bordeaux, Toulouse, Montpellier and Nantes. AFP reports, writes UNN.
Details

Yemen's Houthi rebels claim new attacks on oil facilities and airports across Saudi Arabia
Yemen’s Iran-allied Houthi rebels said they launched attacks at Saudi oil facilities and airports on Saturday while Yemen’s Saudi-backed government said the group also fired three ballistic missiles at coast guard sites in the port city of Aden.
There was no immediate confirmation from Saudi authorities on the Houthi reports, and it was not immediately clear if the reported attacks had hit their targets in the kingdom or been intercepted.
Houthi rebel spokesperson Yahya Saree said the group targeted King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh, an Aramco facility in Yanbu, the Rabigh oil refinery, crude oil pumping stations and the East-West Pipeline.
He also said the group targeted King Fahd International Airport in Dammam, an airport in Najran and an airbase in Khamis Mushait.
The Saudi-led coalition said it destroyed two ballistic missiles fired by Houthis towards Yanbu and Taif on Saturday.
The renewed fighting has shattered a 2022 UN-brokered truce that largely halted cross-border attacks between the Saudi-led coalition, which backs Yemen’s internationally recognised government, and the Houthis, who control the capital Sanaa.
The escalation has opened another front in the US-Israeli war on Iran.
In Yemen, the Interior Ministry of the internationally recognised government said two of the Houthis’ missiles had struck a coast guard headquarters, while a third hit a coast guard building in the Tawahi district.
Houthi spokesman Saree said the group’s forces had targeted Saudi-backed military gatherings at what he called Al-Nasr camp and a naval military base in Aden, saying Saudi officers were overseeing the mobilisation there.
There was no immediate comment from the Saudi-led coalition on that assertion.
Earlier on Saturday, Saudi Arabia’s Civil Defense briefly issued alerts warning residents of potential danger in Taif and Yanbu, as well as in the holy city of Mecca and the kingdom’s second-largest city, Jeddah.
About 10 minutes later, the agency said the threat had passed.
The Houthis warned airlines earlier this month against using Saudi airspace, exempting only the airspace over Mecca and Medina, as they intensified attacks on the kingdom.
(FRANCE 24 with Reuters)

Brazil’s election is a referendum on Israel, and the last hurdle for Latin America’s pro-Israel right
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
17:49:21 UTC
02:49:21 KST

As Brazilians gear up to head to the polls to elect their next President, flags dot the streets of the capital, São Paulo. The flags, however, are not just Brazilian flags. They are Israeli and Palestinian flags — each representing opposing politics with consequences reaching from Latin America to the Middle East.
Brazil represents the final hurdle in a region that has swung drastically to the right over the last 12 months. In a country that accounts for 31% of Latin America’s population and 33% of its economy, the choice between the incumbent Luiz Inácio ‘Lula’ da Silva on the left and Flávio Bolsonaro on the right is instrumental to the broader politics of a region where U.S. dominance is palpable and Zionist allegiances are increasingly audacious.
Across Latin America, Palestine and Israel have become signifiers of opposing politics, reflecting domestic concerns about national sovereignty and domestic security. So as Brazilians prepare for the second round of a highly consequential presidential election on Sunday October 25, voting on issues such as public safety, affordability and corruption, genocide is also on the ballot.
On the one hand, “left-wing organizations today are more aware that Palestine has been turned by Israel—a military enclave of Imperialism—into a global laboratory, where technologies of death are tested and subsequently sold to the rest of the world,” said Soraya Misleh, a Palestinian-Brazilian journalist whose father, Abder Raouf Misleh, was expelled from Palestine during the Nakba.
Simultaneously, Israel has become an exemplar of how to tackle alleged terrorism threats, unbridled by international law. From Nasry Asfura in Honduras to Abelardo de la Espriella in Colombia, Latin America has ushered in a succession of iron-fisted presidents pledging allegiance to the US hegemony while ramping up trade, diplomacy and security coordination with Israel – and Brazil could be next.
Will it be Lula, a persona non grata in Israel who fervently condemns the genocide in Gaza or Bolsonaro, a Christian Zionist who plans to ramp up relations with the apartheid state if elected?
The choice is stark. That is why it is “natural” to see Palestinian flags raised by the left and Israeli flags by the far right, Misleh told Mondoweiss, adding that the display of Israeli flags in Brazil “leaves no doubt as to just how racist, subservient to foreign interests, and violent the far right is.”
Opposing ideologies
Flávio Bolsonaro is the mirror image of his father, former president and self-professed Israel lover, Jair Bolsonaro. He has plainly affirmed that, under his leadership, Brazil “will always defend the right of Israel to survive, the right of Israel to fight for its territory, and to defend its people.”
During a visit to the West Bank in January, he confirmed “full support” for Israeli settlers in the West Bank and pledged to relocate the Brazilian embassy from Tel Aviv to Jerusalem. Following a slim victory in the first round of the election on October 5, Bolsonaro even received premature congratulations from Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.
Bolsonaro’s policies are expected to mirror those of Argentina’s chainsaw-wielding Javier Milei, El Salvador’s millennial dictator Nayib Bukele, and U.S. President Donald Trump, whose approach to interventionism in the Americas has been dubbed the “Donroe Doctrine”. Unsurprisingly, he also plans to join Trump’s Shield of the Americas, a so-called “counter-cartel coalition”, promising to revive a “mano dura” approach to law enforcement, from building maximum-security prisons to designating organized crime groups as narco-terrorists.
This shared enemy narrative also extends to Israel, with whom he has described a sense of “unity” among nations “that want to combat organized crime and terrorism.”
Lula, on the other hand, recalled the Brazilian ambassador to Israel in February 2024 and, speaking at the African Union Summit a few months later, compared Israel’s genocide in Gaza to the Holocaust. In response, Netanyahu called him a “virulent antisemite” and, days later, Foreign Minister Israel Katz declared him a “persona non grata.”
Brazil also joined South Africa’s case against Israel at the International Court of Justice in September 2025 and Lula has accused Israel of genocide on multiple occasions, although he has specifically condemned the Netanyahu government rather than the Zionist project itself.
Trade and contracts
Beyond the rhetoric, under Lula’s leadership, Brazil has taken significant strides towards breaking material ties with Israel. In May 2024, Defense Minister José Múcio Monteiro postponed the signing of a $145 million contract with Elbit Systems for the purchase of 36 armored howitzers. Arms exports to Israel were suspended one year later and, according to official data from the National Petroleum Agency and the Ministry of Development, Industry, Trade and Services, Brazil registered zero direct oil exports to Israel in 2025 despite having been its fifth largest supplier between October 2023 and July 2024.
Yet Lula’s government has fallen short of implementing a full arms embargo and, as a signatory of the Mercosur-Israel Free Trade Agreement (FTA) since December 2007, Brazil has continued to trade with Israel in various sectors. According to Brazil’s official foreign trade statistics, the import of Israeli fertilizers ranked higher than any other product, valued at over $500 billion in 2025 – approximately one third of Israel’s total global exports in this sector.
These products constitute a core component of Israel’s agribusiness sector, which, as UN Special Rapporteur Francesca Albanese reported, “has thrived on Israel-led extractivism and land-grabbing – producing goods and technologies serving Israeli settler-colonial interests, expanding market dominance and attracting global investment – while erasing Palestinian food systems and accelerating displacement.”
Lula’s opponent, however, has proposed expanding relations with Israel, pinpointing the importance of “cooperation in the technological sphere” and suggesting “massive historic agreements – unprecedented in scale.”
Bolsonaro has also promised to sign the Isaac Accords, a series of agreements initiated by Israel and Argentina to increase cooperation in trade, technology and counterterrorism. So far, the initiative has focused mainly on Costa Rica, Panama, and Uruguay, three countries “primed for enhanced cooperation with Israel”. However, in June, Bolsonaro joined 11 other Latin American legislators at a conference in Buenos Aires where they signed a resolution supporting the expansion of the Accords.
If Lula is reelected, “we will continue to demand a complete rupture of economic, military, and diplomatic relations with Israel,” Misleh told Mondoweiss. But Flávio Bolsonaro’s plan to intensify agreements with Israel represents a quantifiably greater threat: “the criminalization and silencing of voices for Palestine in Brazil is set to intensify, amid threats to democratic freedoms. With him, things could get worse. Much worse,” she said.
Christian Zionism in Brazil
Although functionally pragmatic, the rhetoric underpinning the Isaac Accords is rooted in the aforementioned shared-enemy narrative. Even the reference to “Isaac” is part of a manufactured paradigm in which the conflict between Israelis and Palestinians represents a feud between Isaac and Ishmael, Abraham’s sons.
“The issue of Christian Zionism in Brazil has been linked to political developments for much longer than in other countries in the region,” said Nicolás Panotto, an Argentine theologian based in Chile. Under Bolsonaro Sr., “Christian Zionism served as a bridge, what some might call a ‘strategic ecumenism’ between Catholics and evangelicals, to support and promote the far-right in Brazil,” he told Mondoweiss. Nowadays, “there is clearly a more evangelical vision or perspective.” After all, evangelicals constitute approximately 26.9% of the electorate, including Bolsonaro Jr. himself. It is “precisely because I am an evangelical” that relations between Brazil and Israel will improve, he has said.
In evangelical spaces, Misleh told Mondoweiss, it is common to see Israeli flags and symbols: “an instrumentalization of faith that fuels a false religious rhetoric in support of a colonial, supremacist political project,” she said. The Temple of Solomon in São Paulo, for instance, built by the Universal Church of the Kingdom of God in 2014, features limestone—valued at $8 million—imported directly from Jerusalem.
This attempt to manufacture loyalty to Israel is spearheaded by megachurches, parachurches, U.S. missionaries, and, of course, the Evangelical Caucus, a powerful, cross-party group of protestant and evangelical lawmakers in the Brazilian National Congress. After all, “faith-based diplomacy is what has helped nations move their embassies to Jerusalem and stand up against antisemitism,” said Bolsonaro Jr. at the Isaac Accords conference in June.
“He is attempting to consolidate his standing within the evangelical camp in a much more targeted way than his father, who didn’t engage in the same kind of symbolic gestures, such as getting baptized in Jerusalem,” Panotto told Mondoweiss.
And it’s blatantly strategic. During a speech at the Assemblies of God, Brazil’s largest Pentecostal denomination, he even described the current political divide in Brazil as “a spiritual war” in which the left “uses the devil’s weapons.”
