Taiwan plans to build rare earths plant
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
16:43:37 UTC
01:43:37 KST

The Industrial Technology Research Institute (ITRI) plans to build a rare-earth demonstration plant that could meet half the nation’s needs by the end of 2030, as Chinese export controls heighten concerns over industrial supply chains, the institute president said.
In the planning stage, the facility aims to produce 500 tonnes of rare earths annually, ITRI president Chang Pei-zen (張培仁) said in a recent interview.
Construction is targeted for completion by the end of 2028, followed by work to refine production processes and reach the planned output.
Photo: Reuters
The ITRI intends to build the plant in an industrial park to facilitate its eventual transfer to a private company. Funding would need to be budgeted by the National Science and Technology Council, while commercial arrangements, including possible government price guarantees for investors, remain under discussion, Chang said.
Taiwan’s demand for rare earths is relatively small, but the materials are indispensable, he said, adding that the Ministry of Economic Affairs hopes to develop a domestic supply chain and expand production capacity to address concerns about export restrictions.
China’s controls have highlighted risks extending beyond the supply of raw materials to components used in industrial equipment.
Reuters on Thursday reported that Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co (TSMC, 台積電) was exploring alternatives to rare earth components in factory equipment to reduce the risk of disruptions at its advanced chip plants.
TSMC did not comment.
Rare earth magnets are used in motors that move parts in industrial machinery, including equipment in highly automated semiconductor factories, Reuters said.
Supply restrictions could affect manufacturers even when rare earths are not incorporated directly into their finished products.
The ITRI already operates an experimental rare earth production line, but its annual output is only about 5 tonnes, Chang said.
The proposed plant’s target would represent a 100-fold increase.
Equipment at ITRI’s headquarters in Hsinchu County handles rare earth separation and conversion into metals, while some equipment for making high-end magnets is at its Southern Region Campus in Tainan, Chang said.
Rare earth processing is technically challenging, as different elements have very similar properties, making them difficult to separate, he said.
Developing and fine-tuning the separation process can involve hundreds or even thousands of stages and requires substantial experience, Chang said.
The institute aims to refine its production processes by the end of 2030 as it works toward the annual output target. Alongside the technical work, further discussions will be needed on how to provide prospective private investors with sufficient assurances to participate, he said.

Formosa, Taiwan, weight of names
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
16:43:36 UTC
01:43:36 KST

Taiwan heads to the polls next month for local elections. Beneath the campaign ads lies a deeper question: What do we call this place and who gets to decide?
In the pages of the Oxford English Dictionary (OED), that question has been playing out across three centuries. The entries for “Formosa” and “Taiwan” chart an island’s journey from colonial fantasy to self-named reality.
Names are rarely neutral; they are the first act of possession. Nowhere is this more evident than in the OED, where the two entries serve as a linguistic seismograph for one of the world’s most enduring geopolitical fault lines. To read their historical quotations is to watch an island shed the skin of colonial romance and assume the complex, contested identity of a modern nation.
“Formosa” entered the English lexicon not as a place, but as a compliment. In the 1382 Wycliffite Bible, the term appears in the Latin phrase formosa mea (“my beautiful one”), a purely adjectival endearment. Centuries passed before the adjective hardened into a proper noun and when it finally did, it was through the ledger books of the empire.
By 1704, European trading manifests listed “sugar of Formosa” alongside “Japanese silver” and “China tea.” The West knew the island not as a society, but as a commodity. Even its natural endowments were inventoried for extraction: an 1889 entry priced Formosa camphor in the Hong Kong market, while a 1921 botanical report appraised the “crapy appearance” of Formosa oolong teas.
For 300 years, the island existed in the English language as a picturesque backdrop for trade, its indigenous inhabitants reduced to curiosities who made “a drink as strong and intoxicative as sack, out of rice.”
The lexicon shifted violently in the mid-20th century. After 1949, “Formosa” ceased to be a botanical footnote and became a Cold War battleground. The OED’s quotations from that era read like dispatches from the front lines of containment.
A 1950 Baltimore Sun article framed the island as “the last refuge of the Nationalists,” and a 1959 Economist piece tallied “United States aero-naval strength in the Formosa Strait.”
The name had become a geopolitical signifier, a synonym for the free world’s precarious foothold in Asia. Yet even as US admirals drew battle lines, the island’s own identity was quietly evolving.
The dictionary records the moment of transition with telling brevity. A 1972 entry in the Shooting Times carries the parenthetical “Taiwan to most, these days,” an author’s aside that the OED preserved, and one that quietly concedes the old colonial name was becoming an anachronism.
That was not merely a semantic shift; it was a reclamation. In that single parenthetical note, the dictionary captured the slow erosion of imperial nomenclature and the stubborn persistence of local identity.
The “Taiwan” entry, spanning 1958 to 2019, charts the emergence of a sovereign actor. Early citations still bear the scars of diplomatic isolation. A 1979 Time article lamented “disgruntlement and protest over derecognition,” but the quotations quickly pivoted to agency. Taiwan was no longer a refuge or a strait; it was a “silicon island,” an “Asian wunderkind” that “out-traded” its neighbors.
A 1976 Newsweek piece captured a peculiar moment of cultural victory, noting the embarrassment of US teams outslugged by Taiwan’s little league players, baseball being, after all, “as American as apple pie.” By 2000, the New York Times could describe a government committed to making Taiwan a “green silicon island,” a vision of technological sovereignty that would have been unintelligible to the camphor merchants of 1889.
Yet the OED also records the persistent friction of this self-naming. The newest source in its files is no longer a newspaper, but a tweet. A 2019 user observed: “If I were located in the U.S., I would likely be labeled a sinophobe because of my support for Taiwan,” proof that the name remains a political act, dangerous even in digital discourse.
The island’s identity is still negotiated in the space between Beijing’s sovereignty claims and Washington’s strategic ambiguity.
Even the word “Taiwanese” carries weight. In 1969, the Times noted that “63 percent of local government officials are natives of Taiwan,” a statistic that was then, and remains now, anything but neutral.
What the dictionary cannot resolve is the tension between the two names. “Formosa” carries the burden of the external gaze, colonial, romantic, reductive. It is the name given by sailors and merchants who saw beauty and profit, but not people. “Taiwan” is the name claimed by those who lived there, a word that encompasses baseball teams and semiconductor fabs, democratic protests and diplomatic slights.
The OED, in its admirable neutrality, simply records both. It offers no judgement on which name is correct, only evidence of how language bends under the pressure of history.
The dictionary, in the end, is not an arbiter of identity, but a mirror. It shows us that names are never merely descriptive; they are arguments dressed as labels. Formosa speaks of the colonial gaze; Taiwan speaks of a people’s insistence on being called by their own name. The dictionary’s record does not settle the matter. It merely acknowledges that Taiwan’s name, like its history, refuses to stand still.
For this nation, caught between history’s long shadow and the urgencies of the present, the argument is far from over.
Hugo Tseng has a doctorate in linguistics, and is a lexicographer and former chair of the Soochow University English Department.

The danger behind Trump’s new softness toward Beijing is a potential US-China bargain that undermines Taiwan’s core interests. The good guys notch a victory in the AI cybersecurity age
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
16:43:33 UTC
01:43:33 KST

The headlines were unremarkable. Researchers had found a way to weaponize two vulnerabilities in PHP, a programming language used for Web sites and apps, and companies were being urged on Wednesday to install a patch. A smattering of Web sites and services were taken offline while it was installed.
The US said it was looking into government systems and expediting mitigations. The media barely blinked.
However, like a thwarted terror attack, or the Year 2000 problem, the general feeling of a nothingburger can disguise the behind-the-scenes heroics that have — so far — averted catastrophe. That is the case here: an incident that should be considered the most significant victory for the good guys so far in the new artificial intelligence (AI)-cybersecurity age, a boon for the cybersecurity industry eager to prove it is more valuable than ever.
Illustration: Constance Chou
The vulnerabilities — named PHP2Shell — stood to affect about “70 percent of all Web sites in the world,” said Wiz, a cybersecurity firm owned by Google. These deep, underlying flaws, which had existed for more than a decade, allowed an attacker to execute code remotely — like handing a set of keys to an outsider to do and see almost anything it wanted.
“These findings rank among the most severe vulnerabilities discovered in PHP, and arguably in software history,” Wiz wrote.
An abundance of caution has gone global. Web sites belonging to several European governments and local authorities went offline. In the UK, the BBC took parts of its Web site down for maintenance. A US-based human resources company briefly went offline. Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi urged companies to apply the patch quickly. Yet so far, that was all this has amounted to: an abundance of caution.
PHP2Shell was discovered in August with the help of “frontier” AI models, the term given to the cutting edge of what was coming out of the leading labs, from OpenAI to Google. Wiz found the vulnerability in August. So, separately, did Calif, another cybersecurity firm, working with OpenAI as part of a coordinated effort called Patch the Planet, which was launched in the wake of fear around how AI could supercharge the capabilities of cybercriminals and rogue states.
To be clear, this was a far more complex task than simply asking the AI model to find a problem. Rather, this was a concert of model and human specialists, allowing what Wiz described as “an exceptionally complex chain of steps, at the edge of what human researchers could practically achieve.”
A single researcher in Wiz’s team handled in a week what would have taken a “world-class” team months, the firm said.
With the flaws discovered, the mitigation effort kicked in behind closed doors. The team that administers PHP — it is an open-source language — began developing its fix. Top Internet infrastructure firms such as Amazon Web Services and Cloudflare were notified.
The vulnerabilities (and the solution) were made public on Wednesday, with a patch released in the morning — a day ahead of schedule, because some details had been leaked. OpenAI put out a “skill” for its Codex platform that helps companies quickly determine which updates are needed.
Now that the exploit has been made public, hackers will be identifying those weak spots, too, and some have already done so.
Cloudflare chief technology officier Dane Knecht said the company had, before the patch was made available, seen “early attacks emerging” against its clients and was offering them stopgap measures until the weakness had been patched. These attacks are nothing compared with what might have happened had these vulnerabilities been discovered by bad actors first.
The incident underscores the growing importance of specialized cybersecurity firms in the AI age. It was only in February that the stocks of leading security companies such as Cloudflare and Crowdstrike took a bath over investor fears that AI lab Anthropic was going to steal their business. What nonsense that seems today, with the opposite proving true. The new paradigm of security threats has made cybersecurity expertise more valuable, so it is no surprise that Cloudflare shares rose about 7 percent on the news, up 76 percent since that February shock. Crowdstrike is up 146 percent in that time.
Of course, the AI firms are helping defend against a risk they helped create, but that cat is out of the bag now — the same technology that can discover new drugs or write complex code can be used to hack computers. The only course of action is to deal with it. This incident should provide encouragement. The takeaway is that a collaboration between security researchers and frontier AI labs gave the world a head start against a serious threat. These collaborative efforts must continue and be expanded.
We are not out of the woods yet. As ever in cybersecurity, the onus is still on security teams to act. However, these teams do so in full possession of the facts, with a patch ready to go, and in a state of relative calm thanks to trusted sources offering well-considered remedies. The fact that none of this made it to the front pages or nightly news bulletins counts as a battle won in what would be a never-ending war.
Dave Lee is Bloomberg Opinion’s US technology columnist. He was previously a correspondent for the Financial Times and BBC News. This column reflects the personal views of the author and does not necessarily reflect the opinion of the editorial board or Bloomberg LP and its owners.

Apple’s iPhone Duo hits stores with supply short, demand high
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
16:43:32 UTC
01:43:32 KST

Apple Inc quickly sold out of its limited in-store inventory for the new iPhone Duo, underscoring the strong demand for a foldable device that starts at nearly US$2,000.
The phone went on sale on Friday, bringing back the once-familiar sight of people lining up overnight to get their hands on it first. Marking the company’s most radical reinvention in the iPhone’s nearly two-decade history, the Duo is a major bet that Apple can establish itself in a category that is remained a niche so far.
Apple’s latest gadget packed stores from New York to Beijing and Singapore. The early turnout featured customers collecting their preorders, some trying their luck to secure limited inventory for walk-in purchases, and resellers hoping to flip the devices for a higher price.
Photo: Bloomberg
In Singapore, a few hundred people stood in line early Friday, including a family of seven from Myanmar who had camped out overnight.
“This is the first true innovation Apple have had in years,” said Peter Ingram, a chief technology officer visiting from London, who plans to buy it upon his return to the UK. “It is expensive. But I tried it out, played with it in the store. It’s incredible how it’s got no crease.”
In the US, Apple stores received about 50 to 200-plus Duo units per location, and they went fast. A store in Los Angeles had no units left for people who arrived after about 6:30am. The 256-gigabyte star white model, priced at US$1,999, was popular with shoppers.
Large crowds on launch day have mostly dissipated in the past few years after Apple, retailers and wireless carriers began maintaining enough inventory to fulfill most orders through home delivery or appointment-based store pickups. However, the company’s first foldable device arrived in much more limited supply.
Consumers placing new orders for the Duo on Apple’s Web site are being offered delivery at the end of January, though some have seen their shipping estimates move up to as soon as next month or December. The delays mark some of the lengthiest for a new Apple product in the company’s modern era.
Shoppers at the Domain Northside Apple Store in Austin were greeted by new chief executive officer John Ternus, who took the helm last month. At the Fifth Avenue location in New York, the line was already stretching multiple blocks at about 5am, three hours before doors opened to iPhone Duo customers. The launch there was marked by Apple’s senior vice president of marketing Greg Joswiak, and vice president of retail stores Vanessa Trigub.
At the Apple Store in Lawrence Township, New Jersey, about 64km outside Philadelphia, the 256 and 512-gigabyte configurations sold out within the first half hour, leaving the pricier 1 and 2-terabyte (TB) models.
Victor Osorio, a shopper at that location, said even though foldables are not new, “Apple always does something different and adds extra spice to it. I’m not nervous about the form factor but I am about the hinge. I don’t want it to get in the way but it looks OK so far.” Osorio arrived early with his partner, Victoria, who also purchased the Duo and said she was intrigued by the device’s multitasking capabilities.
At the same location, Naveed Abubacker said he trades in his iPhone every year. “Foldable technology has been around for a while and Apple is late to the gate but I’m ready for it,” he said. “If it doesn’t work out for me, I’ll return it.”
In China, Shanghai and Beijing saw a moderate turnout, with most Duo buyers already loyal Apple customers who said they were excited to try out the new design. Many had to register in advance to secure their unit.
“It will take some getting used to,” Andy Shen said at Apple’s Sanlitun store in Beijing. “I chose the Duo mainly because it opens up to a bigger screen to enable better experience with videos, though its other functions are not measuring up to earlier generations, like the camera.”
As one of the most expensive mainstream smartphones ever sold, the Duo had raised questions about just how much demand there would be. Most of the shoppers in Beijing and Singapore looked past the high price and focused on the promise of a truly new Apple product after many years of iterative updates.
The iPhone lineup is Apple’s largest moneymaker, generating about half of the company’s revenue. And the Duo is the biggest single design change in the device’s nearly history. Although the company was not first to market with a foldable phone, it looks to gain an edge with a more polished product built for Apple fans.
Rather than a repeat of the lackluster debut of the Vision Pro headset nearly three years ago, the Duo’s launch is shaping up to be a throwback to the iPhone introductions of old — when demand far outstripped supply. That is the case even with device prices reaching as high as US$3,199 for models with 2TB of storage.
Although the Duo’s cost sets a record for a mass-market smartphone, Apple’s competitors such as Samsung Electronics Co, Xiaomi Corp and Oppo have been raising prices as well. Shortages of memory chips and other components have made consumer electronics more expensive across the board.
The new phones from Apple are difficult to produce because of their advanced hinge and new display technology. They are also only built in a limited number of facilities in China. Apple expanded production in the past few years for its traditional iPhones, including to India, which has helped with supply.
Apple reports its quarterly earnings results on Nov. 2, but those would not include sales of the Duo because the period concluded at the end of last month. It would reflect early sales of iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max models, which debuted on Sept. 18.
Other new versions, such as the entry-level iPhone or the updated Air, would not go on sale until next year, Bloomberg News reported. That marks a change in the company’s usual release schedule, a move meant to help spread out revenue across the year.

WUFI calls for re-examination of Retrocession Day
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
16:43:31 UTC
01:43:31 KST

Oct. 25 should not only serve as a commemorative day for Chinese regimes, but also a day for Taiwanese to shatter the “two Chinas” lie and reaffirm their right to self-determination, the World United Formosans for Independence (WUFI) said yesterday.
On Oct. 25, 1945, the Republic of China (ROC) accepted Japan’s surrender in Taiwan and called the day “Taiwan Retrocession Day,” claiming that Taiwan was returned to China, it said.
On Oct. 25, 1971, the UN General Assembly passed Resolution 2785 which states that the People’s Republic of China (PRC) is the only legitimate representative of China at the UN, it said.
Photo: Screen grab from World United Formosans for Independence’s Facebook page
The two Chinese regimes use the events as basis for claims of sovereignty over Taiwan, WUFI said.
A military surrender and administrative takeover does not equate to a transfer of sovereignty, it said.
The San Francisco treaty, signed in 1951, states that the Japanese government renounces sovereignty over Taiwan and Penghu, but does not specify to whom that sovereignty was to be transferred, it said.
The Treaty of Peace between the Republic of China and Japan, commonly known as the Treaty of Taipei, signed in 1952, also contained no explicit clause transferring sovereignty over Taiwan to the ROC, WUFI said.
The Chinese Nationalist Party (KMT) government portrayed the post-World War II takeover as a “retrocession,” using Chinese nationalism to supplant the right of the Taiwanese to determine their own future, it said.
The 228 Incident, the White Terror era and the decades of martial law showed that being taken over by another regime did not equate to freedom for the people, it added.
UN Resolution 2758 addressed the issue of China’s representation at the UN, but it did not mention Taiwan, it said, adding that the resolution does not state that Taiwan is part of the PRC.
The European Parliament in 2024 passed a resolution stating that UN Resolution 2758 “takes no position on Taiwan” and does not have any bearing on Taiwan’s participation in the UN or other international organizations, it said.
The PRC has never governed Taiwan, yet it used its right to represent China to claim sovereignty over Taiwan and block the nation’s international participation, WUFI said.
The two Chinese regimes have competed over which one represents China, and share the belief that Taiwan belongs to China and that Taiwanese have no right to determine the nation’s future, it said.
That is a historical predicament Taiwan must overcome, it added.
Taiwan is neither territory that can be inherited as a byproduct of the two Chinese regimes’ struggle for representation nor property whose fate can be arbitrarily determined by either of them, it said.
Retrocession Day should be re-examined, WUFI said.
The organization called for the rejection of Beijing’s distortion of UN Resolution 2758, efforts to secure Taiwan’s right to participate internationally, and constitutional reform and normalization of the nation through peaceful, democratic means and self-determination.
Administrative takeover is not retrocession and representing China does not mean owning Taiwan, it said, adding that the nation’s future should be decided by Taiwanese.

There is no escaping tech tycoon villains (at the movies)
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
16:43:31 UTC
01:43:31 KST

There is a striking moment near the end of Musk, a new documentary by Oscar-winning filmmaker Alex Gibney, when the world’s richest man is asked why he considers it important to develop X into what he calls a global platform for collective consciousness.
“I guess ...” Elon Musk replies to his questioner, the billionaire Indian entrepreneur Nikhil Kamath, before his voice trails off. There is a pause of several seconds in which neither man says anything. Eventually, after a couple of false starts, Musk settles on: “To increase our understanding of the universe.”
The exchange — originally broadcast as part of Kamath’s People by WTF podcast in November last year — stands out because it follows more than three and a half hours of a film in which Musk is rarely short of words or solutions. We see his early successes during the dot-com boom, followed by his stewardship of Tesla Inc and SpaceX, the acquisition of Twitter and, ultimately, his alliance with US President Donald Trump.
Photo: AFP
At every step, Gibney depicts Musk as relentlessly accumulating money and power, shrugging off a string of controversies — business and personal — along the way. The section on the Department of Government Efficiency, the Trump administration initiative ostensibly created to identify and cut waste, is especially troubling to watch, particularly when it focuses on cuts to the US Agency for International Development and their impact on projects in Africa. However, when asked to articulate his deeper purpose, the tycoon is lost for words.
Musk represents a prominent example of a shift in contemporary cinema: While multibillionaire tech tycoons have made for convenient villains in the past, recent portrayals are more frequent and less ambivalent. Gibney, 72 — a prolific filmmaker who won the 2007 Academy Award for best documentary feature for Taxi to the Dark Side about abuse by US soldiers — paints a picture of ruthlessness, cynicism and a chronic lack of regulatory oversight. Musk is designed to leave the viewer feeling bleak about the world. As Gibney asks by way of a mission statement: “How could Musk assume so much power, and why had we given it to him?”
That question, to which there is no straightforward answer, speaks to a growing sense of public discomfort with the way superrich tech leaders and their companies have come to dominate the corporate, political and media landscape — as well as our personal lives. The release of Musk came just months after its subject became the world’s first trillionaire following SpaceX’s record-breaking initial public offering, an unheard-of level of wealth that is helping to fund Republican campaigns ahead of the Nov. 3 midterm elections. According to a Pew survey conducted last year, more than half of Americans have an unfavorable view of Musk, while two-thirds had a negative perception of Meta Platforms Inc chief executive officer Mark Zuckerberg.
Another version of Elon Musk appears in Artificial which screened at this month’s London Film Festival ahead of its release this winter. The film, directed by Luca Guadagnino, charts the early years of OpenAI, which Musk co-founded in 2015. Musk left the company in 2018 and has tried unsuccessfully to sue its present incarnation, allowing writer Simon Rich to make the film version played by Ike Barinholtz a form of comic relief — all facial tics and self-importance — rather than anything more sinister.
The role of tech tycoon villain instead goes to Andrew Garfield, who plays OpenAI CEO Sam Altman. The film portrays him as the ultra-ambitious and unscrupulous driving force behind the company that gave us ChatGPT, with the movie’s conscience represented by co-founder and chief scientist Ilya Sutskever (played by Yura Borisov — best known as the kind-hearted henchman in Anora).
Artificial goes on to tell the story of Altman and Sutskever’s eventual falling-out, with Altman fired and swiftly reinstated with the support of Microsoft Corp, OpenAI’s main investor. Garfield plays Altman as increasingly cold and manipulative, swatting aside any concerns about AI safety and the people who get in his way. “I didn’t invent teen suicide!” he yells at one fellow executive, when warned of ChatGPT’s darker potential.
Facebook founder Zuckerberg was the subject of David Fincher’s acclaimed 2010 movie The Social Network and it feels apt that writer Aaron Sorkin should return with a de facto sequel some 16 years later.
In the original movie, the action revolves around a litigation against Zuckerberg during Facebook’s early years. In this fall’s The Social Reckoning he is now well-established — and it is Wall Street Journal reporter Jeff Horwitz (Jeremy Allen White) and Facebook employee-turned-whistleblower Frances Haugen (Mikey Madison) who are out to get him.
The story shows how the duo worked together on Horwitz’s award-winning reporting on Facebook and its algorithm in 2021, with a particular focus on how users can become radicalized and pushed toward extremist groups.
The rather unsubtle point of The Social Reckoning is that Facebook and Zuckerberg are terrible, while journalists and whistleblowers are good. It was not as binary when Sorkin was writing The Social Network, where the Facebook founder could be seen as a misfit simply trying to get his own back on the alpha males and women he believed looked down on him.
Some might see Facebook as a product of the past, with the stakes around the technology developed by OpenAI and rival Anthropic PBC much higher. The drunk woman who delivers a racist diatribe at police officers at the start of The Social Reckoning — radicalized by Facebook, Haugen deduces — might seem trivial compared with the potential for AI to overpower humanity, as is threatened in Artificial.
The power of technology to turn people against each other, only for us all to be overpowered by robots, drives the fear coursing through all these films. “We’ll have to build a bunker,” Geoffrey Hinton (Mark Rylance), Sutskever’s early mentor, warns him early in Artificial. “And hide from the Terminator.”

Atypical worker numbers decline
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
16:43:29 UTC
01:43:29 KST

The proportion of atypical workers compared with overall employment in Taiwan this year fell to a 14-year low, the Directorate-General of Budget, Accounting and Statistics (DGBAS) said on Friday.
Taiwan this year had 793,000 atypical workers — part-time workers and those on temporary and “dispatch” contracts — the DGBAS said, citing a survey conducted in May.
That was 6,000, or 0.67 percent, less than the number last year, it said.
Photo: CNA
Atypical workers accounted for 6.82 percent of the total, who numbered 11.63 million, down by 1,000 from October last year, it said, adding that the ratio was the lowest since 2013.
Census Department Deputy Director Tan Wen-ling (譚文玲) said the decline in the proportion of atypical workers reflected a lower number of temporary and “dispatch” jobs, although the number of part-time workers increased.
Atypical jobs have been perceived as being done by economically disadvantaged people, but the latest survey found that 34.89 percent of atypical workers took on such jobs because of the “special characteristics of the job category,” Tan said, adding that 22.97 percent “preferred this type of employment pattern over others.”
Among atypical workers, 58,000 — or 7.33 percent, wanted a full-time job, down 1.09 percentage points from a year earlier, the survey showed.
The labor participation rate of women aged 15 or older was 52.33 percent, up 1.67 percentage points from 10 years earlier, it showed.
The labor participation ratio among married women aged 15 to 49 was 79.33 percent this year, up 9.95 percentage points from a decade earlier, it showed.
Within that group, those without children had a labor participation rate of 85.44 percent, up 7.03 percentage points from 10 years earlier, while those with children had a labor participation rate of 78.19 percent, up 9.94 percentage points, the survey showed.

Photo: AP
The streets in the area were deserted of people and cars other than a pair of Israeli military vehicles, with an Israeli flag draped on a house taken over by troops.
Higazi Shawer al-Tamimi, 70, a shopkeeper who sells live chickens and feed, and plays a leadership role in the neighborhood, said the army woke him up at 1am and told him and other residents to leave.

“He wants to win it with the blood of the Palestinian people,” he said. “But we won’t go anywhere.”

The governor said 150 families had been affected, while Hebron Mayor Youssef al-Jaabari and local activist Issa Amro put the figure at 250.
“We will find them shelter and provide these people with all the help they need,” the mayor said.

It said the operation would last several days, in line with similar army actions after previous attacks.
However, Netanyahu suggested that bigger action was coming. Asked if he agreed on destroying the Palestinian Authority, Netanyahu, Israel’s longest-serving prime minister, said that he has rejected pressure from three US presidents to work to establish a Palestinian state.
“I will act to neutralize that threat by means I think are better left unspecified right now,” Netanyahu said of the Palestinian Authority in an interview with i24News conducted late on Friday.
There is no evidence that the Palestinian Authority had any involvement in Friday’s attack.

“There is a very big surprise for the Palestinian Authority as well.”

Music workshop praised
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
16:43:24 UTC
01:43:24 KST

The K-12 Education Administration and the Taipei Music Center recently held their sixth songwriting workshop for elementary and junior-high school teachers, introducing how to use artificial intelligence (AI) tools to create pop music, with the aim of bringing songwriting into schools and fostering students’ musical creativity.
Thirty teachers participated in the two-day, 11-hour workshop, learning songwriting techniques they could take back to the classroom to encourage students to explore music and confidently express themselves, K-12 Education Administration official Yeh Hsin-tsun (葉信村) said.
Pop music is closely linked to students’ daily lives and the program helps cultivate the next generation of musical talent, Yeh said.
Photo: Reuters
Educators specializing in a range of subjects, including music, visual arts, performing arts and multimedia music, participated in the program, the Ministry of Education said in a statement on Friday.
The curriculum covered songwriting, using AI tools and music composition so teachers could experience producing a song, the ministry said.
The workshop’s lead instructor was Golden Melody Award-winning music producer Ken Chou (周岳澄), who guided each group of teachers to complete an original song within two days, it said.
The first day introduced AI tools, and artist and repertoire plans, leading teachers to analyze the music industry’s requirements for songs, and understand genres and their creative directions, the statement said.
Teachers later broke into groups to draft song proposals, it said.
On the second day, they analyzed musical styles and beats, found or generated backing tracks and worked with professional songwriters to complete their songs and perform them on stage, it said.
Many high-school music teachers have backgrounds in classical music and are less familiar with the pop music industry, said Huang Mei-chen (黃美甄), executive secretary of the K-12 Education Administration’s Arts and Life Subject Center for Senior High Schools.
The partnership with the Taipei Music Center has helped bring industry experience into the classroom, and given teachers the confidence to teach pop music and songwriting techniques, Huang said.
Taipei Music Center chairman Eric Liang (梁序倫) said that efforts to cultivate musical talent should not focus solely on the music industry, but should take root in schools to make music composition more accessible to students.
The workshop emphasized the importance of creative judgement in the AI era, the ministry said.
While introducing AI tools, it encouraged teachers to consider a song’s content, target audience, style and mood so they could understand what makes music likable, it said.
As AI makes music production more accessible, it is important to develop aesthetic judgement, decisionmaking skills and originality, so that AI serves as an assistant rather than replacing human creativity, the ministry said, quoting teachers who attended the workshop.

A generational reckoning on the streets of Paris
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
16:43:22 UTC
01:43:22 KST

After weeks of mounting tension on the streets of Paris, my wife and I decided to take our six-year-old daughter and leave town during Saturday’s protests. When the main demonstration assembled at 2pm at the Place de la Republique, we were hiking in the forests southeast of Paris near Fontainebleau, once an autumnal retreat and hunting ground for French kings.
After taking the train back and walking to the Metro, we caught a whiff of tear gas in the air. The metro stop by our apartment was closed, so we got off at a nearby station, where we found a crowd of teenagers huddled below the exit stairway, handing out COVID-19 pandemic-era face masks. We grabbed one for each of us, just before a cloud of tear gas sent us all scrambling back down the stairs toward the train, our eyes burning.
There was no escaping the protests, which erupted in France’s high schools late last month. Many young people here, like their peers around the world, lack hope for the future. Burdened by austerity and financial pressures, their schools are deteriorating. Some teachers, overwhelmed by poor working conditions, are absent and not replaced. This summer was also the hottest in France since records began in 1900. The young know that more summers like it, or worse, lie ahead, and they see the adults in charge doing little about it.
Not long after the student protests began, various political factions — some acting in good faith, and some not — tried to attach themselves to the movement, but despite the political jockeying, the students remain at its heart.
Street protests in France are a national ritual. In 2023, large demonstrations erupted when French President Emmanuel Macron announced a plan to raise the legal retirement age from 62 to 64. The reform became law, and the protests subsided. Its central age-related measures were later suspended until 2028.
This time, no similar end is in sight. The French government can withdraw a bill from consideration or rewrite it to secure its passage, but governments today seem incapable of legislating into existence the future young people want and deserve.
With next year’s presidential election looming and the far-right surging in opinion polls, some people I have spoken to predict that the protests would boost far-left forces. Either way, the center is not holding, and I have a difficult time finding anyone here who thinks it deserves to, or even hopes it will.
Where does this leave France? For now, the students’ demands are mostly inchoate. Many older protesters focused on the rising cost of living, echoing the language of “affordability” heard elsewhere. The day after the protests, headlines dwelled on who was responsible for the violence. However, I suspect that the most significant issue might be generational. No country can have a decent future if its youth see none for themselves.
Perhaps one day, the protests would be seen as a step toward a confrontation between the claims of the old and the prospects of the young. Politics has long been organized along lines of class, national belonging, religion or identity. Might age become politics’ defining fault line? If so, we will need to think harder about how power and opportunity are distributed across generations.
Youth politics is hardly new. The living veterans of the 1968 Paris barricades are all pensioners now. Today, pension-related contributions account for about one-third of the French Ministry of National Education’s budget. That partly reflects how the ministry accounts for pension costs, but the figure is nonetheless revealing.
As public debt mounts, and concerns over government borrowing grow, there is much talk about whether France can still afford its welfare state. However, the more important question is what kind of welfare state it wants, and what its priorities should be. How can governments protect people in old age — one of the great achievements of 20th-century democracy — while giving the young a chance at a decent future?
These questions extend far beyond any real or imagined zero-sum tradeoff between pension rights and education spending. At stake is the quality of education, but also our response to global warming and the rise of artificial intelligence.
Older generations are politically formidable. They vote in large numbers and, as France’s population ages, carry ever greater electoral weight. Most high-school students, by contrast, are not old enough to vote.
Older generations also occupy many of the offices through which formal power is exercised. So far, the students themselves have not directed their demands explicitly against older generations, but if these protests are to have lasting significance, it would be because they marked the rumblings of a new politics in which young people demand a greater say over the conditions determining their prospects and those of the planet.
On our walk home, I saw groups of masked teenagers perched on footbridges over the Canal Saint-Martin, their legs dangling, watching trash cans burn. The canal’s bridges also figured in the bloody fighting of the June Days of the Revolution of 1848, when Parisian workers confronted the French National Guard and other government forces.
The political divisions of that era were different. Ours are only now coming into view.
Jonathan Levy, professor of history at Sciences Po, is the author of Ages of American Capitalism: A History of the United States and The Real Economy: History and Theory.
Copyright: Project Syndicate

Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
16:43:18 UTC
01:43:18 KST

German police yesterday said they had detained a suspect following a fire at Adolf Hitler’s mountain retreat, known as the Eagle’s Nest, in the state of Bavaria.
About 200 firefighters were deployed to tackle the blaze at the Nazi dictator’s remote and difficult-to-access Kehlsteinhaus residence, on the peak above Obersalzberg in southern Germany.
Firefighters saw flames rising high into the air as they approached the scene, only to find the building “completely ablaze,” police said.
Photo: AFP
“A suspicious person was taken into temporary custody,” they said in a later statement, adding that nobody was injured in the blaze.
Police spokeswoman Lisa Maier said firefighters struggled to tackle the fire due to its location at an altitude of 1,834m.
The building was only accessible with “heavy breathing apparatus,” she said.
Authorities were on Friday evening alerted to the fire, when a smoke detector triggered a fire alarm at about 9:50pm, police said.
No potential reason for the fire was given, but German media reported that the investigators suspected it was the result of arson.
As snow fell on the Alpine peak, the Eagle’s Nest was still engulfed in flames in the early hours of yesterday, a weather camera showed. The blaze appeared to have been doused by yesterday morning, although smoke continued to rise from the smoldering building.
Officers blocked access to the road leading to the retreat.
The firefighters found no one inside the building.
Maier said the investigation was still ongoing.

Built between 1937 and 1938, the Eagle’s Nest forms part of the toxic legacy of Hitler’s Third Reich, which was responsible for the deaths of millions of Jews along with Roma, LGBTQ people and communists in the Holocaust.

Unfortunately, Jensen Huang is right about the UK
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
16:43:15 UTC
01:43:15 KST

Nobody in the UK wants to agree with a leather-jacket-wearing US tycoon, but it is tough to poke holes in Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s (黃仁勳) diagnosis of what has gone wrong with the UK.
The country has enough intellect, but not enough entrepreneurial spirit, Jensen told politicians and investors gathered in a converted London church last week.
Offered a million ways to win, it tends to find “the one reason not to do it,” he said.
Huang does believe there is talent on this island, a point he underlined by betting millions on five British start-ups. However, there is neither the financial environment nor the regulatory climate to allow British entrepreneurs to think on a grand scale.
As a House of Lords committee has said: “A procession of promising science and technology companies” is moving overseas. Oxford Ionics was bought by US-based IonQ for US$1 billion; OrganOx by Japanese medtech group Terumo for US$1.5 billion. Wise shifted its primary listing to the US. British companies that want to go big also have to go elsewhere.
What happened to the UK? This place once teemed with energetic amateurs, wacky inventors and empire-builders. How did a country that pioneered everything from football to steam engines to the joint-stock company start searching for reasons to not do things?
Most UK-based founders I have spoken with in the past few months offered up the same reason, unprompted: The UK fears risk-taking. Finance there does not have the appetite to support high-risk, high-reward ventures, and the state will not make the political gambles needed to shape a market through rules or procurement contracts.
This is a problem beyond tech. In fact, nothing defines the political and economic culture in the UK today so much as a pathological aversion to risk. Nobody ever wants anything to change, on the off chance it could be dangerous. Fear of what the future might hold has become the national ideology; the main difference between the UK’s major political parties is which vision of the 1970s they prefer.
Much of what holds the UK back can be traced to the same timid mindset. Why, for example, are its businesses chronically short of funds to invest? For one, UK pension money is no longer in equities; last year, pensions held just one-quarter of their assets in equities and 56 percent in bonds — the lowest and highest shares respectively of the world’s seven largest pension markets. The split was 43 percent-38 percent in favor of equities in 2014.
Too much of the country’s wealth is tied up in property. It is seen as a safe bet that increases in value — thanks in part to local councils, few of which dare to take a punt on permitting new building. There is a chance, after all, that it might spoil someone’s view or draw the wrong sort. Any project that survives is constrained by dozens of well-meaning rules. The result is not just a stagnant country, but also one that looks and feels poorer.
Councils fear new neighbors, businesses fear expansion and politicians fear losses or legal challenges. However, fear cannot be a country’s organizing principle.
Any modern liberal democracy has the responsibility to protect its people from the worst that might befall them. That is why welfare systems such as the UK’s exist. However, when countries keep expanding the safety net in a doomed attempt to insulate their citizens from any hazard, the system becomes unsustainable — especially when that same risk-aversion prevents the nation from growing enough to pay for its welfare perfectionism.
If the UK is not there already, it would be soon.
A widely read story in the Wall Street Journal last week outlined the degree to which the system has drifted from its original purpose. Disability payments, first designed for victims of industrial accidents, are today claimed by about 7 million people — more than one in 10. That number has risen by more than 60 percent among working-age adults since 2019; no other Western country has seen a comparable increase. When then-British prime minister Keir Starmer tried to trim just ￡5 billion (US$6.69 billion) off the system’s ￡100 billion-a-year bill, his backbenchers forced him into a U-turn.
Investors, depressed to discover that even a government with a huge majority could not fix welfare, sold gilts. Ten-year borrowing costs have risen from 4.5 percent to 5.5 percent this year, the highest in the G7.
Trying to protect people against every possible peril does not abolish risk; it just shifts it to another set of citizens — who might revolt. Brits need look no further than their French neighbors to see how that turns out.
This is the country that invented cricket and the spinning jenny. It is also the one that invented insurance. Protecting people against risk was a great idea. Such a pity it is the one that has come to define modern UK.
Mihir Sharma is a Bloomberg Opinion columnist. A senior fellow at the Observer Research Foundation in New Delhi, he is author of Restart: The Last Chance for the Indian Economy. This column reflects the personal views of the author and does not necessarily reflect the opinion of the editorial board or Bloomberg LP and its owners.

ANALYTICAL ENGLISH 解析英語(常春藤)

Like Coca-Cola, ketchup has undergone serious rebranding throughout its history. Most people think of ketchup as a sweet, tangy condiment perfect for dipping fries, but this has not always been the case.
Photo: AdobeStock I 照片：AdobeStock
The origins of ketchup are often traced back to southern China. People in coastal towns made a fermented fish sauce sometimes called “kue-chiap.” Easy to store and long-lasting, it became popular with sailors, who carried it with them across the seas. By the 1700s, this sauce had spread across Europe, where people adapted recipes to suit local tastes by using ingredients such as anchovies, shallots, horseradish, and nutmeg.
Modern tomato-based ketchup was developed in the US in the early 19th century, when tomatoes were widely promoted as a healthy food with medicinal benefits. Specifically, they were believed to help treat liver problems. One American doctor promoted tomato ketchup as a cure for indigestion. Although many doctors dismissed these claims, tomato ketchup’s popularity continued to grow across the US. It wasn’t until the explosion of fast food in the mid-1900s that ketchup finally developed its current reputation as a familiar partner for fries, burgers, and hot dogs.
A drink once marketed as a cure and a sauce once associated with health benefits are now ordinary parts of daily meals. Their changing roles show how food, culture, and marketing continually reshape what people eat and drink.
Photos: AdobeStock I 照片：AdobeStock
和可口可樂一樣，番茄醬在歷史上也經歷了重大的形象轉變。大多數人認為番茄醬是一種香甜、濃郁且帶有酸味、很適合拿來沾薯條的調味醬，但情況並非一直如此。
番茄醬的起源通常可追溯至中國南方。沿海城鎮的人們會製作一種有時被稱為「?汁」的發酵魚露。其易於保存且保存期限長，因此大受水手歡迎，他們帶著這種魚露橫渡重洋。到了1700年代，這種醬已傳遍歐洲，人們開始加入鯷魚、紅蔥頭、辣根與肉豆蔻等食材，依照當地口味調整食譜。
現代以番茄為基底的番茄醬是於十九世紀初在美國出現的，當時番茄被當成一種具有藥用益處的健康食物而被廣為推廣。具體來說，人們認為它有助於治療肝臟問題。有一位美國醫師將使用番茄製作的番茄醬宣傳為治療消化不良的藥方。雖然許多醫師並不認同這些說法，但使用番茄製作的番茄醬在美國各地的人氣仍持續上升。直到1900年代中期速食文化迅速興起後，番茄醬才終於建立起今日的形象，成為薯條、漢堡與熱狗的經典搭配。
一種曾被當作藥品宣傳的飲料，以及一種曾與健康益處有所連結的醬料，如今都已成為日常飲食中的普通食品。它們角色的轉變顯示出食物、文化與行銷是如何持續重新塑造人們的飲食習慣。
What Did You Learn?
1. From (A) to (F) below, choose the ONES that are true for both Coca-Cola and tomato-based ketchup.（多選題）
(A) Their first formulas were created by ancient chefs in China.
(B) Sailors played a major role in spreading them around the world.
(C) Their present-day popularity is closely linked to fast-food culture.
(D) They were once promoted as products with health-related benefits.
(E) Their original ingredients have remained mostly unchanged over time.
(F) They were once widely avoided because people believed they were dangerous.
答案：C、D
2. Which word in the passage means “a substance, such as salt or a sauce, that is used to give flavor to food”?（簡答題）
答案：condiment
Words in Use
1. undergo vt. 經歷
三態為：undergo, underwent, undergone。
Sophia underwent several interviews before getting the job.
蘇菲亞在得到這份工作前經歷了好幾場面試。
2. adapt vt. 調適∕改造（以適合……） Jenny adapted her daily schedule to balance work and family life.
珍妮調整了每日行程，以兼顧工作與家庭生活。
3. recipe n. 食譜
Grandma shared her secret cookie recipe with Carol.
奶奶和卡蘿分享了她的祕密餅乾食譜。
4. specifically adv. 確切地說
Specifically, our clients think we need to improve our services.
確切地說，客戶認為我們的服務有待改善。
5. indigestion n. 消化不良
Mandy suffered from indigestion after eating too quickly.
曼蒂因吃得太快而消化不良。
Practical Phrases
1. be perfect for. . . 非常適合……
These shoes are perf ect for walking long distances comfortably.
這雙鞋非常適合舒服地長距離行走。
2. be the case 情況∕情形正是如此
If that is the case, we should change our original plan immediately.
如果情況是那樣，我們應該立刻改變原本的計畫。

Taiwan in Time: Taiwanese opera’s dashing heartthrob
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
16:43:14 UTC
01:43:14 KST

Oct. 26 to Nov. 1
Born backstage after one of her mother’s Taiwanese opera performances, Yang Li-hua (楊麗花) often says that she was already learning the craft in the womb. From a young age, she hoped to follow in her mother’s footsteps as a performer of male lead roles.
But Yang came of age just a bit too late. She landed her first lead role in 1960 at the age of 16, but by then, public interest in live opera performances was declining. After a successful eight-month stint in the Philippines, she found herself without work in 1964.
Photo courtesy of Lisheng Baihe International Entertainment Co
With fewer stage opportunities, Yang turned to new forms of media, first performing on radio, then leading her own troupe on television and starring in movies. She played dashing scholars, martial arts heroes and emperors, gaining legions of adoring female fans in Taiwan and Southeast Asia.
Yang often maintained an androgynous image offstage as well, and was so accustomed to portraying gallant men that she struggled with traditional female roles in her non-opera movies. These characters were often constrained by patriarchal attitudes, enduring bitter lives and sacrificing themselves for others. In 1996, she was voted one of 10 “dream lovers” by the budding LGBTQ movement.
Now 82, Yang continues to promote Taiwanese opera. She recently appeared at a screening of the documentary Emperor on Stage (世紀初戀楊麗花), which explores her life, career and influence.
Photo courtesy of Taiwan Film and Audiovisual Institute
“After watching this film, have you fallen in love with me yet?” she asks the audience in a post-screening video message.
The film opens in theaters on Friday.
TRAVELING CHILDHOOD
Photo courtesy of Yunlin County Department of Culture and Tourism
Yang’s opera roots trace back to her maternal grandfather, who ran a troupe in Yilan’s Yuanshan Township. His daughter, Yang Hao (楊好), fell in love with his disciple, Lin Huo-yan (林火燄), and the two eloped, joining various traveling opera troupes to make a living.
On Oct. 26, 1944, Yang Hao was experiencing contractions before a performance but still managed to finish the three-hour show. There was no time to call a midwife. As her parents were not officially married, Yang Li-hua took her mother’s surname, writes Shih Ju-fang (施如芳) in Yang Li-hua: The Legendary Opera Star and Her Times (如有神在：楊麗花與他的時代).
The end of Japanese rule the following year brought an explosion in Taiwanese opera. Yang’s family continued to travel and grow, partitioning off a room with mosquito nets behind the stage at each stop so they could sleep.
Photo courtesy of Yang Li-hua
Yang learned her first “seven-word tune” at the age of six. From then on, she tried turning everything she saw into seven-word lines, honing her rhyming, intonation and improvisation. She quickly figured out how to make audiences laugh and cry, and at seven, she played her first role, moving the audience to tears with a song about missing her mother.
Yang’s parents sent her to stay with relatives in Yilan so she could attend school, but she often ran away to rejoin the troupe. One day, after visiting her parents, she jumped off the train and sneaked back to the troupe. After a performance, they found her watching from the audience and finally agreed to let her stay. She helped with chores, cared for her siblings, filled in for performers when needed and earned extra food by taking on tasks such as dragnet fishing.
Yang’s parents hoped she would play scholarly characters, but she preferred fighting roles. She trained hard on her own, and once sustained a 6cm gash on her forehead during a swordfight.
Photo courtesy of Public Television Service
Her first leading role was Double Speared Lu Wen-lung (雙槍陸文龍), a character she would reprise 36 years later at the National Theater.
NATIONAL HEARTTHROB
However, the growing popularity of Taiwanese opera movies was drawing audiences away from live performances, forcing many troupes to disband. The overseas Chinese market remained strong, and in 1963, Yang traveled to the Philippines with the Sai Chin Pao Opera Troupe (賽金寶歌劇團). It was her first large-scale production, with a team of more than 50 people. The show was immensely popular over its eight-month stay.
Upon return, Yang had earned enough money to buy her family a two-story apartment in Dadaocheng. However, no more work came in. A neighbor suggested she try radio, and in 1965 she joined Cheng Sheng (正聲) radio station’s Tian Ma Opera Troupe (天馬歌劇團). It was her first regular job with a monthly salary.
Yang insisted on maintaining her hand gestures and eye movements while recording, saying that “without getting into character, I couldn’t convey genuine emotion.” Her stylish, dashing image made her hugely popular, and she received stacks of fan mail every day, many from housewives who listened to her while doing chores.
The troupe put on live shows a few times a year, drawing screaming, tearful fans eager to see the performer they had come to know through the radio.
By the late 1960s, television was overtaking radio. In 1966, Taiwan Television held a contest between opera troupes for its Thursday noontime slot. Tian Ma entered with the politically correct Loyalty to the Country (盡忠報國) and won.
Television brought new challenges. Multiple cameras and limited space in the frame required Yang to adjust her movements, while commercial breaks interrupted the flow. But she soon mastered the medium, and the nation would come to a standstill when her show came on. Crowds waited outside the station to catch a glimpse of her, and she appeared on magazine covers.
MOVIE STAR
In 1967, Yang made her film debut in The Jade Hairpin (碧玉簪), helping revive a fading Taiwanese opera film industry. She would star in 24 films, taking on Mandarin-language productions and modern, non-opera roles for the first time. She practiced in front of a mirror to learn how to act more feminine for these roles, and joked that she was usually the one marrying the woman, but this time, their roles were reversed.
Yang was often paired on set with Hsu Shiu-hian (許秀年), whom audiences called Yang’s “forever bride” — even after Yang married physician Hung Wen-tung (洪文棟) in 1983.
Yang got to play a hero again in Vengeance of the Phoenix Sisters (三鳳震武林), portraying one of the sisters masquerading as a man. At one point, both sisters even fall for Yang’s character, unaware of her identity.
In 1970, Yang was hired as leader and producer of Taiwan Television’s in-house troupe. After a three-year hiatus, she returned to Taiwan Television in 1979, with the troupe named after her. The show soon moved to the evening, and watching Taiwanese opera over dinner remains a fond memory for many Taiwanese.
Yang continued producing television shows and touring. In 1981, she performed on a modern stage for the first time at Sun Yat-sen Memorial Hall. She later performed at the National Theater and Taipei Arena, as well as countless large venues overseas.
Her last production was The Timeless Virtues (忠孝節義), which aired in 2019. At the age of 75, she still rode a horse in a battle scene and continued filming despite falling off once.
After two years of preparation, filming on her documentary began in 2023. The documentary follows Yang as she revisits people and places from her past, sometimes marveling that old props and artifacts have survived.
Taiwan in Time, a column about Taiwan’s history that is published every Sunday, spotlights important or interesting events around the nation that either have anniversaries this week or are tied to current events.

The airport is a key military operations center, and its seizure or destruction in a PRC invasion would be inevitable. Yet that is hardly the only conflict involving Songshan. Taipei Mayor Chiang Wan-an’s (蔣萬安) recent, surprising suggestion that the airport be converted to an AI park is just the latest variation on an old theme. Replacing Songshan airport with some kind of green or park space

The idea that we need to walk 10,000 steps a day originated not in medical research but in a 1960s marketing campaign for a pedometer, says Jack McNamara, senior lecturer in clinical exercise physiology at the University of East London. 01:43:12 KST

More South Korea
I read the editorial “The importance of ties with Japan” (Oct. 22, page 8) with agreement and a sense of dismay. Last month, another editorial “Alliances, security, cooperation” (Sept. 13, page 8) similarly called for more robust Taiwan-Japan relations.
Taiwan is right to deepen its relations with Japan, East Asia’s most populous democracy and a US treaty ally. Yet why does South Korea, the region’s second-largest democracy and another US treaty ally, always seem absent from Taiwan’s strategic discourse?
South Korea sits directly across the Yellow Sea from China. It is geographically the closest US ally to Beijing and hosts the permanently stationed US forces nearest to the Chinese capital.
Of the other East Asian capitals, Seoul is physically closest to Taipei.
Last year, Taiwan’s bilateral trade with South Korea reached US$90.3 billion, surpassing its US$84.9 billion in trade with Japan, making South Korea Taiwan’s third-largest trading partner.
Taipei should also recognize that Japan might not always be uniformly sympathetic to Taiwan’s interests. Former Japanese prime minister Yukio Hatoyama attended a military parade in Beijing in September last year and urged Tokyo to reassess its Taiwan policy.
Japan severed diplomatic relations with Taipei in 1972, nearly 20 years before South Korea did. More than five decades of official Japan-China relations have produced deep historical and institutional ties, embodied in the widely cited “four political documents.” In 1978, Japan and China signed Japan’s only post-World War II bilateral Treaty of Peace and Friendship.
Despite their current tensions, Japanese Minister of Foreign Affairs Toshimitsu Motegi reaffirmed the validity of the documents earlier this month.
These long-standing diplomatic frameworks and historical ties between Tokyo and Beijing could eventually facilitate a rapprochement between Japan and China, potentially leaving Taiwan on the sidelines.
Seoul, by contrast, does not share an equivalent set of foundational political documents carrying comparable weight with Beijing.
Yet deeper South Korea-Japan relations could constrain Tokyo’s room for a rapprochement with Beijing. Seoul and Tokyo share classified military information and regularly participate in joint military exercises involving active-duty personnel, most recently during last month’s Freedom Edge drills.
Last year, two-way travel between South Korea and Japan exceeded 13 million visits, nearly 5 million more than between Taiwan and Japan.
More people traveled to Japan from South Korea than from any other country, followed by China in second place.
SK Group chairman Chey Tae-won, whose conglomerate includes semiconductor giant SK Hynix, has advocated a South Korea-Japan economic community modeled on the EU, including Schengen-style passport-free travel between the two countries.
Imagine if Taiwan could join such a democratic East Asian union. That would require deeper South Korea-Japan ties and, more importantly, serious efforts to bolster Taiwan-South Korea relations, arguably the weakest link in the prospective triangle.
As a South Korean student who deeply values Taiwan, I regret that the potential of this relationship seems to receive little attention within Taiwan.
Taiwan does not need less Japan. It needs more South Korea — and a broader vision for a Taiwan-South Korea-Japan partnership.
Alan Jeong
Northwestern University, Illinois

A Taiwan relations act for ties with Japan
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
16:43:09 UTC
01:43:09 KST

Starting this month, Japan is to allow professional licenses for doctors and other credentialed occupations to list “Taiwan” as their place of origin. That might appear to be nothing more than a one-word change in official documents, but when viewed alongside a series of recent reforms, it becomes clear that Japan’s policy toward Taiwan is gradually shifting.
The prospect of Japan enacting its own version of the US’ Taiwan Relations Act is beginning to come into view.
In 2012, Japan began allowing “Taiwan” to be listed on residence cards issued to foreign nationals. In May last year, it began permitting “Taiwan” to be entered into the nationality field of family registers.
In June, the Japan-Republic of China (ROC) Diet Members’ Consultative Council, an organization established more than half a century ago, changed its official name to the Japan-Taiwan Diet Members’ Consultative Council. This month, the Japanese government completed revisions to its national qualification system, reviewing 322 national qualifications and amending the regulations governing about 100 of them that include a nationality field.
The reforms were hard-won, as Japan’s administrative system has traditionally been quite rigid and resistant to change, with reforms often requiring years of coordination. The changes they introduced — from recognizing “Taiwan” in family registers and national professional licenses to renaming a parliamentary organization from “Japan-ROC” to “Japan-Taiwan” — not only demonstrate the efforts of Japanese lawmakers, but also highlight the heightened attention of Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi’s Cabinet to Taiwan-related issues.
Even more noteworthy is that last month a cross-party Japanese parliamentary group, the Diet Members’ Association for Peace and Stability in the Taiwan Strait, visited Taiwan and met with President William Lai (賴清德). The group’s chairman, Japanese lawmaker Haruo Kitamura, publicly stated that he would promote Japanese versions of the US’ Taiwan Travel Act and Taiwan Relations Act during the autumn Diet session, with the aim of lifting restrictions on ties between Taipei and Tokyo.
Administrative recognition of Taiwan in name does not equate to official diplomatic recognition. Nevertheless, administrative hurdles that once made it difficult to even use the word “Taiwan” in official documents are being dismantled. The experience gained through these reforms would undoubtedly help create favorable conditions for the Diet to advance legislation formalizing Taiwan-Japan relations.
Amid the increasingly volatile situation in the Taiwan Strait, the US already has the Taiwan Relations Act. At a time when the US-Japan alliance is being comprehensively upgraded, enacting a Japanese version of the Taiwan Relations Act has become an urgent priority. Years of parliamentary exchanges between Taiwan and Japan, together with Japan’s gradual implementation of administrative reforms, have produced incremental gains that are now paving the way for a legal framework governing Taiwan-Japan ties.
The shift from China to Taiwan represents more than the change of a word in official documents; likewise, the shift from “Japan-ROC” to “Japan-Taiwan” reflects more than a mere renaming of a parliamentary group. Administrative changes recognizing Taiwan by that name are gradually being implemented, while the legislative branch is picking up the pace.
In the crisp autumn air, the faint footsteps of Japan’s own Taiwan relations act are drawing nearer.
Wang Hui-sheng is a founding member of the East Asian Research Institute.
Translated by Kyra Gustavsen

The last reliable luxury shoppers are retreating in mainland China
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
16:43:06 UTC
01:43:06 KST

Luxury powerhouses including Hermes and Cartier are suffering steeper slumps in China, in a sign that a spending pullback by the country’s wealthy consumers is hitting even the most resilient brands.
Sales at the brands in mainland China fell as much as double-digits in August and last month compared to the same period a year ago, two research firms surveyed by Bloomberg that track industry data said. The drop is significant as Hermes International SCA and Cie Financiere Richemont SA’s Cartier had been relatively unaffected in the country as a broader slowdown in luxury consumption took hold in June, the firms’ data show.
Mainland sales for the 25 largest luxury labels including Louis Vuitton and Gucci have also contracted further, plunging by double-digits in August and last month, the firms said.
Photo: AFP
Business remained weak during China’s National Day holiday, a seven-day break early this month dubbed the golden week, even as consumers spent more on travel, according to people familiar with the matter who asked not to be identified because they are not authorized to speak publicly. Some executives at major luxury houses now fear the slump could become more widespread and persist until next year, the people said.
Concerns are mounting as Beijing’s widening scrutiny of offshore wealth and a cooling artificial intelligence stock rally rattle private fortunes, testing the long-held belief that the luxury industry’s wealthiest clients are largely recession-proof. Global brands had long banked on these top-tier spenders as China’s middle-class retreated during a prolonged property-market slump and wider economic slowdown. Now, they are facing the possibility of their key customers and aspirational shoppers spending less at the same time.
“The recurring message from our annual Asia consumer and luxury trip over the past three years was that conditions were difficult, but that ‘next year would be better,’” HSBC Holdings PLC analyst Anne-Laure Bismuth said in a note this month. “This time, however, meetings in Hong Kong, Xiamen and Shanghai provided no timeline or evidence of a recovery in Chinese luxury consumption.”
Hermes and Cartier did not respond to requests for comment.
Resilient demand from other parts of Greater China, including Hong Kong and Macau, has helped offset some of the declines in the mainland for high-end jewelry brands such as Cartier, research firm JL Warren said. Still, the weakness in one of the luxury group’s largest markets has weighed on their earnings.
Hermes on Thursday reported flat sales in Asia-Pacific for the third quarter. Revenue in the region excluding Japan fell short of analyst expectations for 1.55 percent growth.
The performance in the region — which includes China and accounts for about 42 percent of Hermes’ total revenue — is a sign that the Birkin bag maker is not immune to the spending curbs affecting Chinese shoppers.
China’s macroeconomic environment remains challenging, compounded by sluggish financial markets and ongoing tax-related campaigns, Hermes chief financial officer Eric Du Halgouet said during a post-earnings briefing.
LVMH Moet Hennessy Louis Vuitton SE’s third-quarter results showed a double-digit drop in domestic China sales amid a trademark controversy involving its largest brand Louis Vuitton. Purchases by Chinese shoppers overseas also fell by a mid-single-digit percentage. The weakness contributed to a 5 percent revenue slump in Asia excluding Japan, the group’s only region to post a negative performance.
Gucci sales fell 6 percent in the third quarter, worse than analysts’ expectations, hurt by weak consumption in China. That has contributed to parent Kering SA’s quarterly decline.
Amid the broader economic downturn, Chinese consumers have become more selective about discretionary spending, prioritizing travel, dining and other experiences over highly visible luxury purchases. Even among those still willing to spend, tastes have shifted. Many younger shoppers are gravitating away from prominent logos and status-driven purchases in favor of understated products that emphasize craftsmanship and quality, fueling the rise of so-called “quiet luxury.”
Retail sales growth in August slowed further to 0.4 percent before improving last month. Big-ticket items including jewelry and cars performed the worst, plunging as much as 21 percent in business receipts in the two months.
Comparisons are likely to become less challenging next year after a steep downturn this year, potentially helping major luxury groups return to reported growth, Shanghai-based consultancy Foresight Performance Partners co-founder Jacques Roizen said. However, any improvement in headline numbers is unlikely to signal a meaningful recovery in demand, he said.
“Beneath those comparisons is a structural problem,” Roizen said. “Much of the aspirational middle-class has moved away from luxury, while wealthier consumers have become more cautious. The underlying pressures are unlikely to change quickly.”

Judge rules Cornell’s ‘Jane Doe’ can use pseudonym in suit over alleged gang-rape
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
16:40:21 UTC
01:40:21 KST

The woman at the center of rape allegations against students at Cornell University can continue using a pseudonym in her lawsuit, a judge has ruled.
The New York state judge Phaedra Perry-Bond ruled on Friday that the woman’s privacy interests – particularly concerns for her safety – outweighed any need to publicly disclose her identity in court proceedings.
The woman alleges she was drugged and raped by students at the elite Ivy League university in upstate New York in 2024.
She has become the target of threats, her lawyer, Thomas Giuffra, said earlier this month.
The defendants in the lawsuit have not opposed the request for anonymity, as the woman continues to go by a generic placeholder name “Jane Doe” used in many legal or official situations, especially when a woman’s identity is protected.
But Perry-Bond wrote in a ruling released on Friday that “some members of the public have made it their mission to try and identify Jane Doe”.
The judge warned that “cyberstalking and engaging in or encouraging threats across state lines, whether it be of Jane Doe, of any of the named defendants, or their attorneys, can be considered a federal crime and perpetrators of those acts may be subjecting themselves to prosecution”.
The woman in the Cornell case was 20 at the time of the alleged gang-rape at a fraternity house at the university. She filed her suit on 16 September, prompting prosecutors to reopen a criminal investigation they had initially closed without charges.
Mass protests erupted on Cornell’s Ithaca campus earlier this month, with students criticizing officials’ handling of Jane Doe’s gang-rape allegations, demanding the university president’s resignation and painting “SMASH THE PATRIARCHY” on an administration building.
Protesters shouted “Ban the frats” and held signs saying “At Cornell, rapists are safer than women” and “Stop rape culture.” Some demonstrators directed their anger at Michael Kotlikoff, Cornell’s president, arguing he had failed to keep students safe and chanting, “Kotlikoff, resign!”

Floods in Argentina kill 2, displace over 2,000 amid El Nino
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
16:39:41 UTC
01:39:41 KST

Maryam Ashalem de Andres
24 October 2026•Update: 24 October 2026
Flooding in northeastern Argentina has killed two people and forced more than 2,000 others from their homes, with rising river levels threatening communities across the region, Argentine newspaper Pagina 12 reported Saturday.
Heavy rainfall has caused the Parana, Uruguay and Iguazu rivers to rise, affecting communities near Argentina's borders with Brazil, Paraguay and Uruguay, according to the report.
In Chaco province in northeastern Argentina --mainly in Puerto Vilelas and Barranqueras -- between 1,200 and 1,300 people left their homes, provincial Civil Protection Deputy Secretary Gustavo Santos said Friday.
"This will continue for a couple of months. The river will keep rising and falling constantly," Santos said.
In neighboring Corrientes province, in northeastern Argentina, more than 1,000 people had left their homes, according to a Civil Defense report released Wednesday.
Floodwaters inundated several neighborhoods in Paso de la Patria, a town in northeastern Argentina on the Parana River, after a protective embankment broke under pressure from rising waters.
Two rural workers drowned in Corrientes while moving cattle between islands to protect the animals from the floods.
Authorities warned that rainfall forecast in the upper Parana and Uruguay river basins could cause further river rises next week.
In Misiones province, storms on Thursday and Friday damaged more than 100 homes and forced road and bridge closures as streams overflowed, local media reported.
At Iguazu Falls, located on the border between Argentina and Brazil, the Iguazu River's flow reached 10 times its seasonal average in mid-October.
Several tourist circuits have reopened, but access to the Devil's Throat, the waterfalls' most famous section, remains closed.
El Nino is a climate phenomenon characterized by unusually warm surface waters in the equatorial Pacific Ocean.
