Houthis claim to have struck Saudi airports, oil facilities with missiles, drones
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
16:39:17 UTC
01:39:17 KST

Rania Abushamala
24 October 2026•Update: 24 October 2026
Yemen's Houthi group claimed on Saturday that it carried out seven military operations using ballistic missiles and drones against airports, oil facilities and an air base across Saudi Arabia in retaliation for Saudi airstrikes on Yemen.
In a statement, the group said it targeted King Khalid International Airport in the capital Riyadh.
It also claimed attacks on Saudi oil giant Aramco's facilities in Yanbu and the Rabigh oil refinery, both on the kingdom's western Red Sea coast.
Another operation targeted crude oil pumping stations and the East-West oil pipeline, which transports oil from eastern Saudi Arabia to the Red Sea coast, according to the statement.
The Houthis also claimed to have struck King Fahd International Airport in Dammam, eastern Saudi Arabia, saying the attack was "precise" and disrupted air traffic.
Other operations targeted Najran airport in southern Saudi Arabia, near the Yemeni border, and the Khamis Mushait air base in the southwest, with the group claiming direct hits.
The Houthis said the attacks were in response to Saudi airstrikes on Yemen, alleging that 100 strikes over the last 24 hours had hit civilian sites in the capital Sanaa and other areas under their control, killing and injuring dozens.
The group claimed Saudi Arabia had carried out a total of 3,123 airstrikes and missile attacks since the latest escalation began.
Meanwhile, Saudi Civil Defense said two Houthi ballistic missiles launched toward the Mecca and Medina regions were intercepted, with debris falling in four locations.
Parts of the missiles fell in Wadi al-Mughammas in Mecca, while interception debris fell in Jeddah’s al-Nuzha district, Wadi Jalil in Taif and Masturah in Rabigh, the agency said in a statement.
Providing further details on the debris near Mecca, Saudi Arabia’s AlEkhbariya channel said “fragments of one of the two missiles fell in Wadi al-Mughammas near the holy site of Arafat, 23 kilometers from the Grand Mosque in Mecca.”
Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree, however, denied targeting holy sites in Mecca and Medina.
Saree said the group’s operation targeted oil facilities and military bases, adding that details would be announced “in due course.”
Earlier on Saturday, the Saudi-led coalition in Yemen said it intercepted and destroyed two Houthi ballistic missiles targeting the Saudi cities of Taif and Yanbu.
The Houthis have controlled Yemen's capital, Sanaa, and other parts of the country since 2014.
Saudi Arabia has led a military coalition supporting Yemen's internationally recognized government against the Houthis since 2015.
The latest fighting began in July, after the collapse of a 2022 ceasefire.

Israel detains dozens of Palestinians in West Bank crackdown
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
16:32:55 UTC
01:32:55 KST

Breadcrumb
Israel detains dozens of Palestinians in crackdown on occupied West Bank
Around 70 Palestinians have been detained in less than 48 hours in a sweeping Israeli crackdown on the occupied West Bank, the Palestinian Prisoners’ Society said on Saturday.
The group said Israeli authorities are continuing their offensive across the West Bank, and that detentions have been on the rise since the start of the war on Gaza in October 2023.
The organisation also noted that a crackdown on Hebron, which started on Friday, has spread to other cities.
Arrests were recorded in various cities and towns, including Ramallah, Qalqilya, Jenin, Nablus, Jericho, Salfit, Tubas, Bethlehem, Tulkarem and occupied East Jerusalem.
Data compiled by the group shows that some of those detained have since been released; however, others are facing interrogations.
The data showed that many of those targeted in the crackdown were detainees who had previously been released, including some individuals who were freed as part of prisoner exchange deals.
Rights groups have decried the mass arrests as a systematic policy of persecution, and said the crackdown has extended to relatives and acquaintances of those who were formerly detained.
One of those who were targeted has been identified as Nael Barghouti. According to the official Palestinian Wafa news agency, Israeli forces raided his home in the town of Kobar, leaving his home partially destroyed and heavily vandalised.
The Palestinian Prisoners Society said that most of the detainees who were released said they were subjected to varying degrees of assault, including being blindfolded, shackled, and threatened.
The threats included being warned to not engage in any political activity.
Meanwhile, the rights group also noted that threatening leaflets were distributed across cities in the West Bank.
The development comes as hundreds of families were displaced from Hebron in the middle of the night following large-scale raids and the decision to place the city under lockdown amid a military operation.
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu vowed on Friday to collectively punish residents from a neighbourhood in Hebron, after an attack was carried out on an Israeli army checkpoint.
Palestinian prisoner groups have documented at least 26,000 arrests in the West Bank since the start of the war on Gaza, which does not include those detained in Gaza.

Babcock opens skills centre on Devonport waterfront
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
17:30:17 BST
01:30:17 KST

Babcock has opened a Skills Centre at Devonport Dockyard able to support fifteen hundred technical staff and apprentices a year, and has broken ground on an Integrated Logistics Hub at Sherford that will pull together more than thirty separate logistics sites, according to the company.
Luke Pollard, the Minister for Defence Readiness and Industry and the member for Plymouth Sutton and Devonport, formally opened the Skills Centre, which brings practical training onto the waterfront alongside the work it supports.
The logistics hub at Sherford falls within the Plymouth and South Devon Freeport, on an eighteen point eight acre site with room for a thirty thousand square metre facility. Babcock said it will increase operational capacity and resilience for submarine sustainment and deep maintenance at Devonport, supporting the dual-streaming of Astute class submarines and the transition to Dreadnought.
Pollard said: “Plymouth has always been at the heart of our national defence, and investments like this show how working with industry partners like Babcock can deliver both the skills our Armed Forces need, and the opportunities and growth this community deserves.
“The new Skills Centre will support those already in defence to learn new skills and grow their career and create new pathways for those entering defence for the first time, giving local people the chance to build a career they can be proud of.”
Neal Misell, chief executive of Babcock Nuclear, said: “Today demonstrates our long-term commitment to Plymouth and the wider region, developing the skills, capability and infrastructure needed to bolster the UK’s national defence resilience, while creating opportunities for economic growth and prosperity for future generations. Concluding the day at the new Babcock Capability Centre here in Plymouth city centre was a great chance to share our upcoming plans for the facility with regional partners which will see us relocate around 2000 colleagues into the heart of the city, bringing economic benefits and opportunities as we support the retention and creation of high value jobs into the future.”
Richard May, chief executive of the Plymouth and South Devon Freeport, said: “This is the Freeport doing what it does best – unlocking opportunities and turning plans into real investment. We’re delighted to be working with Babcock to bring this exciting project forward and build on the momentum we’ve created together. It’s a proud moment for everyone involved – and a great example of the defence dividend delivering real benefits for Plymouth and South Devon.”
Councillor Dan Thomas, leader of South Hams District Council, said: “This investment is part of the bigger picture for the South Hams. We promised to support a thriving local economy, create opportunities for good-quality jobs and build strong, resilient communities. By investing carefully and working with our partners, we are turning those promises into practical action that will benefit residents and businesses now and in the future.”

Unknown Publisher

Ternopil region serviceman captured while seriously wounded returns home after four years in captivity
His mother, Olha Chverenchuk, said this in a comment to an Ukrinform correspondent.
"My son took part in fierce fighting on the Lyman axis. That was where he was captured in September 2022. Andrii had a serious wound. He spent six months in hospital," the woman said.
According to Chverenchuk, the circumstances of her son's capture are recounted in the documentary "6th Company." In the film, his fellow servicemen explain that on September 25, two groups of ten men each set out to assault Lyman but fell into an ambush. Russian forces attacked the Ukrainian servicemen. Andrii was wounded and remained in an M113 armored personnel carrier with a fellow soldier. The two began fighting. They later received orders to withdraw into the forest so that artillery units could engage the enemy. Andrii and his wounded comrade, who used the call sign "Znakhаr" (Healer), were captured.
Andrii Chverenchuk is a chemist by education and holds a Candidate of Technical Sciences degree. When Russia launched its full-scale invasion, he was living and working in Kyiv. He joined the defense of Ukraine in the spring of 2022 and served with the 66th Mechanized Brigade.
"During the four years Andrii was in captivity, we wrote him many letters. We hoped they would support our son. Fortunately, he did receive one letter. Later, through the guys who were released from captivity, he sent us his thanks for writing to him. We also know that Andrii was initially held at the Sverdlovsk penal colony, then in Novosibirsk, and later transferred to Kamyshin, where things were the hardest," the serviceman's mother said.
She admitted that it was difficult to describe the emotions she felt when she heard her son's voice on the phone.
"I'm still euphoric. I still can't fully comprehend how happy I am," she said.
The woman said that prayer and faith in God had helped her endure four years of separation from her son and the uncertainty surrounding his fate.

Unknown

Aysar Alais and Rania Abushamala
24 October 2026•Update: 24 October 2026
The Israeli army has forced around 1,500 Palestinians from 250 families to flee their homes in Hebron in the southern occupied West Bank since Friday and plans to displace another 2,500 in the coming hours, the municipality said Saturday.
In a statement, the Hebron municipality said the displaced families lived in the Deir Bahha and al-Jilda neighborhoods, which together are home to 500 families.
Israeli forces marked evacuated homes and distributed notices ordering the remaining families to leave without taking their vehicles, it added.
The Palestinian Foreign Ministry warned Saturday against inflammatory Israeli statements threatening to expand forced displacement and evacuate and destroy neighborhoods in Hebron.
In a statement, the ministry described the threats as attempts to repeat the “Nakba” and carry out ethnic cleansing. It instructed Palestinian embassies and diplomatic missions to take urgent international action to press governments to adopt firm positions against Israeli practices.
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said Friday during an incursion into Hebron that his army was preparing a large-scale military offensive in the occupied West Bank involving the displacement of Palestinians from their neighborhoods and raids on their homes.
“We will do here what we have not done before. We will apply the successful offensive model we implemented in the refugee camps,” he said, referring to military offensives in the northern West Bank.
Siege and evacuation
The Israeli army continued its siege of Hebron for a second consecutive day Saturday as part of a military offensive launched Friday, forcing Palestinians to evacuate their homes.
The army imposed a closure on the city Friday after two Palestinians fired at an Israeli checkpoint. Both attackers and two Israeli soldiers were killed, while three other soldiers were wounded, according to Israeli figures.
The closure was accompanied by a larger deployment of Israeli military vehicles and bulldozers, the blocking of main entrances and roads connecting Hebron to surrounding areas, and raids and searches of homes.
The occupied West Bank, including East Jerusalem, has seen escalating Israeli military attacks and occupier violence since the start of Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza in October 2023.
These attacks have included killing and detaining Palestinians, demolishing homes and other structures, burning mosques and vehicles, bulldozing farmland, preventing farmers from accessing their fields and displacing Palestinian communities, alongside illegal settlement expansion.
Palestinians warn that these measures pave the way for Israel’s formal annexation of the West Bank, undermining prospects for establishing a Palestinian state in accordance with relevant UN resolutions.

Hundreds of protests are held across France
Hundreds of protests were held in France Saturday as nationwide anger grows over the cost of living, with security forces massing to prevent a repeat of violence that marred demonstrations last week, AFP reported.
The main Paris march drew 110,000 people, according to police, and reached its destination without incident but under rain. Some demonstrators chanted "We are not happy" as they peeled away.
Clashes were reported during demonstrations in Lyon, Lille, Marseille, Montpellier, Nantes and Toulouse.
Paris police said that more than 3,000 people were stopped and checked by officers and 65 people were arrested during the demonstration in the French capital.
A march in Marseille drew 17,000 participants, according to police, and 100,000, according to unions, ended without incident.
"We are being reasonable; we understood that we needed to stay away from the shops. But the important thing is to be able to demonstrate," CGT regional general secretary Marc Pietrosino said.
French police fired tear gas to prevent protesters in Lyon, Lille, Montpellier, Nantes and Toulouse from reaching city centres, AFP journalists saw.
Interior Minister Laurent Nunez had warned that authorities "will not tolerate any violence or any disturbance of public order."
French police had arrested 135 people nationwide and seized a variety of weapons, Interior Minister Laurent Nunez said, adding that, so far, "there has been no major incident".
Weapons confiscated included metal balls, lead pellets, fireworks, slingshots, steel balls, improvised weapons, a katana and airsoft weapons, he said.
Hundreds of demonstrators could be seen gathering at Porte d'Italie in Paris, where authorities have said they must begin the only authorised march.
Union representative Murielle Guilbert told reporters it was "scandalous" that President Emmanuel Macron had forbidden protesters from demonstrating "where we wish to demonstrate".
Paris police at the last minute ordered the union-organised march be moved from Bastille, in the centre, to the more remote Porte d'Italie on the southeastern rim.
Unions said they reluctantly agreed. But the Yellow Vests -- a loosely organised group that staged disruptive street protests against President Emmanuel Macron eight years ago -- indicated they would not comply.
The Yellow Vests also said they would hold another round of protests on October 31.
Organisers called for rallies and a sit-in outside parliament and city halls nationwide, condemning the "authoritarian drift" of Macron's government and urging citizens to stand up for "public freedoms".
Thousands of people yelling anti-fascist slogans marched in the city of Orleans against a congress by far-right leader Marine Le Pen's National Rally (RN) party there, AFP journalists saw.
The protest criticised both leading presidential candidate Le Pen and centrist Macron. "Macron resign. Le Pen in prison," the crowd yelled.
The Louvre, d'Orsay, and Picasso museums, as well as the Grand Palais in Paris, were closed Saturday. The culture ministry had called on institutions to take every measure to ensure the safety of visitors and staff, and the protection of artworks.

Israeli bombing cuts off water to large parts of Gaza City, as Israel 'reinstates starvation policy'
Israeli bombing has cut off the water supply to large parts of Gaza City after damaging a main supply line, the Gaza Municipality said on Saturday, amid warnings that Israel is attempting to reinstate its policy of starving Palestinians in the enclave.
In a statement, the municipality said Israeli bombing had damaged a key water pipeline belonging to the Israeli company Mekorot in the Shujaiya neighbourhood.
The bombardment comes despite an October 2025 truce agreement, which Israel has violated on an almost daily basis.
Mekorot is one of the main sources supplying water to the Gaza Strip. Israel exercises comprehensive control over the territory, making this water source, according to experts, a means of exerting pressure on the population.
The municipality added that it was in contact with the relevant authorities to coordinate repairs and restore the water supply as soon as possible.
The disruption to this pipeline comes after groundwater wells and water networks have been subjected to Israeli destruction over the course of three years of genocide.
In an earlier statement to Anadolu, environmental expert Saeed al-Aklouk said that Israel had destroyed more than 80% of Gaza’s water infrastructure.
Since October 2023, Israel has damaged or destroyed 90% of Gaza's civilian infrastructure, with the UN estimating reconstruction costs at approximately $70 billion.
The water crisis coincides with a shortage of flour and the closure of border crossings by the Israeli authorities, who have prevented essential food supplies from entering.
This has made it increasingly difficult for Gaza’s residents to obtain bread in the coastal enclave, where long queues have once again formed outside the few remaining bakeries operating at minimal capacity.
'Policy of starvation'
Hamas warned in a statement on Saturday that Israel was returning to the use of starvation as a policy in the Gaza Strip.
“The [Israeli] occupation’s move towards reinstating its policy of starvation against the people of the Gaza Strip exposes the international community’s utter failure and the complicity of the Board of Peace and its institutions in this criminal Israeli policy," the group said.
It added that Israel was repeating this policy due to the international community's failure to hold Tel Aviv accountable for its previous use of starvation against Gaza's population.
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and former defence minister Yoav Gallant are wanted by the International Criminal Court on war crimes charges, including the use of starvation as a weapon of war.
On Friday, the Euro-Med Monitor warned of a renewed risk of famine in Gaza amid shortages of flour and essential food supplies, the suspension of operations at some bakeries, and the collapse of residents’ purchasing power. These conditions are unfolding as the Israeli blockade and restrictions on humanitarian and commercial supplies continue.

Hurricane Vance remains Category 2 storm off Mexico’s Pacific coast
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
16:25:26 UTC
01:25:26 KST

Maryam Ashalem de Andres
24 October 2026•Update: 24 October 2026
Hurricane Vance continued as a Category 2 storm in the Pacific Ocean, located 615 kilometers (382 miles) south-southwest of Acapulco, according to Mexico’s National Meteorological Service.
The agency reported the storm’s position in an update as authorities continued to monitor its intensity and movement across the eastern Pacific.
Vance’s distance from the coast and its projected trajectory remain key factors in assessing potential risks to coastal communities in southern and western Mexico.
Category 2 hurricanes have sustained winds of 154 to 177 kilometers per hour (96 to 110 miles per hour). They can cause damage to roofs, trees and power lines, depending on local conditions and the storm’s proximity to land.
Heavy rainfall can pose risks even in areas that do not experience the strongest winds, particularly in regions vulnerable to flash floods and landslides.
Authorities advise residents in potentially affected areas to follow official weather bulletins and emergency instructions as conditions evolve.
Mexico is regularly affected by tropical cyclones forming in the Pacific Ocean, particularly during the eastern Pacific hurricane season, which runs from May 15 to Nov. 30.
The country’s meteorological authorities monitor these systems and issue regular updates on their strength, movement and potential effects.
The storm’s development will determine whether additional precautions are needed along Mexico’s Pacific coastline.

Chile passes law establishing annual day of friendship and solidarity with Palestine
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
16:24:13 UTC
01:24:13 KST

Sixteen years after recognising the State of Palestine, Chile will mark its first official Day of Chilean-Palestinian Friendship and Solidarity on 7th January 2027, following the passage of a new law celebrating the historic ties between the two peoples.
Published in Chile’s Official Gazette on Thursday, 22nd October 2026, Law No. 21,843 officially designates 7 January as an annual day of friendship and solidarity with Palestine. The move also reaffirms Chile’s commitment to Palestinian human rights, going beyond a symbolic celebration of the longstanding relationship between the two countries.
The move goes beyond celebrating the historic friendship between the two peoples. It also reaffirms Chile’s commitment to protecting human rights, particularly those of the Palestinian people, in line with UN principles.
The legislation contains two articles. The first establishes 7th January as the annual day of friendship and solidarity between Chile and Palestine. The second provides for commemorative activities celebrating the relationship between the two peoples, while reaffirming Chile’s commitment to the United Nations’ universal human rights protection system.
“Commemorative activities may be held to celebrate friendship and solidarity between Chile and Palestine, reaffirming Chile’s commitment to UN human rights principles and the rights of the Palestinian people”.
First introduced in January 2024, the proposal later moved to the Senate, where several amendments were made before its approval. It then returned to the Chamber of Deputies for a final vote on 22nd September, where it secured majority support, paving the way for it to become law.
During parliamentary discussions, Senator Vlado Mirosevic Explained his support for the legislation, Mirosevic said: “I voted in favour of this bill because it speaks of something that is not foreign to Chile; it speaks of ourselves and our history.”
He emphasised that Palestinians and their descendants had contributed to Chile’s industrial, social and cultural development, while maintaining enduring connections with their ancestral homeland.
Senator Sergio Gahona similarly described the legislation as more than a symbolic gesture,“Voting on this initiative is not simply about setting a date on the calendar, but about profoundly recognising a community that forms an integral part of the soul of our country,” he told the Senate.
Gahona highlighted the contributions of families originally from Bethlehem, Beit Jala and Beit Sahour to Chile’s economic and social development.
The bill received broad support in Congress, securing 100 votes in the Chamber of Deputies and 30 in the Senate. Congresswoman Carolina Tello welcomed the new law, saying it would provide an opportunity to organise events, bring people together and raise awareness about human rights and respect for international law. “On 7 January, we will be able to hold activities and meetings that highlight the importance of human rights and respect for the international community,” she said.
Tello also expressed hope that the law would help raise awareness of the humanitarian crisis in Palestine and prevent similar tragedies elsewhere. “We are happy, and I hope this initiative will help prevent what we are witnessing in Palestine from happening in other parts of the world,” she said, adding: “No to genocide in Palestine.”
The Palestinian Embassy in Chile also welcomed the new law, describing it as an important milestone in relations between the two countries. In a statement shared on social media, the embassy celebrated the publication of Law No. 21,843 on 22 October, officially designating 7 January as the annual Day of Chilean-Palestinian Friendship and Solidarity.
“This law marks a milestone in relations between Chile and Palestine,” the embassy said, adding that it recognises the shared history and strong bonds between the two peoples.
The embassy said that the new annual commemoration would provide an opportunity to celebrate the longstanding friendship and solidarity between Chile and Palestine.
Why 7th January? The date was not chosen by chance. The date holds special meaning for both Chile and Palestine. On 7th January 2011, Chile officially recognised Palestine as an independent and sovereign state under former President Sebastián Piñera.
According to legislative records from the Library of the National Congress of Chile, commemorating this historic decision was a key aim of the initiative from the beginning, reflecting an important milestone in relations between the two countries.
During Senate discussions, Senator Matías Walker highlighted the significance of the date and reaffirmed Chile’s longstanding support for a peaceful settlement and a two-state solution in line with international resolutions.

By Humeyra Pamuk and Enas Alashray
Oct 24 (Reuters) - Iran has ramped up efforts to target US personnel, and lethal plots by Tehran against American citizens have reached “advanced stages”, a senior intelligence official in the Trump administration warned in a memo seen by Reuters.
The alert from Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton came after Washington scaled back staffing at its mission in Saudi Arabia earlier this week in response to intensified attacks by Iran-allied Houthi forces.
Those attacks on one front of the nearly eight-month-old regional conflict triggered by the Iran war have coincided with a rise in attacks on commercial shipping in the Strait of Hormuz.
Earlier this month, sources told Reuters Iran was preparing a more forceful response if the United States resumes large-scale military attacks on its territory.
“Specifically, through various channels, we have received intelligence that Iran has substantially increased efforts to target US personnel,” Clayton wrote to US Secretary of State Marco Rubio in a message dated October 23.
“The lethal plotting efforts by the Iranians against US citizens have reached advanced stages in both the Middle East and certain other countries,” he added.
CIA Director John Ratcliffe was also copied in on the unclassified memo which was first reported by Axios.
The State Department on Wednesday ordered non-emergency government employees and their family members to leave US diplomatic missions in Saudi Arabia and planned to withdraw family members from a number of other missions in the region, US officials told Reuters.
On Saturday, the US State Department updated travel advisories for more than a dozen countries across the Gulf and Middle East, including Saudi Arabia, Qatar, the United Arab Emirates, Iraq and Israel, citing an increased threat from Iran-aligned Houthis.
“When it comes to our staffing at embassies, we constantly evaluate new information about the security environment,” a US official said.
“The threat of Houthi attacks and of Iranian terror plots targeting US officials are informing our decisions on staffing adjustments for embassies on RO Status in the region,” the official said.
The Restricted Operations Status provides the State Department more flexibility in personnel decisions without having to publicly announce a change in the status of a mission.
The Iran war is a week away from entering its ninth month and has significantly weighed on the approval ratings of US President Donald Trump ahead of midterm elections on November 3.
(Reporting by Enas Alashray and Humeyra Pamuk; Editing by Ros Russell and Andrew Heavens)

Yemeni authorities have said that the Houthi militia targeted Aden International Airport, a port in the city’s al-Tawahi district and two coast guard facilities with ballistic missiles.
The information ministry reported renewed ballistic missile attacks on the airport and port in a post on X on Saturday, without providing details on casualties or damage.
Separately, the interior ministry said two ballistic missiles targeted the coast guard headquarters at the ministry’s compound, while a third targeted a coast guard building in the al-Tawahi district. 
Saudi Arabia and the internationally recognised Yemeni government have come under sustained attack from the Houthi militia.

The Houthi militia quickly claimed responsibility for the attack, saying it had targeted a naval base and a military camp overseen by Saudi forces.

His statement did not mention Aden International Airport or specify the weapons used.
The interior ministry said the strikes came after previous attacks on civilian and vital facilities in Aden, including repeated ballistic missile and drone attacks on the international airport.
It warned that targeting vital facilities and public infrastructure threatened the city’s security and stability, endangered civilians and affected institutions providing security and public services.
The Yemeni government and its allies hold Aden and large parts of the country’s southern and eastern provinces, while the Houthi militia control the capital Sanaa and much of northern and western Yemen.
Saudi Arabia has led a military coalition supporting Yemen's government against the Houthi militia since 2015.
Recent escalation between Yemen's government forces and the Houthi militia began in July as a 2022 ceasefire collapsed. 
The group has also targeted Saudi Arabia's energy and civilian sites.

China Focus: Rescue efforts continue after 7.0-magnitude quake in China's Xizang
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
00:12:46 CST
01:12:46 KST

A volunteer makes noodles at a quake-hit village in Maru Township of Baqen County, Nagqu City, southwest China's Xizang Autonomous Region, Oct. 24, 2026. As of 11 a.m. Saturday, 52,450 items or sets of disaster relief supplies had been sent to the quake zone, while more than 2,500 rescue personnel were engaged in relief operations. Authorities have established 35 temporary resettlement sites in the disaster zone. Medical treatment and public health and epidemic prevention efforts are proceeding in an orderly manner, according to the local emergency command headquarters. (Xinhua/Tenzin Nyida)
LHASA, Oct. 24 (Xinhua) -- Rescue and relief efforts continue after a 7.0-magnitude earthquake struck Baqen County of the city of Nagqu in southwest China's Xizang Autonomous Region, local authorities said Saturday.
The earthquake, which struck at 10:33 p.m. on Thursday, has left 16 people dead and 76 others injured. The quake has also damaged or destroyed 339 homes and 20 livestock sheds.
As of 11 a.m. Saturday, all 76 injured people were receiving timely medical treatment, with five of the 11 people initially classified as seriously injured having improved to a mild condition, according to the local emergency command headquarters.
Meanwhile, relief supplies and rescue personnel continue to arrive in the affected areas. As of 11 a.m. Saturday, 52,450 items or sets of disaster relief supplies had been sent to the quake zone, while more than 2,500 rescue personnel were engaged in relief operations.
The supplies include 4,651 tents, 2,000 prefabricated houses, 11,772 folding beds, 5,715 quilts and other cold-weather necessities. A large Wing Loong unmanned aerial vehicle has also arrived at the site.
Authorities have established 35 temporary resettlement sites in the disaster zone. More than 1,600 personnel from Baqen County, 347 firefighters from the Nagqu fire and rescue detachment, and 530 police officers from the Nagqu public security bureau have been deployed, alongside vehicles and search-and-rescue dogs.
Medical treatment and public health and epidemic prevention efforts are proceeding in an orderly manner, the headquarters said.
As of 2 p.m. Saturday, the headquarters said 949 aftershocks had been recorded in the affected areas, including eight measuring 4.0 to 4.9 in magnitude and 33 measuring 3.0 to 3.9.
All temporary speed restrictions on the quake-hit section of the Qinghai-Xizang Railway were lifted on Friday night, according to China Railway Qinghai-Xizang Group Co., Ltd. A comprehensive inspection found no abnormalities, and trains resumed normal operations, the company said.
Power supply in the quake-hit area was fully restored on Saturday night, according to the State Grid.
State Grid Xizang Electric Power Co., Ltd. urgently dispatched teams to the affected area for emergency power restoration after the quake, the state-owned utility said. More than 300 personnel along with vehicles, power generation facilities and emergency equipment have been deployed as of Saturday to ensure power supply for the on-site command center, provide lighting for resettlement sites and restore damaged power lines.
Local authorities said construction on the first batch of prefabricated houses in the quake-affected areas started at around 2 a.m. Saturday. As more units arrive, residents currently staying in tents will gradually move into the better-insulated temporary housing.
"We will ensure that affected residents have safe shelter, warm clothing and bedding, hot meals and clean drinking water," said Pan Zhiqing, Party chief of the Nagqu Municipal Emergency Management Bureau.
At a hospital in Baqen's neighboring Sog County, many injured residents were sent there for treatment overnight. The hospital has arranged medical treatment and prepared hot meals and daily necessities for patients.
Early Friday morning, Norbu Wangchen, a local resident in Sog County, brought more than 100 portions of Tibetan noodles, along with Tibetan tea and tsampa, to the hospital to help those affected by the earthquake.
Help also came from the city of Xigaze, some 700 kilometers away from Baqen.
Du Guoping, who was preparing to open two new restaurants in Xigaze, postponed the openings after learning of the earthquake and headed to the disaster zone with more than 1,500 kg of dumplings.
His team set off at midnight on the night of the earthquake. After a bumpy journey, the team purchased additional supplies, including food containers and bottled water, along the way.
After arriving, Du and his staff set up cooking equipment and prepared dumplings for rescue workers and affected residents. They worked during the day, and at night, the six team members squeezed into two vehicles to rest, keeping the heating on to ward off the high-altitude chill.
With more than 500 kg of dumplings still remaining, Du said the team planned to stay for at least three days to cook all the food they brought.
Watching firefighters, medical personnel and rescue teams race against time at the disaster site left a deep impression on him.
"We feel honored to be able to contribute in our own way," he said. ■

Iran has ramped up efforts to target US personnel, intelligence memo warns
- US intelligence says Iran has stepped up efforts to target US personnel, and “lethal plotting” against American citizens is at “advanced stages”, according to a memo from Jay Clayton.
- The warning came after the US cut staffing at its Saudi Arabia mission and updated travel advice for more than a dozen Gulf and Middle East countries because of rising Houthi threats.
- The wider Iran war is now nearing nine months and is adding pressure on President Donald Trump, with the conflict and regional attacks affecting US security and politics.
AI generated
WASHINGTON - Iran has ramped up efforts to target US personnel, and lethal plots by Tehran against American citizens have reached “advanced stages”, a senior intelligence official in the Trump administration warned in a memo seen by Reuters.
The alert from director of national intelligence Jay Clayton came after Washington scaled back staffing at its mission in Saudi Arabia earlier this week in response to intensified attacks by Iran-allied Houthi forces.
Those attacks on one front of the nearly eight-month-old regional conflict triggered by the Iran war have coincided with a rise in attacks on commercial shipping in the Strait of Hormuz.
Earlier this month, sources told Reuters Iran was preparing a more forceful response if the United States resumes large-scale military attacks on its territory.
“Specifically, through various channels, we have received intelligence that Iran has substantially increased efforts to target US personnel,” Clayton wrote to US Secretary of State Marco Rubio in a message dated Oct 23.
“The lethal plotting efforts by the Iranians against US citizens have reached advanced stages in both the Middle East and certain other countries,” he added.
CIA director John Ratcliffe was also copied in on the unclassified memo which was first reported by Axios.
The State Department on Oct 21 ordered non-emergency government employees and their family members to leave US diplomatic missions in Saudi Arabia and planned to withdraw family members from a number of other missions in the region, US officials told Reuters.
On Oct 24, the US State Department updated travel advisories for more than a dozen countries across the Gulf and Middle East, including Saudi Arabia, Qatar, the United Arab Emirates, Iraq and Israel, citing an increased threat from Iran-aligned Houthis.
“When it comes to our staffing at embassies, we constantly evaluate new information about the security environment,” a US official said.
“The threat of Houthi attacks and of Iranian terror plots targeting US officials are informing our decisions on staffing adjustments for embassies on RO Status in the region,” the official said.
The Restricted Operations Status provides the State Department more flexibility in personnel decisions without having to publicly announce a change in the status of a mission.
The Iran war is a week away from entering its ninth month and has significantly weighed on the approval ratings of US President Donald Trump ahead of midterm elections on Nov 3. REUTERS

What to know about Melania Trump’s Oleshky ceasefire deal
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
16:04:52 UTC
01:04:52 KST

Breadcrumb
What to know about the Melania Trump-brokered ceasefire in Russian-occupied Oleshky
A small city in southern Ukraine, cut off for months by fighting, is set to get a brief pause in the 4 1/2-year-old war so that aid can get in and residents can get out.
US First Lady Melania Trump brokered the localised ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine around Oleshky, a Russian-occupied city she said is "on the brink of disaster."
Ukrainian, Russian and US negotiators reached the deal Friday. Officials on all sides have confirmed it, but they have not released many details.
Oleshky has been without power, heat or water
Oleshky is located in Ukraine's partially occupied Kherson region. It sits on the Dnipro River, which separates Ukrainian forces from the city's Russian occupiers. Moscow's forces captured it on the first day of the full-scale invasion in February 2022. Its buildings were shelled and burned.
In June 2023, floodwaters swamped the city after the Kakhovka Dam collapsed in an explosion that an Associated Press investigation found was likely caused by the Russian military. Hundreds of residents were killed.
Once home to about 24,000 people, the city has had scarce food and medical supplies for months. There is no electricity, heat or running water. Roads out of town are mined and lined with burned-out cars, and drones buzz overhead. With another harsh winter approaching, those still there face death from hunger or disease.
Ukraine has repeatedly appealed for a local ceasefire to organise evacuations. As the occupying power, Russia is obligated under international law to make sure civilians under its control have what they need to survive.
Ceasefire, aid, then evacuations
The deal sets out three stages: a ceasefire, then humanitarian aid delivery, then the evacuation of civilians who want to leave Oleshky, according to Dmytro Lubinets, Ukraine's human rights ombudsman and chief negotiator in the talks.
Before any aid moves, Lubinets said, mines will be cleared on the routes into the city.
Russia's human rights ombudswoman, Yana Lantratova, who took part in the negotiations, said they plan to establish what residents need and then deliver food, medicine, hygiene products and other essentials. She said anyone who wants to leave the combat zone will be guaranteed safe passage.
The pause begins Tuesday and will last several days
Lubinets told the AP that the ceasefire will begin Tuesday, two days before the humanitarian mission starts, and will last several days.
Russia's chief of the general staff, Gen. Valery Gerasimov, said Russian forces "will cease fire on the Kherson axis" from 4 AM Tuesday Moscow time, which is late Monday in the United States. He said Russian forces would also carry out "engineering reconnaissance" and ensure the "humanitarian convoy" can move safely into the city.
Ukraine's General Staff said the ceasefire will begin at 3 AM Tuesday Kyiv time, since Ukraine moves its clocks back an hour on Sunday while Russia does not.
Lubinets said the pause would apply across the Kherson region and neighbouring areas essential to the operation.
Key details have not been released 
Lubinets gave no details on how the ceasefire or the aid mission would be monitored or carried out, citing the sensitivity of the negotiations. He declined to say whether Melania Trump would travel to Ukraine.
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said people who want to leave Oleshky can do so. He would not say whether they would be taken to Russian- or Ukrainian-held territory. Asked how long the evacuation would last, he said only that it would most likely take several days.
"The operation will be carried out gradually and is extremely challenging to implement," Lubinets said.
The first lady took up the issue at the UN
The first lady began talks on Oleshky after she heard about the situation at one of her events during the UN General Assembly session in September, the White House said. She and a representative then worked directly with Russian and Ukrainian leadership to set the terms. She had already been working with officials from both countries on a separate matter.
"When Melania Trump learned about the situation in Oleshky, the negotiation process began under her coordination," Lubinets said. He said the sides spent several weeks discussing ideas and developing "new approaches, mechanisms and tools" to help civilians there survive.
Helping children in conflict zones has become one of her signature issues during her husband's second term. She hosted a UN Security Council meeting on the issue earlier this year.
Last year she wrote to Russian President Vladimir Putin about efforts to reunite families with children she described as "displaced by the war." Her senior adviser, Marc Beckman, says she has helped reunite nearly three dozen children.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has lobbied various world leaders for help reuniting children he says were taken by Russia after the invasion began in 2022. The International Criminal Court in 2023 issued an arrest warrant for Putin for war crimes, accusing him of personal responsibility for the abductions of children from Ukraine.
Tensions between Washington and Kyiv are rising
The development comes as tensions have increased to new highs between the Trump administration and Ukraine's government. Kyiv has faced restrictions on the satellite internet system it relies on to knock down Russian attacks, with President Donald Trump and other top US officials sending mixed messages about who was responsible for throttling the Elon Musk-made Starshield system.
Trump also recently waived new Russia sanctions, agreed with Russia to import diesel fuel, and pushed Zelenskyy to make a deal to end the war. In renewed efforts to revive the peace process, Trump envoy Steve Witkoff travelled to Norway this week for talks with Zelenskyy before meeting Putin in St. Petersburg, Russia.
Zelenskyy did not mention the Oleshky ceasefire during a remote appearance at the Hudson Institute, a Washington think tank, on Friday. He did note that American Patriot missile interceptors were still on hold.
He also stressed the importance of the United States in renewed diplomatic efforts to end the war, including a possible joint meeting with Trump and Putin.

Are Lebanese Shi'ites abandoning Hezbollah? Poll shows majority favor disarming group - analysis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
16:01:01 UTC
01:01:01 KST

Hezbollah may face growing criticism from within Lebanon's Shi’ite community, which has formed the backbone of its support for decades, according to a report from KAN on Saturday.
A recent survey of Shi’ites got attention in regional media. As reported by Israel's KAN public broadcaster and the Lebanese Kataeb.org website, the survey, whose results emerged in mid-October, suggested that many Shi'ites are increasingly questioning the terrorist group.
The main question is whether Hezbollah should keep its arsenal. People also questioned Hezbollah’s conduct in the wars with Israel. However, this did not necessarily mean that Hezbollah is losing its influence over the community.
Respondents said decisions regarding war and peace should be left to the Lebanese state
The survey, conducted by Statistics Lebanon in September among 800 Lebanese Shi'ites, found that 66.4% supported transferring Hezbollah's weapons to the Lebanese state. Another 29.6% preferred that the terrorist organization retain its weapons. The results were significant because Hezbollah has argued that its arsenal is essential for defending Lebanon against Israel.
Roi Kais at Israel’s KAN noted, “A new survey has revealed that about 66 percent of Lebanese Shi'ites support Hezbollah's transfer of weapons to the state, and more than 40 percent express anger and disappointment with its leadership. Amid growing criticism, the support networks and status the terrorist organization has given the sect still maintain its power - as long as no other entity fills the vacuum.”
Notably, Kataeb.org, the website of the Phalange Party (Kataeb Party), a political party in Lebanon, published details on the survey. The Christian Kataeb Party opposes Hezbollah. The website noted that 71.1% of respondents believed that decisions about war and peace should rest exclusively with the Lebanese state. Only 5.9% believed Hezbollah's leadership should have a greater role in determining Lebanon's future.
Only 16.5% of respondents had confidence in Hezbollah's ability to guarantee security
The survey also revealed considerable confidence in the Lebanese Armed Forces. Some 78.5% expressed trust in the army, while 51.1% identified it as the institution best suited to guarantee long-term security. Only 16.5% selected Hezbollah.
These findings raised questions about Hezbollah's traditional claim to represent the security interests of Lebanon's Shi'ites. They suggested that many within the community may prefer stronger state institutions, even if they continue to identify politically or socially with Hezbollah.
The survey also found that 67.4% believed Hezbollah had either failed to achieve its objectives in the war with Israel or had achieved only some of them. Another 42.1% expressed disappointment, anger or concern about Hezbollah's leadership and the consequences of the conflict. Nevertheless, 59.5% continued to express varying degrees of trust in Hezbollah, including 37.1% who reported a great deal of trust.
An earlier survey presented a very different picture. In a June 10 analysis published by Israel's Institute for National Security Studies (INSS), researchers Orna Mizrahi and Moran Levanoni cited a May 2026 survey by Lebanon's Information International in which 87.5% of Shiite respondents opposed disarming Hezbollah, while only 7.9% supported surrendering its weapons. More than 90% opposed ties with Israel.
The contrast with the September findings led to many questions. How can people hold such different views? Is it possible that some of the surveys are biased in their questions or agendas?
Mizrahi and Levanoni argued that Hezbollah's influence rests on its social and economic networks, political power, and the historical marginalization of Lebanon's Shi'ites.
They also noted that intimidation has discouraged opposition within the Shi’ite community. The researchers suggested that weakening Hezbollah's influence would require a stronger Lebanese army and Western and Gulf financial assistance to enable the state to replace Hezbollah's services.
This illustrated the complex relationship between Hezbollah and Lebanon's Shi'ites. Hezbollah is not just a terrorist group. It built networks of social services, financial institutions, and political influence to hedge its bets and take over the Lebanese state.
Now that it is so powerful, it is hard to uproot. Many people in Lebanon feared opposing Hezbollah over the years. For some Shi’ite families, it remains an important source of employment and assistance, even if they have to sacrifice their security due to the wars that Hezbollah has caused.
Lebanese fear Hezbollah-linked facilities could become Israeli targets
KAN highlighted an example from the southern Lebanese city of Tyre, where property owners reportedly opposed opening a branch of Hezbollah-linked financial institution Al-Qard Al-Hassan in their building. They feared the branch could become a target for Israeli strikes. The branches have been targeted in the past.
Hezbollah is attempting to regain support through reconstruction assistance. According to KAN, Hezbollah recently announced aid of up to $14,000 for eligible families in Beirut and its southern suburbs whose primary homes were destroyed, and up to $12,000 elsewhere.
The broader question is whether dissatisfaction will translate into political change. Hezbollah has suffered significant military and leadership losses since the war began, including the killing of Hassan Nasrallah in September 2024.
Yet its influence is rooted in decades of political and social organization. Lebanon did not jump at the opportunity to uproot the group in 2025. In March 2026, a new war broke out, leading to massive destruction of villages in southern Lebanon. Even today, Beirut moves at a snail’s pace.
The survey suggests that support for Hezbollah's terrorist role may be weakening even among its traditional constituency. However, unless the Lebanese state can provide security, reconstruction, and economic opportunities, the criticism won’t lead to major change.

Iran-backed militias in Iraq accuse US of violating airspace, as threats grow - analysis

Iran-backed militias in Iraq accused the United States of violating Iraqi airspace. The statement comes amid tensions between the Iraqi government and Iran-backed militias over efforts to bring weapons under state control, according to a report by Rudaw.
"Standing with the forces of righteousness against the forces of evil is a duty dictated by sound human nature," the IRI said, according to Rudaw. The group sees the conflict involving Iran as a struggle against the US and Israel. The IRI has attacked Israel in the past during the conflict in Gaza.
The Islamic Resistance in Iraq, an umbrella group of Iran-backed militias, continues to support Iran. The group issued a statement amid speculation about a possible new war with Iran.
The militias also accused Baghdad of appeasing the US due to Washington’s pressure on Iraq. The IRI is unhappy that Baghdad has been reducing commercial flights and closing border crossings with Iran. The IRI claimed to have documented 171 violations of Iraqi airspace by US fighter jets and reconnaissance aircraft between September 30 and Friday. The allegations were not independently verified.
The accusations come after the US-led anti-ISIS coalition formally ended its military mission in Iraq on September 30. Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi has sought to use the transition to bring militia weapons under government control. However, several powerful factions have rejected the initiative. The plan is set to take effect by June 2027. Some militias have agreed, while others have rejected the policy.
Some militias opposed to disarmament, others willing to cooperate
According to Rudaw, Kataib Hezbollah and Harakat al-Nujaba remain opposed to disarmament, while Harakat Ansar Allah al-Awfiya and Kataib Sayyid al-Shuhada have expressed willingness to cooperate with government measures.
Zaidi has extended the disarmament deadline to June 30, 2027, by which time "no weapons will remain outside the framework of the state," he said in an interview with Iraqi state media, quoted by Rudaw.
The dispute illustrates a central challenge facing Iraq. Even after the US-led coalition's withdrawal, Iran-backed factions continue to portray their weapons as necessary for confronting Washington and Israel. This puts them increasingly at odds with Baghdad's efforts to assert state authority over armed groups.
The tensions come as the US State Department has warned of increasing regional threats that could affect security in Iraq. On Saturday, the US Embassy in Iraq published an update to the State Department's travel advisory, citing the threat of increased attacks by the Iranian-backed Houthis. The warnings also cite terrorist threats in Iraq, including those posed by Iran-backed militias.
The advisory maintained the existing warning against all travel to Iraq. It noted that Houthi attacks against Saudi Arabia, including strikes on civilian airports and critical infrastructure, could lead to wider regional escalation.
"The hostilities have the potential to escalate rapidly beyond that immediate area," the State Department warned. It also noted that "the Iraqi government cannot guarantee the safety of US citizens against sudden outbreaks of violence and armed conflict."
The advisory specifically highlighted threats from armed groups inside Iraq. "Terrorists, including ISIS and Iran-aligned militias, encourage and conduct attacks against US persons and interests in Iraq," the State Department said.
State Department warns of threats to US citizens, companies
It also warned that militias threaten American citizens and international companies, citing attacks involving drones, indirect fire, and improvised explosive devices. Potential targets include airports, energy infrastructure, hotels, and diplomatic facilities.
The warning illustrates the broader security challenges facing Baghdad. While the Iraqi government seeks to consolidate control over armed factions, Washington continues to view Iran-aligned militias as a threat. The escalation involving the Houthis also highlights how regional conflicts could further complicate Iraq's efforts to maintain stability and avoid being drawn into new confrontations.
The tensions in Iraq come amid other developments involving Iran and Iranian-backed groups across the region. On Saturday, Rudaw reported that US intelligence had warned of increased Iranian efforts to assassinate American diplomats and officials in the Middle East and elsewhere. Citing an Axios report, Rudaw said a memorandum dated Friday from US National Intelligence Director Jay Clayton to Secretary of State Marco Rubio warned that some alleged Iranian plots had reached advanced stages. The report comes as Washington reduces staffing at several embassies amid concerns about regional escalation.
Meanwhile, Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) said on Saturday that it had targeted a gathering center belonging to the Kurdistan Free Life Party (PJAK), an Iranian Kurdish opposition group. The attack took place in Iran but could have implications for Iraq, where Tehran has previously targeted Iranian Kurdish opposition groups. According to Rudaw, clashes between the IRGC and PJAK's armed wing, the Eastern Kurdistan Units (YRK), have intensified over the last week. Iran has used drones and artillery against mountainous areas where the Kurdish fighters operate. Iran's Mehr News Agency described the latest operation as a preemptive strike against PJAK members allegedly preparing attacks.
These developments also come as Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi continues to insist that his government will end the presence of armed factions operating outside state control. In an interview quoted by Rudaw on Friday, Zaidi said that "Iraq will soon, God willing, be a state free of factions, like other countries in the world, and weapons will be exclusively in the hands of the Iraqi security forces."
The developments illustrate the competing pressures facing Iraq. Baghdad wants to consolidate state authority over armed groups, but Iran-backed militias continue to see themselves as part of a wider regional confrontation with the US and Israel. At the same time, Iran's operations against Kurdish opposition groups and reports of threats to American officials suggest that tensions could spread across several fronts.
One example of Baghdad's progress is a new agreement with a Yazidi armed group called YBS in Sinjar in northern Iraq. Baghdad also says it has reached a deal with Turkey for Ankara to leave a base near Bashiqa. However, these may be low-hanging fruit because Iran-backed militias are, in some ways, more powerful. Iran shares a long border with Iraq. It views Iraq as a "near abroad," basically meaning it feels it should control Iraq. It has carried out 1,000 attacks on the Kurdistan Region of Iraq, but also 600 on the rest of Iraq, using militias in some attacks.
For Iraq, the challenge is not only disarming militias. It is also preventing the country from becoming a battleground in a wider regional conflict. The coming months will test whether Zaidi can turn his government's commitments into reality, particularly as the June 2027 deadline approaches.

Emotional struggles are linked to vulnerable narcissism but not grandiose narcissism, meta-analysis finds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
16:00:50 UTC
01:00:50 KST

A new statistical review of data from more than 12,000 adults suggests that difficulties with managing emotions are moderately linked to one specific form of narcissism, while showing virtually no connection to another. The research, published in Personality and Individual Differences, indicates that people with insecure and defensive narcissistic traits tend to struggle with emotional control, whereas those with more boastful, dominant narcissistic traits generally do not report these same struggles. These findings help clarify why past studies on narcissism and emotional health have produced conflicting results, and they may point to specific emotional skills that could be targeted in therapy.
In psychology, trait narcissism refers to a persistent pattern of personality characteristics centered on interpersonal antagonism, which includes feeling entitled, manipulating others, and lacking empathy. Rather than being a single uniform trait, narcissism is generally divided into two main subtypes: grandiose and vulnerable. Grandiose narcissism matches the common stereotype of a narcissist, featuring an outgoing, dominant, attention-seeking, and aggressively self-confident style. Vulnerable narcissism, while sharing the same core of entitlement and self-centeredness, looks very different on the surface, involving introversion, fragile self-esteem, deep feelings of inadequacy, and a heightened sensitivity to rejection.
Both forms of narcissism are associated with problems in relationships, including a lack of care for a partner’s distress, relationship dissatisfaction, and even intimate partner violence; a 2024 meta-analysis found that violence was more strongly tied to vulnerable narcissism (a correlation of 0.25) than to grandiose narcissism (0.11). Because personality traits themselves are deeply ingrained and difficult to change, psychologists often look for modifiable behaviors and skills that might help improve how narcissistic individuals function in daily life. One promising target is emotion dysregulation, which refers to difficulty understanding, managing, and responding to feelings in a healthy way that aligns with a person’s goals and social norms.
“Our broader interest in this area stems from wanting to understand the psychological factors that contribute to the interpersonal difficulties experienced by people with high levels of narcissism,” senior author Megan L. Willis, an associate professor in the School of Behavioural and Health Sciences and the Healthy Brain and Mind Research Centre at Australian Catholic University, told PsyPost. “I’m particularly interested in factors that may be modifiable – that is, things that we may be able to prevent or improve through psychological intervention.”
When psychologists study emotion dysregulation, they often look at several distinct areas where a person’s emotional control can break down. These areas include refusing to accept negative feelings, lacking awareness or clarity about what emotion is actually occurring, struggling to stay focused on tasks when upset, failing to control impulsive behaviors during distress, and lacking effective strategies to calm down. Studies linking narcissism to these emotional difficulties have produced confusing results, with some finding that narcissistic people had worse emotional control and others finding no link or even better emotional control.
Psychologists began to suspect that these contradictions happened because studies were measuring different subtypes of narcissism. For instance, a 2017 study of Chinese university students found that students with vulnerable narcissistic traits reported substantial trouble managing their emotions, while those with grandiose traits actually reported fewer emotional difficulties, which the authors linked to their higher self-esteem. Similarly, a 2020 study of undergraduates indicated that the defensive, self-protective side of narcissism was tied to poor emotion recognition and messy emotional reactions, whereas the assertive, self-promoting side was linked to better emotional management.
To make sense of the growing body of research, a 2024 systematic review summarized the existing literature and observed a consistent link between vulnerable narcissism and emotional struggles, alongside a lack of evidence connecting grandiose narcissism to those same struggles. However, that earlier review only summarized the studies qualitatively rather than mathematically combining their data, and it mixed psychiatric patients with the general public, which can weaken the correlations researchers observe. Willis, lead author Ria Tziliaskopoulos, and their colleagues at Australian Catholic University set out to conduct a full meta-analysis, a statistical technique that pools data from multiple studies to estimate the strength of the relationship between narcissism and emotion dysregulation in the general adult population.
“We wanted to establish the strength of the relationship between emotion dysregulation and narcissism in general, as well as determine whether this relationship differed between grandiose and vulnerable narcissism,” Willis explained.
The researchers searched five major academic databases through January 2026 to find studies written in English that measured both trait narcissism and emotion dysregulation in adults outside clinical settings. They excluded studies focusing on children or specialized groups like psychiatric patients or prison inmates, ensuring the results would reflect everyday adult populations. This screening process yielded 26 eligible studies from 25 reports, encompassing a combined total of 12,209 participants with average ages ranging from 18.7 to 62 years across countries including the United States, Italy, Turkey, China, Iran, and Brazil.
Because each included study used questionnaires to measure personality and emotional habits, the authors categorized the narcissism questionnaires into three groups: those measuring grandiose narcissism, those measuring vulnerable narcissism, and “combined” measures that blended both traits into a single score. For instance, the widely used Narcissistic Personality Inventory counted as a grandiose measure and the Hypersensitive Narcissism Scale as a vulnerable one, while the 2020 undergraduate study’s self-promoting “admiration” scale was counted as grandiose and its defensive “rivalry” scale as vulnerable.
Twenty-two of the 26 studies measured emotional difficulties using a standard questionnaire called the Difficulties in Emotion Regulation Scale, which scores both overall dysregulation and the six specific problem areas like impulse control and emotional awareness. The researchers extracted 80 individual statistical correlations from the 26 studies and used a method called robust variance estimation to account for the fact that several studies contributed multiple data points from the same group of people.
In statistical terms, a correlation ranges from -1 to 1, where 0 means no relationship, positive values mean two traits tend to rise together, and negative values mean one tends to fall as the other rises. By common convention, values of about 0.10 to 0.29 are considered weak, 0.30 to 0.49 moderate, and 0.50 or above strong. When the researchers pooled all 80 data points together without separating the narcissism subtypes, they found a weak positive correlation of 0.15 between overall narcissism and emotion dysregulation. This meant that across the entire dataset, higher levels of narcissism were only slightly associated with greater trouble managing emotions.
When the team broke the data down by narcissism subtype, a sharp divide emerged that helps explain why the overall correlation was so small. Vulnerable narcissism showed a moderate positive correlation of 0.37 with emotion dysregulation across 11 studies. In contrast, grandiose narcissism showed a correlation of 0.04 across 21 studies, a number so close to zero that it was not statistically significant.
“The relationship with vulnerable narcissism was moderate in size, which is quite a meaningful relationship in individual differences research,” Willis noted. “Narcissism reflects a cluster of personality traits, so we wouldn’t expect any single psychological factor to explain it. The size of the relationship suggests that difficulties regulating emotions are an important part of the psychological profile of people high in vulnerable narcissism.”
Measures that combined both forms of narcissism fell right in the middle, showing a weak positive correlation of 0.25 across five studies. Follow-up statistical comparisons confirmed that the link between vulnerable narcissism and emotional difficulties was substantially stronger than the link for grandiose narcissism. The authors also checked whether a few debatable coding choices drove the results. Dropping the grandiose scale of the Pathological Narcissism Inventory, which critics say overlaps too much with vulnerable traits, left grandiose narcissism at 0.03, and dropping the one study that counted the defensive “rivalry” scale as vulnerable narcissism left vulnerable narcissism at 0.37.
“The findings may help explain some of the interpersonal difficulties experienced by people high in vulnerable narcissism,” Willis said. “They tend to be hypersensitive to rejection and criticism, and our findings suggest they are also more likely to have difficulty regulating their emotions. When they feel rejected or criticized, they may struggle to manage the emotions that arise in these situations. This could contribute to hostile or aggressive responses, which can create conflict and damage their relationships with others.”
The researchers then examined the four or five studies that reported scores for each of the six domains of emotional difficulty, pooling all types of narcissism together. They found weak but statistically reliable correlations with three specific problem areas: limited access to effective emotion regulation strategies had a correlation of 0.21, trouble controlling impulses when upset had a correlation of 0.19, and refusing to accept negative emotions had a correlation of 0.18. Meanwhile, narcissism was not statistically linked to lacking emotional awareness (which had a slight negative correlation of -0.08), lacking emotional clarity (0.13), or struggling to focus on goal-directed behaviors when distressed (0.13). The link with emotional awareness was weaker than the link with every other domain.
The authors suggest this pattern means the emotional struggles tied to narcissism may be less about failing to notice feelings and more about how a person reacts once an unpleasant emotion arrives, such as struggling to accept the feeling, acting impulsively, or feeling there is no healthy way to calm down. Because these analyses drew on only a handful of studies and combined all forms of narcissism, they cannot show whether the pattern differs between grandiose and vulnerable traits. The authors note that these specific breakdowns could help explain why people high in narcissism may lash out, blame others, or withdraw during relationship conflicts.
These results align with a study covered by PsyPost in 2024, which also found that emotion dysregulation was tied to vulnerable rather than grandiose narcissism, although that earlier study tested psychiatric outpatients rather than the general adult samples analyzed in the new review.
The findings sit in partial tension with the 2020 study of undergraduates described earlier, which PsyPost covered in 2019, where the self-promoting side of grandiose narcissism was linked to fewer emotional difficulties and better emotional awareness. The meta-analysis included that study but counted its defensive rivalry scale as vulnerable narcissism, and across all the grandiose questionnaires combined, it found no link either way rather than a protective one.
The absence of a link for grandiose narcissism also contrasts with research covered by PsyPost earlier in 2026, which tied both grandiose and vulnerable traits to brain differences connected to hiding one’s feelings. That difference may reflect what was measured: the brain study looked at the specific habit of suppressing outward emotional expressions, while the meta-analysis assessed broader difficulties managing emotions.
As with all research, there are some caveats to keep in mind when interpreting these findings. Every study included in the meta-analysis relied on self-report questionnaires, which depend on participants being both honest and self-aware about their flaws. The authors point to a 2023 study that recorded facial muscle activity and found amplified emotional reactions to negative social evaluation among people with grandiose traits, suggesting questionnaires may miss some of their emotional responses.
“I also wouldn’t interpret the lack of a relationship with grandiose narcissism as definitive evidence that people high in grandiose narcissism don’t experience difficulties regulating their emotions,” Willis cautioned. “All of the studies relied on self-report measures, and people high in grandiose narcissism may be less likely to perceive or report difficulties with emotion regulation.”
All 26 studies also used cross-sectional designs, measuring personality and emotional habits at a single point in time. In addition, half of the studies (13 of 26) recruited only university students, and most were conducted in Western nations, meaning the findings may not apply equally to older adults or different cultural contexts.
“The main caveat is that all of the studies included in our meta-analysis were cross-sectional, so we can’t determine the direction of the relationship,” Willis said. “Difficulties regulating emotions may contribute to the development or maintenance of vulnerable narcissism, vulnerable narcissism may contribute to difficulties regulating emotions, or other factors may explain this relationship.”
One such shared factor the authors raise is early experience: vulnerable narcissism has been theorized to arise partly from childhood trauma or inconsistent parenting, which may also hinder the development of emotional skills. Results also varied widely from study to study, so the pooled correlations are best read as averages rather than as figures that apply equally to every group or questionnaire. Several statistical checks did suggest the findings were unlikely to be skewed by publication bias, the tendency for studies with positive results to be published more often.
Another limitation is that too few studies reported detailed breakdowns of the six emotional problem areas to allow the authors to test grandiose and vulnerable narcissism separately for each specific skill. The authors recommend that future studies routinely report data for all individual emotion regulation subscales alongside total scores, use longitudinal designs that follow people over time, and recruit more diverse samples across cultures and age groups. Even with these limitations, the authors suggest that therapies focused on emotion regulation, such as dialectical behavior therapy or schema therapy, may be worth testing for people high in vulnerable narcissism, though studies have yet to show whether such treatment improves their well-being or relationships.
Looking ahead, the research team is now examining the roots of these traits and how emotional habits take shape over time. In psychology, insecure attachment refers to relationship patterns characterized by anxiety or avoidance that often stem from inconsistent caregiving early in life.
“One of the things I’m particularly interested in now is understanding how vulnerable narcissism may develop,” Willis told PsyPost. “We’re currently testing models looking at the potential role of insecure attachment and difficulties identifying, understanding and regulating emotions. Ultimately, we want to identify potentially modifiable factors that could be targeted through prevention or intervention strategies.”
The study, “The relationship between narcissism and emotion dysregulation: A systematic review and meta-analysis,” was authored by Ria Tziliaskopoulos, Rose Ferguson, Wendy Song, and Megan L. Willis.

After intense and relentless shelling was heard from MSF’s base in Sittwe, Rakhine State, Myanmar, alongside exchanges of gunfire and the sound of aircraft overhead, our team in central Sittwe learned yesterday, 23 October, that at least two people were killed and 17 others injured in this latest escalation.

Paul Brockmann, MSF Operations Manager for Myanmar
All warring parties must make every effort to protect civilians, in line with their obligations under international humanitarian law.

Protector drone flight over Channel was not for Home Office
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
17:00:15 BST
01:00:15 KST

An RAF Protector RG-1 that flew over the English Channel on 14 October was operating in support of defence aims and not in support of the Home Office, according to an answer given in Parliament.
Ben Obese-Jecty, the Conservative member for Huntingdon, had asked for what reason the aircraft was tasked to support the Home Office in the Channel on that date.
Louise Sandher-Jones, the Minister for the Armed Forces, said: “The Ministry of Defence regularly and routinely monitors our waters to protect UK interests, contribute to domestic maritime security, and act as a deterrent against potentially malign activities.
“The deployment the hon. Member refers to was conducted in support of Defence aims, not in support of the Home Office.”
Protector RG-1 is the RAF’s version of the General Atomics MQ-9B SkyGuardian, and the United Kingdom has ordered sixteen of them to replace the MQ-9A Reaper fleet that was retired after two decades of operations over Afghanistan, Iraq and Syria. The aircraft has a wingspan of around twenty four metres, an endurance of more than thirty hours and a maximum altitude above forty thousand feet, and carries Brimstone 3 missiles and Paveway IV bombs alongside its electro-optical and infrared sensors and a maritime search radar.
The aircraft is built to a NATO airworthiness standard and fitted with a detect and avoid system, lightning protection and de-icing, and that certification allows it to fly in unsegregated British airspace alongside civil traffic without a reserved block of sky being set aside for it. The Reaper it replaced could not, and needed segregated airspace or a danger area for every domestic sortie. The fleet is based at RAF Waddington in Lincolnshire with 31 Squadron, and operations are flown from ground control stations on the station.
Surveillance of small boat crossings in the Channel has been contracted out by the Home Office to a commercial operator. The Portuguese company Tekever has operated its AR5 maritime surveillance aircraft over the Channel since 2020 under Home Office contracts, a framework worth up to £1 billion and renewed repeatedly since. The AR5 is a twin-engine fixed-wing aircraft that flies for more than twelve hours and carries maritime and synthetic aperture radars, day and night cameras and receivers for vessel identification and distress beacons.
Paul Webb, managing director of Tekever UK, has said of the work that “drones can identify humans in distress in a much faster way and help rescue teams.” The company has since sold the same system to the Portuguese government and has expanded into supplying uncrewed aircraft to Ukraine.
