The limits of American power: Trump’s reckless gamble against Iran
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
15:54:08 UTC
00:54:08 KST

The limits of American power: Trump’s reckless gamble against Iran
TEHRAN - The U.S.-Israeli war against Iran has exposed the limits of American military power and the dangers of an administration that appears to have mistaken technological superiority for the ability to dictate political outcomes, William H. McRaven, who served in the U.S. Navy, wrote in Foreign Affairs.
Launched on February 28 without a clearly defined rationale or attainable objectives, the war illustrates Washington’s persistent failure to learn from the costly experiences of Vietnam, Afghanistan, and Iraq.
From the outset, the Trump administration’s objectives have been inconsistent. Initially, Washington spoke of regime change and eliminating Iran’s nuclear ambitions. Later, reopening the Strait of Hormuz became a central priority, even though the waterway had not been closed before the war began. Trump’s contradictory statements about these objectives have raised serious questions about whether his administration had a coherent strategy or adequately considered the consequences of military action.
“The war was launched without a clear rationale and with a constantly shifting set of objectives—from changing Tehran’s regime and squelching its nuclear ambitions to, more recently, reopening the Strait of Hormuz, which wasn’t closed until the war started. The results, not surprisingly, have been bad both for U.S. interests and for the Middle East,” McRaven stated.
At the heart of this failure lies an enduring American illusion: that overwhelming military superiority can overcome political, geographical, and strategic realities. Advanced aircraft, precision weapons, and sophisticated intelligence systems can inflict enormous damage, but they cannot automatically force a determined adversary to surrender or produce the political changes Washington desires. Iran’s geography, its capacity to challenge shipping through the strategically vital Strait of Hormuz, and its determination to resist foreign aggression all place significant limits on the effectiveness of American military power.
The administration’s approach has also undermined its international standing. According to the analysis, Washington launched the war without first building international legitimacy or consulting its allies, including neighboring Arab states. Its failure to acknowledge responsibility for an airstrike that reportedly killed 120 students at an Iranian elementary school further damaged its moral credibility. When Trump subsequently sought international assistance to reopen the Strait of Hormuz, the administration encountered resistance from countries whose support it had failed to cultivate.
Such miscalculations reflect a broader problem in American policymaking: the growing concentration of presidential power and the politicization of institutions responsible for providing independent military, diplomatic, and intelligence advice. When personal loyalty takes precedence over professional judgment, warnings about the costs and risks of war may be ignored. The result can be a dangerous cycle in which overconfidence produces reckless decisions, and those decisions generate consequences that military force alone cannot reverse.
The experiences of Vietnam, Afghanistan, and Iraq should have taught Washington that wars without clear objectives, broad international support, and realistic exit strategies can become prolonged strategic failures. Yet the Trump administration appears to have repeated these mistakes, underestimating both Iran’s capacity to resist and the broader regional consequences of attacking it.
Ultimately, the war underscores a fundamental truth: military supremacy does not amount to unlimited political power. Geography, national resistance, international legitimacy, and the quality of leadership remain decisive factors in determining the outcome of conflicts. The central lesson is clear: no amount of firepower can compensate for a reckless strategy, contradictory objectives, and a failure to understand the adversary.

More than 2,000 forced from homes in Hebron amid Israel’s West Bank raids
Palestinians in Hebron are ‘living in fear’ with the city closed, while Israeli forces arrest dozens across the West Bank.
Israel has imposed a lockdown and displaced thousands of Palestinians from their homes in Hebron, as the military conducts raids in the occupied West Bank following the deaths of two Israeli soldiers.
This comes as the Palestinian Authority on Saturday called for international pressure on Israel to protect Hebron’s residents, who said soldiers announced forced evacuation orders over loudspeakers late at night, leaving them with no time to prepare and few places to move to.
Hebron’s Mayor Yousef al-Ja’bari told Al Jazeera on Saturday that 2,200 people had been forced from their homes by Israeli troops and raids.
Later on Saturday, Israel’s defence minister confirmed that “about 2,000” people have been displaced. “They will not be allowed to return to their neighbourhood until we’ve finished dealing with all the Hamas issues in Hebron,” Israel Katz said in an interview with public broadcaster Kan.
Hundreds of Israeli raids have taken place since Friday’s attack by two Palestinian gunmen on an Israeli army reserve base, which killed two Israeli soldiers. The two Palestinians were also killed.
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu ordered a “full lockdown” of the occupied West Bank following the attack.
Mayor al-Ja’bari told Al Jazeera that Hebron residents can neither enter nor leave the city.
Israeli soldiers also fired a stun grenade at Al Jazeera journalists near the Farsh al-Hawa checkpoint in Hebron, as the journalists documented an Israeli operation to bulldoze homes and vehicles in the area.
The Israeli military carried out raids across at least 15 areas of the occupied West Bank on Saturday, Al Jazeera correspondents on the ground reported.
The targeted areas include Jenin and Nablus in the north; Ramallah, el-Bireh, Birzeit, and occupied East Jerusalem in the centre; and Bethlehem in the south.
The Palestinian Prisoner’s Society said Israeli forces arrested about 70 Palestinians in the raids.
Raids in several towns in the Jenin governorate on Saturday evening injured two people, the Palestinian news agency Wafa reported.
Sources told Wafa that two others were injured in separate incidents southeast and east of Jenin.
The Palestinian Red Crescent said early on Sunday that it had treated nine people, including six children, for “suffocation” after Israeli soldiers fired tear gas in Halhul, north of Hebron.
According to a statement early on Sunday, the Israeli military will bar Palestinian workers from entering most areas of the West Bank on Sunday through Monday, and a full closure of crossings into and out of the West Bank will be enforced on Tuesday, the day of the Israeli elections.
The Palestinian Authority, which governs some of the West Bank, called Israel’s actions “collective punishment”, citing the demolition of homes, forced displacement of entire neighbourhoods, and the “closure and siege of Palestinian cities”, and urged the international community to intervene, Wafa reported.
Meanwhile, Hamas said in a statement that the “campaigns and escalations carried out by the occupation and its criminal settlers against our people will only fuel further outrage”.
Hundreds of thousands ‘under siege’
About 200,000 Palestinians live in the city of Hebron, and a further 600,000 in Hebron governorate, making it the West Bank’s most populous governorate.
The 800,000 Palestinians in the Hebron governorate are “now under siege, with all entrances and exits closed since morning”, Issa Amro, a Palestinian activist and political analyst based in Hebron, told Al Jazeera.
“Inside the city, there is no safe place for anyone to hide… the city is really in fear,” Amro said.
Israeli politicians are trying to “capitalise” on the attack ahead of parliamentary elections on October 27, Al Jazeera’s West Bank correspondent Nour Odeh said.
“Netanyahu, his Likud party, and his allies in this right-wing coalition are behind in the polls”, said Odeh, so, in response, they are “trying to put up a brave front, saying they’re combating Palestinians”.
Just days before Israelis are set to vote, Netanyahu avoided answering whether he planned to dismantle the Palestinian Authority, but said that a “big surprise” awaits the organisation.
Rights groups react
Speaking late on Friday, United Nations Secretary-General António Guterres said he was deeply concerned by the closures and reports of home demolitions in Hebron.
“Those closures severely restrict Palestinians’ freedom of movement, access to basic services and livelihoods,” Guterres said.
Mayy El Sheikh, a spokesperson for the UN Human Rights Office in the occupied Palestinian territory, said Israel’s Hebron operation was “yet another episode in a never-ending stream of suffocating measures making life more and more unbearable for Palestinians”.
The Israeli rights group B’Tselem, meanwhile, warned that Israel’s actions amount to “collective punishment and acts that could constitute war crimes”.

Israel turns clocks back tonight: everything you need to know
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
15:47:05 UTC
00:47:05 KST

Israel returns to standard time overnight between Saturday and Sunday, October 24-25. At 2 a.m. on Sunday, clocks move back to 1 a.m., giving everyone an extra hour of sleep. Daylight saving time returns on Friday, March 26, 2027.
Will my alarm ring at the right time?
Most smartphones update automatically, including alarms. To check, open your phone's Date & Time settings and enable automatic time and time-zone updates. The local time zone should be Jerusalem. Manual clocks and some older devices will need adjusting.
Why do clocks change?
Under Israel's Time Determination Law, as amended in 2013, daylight saving time ends on the last Sunday in October. The change means earlier sunrises and earlier sunsets, so mornings grow brighter but evenings darken sooner.
How does it affect sleep and mood?
The extra hour may be welcome, but changes in daylight can disrupt sleep patterns. Melatonin helps regulate the sleep-wake cycle and responds to darkness, while reduced winter sunlight is associated with changes in mood. Effects vary from person to person.
Why not keep daylight saving time year-round?
Supporters of permanent daylight saving time argue it provides more evening light for families and recreation. Critics point to the darker winter mornings, especially for children commuting to school. Israel has debated the idea repeatedly but has kept the twice-yearly changes.
Many Asian, African and South American countries do not change their clocks. Europe's seasonal switches continue despite a 2019 European Parliament vote to end them. In the United States, daylight saving time will end November 1.

IDF, Defense Ministry struggle with amount of reservists seeking mental health care, experts say
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
15:45:28 UTC
00:45:28 KST

The IDF and Defense Ministry are struggling to keep pace with the growing number of reservists seeking mental health care after three years of intense fighting on multiple fronts, according to military reservists familiar with the issue.
The sources say thousands of reservists who have completed prolonged combat deployments are traveling overseas to attend workshops and receive treatment through private nonprofits, seeking help coping with the psychological effects of their military service.
One source said the military should work more closely with these organizations to ensure consistent standards of care.
“It would have been preferable for the IDF to initiate a process with the nonprofit organizations and private bodies to minimize the gaps in diagnosis, oversight, and ultimately treatment,” the source said.
Reservists have also raised concerns about disparities in mental health support between active-duty soldiers and reserve personnel. While soldiers in regular service receive ongoing support, reservists typically get limited assistance toward the end of their operational deployments, and even that support isn’t consistently available.
Military sources serving in the reserves claim that after reservists have once again “become civilians,” the military considers its responsibility fulfilled, leaving them to navigate bureaucracy and the limited support services available on their own.
Mental health specialists in IDF reserves warn of coming PTSD crisis
Reservists specializing in mental health are warning that the IDF and Defense Ministry may be unprepared for a surge in cases of post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) in the coming years.
One source warned that the psychological consequences of the war could continue to emerge long after the fighting ends.
“The psychological shockwaves and outbreaks of post-traumatic stress among hundreds of thousands of combat soldiers and reservists are only beginning and are expected to intensify in the coming years.”
According to estimates by the IDF and the Defense Ministry’s Rehabilitation Department, tens of thousands of soldiers, primarily reservists, are expected to develop PTSD as a result of the war.
More than 7,000 soldiers, most of them combat troops, have already been officially recognized as having psychological disabilities stemming from their wartime service.
The IDF Medical Corps has established the Ta’atzumot Clinic and operates the Combat Stress Reaction Unit to provide mental health care. However, the sources argue that the capacity of these services has not kept pace with rising demand, particularly as fighting continues.
Reservists specializing in mental health also warned of what they described as a “dangerous trend” insofar as many combat soldiers and reservists turn directly to private providers, nonprofit organizations, and alternative treatment programs overseas rather than relying on the military’s official mental health services. Increasing reliance on private providers raises concerns among the sources about the adequacy of the military’s own response.
The Ta’atzumot Clinic reports that approximately 65% of its patients return to military service after treatment. However, military sources in the reserves questioned whether that figure accurately reflects the broader challenges facing soldiers who require mental health care.
The sources questioned why so many soldiers feel abandoned after leaving military service.
“Why do so many soldiers in the field still feel that the military system is quick to ‘discharge them’ or remove them from the statistics as soon as they take off their uniforms, and do the impressive figures reflect the full picture, or only those who managed to reach the forefront of mental health treatment?”
IDF places utmost importance on providing mental health care, military says
The IDF Spokesperson’s Unit said the military places the utmost importance on providing mental health care and has significantly expanded both the capacity and quality of its services since the beginning of the war.
The IDF insisted that its mental health system was prepared for increased demand and has continued to expand and improve its services throughout the fighting, adjusting based on lessons learned.
As part of those efforts, the military has opened new mental health clinics and established a 24-hour mental health hotline available seven days a week.
The IDF also emphasized that it does not simply wait for soldiers to seek assistance. Instead, it identifies those who may need support through structured processing and debriefing sessions held with teams and military units immediately after they complete operational deployments.
The Ta’atzumot Clinic, which treats soldiers currently serving in the military, has also expanded its operations and continues to adjust to changing needs.
Since the beginning of the war, the clinic has increased its staff and expanded its treatment programs, adding occupational therapy, a dedicated treatment track for career military personnel, and an intensive outpatient treatment program.
Soldiers referred to the clinic generally have complex clinical conditions and significant difficulties functioning that cannot be adequately addressed within their military units.
Treatment is intensive and tailored to the severity of each patient’s condition. Its purpose is to support rehabilitation and assess whether a soldier can continue serving, not to keep personnel in the military at any cost.
The IDF stressed that the Ta’atzumot Clinic’s statistics reflect the situation of those patients treated at the facility but not of all the soldiers experiencing post-traumatic symptoms. According to the military, about 65% of patients treated there return to service.
The Combat Stress Reaction Unit, which operates as part of the IDF’s broader commitment to caring for its soldiers, also treats veterans and other discharged personnel experiencing post-traumatic symptoms after exposure to combat.
The unit has treated more than 5,000 new patients, kept wait times short, and expanded access to services in northern and southern Israel, the military reported.
The unit operates in cooperation with the Defense Ministry and provides specialized psychological treatment for combat-related trauma.
In response to concerns about trust in the military’s mental health services, the IDF said that the Medical Corps conducts periodic patient surveys showing most patients are satisfied with the care they receive.
The military also noted that some mental health services fall under the responsibility of civilian agencies, rather than the Medical Corps. These include the Health Ministry, Israel’s health maintenance organizations, and the Defense Ministry’s Rehabilitation Department.
Under Israeli law, the IDF is generally not authorized to provide medical treatment to civilians, except through the Combat Stress Reaction Unit, which is specifically responsible for treating discharged personnel affected by combat.
The Medical Corps also clarified that it does not oppose releasing data on IDF personnel suffering from combat stress reactions. It said figures on combat stress casualties are already being published and will continue to be made available through scientific publications and research conducted by the Medical Corps.
The IDF further stated that, after nearly three years of exceptionally intensive reserve deployments, it has developed a framework known as the “Service Cycle” to better address the changing demands of reserve duty.
The framework recognizes that reserve service is no longer limited to a defined mobilization period followed by discharge. Instead, it can affect reservists, their families, and their military units throughout the year.

Following Israeli strikes on a base in Syria’s northern Idlib province, Barrack denounced the attack as an “unnecessary escalation that does not advance regional stability."
Secretary of State Marco Rubio and his team have maintained a better relationship with the Prime Minister, but believe Israel could do more to strengthen Lebanon's government. They have also expressed frustration with Netanyahu's failure to do more to curb settler attacks on Palestinians in the West Bank, Axios reported.
Final poll finds opposition increasing their lead
The report comes as Netanyahu's polling result worsens ahead of the election, with the latest Maariv poll showing the opposition bloc widening its lead to 54 seats while Netanyahu’s bloc dropped to 48.
The poll also found that 60% of respondents preferred a unity government if the October 27 election failed to produce a clear governing majority, while 23% preferred holding another election. Another 17% said they were undecided.
Of those who favored a unity government, 33% wanted a candidate from the opposition bloc to lead it, while 19% preferred Netanyahu to lead it. Another 8% favored a unity government regardless of who led it.
According to the polling results, Eisenkot led Netanyahu in a head-to-head matchup for prime minister, with 49% support compared with 41% for the incumbent.
Moshe Cohen contributed to this report.

Esti Ayalon Kovo enters Knesset race to stop Jerusalem’s problems from spreading across Israel
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
15:45:06 UTC
00:45:06 KST

Esti Ayalon Kovo has seen what is happening across our country, and is ready to work for a better tomorrow.
A resident of Jerusalem, she has witnessed the challenges facing Israel’s capital, including economically, socially, and where the interests of the powerful and influential haredi community often clash with those of others that live here. Today, she sees parallels between what’s happening in Jerusalem and across the country.
But far from being driven to despair, Ayalon Kovo knows that a brighter future is possible, and she is willing to fight for it.
Born in Ethiopia before immigrating to Israel and having formerly served as head of Israel’s Economic Mission in China, Ayalon Kovo moved to Jerusalem for the future – and she means that quite literally, having chosen it for her children’s education.
Now, she has transitioned from diplomacy to politics to fight for her children, to make sure they can live in a country that can give them the future they deserve. And doing that means both taking on a perceived culture that avoids taking accountability, as well as what she believes is the haredi state-within-a-state, to make sure what has happened to Jerusalem doesn’t happen everywhere else in the country.
For this reason, Ayalon Kovo has joined up with B’Yachad in the 21st slot on its list, believing that only Naftali Bennett can help her achieve the necessary changes to the Jewish state.
Before the elections, In Jerusalem spoke with Ayalon Kovo about her life, career, and what she thinks are the issues in this heated Knesset race.
What brought you to Jerusalem?
I couldn’t imagine being anywhere else. In Israel’s capital. It’s never boring here. We actually came here because my kids got accepted to a school here – and we have loved it. We live in Beit Hakerem; it’s such a special neighborhood.
What got you into diplomacy?
From a young age, before I even really understood the professional options, I felt I wanted to represent Israel around the world. Later on, my interest in the complexity and multifaceted nature of diplomacy drew me to the field.
What made you join B’Yachad and run for elections?
More than anything, I’m in this for my children and their future. To make sure they have the future they deserve, this country needs immediate, serious repair. We need effective governance and thorough plans to tackle the fundamental challenges facing the country, and only Naftali Bennett is capable of delivering this.
What do you think are the defining issues of the election this year?
I see two main issues. First, this country lacks effective leadership that takes responsibility. The result is what we’ve seen, where one failure follows another: Oct. 7, the flydubai hijacking, and more. Second, we need to save Israel as a liberal, Zionist, Jewish, and democratic state. To do that, we simply have to break up the haredi state-within-a-state that’s emerged here regarding enlistment, education, and the workforce. Otherwise, I’m afraid that many of the troubling economic, educational, and social trends we’ve seen in Jerusalem will be seen across the entire country.
What advice do you have for any olim who dream of making change in Israel and running for office?
You didn’t come here to sit back and watch Israel’s story unfold. Take an active part in shaping it. This is your country. Your home.
Getting involved in elections is a great place to start.
If you want change and repair after these difficult past few years, we at B’Yachad would love to have you on our team.

When the 'choosing people' head back to the ballot box, will they take a leap of faith? - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
15:45:06 UTC
00:45:06 KST

It’s the question that everyone – myself included – is struggling with this week: “Who should I vote for?”
It is indeed a quandary, but one that we must address; the right and privilege to choose our leaders is not something to ever take for granted. Israeli elections are not just routine civil events; they are matters of life and death. But it’s a tough, tough choice we face.
Like so many of you reading this, no doubt, I’m torn between two options. On the one hand, the existing government has some very fine people in it. Benjamin Netanyahu is unquestionably one of the outstanding fixtures and figures of Israel; his longevity of nearly 20 years in office has left an indelible mark on the history of the nation.
I have no doubt that virtually every Israeli citizen recalls at least one moment when Bibi brought honor to this country. As both a “war” and a “peace” prime minister, he has steered the ship of state through the most turbulent of waters. His financial acumen, his unshakeable posture vis-à-vis Iran and its nuclear ambitions, and the ground-breaking Abraham Accords are among his standout achievements.
I always felt I had a personal connection to Bibi. I hosted him in my synagogue in the US when he was deputy foreign minister, and it was clear then that he was a rising star. He hosted me in his own home several years ago, when he outlined his future goals, many of which have come to fruition. He has a charismatic presence, and his oratorical skills are second to none. On an international podium, he’s the man you want.
Several pervasive problems with the Netanyahu administration
But there are several pervasive problems I now have with the Netanyahu administration. First is the security issue. Bowing to public pressure, the 2011 freeing of more than a thousand avowed murderers – including arch-terrorists Ahlam Tamimi, mastermind of the horrendous Sbarro bombing, and Yahya Sinwar – in return for Gilad Schalit, laid the groundwork for the Oct. 7 invasion and massacre.
While every life is precious, a strong leader must weigh present gain versus future consequences and make the hard choices, even when they are unpopular. The ensuing deaths of 3,000 Israeli soldiers and civilians – with Hamas still remaining fully armed and threatening – are a black mark on Bibi’s record.
This concern over the government’s ability to protect us is exacerbated by Bibi’s steadfast, arrogant refusal to both accept any blame whatsoever for Oct. 7 nor allow an independent, thorough investigation of the tragedy, rebuffing the legitimate demands of the victims as well as the general public.
A truly great leader, one who sees the nation’s good as his top priority, prepares for the years ahead by grooming a competent successor. But instead of ensuring an eventual, successful change of power, Bibi frustrates the emergence of the next prime minister.
Some of the best candidates were sent abroad, such as UN Ambassador Danny Danon to New York or Tzipi Hotovely to the UK; others like Yuli Edelstein and Nir Barkat were shoved to the side. Bibi is 77 years old this week; no Israeli PM has ever served at that age. Where is the concern for our future?
How can I, as an observant Jew and bereaved father, support this government?
BUT PERHAPS what both aggravates and frightens me the most, as a parent of soldiers, is the stranglehold on the government preventing the ongoing yeshiva study vs IDF service problem from being solved. This issue goes to the nature of what it means to have a Jewish state, and it epitomizes the lack of equality that is keeping this country bitterly divided.
The horrible lashon hara of the leader of the Degel Hatorah faction that recently polluted the airwaves – referring to soldiers as murderers who fight only for their own personal glory rather than to protect the nation, and claiming that Zionism is a desecration of God’s name – is straight out of New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani’s playbook.
How can I, as an observant Jew and bereaved father, support a government that looks the other way when such evil, anti-Torah curses are uttered by members of the coalition?
Now, I accept that there are also good, Israel-loving members in the coalition; but sadly, they are barred from speaking their minds, let alone voting their conscience when scandals such as these arise. “Party discipline” forcibly mutes them, and so, whether they like it or not, they must be judged by the actions of the majority, not by their own personal convictions.
In Jewish law, we learn that if a cow has a single defect that renders it treif, the whole animal is treif, and no part of that cow may be eaten. So, when you vote for one, you are, in truth, voting for all.
Of course, there are legitimate concerns regarding the opposition as well. Are they capable of dealing with the many areas of conflict that inhabit our borders, and beyond? Will they push for a two-state solution (though Netanyahu publicly approved that very idea in his 2009 speech at Bar-Ilan University)?
Will Arabs be accepted as members of a ruling coalition, as happened in Naftali Bennett’s government when Mansour Abbas joined (though Netanyahu had first approached Abbas about joining his coalition)?
Will a new government be able to maintain a strong relationship with America, our principal ally, such as exists today, and repair our relations with the many countries that now condemn us? And will it keep Israel a fully Jewish state, with emphasis on our spiritual nature as well as our secular one?
I believe that the opposition boasts numerous qualified, deeply committed men and women, including a former prime minister, and a distinguished military leader who paid dearly in blood for his devotion to Israel. If they are successful, I predict that numerous other lawmakers, including many from the Likud itself, will join their ranks in due time, forging an even stronger partnership.
The real question is, can we make a leap of faith to effect a change, or are we forever bound to the status quo? It may not always be true that “plus ca change, plus c’est la meme chose,” the more things change, the more they remain the same. I prefer the Greek philosopher Heraclitus’s opinion that “change is the only constant in the universe.”
The Talmud in Berachot recounts that for a long time, only elite, rabbinic veterans were allowed into the grand yeshiva of Yavne, presided over by Rabbi Gamliel. Guards were even posted at the door to keep newcomers out.
But then the sages decided to remove Rabbi Gamliel from his position of authority, due to his arrogance, and install the young rabbi Elazar ben Azaryeh as the new nasi. The doors of the study hall were thrown open, and hundreds of benches were brought in to accommodate the incoming members.
The Talmud says that on that day, there was a massive intellectual breakthrough. There was no matter of Jewish law that was left unresolved; even long-standing disputes that had been stuck for years were successfully analyzed and resolved by the new membership.
I’m not as cynical as Paul and Art; I don’t think we lose when we choose. May we make the right decision as we cast our ballot, and may God bless our leaders with the wisdom and courage to bring lasting peace to our land.■
The writer is director of the Jewish Outreach Center of Ra’anana. rabbistewart@gmail.com

Tourism Ministry launches free food truck tour in US

The Tourism Ministry is taking its culture to the streets of America this month with the launch of the Taste of Israel, Food Truck Tour 2026.
Starting October 25 in North Miami Beach, Florida, a specially designed food truck will embark on a multi-state journey, serving free, authentic kosher-style Israeli food curated by chef Yossi Shitrit.
The culinary initiative aims to introduce the American public to the diverse flavors of Israel, bridging the gap between local culture and international tourism. Operating from 12 to 3 p.m. at each stop, the truck will feature traditional dishes, vegetarian options, and ambient Israeli music. Admission and food samples are entirely free to the public.
After Miami, the truck will travel through another three major US cities. On October 27, it will be in Atlanta; Nashville the following day; and Dallas on October 30.
Shitrit said that his menu is deeply rooted in personal history and cultural fusion.
The convergence of culinary traditions that define Israeli food
“For me, everything begins with taste and memory,” he said. “Even when I create a new dish, the flavors of home are always present. That is what I want to bring along on this journey: the warmth, the generosity, and the convergence of traditions that define Israeli cuisine.”
Michael Izhakov, director-general of the ministry, said the campaign hopes to build a sensory connection to Israel.
“One taste is all it takes to fall in love,” he stated. “Together with chef Yossi Shitrit, we are bringing the flavors and aromas of Israel to the American public: from the spice markets of Jerusalem to the beachfront restaurants of Tel Aviv, and from the Galilee to the Negev.”
The food truck project, produced by the Narrative Group, is an experiential extension of the ongoing “I AM ISRAEL” marketing campaign. Since its launch in June, the digital campaign has generated over 320 million impressions and reached more than 70 million unique users, prompting the ministry to expand its reach into Canada and the United Kingdom.
The strategic focus on American consumers aligns with critical tourism data. The United States remains Israel’s largest source market for inbound tourism. From January through September of this year, 295,000 American tourists arrived in Israel, making up approximately 37% of all inbound travelers. This builds on last year’s footprint, where 448,000 Americans accounted for roughly 34% of total visitors.
By taking the campaign offline and onto the streets, officials hope to sustain this momentum and turn a casual lunch break into a future travel itinerary.
For more, visit tasteofisrael.co/

A journey into the awakening northern Dead Sea
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
15:44:35 UTC
00:44:35 KST

A profound, poetic irony unfolds at the lowest point on Earth.
As the Dead Sea steadily recedes, evaporating at a bittersweet rate of 1.2 to 1.5 meters a year, the surrounding community is doing something entirely unexpected. They are growing.
While the shoreline shrinks, the Megilot Dead Sea Regional Council is actively rewriting the region’s future. Armed with fierce local pride, ambitious hospitality plans, and a culinary obsession with the humble date, a new wave of pioneers is turning this vanishing landscape into one of the country’s most vibrant, resilient travel destinations.
The catalyst for this awakening was the Dead Sea March this weekend, a rare annual event that briefly thawed decades of stagnation and opened a restricted, forgotten world to the public. Locals had long waited for this event, they noted, watching it return perfectly timed with fantastic autumn weather.
For decades, one of the most fascinating corners of the Jordan River basin was completely lost to time. Following intense cross-border incursions in 1968, the historic “Land of the Monasteries” was ringed with roughly 3,000 landmines, locking its striking mid-century Christian sanctuaries behind barbed wire.
Though painstaking demining operations finally concluded in 2019, with the stunning Romanian Monastery the last to be cleared, the area remains a heavily restricted military zone.
While the annual march offers a rare, large-scale public opening to walk among these silent facades, the event leaves a lasting legacy for the rest of the year. The regional thaw has begun.
Today, independent travelers who coordinate ahead with military directives can still experience the haunting beauty of this remote frontier – a poignant reminder of a landscape suspended between a volatile past and a hopeful future.
Visitors can admire the beauty of the various churches from the outside, silent witnesses to the area’s long stagnation, a state that may soon thaw and bring the place back to life.
High-adventure tourism
To understand the true magic of the shifting landscape, you have to get out on the water. The receding sea continuously reveals a surreal, evolving underworld of salt formations you can explore year-round.
Nofei Melach (“Salt Landscapes”), operated by Orit and Jackie Ben Zaken, offers 90-minute educational excursions by motorboat: Jackie frequently runs research charters for the Israel Institute for Oceanographic and Limnological Research, meaning his tour commentary on rising salt “chimneys,” underwater sinkholes, and massive mineral “diamonds” – glittering clusters of salt and mineral crystals – is unmatched (NIS 2,500 per boat, up to 12 passengers).
For a quieter encounter, Itay Yisraeli leads intimate three-hour kayaking tours (NIS 450 for a two-person kayak), giving paddlers the personal sensation of paddling across calm, hyper-saline waters. Detailed itineraries are available on the Official Dead Sea Tourism Portal, and you can book directly on the Dead Sea Rider platform.
New tourism hubs
Back on dry land, the tourism infrastructure is gearing up for a massive evolution. “We parted ways with [the] Tamar [Regional Council] and became an independent regional council,” says council head Aryeh Cohen. “They kept the money, and we were left with the challenges,” he adds with a smile.
Building regulations now permit boutique, three-story hotels. About 10 lodging projects are operating or under development near Kalya and the vibrant street-art hub of Gallery -430. Further south at Mitzpe Shalem, an ambitious blueprint aims to bring 1,000 hotel rooms stretching down to the dramatic cliffs of Nahal Darga.
For an adventure right now, Netanel Schlesinger’s Dead Sea Tourism complex near Avnat serves as the perfect base camp.
“The business started with just four bicycles, but it has since expanded into a tourism center offering a variety of activities,” Schlesinger explains. The site features self-guided smart bikes (NIS 100), off-road Rider vehicles (NIS 250), Jeep tours, and luxury glamping caravans complete with private Jacuzzis and plunge pools.
Visitors can also stop by Cafe Barkai, named for the first light to appear in the east, which partners with a local school to serve travelers.
Where the desert meets the plate
You cannot understand the flavor of the Megilot region without understanding the date. Fed by reclaimed water systems, the local date plantations are the lifeblood of the regional economy, and their sweet harvest has become the literal backbone of the local cuisine. These culinary stops are open year-round for hungry travelers:
Cafe -430 at Lido Junction is a charming espresso cart run by area legend Shimshon Chen.
“I never associate a ‘minus’ sign with my businesses,” laughs Chen, who arrived in 1974, when “the sea reached this spot”, meaning the water came all the way to where his coffee cart now stands.
“I had my eye on this area for years, so I approached the head of the regional council with an idea, and he agreed,” he recounts, saying his simple goal was “To create a charming, delightful spot.” Stop by for fresh pastries baked daily at the nearby Almog Junction.
Me Casa near Avnat is the ultimate highway pitstop that effectively “kicks off” the morning for travelers. Owner Gal Hatzor makes everything from scratch, from the pizza dough to the house-ground burgers and slow-cooked steaks.
“Motorcyclists, for instance, come specifically for the asado and steaks,” he says with pride. “The vegetables come from a local farmer, so local produce finds its way onto the plate here, too.”
Don’t leave without trying their radical artisan ice cream flavors, including vanilla with za’atar, pomegranate, and pretzel with dulce de leche and halva. Some call the place “The Checkers House” (Beit HaDamka), but Hatzor clarifies: “It’s actually chess,” a game he's played for years.
Meanwhile, Buza Ice Cream at Lido Junction is the newest outpost of the famous Galilee-born parlor run by Meital and Liron Davori.
“The ice cream is produced in Sasa, in the Galilee, but the flavors have already begun to take on a local character,” they explain. The menu features a “cotton candy” hit for kids and adult-friendly profiles like “Beirut Nights” (pistachio, rose water, and semolina), yogurt with olive oil, and black coffee with cardamom.
Almog Junction’s Chance restaurant, formerly known as “The Last Chance,” is a legendary family-run Tunisian eatery that has operated since 1994.
“The place exists because it’s impossible to get rid of it – and besides, the customers wouldn’t let us give it up,” says Vered Sinai, who runs the establishment with her 84-year-old father, Dani. The design features river-stone pillars, light fixtures crafted from sajs metal cooking utensils used to make pita, and chandeliers made from traditional Bedouin coffee cups.
The menu is a masterclass in date-infused cooking.
“Dates have become an integral part of the menu,” Sinai notes, serving chicken with lemon and dates, date desserts, and date rolls (makroudh). For breakfast, she serves an inventive date carpaccio enhanced with garlic butter, sage, walnuts, and Bulgarian cheese.
“I saw it at a hotel and got inspired... It’s a delicacy,” she says.
A microcosm of change
The northern Dead Sea is caught in a beautiful, fragile state of metamorphosis. It is a place of profound contrasts: a harsh military past melting into a welcoming tourist future; an ecological crisis met with fierce agricultural innovation.
The annual march may have wrapped up, but the momentum it represents isn’t slowing down. To visit Megilot right now is to catch a glimpse of history in motion – to discover the raw, resilient spirit of a region before the grand-scale resort plans are fully implemented on the ground. The map might be changing, but the spirit of this place is firmly anchored.

The demonstration in Paris "has been completely dispersed," officials announce
The demonstration in Paris "has been completely dispersed along the Cours de Vincennes," following earlier clashes at the rear of the march between protesters and law enforcement, prefectural police reported.
"A Gendarmerie helicopter has been deployed to support ground units and locate any remaining groups of rioters," the same source added, noting that "more than 500 rioters" had been present toward the end of the demonstration. A water cannon and tear gas grenades were used in response to projectiles being thrown at police.
Nearly 1,000 arrested Saturday in French protests, number likely to rise – interior minister
Nearly 1,000 people were arrested by law enforcement on Saturday on the sidelines of protests by high school students and demonstrations against the high cost of living in France, Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez stated during a press briefing.
"As I speak to you, we are at nearly 1,000 arrests," he said, adding, "I believe this figure will increase significantly." He noted that last Saturday – a day marked by unprecedented violence and looting – there had been 385 arrests by this same time (around 7pm).
🎥 Paris demonstrations end in violence
Video by FRANCE 24 correspondent Ludovic de Foucaud shows black-clad rioters aiming projectiles at authorities towards the end of an otherwise peaceful protest in Paris. Police reportedly retaliated by firing water cannon and tear gas.

A non-stop display of shame." – post on X by leader of left-wing party, "France Unbowed" (La France Insoumise – LFI) and presidential candidate, Jean-Luc Mélenchon.
"More than 500 rioters are attacking law enforcement" – according to police at end of Paris march
Towards the final leg of the Paris protest route, vandals attempted to break into a car dealership at Vincennes Court, reported French police via a post on X.
"The swift intervention of law enforcement prevented them from doing so and secured the business," wrote the post.
Interior ministry says 410,000 protesters marched across France versus 'nearly 800,000' claimed by organisers
A total of 410,000 people took part in demonstrations across France on Saturday – including 110,000 in Paris – as part of a day of rallies focussed on purchasing power and the defence of public services, the Interior Ministry told AFP. The turnout was slightly lower than last week, which saw 550,000 people take to the streets.
Meanwhile, according to the union responsible for organising the authorised events, 800,000 people participated in the demonstrations nationwide on Saturday, with 250,000 in the capital.
Clashes broke out in several cities, including Paris, Lyon, Rennes, Nantes, Bordeaux, Nice, and Marseille.
Demonstrator sustains serious hand injury in Toulouse
One person sustained a serious hand injury during clashes with law enforcement at the end of the demonstrations in Toulouse on Saturday, prefectural authorities told AFP.
AFP journalists observed a protester being evacuated by firefighters following the incident that occurred as the demonstration was dispersing from the Les Arènes district, in the west of the city centre.
"As a crowd was being dispersed, one individual was attended to by emergency services for a serious hand injury," the Haute-Garonne prefecture confirmed, adding the circumstances around the injury are not yet known.
According to an anonymous medic who happened to be in the crowd and treated the injured person, the individual suffered a "severe injury to their right hand, with several fingers torn off," allegedly caused by the explosion of a device nearby.
Saturday’s demonstration in Toulouse drew between 26,500 participants according to local authorities; and 80,000, according to the CGT trade union.
Police deploy water cannon and tear gas towards end of Paris march
Clashes erupted as a mass march drew to a close in Paris on Saturday, a week after widespread rioting and looting. More than 400,000 people rallied across France over school funding and soaring living costs, mounting a fresh challenge to President Emmanuel Macron’s government.
The Paris march began peacefully. But near its endpoint at Porte de Vincennes, some protesters threw projectiles while police fired volleys of tear gas and used water cannons to disperse people.
26,000 march in Toulouse – according to local authorities
Demonstrators tallied 26,000 in the southwestern city of Toulouse on Saturday, according to local authorities.
Around 10,000 people demonstrate in Lyon despite bans
Nearly 10,000 people marched through the streets of Lyon on Saturday, in spite of lacking pre-authorisation and an expanded ban on gatherings in the city centre, according to estimates by the Rhone prefectural authorities as of 4.30pm.
Throughout the day, protesters gathered at various locations across the city, forming groups of differing sizes. According to the prefecture, demonstrators moved "in a very erratic manner, without any clearly defined objective" over the course of the afternoon.
Police remained mobile in response, dispersing the groups to prevent escalation and at times, deploying tear gas. They aimed to prevent the marches from growing larger or heading toward the Presqu'île shopping district, where shops were looted and the tourist office was set on fire on October 17, AFP journalists observed.
Armoured "Centaure" vehicles were deployed.
Police say 110,000 demonstrate in Paris, but 'situation remains calm'
Parisian prefectural police confirm at least 110,000 people have marched in Paris; but that the "situation remains calm" – according to a report by AFP.
Paris police said that more than 3,000 people were stopped and checked by officers and 65 people were arrested during the demonstration in the French capital.
The National Gendarmerie reports protesters aiming fireworks at law enforcement in Dijon
Clashes in Nantes, as protesters enter the restricted zone; water cannon deployed, tear gas fired
Clashes have broken out on Saturday in Nantes between law enforcement and protesters who managed to reach the city centre – an area where the local prefecture had prohibited demonstration, according to observations by an AFP journalist.
The procession of several thousands set off in the early afternoon on the Île de Nantes, outside the restricted zone. Upon attempting to cross the Loire River – which separates the island from the city centre – protesters encountered police and security forces.
Blocking access to the bridge, the authorities deployed a water cannon and tear gas, while some protesters threw small projectiles in their direction.
The group then turned back, crossing the Loire via a different bridge to enter the area where the prefecture had officially banned all gatherings. Amidst the rain and occasional fireworks set off by participants, the front of the march was pushed back by security forces using stun grenades, tear gas, and a physical charge.
Shortly before 4pm, the procession reached the centre of Nantes, met with further rounds of tear gas.
'French police using tear gas' – AFP
French police have fired tear gas at protesters in several cities on Saturday amid fresh demonstrations, according to AFP journalists.
Riot squads fired tear gas at protesters in Lyon, Lille, Toulouse and Nantes, hours after Interior Minister Laurent Nunez warned: "We will not tolerate any violence or any disturbance of public order.
Jordan Bardella re-elected president of far-right National Rally amid protests
Jordan Bardella was re-elected on Saturday as president of the National Rally (Rassemblement National)–France’s primary opposition party – during a congress in Orléans, a city to the southwest of Paris, at an event that coincided with a demonstration against the far right, organised by figures from France's political left.
Running unopposed, he secured 98.98% of the vote.
"To lead Marine to the Élysée, I will need you," Jordan Bardella told several thousand party members.
Bardella is a Member of the European Parliament (MEP) and has led the National Rally, founded in 1972, since 2022. He is set to deliver a speech on Sunday at the Zénith d'Orléans, which will be followed by an address from Marine Le Pen, a candidate in the 2027 French presidential election.

'You can't police yourself into social cohesion'
“You can't police yourself into social cohesion. You can't police yourself into a political future,” Andrew Smith, historian of modern France at Queen Mary University of London, told FRANCE 24, identifying a central paradox confronting the French Republic: the state may possess the means to impose public order, yet lack the political capacity to address the grievances driving mass mobilisation. Russian Chemical Giant Linked to Missile Fuel Production Goes Up in Flames After Drone Strike
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
15:39:44 UTC
00:39:44 KST

- Category
- War in Ukraine
Russian Chemical Giant Linked to Missile Fuel Production Goes Up in Flames After Drone Strike
A drone attack struck the Tolyattikauchuk petrochemical plant in Russia’s Samara region overnight on October 24, triggering a large fire at a facility producing synthetic rubber, gasoline additives, and chemicals with applications in solid rocket propellants.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to the monitoring channel Exilenova+ on October 24, the attack targeted the industrial complex in the city of Tolyatti. Local residents reported a significant fire around 6:30 a.m., while drones were reportedly still flying over the city.
Footage circulated on social media showed thick black smoke rising from the industrial area. Russian authorities issued a drone threat warning across the Samara region, while a local airport temporarily suspended operations.
Local reports also indicated that workers at the nearby AvtoVAZ automotive plant were evacuated following the attack. The extent of damage to Tolyattikauchuk and any casualties have not been independently confirmed.
According to the OSINT-Varta database, Tolyattikauchuk is one of Russia’s largest petrochemical facilities, with an estimated annual synthetic rubber production capacity of approximately 260,000 metric tons.
The plant manufactures butadiene, isoprene, hydrocarbon products, and methyl tert-butyl ether (MTBE), a chemical additive used to increase the octane rating of gasoline.
Several of these products have military applications. Butyl rubber is used in tires for military vehicles, while synthetic rubber compounds can serve as polymer components in composite solid rocket propellants.
These materials connect the facility to supply chains supporting Russia’s defense industry, although the proportion of its production used for military purposes remains unclear.
The facility was previously targeted on April 4, when long-range drones struck both the Tolyattikauchuk and KuibyshevAzot chemical plants in Russia’s Samara region. The attack triggered explosions and a major fire.

Brazil’s Lula and Bolsonaro about even ahead of election run-off: Poll
The race between Brazil’s president and the right-wing senator has tightened in recent days.
Brazilian President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva and Senator Flavio Bolsonaro remain about even on the eve of Sunday’s election run-off, shows a CNT/MDA poll.
The right-wing senator, the eldest son of former President Jair Bolsonaro, would receive 46.3 percent of the vote compared with 45 percent for the leftist Lula, according to the poll released on Saturday. Last week, the poll showed Bolsonaro leading Lula 46.8 percent to 45.9 percent.
MDA surveyed 2,032 people from October 21 to October 23, with a margin of error of 2.2 percentage points.
The poll comes the day after the final debate before the presidential run-off.
The candidates questioned each other on Friday about Brazil’s economy, infrastructure and regional development.
Bolsonaro accused the incumbent of allowing organised crime to expand, driving families into debt and not addressing the higher cost of living.
“He doesn’t know what hunger is,” Brazil’s first working-class president said of Bolsonaro. “He doesn’t know Brazil.”
Sunday’s vote comes after Bolsonaro finished first in the initial round of voting on October 4 with 47 percent to Lula’s 45 percent.
A Datafolha institute survey published on Thursday suggested the pair are now tied with 50 percent support each, compared with Bolsonaro’s four-point lead in polls published two weeks ago.

North Korea improves ballistic missiles and mass-produces drones with Russian support – NYT

North Korea improves ballistic missiles and mass-produces drones with Russian support – NYT
North Korea is continuing to upgrade its ballistic missiles and has launched the mass production of attack drones, largely thanks to its cooperation with Russia.
Source: The New York Times
Details: The Russians are sharing their developments with Pyongyang in exchange for soldiers, workers and weapons.
North Korea is modernising its armed forces and weapons with the help of Russia, having renewed military cooperation following the start of the full-scale Russian invasion of Ukraine.
In early October, Pyongyang tested a tactical ballistic missile that it claims is capable of carrying a nuclear payload. South Korea and Japan estimated it flew about 700 km (430 miles), while North Korea claimed a range of 1,000 km (621 miles).
"South Korea usually responds to North Korean missile tests with brief statements condemning them as provocative. But five days after the North's launch, it test-fired its own hypersonic ballistic missile for the first time, observed by President Lee Jae Myung, indicating that Seoul has grown increasingly uneasy over the rapid advancement of North Korea's missile technology," the NYT writes.
Specifically, Pyongyang has access to Russian deployment data and feedback. Anton Ponomarenko, an analyst, noted that this has allowed them to improve the accuracy and manoeuvrability of their weapons, making the threat to South Korea "more substantial".
Russia has also helped North Korea develop its own unmanned systems and their mass production.
"Pyongyang has learned from the conflict in Ukraine and the Middle East that inexpensive drones can overwhelm costly air defence systems. During a North Korean drill last month, a drone swarm attacked a target island, while cruise and ballistic missiles struck simultaneously from different directions. North Korea's evolving tactics will eventually force South Korea and its allies to redesign their air defences at exorbitant costs," the NYT explained.
Background:
- Bloomberg reported this September that Russia is involving North Korean citizens in the production of military drones, particularly at facilities in Alabuga, Tatarstan. Up to 25,000 North Koreans are believed to be working at Russian military plants.
- In addition, a North Korean missile forces unit, which could be equipped with 120 ballistic missiles and six launchers for strikes against Ukraine, has begun deploying in western Russia.
- Ukrainska Pravda previously reported that in August, Russia had asked North Korea to provide KN-30 ballistic missiles. In June 2026, North Korea announced the testing of a modernised 240mm multiple-launch rocket system, a tactical ballistic missile and a 155mm long-range artillery shell.

Ukraine’s military says Starlink satellite connection stable after recent restrictions
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
15:31:14 UTC
00:31:14 KST

Ukraine’s military has a “stable connection to Starlink”, the Ukrainian government said, 10 days after its ability to use the satellite communications system was suddenly restricted.
But hours after the announcement, SpaceX CEO Elon Musk, whose company owns Starlink, accused the Ukrainian military of violating the company’s terms. Neither Musk nor the US government, which operates Starshield using Starlink technology, took responsibility for imposing the curbs.
“Ukraine military violated Starlink terms of service and used it for offensive drone strikes to kill people. That loophole was closed last week,” Musk said in a social media post.
Serhiy Beskrestnov, a Ukrainian presidential adviser, said on the Telegram app that the country is “physically unable” to use Starlink for long- and medium-range attack drone operations.
Ukraine’s general staff and defence ministry did not immediately comment.
The Starlink satellite terminals, which are produced by Elon Musk’s SpaceX but managed by the US government, are a key component of Ukraine’s military operations. Sudden speed restrictions on the terminals, which capped operations at speeds of 160km/h (99mph), led to the failure of several Ukrainian combat missions earlier this month.
The military’s ability to intercept Russian attack drones was hampered and some Ukrainian operations to strike behind enemy frontlines were cancelled. Russia was able to launch ballistic missiles at Ukraine without any advance warning from the US.
The speed restrictions coincided with the announcement by Donald Trump of a US deal to buy Russian diesel, although the US president initially denied that his administration was behind the decision to cut intelligence sharing with Ukraine.
“I don’t know if it was anybody, but it wasn’t me, and I don’t think it was Elon,” Trump said, referring to Musk, SpaceX’s chief executive.
However, the US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, appeared to throw suspicion on Musk when he defended Trump last Wednesday. “The president has nothing to do with the decisions that are made by Starlink and Starshield and by Mr Musk,” Rubio said. “That’s a private company. The president doesn’t run that company and can’t direct that company to do anything.”
Musk was quick to blame the limits on Starshield on the Trump administration, writing on X last week that the systems were “owned and controlled by the US government”. “Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately Potus [president of the United States],” he wrote.
The US vice-president, JD Vance, backed Musk on Thursday, saying the billionaire “doesn’t want to get in the middle of what is a war between two state actors without the United States government effectively directing him on what to do”.
Ukraine’s president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, blamed both parties: “It was a message from [the] American government to limit the speed … And technically, SpaceX did it.”
There were no similar restrictions on Starshield terminals in EU countries and that they applied only to Ukraine, he added. “In other words, this is a planned operation.”
He said the decision would “bring a lot of human losses … of course people would die”.
Announcing the restoration of the system on Saturday in a diplomatic video address on the Telegram app, Zelenskyy expressed his gratitude to his US allies, including Trump and the US state department, for resolving the operational issue: “The most important development for today is that Starlink and Starshield have resumed operations at their pre-restriction speeds. The speeds are now at the level we need.”
The restoration began overnight. “By this morning, the speeds were already sufficient for operational use,” Zelenskyy said. “This is very important and significant for our frontline logistics and for defending Ukraine against jet-powered Shaheds.”
On Thursday, Trump had claimed the service was running again at full speed, but a European official speaking to the Associated Press denied the service was fully functioning.
When asked by reporters whether he would tell Musk to stop “messing around” with Ukraine’s access to Starlink on Friday, the US president said: “I’ve not spoken to him. I might have to … I’ve heard it was fixed. But if it’s not, I’ll speak to him … If there is a problem, I’ll get it straightened out.”
He then described Musk as a “very brilliant” and “very good” person.
Reuters contributed reporting

Israel brings talks with Lebanon to a standstill by refusing to withdraw from ‘pilot zones’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
15:31:02 UTC
00:31:02 KST

Israel brings talks with Lebanon to a standstill by refusing to withdraw from ‘pilot zones’
Talks between Lebanese and Israeli officials, hosted by the US in Tampa, Florida, this week, concluded without any breakthroughs, The New Arab reported on Thursday, citing its own sources.
The discussions were held at US Central Command headquarters, the Pentagon's Middle East operations arm. They come as Israel has continued its attacks on Lebanon this month, carrying out air strikes and home demolitions in the Nabatieh, Bint Jbeil, and Sidon districts.
The New Arab said it was told there was "intransigence in Israeli positions, while the Lebanese side is holding firm to its demands that steps must be reciprocal".
The Lebanese Armed Forces (LAF), largely funded by the US, has also rejected direct military-to-military coordination with the Israelis, instead preferring a third-party verification mechanism to be employed by the United Nations and allies such as France.
Israel has bombed Lebanon consistently since October 2023, after the Hamas-led attacks on southern Israel ignited the region.
A November 2024 ceasefire brokered by the former Biden administration did little to curb Israel's insistence that it was targeting Hezbollah leaders and weapons depots across the country, including in the capital, Beirut.
But it wasn't until this year that Israel significantly ramped up its military operations, mounted a ground invasion, and occupied long stretches of the south and east of Lebanon.
Since the US and Israel launched their joint war on Iran on 28 February, which prompted Hezbollah to launch attacks on Israel in defense of its ally, Israel has killed more than 4,300 Lebanese and displaced one million people in the country.
Lebanese officials have prioritized returning the displaced to their lands and demanded a timetable to do so from the Israelis, but there has been no movement on the issue since the US-sponsored framework was signed by the two sides in June.
Lebanon and Israel agreed to a trilateral framework with the Trump administration in Washington earlier this year, following five rounds of talks hosted by Secretary of State Marco Rubio.
The three countries held what was billed as a historic signing ceremony on 26 June.
Rubio said it was "the beginning of the beginning" in remarks to reporters at the time.
He later added the US would commit $100m in "humanitarian assistance in coordination with the UN" for affected communities, though he did not specify whether it was just for Lebanon or also for northern Israeli border towns.
Rubio said the LAF would be "reimbursed" by the Trump administration to the tune of $30m.
The framework led to the creation of the Military Coordination Group for Lebanon, which Washington would facilitate.
But the "pilot zones" that the Israelis pledged to withdraw from, in order to allow the LAF to take over, have not been expanded since July, with the Israelis claiming that the LAF have not had the capacity to disarm Hezbollah fighters.
Hezbollah is the key party to the conflict that was not represented in the talks.
It remains the country's most powerful military organization and far outmatches the LAF's capabilities. It was formed in the 1980s in response to the illegal Israeli occupation of Lebanon.
It has insisted that it cannot disarm while Israel remains a threat to Lebanon, and as Israeli officials normalize rhetoric about expanding Israel's borders to the north.

Bluebottle maker opens Sydney plant for forty vessels
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
16:30:48 BST

Ocius Technology has opened an engineering, production and maintenance hub for its Bluebottle uncrewed surface vessels in Sydney, together with a round-the-clock global operations centre, as it scales up to deliver forty more vessels under an Australian government investment of 176 million dollars, according to the company.
Pat Conroy, the Australian Minister for Defence Industry, opened the site on 16 October at a ceremony attended by the Royal Australian Navy, customers and partners. The expansion follows the opening earlier in the week of the company’s first overseas maintenance base in Auckland, run through its subsidiary Ocius New Zealand.
Robert Dane, the chief executive, said: “The opening is an important next step in Ocius’ evolution and our ability to deliver sovereign maritime technology at scale for customers in Australia and around the world.
“It brings together the people, technology and manufacturing expertise needed to build Australia’s Bluebottle fleet at pace, sustain vessels already operating at sea and respond to increasing global demand.
“Ocius began as an R&D operation at UNSW. Today, we have a major Australian manufacturing base, a 24/7 Global Operations Centre and an expanding international presence. That progression shows what Australian innovation can achieve when world-leading research is transformed into operational technology at scale.”
Conroy was blunter about what the vessels are for: “Ocius is a great Australian success story, developing world-leading maritime technology right here in Sydney. Ocius is a prime example of Australian innovation and ingenuity that has created over 70 jobs over the last 12 months, while supporting other small businesses and jobs through its supply chain.
“I’ve said before that I want potential adversaries to understand that when they see an Ocius Bluebottle USV, it is a signal to get out of our ocean. These new facilities will help deliver Bluebottles to the Royal Australian Navy, meet demand for Bluebottles from around the world, and boost Ocius’ maritime operations capability.”
Tim Ayres, the Minister for Industry and Innovation, said facilities of this kind “show the strength of Australian advanced manufacturing, turning home-grown research and innovation into high-value jobs, sovereign capability and products that can compete globally.”
Bluebottle vessels run on solar, wind and wave energy and can stay at sea for extended periods, providing persistent intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance without a crew. The company describes them as satellites of the sea. A hybrid variant carrying diesel as a supplementary fuel source is built at the same facility, and the Sydney site also houses research areas working on the sensor, autonomy and mission systems. The workforce has grown past 130.
Bluebottles have achieved AUKUS Authorised User Status and are in service with the Royal Australian Navy, the Australian Border Force, the Royal New Zealand Navy, and with the United States through the prime contractor ThayerMahan.

Saudi Arabia will not host the Russian-backed Intervision song contest this year, with the event potentially postponed until 2027, the state-run news agency TASS reported, citing an unidentified source.
The source said a “combination of circumstances” had made it impossible to stage the competition in Saudi Arabia in 2026, without elaborating.
The decision leaves the future of Russia’s alternative to Eurovision uncertain a year after Moscow revived the Soviet-era competition.
A source in Riyadh had already cast doubt on the event in August, telling TASS that its dates, participants and program remained unclear.
Saudi Arabia was announced as the next host during the final of the September 2025 contest in Moscow. Saudi officials later said Russia had yet to formally hand over responsibility for organizing the event.
Russian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov expressed hope in May that escalating tensions in the Middle East would not disrupt plans for the second edition.
Russia revived Intervision after being barred from Eurovision in 2022 following its full-scale invasion of Ukraine. Eurovision’s organizers said Russia’s participation could bring the competition into disrepute.
Culture Minister Olga Lyubimova subsequently proposed bringing back Intervision, which was held in the Polish city of Sopot in the late 1970s and early 1980s and featured performers from the Soviet Union and other socialist countries.
President Vladimir Putin signed a decree ordering the competition’s revival in February 2025, with Russian authorities allocating 750 million rubles ($9.3 million) to stage it.
Organizers said the Moscow contest drew participants from 22 countries. Russia was represented by the pro-Kremlin singer Shaman.
Vietnamese singer Duc Phuc, who won his country’s version of “The Voice” a decade earlier, took first place. Kyrgyzstan’s Nomad group finished second, followed by Qatar’s Dana Al Meer.

Denmark to Purchase New U.S.-Made Anthem Cruise Missiles
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
15:23:25 UTC
00:23:25 KST

Denmark will purchase Norwegian Joint Strike Missiles from Kongsberg to arm its F-35s, as well as new Anthem cruise missiles from the American company Covenant for launch from ground-based launchers. The Anthem was first publicly unveiled in early September.
The Danish Ministry of Defence announced the procurement.
According to the ministry, the goal of the procurement is to strengthen national and collective deterrence. These are weapons that NATO needs and that contribute to Denmark’s security.
The missiles are among various types of long-range, high-precision weapons that, thanks to advanced navigation technologies, can strike targets at great distances with high accuracy.
Covenant is an American defense company with an Israeli engineering and manufacturing base, founded in 2024 by Michael Kaufman and Ofir Dayan. Kaufman, an American-Israeli entrepreneur who previously worked with Peter Thiel, became the company’s CEO, while Dayan became the CTO. Covenant is headquartered in Washington, D.C., and operates a research and development and manufacturing complex covering approximately 3,000 m² in northern Israel.
Over the past two years, Covenant has raised more than $250 million in investments. Its investors include Andreessen Horowitz, Peter Thiel’s Founders Fund, Lux Capital, 8VC, Lightspeed, Altimeter, and the Israeli fund Aleph. The company has brought together more than 200 employees in the U.S., Germany, and Israel, including engineers with experience working at major defense corporations.
Covenant publicly unveiled its flagship product—the Anthem long-range cruise missile—only on September 9, 2026, after two years of development. At the time of the presentation, the company had already reported over 200 test flights of the missile and approximately $150 million in orders. Among its customers, the company named the U.S. Army and Navy, as well as international partners.
The Anthem is a ground-launched missile capable of carrying a payload weighing over 200 kg. It uses a solid-fuel rocket engine for launch. The developer has not publicly disclosed the exact flight range.
The missile is being developed with mass production and large-scale deployment in mind, alongside other long-range weapons such as the Tomahawk and JASSM-ER. According to Covenant’s management, once full-scale serial production begins, the target price for the Anthem will be several hundred thousand dollars.
To ensure mass production, Covenant has engaged three suppliers of solid-fuel rocket engines and has been working to bring on a fourth. The company has also signed long-term agreements for more than 4,000 rocket engines over the next two years. This approach is intended to reduce dependence on individual suppliers as production scales up.
The company is rolling out Anthem production in the U.S., Germany, and Israel. Once they reach full capacity, the facilities in Dallas and Saxony are expected to produce 5,000 missiles each per year, while the site in northern Israel will produce an additional 2,000.
The Joint Strike Missile (JSM) is a fifth-generation strike missile from Kongsberg, designed to overcome modern air defense systems.
It was developed based on the NSM naval missile. The air-launched variant, like the base version, is capable of engaging surface and ground targets, making it a versatile weapon.
The JSM’s stated range is 350 km. The warhead weighs 120 kg, and the missile’s total weight is 416 kg. It is 4 m long and has a diameter of 480 mm.
The missile can be stored in the internal bay of an F-35A fighter jet, preserving the aircraft’s low-observability characteristics.
The missile uses a high-precision navigation system that ensures a low-altitude flight profile. For terminal guidance, it employs a modern infrared seeker with imaging capability.

Former US vice-president Kamala Harris returns to US campaign trail with midterms, 2028 in view
- Kamala Harris is back on the campaign trail to help Democrats in close midterm races, starting in Nevada and visiting several battleground states.
- She attacked Donald Trump’s record and urged voters to back Democrats, while stressing, “2028 don’t matter if we don’t do 2026 right.”
- Harris has not decided on a 2028 White House run, but her return will renew debate about her future after losing in 2024 and facing a crowded Democratic field.
AI generated
NEW YORK – Kamala Harris is returning to the campaign trail to help Democrats in some of the tightest US midterm races, putting the former vice-president back before voters as she weighs whether to make a third run for the presidency in 2028.
The Democratic Party’s unsuccessful 2024 standard-bearer has made relatively few public appearances in 2026. But with her party trying to break the Republican hold on Congress on Nov 3, Harris is rallying in Georgia, Mississippi, Nevada, New Hampshire and Wisconsin, a return likely to renew questions about her political future as a crowded field of potential 2028 contenders takes shape.
Harris kicked off her tour in Las Vegas on Oct 20 with a new stump speech attacking what she described as the cruelty of President Donald Trump, mixed with the aspirational aphorisms that have long been her calling card as the first black and Asian person and first woman to become vice-president.
She spoke to scores of Culinary Workers Union members alongside gubernatorial candidate Aaron Ford, Nevada’s first Black attorney-general, who she said would be the “first black governor west of the Mississippi”.
“We got a serious fight in front of us,” Harris said. “We are witnessing pure brutality come out of what is undoubtedly the most corrupt, callous and incompetent presidential administration.”
Like Trump, who is jetting around the country for Republican candidates, Harris is not broadly popular among voters. A Reuters/Ipsos opinion poll in June showed 39% of Americans viewed her favourably, but the figures were starkly partisan: 82% of Democrats viewed her favourably, compared with 7% of Republicans and 33% of independents.
“At the end of a campaign, you bring out your heavy hitters,” said Elaine Kamarck, a senior fellow at the Brookings Institution and a member of the Democratic National Committee. “That’s what’s going on here with her, and frankly with Trump.”
The day after Las Vegas, Harris led chants of “Mississippi matters!” to a crowd supporting Scott Colom in the city of Columbus. Colom is seeking to become the first Democratic US senator elected in Mississippi since 1982, and polls show an unusually tight race with Republican Cindy Hyde-Smith.
Harris opened with advice she said she gives young people she mentors: “Never let someone else’s limited ability to see your capacity be a limitation on your ambition,” she said. “Let me repeat that.” And she did, louder than the first time, drawing cheers from the crowd.
Undecided on 2028
If Harris decides to run again for the White House in 2028, she would likely be among the most high-profile names in what is expected to be a crowded Democratic field.
But Harris also carries the baggage of past defeats: she lost the 2024 presidential election to Trump, and her first White House campaign ended before the 2020 Democratic nominating contests began.
A 2028 campaign would also force Harris to revisit the Democrats’ chaotic 2024 race, when then President Joe Biden abruptly ended his re-election campaign over questions about his health and mental acuity and she replaced him as the nominee.
Harris has since called Biden’s decision to seek re-election “reckless” in her memoir 107 Days, a reference to the short campaign she inherited. In October, she offered her clearest criticism yet of his support for Israel’s war in Gaza, rebuking the Israeli government’s “horrific conduct” and saying the US should have “acted sooner and more forcefully”.
“All these things will be relitigated,” Kamarck said. “What happened to Biden? Did she know? Did she think he was losing it? And on and on and on.”
Scott Ferson, a Democratic strategist and author of How The Democrats Lost America, said the party has tended to give short shrift to candidates who have lost, though voters disillusioned with Trump may also view Harris in a new light.
“She has that kind of crossover appeal,” Ferson said, “particularly with people who left in 2024 or stayed home”. Her implicit message, he suggested, is “Do you regret staying home?”
In October, as she wrapped up an appearance on the Baby, This Is Keke Palmer video podcast, Palmer asked her if she would run again.
“Oh, girl, come on!” Harris said, laughing while gripping the hands of the Hollywood movie star. “I haven’t decided yet.”
“But the midterms, the midterms, the midterms,” Harris went on. “2028 don’t matter if we don’t do 2026 right.” REUTERS
