A group preparing mass riots and recruiting young people through social media has been exposed in Moldova
Kyiv • UNN
Searches were conducted in Moldova as part of an investigation into preparations for violent riots and the recruitment of young people through fake accounts.
On October 24, the Moldovan police reported that they were investigating the activities of a group suspected of preparing violent acts and mass riots. Together with officers from the Information and Security Service (SIS) and PCCOCS prosecutors, the police conducted searches in Chișinău, as well as in the central and northern regions of the country. Newsmaker reports this, UNN writes.
Details
According to the investigation, since October 2026, the group’s members had been planning violent actions in the hope of obtaining financial gain. To implement their plans, the group’s members created several fake accounts on social media. In this way, they attempted to recruit young people to participate in protests that were supposed to escalate into mass riots. The investigation alleges that the suspects posted calls for violence on social media and used manipulation techniques to conceal from young people the real consequences of their possible actions.
The searches were conducted with the support of fighters from the Fulger Special-Purpose Battalion. The police уточнили that during the investigative actions, they seized evidence confirming preparations for riots.
At present, the individuals involved in the case are cooperating with the investigation. Law enforcement agencies continue their investigation to clarify all the circumstances of the case and identify other possible members of the group.
Law enforcement officers urged citizens not to fall for manipulation and not to respond to calls for violence and illegal actions. The police reminded the public that participation in incitement to violence and the destruction of state property may result in legal, including criminal, liability.

Sudan legal amendment puts journalists at risk of death penalty
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
15:18:35 UTC
00:18:35 KST

Breadcrumb
Journalists, politicians face death penalty under Sudan legal amendment, activists warn
A recent amendment to Sudan's 1991 criminal code could mean that journalists and politicians could now face the death penalty for online posts, rights groups and activists have warned.
The amendment now includes media publications and electronic media as potential crimes against the state.
The development comes amid an armed conflict between the Sudanese forces and the notorious RSF paramilitary group, which has raged on since 2023 and significantly hindered freedom of expression and journalism in the country.
It also comes at the same time the government implemented a mechanism designed to tackle cybercrime. However, activists state this has been used to monitor publications, media outlets and potential dissidents.
Sudanese journalist Majid Mohammed told The New Arab that the increasing punishment for those who publish content online is inconsistent with the government’s stated goal of opening and improving dialogue with citizens in the country.
“The amendments have failed to distinguish between the freedom of Sudanese people and enemies in Sudan who may use social media or online platforms to harm the state,” he said.
He urged a “review of the amendments, because their implementation will create and directly lead to the end of any dialogue initiatives and will create a negative climate for any consensus and agreements".
He also noted one of his biggest concerns was it would prevent the press from fulfilling its role towards the nation and civilians, and from assisting state institutions from carrying out their responsibilities through monitoring, oversight, and combating misinformation.
Amendment to penal code
Earlier this week, Abdel Fattah al-Burhan, the commander-in-chief of the Sudanese Armed Forces, issued a temporary decree under the Miscellaneous Amendments Act of 2026, which included changes to several laws.
The amendments were published in a special supplement to the Official Gazette.
Article 51, which pertains to inciting war against the state and includes terms such as the training of individuals, collecting weapons, or attempting to support or incite such actions, was amended to include electronic and media publications.
The original article states that anyone charged with the aforementioned “shall be considered to have committed the crime of inciting war against the state and shall be punished by death or a lesser term of life imprisonment, with the possibility of confiscating all their assets”.
Backlash against the amendment
According to local media reports, the amendments have sparked backlash among journalists, activists and politicians, and since the change, there has been a marked decrease in discussions, posts and articles on social media from Sudan.
Some activists have decried the move, stating that the government will likely exploit the amendment, and interpret any dissent or expressions of opinion as a crime against the state under the penal code.
The Sudanese Journalists Syndicate announced in a statement on Friday that it stood firm in its rejection of the amendment to Article 51 of the 1991 Criminal Code, and Prime Minister Kamil Idris’ decision to establish the National Mechanism for Combatting Cybercrime.
The syndicate said there would be serious repercussions to the measures, and press freedoms, and the right to access certain information, particularly in light of the ongoing war, would be severely hindered.
It cautioned against granting further powers for the state to monitor and track media outlets and social media platforms, or act against publishers based on vague descriptions and the wording of the penal code.
The political group The Radical Change Alliance also this week rejected the amendments, demanding that the changes be repealed and calling for an end to the prosecution of journalists and activists.
Human rights activist Othman Saleh told The New Arab that “the intention behind this amendment is clear – it's to restrict freedom of publication, expression and press. It also hinders the work of activists and journalists who document violations from all sides, and analyse and express opinions on all issues”.

Why popular airplanes are getting scrapped years early
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
15:18:30 UTC
00:18:30 KST

GOODYEAR, Ariz. — An Airbus A320neo, one of the world's most popular planes, rolled off the Mobile, Alabama, factory line in July 2022, painted bright yellow for its next destination: Spirit Airlines.
It was built to fly for decades. But this May, less than four years later, it was stripped for parts worth millions and crushed, the steel teeth of an excavator tearing through its fuselage at a facility on the outskirts of Phoenix.
More aircraft are getting dismantled years, if not decades, earlier than expected, industry executives told CNBC. It is the result of a shortage of parts, none more precious and expensive than aircraft engines, that has exasperated airlines and driven up costs for years.
Even after the engines are removed, firms are looking for parts as varied as landing gear and antennae to sell.
"It's the first time in my career that involved purchasing an aircraft that's less than five years since date of manufacture," said Bill Thompson, vice president who leads aircraft and engine acquisition for the Americas at aviation asset management and trading firm EirTrade Aviation, which bought the less than 4-year-old Airbus A320neo earlier this year.
He said the company paid "single-digit" millions each for that airplane and a similarly aged one, and it expects to make a profit from selling the more than 1,000 parts it took off them before they were crushed.
"I don't know if you're going to sell the coffee makers but you never know. Sometimes you do," he said.
'Don't fall in love with the metal'
Twenty-one newest-generation aircraft were torn down from June 2025 through this past August, according to aviation data and advisory firm IBA Group. The scrapped planes were 6.4 years old on average, and included mostly Airbus but also some Boeing planes. That compares with an average retirement age for narrow-body airplanes of 21.7 years, IBA said.
"Anytime that you end up with any period of market softness in aircraft availability, engine availability, it's going to cause investors to look at other options," said Simon Goodson, CEO of AerFin, a company that buys, sells, repairs and leases aircraft and parts. "We always say to our aircraft and engine traders, 'Please don't fall in love with the metal.'"
Hundreds of aircraft are retired each year as manufacturers ramp up production for airlines, so older planes are swapped out for newer, more fuel-efficient models.
But aside from retiring aging planes, some owners don't want to wait around for replacement parts or repairs on younger jets.
"A year might not sound that long, but does three or four years?" said Dave Querio, CEO of Ascent Aviation Services, a company that repairs, modifies, stores and disassembles aircraft, based in Marana, Arizona, outside of Tucson. "That's the issue for the aircraft that came in in '23, '24 and '25."
In some cases, owners can reap more for the parts than they can selling the plane or paying storage costs and waiting for it to get back in the air again.
Querio said he hasn't seen "the volume of younger aircraft being torn down as I'm seeing today."
Hot engine market
A major reason for the young retirements is the long wait and rising prices for jet engines.
One problem is that cutting-edge engines that burn hotter and use less fuel are coming up for maintenance far earlier than airlines expected.
The maintenance requests have kept engine repair and overhaul facilities backed up, from those owned by manufacturing giants GE Aerospace and RTX unit Pratt & Whitney to smaller, independent ones. Airlines and leasing firms have been hunting for spare parts and engines anywhere they can find them, like here in Goodyear, Arizona.
The trend has added more fuel to the already hot secondhand parts market. An engine fan blade could cost $50,000 or even more than $100,000 for bigger jets, Goodson said. Engines that power some Airbus A320neo aircraft have 20 of those blades. A disc for the engine, meanwhile, could cost between $1 million and $2 million.
An engine recall because of a manufacturing defect has backed up repair shops and grounded hundreds of Airbus planes around the world. Spirit Airlines bore the brunt of that problem in the United States, years before the airline collapsed.
The engine is made by Pratt & Whitney, which issued the recall in 2023 after discovering contaminated powdered metal used in making some parts. Those engines are worth close to $17 million this year at the high end, up 60% from the upper end of the range in 2019, according to IBA.
Airlines are removing some engines off retired planes to keep current aircraft flying while they wait for engines to come back from the shop.
"So you're just playing Legos and moving engines on and off aircraft," said Mike Stengel, a partner at AeroDynamic Advisory, an aerospace consulting firm.
The problems are driving up the cost to buy or rent one of the popular engines to record levels.
Renting one is ranging from about $160,000 to $180,000 a month, according to IBA data. A competing engine for the A320neo family made by CFM International, a joint venture of GE Aerospace and France's Safran, is far from a bargain, renting in a similar range of $130,000 to $180,000 a month.
Spirit Airlines' ghost planes
The problems with young retirements predate Spirit's collapse.
The 4-year-old Airbus plane that was torn down outside Phoenix in May is a key example. The aircraft was put in storage because of the engine recall, and it stayed until it was torn apart.
But the company's demise has brought more of its Airbus fleet to the market, forcing owners to figure out if it's worth the wait for engines or other parts.
CNBC visited AerSale's facility in Goodyear on a scorching day in late June, less than two months after Spirit collapsed, where dozens of the idle yellow planes were stored. It was so soon after the airline's demise that a former Detroit-based Spirit captain, Glenn Zecchin, popped in and asked about opportunities to ferry Spirit's aircraft to the desert, and to peek in on his former airline's planes.
"I knew the airplanes were there, and I wanted to see what happened," said Zecchin, who is now flying corporate jets.
A jet parked at the storage facility and maintenance hangar still had Spirit in-flight menus and safety cards in the bungee cord seatbacks. Pilot manuals were still in the cockpit.
Not all of these aircraft will be destroyed. Some companies that owned Spirit's planes before bankruptcy will just sell their parts, but some may keep the planes in storage. Other aircraft may go on to fly for other airlines, with potential carriers ripping out Spirit's tight 28-inch seat pitch for something roomier.
But as long as they're not flying, it means paying storage fees, which vary by aircraft type. Some planes in desert facilities — selected because the arid climate can preserve the aircraft better and avoid corrosion — can sit for decades.
Others won't make it back into the air if there's enough demand for the parts and too long of a wait to get the plane flying again.
"After you get rid of all the valuable equipment and sell it back into the aftermarket, what's really left is just a metal carcass that you will literally take a crane and crush," said AeroDynamic's Stengel. Then the owner can "sell it to recyclers that will make of it what they will, maybe into beer cans or something outside of aerospace."
Ascent's Querio said some owners opt to take that route.
"It's a little melancholy to watch it at times," he said. "But sometimes, it's kind of a thrill to ... see how fast an aircraft can be crunched up and sent off to the smelter."
— CNBC's Erin Black contributed to this report.

Starlink in Ukraine Back to Normal After Week of Throttling
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
15:18:06 UTC
00:18:06 KST

Ukraine said on Saturday that the Starlink satellite system and its military version Starshield were now fully functional after over a week of restrictions that disrupted military operations and intensified tensions with the U.S.
Problems with Elon Musk's SpaceX-owned systems came after U.S. President Donald Trump announced a deal to buy Russian diesel while pressing Kyiv to stop striking Russian oil refineries.
Ukrainian officials said the restrictions, which capped operations at speeds of 160 kilometers per hour (kph), hampered the military's ability to intercept Russian attack drones and forced the cancellation of some operations.
"The main thing for today is that Starlink and Starshield have resumed operations at their pre-restriction speeds. The speeds are now at the level we need," President Volodymyr Zelensky said on the Telegram app.
According to Zelensky, the speeds started returning to normal overnight. Ukraine's Defense Ministry said on Saturday the connection remained stable at over 400 kph.
Ukraine does not rely on the systems for long-range drone operations on Russian territory, including attacks on refineries.
But Starlink remains vital for frontline communications, and the deployment of Starshield-enabled medium-range attack drones has helped Ukraine gain the upper hand in several areas of the battlefield this year.
Limitations order
The restrictions sparked outrage in Ukraine, particularly as they coincided with disruptions to allied warnings about incoming Russian missile attacks. Kyiv later said it continued to receive U.S. intelligence.
Neither Musk nor the U.S. government has acknowledged responsibility for restricting Starlink or Starshield in Ukraine. Both have said publicly that any such decision could only have been taken by the other.
Reuters has reported that the order to throttle Starshield came from inside the White House. Previously, U.S. administrations had several times asked SpaceX to turn Starlink on or off in various countries, sources said.
On Friday, contradicting his previous statement that the services had been fully restored, Trump said that if problems persisted, he would "get it straightened out."

In countries like the UK, Norway and Sweden, protests are allowed right in front of Parliament,” the educationist said at an event in Mumbai.“In India, it was far from Parliament. Even when it was just Jantar Mantar, it was too far,” he added.Wangchuk was referring to demonstrations held at Delhi’s Jantar Mantar, the capital’s now-denotified designated protest site, in June and July following the NEET-UG paper leak in May.The protests, in which Wangchuk played a key role by undertaking an indefinite fast for over 20 days before being removed and taken to a hospital, ended with the resignation of then-Union education minister Dharmendra Pradhan on July 25.His remarks came amid ongoing protests in Delhi demanding the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner (CEC) Gyanesh Kumar over alleged irregularities in the Special Intensive Revision of electoral rolls.

That is the example of Sri Lanka, Bangladesh,” Wangchuk remarked, referring to the youth- and student-led demonstrations in the two neighbouring countries that culminated in the ouster of the incumbent governments.

HONG KONG, Oct. 24 (Xinhua) -- InnoCarnival 2026 opened on Saturday at the Hong Kong Science Park under the theme "Lead with I&T Dream to Fly High", showcasing a number of exhibits of local innovation and technology (I&T) achievements.

Ancient wheat, modern revival: Türkiye reclaims agricultural heritage through heirloom seeds
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
23:16:24 CST
00:16:24 KST

ANKARA, Oct. 24 (Xinhua) -- A hundred years ago, Hatice Alkan kept a sack of wheat seeds in her dowry chest, a traditional blessing of abundance and prosperity.
Alkan raised children, grew old, but forgot the seeds. She would never have imagined that her great-grandson would plant them and help revive a traditional wheat variety known as "red wheat" a century later, and that this would also spur a wider effort to recover and cultivate Türkiye's ancestral seeds that have fallen out of use in modern agriculture.
Across the Anatolia peninsula, farmers, researchers and local institutions have worked to recover crop varieties that may have been displaced by alternatives offering higher yields, more uniform growth and easier harvesting.
Beyond their agricultural value, these heirloom varieties can preserve genetic diversity and traits shaped by generations of cultivation under specific environmental conditions.
In northeastern Türkiye, one such crop is Kavilca, an ancient wheat variety traditionally grown in the provinces of Kars and Ardahan. The region's harsh continental climate, marked by some of the coldest winter temperatures in Türkiye, has helped shape local agricultural practices.
Kavilca is valued for its adaptation to these conditions, making its continued cultivation significant for both regional farming heritage and the conservation of traditional crop varieties.
In 2017, Mirasimiz Yerel Tohum Project, or "Our Heritage, Local Seeds," was launched as a national initiative under the auspices of Emine Erdogan, wife of President Recep Tayyip Erdogan, and the Ministry of Agriculture and Forestry.
Its collection efforts seek out seeds kept in household chests and wrapped in cloth, echoing traditional practices in Turkish brides' dowry chests.
Once collected, seeds can be identified, conserved in seed banks, multiplied, and studied for potential use in agricultural research and breeding. Some varieties may subsequently be registered or made available for wider cultivation, linking household preservation practices with more systematic efforts to protect Türkiye's agricultural genetic resources.
Meanwhile, the Turkish government also helps farmers to reduce the financial burden of adopting traditional varieties.
In 2021, 56 tonnes of kavilca seeds were distributed to 160 producers in Kars and Ardahan to expand cultivation. The farmers received a grant subsidy to cover 75 percent of eligible costs, as an incentive to cultivate a crop that might otherwise remain marginal.
At the Ataturk Agricultural Research Farm, operated by the Ankara Metropolitan Municipality, 45 local seed varieties and cultivars have achieved genetic and developmental stability after three years of selection and cultivation.
Products grown from heirloom seeds, including the traditional Ayas tomato and Ankara melon, have reached modern supermarket shelves, offering a potential route from conservation to commercial production.
Agricultural engineer Fatma Zehra Mutlu told reporters that the seeds would be distributed free of charge to local farmers, where they could complete their growing cycles under natural conditions.
Meanwhile, more than 1,500 indigenous seed samples were collected nationwide between 2020 and 2022 and stored in the national seed gene bank, according to reported figures. The government has also pursued the certification and registration of native varieties to support their formal market circulation.
Türkiye was updating its National Biodiversity Strategy and Action Plan to align with the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework, the international roadmap adopted in 2022 to halt and reverse biodiversity loss, said Ibrahim Yumakli, Türkiye's minister of agriculture and forestry, last Friday at the Leaders' Summit of the 17th Conference of the Parties to the UN Convention on Biological Diversity (COP17) in Yerevan, Armenia.
Describing the protection of biodiversity as a responsibility to future generations, the minister said Türkiye hopes to use the upcoming COP31 climate conference in Antalya to help translate climate commitments into concrete action and strengthen connections among climate policy, biodiversity conservation, land, and food security. Australia upgrades highway rest areas to improve road safety
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
23:16:20 CST
00:16:20 KST

CANBERRA, Oct. 24 (Xinhua) -- Two rest areas in remote South Australia have been newly built or upgraded under a 4.25-million-Australian-dollar (about 2.77 million U.S. dollars) project aimed at reducing driver fatigue and improving road safety, the federal government announced on Friday.
According to a joint statement by the federal and South Australian governments, major works have been completed on a new heavy vehicle rest area along Olympic Dam Highway at Pimba and an upgrade of an existing rest area along Stuart Highway at Arcoona.
The project, jointly funded by the two governments, is expected to improve safety for approximately 950 vehicles, including 330 heavy vehicles, that travel past the sites daily.
Both rest areas can accommodate four triple road trains at a time, with separate parking spaces available for smaller vehicles.
Federal Assistant Minister for Regional Development Anthony Chisholm said driver fatigue was one of the most significant contributors to serious incidents involving heavy vehicles.
"We know that fatigue is one of the most significant contributors to serious incidents involving heavy vehicles," he said.
The Stuart Highway stretches approximately 2,700 km between Port Augusta in South Australia and Darwin in the Northern Territory, serving as a major transport, agriculture, mining and tourism corridor.
According to the statement, 51 crashes were reported on a section of the highway between 2020 and 2024, resulting in four deaths and eight serious injuries. ■

DANDONG, Liaoning, Oct. 24 (Xinhua) -- China's top political advisor Wang Huning on Saturday accompanied Kim Jong Un, general secretary of the Workers' Party of Korea and president of the State Affairs of the Democratic People's Republic of Korea (DPRK), on a visit to Dandong in northeast China's Liaoning Province.
Wang, a member of the Standing Committee of the Political Bureau of the Communist Party of China (CPC) Central Committee and chairman of the National Committee of the Chinese People's Political Consultative Conference, conveyed General Secretary of the CPC Central Committee and Chinese President Xi Jinping's cordial greetings and best wishes to Kim.
On Saturday morning, Wang greeted Kim at the square of the Memorial Hall of the War to Resist U.S. Aggression and Aid Korea and accompanied him to present a flower basket to the memorial tower.
The national anthems of China and the DPRK were played, and honor guards laid the flower basket. Kim approached the flower basket and arranged the ribbon, which read, "The martyrs of the Chinese People's Volunteers (CPV) are always remembered." In a solemn atmosphere, all present paid silent tribute to the martyrs.
Inside the memorial hall, Kim viewed the historical artifacts showcasing the bravery of the martyrs and the side-by-side fighting of Chinese and DPRK soldiers, and gifted a historical photo bearing his personal inscription to the hall.
During their meeting, Wang said on the occasion of the 76th anniversary of the CPV's entry into the DPRK to fight in the War to Resist U.S. Aggression and Aid Korea, General Secretary Kim Jong Un's special trip to Dandong fully demonstrates how much the party and government of the DPRK value the China-DPRK friendship forged with blood.
He said the visit is highly significant, as it not only carries forward the traditional friendship between China and the DPRK and consolidates the popular support for friendship, but also deepens political mutual trust and advances cooperation and development.
In September last year and June this year, General Secretary Xi Jinping and General Secretary Kim Jong Un made historic mutual visits and reached a series of important common understandings, guiding the traditional friendly and cooperative relations between China and the DPRK into a new historical period, Wang said.
China stands ready to work with the DPRK to unswervingly implement the important consensus reached between the top leaders of the two parties and two countries, and take their common socialist cause as a bond to further develop China-DPRK relations, Wang said.
The opening of the new China-DPRK Yalu River bridge can be taken as an opportunity to expand personnel exchanges and trade cooperation and better benefit the two peoples, he said.
He called for strengthening strategic communication and collaboration to foster a peaceful and stable external environment for safeguarding their respective sovereignty, security and development. ■

Across China: Climbing Hainan gibbon population demonstrates China's environmental protection efforts
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
23:16:10 CST
00:16:10 KST

HAIKOU, Oct. 24 (Xinhua) -- Before the morning mist fully lifts, the clear calls of Hainan gibbons already echo through the valleys of Bawangling, part of the Hainan Tropical Rainforest National Park in south China's Hainan Province.
The tropical rainforest in central Hainan is China's most concentrated, best-preserved, and largest contiguous continental-island-type tropical rainforest, and it forms an important part of the world's tropical rainforest system. Established in 2021, the national park covers about 4,269 square kilometers.
According to the park administration, 91 new wildlife and plant species have been discovered in the past five years, and more than 95 percent of Hainan's primary forest and over 55 percent of its natural forest have been effectively protected.
As the world's most endangered gibbon, the Hainan gibbons have long been the rainforest's "top star," with their swinging figures through the canopy the most direct proof of improving ecology in Hainan and also China at large.
Listed as critically endangered by the International Union for Conservation of Nature, the Hainan gibbon once teetered on the brink of extinction, with fewer than 10 individuals remaining in just two groups. The Bawangling area is the species' only known habitat.
The gibbons are back in the spotlight as Saturday marks International Gibbon Day.
Data from the National Forestry and Grassland Administration showed that the population of Hainan's resident gibbons has increased to 44 in seven groups, making it the only gibbon species in the world with a continuously growing population.
Hainan gibbons have long arms and oval faces. The apes are gentle by nature and have unique calls. They feed mainly on ripe berries, tender leaves and twigs, and flower buds, and sometimes also eat honey, insects and bird eggs. Adult males have black fur, while females have golden fur. Females give birth to only one baby gibbon every two to three years.
In recent years, Hainan has stepped up efforts to improve and expand the gibbons' habitat. Measures include relocating residents from core protected areas, restoring degraded ecosystems and building ecological corridors.
Local authorities have also set up professional monitoring teams to conduct on-site monitoring and track the population through surveys. In addition, Hainan's forestry authorities have also established a global think tank for the national park, forming a joint global research mechanism.
Chen Qing, a forest worker involved in gibbon monitoring, has spent years observing the primates through binoculars, photographing them and recording their movements and behavior in a notebook.
Chen has also joined forest protection efforts organized by the Hainan forestry authorities and civil society organizations, planting fruit trees and building rope bridges for the gibbons.
"When we were short-handed, I brought my family members to the front line," Chen said. "We have restored and improved a large area of their habitat."
The gibbons' growing population reflects China's broader efforts to protect its natural environment, authorities said.
Fu Mingkai, a local guide, said the rainforest is a globally important gene pool of germplasm resources and home to many plants and animals unique to Hainan.
"For example, the Hainan gibbon and the Hainan peacock pheasant, both of which have very high requirements for their habitat, have been found here," he said.
Their presence and population recovery show that the rainforest is healthy and full of vitality, he added.
"Thanks to strict protection in recent years, the vegetation has recovered and biodiversity in the rainforest is improving," Fu said.
"The rainforest is the Hainan gibbon's home, and it is my home too," Chen said. "I am sure that one day there will be more gibbons singing songs in the morning to awaken the primeval tropical rainforest." ■

Democrats want to kill Trump’s diesel deal. Working Americans will pay the price
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
15:13:59 UTC
00:13:59 KST

Democrats want to kill Trump’s diesel deal. Working Americans will pay the price
With Americans struggling from soaring energy prices, and businesses across the country trying to keep their heads above water, the Democrats’ apparent priority is to threaten companies that might help ease the pressure.
According to an October 22 Washington Post report, Senate Democrats are preparing to investigate American companies involved in US President Donald Trump’s decision to ease sanctions on Russian diesel. The Senate Foreign Relations Committee has reportedly asked businesses to preserve relevant documents ahead of possible congressional investigations, should Democrats regain control of Congress in the November midterms.
For a party that claims to champion working Americans, this is a peculiar way of demonstrating its concern.
Diesel is the lifeblood of the American economy. It powers the trucks that carry food to supermarkets, the tractors that harvest crops, the machinery that builds homes and roads, and the locomotives that move freight across the vast country.
Yet the people who depend on it have too often been treated as an afterthought by the Washington establishment. They live and work in the industrial towns, farming communities and sprawling rural counties that coastal political elites dismiss as flyover country.
Just recall Hillary Clinton’s infamous 2016 description of millions of Trump supporters as a “basket of deplorables” – a perfect crystallization of the contempt that many ordinary Americans felt was directed at them by the Democrats.
A decade later, that perception is unlikely to be helped by the Democratic lawmakers’ threats to investigate businesses for participating in an arrangement intended to bring additional fuel to the market.
The timing makes those threats extra galling. America is facing an energy crunch aggravated by the Trump administration’s own military campaign against Iran. There is no reason to pretend otherwise. Yes, the president’s decisions helped disrupt global energy markets, and Americans are entitled to demand answers about their consequences.
But recognizing that responsibility does not mean opposing every subsequent attempt to alleviate the damage.
Trump’s decision to temporarily ease restrictions on Russian diesel represents an effort to increase available supplies at a time when the market desperately needs relief. It is a pragmatic response to an immediate economic problem, whatever one thinks of the circumstances that created it.
And now Democrats are determined to make that response costly for the companies willing to participate.
Congress has every right to examine whether the administration acted within its legal authority. But threatening private businesses with investigations for engaging in transactions authorized by the federal government is another matter entirely. If those companies comply with the law, why should they have to fear becoming targets of a future congressional majority?
The actual volume of Russian diesel involved is almost beside the point. Moscow initially pledged to release some 300,000 metric tons of diesel, with further shipments promised in the following months – a modest quantity compared to America’s enormous fuel consumption.
But that’s not what the markets will be reacting to. They react to expectations, regulatory certainty and the willingness of businesses to undertake transactions without fearing political retaliation. And now, even a lawful, government-authorized energy deal could expose companies to years of investigations simply because a different party took power.
Just imagine the chilling effect.
Today, the dispute concerns a relatively small quantity of fuel from one supplier. Tomorrow, the same approach could be applied to other commodities, trading partners or commercial arrangements that fall afoul of Washington’s shifting ideological priorities.
In effect, the Democrats want to hold American energy security hostage to domestic political warfare.
And for what? The ostensible objective is to keep pressuring Russia.
For years, Moscow has faced sweeping Western sanctions, restrictions on financial transactions and efforts to shut its energy exports out of international markets. None of this has forced Russia to accept any of the West’s demands.
Russia has shown it can adapt and endure economic pressure. While not entirely painless, sanctions have consistently failed to produce the political outcome their advocates have called and hoped for.
Meanwhile, Moscow has repeatedly signaled that it remains prepared to negotiate to reasonable counterparts that would take Russia’s own security concerns and national interests into account. Whether those positions are acceptable to Washington is a matter for diplomacy – and refusing to talk altogether is not diplomacy.
Trump is willing to acknowledge that Russia remains a major power with which the US must eventually find a workable relationship. It’s the baseline level of recognition of political reality one expects from the leader of a major world power.
What the Democrats are doing is the international-politics equivalent of pressing their hands to their ears and shouting ‘La La La’ at the top of their lungs.
The truck driver paying more at the pump, the farmer counting operating costs for the next season and the small-business owner watching expenses climb have little interest in Washington’s political theater. They want affordable fuel, predictable costs and a government that remembers whom it is supposed to serve.
Threatening investigations to discourage companies from helping supply the American market is not sending the message the Democrats seem to think it’s sending. It suggests that, to them, political obedience matters more than keeping the country running.
And ordinary Americans could once again be left paying the bill.
The statements, views and opinions expressed in this column are solely those of the author and do not necessarily represent those of RT.

Report: Netanyahu told diplomats to back Argentina's call for Falklands talks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
15:08:39 UTC
00:08:39 KST

Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu instructed Israeli diplomats to support Argentina's call for negotiations over the future of the Falkland Islands and acknowledge Argentina's historical connection to the territory, The Telegraph reported Saturday, citing sources familiar with the matter.
The reported shift in Israel's position follows Britain's decision last month to impose sanctions on Israeli settlements in the West Bank. According to The Telegraph, the move reflects growing tensions between Jerusalem and London over Britain's policies toward Israel and the Palestinians.
The Falkland Islands, known in Argentina as the Malvinas, are a British territory in the South Atlantic, roughly 480 kilometers (about 300 miles) east of Argentina's coast. The dispute dates back centuries and culminated in 1982 when the two nations fought a war over the islands. Although Britain won, the Argentinians still claim the islands.
The diplomatic push comes as Israel seeks closer ties with right-leaning governments in South and Central America, while facing growing criticism from traditional European allies over the Gaza war and settler violence in the West Bank.
The change would not amount to formal Israeli recognition of Argentina's sovereignty claim over the islands, but has raised concerns in Britain that Israel could go further if London imposes additional sanctions on settlements, the newspaper reported.
However, an Israeli Embassy spokesman in London, Alex Gandler, denied that Netanyahu had issued such an instruction. Israel's Foreign Ministry also denied the report, saying: "The report is incorrect. There is no change in our position on the issue."
I categorically deny this allegation. No such directive exists.
Israel's Ambassador to the United Nations, Danny Danon, addressed the dispute at a UN session last week, calling for direct negotiations between Britain and Argentina. Sources cited by The Telegraph described his remarks as a significant departure from Israel's previous position, particularly because they acknowledged Argentina's historical connection to the islands.
Danon said Israel recognized the importance Argentina attached to the issue and its efforts to resolve it through diplomatic channels and in accordance with international law. He also called for direct, constructive and practical dialogue and said any progress should take into account relevant historical, legal and human considerations.
One source told The Telegraph that the wording of Danon's statement had been approved at the highest levels of the Israeli government. The source described the intervention as the first time Israel had become involved in the dispute.
The report linked the shift to Israel's close relationship with Argentine President Javier Milei, who has strongly supported Israel throughout the Hamas-led October 7, 2023, attack. Milei attended Israel's Independence Day celebrations this year, where he lit a ceremonial torch.
Israeli officials cited by The Telegraph also pointed to deteriorating relations with Britain, particularly over the sanctions and critical statements by British leaders. The newspaper reported that the Israeli position could further strain ties amid the dispute over Israel's West Bank policies.
Britain's decision to sanction settlements has brought bilateral relations to their lowest point in decades, following London's recognition of Palestinian statehood last year and its criticism of Israel's conduct in the war in Gaza.
The sanctions announced last month by British Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband expanded Britain's human rights sanctions framework to cover violations of international humanitarian law. The measures allow restrictions on individuals and entities involved in settlement construction, expansion and financing.
The new regulations took effect days before the October 19 deadline for bids on a construction tender in the E1 area of the West Bank, east of Jerusalem. Britain and other countries had warned contractors that participating in the tender could expose them to legal and reputational consequences. The planned construction between Jerusalem and the Ma'aleh Adumim settlement is opposed by Western governments because it could sever the territorial contiguity needed for a future Palestinian state.
Britain has also announced plans for a trade ban on settlements, joined by Canada and France. The British government has said the measure could take six to nine months to enter into force because of the legislative process required.
The measures followed Britain's adoption of the International Court of Justice's 2024 advisory opinion, which found Israel's continued presence in the occupied Palestinian territory unlawful. Separately, the Fourth Geneva Convention prohibits an occupying power from transferring parts of its civilian population into occupied territory.
In response to Britain's moves, Foreign Minister Gideon Sa'ar announced the closure of the British Consulate in Jerusalem. Seven British diplomats will continue to operate in the city under a reduced diplomatic presence.
At a UN Security Council meeting in February, Sa'ar had invoked the Falklands dispute while accusing Britain of hypocrisy over its opposition to Israeli settlements. Addressing then-British Foreign Secretary Yvette Cooper, he argued that Britain's position on Israeli residence in the West Bank contradicted international law and the Balfour Declaration.
"It is our country; it's not 13,000 kilometers from our country, like the Falkland Islands. The Argentinians call it the Malvinas Islands – a dispute you haven't solved with Argentina until today," Sa'ar said.
Despite the political tensions, Israeli government sources told The Telegraph that the two countries continued to cooperate closely on security and hoped to maintain the relationship.
Israel also has practical reasons to stop short of formally endorsing Argentina's claim. Intelligence cooperation with Britain gives Israel an additional channel into the Five Eyes intelligence-sharing alliance, while Israeli companies have commercial ties with British firms involved in the Sea Lion oilfield project near the Falklands.
Britain's Foreign Office has not commented on The Telegraph's report.

Beyond Iran’s famous cities: villages that deserve a place on every traveler’s itinerary
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
15:08:09 UTC
00:08:09 KST

Beyond Iran’s famous cities: villages that deserve a place on every traveler’s itinerary
TEHRAN - Iran’s historical cities are renowned for their grand mosques, Persian gardens, traditional bazaars and Silk Road heritage. Yet beyond the familiar destinations of Isfahan, Shiraz and Yazd, to name a few, lies another side of the country: a landscape of mountain villages, ancient mud-brick settlements and rural communities whose traditions offer a different perspective on Iranian life.
Scattered across the country’s mountains, valleys and desert margins, these places reveal the diversity of Iran’s geography, architecture and cultural heritage. Some are easily reached on a day trip from a nearby city, while others require more time and effort to explore. Together, they offer travelers an opportunity to look beyond the country’s best-known attractions and discover the character of its rural regions.
Kandovan, life inside volcanic rock
In northwestern Iran, Kandovan stands out for its unusual architecture. Located near Tabriz, the village is known for its cone-shaped rock formations, in which generations of residents have carved homes and other living spaces.
Often compared with Cappadocia in central Turkey, Kandovan belongs to a small group of settlements where people have continued to inhabit rock-cut dwellings into modern times. Its distinctive landscape, shaped by volcanic activity and centuries of human adaptation, gives the village an appearance unlike that of most Iranian settlements.
Unlike archaeological cave sites preserved primarily as historical attractions, Kandovan remains a living community. Its homes illustrate how residents have adapted traditional building practices to the surrounding geology and climate.
The village is also one of the more accessible rural destinations for travelers visiting Tabriz, making it a convenient introduction to Iran’s countryside.
Palangan, a village climbing the Kordestan’s mountains
In Kordestan province, western Iran, Palangan is celebrated for its stepped architecture and dramatic mountain setting. Traditional houses rise above one another along the slopes, creating a compact settlement that appears to grow out of the surrounding terrain.
The village offers a glimpse into rural Kurdish life, including local food traditions and the close relationship between communities and their natural environment. Its river, mountain scenery and stone-built houses make it a popular destination for visitors from nearby areas.
Local restaurants serving river fish provide an opportunity to sample regional cuisine, while the surrounding hills offer a setting for walking and exploring.
Palangan is among several stepped villages found across the Kurdish mountain regions of western Iran. Although some rural settlements in the area remain relatively difficult to reach, Palangan can be visited from nearby urban centers, including Sanandaj, with onward travel arrangements.
Masuleh, where rooftops become streets
Further north, in Gilan province, Masuleh offers another striking example of architecture adapted to mountainous terrain. Its traditional houses are built along a steep slope, with the roof of one building often serving as a walkway or courtyard for the house above it.
The arrangement gives the village its distinctive stepped appearance and makes pedestrian movement an integral part of its architectural character.
Set amid the mist-covered mountains of northern Iran, Masuleh is known for its humid climate, lush surroundings and frequent clouds that drift through the settlement. Its popularity among domestic travelers means that its streets can become crowded, particularly during busy travel periods.
Nevertheless, walking trails leading into the surrounding mountains offer opportunities to escape the busiest areas and appreciate the landscape. Within the village, rooftops and narrow paths remain important spaces for everyday encounters, reflecting a strong sense of community.
Masuleh is therefore both a scenic destination and an example of how traditional settlements developed in response to steep terrain and local living conditions.
Gazor-Khan, gateway to the Alamut Valley
For travelers interested in history and mountain landscapes, Gazor-Khan in Qazvin province offers a combination of both. The village is best known as the gateway to the ruins of the UNESCO-listed Alamut Castle, a fortress associated with the Nizari Ismaili community, whose members became known in medieval sources as the Assassins.
Perched high above the Alamut Valley, the fortress occupied a strategic position and became an important center of the Nizari Ismaili state. Its history is closely associated with Hassan-i Sabbah, who established his base there in the late 11th century.
The Mongol campaign led by Hulagu Khan resulted in the fortress's capture and destruction in the 13th century. Although much of the original structure has disappeared, the remaining ruins and surrounding mountain scenery continue to attract visitors.
Beyond the historic site, Gazor-Khan is a quiet mountain village surrounded by orchards, including apple, apricot and cherry trees. In spring, flowering trees add color to the landscape, while hiking routes provide opportunities to explore the valley.
The journey requires more planning than a visit to villages close to major cities, but the combination of history, scenery and rural life makes it a rewarding destination.
Abyaneh, a living link to Iran’s past
Located near Kashan, at the foot of Mount Karkas, Abyaneh is among Iran’s best-known historic villages. Its red earthen buildings, wooden balconies, narrow lanes and traditional dress give it a distinctive appearance.
The settlement is often associated with Iran’s pre-Islamic past, although its long history spans multiple periods. Its architecture reflects the use of locally available materials, particularly the red soil that gives the buildings their characteristic color.
Abyaneh is also notable for the preservation of elements of local language and cultural traditions. Some older residents speak a distinctive local dialect, while traditional clothing remains an important part of the village’s cultural identity.
Men have traditionally worn dark coats and loose trousers, while women’s clothing is known for its colorful patterns and white headscarves. These customs provide a visible connection to regional traditions that have endured alongside broader changes in Iranian society.
Abyaneh’s popularity, however, has brought challenges. Visitors can fill its narrow streets, particularly during peak travel periods, and the village can sometimes feel more like an open-air heritage site than an ordinary rural community.
Nain, desert heritage beyond the main tourist routes
Between Yazd and Tehran, Nain offers a quieter encounter with Iran’s desert heritage. Although technically a small town rather than a village, it deserves attention for its historic architecture and relatively understated place on many travel itineraries.
The town is known for its historical Jameh Mosque, an old bazaar, traditional water reservoirs and the remains of Narenj Castle. Together, these structures reflect the architectural and engineering traditions that helped communities survive in Iran’s arid central regions.
Traditional water reservoirs, known as ab-anbars, were designed to store water for use during dry periods. Along with other water-management structures, they demonstrate the importance of adapting settlement patterns and architecture to scarce water resources.
Parts of Nain’s historic fabric have deteriorated, and some old buildings remain in poor condition. Yet the town’s less commercialized atmosphere can offer a different experience from more heavily visited heritage destinations.
Its contrast between historic quarters and newer neighborhoods also reveals how traditional settlements have evolved as residents adapt to contemporary life.
Kharanaq, traces of an ancient Silk Road settlement
Northeast of Yazd, Kharanaq is known for its abandoned mud-brick settlement and atmospheric ruins. The village developed along historic travel routes and is associated with the network of settlements that supported movement across central Iran.
Its old buildings, narrow alleys and earthen walls form a dense architectural landscape. Some structures are believed to date back many centuries, although the history of individual buildings varies.
Walking through the abandoned quarter offers a sense of how communities once organized their homes and passageways in a desert environment. From elevated points, visitors can see the settlement against a backdrop of surrounding mountains and open terrain.
The ruins are also vulnerable. Weathering, erosion and uncontrolled visitor access can accelerate the deterioration of fragile earthen structures. Exploring the area responsibly means avoiding unstable buildings, staying on established paths where possible and respecting any restricted areas.
Kharanaq can be combined with visits to Meybod and the Zoroastrian pilgrimage site of Chak Chak, making it a possible addition to a wider itinerary from Yazd.
Meybod, desert architecture and ingenious design
Meybod, another historical settlement near Yazd, offers a broader view of the architectural traditions of Iran’s central desert. Although it is a town rather than a village, its historic structures make it a worthwhile stop for travelers interested in the region’s cultural heritage.
One of its principal attractions is Narin Castle, a large earthen fortress whose origins extend back into antiquity. The town also preserves traditional water reservoirs and a historic pigeon house.
Pigeon houses were constructed to shelter birds and collect their droppings, which were used as agricultural fertilizer. Their design reflects the resourcefulness of communities that relied on locally available materials and developed practical solutions to meet everyday needs.
The pigeon house in Meybod is among the notable surviving examples of this building tradition in Iran.
Together, the castle, water-storage structures and pigeon house illustrate how architecture in the desert served practical purposes while also becoming part of the region’s distinctive cultural landscape.
Why Iran’s rural destinations matter
Exploring Iran’s villages and smaller historic settlements offers more than a change of scenery. These places reveal how people have adapted to different environments, from the volcanic formations of the northwest to the steep mountains of Kordestan and the water-scarce landscapes of the central plateau.
Their architecture reflects local responses to climate, geology and available resources. Their languages, clothing, food and customs also demonstrate the country’s regional and ethnic diversity.
For travelers whose itineraries focus on Iran’s famous cities, adding even one or two rural destinations can broaden their understanding of the country.

Security forces deploy as Milan braces for another day of protests

Hundreds of Italian soldiers deployed as thousands protest in Milan
The Italian government sent hundreds of soldiers to the country’s fashion and financial hub ahead of anticipated unrest.
Milan, Italy – Thousands of protesters took to the streets across Italy to demonstrate against Giorgia Meloni’s right-wing government and the rising cost of living, a week after clashes with police and looting during demonstrations in Milan.
Protests were called in eight Italian cities on Saturday, including the fashion and finance capital, Milan, where the government deployed hundreds of soldiers.
As soldiers spread out and luxury boutiques were boarded up, two demonstrations marched through the streets of the northern city.
Around 50 people gathered spontaneously in Cordusio Square, heading towards the central Castle square and chanting, “We are all antifascists”.
Small groups joined the main demonstration along the way, swelling its ranks. Many of the protesters were young people.
At its peak, the protest drew around 10,000 people.
“I believe that the main obstacle to our future is our state,” Riccardo, a 17-year-old student from Milan who did not give his last name, told Al Jazeera.
“We are here because of the rising prices and because I believe that our government has no respect for its citizens,” another 17-year-old student from the province of Pavia added, without giving his name.
“There are four people in my family. My mother works in a factory, but my father is about to lose his job. It’s hard to make ends meet on just one salary,” he said.
For almost four hours, the protesters walked around the city centre, heading southeast while being watched by riot police. They finally stopped at 7:30pm local time (17:30GMT) in front of Milan Polytechnic University.
There were no security incidents in Milan, but protesters clashed with police in other cities, including Turin and Rome, Italy’s ANSA news agency reported.
Police said nine people were arrested in protests across Italy on Saturday, with a total of 371 briefly detained.
‘We distrust this government’
Saturday’s demonstrations followed an announcement online of a new round of protests by a newly formed group calling itself the ‘October 17 Movement’. It has been the main driver of demonstrations alongside student federations, grassroots trade unions and antiwar coalitions.
“Those who deny our future are truly violent,” the group said on Instagram. “We distrust this government because we see it as authoritarian.”
In response to last weekend’s looting, the government announced a series of new security measures, including the deployment of 500 soldiers to Milan on Saturday.
On Friday, police carried out raids and searches in several cities for people suspected of taking part in looting and rioting in last weekend’s protests, reported the Italian news agency Adnkronos. Another 150 raids were carried out on Saturday morning in the northern region of Lombardy.
On its Telegram channel, the October 17 Movement said many of those planning to demonstrate wanted to voice their dissent peacefully.
“We must be peaceful. If we give [the police] an excuse, they will charge against us,” a participant identified as E said on Thursday.
Others have stressed that there is no distinction between those who engage in violence and peaceful protesters. “It’s just us,” said a member identified as Q.
Protesters decided to keep the location of the demonstration secret until the last minute, with three meeting points announced on their social media accounts on Saturday afternoon.
Police confirmed to Al Jazeera that they had located and were questioning the administrator of the group’s Instagram page. According to the Italian daily Corriere della Sera, he is a 30-year-old Italian-Moroccan freelance journalist and researcher. He is currently under investigation on suspicion of “inciting crimes”.
Most of the arrested protesters were under 18.
Some joined the protests last weekend after being unexpectedly added to a Telegram group, Corriere della Sera reported.
“They said that they would raise chaos and we could take a lot of goods,” one of them said.
Lawyer Michele D’Agostino is defending two demonstrators, aged 21 and 15.
“[The youngest one] didn’t even know the reasons behind the protest; he had just seen it on TikTok and decided to check it out with a friend,” D’Agostino told Al Jazeera.
“He was not among the looters, but he did not realise the seriousness of what was happening,” he said.
The public prosecutor has blamed social media for misleading young people into taking part in what he described as “insurrectional acts”.
Justice Minister Carlo Nordio told Sky TG24 that there was a need to “expand the capacity of our youth detention facilities” in response to the mass arrests of under-18s.
“Looting is wrong, but I cannot understand why it makes more noise than what happens in southern Italy, where people are facing fuel shortages,” said a 17-year-old student, whose family is originally from Senegal and who joined the demonstration in Milan.
Earlier this week, truck drivers set up roadblocks in several regions of southern Italy to protest against soaring fuel prices, leaving many markets without supplies for days. On Thursday, the government sought to offer them some relief by granting tax breaks and establishing a special fund for farmers and fishermen.

Netanyahu says Israel mulling over crypto ahead of possible sanctions
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said he is exploring the use of cryptocurrency to circumvent potential financial sanctions on Israel, drawing criticism from opposition figures who said it would turn the Jewish state into an economic pariah like Iran.
“We need to prepare ways to evade banking sanctions through an alternative economic system,” Netanyahu said in an interview with Israel’s Channel 10. “You know what that means – the currencies that can bypass them. I’m working on that too.” Asked whether he meant crypto, the Prime Minister said: “Very correct.”
Netanyahu was speaking ahead of the Oct 27 election, where he faces a strong challenge from former general Gadi Eisenkot.
Opposition leader Yair Lapid said the Prime Minister’s proposal for evading potential sanctions “belongs to countries like Iran, Russia, and Venezuela – nations whose banks are cut off from the world, whose companies cannot accept payments, and whose young people are fleeing”.
“That’s his vision,” Lapid added in a post on social media platform X.
In September, 12 major countries, led by Britain, pledged coordinated measures against Israeli settlements in the West Bank. British Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband said the moves would also cover individuals and companies providing financing, construction and other services to the settlements.
That raised fears of sanctions on Israeli banks that could rattle the tech-export-driven economy.
“The concern is that foreign banks will cease providing correspondent services to their Israeli counterparts, effectively severing Israel’s ability to conduct international economic activity,” said Yair Avidan, a former banking supervisor at the Bank of Israel.

In the interview, Netanyahu also warned that decades of US military aid would end, forcing Israel to finance its defence on its own.
“If you think we will continue receiving what I secured twice – tens of billions of dollars in American aid for the defence budget – you’d better prepare yourselves and get used to the idea that this will not continue,” he said. “That is because America has changed, not because Israel has changed. It will end. It is only a matter of time.”
Netanyahu said Israel has two more years with US President Donald Trump, but must prepare for a less favourable Washington after he leaves power.
The US and Israel have agreed a memorandum of understanding which runs through 2028 and provides US$3.8 billion (S$4.9 billion) annually, largely for military procurement from the US.
Washington extended a supplement of at least US$15 billion during three years of war triggered by Hamas’ October 2023 attack on Israel, which claimed the lives of 1,200 Israelis.

The Joint List is “decisive” in efforts to prevent Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu from remaining in power, its parliamentary leader Ahmad Tibi said, outlining conditions for providing an alternative government with a parliamentary safety net.
In an interview with Anadolu, Tibi described next Tuesday’s Knesset elections as “important, fateful and dangerous,” saying his alliance was prepared to cooperate with the Jewish opposition without joining its government.
The Joint List brings together Tibi’s Arab Movement for Change, the Democratic Front for Peace and Equality and the National Democratic Assembly, known as Balad. A poll published Friday by the Israeli newspaper Maariv projected that it would win nine seats.
Tibi predicted increased turnout among Arab citizens, who account for about 20% of Israel’s population of more than 10 million.
He expected neither Netanyahu’s bloc nor the Jewish opposition to secure the 61 seats required for a parliamentary majority, in line with various opinion polls.
“The Jewish blocs — the opposition and the ruling coalition — are evenly matched. Even if the United Arab List, led by Mansour Abbas, is added to the opposition bloc, it would reach only 56 or 57 seats, which would not be enough to bring down Netanyahu’s government,” Tibi said.

“Only the Joint List is the decisive list that guarantees the removal of the government of Benjamin Netanyahu, (Finance Minister Bezalel) Smotrich and (National Security Minister Itamar) Ben-Gvir,” he said.
“The stronger the Joint List, the easier it will be to remove the government of crime, war and failure: Benjamin Netanyahu’s government.”

“Netanyahu will not be able to form a right-wing government. He wants to prevent (Yashar leader Gadi) Eisenkot or the opposition from forming a government, so he wants to remain prime minister of a caretaker government,” he said.
“We in the Joint List are willing and ready to cooperate to prevent him from continuing to head a caretaker government. Parliamentarily, this is possible.”

“I do not want to go into the details. This is possible parliamentarily, and the Joint List will help and vote in favor of it,” he said, adding that his alliance had been the first to propose removing Knesset Speaker Amir Ohana.
“We want to vote against him (Netanyahu) alongside the opposition and vote in favor of the opposition. This is natural, but it will change the current rules of the game inside parliament.”
Asked about the conditions for providing a parliamentary safety net to Eisenkot, a former Israeli military chief, Tibi said any arrangement must provide safeguards for Arab citizens.
“There must be a safety net for our community and our issues: crime and violence, personal security, house demolitions, the Kaminitz Law, an end to incitement and racism against our doctors, our nurses, bus drivers and every Arab in this country, much larger budgets and infrastructure,” he said.
The Kaminitz Law concerns enforcement against unauthorized construction, including the demolition of Arab homes.
“We also want a political horizon, which is an important source of hope. We will raise all these issues with anyone who wants us to help provide a safety net or support votes here and there,” Tibi said.
He stressed that such support would not mean joining an opposition-led government.
Eisenkot has said he wants a “Zionist government” committed to what he described as a “Jewish Israel” and aligned with his political and security positions.
“That is for those who want to join the government. We are not there,” Tibi said.
“We do not want to be responsible for incursions into Al-Aqsa Mosque, a war in Gaza, the continuation of Jewish terrorism and settlement activity, or house demolitions.”
Joining a government or coalition would entail “collective responsibility,” he said, while other arrangements could allow cooperation on specific issues.
“This will contribute to removing Netanyahu’s government and paving the way for an alternative government that is less bad,” he said.
“The next government will not be our dream government. It will not be a government of peace, but it will be less bad than the government of Netanyahu, Smotrich and Ben-Gvir.”
Asked whether he meant an Eisenkot-led minority government supported by the Joint List from within the Knesset, Tibi declined to elaborate.
“We will see the numbers, the results, how the current opposition behaves and which direction it wants to take,” he said.
“There are those calling for a national unity government. That would be bad, and it is not what the public wants, even the Israeli public. So we want to wait. We are pushing to bring down this government and establish an alternative.”
Tibi said the coming election differed from previous votes because of the policies and plans of the current government.
“We are talking about a criminal and fascist government that has committed and plans to expand war crimes: ethnic cleansing, incitement against our community inside Israel, spreading crime, house demolitions, Jewish terrorism in the occupied territories and war crimes in Gaza,” he said.
He accused Smotrich of threatening to extend settlement policies to Galilee and said Smotrich and Ben-Gvir were threatening to bring down the Palestinian Authority and annex Palestinian territory.
Tibi also warned of “rising racism against Arab citizens and treating them as enemies.”
“This is a real threat to our existence, our future and our collective identity,” he said.
“That is why these elections are important, fateful and dangerous. We sense that our public is mature and wise, and wants to bring about change, exert influence and defend itself through voting.”
Tibi said indicators pointed to increased participation among Arab voters.
“There is an upward trend in turnout. Today, the figure stands at 62%. At the same point before the previous election in 2022, it was 48%, so there is a clear difference,” he said.
“We want it to reach at least 70%. Some towns will reach that level.”
Higher Arab turnout could help remove Netanyahu from power and push one or two small right-wing lists below the electoral threshold, he argued, naming the lists of Ofer Winter and Yoaz Hendel as potential losses for Netanyahu’s camp.
Asked about expectations that increased Arab participation could also mobilize right-wing voters, Tibi said Jewish turnout might rise by two to four percentage points.
“Alongside increased Arab participation, this rise also contributes to pushing the small right-wing lists out,” he said.
“This will move Benjamin Netanyahu further away from being able to secure a decisive outcome in his favor.”
Tibi outlined several possible post-election scenarios, including an opposition-led government, a Jewish national unity government or Netanyahu remaining at the head of a caretaker administration until another election.
“Netanyahu wants to remain prime minister of a caretaker government and return to elections again in March or April. We will try to use our strength as the Joint List to thwart this scenario,” he said.
Asked about right-wing election campaigns focusing on Arabs at the expense of economic and social issues, Tibi accused right-wing politicians and media outlets of using hostility toward Arabs to rally their supporters.
“The lowest common denominator is spreading hatred and incitement against everything Arab and everything Palestinian,” he said.
“That is why there is incitement against us, against Arab doctors, medical teams, drivers and pharmacists, on right-wing channels and among right-wing politicians.”
“They believe this incitement and hatred will consolidate the right-wing base on the eve of the election. This is very dangerous and threatens those being targeted-- Arabs,” he added.
Tibi also suggested Netanyahu might seek a military confrontation to influence the political landscape.
“Netanyahu would like to launch a war before the election. If he could, he would. It is said that Trump prevented him from doing so,” he added.
“He may do it after the election to impose a national unity government. All these scenarios are possible.”
Asked whether an election defeat for one side could trigger internal unrest, Tibi warned that a right-wing loss could lead to increased incitement, threats and attacks against Arab leaders, left-wing figures or opposition leaders.
“Netanyahu has no red lines. He was a partner in the incitement against Yitzhak Rabin back then, until he was killed,” Tibi said.
“He will also fuel the incitement machine at a greater and fiercer pace.”
Rabin, a former Israeli prime minister whose Labor government signed the Oslo agreement with the Palestine Liberation Organization in 1993, was assassinated by Jewish extremist Yigal Amir on Nov. 4, 1995, as he left a peace rally in Tel Aviv. The assassination followed intense political polarization and right-wing protests against the agreement.
Tibi predicted that the Joint List would win at least nine seats.
“If turnout among Arab citizens rises to 70%, 71% or 72%, we could win nine or 10 seats,” he said. “With those numbers, we will bring down Benjamin Netanyahu.”

Review under way on array that detects nuclear tests
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
16:00:02 BST
00:00:02 KST

An independent review has been commissioned into ways of reducing the ground vibration reaching the Eskdalemuir seismic array, the installation that gives Britain its contribution to global nuclear test detection, and it covers putting sensors down boreholes and processing the signal differently, according to answers given in Parliament.
Luke Akehurst, the Labour member for North Durham, put four questions to the Ministry of Defence on the array, its monitoring equipment and the restrictions it places on wind farm development nearby.
Luke Pollard, Minister of State for Defence Readiness and Industry, said: “Monitoring equipment at the Eskdalemuir Seismometer Array is continually reviewed to ensure it meets national requirements and the requirements of the Comprehensive Nuclear Test-Ban Treaty Organisation International Monitoring System.
“There is currently an ongoing independent review of mitigation proposals for reduction of seismic ground vibration received at the Eskdalemuir seismic array and the effect on the detection capability of the array, commissioned by the Ministry of Defence and Department for Energy Security and Net Zero. This includes a review of borehole emplacement and digital signal processing approaches.”
Asked when the science behind the restrictions on wind energy development around the array was last independently reviewed, Pollard said: “The current methodology used to assess the impact of wind turbines on the Array’s ability to detect underground seismic events has been developed using specialist scientific advice and remains the basis for safeguarding decisions. The methodology itself was retained as part of the revised safeguarding approach published in March 2026 following public consultation.”
On whether upgrading the array could allow more onshore wind to be built, Pollard said: “The Ministry of Defence (MOD) has worked closely with the Department for Energy Security and Net Zero (DESNEZ) over onshore wind deployment in the vicinity of the Eskdalemuir Seismic Array, which supports the United Kingdom’s obligations under the Comprehensive Nuclear-Test-Ban Treaty. As part of this work, the MOD supported experimental testing of alternative technologies and has considered assessments undertaken by specialist technical advisers and independent seismology experts.
“DESNZ has recently consulted on a revised approach to managing onshore wind turbine interference in the vicinity of the Array. The MOD and DESNZ have also commissioned an independent scientific review of alternative technological solutions.
“Previously, evidence made available to the Department has not demonstrated that proposed alternative technological solutions provide viable mitigation for operational use. The consultation responses and independent scientific review are currently being considered and DESNZ will publish a government response reflecting the outcome of both processes soon.”
Eskdalemuir sits in Dumfriesshire and feeds the International Monitoring System run by the Comprehensive Nuclear-Test-Ban Treaty Organisation in Vienna, which watches for the seismic signature of an underground nuclear explosion anywhere in the world. Turbine blades and towers transmit vibration into the ground, and that noise competes with the signals the array is there to hear. A safeguarding zone restricts development around the site, and that zone has become contested as onshore wind expands across southern Scotland.

Only one in six Poles knows where the nearest shelter is located — survey

Unknown Publisher

Only one in six Poles knows where the nearest shelter is located — survey
Kyiv • UNN
Nearly 60% of Poland’s residents do not know the location of the nearest shelter. Only 15.7% of respondents can name its exact location.
Almost 60% of Poland’s residents do not know where the nearest shelter or refuge is located near their home. Only 15.7% of those surveyed can name such a place precisely. This is evidenced by the results of a United Surveys by IBRiS study for Wirtualna Polska, reports UNN.
Details
In the poll, the results of which were published on October 24, 2026, respondents were asked whether they knew where the nearest shelter or refuge was located near their place of residence.
58.7% of participants answered: "I don’t know." Another 8.4% said that they were not interested in the subject, while 1.3% considered the question too difficult.
"Overall, almost 70 percent of Poles cannot name a single facility where they could seek help in the event of a threat," the post says.
By contrast, according to the study’s results, 15.7% of respondents know the exact location of the nearest shelter or refuge. Another 15.9% have an approximate idea of where such a place is located.
"This means that only one in six Poles feels fully prepared for a crisis situation. Not many more—15.9%—know about such a place ‘more or less,’" the study says.
The United Surveys by IBRiS study was conducted from October 16 to 18, 2026, on a representative sample of 1,000 people. According to the information available, the results clearly demonstrate that "the issue of security and crisis preparedness must return to news headlines and educational programs."
Reminder
In Ukraine, the rules for access to shelters located in schools and kindergartens have been clarified. From now on, people who are not involved in working at these institutions may take shelter there from shelling only by a separate decision of the local authorities and subject to compliance with the specified safety requirements.
