13:14:26 UTC
22:14:26 KST

Germany is negotiating a deal with Ukraine to purchase Bars jet-powered drones, a German official with knowledge of the matter told the Kyiv Independent on Oct. 24.
Berlin is discussing the deal with Kyiv as Germany plans to buy thousands of deep-strike weapons from European arms companies, as initially reported by Bloomberg on Oct. 23.
According to officials Bloomberg spoke with, Germany’s future strategic thinking involves using masses of cheap missiles to overwhelm enemy air defenses. Currently, Germany’s army only operates midrange Taurus cruise missiles, while the U.S. warned its allies to expect years-long delays for missile deliveries.
The Bars jet powered drone has a range of 1,000 kilometers and can reach speeds of up to 700 kilometers per hour. The manufacturer of the drones is not publicly known for security reasons.
The Ukrainian army launches around 2,000 of these drones per month, targeting Russian oil refineries, power plants, and substations, a representative of the company told Ukrainian media outlet NV in September.
Germany and Ukraine signed a deal to jointly produce Bars in July 2026 as part of the Build with Ukraine initiative. Under the first stage of the deal, Germany would finance the production of the drones, while all manufactured equipment would be sent to Ukraine’s Armed Forces.
Recently, President Volodymyr Zelensky said that Bars have proven to be one of the most effective interceptors against Russian jet-powered drones, as Moscow escalates attacks on Ukrainian cities, Ukrinform reported on Oct. 10.
Germany has emerged as the biggest foreign partner in Ukraine’s burgeoning defense tech sector. A September report from the Kyiv School of Economics Institute found that there were 36 joint ventures between Ukrainian and German firms, as Berlin prioritizes deep-strike technology and intelligence.

Source: Zelenskyy in a video address
Quote: "Starlink and Starshield are back to operating at the speeds they were capable of before these restrictions were imposed. Now we have the speed we need."
Details: Zelenskyy said speeds began to recover overnight and that by morning they had reached the level needed for military use.
"This is very important; it is significant for our frontline logistics and for protecting Ukraine from jet-powered Shahed drones," he noted.
Prior to this, the defence forces and experts from the Ministry of Defence recorded Starlink and Starshield operating at speeds exceeding 161 km/h.
The Ministry of Defence later officially confirmed that it was recording Starlink and Starshield speeds exceeding 400 km/h and that the connection was stable.

- On 16 October, US President Donald Trump claimed that the White House had not been involved in restricting Ukraine's use of the system.

Dominican Republic becomes latest Latin American country to adopt IHRA antisemitism definition amid regional shift to the right
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
13:10:00 UTC
22:10:00 KST

On August 24, the Dominican government adopted the International Holocaust Remembrance Alliance (IHRA) working definition of antisemitism, infamous for equating opposition to Israeli apartheid and Zionist colonialism with antisemitism. President Luis Abinader made the announcement in Santo Domingo, while speaking at an event organized by the U.S. Zionist organization Combat Antisemitism Movement. Subsequently, a statement from the Dominican Foreign Ministry justified the decision by invoking a supposed official policy against hate and discrimination dating back to 1938 when, according to the text, “the Dominican State was the only one to offer asylum in Sosúa to a significant number of Jewish refugees fleeing the war crimes perpetrated by the Nazi regime”.
In 1938, the racist and genocidal Trujillo dictatorship was in power. Just as the Israeli regime pushes for the redefinition of antisemitism to shield itself, in Orwellian fashion, Abinader is rewriting the past to accommodate the neo-Trujilloist present.
It is not surprising that the Dominican government, led by Abinader, would uphold the Trujilloist legacy. This is a government that has denied the significance of slavery during the Spanish colonial period that preceded the formation of the Dominican state, that does not officially commemorate the genocide against Haitians in 1937, known as the Parsley Massacre, and that denies the existence of widespread racism in the Dominican Republic while keeping more than 200,000 Dominicans of Haitian descent stateless. President Abinader boasts of following the ideas of dictator Joaquín Balaguer, one of the Trujillo era’s main ideologues. Abinader follows in Trujillo’s footsteps regarding what Dominican racists dub “the Haitian problem,” as shown by his policy of mass deportations and the construction of a border wall—an aggiornamento of the Trujillo-era political program known as the “Dominicanization of the border.”
Today’s neo-Trujilloist regime, with its apartheid policies of racial mass deportations, denationalization and statelessness, is coherent in its support of the genocidal Israeli regime and in claiming the legacy of the dictatorship. This is the true significance of the Dominican endorsement of the IHRA definition through a statement that upholds the legacy of a totalitarian regime that extorted and killed Jewish refugees.
In the context of the ongoing genocide in Gaza, the Dominican government has signed agreements with Israel on issues such as water management and has acquired Israeli weapons. By adopting the IHRA’s working definition of antisemitism, Abinader now threatens to further erode the weak democratic rights that still exist in this Caribbean country by moving in the direction of weaponizing accusations of antisemitism to criminalize solidarity with Palestine.
Abinader’s total subordination to Trump is another key driver of his support for Israel. The Dominican government has aligned itself with the pro-Trump “Shield of the Americas” regional coalition and has made its airports available for U.S. military operations in the Caribbean and against Venezuela; it has even agreed to accept deportees from third countries arriving from the U.S.
The Dominican government’s alliance with Israel is part of this broader trend, and one of the clearest indicators of the region’s shift to the right is the intensification of ties with Israeli apartheid.
The IHRA definition and the regional shift to the right
Due to a combination of strong U.S. interference and the decline of center-left parties, elections over the past year have brought right-wing governments to power in Bolivia, Chile, Honduras, and Colombia. In the cases of Bolivia and Colombia, which had no diplomatic relations with Israel, these were immediately reestablished. In Chile and Honduras, where relations had been degraded by the withdrawal of ambassadors, there was a full diplomatic normalization.
The Venezuelan government’s capitulation to Trumpism, following the U.S. military attack on January 3, 2026, and the kidnapping of Nicolás Maduro, is also part of this regional shift to the right. Interim president Delcy Rodríguez reestablished diplomatic relations with Israel in August, following a campaign of “disaster diplomacy” by Netanyahu, who took advantage of the twin earthquakes in northern Venezuela that left more than 6,500 dead and tens of thousands injured. Relations had been broken since 2009.
In turn, the adoption of the IHRA’s definition of antisemitism has become an indicator of how closely Latin American regimes align with the objectives of Israeli foreign policy and their willingness to criminalize solidarity with Palestine. The definition in question was drafted in 2004 and adopted by the IHRA in 2016, after which it was promoted by Israeli foreign policy as part of its “new antisemitism” doctrine, which views opposition to Israel as the most significant form of antisemitism. Its text includes questioning the democratic character of the State of Israel among its examples of antisemitism. The definition was referenced in a Trump executive order in 2019 and in Latin America it has been adopted by right-wing governments in Argentina, Colombia, Costa Rica, Panama, Guatemala, and Uruguay before being adopted by the Dominican Republic.
Over the past two years in Argentina, legal proceedings have been initiated, using the IHRA definition, against Alejandro Bodart, Vanina Biasi, and Mariano Soria, leaders of the Left and Workers’ Front-Unity, a Trotskyist coalition that holds four seats in the National Congress. In Brazil, socialist leader Zé María of the PSTU and the Jewish journalist Breno Altman have been criminalized for criticizing the Israeli state and calling for Palestinian freedom “from the river to the sea.” Zé María was sentenced to two years in prison, Altman was fined, Bodart won an appeal that overturned his conviction, and the cases against Biasi and Soria remain open.
Kenneth Stern, the main drafter of the IHRA definition, who describes himself as a liberal Zionist, has criticized its use by right-wing Jewish sectors to limit freedom of expression and foster a McCarthyist environment, citing the case of Germany, where authorities have used it to label Jewish people as “anti-Semites” for opposing Israeli crimes in Gaza. Stern recommended the U.S. Senate in 2025 to not adopt the IHRA definition.
Dominican legal scholar Jaime Rodríguez has pointed out that, within the Dominican legislative framework, the Abinader administration’s endorsement of the IHRA definition is not yet legally binding, though he has warned of the risks of censorship and persecution that would result from moving forward with enshrining it into law. Democratic guarantees and freedoms in the country are already fragile, and the alliance with Israel has contributed to their weakening, as evidenced by the Dominican government’s use of the Israeli spyware Pegasus against journalists.
But the peril is an even greater one. There is a clear affinity between the Neo-Trujillista regime led by Abinader and the Zionist project, as Israel is viewed by the Dominican right as a blueprint for Dominican apartheid. Neonazi organizations regularly wield Israeli flags at racist marches against Haitians. Much like Trujillo in 1938, Abinader is unconcerned about antisemitism or discrimination more broadly, as the regime he leads is carrying out a brutal crackdown on Haitian migrants and Dominicans of Haitian descent, conducting a campaign of more than one million deportations over the past six years during which dozens of people have been killed and many more subjected to horrific violence. Normalizing genocide abroad is a way of normalizing apartheid and ethnic cleansing it at home.

US updates Israel travel warning, cites growing threat from Iran-backed Houthis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
13:09:00 UTC
22:09:00 KST

The US State Department issued an updated travel advisory notice for Israel on Friday, warning of an increased threat of armed attacks by Iran-backed Houthi terrorists and the potential for a rapid escalation of regional hostilities.
The update did not change Israel's overall travel advisory classification, which remains at Level 3, urging American citizens to reconsider travel due to terrorism and unrest. The existing risk indicators and restrictions on travel to certain areas of the country also remain unchanged.
In its warning on armed conflict, the State Department cited previous Houthi attacks against Saudi Arabia, including strikes on civilian airports and critical infrastructure that resulted in civilian casualties and major travel disruptions.
The department warned that hostilities involving the Houthis could escalate rapidly beyond the areas immediately affected, potentially posing additional risks to travelers across the region.
The updated warning comes against the backdrop of previous missile threats originating from Yemen, which have required Israel to activate air defense systems and issue civilian alerts.
US maintains restrictions on travel to Israeli border areas
Despite the updated regional threat assessment, Washington has not raised its overall warning level for Israel. The State Department continues to advise Americans to reconsider travel because of terrorism and unrest, while maintaining stricter Level 4 restrictions in several designated areas.
These restrictions cover areas north of the Route 85, Route 90, and Route 87 boundaries in northern Israel; locations within 11.3 kilometers of the Gaza Strip; and areas within 2.4 kilometers of the Israel-Egypt border, except near the Taba crossing, also known as the Menachem Begin crossing.
The State Department said Israeli authorities restrict travel in the designated northern areas because of IDF activity and presence, and instructed Americans not to travel there for any reason.
US government employees working in Israel face the same geographical restrictions. Official travel to these areas requires approval from the US Embassy's security office.
The advisory also reiterated that, as of August 26, family members are permitted to accompany US government employees stationed in Israel. However, Washington warned that additional security measures affecting US personnel could be introduced as conditions evolve.
The State Department emphasized that Israel's security environment remains complex and can change rapidly, warning that violence could occur without advance notice.
Regional tensions could also prompt airlines to cancel flights or reduce services to and from Israel, potentially disrupting travel plans even in areas not subject to the highest-level restrictions.
Americans urged to prepare for missile and drone threats
The advisory urged American citizens planning to visit Israel to remain vigilant, avoid demonstrations and large gatherings, and familiarize themselves with emergency procedures.
Travelers were advised to identify nearby bomb shelters and download the Home Front Command's Red Alert application, or similar services, to receive real-time warnings about incoming rockets, missiles and armed drones.
Israel's Home Front Command emergency warning systems have been used during previous missile attacks, providing residents with alerts intended to help them reach protected areas.
The military has also updated its advance-warning capabilities to give civilians more time to prepare for certain missile threats.
The State Department encouraged American travelers to enroll in its Smart Traveler Enrollment Program, which enables the US Embassy to distribute security updates and contact citizens or their emergency contacts during a crisis.
Americans were also urged to develop independent evacuation plans that do not rely on US government assistance, follow instructions from local security officials, and exercise particular caution near checkpoints and areas with a significant security presence.
The advisory further recommended purchasing comprehensive travel insurance that covers emergency medical treatment, evacuation assistance, and trip cancellations.
The warnings underscore the continued importance of civilian preparedness amid regional missile and drone threats, with Israeli authorities having previously reviewed the timing and operation of emergency alerts during periods of heightened tensions.
Although the October 23 notice highlighted the increased potential for Houthi aggression, it did not announce additional restrictions on travel to Israel or a change in the State Department's assessment of the country's overall travel risk.

Beyond the ballot, October 7 families call for a different kind of Israeli politics
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
13:08:47 UTC
22:08:47 KST

Moshe Shapiro wants Israelis to learn to live together with the same seriousness with which they learned to protect wildflowers.
Shapiro, whose son Aner was killed on October 7, 2023, while throwing grenades back out of a roadside shelter to protect fellow Nova music festival-goers, is among the bereaved relatives behind Hamechane, an initiative seeking to make social cohesion a national responsibility.
Ahead of the elections, he joined Hoda Daxa and Shai Zohar in an interview with The Jerusalem Post about what that would require – and whose place in Israeli society needs to be recognized.
“Unity is an operating system, an approach,” said Zohar, the uncle of Capt. Omer Neutra, a lone soldier from New York who was killed on October 7. His body was taken to Gaza and returned in November 2025. Daxa’s husband, Col. Ehsan Daxa, commander of the 401st Armored Brigade, was killed commanding troops in northern Gaza in October 2024.
For Shapiro, the wildflower campaign offers an example of how such a change can take root. Beginning in the 1960s, it combined legal protection with public education, turning a cause championed by a small group into something generations of children grew up knowing. He wants respect for others, even across deep disagreements, to become just as ingrained.
A search for common ground
“Hamechane,” meaning “the denominator,” expresses the search for common ground. The organization’s members include bereaved families, captivity survivors, and people wounded in the Israel-Gaza War. They want the next government to establish, within its first 100 days, a national framework for social cohesion.
For the three interviewees, the urgency comes from lives they are trying to honor, and a country they fear could repeat its failures.
Zohar argued that the divisions preceding October 7 helped bring Israel to catastrophe. He regards internal polarization as the country’s greatest existential threat and warned that, without addressing it, Israelis risk paying that price again. He cautioned that Israelis cannot risk slipping backward, that it is “something we must prevent at all costs.
“We have already paid an immense price,” he added.
His warning accompanied a more personal admission: Until he heard Daxa, a member of Israel’s Druze community, speak about the Nation-State Law, he had not understood what it meant to her community.
“It went over my head,” he said. “Today I understand it better.”
The 2018 Basic Law reserves national self-determination in Israel to the Jewish people, defines Hebrew as the state’s language, and gives Arabic special status. It contains no explicit guarantee of equality. Druze critics have argued that it excludes them from the country to which they belong and for which their community’s soldiers fight.
The High Court upheld the law in 2021, interpreting it as compatible with equality protections. The dispute nevertheless returned during the war: In November 2023, Druze spiritual leader Sheikh Muwaffaq Tarif called for constitutional recognition of the community’s rights, while the coalition promised separate legislation on Druze status.
For Daxa, the question of belonging also arises in ordinary encounters. She recalled traveling by train with her children and speaking Arabic. Nobody said anything, she explained, but she noticed passengers’ discomfort.
“Hatred doesn’t distinguish,” she said.
She was explicit about the limits of a unity understood only as solidarity among Jews.
“There are partners here,” she said, describing people who already feel part of Israeli society and want to contribute as active participants.
The group’s work, she explained, begins with what its members have come to understand through loss. They bring different opinions and will vote for different parties. What makes conversation possible is a willingness to learn rather than being certain that one side is right and the other wrong.
“We come with an open heart,” she said.
Shapiro described a yearlong process of developing a shared vision. He had participated in other initiatives, including efforts to encourage dialogue during the judicial reform legislation dispute. In Hamechane, he found religious and secular Jews, ultra-Orthodox (haredim), Druze, and people from the Right and Left.
“This is the face of Israeli society,” he said.
The relationships formed through that process imbued him with the confidence that cooperation is possible. Nobody, he emphasized, has had to conceal or abandon their opinions.
His own family contains sharp political differences, he said. Learning to handle them means recognizing that the relationship matters, while allowing disagreement to be expressed respectfully, he explained. He wants that responsibility extended to the country.
His grandfather Haim-Moshe Shapiro signed Israel’s Declaration of Independence and served as a minister. Before the Six Day War, he pressed prime minister Levi Eshkol to bring opposition parties into the government and appoint Moshe Dayan defense minister.
Moshe recalled his grandfather’s insistence on bringing political rivals into government as Israel faced the prospect of war. In June 1967, just before the Six Day War, the government was expanded to include two opposition parties: Gahal, led by Menachem Begin, and Rafi, whose members included Dayan. Begin joined the cabinet, and Dayan became defense minister.
Aner’s writing gives that inheritance another voice.
Kaleidoscope of religious, secular, right-wing, left-wing
In a social media post written before October 7, Aner reacted to graffiti defacing an image of the Lubavitcher Rebbe. He questioned the categories through which Israelis were seeing one another: religious, secular, right-wing, left-wing. People were speaking in black-and-white terms, dividing the world between those on their side and “them.”
“There really is no ‘them,’” he wrote at the time.
In an essay on otherness, boundaries, and dialogue, psychoanalyst Shmuel Ehrlich links the possibility of dialogue to recognizing the other’s humanity and accepting that conflicting feelings can coexist within a relationship. His account echoes the openness the three describe: making room for complexity, in ourselves as well as in those with whom we disagree.
During the shiva for Aner, Moshe recalled that he saw cooperation between people from opposing political camps and believed the divisions his son had written against were receding. He now describes the return of that hostility with disappointment.
Hamechane aims to make cooperation endure beyond emergencies. Alongside its call for government action, Hamechane seeks to encourage personal connections and dialogue between people from different backgrounds through schools, workplaces, and communities.
Shapiro envisages teaching children from a young age about different communities and how to listen to others and handle disagreement. He also wants action in communications, including measures against online activity that inflames hatred. He worries about political speech that reduces entire groups to caricatures.
Politicians, he said, have begun to sound like bots. He wants people to return to speaking like people, addressing substance rather than circulating slogans.
These are proposals for what a national effort could address. The initiative has not settled the precise structure of the body it seeks. Its representatives say elected officials and professionals should develop that framework, with responsibility extending across government and society.
Daxa acknowledged that the group does not possess all the professional answers. Recognition of polarization as a national danger, she believes, would itself mark a beginning.
Her husband’s example gives her a way to describe the conduct she hopes to encourage. Whatever the subject, including haredi enlistment, Ehsan could articulate the other person’s perspective.
“Even if he didn’t agree, he still had the ability to see, understand, and respect,” she said.
For Zohar, Omer’s life offered a similar example of connection. Raised on Long Island, he came to Israel to serve in the IDF. His uncle described him as someone who brought people together, linking Diaspora Jewry and Israel.
Honoring that life, Zohar said, means taking responsibility for the society that remains.
Shapiro returned to the subject of the shelter where Aner died. Apart from the two friends he arrived with, he said, his son did not know the people behind him. One of those friends was Hersh Goldberg-Polin, who was taken hostage from the shelter and murdered by his Hamas captors alongside five other hostages in a tunnel in Rafah in August 2024.
For Aner, Moshe said, the politics, religious identities, and backgrounds of the people inside the shelter with him did not determine whether he would protect them.
“We’re not asking people to sacrifice their lives,” Moshe said.
What he asks is that they listen, make room for others, and recognize that disagreement does not cancel their obligations to one another.
Among the words Aner left behind were lines his father read aloud during the interview:
“There are wars we have no choice but to fight.
There are battles we cannot help but lose.
And there is hatred looking for a place, now finding fertile ground.
There is also time to wake up and love.”

&quot;As long as Putin is in the Kremlin, the war will not end&quot;: Fire Point co-owner Shtilerman, in an op-ed for Le Monde, called on the West to make Putin&apos;s removal
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
16:05:53 EEST
22:05:53 KST

"As long as Putin is in the Kremlin, the war will not end": Fire Point co-owner Shtilerman, in an op-ed for Le Monde, called on the West to make Putin's removal
Kyiv • UNN
Denys Shtilerman said that the war would not end as long as Putin remains in the Kremlin. He proposed four steps to weaken his power.
As long as Vladimir Putin remains in the Kremlin, Russia’s war against Ukraine will not truly end—even if he signs a ceasefire and talks about “peace.” Therefore, Europe and the United States must set the removal of Putin from power as a strategic objective. Denis Shtilerman, co-owner and chief designer of Fire Point, writes this in a column for the French newspaper Le Monde, reports UNN.
Details
Shtilerman begins with a parallel to the film "The Death of Stalin": a regime that had seemed unshakable just a day earlier began to falter as soon as the dictator was gone. In his view, this is precisely how the West should look at Putin—not speculate about who might oppose him, but take concrete measures capable of accelerating his fall: in the political, economic, military and intelligence spheres.
Ukraine and its partners have learned to strike Russia’s war machine, while sanctions, isolation and diplomatic pressure are necessary, the author notes. But neither missiles nor sanctions alone eradicate Russian militarism: they weaken the Kremlin’s means, while its core remains intact. Putin may well sign a ceasefire, Shtilerman writes, but that will change nothing.
As long as he remains in the Kremlin, the war against Ukraine will not truly end
Why Putin needs war
In the author’s view, Putin needs a permanent conflict—not necessarily an armed one: an open war in Ukraine, a hybrid or even open war in Europe, and a global one against the West. His rule requires an enemy, a sense of a besieged fortress and constant mobilization. If Putinism previously secured loyalty through stability and rising incomes, it is now sustained by fear, revanchism and the myth of restoring the empire.
Peace would confront Putin with questions that would be more dangerous to answer than continuing to fight: what hundreds of thousands of people died and were wounded for, what will happen to the armed and traumatized veterans who return home feeling betrayed, and how to explain that Ukraine, which he promised to “break,” survived.
What Shtilerman proposes
The co-owner of Fire Point emphasizes that this is not about invading Russia or installing a pro-Western puppet there—who governs the country will be decided by Russians themselves. But weakening Russia is not enough; Putin’s personal power must be weakened. To this end, he proposes four steps.
Destroy the myth of Putin as the “defender of Russia.” According to Shtilerman, strikes on Russian territory have not only a military but also a political objective: they disprove Putin’s promise that Russians can wage war without consequences for themselves.
Not a week goes by without my drones and missiles striking his country
Russians, he adds, must understand: the war came to them because Putin brought it to Ukraine first.
Turn Putin’s inner circle from his shield into a weak spot. Those who finance the war, carry out criminal orders or conceal his wealth must lose their assets, freedom of movement and their families’ future in the West. The author recalls that after Putin’s March meeting with business leaders, Russian billionaires reportedly transferred about 400 billion rubles (€4–4.2 billion) to the budget in “voluntary” contributions to cover the deficit and military expenditures—and must be held accountable for it.
Strip Putin of legitimacy in the West. The ICC arrest warrant against him and the special tribunal concerning the crime of aggression must not remain a formality: the tribunal must bring charges against named individuals, and the warrant must be enforced.
Negotiations with Russia, Shtilerman suggests, may be necessary, but not Putin’s rehabilitation: no summit should restore the status quo with the person responsible for the biggest war in Europe since 1945.
Make the prospect of a future without Putin a reality. The allies must agree on an offer for post-Putin Russia: gradual easing of sanctions, restoration of economic ties and security dialogue—in exchange for the withdrawal of troops, the return of abducted Ukrainian children, reparations and a commitment to comply with international law.
Stilerman acknowledges that Putin’s departure does not guarantee a democratic Russia: his successor could turn out to be brutal, revanchist, and hostile toward the West. But it would no longer be Putin—and in his view, that is the crucial difference. Putin’s disappearance does not promise lasting peace, he concludes, but his remaining in power guarantees that there will be no peace.
We remind you
In July, Stilerman stated that the war could end only after a full return to the 1991 borders, and warned that freezing the war at its current stage would have negative consequences for Ukraine’s security and economy. At the time, he also confirmed that a Flamingo missile had struck the Avitek plant in Kirov, which produces components for the Tor air defense system and Kh-101 missiles.

Fair by design, simple in practice: what can Riga teach Brussels?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
13:02:08 UTC
22:02:08 KST

Four proposals for how EU digital consumer protection rules can strengthen trust without holding back Europe’s growing businesses.
By Ben Brake, Director General of DOT Europe.
The Baltic economies are among the most digitalised in Europe. For many Latvian businesses, from online retailers to subscription services and apps, the Single Market is not a distant ambition. It is their customer base from day one. That makes Riga a useful place to consider a question Brussels is currently grappling with: how far should the EU go in regulating the design of online services?
Two pieces of legislation will shape the answer. The recently proposed EU Kids Act aims to ensure age-appropriate access to online services. It also calls for safety by design, including restrictions on features such as autoplay and engagement-based rewards on social media and video-sharing platforms. The Digital Fairness Act, expected this November, will examine automatic subscription renewals, personalised offers, influencer marketing, and how websites and apps present choices to consumers.
Our industry supports the goal of protecting consumers online, especially minors. The question is how to achieve this without adding complexity that falls most heavily on small and growing businesses. This matters particularly now, when Europe has made competitiveness and simplification key priorities. As I arrive in Riga with a business delegation, I see four areas that could make a decisive difference.
One European Rulebook, Not 27
For a company in Riga selling to customers in Berlin or Lyon, few things are as costly as rules that change at every border. Over the past year, several Member States have developed their own laws governing minors’ access to social media, each taking a different approach.
The European Commission was right to signal that a European-wide solution should take precedence, and the Kids Act sends precisely that message. The Digital Fairness Act should follow the same logic. Where it regulates, it should provide full harmonisation, leaving no room for additional national requirements that would recreate the very fragmentation the Act is meant to prevent.
Small, open markets with extensive cross-border trade, such as Latvia, demonstrate most clearly why this matters. A rule interpreted differently in every country is, in practice, 27 different rules.
Enforce Existing Rules First
Europe is not starting from a blank page. The Digital Services Act (DSA) already prohibits deceptive interface design on online platforms and requires a high level of protection for minors. The Unfair Commercial Practices Directive and the Consumer Rights Directive already cover misleading practices, pricing and contracts.
In Latvia, the Consumer Rights Protection Centre (PTAC) already supervises compliance with the DSA.
Before introducing new obligations, the EU should establish where existing rules genuinely fall short and where they are simply not yet being enforced consistently. Clear guidance and coordinated enforcement can often deliver more for consumers than another law, and do so faster.
Simplification Businesses Can Actually Feel
Simplification should not remain a promise made in policy announcements. The Digital Fairness Act offers an opportunity to make consumer protection rules easier to apply, rather than simply expanding them.
During the Commission’s public consultation, businesses and their associations proposed concrete solutions. One is to reduce repetitive information requirements for recurring transactions, such as in-app purchases. Another is to strike a better balance in withdrawal rights for digital subscription services while preserving consumers’ right to change their minds.
For a start-up with a small legal team, such changes free up time and money to invest in better products.
Simpler rules can also mean better protection. A consumer who receives one clear notice is likely to read it. A consumer who receives ten may read none of them.
Clear Boundaries Between Laws
The EU Kids Act and the Digital Fairness Act partly cover the same areas: addictive design, engagement-based features and the protection of vulnerable users.
Add other existing consumer protection laws, and a company may find itself having to comply with several sets of obligations for a single feature, potentially overseen by different authorities.
Each piece of legislation needs a clearly defined scope. The EU should explain how these laws fit together before they enter into force, not afterwards.
Legal certainty matters most to those with the fewest lawyers. These are the smaller companies deciding whether to invest and expand across the Single Market.
Consumer trust and competitiveness are not opposing goals. European digital businesses depend on customers who trust them, and consumers benefit from a market in which new services can grow.
Latvia shows that a small, open economy can achieve both. The Digital Fairness Act should be designed with businesses like those operating in Riga in mind. If it is consistent across Member States, builds on what already works and is simple to apply, it will serve the entire Single Market well.

A hidden bias in human language challenges 70 years of science
- Date:
- October 24, 2026
- Source:
- University of Vermont
- Summary:
- A groundbreaking study challenges 70 years of assumptions about how human language works. By analyzing billions of word uses, scientists discovered that meaning is organized around power, danger, and order rather than emotion alone. Even more surprisingly, human language shows a powerful hidden preference for safety, suggesting that our words may reflect ancient survival instincts.
- Share:
Researchers at the University of Vermont have discovered a surprising pattern in human language that challenges a scientific theory widely accepted for more than 70 years. Their findings suggest that the meaning of words is shaped by something more fundamental than emotion: our understanding of power, danger, and order.
The study, published in Science Advances, introduces a new approach called "ousiometrics," which uses mathematical methods to measure the essential meaning of language. Its most striking finding is that the words people use show a consistent and widespread preference for safety over danger.
This hidden safety bias could transform how researchers study language, understand human behavior, and develop artificial intelligence systems that interpret what people say and write.
Scientists Discover a Hidden Safety Bias in Human Language
Since the 1950s, much of the scientific understanding of word meaning has relied on a framework developed through pioneering research by psychologist Charles Osgood and others. Known as the VAD model, it describes meaning through three emotional dimensions: valence (positive vs. negative), arousal (excited vs. calm), and dominance (controlling vs. submissive).
This approach became influential in psychology, linguistics, and artificial intelligence, particularly in systems designed to identify the emotional tone of written language.
However, the University of Vermont researchers found evidence that this long-established model overlooks important aspects of how meaning is organized.
Their analysis examined billions of individual uses of more than 20,000 words across a wide range of real-world texts. Using advanced computational techniques, the team identified a different underlying structure. They found that the three dimensions in the traditional VAD model are not independent of one another, as previously assumed.
Instead, their results indicate that word meaning can be more effectively described through three separate dimensions: power (weak vs. powerful), danger (safe vs. dangerous), and structure (ordered vs. chaotic).
The research, supported by the US National Science Foundation, Google, MassMutual, and other funders, found that this new framework accounted for more than 90% of the variation in measured word meaning. The traditional VAD approach explained approximately 72%.
That improvement could be especially important as large language models, automated content moderation, and other AI technologies increasingly depend on understanding human communication.
Why Human Language Favors Safety Over Danger
One of the study's most unexpected discoveries emerged when the researchers examined how words actually appear in everyday communication.
Across books, news reporting, social media, and spoken language, words associated with safety appeared much more frequently than those associated with danger.
This finding offers a new explanation for a familiar phenomenon called the Pollyanna principle, which describes the tendency for human language to lean toward positive rather than negative words.
For decades, researchers generally interpreted this pattern as evidence that people favor positive emotional expressions. The new analysis suggests that something more fundamental may be responsible.
According to the researchers, the apparent preference for positivity largely reflects an underlying preference for safety.
"The Pollyanna principle's positivity bias," the study concludes. "is, in fact, a one-dimensional projection of an underlying safety bias."
"This is a big observation that comes out of this work," said Peter Dodds, director of the UVM's Complex Systems Institute and senior author of the study. "Expressions of safety are crucial to all language."
Could Human Language Be Shaped by Survival?
The discovery raises an intriguing possibility: the structure of human language may reflect evolutionary pressures associated with staying alive.
From this perspective, words do more than communicate feelings. They also help people recognize threats, evaluate uncertainty, establish trust, and coordinate actions with others.
Being able to distinguish between safety and danger is essential to survival. The researchers suggest that this basic human priority may also influence how meaning is organized in language.
Throughout daily life, people constantly exchange information about whether individuals, places, situations, and behaviors are threatening or safe. The new findings suggest that these distinctions may be more central to communication than previously recognized.
They also offer a different interpretation of why positive language is so common. Rather than simply expressing happiness or approval, many positive words may convey a sense of security, stability, or predictability.
Julia Zimmerman, a postdoctoral researcher in UVM's Computational Story Lab and a co-author of the study, said the three newly identified dimensions reflect experiences that are fundamental to human life.
"Power, danger, and structure," she said, "are relevant to every person that's ever lived."
Researchers have also long recognized that people tend to favor language associated with goodness and low aggression. The team argues that these familiar tendencies may arise from the same deeper pattern.
"We now understand," the team writes, that these are "shadows of an underlying linguistic safety bias."
Although the results are consistent with a possible connection between language and survival, they do not establish that evolutionary pressures directly caused the safety bias.
A Discovery That Could Change How AI Understands Language
The findings have implications that extend well beyond linguistics.
Many artificial intelligence systems use sentiment analysis to determine whether language expresses positive, negative, or neutral feelings. Some approaches also draw on the traditional VAD framework to measure emotional meaning.
If that framework does not fully capture the underlying structure of language, systems built around it could overlook important distinctions in what people communicate.
The researchers suggest that incorporating power, danger, and structure could eventually help AI models interpret language more accurately and explain their assessments more clearly. This may be particularly useful when analyzing trust, risk, and decision-making.
In linguistics, the findings offer a different way to understand the foundations of meaning. Instead of treating emotional tone as the primary organizing principle, the new framework emphasizes distinctions related to strength, safety, and predictability.
Psychology could also be affected. Decades of studies have used the VAD model to investigate emotions, perception, and behavior. A different set of fundamental dimensions could encourage researchers to reconsider how some of those findings are interpreted.
The discovery may also interest neuroscientists. The human brain is highly sensitive to threats and signals of safety, and the newly identified linguistic bias suggests that these biological priorities may be reflected in language. This potential connection could help researchers explore relationships between brain activity and symbolic communication, although further research would be needed to establish them.
A New Tool Measures the Hidden Meaning of Words
To investigate these patterns, the researchers created analytical methods designed to measure meaning across enormous collections of written and spoken language.
One of their central innovations is the "ousiometer," a tool that rapidly evaluates the essential meaning of large bodies of text and produces an average meaning score.
(The word "ouisa" comes from Ancient Greek and is a root for the English word "essence.")
The ousiometer builds on an earlier tool developed by the research team called the "hedonometer" (a happiness meter). While that instrument measures the overall emotional tone of language, the new approach examines broader patterns of meaning.
The researchers demonstrated that the ousiometer can analyze material from remarkably different sources, including Jane Austen's novels, Arthur Conan Doyle's Sherlock Holmes stories, the New York Times, Wikipedia, Twitter, and transcripts of talk radio programs.
The tool can also track how meaning shifts as a story unfolds.
For example, the researchers analyzed an English translation of Victor Hugo's Les Misérables and mapped its changing meaning throughout the novel.
They called this changing pattern an "ousiometric trajectory." The visualization resembles the twisting shape of a multicolored protein, with the narrative moving across a grid based on four contrasting pairs: dangerous/safe, weak/powerful, gentle/aggressive, and bad/good.
By following this path, researchers can observe how the underlying meaning of the text changes from one section of the story to another.
Why Counting Word Frequency Changes the Results
Another important innovation involved distinguishing between words themselves and how often people actually use them.
In linguistics, researchers describe individual words as categories called "types," while each appearance of a word in text is known as a "token."
(For example, as a category "apple" is a type and every time the word "apple" is used in a sentence is a token.)
This distinction matters because a word that appears millions of times contributes much more to everyday communication than one that is rarely used.
Earlier research often gave each word equal importance, regardless of its frequency. The Vermont team instead incorporated how often words appear in real communication, allowing patterns to emerge that might otherwise remain hidden.
This approach was particularly important for identifying the widespread preference for safety-related language.
The ten-member research team was led by Peter Dodds and Chris Danforth, professors in UVM's College of Engineering and Mathematical Sciences. Their collaborators included researchers from the Santa Fe Institute, the Complexity Science Hub in Austria, Howard Hughes Medical Center, the University of California, Berkeley, the University of Adelaide, and MassMutual Data Science.
Rethinking What Human Language Reveals About Us
Understanding this hidden safety bias could have consequences for how researchers study communication across society.
If words consistently reflect a preference for safety, that tendency may influence how stories are told, how information spreads, and how people interpret events and experiences.
The findings could eventually inform research into political communication, mental health messaging, and AI systems designed to interact with people.
More broadly, the study challenges the idea that human language can be understood primarily through emotions such as happiness, fear, and excitement.
Instead, the researchers propose that meaning has a deeper structure connected to power, danger, and order. Their findings suggest that language may reflect the challenges humans face when navigating uncertain environments, maintaining relationships, and identifying threats.
By revealing this previously overlooked structure, the team offers a new way to understand what words communicate and why certain kinds of meaning dominate everyday conversation. Human language, their research suggests, may be more closely connected to our fundamental need for safety than scientists have traditionally recognized.

Tensions rise in Albania as protesters burn symbolic pillows outside prime minister’s office
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
12:56:38 UTC
21:56:38 KST

Opposition supporters and students mobilised in the Albanian capital, with riot police using water cannons on large groups of protesters. Authorities said 2,500 police officers were deployed to the streets of Tirana.
Thousands of people rallied for a fresh anti-government protest in the Albanian capital Tirana on Saturday, with police firing tear gas to disperse the crowd.
In the latest of several clashes between police and protesters since mid-October, government buildings were attacked and dozens of demonstrators were detained. Authorities said that more than 300 protestors and police have been injured.
The protesters had heeded calls from organisers for students and others around Albania to attend the rally. Various groups, including university professors, artists and opposition parties, have announced their support or attendance.
Supporters of the opposition Democratic Party earlier gathered outside the prime minister's office for around an hour and a half, setting fire to pillows that Rama had placed there as a symbolic invitation to dialogue with students.
The demonstrators then headed towards the Ministry of Education, where a separate student protest took place.
For their part, high school and university students are demanding lower tuition fees, greater state investment in education and protesting corruption in the education system. Some have joined a broader anti-government movement calling for the resignation of the prime minister.
Prime minister Edi Rama issued a stern warning against violence, pledging a sustained response from the authorities.
"All those who glorify violence, all those who echo violence, and all those who perpetrate violence must understand that just as the urban terror was intense, concentrated, and prolonged, so too will the response from the state be prolonged and persistent," Rama said.
Anti-government protests refuse to die down
Anti-government protests started in May, sparked by a luxury hotel project linked to US President Donald Trump's family, which scientists said in July had already caused irreparable damage to a once pristine stretch of Albania's coast.
Anger over the resort development has morphed into a broader push against corruption, amid ongoing demands for Prime Minister Edi Rama to step down.
Rama has blamed "foreign actors" for the violence and accused both Russia and Iran of driving online misinformation.
The prime minister has also called for "dialogue".
The demonstrators have distanced themselves from any political party, and regularly carry signs accusing both Rama and longtime opposition leader Sali Berisha of corruption.
They chanted "Rama in prison" and "Berisha in prison" on Saturday, blaming the entire political class for the crisis.
The prime minister had earlier published photos of around 40 people, identified by their initials, whom he accused of violence, and renewed his call for the heads of dozens of public institutions to resign.

Elections must not deflect attention from Israel’s international crimes, rights group warns
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
12:56:33 UTC
21:56:33 KST

Amnesty International on Saturday warned that upcoming elections must not deflect attention from Israel’s international crimes, urging continued scrutiny and accountability, Anadolu reports.
In a statement, Erika Guevara Rosas, Amnesty International’s senior director for research, policy, advocacy and campaigns, said Palestinians have little reason to expect the outcome to deliver positive human rights change as much of the world’s attention focuses on Israel’s upcoming parliamentary elections on Oct. 27.
Explaining this, she pointed out that electoral candidates have “shamelessly exploited” anti-Palestinian sentiment or even threatened to step up human rights violations and crimes under international law in a bid to score political points.
“Candidates have used dehumanizing rhetoric against Palestinians, promised to further entrench Israel’s illegal annexation measures in the occupied West Bank, and threatened further devastation of the occupied Gaza Strip,” Rosas noted.
The rights advocate underlined that across the occupied West Bank, including illegally annexed East Jerusalem, Israel continues to “ruthlessly displace” families and carry out home demolitions while imposing military restrictions on Palestinian farmers.
“In the occupied Gaza Strip, where Israel’s genocide continues unabated, a year after the so-called ceasefire, killings of Palestinian civilians continue, and the expansion of access-restricted zones and the indefinite delay of reconstruction have left Gaza’s population trapped in a state of protracted displacement and despair.”
– International community urged to increase pressure on any incoming government
She went on to say that “persisting impunity for decades of atrocity crimes” associated with Israel’s “cruel system of apartheid and its brutal unlawful occupation,” perpetuated by successive Israeli governments, has only fueled more crimes against Palestinians.
“Millions of people, including Palestinians in the OPT, as well as civilians in Lebanon and Syria, face the consequences of Israeli policies and actions, yet have no say or vote in the elections that will impact their lives,” added Rosas.
She called on the international community to increase pressure on any incoming government to “stop Israel’s genocide in Gaza, dismantle its system of apartheid, end the ethnic cleansing of communities in the West Bank, and end its unlawful occupation of the OPT.”
Rosas stressed that they must also pressure Israel to end unlawful attacks and abide by its obligations under international humanitarian law across the region, withdraw its troops from southern Lebanon and allow the return of displaced Lebanese people to their towns and villages.
“States can and must act now to hold Israel accountable and halt its relentless assault on human rights in the region,” she said.
The official added: “This includes suspending the EU-Israel Association Agreement, imposing an arms embargo on Israel, and ending any cooperation that may contribute to maintaining Israel’s unlawful occupation of Palestinian territory.”

Harris returns to campaign trail as 2028 White House questions loom
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
12:54:06 UTC
21:54:06 KST

Kamala Harris is stepping back into the political arena to help Democrats compete in closely contested midterm races as the former vice president weighs whether to seek the presidency again in 2028.
Harris, the Democrats’ unsuccessful 2024 presidential nominee, has made relatively few public appearances this year.
But with the party seeking to break Republicans’ hold on Congress ahead of the Nov. 3 elections, she is campaigning in Georgia, Mississippi, Nevada, New Hampshire and Wisconsin. The tour could renew speculation about her political ambitions as a growing field of potential 2028 presidential contenders begins to emerge.
She launched the tour Tuesday in Las Vegas with a new stump speech criticizing what she described as President Donald Trump’s cruelty, while drawing on the aspirational messaging that has long defined her public appearances. Harris made history as the first woman and the first Black and South Asian American to serve as vice president.
She spoke to scores of Culinary Workers Union members alongside gubernatorial candidate Aaron Ford, Nevada’s first Black attorney general. Harris said Ford would become the “first Black governor west of the Mississippi” if elected.
“We got a serious fight in front of us,” Harris said. “We are witnessing pure brutality come out of what is undoubtedly the most corrupt, callous and incompetent presidential administration.”
Like Trump, who is traveling around the country to campaign for Republican candidates, Harris is not broadly popular among voters. A Reuters/Ipsos opinion poll in June showed that 39% of Americans viewed her favorably, but the figures were sharply divided along partisan lines: 82% of Democrats viewed her favorably, compared with 7% of Republicans and 33% of independents.
“At the end of a campaign, you bring out your heavy hitters,” said Elaine Kamarck, a senior fellow at the Brookings Institution and a member of the Democratic National Committee. “That’s what’s going on here with her, and frankly with Trump.”
The day after her Las Vegas appearance, Harris led chants of “Mississippi matters!” before a crowd supporting Scott Colom in Columbus, Mississippi. Colom is seeking to become the first Democrat elected to the U.S. Senate from Mississippi since 1982. Polls show an unusually tight race with Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith.
Harris opened with advice she said she gives young people she mentors: “Never let someone else’s limited ability to see your capacity be a limitation on your ambition,” she said. “Let me repeat that.” She repeated the line more loudly, drawing cheers from the crowd.
If Harris decides to run for the White House again in 2028, she would likely be among the most high-profile names in what is expected to be a crowded Democratic field.
But Harris also carries the baggage of past defeats. She lost the 2024 presidential election to Trump, and her first presidential campaign ended before the 2020 Democratic nominating contests began.
A 2028 campaign would also force Harris to revisit the Democrats’ tumultuous 2024 race, when then-President Joe Biden abruptly ended his reelection campaign amid questions about his health and mental acuity, and Harris replaced him as the party’s nominee.
Harris has since called Biden’s decision to seek reelection “reckless” in her memoir, “107 Days,” a reference to the short campaign she inherited. This month, she offered her clearest criticism yet of Biden’s support for Israel’s war in Gaza, rebuking the Israeli government’s “horrific conduct” and saying the U.S. should have “acted sooner and more forcefully.”
“All these things will be relitigated,” Kamarck said. “What happened to Biden? Did she know? Did she think he was losing it? And on and on and on.”
Scott Ferson, a Democratic strategist and author of “How the Democrats Lost America,” said the party has tended to give short shrift to candidates who have lost elections. However, voters disillusioned with Trump may also view Harris in a new light.
“She has that kind of crossover appeal,” Ferson said, “particularly with people who left in 2024 or stayed home.” Her implicit message, he suggested, is: “Do you regret staying home?”
Earlier this month, as Harris wrapped up an appearance on the “Baby, This Is Keke Palmer” video podcast, Palmer asked whether she would run again.
“Oh, girl, come on!” Harris said, laughing as she gripped the hands of the Hollywood star. “I haven’t decided yet.”
“But the midterms, the midterms, the midterms,” Harris continued. “2028 don’t matter if we don’t do 2026 right.”

Met police confirm giving Duchess of Sussex letter about father’s alleged offending

The Metropolitan police have confirmed they gave a letter to the Duchess of Sussex in 2019 concerning “alleged offending” involving her father, after accusations arose on Friday about Thomas Markle Sr having child sexual abuse images.
Scotland Yard said it had received a letter in January 2019 making a number of allegations about offending outside Britain.
The police force said it had passed the information on to the Duke and Duchess of Sussex’s office, but it did not pass it on to “other law enforcement agencies”.
The Sun newspaper published claims that Meghan’s half-brother, Thomas Markle Jr, claimed he had found a stash of images belonging to their father at his former home in the Philippines.
On Friday, Meghan said she had been made aware of these allegations by the Met, and that she was “deeply distressed” by them.
The duchess, who is estranged from her father said in a statement she had broken off contact to protect her children, Prince Archie, seven, and Princess Lilibet, five. He has never met them.
Meghan and Prince Harry recently moved back to the UK from the US.
Meghan’s father has denied the allegations and told the Daily Mail the accusations were “sick lies”.
The Met said it was considering whether to refer itself to the Independent Office for Police Conduct (IOPC) to review its actions.
In a statement, a Metropolitan police spokesperson said: “Following a thorough review of Met police systems and records, we have confirmed that in January 2019, we received a letter containing a number of claims about alleged offending outside the United Kingdom. It was sent to the MPS (Metropolitan Police Service) Protection Command to raise concerns in relation to the security of the Duchess of Sussex.
“The letter was reviewed and a decision was made that it should be passed to the office of the Duke and Duchess of Sussex for their awareness. The details of the allegations in the letter were not shared with other law enforcement agencies.
“The MPS is reviewing the handling of this matter in 2019 and considering whether a referral to the IOPC is necessary to review our approach.”
In a statement on Friday, issued through her spokesperson, the duchess said: “I am deeply distressed at the news that has come to light in the last 24 hours, and my thoughts are with any children who may have been harmed.
“In 2018, a letter was sent to the Metropolitan police and Royalty and Specialist Protection [Rasp]. That letter was subsequently shared with me. It made troubling and disturbing allegations against my father and I was given assurances that these were being investigated.
“I hope it can now be understood that, despite certain media publications’ distortion over the years, any distance from my father, and my choice to not allow him to have contact with our children, was for one reason: to protect them. I trusted that the authorities were doing the same for other families.
“Although the breadth of what has now been uncovered is more sickening than one could ever imagine, my sincerest hope is that justice will be fully served and that the priority remains the safety and protection of innocent children.”
She later said she had misremembered the year the Met had contacted her, and confirmed it had been 2019, not 2018 as she said on Friday.
A spokesperson for the Duchess of Sussex said: “In recalling events from more than seven years ago, without the benefit of a diary entry or contemporaneous record, it is understandable that she may have been mistaken by a few months.
“If the MPS holds a time-stamped record confirming that the letter was reviewed in 2019, that should be treated as the accurate reference point for when it was received and shared with the duchess.
“I think it is reasonable to recognise that she is doing her best to recall the precise timing of events that were not diarised at the time, and that any discrepancy of a few months is an understandable consequence of that passage of time.”
Sources said that although Meghan was made aware of the allegations in 2019, she had been unable to speak publicly to avoid jeopardising any future investigation and because speaking out could have resulted in legal action against her.
The Sun reported that Markle Jr told detectives in the Philippines he had discovered “hundreds, if not thousands” of child sexual abuse images on computers and mobile phones stored in four large boxes at the home in Cebu where Markle Sr was living until he returned to the US in May after having a stroke.
Markle Jr, 60, said he had also contacted the FBI in the US, the Sun reported.

Is Iran planning attacks on Americans; why is the US on alert?

Is Iran planning attacks on Americans; why is the US on alert?
US intelligence memo warns that Iranian plots against US citizens in the Middle East ‘have reached advanced stages’.
United States intelligence agencies have warned that Iran is in “advanced stages” of plans to target US personnel abroad, prompting Washington to place staff on high alert in the Middle East, according to US officials and an official memo cited by Axios and The New York Times (NYT).
The alert comes as the US and Israel signal they may be preparing for a new military campaign against Iran, which Tehran has reportedly threatened to retaliate against, in part by targeting communications cables in the Gulf.
The heightened threat assessment has prompted Washington, already on guard over escalating attacks by Iran-backed Houthis, to trim Washington’s diplomatic presence in the Middle East, the NYT has reported, citing officials.
Here’s what we know about the latest US warning, and how it fits into the broader US-Iran conflict:
What has the US said about Iran’s alleged plans to attack Americans?
A warning about Iranian plans to target US citizens was detailed in a memo sent by Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton to Secretary of State Marco Rubio, first reported by US news site Axios.
In the memo, Clayton wrote that US agencies had received intelligence indicating that Iran has “substantially increased efforts to target US personnel” overseas, with lethal plots reaching “advanced stages” in the Middle East and other countries.
The NYT, which also reported on the memo, cited unnamed US officials as saying threats to American officials, including ambassadors, had been assessed in recent weeks, and that Iran had lined up potential targets in Europe.
The officials said some intelligence indicates Iranian operatives are already active within the US.
What evidence has Washington presented, and what remains unverified?
Washington has not publicly commented on the memo, although the NYT cited a US official as confirming its authenticity on behalf of President Donald Trump’s administration.
Another official cited by the NYT played down Iran’s ability to execute attacks inside the US and elsewhere, saying it lacks the capacity to follow through on all its ambitions.
Why have US officials raised the alarm now?
According to officials cited by the NYT, US agencies deem Iranian threats to US citizens in the Middle East to be “at the highest level” since the US-Israel war on Iran began in February.
This assessment is behind the US’s recent moves to withdraw staff posted in the region, the NYT added.
In the background are reported US and Israel plans to initiate a new military campaign against Iran following the US mid-term elections next month. On Friday, Trump said the US “may do another little epic fury”, using the codename for the US-Israel war against Iran that began on February 28.
Which countries has the US withdrawn diplomats from?
On Wednesday, the US Department of State announced it was removing non-essential staff in its embassy in Saudi Arabia, citing escalating attacks by the Iran-backed Houthis in Yemen against Saudi infrastructure.
Staff levels have also been quietly reduced at other US diplomatic missions in the region, several US media have reported. That includes embassies in the United Arab Emirates, Bahrain, Kuwait, Qatar, Jordan and Lebanon, according to CNN.
A US official cited by the NYT said the threat of Houthi attacks and “Iranian terror plots targeting US officials” were driving US staffing decisions.
Has Iran responded?
Iran has not responded to news of the US intelligence memo accusing it of planning attacks on US personnel.
However, Iranian officials have repeatedly threatened and carried out attacks against US bases and those of its allies in the region. The Pentagon has confirmed that 21 US military personnel have been killed in the Middle East since the war on Iran began.
On Wednesday, Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) warned that Tehran would follow a new “offensive” strategy if the US renewed attacks.
That means Tehran would no longer limit its military operations to retaliatory strikes, said IRGC spokesman Hossein Mohebbi, adding that the quality, range and power of Iranian missiles had improved.
Tehran also has in-depth plans to target undersea communications cables in the Gulf in the event of new US-Israeli attacks, the Reuters news agency reported, citing two senior Iranian security officials.
Previously, Iran’s security chief Mohsen Rezaei warned that cables, data centres and artificial intelligence facilities across the region could come under attack if war with the US breaks out again.
Has Iran previously been accused of plotting attacks against Americans?
Yes, US authorities have long accused Iran of being behind plots targeting US citizens, including assassination attempts against Trump on US soil.
In March this year, a Pakistani national was convicted by a US court of plotting to assassinate Trump and other US politicians on the orders of Iran’s IRGC.
An Iranian IRGC member was charged in 2022 with trying to assassinate former US National Security Advisor John Bolton. The individual allegedly “attempted to pay individuals in the United States $300,000 to carry out the murder in Washington DC or Maryland”, according to the US Department of Justice.
Last year, the US intelligence community warned that Iran would “continue to directly threaten US persons globally”, specifically targeting officials it believed were involved in the 2020 assassination of IRGC Quds Force commander Qassem Soleimani.
This month, the US abruptly withdrew bombers from an airbase in England, United Kingdom, citing concerns about a potential attack. That followed a security incident at the base, after which the UK arrested several men on suspicion of working with Iranian intelligence.

NASA’s asteroid Bennu samples reveal a 4.5-billion-year-old secret
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
12:50:06 UTC
21:50:06 KST

NASA’s asteroid Bennu samples reveal a 4.5-billion-year-old secret
- Date:
- October 24, 2026
- Source:
- ETH Zurich
- Summary:
- Tiny samples from asteroid Bennu are rewriting scientists' understanding of how our Solar System formed. New evidence suggests that Bennu was born where material from the inner and outer Solar System mixed, with Jupiter playing a surprising role in shaping its formation.
- Share:
Samples collected from asteroid Bennu by NASA are revealing surprising new details about how our Solar System formed approximately 4.5 billion years ago. A new chemical analysis challenges earlier theories about the asteroid's birthplace and suggests that Jupiter played an important role in shaping the materials from which Bennu and other ancient objects formed.
Bennu completes one orbit around the Sun every 1.2 years and makes a relatively close approach to Earth about every six years, coming within roughly 300,000 kilometers (186,000 miles). NASA's OSIRIS-REx mission traveled to the asteroid, collected material from its surface, and successfully delivered the samples to Earth in 2023.
On September 23, 2023, a capsule carrying approximately 120 grams of asteroid material landed in the Utah desert. Scientists around the world subsequently received small portions of the precious cargo for detailed study.
Among them was Maria Schönbächler, Professor of Isotope Geochemistry at ETH Zurich, whose laboratory received half a gram of Bennu material. Her team immediately began examining the samples for clues about the asteroid's history.
The research, now published in Science Advances, has uncovered a distinctive chemical signature that not only helps identify Bennu's origins but also provides new evidence about the processes that shaped the early Solar System.
Bennu's Chemical Fingerprint Reveals Its Cosmic Relatives
To investigate Bennu's origins, the ETH Zurich researchers examined isotopes of three elements: iron, titanium, and chromium.
Isotopes are different forms of the same chemical element that contain varying numbers of neutrons, giving them slightly different masses. By measuring the relative amounts of these isotopes, scientists can identify a material's chemical fingerprint. These patterns provide clues about where an asteroid's ingredients originated and, in some cases, when they formed.
The analysis revealed that iron and titanium are distributed remarkably evenly throughout Bennu's material. It also uncovered a close chemical relationship between Bennu, the asteroid Ryugu, and a rare group of primitive meteorites known as CI meteorites.
CI meteorites are carbon-rich remnants of the early Solar System that have undergone relatively little alteration over billions of years. They are exceptionally uncommon among meteorites recovered on Earth.
Bennu, Ryugu, and CI meteorites share strikingly similar isotopic fingerprints, suggesting that their original materials came from the same reservoir of ancient cosmic dust. Their chemical signatures also differ substantially from those of other known asteroids, meteorite groups, and planets.
These similarities offer an important clue about where these objects formed and what conditions existed during the Solar System's earliest stages.
Scientists Discover Bennu's Unexpected Birthplace
For years, researchers generally believed that primitive asteroids like Bennu originated in the outer Solar System, perhaps in the same distant regions where comets formed. They also suspected that Bennu's original material came together relatively late in the Solar System's development.
The new findings challenge both assumptions.
Instead, the researchers propose that the material that became Bennu, Ryugu, and CI meteorites accumulated near a boundary known as the water-ice line.
This boundary marks the region in the disk surrounding the young Sun where temperatures were low enough for water vapor to freeze into ice. Around 4.5 billion years ago, it may have been a particularly important meeting place for material traveling from different parts of the developing Solar System.
Dust originating in both the inner and outer regions mixed near this boundary. Water ice helped the smallest particles stick together, allowing them to gradually accumulate into larger bodies.
"Bennu is a hybrid: the material does not clearly match either the inner or the outer Solar System," says Schönbächler.
Its unusual chemical composition suggests that Bennu formed from a combination of materials originating in both regions rather than from a single, isolated source.
Jupiter May Have Played a Crucial Role in Bennu's Formation
The researchers also developed a scenario explaining how this mixing could have occurred, with Jupiter emerging as a key player.
Jupiter began forming extraordinarily early in Solar System history, within approximately one million years of the Sun's birth. At that time, the young Sun was surrounded by a rotating disk of gas, dust, and ice.
Within this disk, countless small particles gradually collided and stuck together, building larger objects through a process called accretion. Over time, some of these growing bodies became asteroids and planets.
As Jupiter rapidly increased in mass, its immense gravitational influence began reshaping the distribution of material throughout the disk.
The researchers suggest that the growing gas giant acted somewhat like a structural barrier, preventing most larger particles from crossing its orbital region while still allowing finer dust to move around it.
This fine material, originating from different parts of the disk, could then mix extensively near the water-ice line.
According to the proposed scenario, the parent bodies of Bennu and Ryugu, along with the objects that produced CI meteorites, formed from this thoroughly mixed material.
Jupiter may therefore have helped determine not only where these ancient asteroids formed but also which ingredients became incorporated into them.
Ancient Dust and Ice Reveal the Ingredients That Built Earth
The proposed formation scenario could also explain two of Bennu's most intriguing characteristics: its abundance of water-bearing material and its chemical resemblance to the Sun.
Near the water-ice boundary, ice could evaporate as temperatures changed, releasing water vapor that later condensed again in cooler regions. This process would have helped concentrate water in the material from which Bennu formed.
Meanwhile, Jupiter's influence may have limited the movement of larger particles, leaving the asteroid's parent material dominated by fine dust.
Because these tiny particles could circulate and mix efficiently throughout the disk, they preserved a chemical composition that closely resembles the overall elemental mixture found in the Sun.
The process is somewhat similar to the way fine household dust spreads and settles across many different surfaces rather than remaining in one location.
This extensive mixing could explain why Bennu's material retains such a representative sample of the ingredients present during the Solar System's earliest history.
"Bennu may offer our best glimpse of the original mix of chemical elements from which the terrestrial planets were ultimately built," as Schönbächler states.
Bennu is considered an exceptionally primitive asteroid because its material formed approximately 4.5 billion years ago and has experienced relatively little chemical alteration since then.
That makes its samples particularly valuable for reconstructing the conditions that existed before Earth and the other rocky planets finished forming.
By studying the asteroid's chemistry, scientists can better understand how the Solar System developed and which processes determined the composition of its planets.
Bennu's water-bearing minerals and organic compounds also make it important for investigating how early Earth obtained some of the chemical ingredients necessary for life.
Although these findings do not establish exactly how those materials reached our planet, they provide valuable evidence about where such ingredients originated and how they were distributed throughout the young Solar System.
A New Mission to Mars' Moon Could Reveal More
Despite the new discoveries, several questions remain unanswered.
"We are now wondering whether other asteroids have the same isotopic signature as Bennu and Ryugu," Schönbächler goes on to state.
Researchers also want to determine more precisely how Jupiter influenced the movement of dust and whether its gravitational effects were responsible for favoring the accumulation of particularly fine particles.
Additional asteroid samples could help scientists test the proposed formation scenario and establish whether Bennu's chemical signature is shared by other ancient bodies.
With the Bennu analysis now complete, Schönbächler is looking ahead to another opportunity to examine material from the early Solar System.
Japan's space agency, JAXA, is preparing a sample-return mission to Phobos, one of Mars' two moons. The mission is scheduled to launch at the end of October 2026, with the goal of collecting material from the Martian moon and bringing it back to Earth.
"It would be exciting to also obtain this material to analyse it in my laboratory," she says.
Schönbächler plans to apply to JAXA for access to the samples. However, the scientific community will need to be patient. The capsule carrying material from Phobos is not expected to return to Earth until 2031.
Those future samples could provide another important piece of the puzzle, helping researchers determine how different regions of the early Solar System exchanged material and ultimately produced the planets, moons, and asteroids we observe today.

Brennecka, Thomas S. Kruijer, Josh Wimpenny, Martin Bizzarro, Jessica J. Barnes, Ann N. Nguyen. Nucleosynthetic constraints on the origin of Bennu and CI-like asteroids.
