Roundup: Ebola's cross-border spread tests Africa's defenses as vaccine trial begins
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
18:51:09 CST
19:51:09 KST

KINSHASA, Oct. 24 (Xinhua) -- Africa's fight against Ebola faces mounting challenges as the virus spreads across national borders, with the second death in Kenya and uncertainties over the source of Nigeria's first infection complicating containment efforts, even as a major vaccine trial launched Friday in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) offers fresh hope.
The latest developments in the disease's spread have heightened concerns over gaps in cross-border surveillance and regional preparedness, with Uganda tightening transit restrictions amid fears of further spread. Scientists, meanwhile, are racing to develop vaccines against the Bundibugyo virus as the DRC battles its deadliest Ebola outbreak on record.
According to the World Health Organization (WHO), the outbreak has now affected five countries, including four in Africa. The Africa Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (Africa CDC) has previously described it as the most geographically widespread Ebola outbreak ever recorded on the continent.
In the DRC, the outbreak has claimed 4,687 lives among 9,704 confirmed cases as of Oct. 20, spreading to eight of the country's 26 provinces.
KENYA REPORTS SECOND DEATH
Kenya's Ministry of Health announced late Friday that a 65-year-old woman receiving Ebola treatment had died, bringing the country's death toll to two among nine confirmed cases.
The woman, a close family member of the country's first confirmed Ebola patient, had been placed under quarantine before developing symptoms on Oct. 13. She was admitted to a treatment facility the same day but died Friday evening.
The first patient, who had traveled from the DRC through Uganda, died in Nairobi on Oct. 5.
All eight subsequent infections have been linked to the initial case, including four family members and four healthcare workers. The seven surviving patients remain under treatment at two isolation facilities.
Kenyan authorities said there was "no evidence of community transmission" beyond the identified cluster, while the WHO reported Friday that all 135 contacts of the initial patient had been traced and quarantined.
NIGERIA CASE RAISES QUESTIONS OVER INFECTION SOURCE
In Nigeria, new genomic findings have suggested a close link between the viruses detected in the country's first Ebola patient and Kenya's initial case, as conflicting accounts of the patient's travel history complicate efforts to trace the source of infection.
Nigerian Coordinating Minister of Health and Social Welfare Muhammad Ali Pate said Friday that genomic sequencing showed the virus detected in the country's only confirmed Ebola case was "highly similar" to that found in Kenya's first imported case, "differing by just one mutation."
The Nigeria case was confirmed in Abuja, the capital, on Oct. 20. According to the WHO, the patient arrived in Nigeria on Oct. 3, developed symptoms four days later and tested positive for the Bundibugyo virus on Oct. 20.
According to Swiss media reports citing Switzerland's Federal Department of Foreign Affairs, the patient is a Swiss national married to a staff member of the Swiss Embassy in Abuja. Official sources said neither the woman nor her husband, who is in isolation, had traveled to the DRC, contradicting an earlier account by Ugandan authorities.
The Ugandan Health Ministry said Friday the patient had shown no symptoms when departing from the country, adding that investigations were continuing to establish when her symptoms began and where she might have been exposed.
According to the WHO, Nigeria had identified 44 contacts as of Oct. 20 and intensified surveillance and infection prevention measures. Nigeria's health authorities said the patient was showing signs of recovery, with no evidence of community transmission.
UGANDA TIGHTENS TRAVEL RESTRICTIONS
On Friday, Uganda announced additional precautionary measures, including restrictions on travelers with a history of travel to the DRC.
In a statement, the Ugandan Health Ministry said such travelers would no longer be permitted to transit through the country.
Authorities also reinstated traveler locator forms for all passengers, reinforced infection prevention measures at entry and exit points and health facilities, and strengthened nationwide surveillance.
The ministry stressed that Uganda remains free of Ebola.
Uganda reported 20 confirmed cases, including two deaths, before the end of the outbreak was officially recognized by the WHO and Africa CDC on Aug. 27, after 42 consecutive days without a new confirmed case.
The WHO, meanwhile, reiterated Friday that it does not recommend travel or trade restrictions on affected countries, calling instead for stronger surveillance, timely case detection and coordinated cross-border preparedness.
VACCINE TRIAL OFFERS HOPE
As countries stepped up efforts to prevent further spread, a major clinical trial evaluating vaccines against the Bundibugyo virus began Friday in Bunia, the capital of the DRC's hardest-hit Ituri province.
The Phase 2/3 trial was launched with the vaccination of its first participant.
Despite the scale of the ongoing epidemic, no vaccine has been approved specifically against the Bundibugyo virus.
The trial will assess the safety, immune responses and effectiveness of several vaccine candidates, using an adaptive platform design that allows multiple vaccines to be evaluated within a single study.
The WHO said the trial is a critical step toward establishing whether candidate vaccines could effectively protect people against the virus.
The agency has warned that Ebola infections in the DRC had rebounded after a brief decline, with the latest seven-day moving average suggesting "renewed intensification of transmission."
It said that escalating insecurity, population displacement and restricted humanitarian access were further complicating response operations and increasing the risk of undetected transmission. ■

9 Unique Apps to Try on the iPhone Duo
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
10:45:00 UTC
19:45:00 KST

Despite seven years of Android folding phones, Apple's iPhone Duo launch has spurred developers to create quirky, weird, and fun apps that experiment with the folding design (leaving Android owners feeling like second-class citizens yet again).
I've reviewed almost every folding phone in the past decade, and my inbox has never seen this many app pitches from indie developers wanting to show off their app for Apple's first foldable.
Some of these apps aren't necessarily new but use the phone's hinge to offer fresh experiences. You'll also find a “Made for iPhone Duo” badge on apps that make best use of the larger screens on the App Store. From a game that has you closing the phone to grill a piece of toast to a clever way to memorize flash cards, here are nine unique apps to try on your new Apple handset.
Battlefleet Duo
Board games will have a field day on the iPhone Duo, and Battlefleet Duo is the best example. On the larger 7.6-inch screen, you get a sprawling canvas, but in tabletop mode, you can view your ships on the bottom screen and the enemy's fleet above. That's especially great if you have a friend with the iPhone Duo, as you can play local multiplayer and sit across from each other just like you would with the old-school Battleships. You can play two free battles every day, or unlock unlimited battles with a one-time $5 purchase—no ads or subscription.
Flipcorder: Retro Camcorder
Reminiscing about the long-lost days of the pre-smartphone era? Flipcorder offers simple pleasure, turning your iPhone Duo into a camcorder, so you can make new memories that feel like the old days. Open the app, and the outer display will show a “closed lens”—open the Duo to “take the cap off,” then start recording. The user interface is retro, and video clips have a filter to emulate VHS (it has a MiniDV filter too). I really like that you can view your “tapes” and everything is cataloged by day, so you can see 30 minutes of footage in one stitched-together clip.
As you’re recording, the person on the other end can see a preview of the video on the outer display—that kind of dual-display experience is only available to camera apps, so if you were hoping to read a book and have the outer display appear as the book cover, that's sadly not possible at the moment.
RectoVerso: Flashcards
Flashcard apps are a dime a dozen, but nothing quite captures the physical experience of flipping around a flashcard like RectoVerso. This $13 app lets you import your own text—your classroom notes or even a PDF—and uses Apple Intelligence to automatically create flashcards on the subject matter. Alternatively, you can import decks from Anki, another popular flashcard app, or write your own. The magic is when you're actually studying. Don't know the answer? Slightly open the iPhone Duo, and the answer will gradually appear—fully open, and you get the full answer. That way you can bang your hand on the desk and say, “Ah, I totally knew that.”
PianoFold
Who doesn't love a rhythm game? Pop your iPhone Duo into a 90-degree angle and let the blocks in PianoFold reach the middle crease—that's when you tap the corresponding column. You need to time your taps perfectly, unless you enjoy listening to Bach get butchered in real time. There are 40 levels across eight chapters, and the game rates your performance (out of three stars) at the end of each song. You can retry as many times as you'd like. The first two chapters are free, though you can also play one song for free every day. For full access, you'll have to pony up $5. There are no ads and no subscription.
Toastie
When I showed my wife Toastie, she remarked that it might be the first time she ever wanted an iPhone (she uses a Pixel). That's high praise! This delightful $3 app asks you to construct a sandwich on the iPhone Duo's inner screen. Each recipe has specific instructions you have to follow, and when you're done, you'll need to close the iPhone for a few seconds—however many the recipe says—to “grill” your sandwich. Open the phone back up, and it's ready to serve! That is, if you haven't burned it. There are only 10 recipes, so you'll probably get through this quickly. But hey, at least you can say you've used the world's most expensive toaster.
Portal
Want to focus? Or relax? Portal lets you play relaxing soundscapes—listen to a volcano's bubbling lava or waves crashing on a beach—but you can also see these sights on the Duo's 7.6-inch canvas, in tabletop mode, or on the outer screen in tent mode. It's very relaxing and an excellent companion for travelers who rely on a sound machine to fall asleep. You can also follow calming breath exercises, or set focus timers to get stuff done. The app boasts more than 100 vistas, from Iceland's black beaches to enchanting UK woodlands. The app is free, though you can only access three portals refreshed monthly. Full access costs $3 a month, $30 per year, or $100 for a lifetime membership.
If you like the idea of Portal, you might want to check out Fold Focus, though it's designed to help you get work done rather than relax. Close the Duo to focus on a task, and the pixel animation on the outer display will start building a city. Open your phone before the timer ends and everything will come crashing down.
FirstSeed Planner
Want to try a new calendar app? Maybe your current one isn't optimized for the Duo (ahem, Google Calendar). Try FirstSeed Planner. The developer has fully enabled Duo support, letting you view the calendar on one screen and a daily planner on the other. It supports drag-and-drop actions between the two halves of the screen, and I also love the space at the bottom for writing notes for the day. And when Apple enables stylus support on the Duo later this year, you can handwrite in FirstSeed, making your Duo feel more like a paper planner. It's free, but the Pro version costs $3.49 per month, $30 per year, or $90 for lifetime access. The paid versions unlock features like automatic backups and weather forecasts.
Delta Emulator
If you’re big on retro gaming, you’ve probably heard of Delta. The popular emulator just rolled out its biggest update yet, headlined by support for the folding iPhone Duo. Prop the Duo at a 90-degree angle, and custom skins transform the device into a classic clamshell like the Nintendo DS—complete with automatic sleep mode when you close it. Just remember: It’s strictly an emulator, so you’ll still need to source your own ROMs responsibly.
Tiny Computers
Bring your favorite PCs and Macs back to life with Tiny Computers. This $4 app houses a library of 10 computers, from the Commodore 64 to the iMac G3. Fold the Duo into tabletop mode to bring the museum of machines to life—a vintage screen up top and a functional, clickable keyboard below. The operating systems are interactive, so you can run retro paint apps, secret terminal commands, or kill time with classic desktop games like Solitaire.

Snyder hopes to finally face Yazdani in Astana
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
10:32:48 UTC
19:32:48 KST

Snyder hopes to finally face Yazdani in Astana
TEHRAN - Kyle Snyder has never faced Hassan Yazdani in an official match, given that the two superstars have built their individual legends in disparate weight classes.
The paths of the fellow 2016 Olympic and multi-time world champions may finally cross this week in Astana, and both – along with the entire wrestling world, no doubt – would like to see them face each other.
“I spoke with Yazdani maybe a month ago and we both said it would be great to compete against each other at this tournament, so hopefully it happens,” Snyder said at a press conference Friday on the eve of this year’s World Championships, where he will attempt to defend his freestyle 97kg title and claim a fifth gold overall.
For Snyder, the ninth World Championships of his career could hardly be more challenging -- and exciting.
“I think that this is the deepest weight class that I’ve ever wrestled in in my life,” Snyder said. “There’s a lot of really tough guys in the weight class. That’s what makes it exciting.”
It’s not hard to see what has gotten the juices flowing for the 30-year-old two-time Olympic medalist.
A week before the 97kg competition begins, one known factor is that Snyder, as the top seed, faces a potential quarterfinal (!) clash with longtime nemesis and eighth seed Abdulrashid Sadulaev, who will be chasing a seventh world gold.
What remains unknown is who Snyder will have to first beat to get to the quarterfinals. And, as he pointed out in the press conference at Barys Arena, any one of a number of unseeded wrestlers are capable of taking down the reigning champion in the first round.
Topping that list is Yazdani. After taking a second career Olympic silver at the 2024 Paris Olympics at 86kg, he took the great leap upward this year to 97kg. Yazdani showed he could handle the extra weight by defeating world silver medalist and Paris bronze medalist Amirali Azarpira in a two-match playoff to make the world team.
Snyder said he was impressed with Yazdani and said he appeared to have no difficulty making the transition in terms of power.
“When I watched him wrestle Azarpira, I didn’t see any difference between [the two. They] both looked similar in regard to strength, and I think Azarpira is one of the strongest guys in the weight class,” Snyder said.
Snyder has gotten a tiny glimpse of what he might expect should he face Yazdani in Astana.
“I wrestled Yazdani one time in practice, for about 20 minutes,” Snyder said. “It was many years ago, so we haven’t wrestled in a while.”
Still, he knows that Yazdani could not have accomplished what he did without having what Snyder called “the will of a champion.”
“He’s so determined, he’s so resilient. I think about all the things that he has gone through and experienced in his career. All of the legends that he has defeated. There aren’t many wrestlers who have had that level of experience.
“And then, of course, tactically everyone knows he’s going to underhook you, he’s going to wrestle at a really high pace immediately when the match starts. He’s a good scrambler, he has good leg attacks. So, being ready for all those different things. I think that he’s a very worthy competitor.”
As for Sadulaev, when pressed Snyder singled him out as his toughest foe. The two have had epic battles in the past that have been dubbed “Snydulaev.”
“I haven’t wrestled Yazdani so I don’t know what that match would be like,” Snyder said. “But, just from my past, Abdulrashid Sadulaev is the toughest competitor.”
Still, experience keeps Snyder from looking ahead to a potential encounter.
“We’ll be in the same quarter, but we both still got to win in order to wrestle each other,” Snyder said. “I think at a tournament like this that the wisest thing to do is take it match by match, because there are a lot of guys who are unseeded who I potentially wrestle first who are really high-level champions in the sport.
“We’ve spent all summer preparing for all the different guys I could wrestle in the bracket…The guys in my weight class are so talented and there’s going to be a lot of matches that come down to one exchange, one point, one second.”
It is interesting to note that 10 years after all three struck gold at the 2016 Rio Olympics, Snyder (97kg), Sadulaev (86kg) and Yazdani (74kg) are competing in the same weight class.

HAMOUD, Jordan – Prayer services had just started at a church in Jordan on Oct 23 when Nasser al-Burqan heard what he thought was an exploding air-conditioner. Then the blasts kept coming. He soon realised it was gunfire.
Some people ran away. He said others, some bleeding, tried to hide in their place of worship where a funeral for his relative had been taking place. Word spread among those gathered that there were fatalities.
When the shooting finally stopped after several minutes, Burqan said he got a good look at the assailants behind what the Jordanian authorities described as an act of extremist terrorism that killed eight people.

Son shot in the leg
A short while later, his son, who also attended the mass, called him to say he had been shot in the leg and was being treated in hospital.
The attack at the Greek Orthodox Hamoud church in Karak governorate, about 120km south-west of the capital Amman, shocked the community, part of Jordan’s Christian minority.
Such attacks are rare in Jordan, although authorities in the US-allied kingdom say they have repeatedly foiled plots by Islamist militants in recent years.
Jordan’s King Abdullah, a US partner in the fight against militant Islamist groups, visited Karak hours after the attack and said the perpetrators would be punished “with an iron fist”.

Army seeks new ways to power troops on the battlefield
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
11:30:58 BST
19:30:58 KST

UK Defence Innovation has opened a Tactical Power Challenge worth £2.45 million seeking better ways to generate, store, distribute and manage electrical power for deployed forces, run on behalf of the British Army with support from the Defence Science and Technology Laboratory, according to UK Defence Innovation.
The competition is being delivered in partnership with Australia’s Advanced Strategic Capabilities Accelerator and closes at noon on 10 November. Further detail is available on the government’s competition page.
The organisation said the challenge seeks innovative solutions to improve the generation, storage, distribution and management of electrical power for deployed forces.
Power has become one of the quieter constraints on how the Army fights. A dismounted section now carries radios, electronic warfare detectors, night vision, counter-drone equipment, tablets and the batteries for all of it, and the weight of those batteries competes directly with water and ammunition. At formation level the problem scales up into generators, fuel convoys and the thermal and acoustic signature that a diesel generator park produces for anyone looking.
Ukraine has made the point sharply over the past four years, because units operating dispersed and under constant observation cannot run a visible generator, and the fuel resupply that a traditional headquarters depends on is one of the easiest things for a drone operator to find and hit. Silent generation, solar and battery hybrids, and power management that lets one source feed several systems have all moved from convenience to survivability.
The Australian partnership places the competition inside a wider pattern of British and Australian innovation work, with the Advanced Strategic Capabilities Accelerator performing a similar function to UK Defence Innovation. Running a challenge jointly gives a successful supplier two potential customers and gives both armies a chance of fielding compatible equipment, which matters more as the two countries work together under AUKUS Pillar Two on autonomy, artificial intelligence and electronic warfare.
UK Defence Innovation was established to replace the Defence and Security Accelerator and to put a single organisation in charge of pulling new technology into the department at pace, with a budget ringfenced under the Strategic Defence Review. Competitions of this kind are its main instrument, offering a defined sum against a defined problem on a short timetable.

With his first smartphone, Lula seeks to catch up to Brazil's online generation
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
10:17:02 UTC
19:17:02 KST

With his first smartphone, Lula seeks to catch up to Brazil's online generation
SAO PAULO/BRASILIA, Oct 24 - Just days before his 81st birthday, Brazilian President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva this week took ownership of a brand new smartphone, one that former aides said was his first ever.
Lula's choice to finally adopt a foundational artefact of modern life may be a tacit acknowledgment that he has failed to keep pace with a Brazilian electorate that now spends much of its life online. That may count against him in Sunday's presidential runoff.
"I’m becoming the king of selfies, a real internet user," Lula told supporters at a recent rally in Brasilia, hinting at his renewed efforts to better navigate social media campaigning.
Lula’s new technological adventure illustrates a generational shift in Brazilian politics, where a candidate's ability to convert millions of followers across platforms like TikTok, Instagram and WhatsApp into votes can now catapult them to the upper echelons of Brazilian power.
During congressional elections that took place alongside the first round of this month's presidential vote, a number of younger, social media-savvy candidates dominated their races.
Running for the right-wing Liberal Party, Nikolas Ferreira, 30, and Lucas Pavanato, 28, both took more than 3 million votes in their respective races, while leftist candidates who were elected with over half a million votes each included Erika Hilton, 33, and Ana Elisa Silva, who is just 21.
LULA LEARNS THE ROPES
Lula, a former shoeshine boy turned metal worker, trade union leader and global leftist icon, first ran for president in 1989, and is seeking an unprecedented fourth term in office. Standing in his way is right-wing Senator Flavio Bolsonaro, who is the son of ex-President Jair Bolsonaro and surprised pollsters by topping the first-round vote. The 45-year-old senator has been engaging voters directly with his own YouTube channel.
Ana Elisa Silva, a law student from Minas Gerais, joined Lula's inner circle to help him better navigate the unfamiliar social media landscape after his disappointing first-round performance.
"In my view, digital communication is not a generational privilege," Silva told Reuters. "Age may influence familiarity with certain platforms and formats, but it does not determine the ability to communicate, mobilize, or build a community."
For a politician like Lula — who freely admits his distaste for cellphones — the change required some adjustments, Silva said.
"His political communication trajectory predates the internet. (It was) forged through his relationships with workers, trade unions, grassroots movements, and massive rallies," she said. "This experience remains important, but it needs to align with changes in how people consume information, especially young people."
THE EVOLUTION OF POLITICS
The emerging power of so-called "influencer politicians" represents the natural evolution of a phenomenon that started with politicians reaching out to social media figures for campaign support, said Maximo Zaldivar, regional director for Latin America and the Caribbean at the International Foundation for Electoral Systems.
"The influencer has their own political capital," Zaldivar said, referring to their amassed followings across social media platforms. "That's what they bring to the table and no politician can compete with that."
Among "influencer politicians," Ferreira sits in a league of his own. A staunch Bolsonaro supporter and the son of an evangelical pastor, he boasts nearly 25 million followers on Instagram, equivalent to more than 10% of Brazil's population.
Though anyone can jump on social media, success demands commitment and consistent messaging, said Julia Zanatta, 41, an influential conservative lawmaker from southern Brazil with over 1 million followers on Instagram. She secured more than half a million votes in this month's election.
“I never thought about whether I'd reach more people or if I'd displease anyone,” she said. REUTERS

Ukraine receives only 24 Patriot missiles from USA over past three months - Zelenskyy
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
13:15:34 EEST
19:15:34 KST

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy stated that Ukraine has received only 24 interceptor missiles for its U.S.-made Patriot air defense systems over the last three months—a quantity far short of what is actually needed.
In an interview with ABC News on Friday, he noted that 30 ballistic missiles were fired at Kyiv just this past Thursday evening.
According to Zelenskyy’s estimates, Ukraine requires an average of 350 Patriot interceptor missiles per month.
Asked if he believes Putin requested that Trump to turn off intelligence-sharing between the U.S. and Ukraine, Zelenskyy responded, "I don't know. I hope, I trust and I hope God bless. No."
The President of Ukraine noted that he does not feel betrayed by the United States, but expressed regret over the lack of American aid. "I feel what I feel. It's not supportive," Zelenskyy said.
He emphasized that he is grateful for the partnership in the war against the Russian Federation, but suggested that, at times, he may not be as "polite" as other partners expect him to be. "Of course I'm a normal person, I'm just human, maybe not such a big humanitarian as Putin, of course … Like between friends, like in the family, you have to be honest, not to play games. I don't play games with Trump. This is my difference between me and Putin. I don't play with him any games. I'm direct, honest," Zelenskyy said.
The Ukrainian head of state believes that this is Trump’s personal decision “to be friends with Putin or not," but suggested that “they're in quite very good relations.”
Zelenskyy stated that the Ukrainian side is "ready to stop this war as quick as possible," but noted that the Russian Federation currently controls more than 19% of Ukrainian territory, and that Ukraine is not prepared to cede any further territory for the sake of ending the war.
As earlier reported, by June 2025, the U.S. military will likely have used up to two-thirds of its stockpile of missile-defense interceptors, even as American defense companies ramp up production. Specifically, Lockheed Martin is working to increase its annual production capacity for advanced PAC-3 interceptors, used in Patriot missile systems, from approximately 600 to 2,000 units. According to Bloomberg, the shortage in missile stockpiles has already affected supplies to other U.S. allies.
German authorities are seeking permission from the USA to assemble an advanced version of the Patriot interceptor missiles at facilities in Germany, stated German Defense Minister Boris Pistorius.
Zelenskyy has stated that Ukraine is not the top priority for suppliers of American PAC-2 and PAC-3 missiles for Patriot air defense systems, as the majority of these have long been directed to the Middle East. According to the president, Ukraine is also working with European and other nations around the world to secure additional missile supplies to protect its population.
According to him, Ukraine received 675 missiles throughout 2023, and 364 in 2025—yet the number of Russian missile strikes has increased during this period. For 2026, the delivery of 264 PAC-3 and PAC-2 missiles was planned. The PAC-3 missiles are supplied by the United States through the PURL program. "All our partners—both Americans and Europeans—are aware of the sums they are contributing and know exactly how many missiles they are providing us. There are also separate bilateral agreements with various European nations and countries in the Middle East. But, unfortunately, you can see a downward trend, and this depends primarily on the American side," Zelenskyy stated in August of this year.
On October 21, Ukrainian Minister of Defence Yevhen Khmara and Commander-in-Chief of the Armed Forces of Ukraine Mykhailo Drapaty met with a delegation from the American defence company Lockheed Martin, led by Orlando Sanchez Jr., President of Lockheed Martin Aeronautics. The discussions focused on the importance of stable arms supplies and future cooperation. In particular, the parties addressed increasing the delivery of PAC-3 interceptor missiles to counter the threat of strikes by Russian ballistic missiles.

Russia is conducting a campaign of hybrid attacks and sabotage across Europe, and Britain is working with the United States to deter and contest activity that threatens Euro-Atlantic security, according to an answer given in Parliament.
Jim Shannon, the Democratic Unionist Party member for Strangford, had asked what steps are being taken to work with the United States to reduce the Russian threat to both home territories.
Louise Sandher-Jones, the Minister for the Armed Forces, said: “As our closest defence and security partner, we engage and collaborate with the US regularly on a range of issues. We know Russia is conducting a campaign of hybrid attacks and sabotage across Europe. The UK does not seek confrontation with Russia, but we will continue to deter and contest activity that threatens Euro-Atlantic security.”
Answering a separate question from Shannon on support for Poland and Lithuania, Sandher-Jones said: “The UK stands ready to defend every inch of Allied territory, with NATO remaining the cornerstone of the UK’s defence and security. This is reflected in our commitment to reach NATO’s defence spending target of 3.5% of GDP by 2035. Article 5 of the North Atlantic Treaty makes clear that an armed attack against one NATO Ally is considered an attack against the entire NATO Alliance.
“As the third-largest cash spender on defence in NATO, the UK contributes significantly towards the security of NATO’s eastern flank, which includes Poland and Lithuania. This is demonstrated through rotational air policing, troop deployments, and joint exercises, including maritime surveillance in the Baltic region. NATO is a defensive alliance and does not seek confrontation with Russia, but Russia should understand that any attack on a NATO ally would be a grave miscalculation.”
Wes Streeting told the Defence Committee this month that hybrid activity of this kind amounts to state backed terrorism. European governments have attributed arson, parcel bombs, rail sabotage, cable damage and drone incursions over airports and military sites to Russian intelligence services or to proxies recruited through messaging apps.

12 Absolutely Banging Proper Watches Under $400
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
10:15:00 UTC
19:15:00 KST

The wonderful counter to rising prices at the very top end of the watch world is that, frankly, things have never looked better for those seeking proper mechanical watches on a budget. Entry-level timepieces keep getting better and cheaper—and this isn't just from newly established microbrands hoping to make a name for themselves, but from the major players, too.
Recently, I was asked to pick a couple of wallet-friendly watches for WIRED's Gear newsletter, and it sent me down a glorious rabbit hole where I was genuinely surprised by superb timepieces well below what WIRED has previously set for affordable watches (the sub-$1,000 bracket). Far from dropping three figures on a decent automatic, you can now get almost anything you desire from a watch for far less than $500.
To check my math and make sure I wasn't going slightly crazy, I reached out to WIRED's wider circle of watch experts with a devilishly tricky, unenviable challenge: Pick their favorite mechanical watch for less than $400, the sort of price where quartz watches dominate. It was a hard ask, but they delivered. Here's the list—all are exceptional value, and watches we'd be delighted to sport on our wrists.
Caravelle Sea Hunter
Caravelle has no right to make a mechanical dive watch this attractive and capable for a mere $300, but here it is. The secret to its timeless look is that Bulova's budget brand sensibly fashioned this modern Sea Hunter heavily on the diver's design from the late 1960s, while bumping the size up to a more modern 39 mm. Elegant and stylish, it's practically a GADA (go anywhere, do anything) watch. But with 200 meters of waterproofing, a 120-click unidirectional bezel, and a 42-hour power reserve, the Sea Hunter is a compelling sports watch. Throw on a rubber strap for diving, a nato for casual (our pick is Artem), or stick with the three-link steel bracelet for a more classic look.
Orient Bambino Version 7 38 mm
Unquestionably one of the best-value automatic dress watches you can buy today, the $295 Orient Bambino’s timeless 38-mm design with white dial and leather strap has been carefully shrunken down from the original 40.5-mm casing, making this piece incredibly wearable (both in these smaller watch times and when case sizes inevitably get larger again.) You can view the automatic Japanese movement through the exhibition case back, and there's even 30 meters of water resistance—not that you should be swimming with such a watch. Want something less traditional? Go for the pink dial with a stainless steel bracelet.
Brew Metric Lite Retro
This new smaller take on Brew's original Metric Retro is the choice of Mike Christensen, British GQ's lifestyle director and watch editor. Cashing in on the current trend for very small watches, Mike loves that this 30-mm piece is wearable for both men and women. “This li'l Brew number is so retro they decided to call it exactly that,” he says. At just $375, the stainless steel Metric Lite Retro, complete with a matching bracelet, uses an automatic movement visible through the open caseback. It has 50 meters of water resistance, and even sapphire crystal atop the striking dial. Proper retro charm that's forgiving on the bank balance.
Timex Marlin 1965 Reissue Hand-Wound
Chris Hall, a watch expert who writes for WIRED, The New York Times, Financial Times, and others, as well as his excellent The Fourth Wheel Substack, recommends the Timex Marlin 1965 Reissue Hand-Wound at $259. “It was the model that marked Timex’s return to mechanical watches about a decade ago, and unlike so many watches at this level, it isn’t a rip-off of something else: It’s a tribute to one of Timex’s own designs,” Hall says. “It’s small, quirky, and very much its own thing. Never mind the mechanics, getting real personality and credibility at this price is what’s really impressive.” At 34 mm on a leather strap, the design feels pure, and the 30-meter water resistance is a bonus.
Sea-Gull 1963 “International Edition”
Looking a little further afield can often pay off in the watch world. A prime example is the Sea-Gull 1963, a hand-wound mechanical chronograph based on a vintage pilot's timepiece originally built for the Chinese Air Force back in 1961. Many call this watch the gateway drug to watch collecting, but there are a few different versions. Here we've gone for the “International Edition,” which seems to be a budget model of the 1963 Sea-Gull, as it sells alternative iterations for more on its own website. The design is faithful (including the ST1901 movement), the 38-mm size is perfect, and you can't argue with the unfathomably low $269 price.
Baltic HMS
Founded in 2016 by Etienne Malec and debuting on Kickstarter in 2017, this French micro-brand was inspired by the watch collection Malec inherited from his late father, whose family hailed from northern Poland near the Baltic Sea. The brand has quickly become a darling of watch reviewers, so it's no surprise that two of WIRED's watch experts have chosen the 1940s-inspired three-hand HMS (cheating ever so slightly as the HMS clocks in at $430).
Robin Swithinbank, who writes on watches for The New York Times, Financial Times, and Business of Fashion, and hosts the Luxury Society Podcast, has been won over by the 38-mm HMS 002 Silver (above right). “At any price, I like my watches simple, legible, and hardwired with the kind of style that never dies. Baltic absolutely nailed it with this,” he says. Powered by an automatic Miyota 8315 movement with a 60-hour power reserve, it also has 50 meters of water resistance.
Tim Vaux, who writes for both Hodinkee and British GQ about watches, prefers the HMS 003 Salmon (above left). It's smaller than the 002 at 36.5 mm, but still uses the Miyota 8315 movement. “In 2026, there’s no need to look at the household names anymore. The HMS 003 has one of the most classically configured dials you’ll find at any price,” Vaux says. “Walk into a room wearing this and nods of approval will come from all angles. With the Salmon dial, you can’t go wrong.”
Bulova A-11 Hack Watch
As Caravelle's big brother, Bulova has appeared in our bargain watch roundups before. Still, this time, Felix Scholz, editor-in-chief of Revolution Australia and cohost of OT: The Podcast, chose the A-11 Hack Watch, on sale for just $357. “Military watches hold a special place in the hearts of watch enthusiasts,” Scholz says. “And while they might not be rare or intrinsically valuable, the hacking watches produced by numerous American makers during the Second World War are among the greatest.”
Legible and functional, Scholz says such pieces are a true slice of history, and that Bulova is one of the historic manufacturers of this type. “The A-11 Hack captures the spirit, but the less martial blue dial feels contemporary, and doesn't make you look like you're LARPing as a reenactor.”
Citizen Tsuyosa
Pickings are admittedly slim for genuine automatic GADA (go anywhere, do anything) watches under $400, but take a look at the $396 Citizen Tsuyosa with its classic black dial and integrated stainless steel bracelet. It features a 40-mm case, 50 meters of water resistance, sapphire crystal, 42-hour power reserve, and a 3 o’clock date window that will see you from beach to boardroom. If black is too serious, Citizen offers several dial hues (gold and green is a nice combo).
WIRED's top pick, however, is the new, more wearable 37-mm range conveniently on sale right now at just under our $400 target. If you venture above $600, park Citizen and go for the Lorier Falcon or Traska Commuter 36 instead.
Vostok Amphibia
WIRED watch expert Laura McCreddie-Doak has seen our Chinese chrono option and upped the ante with this Russian dive watch. Vostok traces back to the Soviet Union's Chistopol Watch Factory, a supplier to the USSR Ministry of Defense during World War II. This Amphibia 420269 (there are many, many other models) has a 2416B automatic movement that offers a 31-hour power reserve. Bafflingly just $151 on a steel bracelet, it's rated for 200 meters of water resistance, thanks to its unique, pressure-tightening case design. “This watch needs no other justification for inclusion on this list other than it was worn by Bill Murray as Jacques Cousteau-alike Steve Zissou in Wes Anderson’s The Life Aquatic,” says McCreddie-Doak.
Seiko 5 Sports
Finally, we come to the almost inevitable inclusion of the Seiko 5 Sports automatic. The familiar and affordable Seiko 5 Sports line began in 1968 as a tougher, sportier evolution of the 1963 Seiko Sportsmatic 5. The lineup is still going strong with dozens of variants plus a back catalog of thousands. That explains why, for the second time on this list, two of our experts chose the 5 Sports.
WIRED watch writer and author Josh Sims says the Seiko 5 Sports “is the MPV of watches: dependable, rugged, adaptable, as happy in the city as out of it. For my money—and this really is a lot of watch for, relatively, not a lot of money—it also has the cool of not being Swiss. Seiko isn’t just a giant of Japanese watchmaking; it’s a giant of watchmaking that deserves more r-e-s-p-e-c-t, and remains as relevant as ever.” Sims has gone for the SNSX Series that starts at $385.
Holly Ross, as executive editor of Vanity Fair’s On Time watch supplement, has gone for the Seiko 5 SRPE71 (pictured above), a model that's not new but still available if you look. “What is not to love about this chic, timeless, durable, and mechanical Seiko 5? And for a neat $320, it makes it even more desirable.”

‘No hesitation in detaining youth’: Congress targets government over US national VanDyke’s release in Myanmar arms case
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
10:13:28 UTC
19:13:28 KST

Congress asks why US national accused in Myanmar arms case was allowed to return home
NEW DELHI: Congress on Saturday questioned the decision to allow US national Matthew VanDyke, an accused in the Myanmar arms training case, to return to his home country, asking why a foreign national accused of terrorism was being granted such liberty while young activists protesting against alleged “vote chori” were being detained.Congress general secretary in charge of communications Jairam Ramesh raised the issue in a post on X, referring to VanDyke's release and the extension of permission for him and six Ukrainian nationals to remain outside India until February 24 next year.
“US national Matthew VanDyke, arrested for conspiring to carry out terrorist activities against India, was released yesterday and allowed to return home for 4 months. Why has such liberty been extended to a foreign national accused of terrorism?” Ramesh asked.He also criticised the government's handling of protests against alleged electoral irregularities.“This even as the government has shown no hesitation in detaining and arresting youth activists and peaceful protesters during the anti-vote chori protests this past month,” he said.
Ramesh further pointed to the issue being raised during US secretary of state Marco Rubio's visit to India in May, noting that the American official had visited again this week.
Congress raises questions over US intervention
Ramesh had previously accused Prime Minister Narendra Modi of being a “compromised PM” following VanDyke's release in September.The Congress leader had claimed that Rubio raised the matter during his May visit to India and that US ambassador to India Sergio Gor also took it up with foreign secretary Vikram Misri.On September 8, Ramesh claimed that charges under the Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act (UAPA) had been dropped against VanDyke. He alleged that this contrasted with what he described as the widespread misuse of the law against Indian citizens and delays in such cases.After VanDyke was released on September 24, Ramesh alleged that the prime minister had “failed” to protect India's elections, institutions and national security.
Court allows seven accused to remain abroad till February 24
A Delhi court on Friday extended until February 24, 2027, the permission granted to VanDyke and six Ukrainian nationals to remain outside India while the National Investigation Agency (NIA) continues its probe into the Myanmar arms training case.Special Judge Prashant Sharma passed the order after hearing applications filed by the seven accused. The proceedings were held in-camera.The NIA sought additional time to investigate several aspects of the case, with its counsel Rahul Tyagi making submissions to that effect. The agency told the court that further investigation was needed to verify alleged offences under the UAPA in connection with the import and recovery of large quantities of drones and accessories through India.VanDyke appeared in person before the court on Friday and was permitted to return to the US.The other six accused attended the hearing through video conferencing, citing health issues.The seven foreign nationals had earlier been permitted to stay in their home countries until October 23 after seeking six weeks to meet their families.
The NIA has alleged that VanDyke and the six Ukrainian nationals entered India on tourist visas, travelled to the northeastern region without the required permits and crossed from Mizoram into Myanmar, where they allegedly trained ethnic armed organisations.The accused were arrested on March 13 over allegations of training insurgent-linked groups in Myanmar.The agency had initially invoked provisions of the UAPA, including those relating to conspiracy.However, its chargesheet did not include the UAPA provisions and instead invoked Sections 21 and 23 of the Immigration and Foreigners Act. These provisions cover offences that can be compounded before the Foreigners Regional Registration Office (FRRO).The NIA had previously indicated that its investigation into the alleged terror-related aspects was continuing and that further allegations could be included in a supplementary chargesheet.

Why do some women become the strongest defenders of patriarchy
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
10:13:21 UTC
19:13:21 KST

Delhi University women took to streets demanding safety after news report of a gangrape near a girls college.
“Sir, let me say that I am not a feminist. I consider myself as a human being. As a human being we feel that it is our duty to help women, minorities, Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes, OBCs, and also the neglected class.”
Mamata Banerjee in Lok Sabha on Women’s Day, 2008.
Oxford dictionary defines feminism as 'the belief and aim that women should have the same rights and opportunities as men or the struggle to achieve this aim.'Then why is it that some of us distance ourselves from this term? And why is it that some women uphold the very patriarchy that restricts them?
Why do some women keep patriarchy aliveA group called the NCMIndia Council for Men Affairs recently took out a 'Long Live Patriarchy' march that went viral on social media. The group also had women holding the banner. "In the name of equality, these girls don't want to do jhaadu-pocha, clean utensils or raise kids. They just want freedom, money and debauchery," one of the women at the march said. "Equality does not mean freedom to drink, smoke, roam around at night. Women are misusing their independence. Azaadi does not mean shaming men."TOI spoke to Dolly Kumari, who is also a member of the group that actively raises men's issues, and asked her what patriarchy meant to her."Patriarchy cannot be understood simply as a system created by men to oppress women. When a woman speaks about men's issues, some people may find it surprising because they expect her to speak only from a particular gender-based perspective. But I do not believe empathy should have a gender. Supporting men who experience injustice does not mean denying the difficulties women face," she said."My objection is to the idea that everything traditional must be condemned as patriarchal and, therefore, bad. If a man wants to protect and provide for his family, and a woman willingly chooses to trust him in that role, why should society automatically call that oppression or brainwashed women?"Oxford dictionary defines patriarchy as 'a society, system or country that is ruled or controlled by men.'
It would appear, then, that women supporting patriarchy would be an anomaly. However, Dolly said that the purpose of their 'Long Live Patriarchy' initiative was to raise awareness of men's rights, which "we have been organising on Gandhi Jayanti for nearly a decade.""Equality should not become a competition between men and women. Women deserve justice, and so do men. We need a society where both can express their pain, seek support, and live with dignity without being judged by gender stereotypes," said Dolly."In the traditional Indian family, men were often expected to provide, protect and take responsibility for their families while women traditionally took on many responsibilities related to the home and children. These roles evolved within the social and economic realities of their time although it resulted in unequal rights and restrictions. Our history is not simply a story of oppression and therefore patriarchy should prevail."
Is the 'aurat hi aurat ki dushman' concept real? Does different treatment of a son from daughter and parenting play a role in keeping misogyny alive? Or is this 'aurat hi aurat ki dushman hoti hai' syndrome.Devika Anand, a psychologist at Rise and Mind, believes that the answer lies partly in the way gender roles are normalised within families and communities."I think one way to understand this is that we don't always question the systems we grow up in, particularly when those systems are presented to us as normal, moral, or necessary. When a woman grows up learning that a good woman is one who sacrifices, adjusts, tolerates, or puts others before herself, these expectations can become deeply embedded in her understanding of what it means to be a woman," she said.Over time, these expectations may stop feeling like restrictions and start being seen as values. A woman may even derive a sense of identity or self-worth from having lived up to them, sometimes at considerable personal cost."When younger women choose differently, it can challenge not just her beliefs but also the meaning she has attached to her own sacrifices," Devika explained.This explains why some women who have experienced restrictions themselves may go on to impose similar expectations on younger women. Having spent years adjusting to restrictive norms, they may come to regard them as an inevitable part of life rather than something that can be challenged."There can also be a need to make sense of one's own experiences. If someone has made significant sacrifices because she believed there was no alternative, acknowledging that those sacrifices were unnecessary or unfair can be painful. It may bring up feelings of anger, grief, or regret. Believing that younger women must make similar sacrifices can sometimes help preserve the sense that those sacrifices had a purpose," Devika said.When certain expectations are repeatedly reinforced within families and communities, they can become the default way of relating to others. A woman may reproduce the same expectations she experienced, not necessarily because she wants younger women to suffer, but because she has learned to see those expectations as responsible or appropriate behaviour.
From 'mere sar mei dard hai, iska karan marrd hai' to 'ek sutta, 2 chai, marrd jaat haye haye', the protest saw viral slogans. (PTI image)
Can patriarchy give women a sense of power? "Power doesn't always mean having equal power within a system. Sometimes, it means having more power than someone else within that system," Devika said.In a patriarchal family, a woman may have limited autonomy in relation to men but still hold considerable authority over younger women, daughters-in-law or other women in the household. She may have little influence over the rules themselves but gain status by enforcing them."This can give her a sense of belonging, security, or control in an environment where her own power is otherwise limited," Devika explained.There can also be a psychological incentive to conform. If a woman receives approval, respect or recognition for upholding family traditions, questioning those traditions may threaten not only her beliefs but also her position within the family or community.When tradition becomes a question of freedom Calling kindness, compassion, empathy and nurture 'qualities' that women should have, Dolly said, "I feel that relationships are increasingly being discussed in terms of personal freedom, sometimes without equal emphasis on duties, compromise, commitment, and mutual accountability."Dolly believes that a woman does not have to reject tradition to prove that she is empowered. "I come from a traditional, patriarchal family, yet my father always encouraged me to participate in activities that people might traditionally associate with boys. I played sports, learned to ride a bike, built a career in technology, and today have a beautiful family of my own. Growing up with two brothers also gave me a personal experience of sharing opportunities and responsibilities across gender lines. That experience is one of the reasons I believe that having a traditional father or growing up in a strict household does not automatically mean being oppressed. Tradition and discipline are not inherently oppressive," she said.Devika, too, cautions against labelling every woman who holds a traditional belief as a victim of internalised misogyny, which may include judging women more harshly than men, policing other women's behaviour, or believing that women are inherently less capable or less deserving of autonomy," she said.
When women challenge the rules they grew up with A 65-year old influencer from Haryana called Tai Savitri, who recently went viral over her commentary on society and patriarchy, told TOI that even though her experiences have been bitter, it was her educated children that taught her to become a feminist. "I was less educated. My kids got good education so I learnt a few things from them. It was also a feeling that I should do something for the women," she told TOI.She recalled facing criticism in her village, even though her family did not offer much resistance to her views."Yes, I have also heard that aurat hi aurat ki dushman hoti hai but I think it is more because of lack of education that pitied one woman against the other, a system wherein one woman was the slave of another. This created a scenario where women did not want other women to succeed in life," she said.In one of her viral videos, Savitri compared women who restrict other women to dogs that have become accustomed to living on a leash. "You must have seen dog owners taking their pets out. Even if they let go of this leash, by mistake or deliberately, you will notice that the dog itself will hold the leash in his mouth and give it back to his owner. Because the dog has now developed a habit of living like a slave and it has accepted its fate. It is the same with women who try to show other women in poor light. It is the same slave mentality. My only message to women is kutta nahi sher bano (don't be a dog, be a tiger). Whoever tries to put a leash on you or make you a slave, rip them to shreds," she said.
Patriarchy gives some women a sense of belonging There is a distinction between having a choice and the freedom to make that choice. Holding a traditional belief is not the same as denying another woman the right to choose differently. The consequences of that belief, and the degree to which it is imposed on others, matter.Women who defend patriarchal expectations are not necessarily motivated by a single cause. Their views may be shaped by the values they grew up with, the sacrifices they have made, the security they derive from their place within a family or community, or a genuine belief that traditional arrangements offer stability.The question, then, is not simply why some women become flagbearers of patriarchy. It is also why a system that can restrict women's choices sometimes offers them identity, belonging or authority in return—and what it would take for women to feel secure enough to question it.Perhaps the more useful question is not whether women are their own enemies, but whether a society that teaches women to measure their worth through sacrifice, obedience and conformity gives them enough room to imagine a different way of living.

Five takeaways from Trump's midterm campaign rallies
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
10:12:10 UTC
19:12:10 KST

Five takeaways from Trump’s midterm campaign rallies
WASHINGTON - President Donald Trump is in the midst of a nationwide campaign blitz ahead of the November midterm elections, holding near-daily rallies to boost turnout for Republicans who are fighting to keep control of Congress.
In his 90-minute stump speeches, Trump defends his economic policies, boasts about crowd size, mocks protesters and has even admired a fellow Republican’s buttocks.
Here are five takeaways from Reuters coverage of the president’s appearances, staged mostly in Republican-friendly areas across the country:
Trump’s economic pitch collides with voter reality
At the start of the month, Trump said he had done a “bad job” explaining his economic record.
He has tried to remedy that at his rallies, pointing to a record-low poverty rate, low unemployment, record highs in the stock market and cheaper prices for some food items.
But his sales pitch is colliding with voters’ concerns about how much they are spending on gas, groceries and other everyday expenses.
Consumer prices accelerated in September as the cost of gasoline surged. The nationwide average price of gas is US$4.27 a gallon (S$1.44 per litre) - nearly 40% higher than a year ago, according to AAA. Trump has repeatedly promised that gas prices will fall once the Iran war ends.
The disconnect was evident outside Trump’s rally in rural Kansas, where Chester Daniel, a 90-year-old military veteran and Trump supporter, said the economy has “a long way to go” to help working people.
“Prices? Too high! We will never go back to what they were when this all started, but they need to come way down,” Daniel said.
“I don’t know how these young people make a living for their family.”
Rally map shows Republicans playing defence
Trump’s travel map signals just how difficult it will be for Republicans to retain control of Congress, with the president forced to play defence deep in conservative territory.
Trump has travelled twice to Texas for Republican Senate nominee Ken Paxton, campaigned for Republican Senate incumbent Roger Marshall in Kansas and made two stops in Ohio for Senator Jon Husted.
Trump also rallied for Republicans in competitive races in Alaska, Iowa, Montana and South Carolina. He is set to visit Mississippi on Oct 26.
Those are places Republicans are accustomed to winning easily, not battlegrounds where Trump would spend time during the crucial final weeks before an election.
Paxton narrowly trails Democrat James Talarico in polls, while Marshall faces a serious challenge from Democrat Adam Hamilton in a state that has not elected a Democratic senator in nearly a century.
Husted trails former Democratic Senator Sherrod Brown in polls in Ohio, and Republican Senate hopeful Ashley Hinson is in a close race against Democrat Josh Turek in Iowa.
Notably absent from Trump’s travels so far with less than two weeks until Election Day: Michigan, Maine, Minnesota and New Hampshire – also home to tight Senate races.
He is soon poised to hit some of those locations. He is scheduled travel to Michigan on Oct 25 and has said he also plans to go to Maine.
Trump’s boasts about big crowds meet uneven reality
Trump has made crowd sizes a recurring theme of his midterm rallies, portraying packed arenas and thousands of people he says are stranded outside as evidence of his persisting popularity.
But actual turnout on the campaign trail in recent weeks has been uneven. Some rallies have drawn capacity crowds but have shown little sign of the overflow Trump described.
At others, large sections of seats remained empty even in modest-sized venues.
“I’m doing these every night, and no matter where I go, it’s the same thing. It’s massive crowds,” Trump said at a rally in North Carolina on Oct 20.
“We have big screens outside. Thousands and thousands of people. There’s something going on that’s very special.”
The venue was filled to capacity, but there were no signs of crowds outside waiting to get in or watching on screens.
At an Oct 7 rally in San Antonio, Texas, Trump said lines stretched over 3km outside the arena even as sizable sections inside remained empty.
Crowd sizes are not always an accurate measure of political support, but Trump has pointed to them as a sign of strength even as his approval rating has fallen to 31%, the lowest of either of his presidential terms, according to a Reuters/Ipsos poll released on Oct 19.
Trump is not on the ballot on Nov 3. For Republican candidates, the question is whether the enthusiasm he generates among his supporters can translate into votes for them.
France becomes a ‘bete noire’ for midterms
Trump has often used French President Emmanuel Macron as a foil in his campaign stump speeches, claiming he strong-armed Macron into raising prescription drug prices in France by threatening tariffs on a popular French export, champagne, and other goods.
But in the last week or so Trump has seized on another narrative about France, casting its violent unrest of recent weeks as a warning of what he says could happen in the US if Democrats win in the midterms.
Trump has blamed the unrest on migrants and Muslims, following a familiar playbook that has featured in his politics for more than a decade.
“What the hell happened to France?” Trump told a crowd in a livestock competition arena in Clemson, South Carolina, on Oct 21.
Notably, the French protests have taken a larger role in Trump’s recent speeches than two other major foreign policy headaches he has been unable to resolve: Russia’s invasion of Ukraine and his war against Iran.
“They’ll end one way or another,” Trump said of the two conflicts at his Clemson rally. He did not elaborate on how they might end, but complained that he was not awarded the Nobel Peace Prize for his work to resolve conflicts around the world.
Trump puts the body in body politic
Trump has long had a fixation on the human physique that stretches beyond the body politic.
This campaign season, Trump has given particular attention to Husted, a 59-year-old former college football player for the University of Dayton.
At rallies in Ohio, Kentucky and North Carolina, Trump marvelled at Husted’s physique, at one point saying his backside is “like a pile of muscle.”
“Then I looked at his legs, and I said, ‘Man, his feet are big.’ Then I looked at his shoulders, and I tapped him on the shoulder, and it actually hurt my hand. It was like a piece of steel. I said, ‘This guy’s a monster,’” Trump said.
Trump had similar praise on Oct 23 for Robert F. Kennedy Jr, his secretary of health and human services, telling a campaign rally in Florida that the 72-year-old “has the body of a 30-year-old.”
Such riffs are familiar terrain for Trump. At the close of his 2024 campaign, he used a Pennsylvania rally speech to tell a crude story about PGA legend Arnold Palmer’s prowess beyond his golf game.
Trump’s focus over the years on people’s physical attributes has also included mocking the weight and looks of his opponents.
Trump finds even some of his friends lacking in fashion sense, including the rumpled Paxton.
“Some may not like the way he dresses,” Trump said about him at the Republicans’ midterm convention in Dallas in mid-September, adding: “I don’t.”
That has not stopped Trump from campaigning for Paxton, however. He returns to Texas on Oct 27 for two more campaign rallies. REUTERS

Kyiv's power ring under attack: why the capital faces a winter of blackouts
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
13:06:00 EEST
19:06:00 KST

Kyiv's power ring under attack: why the capital faces a winter of blackouts
Hopes for a mild winter or inaccuracies in Russian strikes will not help Kyiv get through this winter without problems with its electricity supply. The only question is how long the power cuts will last and whether air defence forces and power engineers will manage to prevent the worst-case scenario.
The Russians are continuing their systematic attacks on Kyiv and Kyiv Oblast, seeking to completely destroy the city's combined heat and power plants and break the so-called power ring in order to plunge the capital entirely into darkness and cold.
The city has already lost a significant proportion of its own power generation capacity, while strikes are destroying substations through which electricity is supplied from other regions. In the event of severe frosts and further hits, a scenario involving 20 hours without electricity no longer seems far-fetched.
What is Kyiv's power ring, what risks does damage to it pose, and what should the capital's residents prepare for?
What is Kyiv's power ring?
This article does not disclose any sensitive information. The configuration of the power system is no secret to Russia, as Ukrenergo, Ukraine's state-owned electricity transmission operator, has warned. What does remain secret are the protection systems, equipment redundancy arrangements and power restoration procedures following attacks.
In the narrow technical sense, Kyiv's power ring is a system of high-voltage power lines and 330-kilovolt (kV) substations that connects the capital to Ukraine's integrated power grid and enables electricity to be transmitted to the city from different directions.
A key element of the capital's power supply is the 750 kV Kyivska substation, through which electricity from the Rivne and Khmelnytskyi nuclear power plants can be delivered to the capital.
Given their strategic importance, these facilities are under constant attack by Russian forces. The aim is to cut Kyiv off from Ukraine's integrated power grid and cause a blackout.
Put simply, the ring is a kind of road network for electricity. Transmission lines carry electricity to the capital, while substations step down its voltage and feed it into distribution networks for consumers.
If one section of this "road" is damaged by attacks, electricity flows can be rerouted through other lines. This helps maintain the power supply after damage occurs.
The ring is a critically important element of Kyiv's energy supply because the city consumes far more electricity than its own sources generate.
How much electricity does Kyiv consume, and why have power cuts begun?
Kyiv is the largest consumer of electricity in Ukraine. According to estimates by energy experts, the city consumes 1-1.2 GW, or 12-15% of the national total. In winter, depending on the temperature, demand can rise to 1.8-2 GW.
In 2025, before the large-scale winter attacks, local generation played a key role in supplying electricity to the city. According to sources at one of the energy companies who spoke to Ekonomichna Pravda, it may have accounted for as much as 1.3 GW. This came primarily from Kyiv CHP-5, CHP-6 and Darnytsia CHP (CHP-4) – combined heat and power plants (CHP plants) that produce both electricity and heat for the city's district heating network.
These plants are now no longer able to generate electricity. Nevertheless, all three CHPs were hit again by the Russians during the large-scale attack on the night of 13-14 October.
The capital is now forced to rely more heavily on electricity supplied from other regions via the power ring. The problem is, however, that its key components have been under constant attack for more than a month. Some of these attacks result in damage to equipment.
To cause significant problems, the Russians do not necessarily have to destroy the entire power ring. It is enough to damage a few critical nodes through which a large share of the electricity flows.
As a result, a situation may arise where there is electricity in the system, but the grids cannot transmit it to the capital in the required volume. If the city lacks its own power generation, the situation becomes even more complicated.
Under such conditions, dispatchers are forced to restrict consumption, including by introducing emergency or scheduled power cuts. This makes it possible to maintain a balance between available capacity and consumption and to prevent a large-scale failure in the power system.
The time needed for repairs depends on the extent of the damage. Some equipment can be repaired quickly. Replacing a large power transformer or other complex equipment may take longer, especially if the necessary equipment is not held in reserve.
Further complications are caused by repeat attacks, air-raid warnings being in effect for long periods, risks to repair crews and government attempts to reduce the proportion of energy company employees eligible for deferral from mobilisation. Following emergency repairs, the situation can deteriorate again, as strikes have been relentless lately and power workers face the risk of further attacks.
What to expect this winter
The main risk for Kyiv is a combination of three factors: low air temperatures, high consumption and Russian strikes that restrict the ability to transmit electricity to the capital. Given this combination, even fully functioning power generation in other regions does not guarantee that Kyiv will receive enough electricity, making various scenarios possible.
In a relatively favourable scenario, energy workers will repair damaged equipment and new strikes will not cause critical losses. In that case, restrictions may be moderate, although avoiding power cuts altogether will be difficult. For consumers, this would mean 8-10 hours without electricity per day.
If the attacks continue and some equipment remains damaged, Kyiv could face longer power cuts during moderately cold spells. Under this scenario, outages could last 12-16 hours per day.
The worst-case scenario involves regular large-scale strikes on key substations and other elements of the power system amid severe frosts. In that case, restrictions could last up to 20 hours per day. However, sources in the energy sector interviewed by Ekonomichna Pravda do not believe in a scenario in which the Russians would manage to destroy everything and "plunge Kyiv into darkness".
The consequences will depend on which facilities are damaged, how quickly they can be repaired and how much electricity can be transmitted to the capital.
A separate challenge is keeping critical infrastructure running, including water supply pumps, heating systems, transport, hospitals and communications.
Read also: No electricity means no water: an interview with the deputy CEO of water utility Kyivvodokanal
The capital needs approximately 200 MW of generating capacity for these purposes, primarily from combined heat and power units and high-capacity generators. According to Ekonomichna Pravda's sources, 150 MW of distributed generation has been brought into operation in Kyiv. By the end of 2026, this is expected to increase to 180-185 MW. Private facilities accounting for another 55-60 MW could become operational before winter, around half of which are already ready.
* * *
It is clear that protecting energy facilities critical to Kyiv from ballistic missiles depends primarily on the effectiveness of air defence. The engineering protection built at most substations can reduce the impact of individual strikes, but it cannot guarantee the survival of critical equipment after a direct hit.
Amid a shortage of missiles for Patriot systems, it is important to have the necessary amount of backup equipment, trained repair crews and clear action protocols for crisis situations.
Experience from previous winters shows that energy workers have learned to work under conditions of large-scale destruction. However, this does not cancel out the physical limitations of the grid and does not guarantee an uninterrupted electricity supply under every attack scenario.
Three things will be decisive for Kyiv this winter: how much electricity can be delivered to the city, how quickly energy workers can repair damaged equipment and whether backup generation can sustain critical facilities.
How long the power cuts last will depend on this. Kyiv can get through the winter without a collapse of its power supply, but it would be naive to expect the capital to avoid prolonged power outages if constant attacks continue.
By Mykola Topalov

China Great Wall Museum in Beijing reopens after renovation, upgrade
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
18:03:14 CST
19:03:14 KST

BEIJING, Oct. 24 (Xinhua) -- The China Great Wall Museum at the foot of the renowned Badaling Great Wall in Beijing reopened to the public on Saturday after an extensive renovation and upgrade.
Located in Yanqing District on the outskirts of the Chinese capital, the museum first opened in 1994 and closed in April 2022 for redevelopment.
Construction began in December 2023, with a building built to better blend the museum into the surrounding mountains and vegetation.
The museum, with a floor area of 16,000 square meters, features exhibition areas, educational and public service areas, collection storage areas and research spaces.
Its permanent exhibition and special thematic displays explore the Great Wall's history and culture. The permanent exhibition features more than 700 cultural relics, including many on loan from museums across China.
The displays trace over 2,000 years of the Great Wall's construction efforts and showcase how its preservation methods have advanced, from emergency protection to systematic conservation.
Visitors can also better understand the Great Wall's historical roles. Beyond its function as a military defense structure, it also gradually became a site of exchanges and integration among China's ethnic groups.
On the museum's second floor, visitors can enjoy expansive views of the imposing Badaling section outside the venue through glass curtain walls.
The Great Wall, a UNESCO World Heritage Site, stretches more than 20,000 kilometers across 15 provinces, municipalities and autonomous regions. Beijing has about 520 kilometers of Great Wall sections in total, and the Badaling section is the most visited. ■
