Owners of mobile phones that are not set to update their time automatically, or users who prefer not to rely on automatic updates, can adjust their devices manually. They can also restore automatic date and time synchronization at any point.
Android
Android menus vary across models, but time settings are generally found in the device's main Settings menu or under the clock settings.
In Settings, select "Date & Time" and disable the "Automatic date and time" option. Then select the appropriate time zone – Jerusalem – and set the time and date manually.
iPhone
In Settings, select "General," then "Date & Time." Turn off "Set Automatically," select the appropriate time zone and adjust the clock manually.

Ray-Ban Meta Audio Review: The Best Smart Glasses
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
09:15:00 UTC
18:15:00 KST

I am very lost in Los Angeles. I’m also sweating because I'm running as fast as I can, slapping my hands against the wet glasses frame on my face to boost the volume of the pulsing techno beats blasting into my ears—and anyone else’s if they happen to be nearby. It’s only the second time I’ve gone on a run in the city, and I decide to let myself get completely off course.
“Hey Meta,” I pant. “I need to get back; tell me where to go.”
The music dims, and the AI agent barks turn-by-turn directions in my ears. After getting turned around a couple of times, I eventually make it back. The navigation wasn’t perfect, but it got me where I needed to be.
This feature has long been available in Meta’s smart glasses. But now I’m wearing the new Ray-Ban Meta Audio, camera-free glasses the company announced in September. The only big change between these and Meta’s other glasses is the lack of a camera, but losing that one feature makes a world of difference.
It makes sense that Meta started with cameras on its glasses. After all, its primary breadwinner is Facebook, a visual platform driven by all the photographs and memes your uncle can use AI to generate. The platform is designed to capture content and beam it to the world—sometimes whether people like it or not.
It took waves of privacy controversies for Meta to finally ditch the cameras. People have found the camera-enabled glasses creepy, calling Meta’s products “pervert glasses” because they have been used by weirdo pickup artists to record people without consent. Some users also shared techniques for removing the indicator light on the glasses designed to let people around the wearer know they’re recording. (Meta released a software fix for this that disables the cameras entirely if the indicator light has been tampered with.)
It didn’t help that the company tried to put facial recognition technology on the glasses, which it denied at first, then later admitted to, and removed. In September, the company was sued for its facial recognition systems. (Meta insists that all the very public pushback did nothing to encourage it to release audio-only glasses.)

Trump’s Iran pause is for November
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
09:12:09 UTC
18:12:09 KST

President Trump’s pre-midterm pause on strikes against Iran landed as a claim of diplomatic momentum, not a concession of failure. The pause was framed as proof that negotiations are working. Look closer, and a different mechanism appears. The war meant to project strength has become an electoral liability, and the president’s response is to bury its most visible costs until voters have finished deciding. Then the option can reopen.
The White House insists Washington is negotiating from strength. Military options remain on the table. The blockade stays in force. The administration has not ended the war, only hidden its sharpest edges from the campaign season. That sequence matters. It allows Republican candidates to campaign without the immediate risk of new strikes or another energy-price spike, while preserving the argument that renewed action may be warranted later. Nothing has been settled. Everything has been postponed.
Trump’s political identity rested on rejecting costly, open-ended foreign interventions. His appeal to swaths of the MAGA movement included the claim that American leaders had squandered resources and neglected domestic problems chasing overseas conflicts. “America First” was a promise about priorities as much as power.
The Iran war has strained that promise to its breaking point.
Back in February 2026, it looked like a pressure campaign: force Tehran to accept Washington’s terms. Months later, it’s a drawn-out confrontation with no clear settlement. Rising fuel prices, stubborn inflation, and the uncertainty over how long the war will last have turned it into a domestic political problem.
Consumer sentiment has fallen close to a record low, dragged down by rising living costs linked to the conflict.
This creates a tension the Republican coalition cannot easily absorb. Some supporters prioritize nationalist strength and a confrontational stance toward Iran. Others were drawn by pledges to avoid costly wars and focus on economic grievances at home. An extended conflict makes satisfying both impossible. Pausing attacks before the midterms offers a way to postpone the reckoning.
The question is whether this pause is a genuine step toward peace or simply an attempt to protect Republicans from the political costs of an unpopular war. The attacks may have stopped, but the naval blockade remains in place, economic pressure on Iran continues, and neither side appears any closer to a lasting agreement. Trump has ruled out further strikes before 3rd November. What he has not ruled out is a return to military action once the election is over. This sequence allows the administration to present the pause as controlled progress, lets Republican candidates campaign without the immediate risk of new strikes or energy-price spikes, and preserves the option of arguing later that renewed action may be warranted.
The reports tell a different story than the public messaging. The Pentagon has been instructed to prepare for a potential resumption of large-scale operations. Discussions involving Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu have touched on a major new operation before elections in both countries. The White House calls such reports false. But the military remains on alert, and preparations are being finalised.
For many MAGA voters who supported Trump in part because he promised to reject endless wars, a purely electoral pause represents a significant contradiction.
An unpopular foreign war won’t turn MAGA loyalists into Democrats. The real hazard for the GOP is exhaustion: an endless conflict paired with painful pump prices gives frustrated voters every reason to leave their ballots on the kitchen table.
By removing the immediate threat of renewed attacks, Trump can try to prevent the war from becoming the dominant symbol of Republican failure and shift attention toward negotiations. If the conflict remains relatively quiet until November 3, Republican prospects improve. If Democrats gain control of one or both chambers, congressional scrutiny of military spending and presidential war powers would intensify.
This is where the powerless ballot enters the picture. Elections are meant to give citizens influence over decisions made in their name. That relationship weakens when a president can temporarily reduce the visibility of a policy’s costs until after ballots are cast, then resume the same course. Trump’s approach could turn the midterms into a debate over whether he appears willing to pull back from the war, rather than whether his Iran policy has actually changed. Americans are already feeling the strain of higher living costs, and consumer confidence has fallen sharply. A brief pause in the fighting will do little to ease that burden, much less resolve the underlying conflict. What is needed is a lasting diplomatic settlement, not a temporary break that leaves the same problems unresolved.
Neither a Republican nor a Democratic outcome automatically resolves the strategic problem. Iran has its own calculations.
Iranian officials continue to demand sanctions relief and an end to the blockade while Washington insists on further concessions. A pause that leaves these disagreements unresolved may simply delay the next confrontation.
The bigger question is not whether Trump keeps his promise before the election, but what he plans to do once the votes are counted and the political pressure has eased. If the coming weeks bring a verifiable agreement backed by credible safeguards, the pause could be a genuine first step toward ending the war. If instead November 3 is treated as the moment political restraints disappear, then the restraint will have functioned primarily as an electoral maneuver.
In that case the danger is clear. Voters are being asked to endorse the appearance of an ending while the means to continue the conflict remain intact. The ballot becomes a ratification of a decision already made elsewhere.
If the fighting resumes after the votes are counted, the question will no longer be whether Trump delivered peace, but whether his supporters were ever given a genuine choice between peace and a war that had only been postponed.

NAIROBI, Oct. 24 (Xinhua) -- Kenyan authorities on Saturday continued to search for seven people still missing after a multi-story building collapsed in a suburb of Nairobi on Friday.
"Search and rescue operations are ongoing at the site of the building collapse in Eastleigh. Two injured people have been taken to Kenyatta National Hospital," the Kenya Red Cross Society said in an update issued late Friday.
Onesimus Kipchumba Murkomen, cabinet secretary for the Ministry of Interior and National Administration, said Friday night that 11 shops on the building's ground floor and in the basement were occupied at the time of the collapse.
"Seven people have been reported missing. The rescue team has made contact with some of them, and efforts are underway to rescue those trapped in the rubble," he said.
All 67 construction workers at the site have been accounted for, Murkomen said, adding that 66 escaped unhurt, while one was hospitalized and is in stable condition.
The seven missing people are believed to have been inside the shops when the building collapsed, he said.
Authorities have yet to determine whether the collapse damaged or compromised the structural integrity of adjacent buildings.
Investigations are underway to establish whether any regulatory or professional violations contributed to the collapse, and local authorities have launched a manhunt for the building's owner. The National Construction Authority said it has identified the developer, contractor and registered professionals associated with the building.
"Details regarding rescue operations, the status of the site, and actions being undertaken by the multi-agency team will be shared in due course," the regulatory body said.
Building collapses have occurred repeatedly in Kenya in recent years, with experts blaming weak enforcement of construction regulations and a lack of routine safety inspections by government officials as among the causes. ■

BRATISLAVA, Oct. 24 (Xinhua) -- Polling stations opened at 7 a.m. (0500 GMT) on Saturday in Slovakia for local and regional elections, with voters set to elect representatives to municipal and regional council bodies for four-year terms.
Voting will continue until 8 p.m. (1800 GMT), with 6,029 polling stations established across 2,926 municipalities, towns, cities and city districts. Nearly 4.41 million people are eligible to cast ballots.
Voters are electing mayors, members of municipal and city councils, governors of self-governing regions and regional councillors. In the capital Bratislava and the eastern city of Kosice, voters are also choosing district mayors and members of district councils.
Voting is restricted to polling stations in voters' places of permanent residence.
Both Slovak citizens aged 18 and above and eligible foreign nationals may vote. Slovak voters must present a valid identity card, while foreign nationals are required to show an identity card indicating a long-term residence permit. ■

Expert warns of complex ecological fallout from Mongolia grassland fire linked to Japanese company
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
17:06:24 CST
18:06:24 KST

TOKYO, Oct. 24 (Xinhua) -- A large grassland fire in Mongolia reportedly linked to activities by a Japanese company's subsidiary may have caused extensive ecological damage, with its broader environmental impact requiring comprehensive assessment, an expert said.
The fire broke out on Oct. 8 in the Numrug Strictly Protected Area in Mongolia's eastern province of Dornod. The flames were extinguished on Oct. 16, according to Mongolian media reports. Japanese telecommunications operator KDDI said on Oct. 20 that the fire was linked to activities by its Mongolian subsidiary Mobicom.
The fire may have affected not only grasslands but also riverbanks, wetlands and other ecosystems, said Wang Qinxue, a researcher at Japan's National Institute for Environmental Studies who has long studied the region's ecological environment.
A comprehensive assessment is needed to determine whether soil conditions can recover alongside vegetation, whether wildlife can safely survive the winter and whether the fire has caused any transboundary environmental pollution, Wang said.
Preliminary data released by Mongolia's Ministry of Environment and Climate Change showed that the fire had burned about 530,000 hectares of land, including approximately 470,000 hectares within the Numrug Strictly Protected Area, accounting for 79.8 percent of the reserve's total area.
Located in eastern Mongolia near the Chinese border, the reserve features a mix of grasslands, forests, rivers and wetlands. It provides habitats for a variety of wildlife and plays an important role in conserving local biodiversity, Wang said.
Even if vegetation regrows the following year, plant species composition and soil conditions may not recover at the same pace, he said.
Assessing damage to forest ecosystems is particularly complex, requiring an examination of tree survival rates, the availability of seed sources and the growth of new seedlings to determine the extent of damage and the potential for recovery, Wang added.
The fire's potential transboundary ecological effects also warrant further investigation. It remains necessary to determine whether ash and sediment could be carried into rivers and wetlands by surface runoff and whether smoke from the fire had crossed national borders through the atmosphere, Wang said.
Citing research on Mongolia's Dornod Province, Wang said fire occurrence from autumn through the following spring was associated with the number of dust storm days in spring.
Reduced vegetation cover after a fire leaves soil more vulnerable to wind erosion and makes surface materials easier to transport by wind, he said.
Wang called for systematic surveys of the burned areas, categorized by ecosystem type, to scientifically assess the actual damage and determine the scope for ecological recovery. ■

BEIJING, Oct. 24 (Xinhua) -- Saturday marks United Nations Day, commemorating the anniversary of the UN Charter's entry into force in 1945.
On multiple occasions in recent years, Chinese President Xi Jinping has reiterated China's support for the international system with the United Nations at its core, and called for upholding the authority of the United Nations, practicing true multilateralism, and observing the purposes and principles of the UN Charter.
The following are some highlights of his remarks.
Sept. 13, 2026
At the 18th BRICS Summit in New Delhi, India, Xi said all countries, regardless of their size, strength or wealth, are equal members of the international community.
"Global South countries should hold high the banner of multilateralism, uphold the authority and role of the United Nations, support multilateral institutions in advancing reform and increasing efficiency, and ensure the equal participation of all countries in international affairs," he said.
July 17, 2026
At the opening ceremony of the 2026 World AI Conference and High-Level Meeting on Global AI Governance held in Shanghai, Xi said that AI is an invaluable asset that encapsulates humanity's collective wisdom.
"We should practice true multilateralism and recognize the important role of the United Nations," he said. "We should enhance alignment and coordination on AI development strategies, governance rules and technical standards, so as to form a consensus-based global governance framework at an early date to make this frontier technology better benefit humanity."
Sept. 1, 2025
At the "Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO) Plus" Meeting in north China's port city of Tianjin, Xi said the purposes and principles of the UN Charter and other universally recognized basic norms of international relations must be observed comprehensively, fully and in their entirety.
"We should firmly safeguard the status and authority of the United Nations, and ensure its irreplaceable, key role in global governance," he said.
Aug. 30, 2025
When meeting with UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres on the sidelines of the SCO Summit 2025, Xi said that China will always be a trustworthy partner of the United Nations.
China is willing to deepen cooperation with the United Nations, support the United Nations in playing a central role in international affairs, and jointly shoulder the responsibility of safeguarding world peace and promoting development and prosperity, Xi told Guterres.
June. 28, 2024
At the conference marking the 70th anniversary of the Five Principles of Peaceful Coexistence held in Beijing, Xi said that in the face of new developments and challenges, "the authority and central role of the United Nations can only be strengthened rather than weakened."
"The purposes and principles of the UN Charter are never outdated, and they are getting ever more important," he said. "China advocates the vision of global governance featuring extensive consultation and joint contribution for shared benefit, and China believes in true multilateralism." ■

Thirty-three British warships left service since 2010
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
10:01:44 BST
18:01:44 KST

Thirty-three Royal Navy warships have been taken out of operational service since 2010, of which eight have been sold, fifteen recycled and ten are still waiting to be disposed of, according to an answer given in Parliament.
Andrew Rosindell, the Reform UK member for Romford, had asked how many warships had been taken out of service, sold or scrapped in each year since 2010.
Luke Pollard, Minister of State for Defence Readiness and Industry, said: “Since 2010, 33 Royal Navy warships have been taken out of operational service. Of these, 8 have been sold, 15 have been recycled and 10 are pending disposal.
“As vessels may be withdrawn from service in one year and sold or scrapped in a later year, these categories are not mutually exclusive, and the figures should not be aggregated.
“As set out in the Defence Investment Plan, this Government is investing in new frigates, amphibious ships, new submarines and new standardised vessels alongside a new Hybrid Navy of uncrewed and autonomous systems to increase our Navy’s lethality and deterrence.”
Thirteen new frigates are being built across two classes, eight Type 26 anti-submarine ships on the Clyde and five Type 31 general purpose ships at Rosyth, and Norway has since selected the Type 26 design for its own fleet. Three Fleet Solid Support ships are under construction to resupply the carrier groups, new transport ships are planned to take over from the amphibious and Bay class vessels. The submarine service is completing the Astute class before moving to the four Dreadnought ballistic missile boats and then to SSN-AUKUS attack submarines, which ministers have said will be delivered at a rate of one every eighteen months from the mid-2030s.
The period covered includes the retirement of the Type 42 destroyers, the progressive withdrawal of the Type 23 frigates, and the decision to dispose of the amphibious assault ships Albion and Bulwark, the latter of which is being sold to Brazil.

Hong Kong and mainland Chinese police have arrested 33 people in a joint crackdown on a syndicate that allegedly stole credit cards from residents who had travelled north to Shenzhen, with losses exceeding HK$1.8 million (US$229,500).
Superintendent Tsang Chun-kit of the Crime Kowloon East Regional Headquarters said on Saturday that “card carriers” then immediately crossed the border to buy mobile phones and resell them for cash, all before the victims could realise what had happened.
“All the victims had been to tourist hotspots in Shenzhen for leisure before the crime happened,” Tsang said. “They didn’t check their personal belongings after the trip until banks notified them of abnormally large transaction records.”
The Kowloon East regional technology and financial crime unit shared intelligence with Shenzhen’s Public Security Bureau and carried out an in-depth investigation before separate enforcement action was taken, he explained.

Seven projects by RIBA award-winning Nakshabid Architects
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
09:00:00 UTC
18:00:00 KST

Seven projects by RIBA award-winning Nakshabid Architects
Who is RIBA International Prize winner Nakshabid Architects? In this roundup, we get to know the Dhaka-based studio through seven of its key projects spanning Bangladesh.
Founded by Bayejid Khondoker in 2003, Nakshabid Architects’ extensive portfolio is concentrated in Bangladesh and encompasses both public and private projects – from residential blocks to mosques and museums.
Last week saw the studio’s Green Field Factory named the fifth winner of the biennial award, presented by the Royal Institute of British Architects (RIBA) to the world’s best new building outside the UK.
Praised for its focus on passive design principles and the prioritisation of employee wellbeing, the studio considers its latest award to be a recognition of Bangladesh’s architectural contributions at a global scale.
“We see the prize as a recognition of what architecture from Bangladesh can contribute to global conversations on climate and the dignity of labour,” the studio told Dezeen.
Alongside the award-winning Green Field Factory, recent projects undertaken by the 20-person studio include the government-commissioned renovation of the Bangladesh Military Museum in Dhaka, which reached completion in 2022 with a glass geodesic dome.
Central to its architectural approach, the studio said, is forging connections between a building and its “socio-ecological context” in a bid to reframe functional programmes as places of gathering.
“We believe that architecture must respond directly to its socio-ecological context, transforming ordinary programmes into meaningful collective experiences,” the studio said.
“We approach every project as a shared undertaking, listening closely to the people who will use it, the climate it sits in and the building traditions around it before we draw,” it continued.
“In this way even the most functional programmes become places of gathering, where light, air, landscape and everyday social life are woven into the architecture itself.”
Read on for a look at seven of the studio’s key projects:
Green Field Factory, Rangpur, 2017
The Green Field Factory, a rug factory in Rangpur, was designed by Nakshabid Architects to dismantle workplace hierarchies and is the fifth winner of the RIBA International Prize.
Fronted by a monumental green facade, the seven-storey building was informed by the traditional Bengali home, incorporating natural ventilation and biophilic design principles.
Aman Mosque, Narayanganj, 2018
A pair of intersecting arches form an “invisible dome” that frames the interior of Aman Mosque, a cubic prayer hall completed by the studio in Narayanganj.
Set within a sunken circular courtyard, the mosque is defined by its solid concrete volume, which is adorned with triangular perforations that filter light into the space.
Shaptak Insignia, Dhaka, 2021
A concrete facade punctuated with square openings was designed to limit heat gain and control daylight access at the Shaptak Insignia apartment tower in Dhaka.
Comprising two blocks, the residential block contains 18 units on a 670-square-metre plot, with each apartment complete with a balcony and a stepped terrace.
Urban Legacy, Dhaka, 2021
A pair of slender, red-brick residential towers make up the studio’s Urban Legacy project in Dhaka.
Its jagged form is defined by cantilevered balconies, which are enclosed by horizontal louvres and complete with greenery intended to shade and cool the apartment interiors.
“Cascading vines and planters spill from every terrace and the brick-walled garden base, turning the building into a vertical green landscape,” the studio said.
Aman Cement Factory Mosque, Sirajganj, 2022
An arched entrance guides visitors beyond the tiered brick exterior of the Ullapara Mosque, which Nakshabid Architects completed on the grounds of a cement factory for its workers.
Spread across two storeys, the mosque was built using locally-sourced brick, concrete and glass in a bid to blend “tradition with modernity”.
“[The mosque] has become a place where factory workers and neighbours gather for prayer, social events and community life,” the studio said.
Bangladesh Military Museum, Dhaka, 2022
Looking to redefine museum culture in Bangladesh, Nakshabid Architects conceptualised its design for the Bangladesh Military Museum in Dhaka as a “vibrant civic destination”.
Its curving concrete structure contains cafes, galleries, an amphitheatre and an arena, which is sheltered by a 120-feet glass geodesic dome.
Nurpur Graveyard, Rangpur, 2023
Nakshabid Architects intended for the Nurpur Graveyard, a Muslim graveyard in Rangpur, to also offer a place of leisure for the local community.
To do this, the site accommodates a healthcare facility and an education space – or madrasa – with future expansions expected to include a mosque.
“Nurpur Graveyard is a place that diminishes the typical boundaries of graveyards,” the studio said.

New York Archdiocese close to settling sexual abuse claims for over US$800 million
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
09:00:00 UTC
18:00:00 KST

New York Archdiocese close to settling sexual abuse claims for over US$800 million
Maya King and Jeffery C Mays
- The New York Archdiocese is close to a settlement worth more than US$800 million for 1,300 sexual abuse claims, after years of legal pressure and fears of bankruptcy.
- Plaintiffs’ lawyers said all survivors signed the revised deal, though the archdiocese said, “We are not quite there yet,” and a few holdouts delayed final approval.
- The deal would offer at least US$250,000 per person, add US$20 million for holdouts, and force the archdiocese to publish names of credibly accused clergy and lay leaders.
AI generated
NEW YORK – The Archdiocese of New York and plaintiffs’ lawyers were closing in on a settlement on Oct 23 in which the Church would pay more than US$800 million (S$1 billion) to settle claims from 1,300 people who said they had been sexually abused by its clergy members and lay leaders.
The plaintiffs’ lawyers said that they had finalised the settlement with the archdiocese and that all of the plaintiffs had signed off on it.
But Joseph Zwilling, a spokesperson for the archdiocese, said in an interview on the night of Oct 24 that the parties were still working to finalise the agreement.
“We are not quite there yet,” he said.
Terms of the settlement would call for each plaintiff to have the option of receiving a lump-sum payment of at least US$250,000, or a potentially larger payout after a review of the extent of the abuse each plaintiff has claimed, according to the plaintiffs’ lawyers.
The proposal would end a multi-year saga that threatened to bankrupt the United States’ foremost Roman Catholic archdiocese.
The terms of the proposed settlement required that all 1,300 plaintiffs accept it, and there were some holdouts, who argued that the proposal did not do enough to rectify the harms they had experienced. Progress was also stymied by the deaths of some plaintiffs.
“Tonight, we were able to finalise the settlement with the Archdiocese,” Trusha Goffe, an attorney with Jeff Anderson & Associates, wrote on Oct 23 in an e-mail to the firm’s nearly 300 clients who say they were abused.
“All of the survivors agreed to the revised deal. This means that the settlement you agreed to will move forward.”
Lawyers for the plaintiffs said they had repeatedly warned their clients that if they did not accept the proposal, the archdiocese would most likely declare bankruptcy, reducing the size of any eventual payout and extending the length of the already years-long litigation.
To appease the handful of plaintiffs who were resistant to the proposal, the lawyers said, the archdiocese negotiated with one of its insurers to increase the amount of money it would pay the holdouts.
They would now receive a pot of US$20 million to be evenly distributed among them – an uncommon arrangement that hinged largely on the availability of insurance funds.
“The survivors showed an amazing amount of perseverance and patience here,” said Paul Mones, a veteran lawyer whose Los Angeles-based firm represents 33 of the plaintiffs against the archdiocese.
“After a lifetime of pain and struggle, they mustered the energy to push that final mile. And hopefully this deal will give them a degree of solace and healing.”
The Archdiocese of New York, which includes Manhattan, the Bronx, Staten Island and a handful of Hudson Valley communities, would be the latest Catholic institution to pay hundreds of millions of dollars to settle claims of sexual abuse.
In June, the Archdiocese of San Francisco agreed to pay US$395 million to settle claims from more than 530 people who said clergy members and lay leaders had abused them.
In 2024, the Archdiocese of Los Angeles settled similar claims for more than US$1 billion – one of the largest sexual abuse settlements in church history.
The agreement with the New York Archdiocese also requires it to publish on its website the names of the clergy members and lay leaders who were credibly accused of sexual abuse, and to keep that list updated with any future substantiated claims of abuse.
The accusers and their lawyers said they thought these requirements would not only illuminate past abuses, but also help to prevent future ones. It is unclear what disclosures, if any, the archdiocese would have faced if it had declared bankruptcy.
In her e-mail, Goffe said she would have more details about the settlement process in the next two weeks but wanted to emphasise “what an achievement” the agreement represents. NYTIMES
- This article originally appeared in The New York Times.

The forecast indicates that Bulgaria will outperform the European Union and eurozone economies throughout the three-year period, although inflation is expected to remain higher.

EY expects the EU economy to grow by 1.4% in 2026, followed by 1.7% in 2027 and 1.4% in 2028. Growth in the eurozone is forecast at 1% this year, 1.4% next year and 1.3% in 2028.

Russia Transferred Non-Nuclear Submarine Technology to China
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
08:54:11 UTC
17:54:11 KST

As part of a cooperation that has been ongoing since the 2010s, Russia transferred technical documentation and materials for submarine testing to China. The technology exchange continued even after the start of Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.
This is stated in the report “A Marriage of Convenience?” by the research organization Center for Advanced Defense Studies (C4ADS).
According to experts, Sino-Russian cooperation encompasses noise-reduction technologies, non-nuclear propulsion systems, automated command, control, and weapon management systems, as well as submarine hull design.
China’s submarine fleet, particularly its non-nuclear component, initially relied on Soviet and Russian technologies, although the Chinese Navy later transitioned to domestically produced platforms. At the same time, U.S. government sources claim that China’s nuclear submarine program continues to receive significant Russian technical assistance, particularly in the area of reducing acoustic signature.
The Russian Central Design Bureau for Marine Engineering Rubin—a subsidiary of the state-owned United Shipbuilding Corporation (USC)—plays a key role in the cooperation between the two countries. The bureau is subject to sanctions imposed by the U.S., the EU, and Japan.
Trade data confirms this cooperation. According to these data, from at least August 2015 through April 2023, Rubin collaborated with procurement agencies of the People’s Liberation Army of China and China Shipbuilding and Offshore International Co., Ltd. (CSOC) on the joint development of submarine technologies.
CSOC is the foreign trade division of the China State Shipbuilding Corporation (CSSC), which builds civilian and military vessels.
During this period, Rubin made 12 deliveries to the PLA Navy’s procurement agencies and CSOC with a total value of over $80 million. According to the report’s authors, the vague descriptions of these deliveries likely pertain to conceptual designs for a non-nuclear submarine.
In particular, two deliveries from Rubin to CSOC in October 2019 and January 2020 included documentation regarding various submarine-related tests. Among them were tests to evaluate cavitation, a natural phenomenon that impairs the stealth capabilities of submarines.
According to a maritime security expert consulted by the report’s authors, these details indicate that Rubin helped CSOC test the effectiveness of Chinese technologies for reducing submarine noise.
Available data also indicates that from December 2019 to September 2022, CSOC supplied Rubin with materials for submarine testing. These included control devices and components for test consoles used to evaluate the submarine’s information and control system. Documents related to a shipment in September 2022 also mention a contract for joint design and production.
As a reminder, in late September, Ukrainian hackers claimed to have obtained a large cache of technical documentation related to Russian naval systems. According to their statement, the breach encompassed the scientific, technical, design, testing, and operational infrastructure of Russian naval developments related to the submarine fleet, navigation, hydroacoustics, and marine robotics.

Iran drops four places to sixth at Nagoya Asian Para Games
TEHRAN - Iran concluded its campaign at the 2026 Asian Para Games in Nagoya in sixth place, suffering a four-position decline from its runner-up finish at the previous edition in Hangzhou, China, in 2023.
The Iranian delegation collected 102 medals, including 26 gold, 36 silver and 40 bronze, compared with 131 medals — 44 gold, 46 silver and 41 bronze — at Hangzhou.
Despite the decline in the overall standings, several Iranian athletes delivered outstanding performances, demonstrating the country's continued strength in para-athletics and swimming.
Among the most successful competitors was Sina Zeighaminejad, who emerged as one of Iran's leading gold medalists in para swimming. He secured three gold medals, underlining his remarkable consistency and establishing himself as a key figure in Iran's medal-winning campaign.
Another standout performer was Elham Salehi, who captured two gold medals in para-athletics. Her achievements provided a significant boost to the Iranian delegation and highlighted the important contribution of female athletes to the country's success.
Alireza Zare also produced an impressive performance, winning two gold medals in para-athletics. His achievements included a record-breaking run in the men's 200-meter T35 event, where he clocked 24.83 seconds to secure the title.
While these individual successes offered encouraging signs, Iran's overall results reflected a noticeable decline compared with Hangzhou. The delegation won 18 fewer gold medals and 29 fewer medals overall, although it also competed with a smaller squad.
Meanwhile, China reaffirmed its dominance of Asian para sports, finishing comfortably at the top of the medal standings with an extraordinary 435 medals, comprising 207 gold, 117 silver and 111 bronze.
Host nation Japan secured second place with 64 gold, 60 silver and 62 bronze medals, while Uzbekistan finished third with 45 gold, 49 silver and 51 bronze.
India claimed fourth position with 30 gold medals, followed by South Korea with 29, leaving Iran sixth with 26 gold medals.
China's commanding performance demonstrated its considerable depth across multiple disciplines and reinforced its position as the continent's leading para-sport powerhouse.
For Iran, the Nagoya Games presented a mixed picture of individual excellence and collective disappointment.
Although champions such as Zeighaminejad, Salehi and Zare delivered memorable performances, the four-place drop in the rankings underlined the need for stronger preparation, investment in emerging talent and improved competitive depth.
The challenge now facing Iranian para sports is to build on these individual achievements and regain a place among Asia's leading delegations at future international competitions.

Germany plans to replenish its stockpile of precision-guided weapons with several thousand missiles from European arms manufacturers. In particular, the country is in talks with Ukraine regarding Bars jet-powered drones.
Source: Bloomberg
Details: According to Bloomberg, the Ukrainian jet-powered UAVs are among four main options being considered by the German Defence Ministry. In addition to Bars, Germany is discussing a contract worth more than €1 billion to purchase Anthem ground-launched cruise missiles from US company Covenant.
Germany is also considering Ruta missiles from the Dutch company Destinus, which have been used in Ukraine, and the HS1 high-speed missile being developed by German-British defence start-up Hypersonica, the financial news agency's sources said.
"They are also in talks with Ukraine to co-produce and acquire the Bars cruise missile, whose manufacturer has not been made public, people familiar with the negotiations said," Bloomberg reported.
The Bars jet-powered drone has a strike range of up to 1,000 km and can carry a warhead weighing up to 60 kg. The UAV can reach speeds of more than 700 km/h. Bars operates as a modular platform which, depending on its fuel load and warhead weight, can be used for long-range and mid-range strikes as well as strikes near the front line.
The manufacturer of Bars drones is capable of producing around 600 jet-powered drones per month. The company is also working on upgrading the drone to the Bars 2.0 version.
Background: Earlier, Ukrainska Pravda reported that Ukraine and Germany signed an agreement in July 2026 on the joint production of Bars UAVs. During the first stage of the project, Germany will finance drone production, with all the systems produced to be supplied to Ukraine's defence forces.

AI glasses create new growth potential for Taiwan optical industry
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
08:32:11 UTC
17:32:11 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Taiwan's optical lens makers are expanding into AI glasses as the emerging market creates new business opportunities beyond smartphones, CTEE reported Saturday.
As Meta, Google, and other major technology companies introduce new models, AI glasses are moving closer to everyday consumer use. Research firm IDC estimates global shipments will reach 13.04 million units this year and increase to 16.18 million next year.
Genius Electronic Optical Co. has been developing optical components for AI glasses and augmented and virtual reality (AR and VR) devices in recent years. The company is already working with US clients and is also in talks with Chinese brands.
Although orders for VR lenses have slowed, activity in AI glasses and AR products is picking up. These applications share some of the same technical requirements as smartphone cameras, including compact designs, high resolution, and precise assembly, while also requiring lightweight components, according to Pocket Securities.
Asia Optical Co. has spent years developing metalens technology using nanoimprint lithography, a process that uses a stamp-like mold to transfer nanoscale circuit patterns onto a light-sensitive coating on a wafer. The company holds related manufacturing patents, according to Business Next.
It said the technology could significantly lower the cost of optical waveguide lenses used in AR glasses, potentially making eyewear with built-in displays more affordable. Asia Optical is also exploring the use of metalens technology in sensing modules for AI glasses.
Kinko Optical Co. is focusing its AR, VR, and mixed reality development on optical waveguides and optical engines, which help deliver images to the wearer's eyes. The company expects its investments in AR technology to begin generating returns next year.
Ability Enterprise Co. is starting with specialized applications such as sports glasses. It is participating in a smart sports glasses project under an electronics manufacturing services model, producing devices based on designs provided by clients.
Depending on customer needs, the company may expand into original design manufacturing, which also includes product design.

Taiwan’s NCIST investigates origin of Hsiung Feng III missile part
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
08:32:00 UTC
17:32:00 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) – The Kaohsiung-based National Chung-Shan Institute of Science and Technology said Friday that it found a suspected Chinese component in its air-launched Hsiung Feng III missile, CNA reported.
NCSIST is developing Hsiung Feng III missiles for the country's indigenous defense fighter under its Hsiung Chih Project. The institute test-fired the missiles near Pingtung County’s Jiupeng Military Base in July and is still optimizing the design, per the Liberty Times.
Current ship-fired and ground-launched Hsiung Feng III missiles weigh between 1,300 and 1,400 kilograms, Liberty Times said. The missile must be scaled down below 1,000 kg to be safely carried by IDFs, though at the cost of a shorter effective firing range.
Storm Media reported that NCSIST discovered a communication signal filter that may be of Chinese origin during an inspection. The institute said the component has not been installed and it has contacted the supplier for an explanation.
The institute said the metallic filter has no transmission capabilities or embedded electronic components. It added that it conducts routine inspections to weed out Chinese components.

Israel launches major West Bank operation after soldiers killed
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
08:31:57 UTC
17:31:57 KST

Breadcrumb
Israeli forces displace Hebron families after deadly attack
Israeli forces pushed into the occupied West Bank city of Hebron on Saturday and displaced around 250 families, some in the middle of the night, vowing to exact a heavy price for a deadly attack on soldiers.
The Palestinian Authority called for international pressure on Israel to protect residents, who said soldiers announced the evacuations over loudspeakers late at night as they packed what they could and left.
Israeli forces have already demolished some buildings in the immediate vicinity of where the attack took place.
Israel's military began largescale raids on the occupied West Bank on Friday, which it said would last several days and include searches and building demolitions, after two Israeli soldiers and two Palestinians were killed in a clash at a military checkpoint.
Hebron governor Khaled Dudin told AFP the army started in the attackers' neighbourhood "but there is no guarantee that the operation will not expand", calling it a form of "collective punishment".
Yousef Zouhair Al-Jabari, head of Hebron's municipality, said around 1,300 people faced losing their homes, in addition to the 1,200 already displaced.
ICC fugitive Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu is locked in a tight race to keep his job in Tuesday's vote, having campaigned on promises to keep Israelis safe, and he and his right-wing allies visited the scene of the incident to pledge an even harder line on Palestinian resistance.
Israeli forces were searching targets and questioning suspects to "locate and dismantle terrorist infrastructure" in the Hebron area from where they said the attackers had emerged, according to a joint statement from the Israeli military and Shin Bet domestic security agency.
Forces were also "demolishing illegal structures that could pose a security threat at the site of the encounter", they said, adding that "counterterrorism operations" were underway at dozens of locations.
Netanyahu threatened on Friday to collectively punish the neighbourhood from where the attackers came by demolishing it.
Palestinian group Hamas, without claiming responsibility, praised Friday's attack on two Israeli soldiers as a "heroic operation" and called on supporters to carry out more.
A Hebron-based AFP photographer heading to another assignment witnessed the gun battle break out at the Farsh al-Hawa checkpoint between the soldiers and two men armed with a handgun and an automatic rifle.
Israeli forces eventually shot dead the two Palestinians.
Netanyahu later ordered a lockdown in the occupied West Bank.
Visiting Hebron, the premier said he and Defence Minister Israel Katz were "considering a very extensive IDF operation in Judea and Samaria, such as has not been carried out since" the 1967 war.
The first step would see Israeli forces "enter the neighbourhood from which the terrorists came, evacuate the residents, go from house to house, and destroy the terrorist infrastructure", he said.
The military would apply a model previously used in refugee camps in the northern West Bank, he said, the scene of a large-scale assault in January 2025 that forcibly displaced thousands of Palestinians.
Israeli rights group B'Tselem called for urgent international pressure to prevent Israel from pursuing "plans for collective punishment and acts that could constitute war crimes".
UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres, through a spokesman, voiced concern over Israeli closures that affect Palestinian livelihoods and called for a halt to violence on all sides.
'Exactly like Gaza'
Far-right Israeli Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich, who also holds a position within the defence ministry, called for a large-scale military offensive in the West Bank "exactly like in Gaza".
He said authorities were "sending an unequivocal message to our enemies: if you mess with the Jews, you will pay a very painful price".
National Security Minister and far-right firebrand Itamar Ben Gvir said the Ramallah-based "Palestinian Authority must be dismantled".
"It is impossible for there to be an authority within Judea and Samaria that incites murder, calls for murder, and works for murder," he told reporters.
No evidence suggests that the Palestinian Authority, which exercises limited self-rule in parts of the West Bank, was connected to Friday's attack.
Both Ben Gvir and Smotrich are prominent advocates of illegal Israeli settlements in the West Bank, which have proliferated under Netanyahu's government.
Netanyahu vowed to "pursue Hamas terrorists" everywhere, adding: "You have no place to hide."
Israel vowed to obliterate the group in the wake of the 7 October attacks, later a war on Gaza that has killed over 74,000 Palestinians and been determined a genocide by UN experts and leading rights groups.
The army crackdown on the occupied West Bank comes as Israeli settlers, often under army protection, continue attacks against Palestinian olive harvesters.
According to an AFP tally based on data from the Palestinian health ministry, Israeli forces and settlers have killed 1,117 Palestinians in the territory since the start of the Gaza war in October 2023.

Seoul’s useless placation is a warning for all US trade partners
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
08:30:09 UTC
17:30:09 KST

Advertisement
Opinion
Seoul’s useless placation is a warning for all US trade partners
Clearly, appeasement doesn’t work and dependence just feeds leverage. Collective action is the only effective stand that states can take
3-MIN READ3-MIN
3
 Listen
Zhou Xiaoming is a senior fellow at the Centre for China and Globalisation in Beijing and a former deputy representative of China’s Permanent Mission to the United Nations Office in Geneva. 
The anxiety gripping Seoul is palpable. Under US pressure, South Korea signed a US$350 billion investment deal last November for a 10-percentage-point tariff reduction, billing it as a strategic alliance. Barely a year on, the facade has crumbled.
Last month, US President Donald Trump announced a US$200 billion tranche of the deal with no South Korean official present. Blindsided, Seoul restated its “commercial viability” clause. Trump’s response was blunt. “If they don’t want to do it, that’s OK with me. I’ll just charge them more,” he told reporters. “Tell them if they don’t sign shortly, I’m going to double it up.”
For South Korea, the numbers are sobering: US$350 billion represents 18 per cent of its annual gross domestic product. Even if much of it is channelled through loans, guarantees and corporate outlays, it risks upward pressure on the won, crowding out domestic investment and political exposure if projects underperform.

NASA’s FIRMS satellite service detected a thermal anomaly at the substation, which may indicate a fire.
Sevastopol, Simferopol, Yalta, Feodosia, Dzhankoi, Alushta, and Yevpatoria were left without power.

Interview: Xi's vision for global governance responds to changing world, says Tajik expert
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
16:10:41 CST
17:10:41 KST

DUSHANBE, Oct. 24 (Xinhua) -- The Global Governance Initiative (GGI) proposed by Chinese President Xi Jinping reflects the objective transformation of the world system and responds to the aspirations of most countries for a more just and equitable system of global governance, said Rahmon Ulmasov, a professor at the Russian-Tajik (Slavonic) University.
In a recent interview with Xinhua, Ulmasov described the initiative as one of China's most significant initiatives in recent years, saying it came at a time when the existing global governance system was facing serious challenges.
"Geopolitical conflicts, sanctions and trade wars are intensifying, while the gap between developed and developing countries is widening. At the same time, existing international institutions are becoming increasingly inadequate in addressing global problems," Ulmasov said.
Against this backdrop, he said, reforming and improving global governance has become increasingly important to ensure that international institutions can better respond to emerging challenges and reflect the interests and concerns of countries around the world.
Ulmasov noted that the GGI builds on China's previously proposed Global Development Initiative, Global Security Initiative and Global Civilization Initiative.
"Together, they form a coherent Chinese vision for international development, based on the interconnection between development, security, dialogue among civilizations and the improvement of global governance," he said.
He stressed that global governance should be based on equality among countries and decision-making through consultation, which is in line with the core principles of the GGI.
In his view, effective global governance also requires countries with different political systems, civilizational traditions and national interests to strengthen dialogue and seek common ground while respecting their differences.
"The ability to build cooperation despite differences is one of the most important elements of modern multilateral governance," Ulmasov added. ■

Yemen's Houthi group said it launched attacks on Saudi oil facilities and airports on Saturday, including a Saudi Aramco facility in Yanbu, the Rabigh oil refinery and King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh.
The group's military spokesperson, Yahya Saree, said it also targeted King Fahd International Airport in Dammam, Najran airport, and an air base in Khamis Mushait.
Saudi authorities did not immediately confirm the attack.
Iran's Pezeshkian blames US for interim deal failure,
Iranian President Massoud Pezeshkian, in remarks broadcast on state TV on Saturday, blamed the United States for the failure of an interim deal with Iran, but said there should be a new attempt at concluding it.
"We were having negotiations, the cowards (Americans) messed everything up...I still think we should go and conclude it," Pezeshkian said.
Iran remains open to talks with the US under a Pakistan-brokered interim deal reached in June to end the conflict, Tehran’s ambassador to Islamabad said Saturday, accusing Washington of undermining diplomacy and prolonging the standoff over the Strait of Hormuz.
Ambassador Reza Amiri Moghadam said Iran recently told Pakistan it was prepared to reopen the Strait of Hormuz if Washington lifted its naval blockade, but accused US President Donald Trump of rejecting the proposal and insisting the blockade of Iranian ports would continue.
Palestinian Authority calls for intl pressure on Israel
The Palestinian Authority called on Saturday for international pressure on Israel to protect Palestinians after some residents of the West Bank city of Hebron were displaced from their homes in response to an attack that killed Israeli soldiers.
Confronting "the growing threats to expand the scope of forced displacement and destruction requires urgent international action that goes beyond condemnation to adopt tangible and deterrent measures", the PA's foreign ministry said in a statement.
Yemen's Houthis claimed an attack on Saturday on a naval base and a military camp in Aden, the interim seat of the internationally recognised government, after blasts were heard there.
"Our armed forced targeted Saudi enemy concentrations at the so-called Al-Nasr camp and the naval base in Aden," Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree said, adding that the sites were overseen by Saudi forces.
Saudi strike kills five members of same family in Hodeida
Yemen's Iran-backed Houthis on Saturday said a Saudi strike on Hodeida killed five members of the same families, as both sides press attacks.
"Five people, the head of the family, two of his children and his two wives, have been martyred and his daughter wounded as a result of a Saudi enemy air strike on the home of citizen Abdulwahed al-Wasabi in the Al-Tuhayta district" of Hodeida, the Houthis' Al-Masirah TV channel reported.
Houthi media reported that Saudi strikes killed 11 people in Yemeni capital Sanaa on Saturday, shortly after the Saudi-led coalition fighting them said it had intercepted two missiles targeting Saudi cities.
The Houthis' Al-Masirah outlet reported a series of "Saudi enemy airstrikes" targeting Sanaa, including one on a house that killed at least four people and wounded several others.
A separate strike at a residence building for cement factory workers in the Sanaa governorate killed six women and one child and wounded three others, the broadcaster said.
Two people wounded in Friday's attack on a church in southern Jordan have died of their injuries, bringing the number of people killed to nine, health minister Ibrahim al-Bdour told AFP on Saturday.
"The number of victims who died in the terrorist attack on the church in the village of Al-Hamoud in Karak has risen to nine following the death on Saturday of a second casualty who had been in a critical condition," the minister said.
The Israeli military forced around 1,200 Palestinians to leave their homes in Hebron in the occupied West Bank, a Palestinian official said on Saturday, a day after a Palestinian attack killed two Israeli soldiers.
Yousef Zouhair Al-Jabari, the head of Hebron's municipality, said around 1,300 faced losing their homes in addition to the 1,200 already displaced.
He also said the Israeli operations were motivated by parliamentary elections on Tuesday, when Netanyahu's right-wing coalition may lose its majority, opinion polls show.
Jordan's king orders security forces to respond firmly to
Jordan's King Abdullah chaired a security meeting on Saturday and ordered security forces to respond firmly and pursue those behind a church attack in Karak Governorate that killed and wounded civilians, the royal court said.
A person wounded in Friday's attack on a church in southern Jordan has died of their injuries, bringing the number of people killed to eight, Health Minister Ibrahim al-Bdour told AFP on Saturday.
"The number of victims who died in the attack on the church in the village of Hammoud in Karak has risen to eight following the death of one of the injured who was in critical condition," the minister said.
Another 26 people remain hospitalised, including one in critical condition, he said.
Gunmen stormed the compound of a Greek Orthodox church in the village of Hammoud in Karak governorate during a funeral procession on Friday and opened fire, Jordanian authorities said.
"A terrorist group has carried out a horrific act, one that is condemned in every respect, and the security services are working round the clock to track them down," Interior Minister Mazen al-Faraya told a press conference.
Turkey's foreign minister will tell his Yemeni counterpart on Saturday that Houthi attacks on civilians are "unacceptable" and express hope the conflict can be resolved through dialogue, a Turkish foreign ministry source said.
Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan is due to meet Yemen's Afrah al-Zouba in Istanbul, a day after hosting talks with senior European and regional diplomats.
The Houthis have been at war since 2014 with Yemen's internationally recognised government.
Following an uneasy four-year truce, fighting reignited in July, months into the US-Iran conflict that has plunged the wider region into crisis.
Iranian President Massoud Pezeshkian will meet his Russian counterpart Vladimir Putin in Moscow next week, Iranian media reported.
Pezeshkian is due to visit Russia for a meeting of gas-exporting countries.
Russia and Iran, two of the most sanctioned nations on earth, have grown closer together in the years since Moscow launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.
"The Iranian president will visit Moscow to attend the summit of gas-exporting countries that will take place on Tuesday, October 27," the Tasnim news agency reported, citing Tehran's ambassador to the country, Kazem Jalali.
The two leaders will discuss economic cooperation as well as "questions of geopolitics", Jalali was quoted as saying.
Saudi-led coalition says it destroyed Houthi missiles
A Saudi-led coalition fighting Yemen's Houthis said it destroyed two ballistic missiles firedby the Iran-aligned group towards Taif and Yanbu on Saturday, as fighting between the sides continued.
Saudi Arabia's Civil Defence briefly issued alerts on Saturday warning of potential danger in Taif and Yanbu, as well as the holy city of Mecca and its second-largest city, Jeddah.
The service issued notices around 10 minutes later saying the danger had passed.
Saudi civil defence issues 'potential danger' warning
Saudi Arabia's civil defence agency broadcast warnings of "potential danger" for four of its western provinces, including that of Mecca, home to Islam's holiest city, on Friday, without saying why.
The alerts, which also covered the major Red Sea city of Jeddah, nearby Taif and the coastal oil hub of Yanbu, were all rescinded minutes later.
Residents were instructed to "proceed to the nearest safe place" by the agency. The agency also repeated a legal warning against sharing images or information related to "countering missiles and drones".
Netanyahu says Palestinian Authority in for 'big surprise'
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said that the Palestinian Authority was in for a "big surprise" after he ordered a major military operation in response to an attack on soldiers in the West Bank.
Netanyahu, days ahead of elections, declined to answer directly when he was asked if he would dismantle the Palestinian Authority but said he favoured "ruse and surprise".
"We transformed the Middle East. I said that we would change things and we have," Netanyahu told i24News in an interview conducted late Friday.
"There is a very big surprise for the Palestinian Authority as well."
The Saudi-led coalition fighting Yemen's Houthis said on Saturday it had intercepted a ballistic missile launched towards Riyadh by the Iran-backed group.
Two explosions rang out in Riyadh early Saturday, an AFP journalist in the Saudi capital said, as the Houthis keep up strikes on the kingdom.
An early warning system was activated to alert residents to a potential threat, the Saudi civil defence said.
"Air defences intercepted and destroyed a ballistic missile launched by the Houthi terrorist militia toward Riyadh," coalition spokesman Turki al-Malki posted on X.
Iran said on Saturday that US military ships would never be allowed to enter the Gulf "under any circumstances" and that President Donald Trump would "take that dream to his grave".
The remarks came amid mounting US and Israeli threats of renewed attacks on Iran, as US ambassador to Turkey Tom Barrack warned that Washington could "absolutely" strike Iran as soon as this weakened.
"We will not allow US military ships in the Persian Gulf under any circumstances and at any time," said Iran's armed forces chief of staff Ali Abdollahi, according to Iranian state television.
"The US president must dream of seeing the armed forces enter the Persian Gulf. He will take that dream to his grave."

Monitoring systems at the Ministry of Defense have recorded the restoration of Starlink/Starshield performance at high speeds, Ukrainian Defense Minister Yevheniy Khmara reported.
"We are recording speeds of over 400 km/h; the connection is stable. This is yet another example of how direct dialogue and the persistent stance taken by the President of Ukraine at the highest level yield results. And this result is, above all, vital for our front line, for our military personnel, for the operation of drones, and for logistics and communications," Khmara commented in response to journalists' questions on Saturday.
He emphasized that the Ministry of Defense continues to monitor and document the performance of Starlink/Starshield.
Earlier on Saturday, sources within the Ministry of Defense told Interfax-Ukraine that the Ukrainian Defense Forces and the Ministry of Defense had observed the restoration of Starlink/Starshield connectivity at speeds exceeding 161 km/h.
According to the Ministry of Defense sources, as of the morning of October 24, Starlink/Starshield was confirmed to be operational at speeds above 161 km/h. The agency continues to monitor its performance, conduct tests at higher speeds, determine upper limits, and assess the full extent to which the service has been restored.

Sonia Gandhi makes X debut, recalls first meeting with Rajiv Gandhi ahead of book launch
NEW DELHI: Congress Parliamentary Party chairperson Sonia Gandhi made her debut on social media platform X on Saturday, sharing a video in which she recalled her first meeting with former Prime Minister Rajiv Gandhi and offered a glimpse of her upcoming book, Belonging: A Journey of Love.The book, Sonia Gandhi's first, is scheduled to be launched on November 10. It recounts her personal journey, including her memories with Rajiv Gandhi and experiences from her younger days to the present.
In the nearly two-minute video accompanying her first post on X, Sonia Gandhi recalled meeting Rajiv Gandhi at the Varsity Restaurant, a Greek eatery in Cambridge, England, where they were students.The video featured photographs of the couple and the restaurant where they first met.
"In a small Greek restaurant in Cambridge, my journey of love began. Rajiv and I created a world filled with love, laughter and memories. On 10th November, I share that world with you," she wrote in her post.
Sonia Gandhi recalls meeting Rajiv Gandhi in Cambridge
Speaking in the video, the Congress MP recalled looking for Italian food while living in England, where she said the food available at the time did not suit her preferences."Food in England in those days was awful. In those days, you didn't have so many restaurants, you know, like you have today," she said.
She explained that she was looking for a place serving food closer to what she was accustomed to, particularly Italian cuisine, when she discovered the Greek restaurant."And then, we discovered this place (Varsity Restaurant). It was a Greek restaurant where many European students, but also Indian students, used to go for their meals. And, of course, I learned that it was the same for him," she said.Sonia Gandhi also recalled that a common friend introduced them. Then, you know, we became friends. Then going to parties with friends, or going to see sights, or… We went to a Valentine party where there were lots of students," she said.Describing what stood out to her about Rajiv Gandhi, she said his gentle nature had left a lasting impression."He was a very gentle-looking person. Of course, he was very good-looking. But that gentleness came through. So that was something which really touched me and struck me. So that, of course, I'll never forget when I first met him," she said.Sonia married Rajiv Gandhi on February 25, 1968.

Most defence tech firms report a declining market
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
09:00:52 BST
17:00:52 KST

Seventy-three per cent of defence-oriented technology firms surveyed said the market had declined, eighty-seven per cent had been hit by funding delays and reductions, and ninety-three per cent were reassessing investment or recruitment in the sector, according to evidence given to the Defence Committee.
Julian David, chief executive of techUK, was giving evidence on the implications of the Defence Investment Plan for British industry.
He said: “Last time we were here, we reported on our survey of members, and 73% said that the market has declined; that was in May. Funding delays and reductions have hit 87% of respondents, and 93% of them are now reassessing investment or recruitment of people to focus in this sector.”
David said members had expected the opposite when the plan was published, telling the committee: “From a tech point of view, defence-oriented tech members expected, therefore, that there would be a big uptick in the focus on tech and that orders would flow, particularly to SMEs. We have not found that to be the case.” He added that techUK had checked again with members since the survey and “they have not really seen a lot of progress.”
On the effect on smaller firms he said: “The problem, particularly from an SME point of view, is that they live off the cash flow. If there is no cash flow or no predictable path to cash, they are going to either try to find markets elsewhere or cut back and wait and see.”
David also raised departmental staffing, saying: “I would highlight the fact that, in terms of delivery, the MOD is still not properly staffed in order to deal with procurement, particularly of new things and from smaller companies. Sometimes that is disguised, in that one commercial team’s headcount is 70%, with a gap of 30%, but 40% of the team is filled by contractors who cannot fulfil the whole process of sign-off authority.”
Arnab Dutt of the Federation of Small Businesses gave figures from his own organisation’s research, telling MPs that only thirteen per cent of small businesses use pipeline documentation to find public opportunities, against twenty-eight per cent who use active procurement platforms, and that sixty-two per cent of small businesses looking for public sector contracts report that finding suitable opportunities is difficult.
Dutt said: “Another awful piece of research is that 19% of companies that have already engaged with the MOD said that they will not be doing so again because of the systemic barriers and the level of hard work and engagement. Among that 19%, there could be some brilliant businesses, so that is another issue.”
He told the committee that the Federation had received minimal consultation on the plan, describing it as the organisation’s main bugbear since publication.
David told MPs that of £7.5 billion of small and medium-sized enterprise spend by May 2028, only £2 billion is direct and £5.5 billion indirect, and that the department tracks progress without committing or delivering. He said what is needed is targets and performance indicators for the people doing the procurement, measured as they go, “as opposed to waiting until the end of 2028 and then asking whether it happened.”
He also raised the departmental definition of a small or medium-sized enterprise, which differs from the one in the Procurement Act and the fair payment code, meaning firms used to reporting one way now have to report another.

Spain tests new anti-drone systems at army exercise
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
07:58:40 UTC
16:58:40 KST

- EM&E Group used remote weapon stations on 4x4 and 6x6 vehicles and a jamming robot to down drones at Spain’s ATLAS 26 exercise.
- The systems were shown as configurations of ARACNE, the counter-drone system EM&E is developing with Indra for the Spanish Armed Forces.
Spanish defense company EM&E Group used remote weapon stations on armored vehicles and a jamming-equipped ground robot to detect and shoot down several drones during the Spanish military’s ATLAS 26 counter-drone exercise this week at the Médano del Loro firing range in Huelva, in southwestern Spain.
The exercise was led by Spain’s Chief of the Defence Staff, organized by the Maneuver Support Command and directed by the Spanish Army’s Anti-Aircraft Artillery Command. EM&E, formerly known as Escribano Mechanical & Engineering, said it took part with several configurations of ARACNE, the counter-drone system it is developing with Indra Group through a joint venture.
Two 4×4 tactical vehicles took part fitted with EM&E’s GUARDIAN 2.0 remote weapon station as a hard-kill option, meaning they physically destroy drones with gunfire instead of disrupting them electronically. The company also fielded its FEROX 6×6 armored vehicle carrying the GUARDIAN L-HIT remote station, which it uses to both detect and engage drones, and deployed its AUNAV LINK robotic vehicle with an integrated electronic warfare package that jams the radio links between a drone and its operator to block or distort its communications.
EM&E said the systems detected and shot down several drones during the exercise, without giving numbers or details of the targets.
ARACNE is one of the Spanish Armed Forces’ main counter-drone programs. The roughly 30.24 million euro ($34 million) effort covers 14 systems for the military, seven fixed and seven mobile, intended to protect critical infrastructure and military convoys, with mobile versions mounted on Vamtac ST5 tactical vehicles. The system pairs Indra’s sensors and command software with EM&E hardware, including a SmartEar radio-frequency scanner that monitors frequencies from 400 MHz to 6 GHz within about 6 km (3.7 miles) and an EM&E electro-optical station that can spot targets more than 14 km (8.7 miles) away with its daylight camera and up to 23.1 km (14.4 miles) with its thermal channel.
Indra and EM&E also demonstrated ARACNE at last year’s ATLAS 25 exercise, held at the same Huelva range from Oct. 20 to 24, 2025, where Indra said the system’s command and control software stood out for its ability to combine data from its own sensors and third-party sensors. A counter-drone system that Indra continues to develop under the ARACNE project also protects the Spanish contingent deployed with NATO in Lithuania, and Indra said in March 2026 that it had drawn interest from several countries on the alliance’s eastern flank.
The ATLAS exercises bring together Spanish military units and industry to test systems for detecting, identifying and defeating drones, and EM&E’s demonstrations this year added ground robotics and electronic warfare to the gun-based options shown on its vehicles.

Russian-Indian BrahMos missile is getting future-ready
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
07:47:51 UTC
16:47:51 KST

Russian-Indian BrahMos missile is getting future-ready
The BrahMos corporation is working to add more destructive power and reach to its namesake supersonic cruise missile, following its spectacular combat successes last year.
The operational and functional parameters of the missile are being upgraded, and new versions are in the works, the CEO and managing director of the joint venture between India and Russia, Jaiteerth Joshi, told local media recently.
Named after the Brahmaputra and Moskva rivers, the BrahMos is engineered for high-precision, long-range strikes. The missile offers militaries the versatility to engage threats using land, sea, and underwater platforms.
BrahMos earned its stripes last year when the Indian and Pakistani militaries briefly clashed with missiles and drones, following a terrorist attack on civilians in India’s Jammu and Kashmir state.
As the two militaries tested each other with drones, India fired BrahMos missiles to strike hardened high-value targets, including hangars reportedly housing Pakistan’s US-made F-16 fighter jets.
India has said there was not a single interception of the BrahMos during the clashes, dubbed Operation Sindoor, and buyer interest has risen since.
BrahMos Aerospace is a joint venture between India’s DRDO and Russia’s NPO Mashinostroyeniya.
BrahMos’ trajectory into the future
BrahMos started as a land-launched cruise missile, but its developers have worked to give it more flexibility and lethality as battlefield needs evolved and expanded.
The missile, which flies at nearly three times the speed of sound and carries a 200 to 300 kg warhead, had an initial range of 290 km but continuous upgrades have extended its reach.
In 2023, the Indian Air Force (IAF) successfully tested a version with a 450 km range. Mated to the Su-30MKI fighter, this variant, called the BrahMos-A, offers the IAF a standoff precision strike capability that few air forces in the world can match.
There is also a Block III land-attack variant, which can fly very low and approach targets from unexpected angles – dodging any defenses the enemy may try to throw at it.
The BrahMos corporation is working on a long and ambitious list of upgrades. At the top of the current development efforts sits a lighter, air-launched variant.
Christened the BrahMos-NG, it can be flown on the IAF’s other fighter jets, including the domestically produced Tejas light combat aircraft. The Su-30MKI will be able to sortie armed with three of these missiles.
The BrahMos-NG will feature higher domestically-produced content and advanced materials. The Indo-Russian joint venture expects to unveil this prototype by 2027-28.
The BrahMos corporation is also working on a very long-range missile. This version would be able to strike targets up to 1,500 km away, far more than the 290 km range of the original missile unveiled in the early 2000s.
This long-range version is at the conceptual stage, and the company is discussing further upgrades with its Russian joint venture partner. Joshi has told Indian media outlets in recent interviews that the range-extension program will proceed in phases, with test firings from land, sea, and air to validate the missile’s operational capabilities.
Also, on the missile maker’s drawing board is a hypersonic version – the new frontier of modern warfare – currently called BrahMos II.
The concept aims to integrate advanced technologies, state-of-the-art design, and smart materials to field a hypersonic futuristic weapon that will dominate fast-evolving battlefield technology.
BrahMos II will have an “air-breathing” scramjet engine that would boost it to a top speed of Mach 5.
BrahMos is seeing high global interest
The missile has already been sold to multiple countries, and many others have shown an interest in buying it.
One of the first foreign customers of the Indo-Russian missile was the Philippines, with Manila signing a $375 million contract in 2022. The first batch of BrahMos missiles was delivered to the country in April 2024, and the second in April 2025.
In June this year, India confirmed it had a deal with Vietnam to supply the missiles.
Indonesia, which has also evinced interest, has moved forward with procurement plans.
In addition, over a dozen nations including Malaysia, the UAE, Saudi Arabia, Egypt, Chile, and South Africa have evaluated or expressed a formal interest in the BrahMos missile system.
BrahMos is gearing up for a demand surge
The BrahMos project is a trailblazer in India’s defense industry. It broke the shackles of excessive bureaucratic controls that were once the hallmark of Indian state-owned defense corporations that had forced the country to remain a major arms importer.
Effective management and the synergizing of commercial viability, strike capabilities, and indigenization have helped the missile become the battlefield success it is, whie making inroads into the global arms market.
With a burgeoning order book, BrahMos corporation is prioritizing the fulfillment of orders received from the Indian armed forces, for whom the missile is a primary strike weapon. India recently contracted for more BrahMos launchers and fire-control systems, so more of its warships can be armed with the missile.
The missile maker now has production facilities in four Indian cities: Hyderabad, Nagpur, Pilani and Lucknow. Research and development clusters, nicknamed ‘tech-bricks’ have been set up to work on niche technologies for the next generation missiles.
The supply chain is being expanded to make it more robust and resilient – and to meet an expected surge in demand. For this, the company will expand the industry partners for each system and subsystem to up to 45, from the current one or two partners.
India’s arms export ambitions ride on BrahMos
New Delhi is gradually setting its sights to make a complete transformation from being one of the biggest arms importers to a major defense exporter.
It also simultaneously wants to see more domestically produced components and technology being used in its products. Indian defense exports registered an impressive 67% annual growth to reach $4 billion in the financial year ended March.
The federal government’s annual defense production target is $31 billion by 2029, of which defense exports are pegged at $5.5 billion.
BrahMos will be key to New Delhi’s ambitious goals to emerge as a major global arms exporter.
