What Does Bulgaria's President Actually Do?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
06:30:00 UTC
15:30:00 KST

Prices Keep Bulgaria’s Public Tension High Despite Gradual Decline
Bulgaria’s Public Tension Index edged down to 6.10 points in the third quarter of 2026 from 6.22 in the previous quarter, continuing its decline at a slower pace
On Sunday, Bulgarians will choose a head of state for a five-year term beginning in January 2027 and most of them will do it knowing that the person they elect will not run the country. Bulgaria is a parliamentary republic. The prime minister and the Council of Ministers set policy, parliament passes the laws, and the president has no right to propose legislation, no seat in the cabinet and no say over the budget beyond a veto that 121 of the 240 MPs can override.
That makes the office sound weaker than it is. The president is the one official every adult Bulgarian votes for directly, commands the armed forces, represents the country abroad, decides when an election is called and, at moments of political deadlock, picks the people who run the state while parliament cannot. Over the past five years of snap elections those moments became routine, and the presidency grew into one of the most consequential institutions in the country, which is exactly why parliament moved in 2023 to cut it back.
Bulgaria had no president for most of its modern history. From 1879 the head of state was a prince (knyaz), and from 1908 a tsar, until a referendum on September 8, 1946, abolished the monarchy and opened the way for the People's Republic. Under communism the role passed to a collective body, first the Presidium of the National Assembly and from 1971 the State Council, which Todor Zhivkov chaired until his removal in November 1989.
The modern presidency was born in the turbulence that followed. In April 1990 parliament made Petar Mladenov, Zhivkov's successor at the head of the State Council, the country's first president. He lasted three months, resigning in July after a recording surfaced in which he was heard telling colleagues during a December 1989 protest that it would be better if "the tanks came." The Grand National Assembly then elected dissident philosopher Zhelyu Zhelev in August 1990, and the constitution it adopted on July 12, 1991, turned the presidency into a directly elected office. Zhelev won the first popular vote in January 1992.
Since then the office has been held by Petar Stoyanov (1997–2002), Georgi Parvanov (2002–2012, the only president so far to serve two full terms), Rosen Plevneliev (2012–2017) and Rumen Radev (2017–2026). When Radev resigned in January 2026 to found Progressive Bulgaria and run for parliament, Vice President Iliana Yotova became the first woman and the first vice president to take over the office, serving out the remainder of his term. The presidency sits at 2 Dondukov Boulevard in central Sofia, which is why Bulgarians use the address as shorthand for the institution.
Further reading: Tanks, Mandates and Caretakers: The Story of Bulgaria’s Presidency Since 1990
The constitution sets four conditions. A candidate must be a Bulgarian citizen by birth, be at least 40 years old, meet the requirements for election to parliament and have lived in Bulgaria for the previous five years. The term is five years, and a president can be elected only twice, consecutively or not. Once in office, the president cannot sit in parliament, hold any other state, public or business post or serve in a party's leadership.
President and vice president are elected together on a single ticket. To win in the first round a ticket needs more than half the valid votes with turnout above 50 percent. If either condition is missed, the top two tickets go to a runoff a week later, where the higher vote wins regardless of turnout. No Bulgarian president has ever been elected in the first round, and with turnout this year expected below 40 percent, the November 1 runoff is all but certain.
The vice president has no independent powers of their own. The office exercises whatever authority the president delegates by decree, in practice the handling of pardons, citizenship and asylum, and steps in if the presidency falls vacant, completing the term. If both offices are empty at once, the Speaker of parliament acts as head of state until a new election, which must be held within two months.
The president's main tool against parliament is the right to return a law for reconsideration before signing it. The veto can be used only once per law, and the National Assembly overrides it by passing the text again with the votes of more than half of all MPs, 121 of 240, after which the president must promulgate it. Against a government with a stable majority, such as Progressive Bulgaria's 131 seats today, a veto delays a law and forces a public debate, but it rarely stops one.
The stronger instrument is the Constitutional Court. The president is one of the few institutions that can ask the court to strike down a law or to give a binding interpretation of the constitution, and also appoints four of its twelve judges. The president can also formally propose constitutional amendments, although parliament decides on them.
Most presidential decisions take the form of decrees, and most decrees must be countersigned by the prime minister or the relevant minister, which keeps the government in the loop on appointments, awards and similar acts. The exceptions are the ones that matter politically: scheduling elections, dissolving parliament, returning laws, handing out mandates to form a government and appointing a caretaker cabinet all happen on the president's signature alone.
Those mandates are where the office becomes central in a fragmented parliament. After an election the president hands the first mandate to form a cabinet to the largest parliamentary group and, if that fails, the second to the next largest. The third mandate goes to any group of the president's choosing, a real discretion that has decided governments in the past. If all three fail, the president dissolves parliament, schedules a snap election and appoints a caretaker government to run the country until a new parliament elects a cabinet. Bulgaria has had a dozen caretaker governments since 1990, seven of them in the last five years.
The president is supreme commander-in-chief of the armed forces and chairs the Consultative Council for National Security, which brings together the government, parliamentary leaders, the military and the security services. The council has no executive power, but convening it is a political signal. The president appoints and dismisses the senior military command and confers the highest ranks, though only on the government's proposal, and the constitution allows the head of state to declare war or martial law when parliament is not sitting, subject to its later approval.
Abroad, the president represents Bulgaria, receives the credentials of foreign ambassadors and, on the government's proposal, appoints and recalls Bulgaria's own heads of mission. Foreign policy itself belongs to the cabinet, and the president usually does not represent the country at European Council summits, where the prime minister sits.
The president also signs the decrees that appoint several of the state's most powerful officials once other bodies have chosen them, including the prosecutor general and the heads of the two supreme courts. The president may send a nomination back once, but a repeated proposal must be signed.
Some of the presidency's most sensitive work happens far from the headlines. The president grants, restores and revokes Bulgarian citizenship, grants asylum, pardons convicted criminals and can write off uncollectable debts to the state. By long tradition these powers are delegated by decree to the vice president. A presidential commission reviews the requests, but its members have been kept anonymous, and the motives behind individual pardons are not routinely published, which is why critics are now calling for the process to be opened up.
The president also awards state orders and decorations, renames towns and villages, schedules local elections and national referendums once parliament has approved them and addresses the nation on New Year's Eve.
While in office, the president and vice president cannot be detained or criminally prosecuted, and they bear no liability for acts performed in the course of their duties, with two exceptions. They can be removed for high treason or for violating the constitution. An impeachment motion needs the signatures of at least a quarter of MPs and must then be approved by more than two-thirds of the National Assembly, 161 votes, before the case goes to the Constitutional Court, which has one month to rule. If the court finds the president guilty, the mandate ends.
The bar is high enough that it has never been cleared. The nationalist Ataka party tried to start proceedings against Rosen Plevneliev in 2013 after he backed early elections during that year's protests, but it could not even gather the support to put the motion on the agenda. A president can otherwise leave office early only through death, a permanent illness that prevents the work, or resignation, which must be submitted before the Constitutional Court.
For most of the post-communist era the caretaker power was a formality, used briefly between elections. That changed after 2021, when Bulgaria entered a cycle of eight parliamentary elections in five years. Each failed parliament left Radev to appoint another caretaker cabinet, and the governments of Stefan Yanev and Galab Donev, both men ran the country for long stretches, signing off on energy contracts, defense decisions and the handling of the war in Ukraine without any parliamentary majority behind them. Critics argued that the president had effectively become the head of the executive.
Parliament answered on December 20, 2023, when GERB, We Continue the Change, Democratic Bulgaria and the Movement for Rights and Freedoms passed the sixth amendment to the 1991 constitution. Alongside a large judicial reform, it took away the president's free choice of caretaker prime minister. The president must now pick from a short list of officials: the Speaker of parliament, the governor or a deputy governor of the Bulgarian National Bank, the chair or a deputy chair of the National Audit Office, or the Ombudsman or a deputy. The list was quickly nicknamed the "house book," after the old apartment-building ledgers where residents were recorded.
The Constitutional Court struck down most of the 2023 package in July 2024, including the judicial changes, but split six to six on the caretaker provisions, so they survived. A second challenge brought by Radev and two groups of MPs failed in July 2025 for the same reason, when only six of the twelve judges, one short of the required seven, found the rules unconstitutional. The practical effect has been visible since. In 2024 Radev had to appoint Audit Office chair Dimitar Glavchev, a long-time GERB figure. In February 2026 Yotova said ten eligible officials had turned her down before Andrey Gyurov, then a suspended BNB deputy governor, accepted, and complained that the amendments had left the presidency without a real choice.
The politics have since turned upside down. Radev, now prime minister with a majority of his own, announced on August 24 that his government will propose restoring the president's free hand over caretaker cabinets, arguing that "when the President's hands are tied, the procedure almost came to a standstill." No text has been tabled yet. If the change goes through, it would hand back the power to the president.
This article is part of Novinite's editorial series on Bulgaria's October 25 presidential election. It was not commissioned or paid for by any candidate, party or initiative committee, and it does not endorse anyone.

Powerful M7.2 earthquake strikes off Vanuatu’s Espiritu Santo coast
A magnitude 7.2 earthquake struck off the western coast of Espiritu Santo island, Vanuatu, in the Pacific Ocean early Saturday, Qazinform News Agency reports, citing the Kazakhstan National Data Center.
The earthquake occurred at 7:31 a.m. Astana time (02:31 UTC) at a depth of 10 kilometers (6 miles), according to the Institute of Geophysical Research of the National Nuclear Center of Kazakhstan.
Seismologists located the epicenter at 14.05 S, 165.52 E, recording body-wave magnitude mb=7.0.
As Xinhua reported, the quake prompted the Pacific Tsunami Warning Center to issue a tsunami warning.
No casualties or property damage have been reported so far.
On Saturday, a 7.0-magnitude earthquake struck Baqen County in Nagqu City, southwest China’s Xizang Autonomous Region, killing 16 people and injuring 46 others.

Permanent secretary pressed five times on backloading
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
07:00:43 BST
15:00:43 KST

The Permanent Secretary at the Ministry of Defence was asked five times by a member of the Defence Committee whether the Defence Investment Plan settlement is backloaded, telling MPs at one point that he was not sure he understood the definition and finally that there was not more he could give the committee.
Jeremy Pocklington was giving evidence alongside Wes Streeting, the Secretary of State for Defence.
Derek Twigg, the Labour member for Widnes and Halewood, put it to Streeting that John Healey’s resignation letter had said the funding settlement was insufficient, and that the extra support was backloaded when the pressure of operations and the imperative to speed up readiness falls in the first two years.
Streeting said extra funding was won by Dan Jarvis during the Defence Investment Plan process and brought in the Permanent Secretary, who had been party to those discussions.
Twigg asked: “Is it backloaded or not?” Pocklington began: “Additional resource DEL was given to the Department between the time of John Healey’s resignation and Dan Jarvis settling the DIP.”
Twigg interrupted to say he wanted a straight answer for the committee and repeated the question. Pocklington said: “The overall departmental spending is on a rising profile, so by the end of this Parliament it will be 27% higher in real terms than at the start.”
The chair, Tan Dhesi, intervened twice to ask for an answer, and Pocklington said: “I am keen to help the Committee. I can read out what our spending totals are for each year.” Asked again, he said: “I am not sure I understand the definition.”
He then said: “We received additional support between the time between the time of John Healey’s resignation and Dan Jarvis that meant that the spending power of the Department has actually increased by £15 billion. It was a lower amount at the time that John Healey resigned. We do have additional support, including, in particular, additional support for RDEL for readiness.”
Asked a final time whether he agreed with the previous Secretary of State on the point, Pocklington said: “I think the settlement had changed. There is not more that I can give to the Committee.”
On the trajectory of spending, Streeting told the committee that defence spending was 2.3 per cent of national income when Labour came to office and will be 2.7 per cent in 2027-28, and that the Chancellor has said he will plug a £4.7 billion gap at the Budget with more to come at the spending review.
Twigg pressed him on whether there is any commitment to reach three per cent by 2030. Streeting said: “But we would not normally, and we do not normally, set out ahead of spending reviews what the control totals will be.”
Dhesi told him: “It seems palpable to many of us that we are not meeting the moment, and that is why there is a sense of exasperation.” He noted the committee had visited Denmark, which has gone from spending 1.3 per cent of national income on defence to 4.99 per cent within four years.
Streeting said: “And in those cases, Chair, look at the cost of borrowing in those countries. We are not comparing like with like.” He said the debt-to-GDP ratio is around a hundred per cent and that roughly one in every ten taxpayer pounds goes on servicing debt interest.

How Ukrainians in US advocate for Ukraine’s interests
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
09:00:00 EEST
15:00:00 KST

How Ukrainians in US advocate for Ukraine's interests
For decades, the Ukrainian community in the U.S. has been working to ensure that relations between Ukraine and the U.S. remain strong and that Ukraine has reliable partners in Washington.
The Ukrainian Congress Committee of America (UCCA), a nonpartisan organization of Ukrainian Americans, has represented the community's interests since 1940. Our position does not depend on which party is in power; our mission is to defend Ukraine's interests. In our work and communications, we consistently explain to the American public that supporting Ukrainian sovereignty is important for America itself.
One focus of our advocacy is increasing economic pressure on Russia. As part of this effort, we have supported legislative initiatives by Senators Lindsey Graham and Richard Blumenthal to strengthen sanctions against the Kremlin.
The latest decisions by U.S. President Donald Trump's administration – in particular, regarding the return of Russian diesel fuel to the global market and the easing of sanctions against Russia – contradict our position on the need to increase economic pressure on the Kremlin, as they provide Russia with additional resources to continue the war.
While the U.S. Administration might couch the rationale for the diesel deal to 'lower fuel prices' for American consumers, the easing of sanctions should be evaluated in light of their consequences. A decision that claims to offer only minor benefits for U.S. citizens but simultaneously increases Russia's revenues – which it uses to finance the war – runs counter to the long-term security interests of the U.S., and most importantly to worldwide democratic values and principles.
Similarly, we disagree with the U.S. government's criticism of Ukrainian strikes on Russian oil infrastructure as an argument in favor of making concessions to the Kremlin. Ukraine is defending itself against a state that launched a full-scale invasion on Feb. 24, 2022, and still shows no willingness to end its aggression. Unilateral concessions by partners do not, in and of themselves, guarantee peace.
Moreover, the experience of recent years shows that Vladimir Putin is not seeking a compromise for the sake of a just peace, but rather the opportunity to continue the war on terms favorable to himself. Therefore, in its communications with the American audience, the UCCA strives to clearly explain Russia's true intentions and outline the real mechanisms for deterring the aggressor.
At the same time, we see that concerns about such decisions are shared not only by Democrats but also by Republicans in Congress. This is important because support for Ukraine must not become a pawn in intra-party struggles.
Not just protests
When talking about the influence of the Ukrainian community in the U.S., it is important to understand the unique characteristics of the American political system. American democracy has its own mechanisms for influencing the government, and mass street protests are just one of them. They can draw attention to an issue, but they do not guarantee a change in political course.
Large-scale demonstrations on various domestic and foreign policy issues take place regularly in the U.S.. However, our experience shows that if we want to achieve concrete results for Ukraine, we must work simultaneously on many levels – in Congress, in the media, with civil society organizations, business representatives, and various ethnic communities.
The UCCA's activities are not limited to public events; we also maintain regular contact with members of the House of Representatives and the Senate, convey our position to political circles in both parties, collaborate with journalists, and strive to ensure that Ukrainian issues remain on the American public agenda.
We have developed partnerships with other communities, including Polish, Baltic, Georgian, Jewish, and Cuban. For example, in 1994, the UCCA was instrumental in founding the Central and East European Coalition (CEEC), which unites the concerns of over 20 million Americans citizens of Central and East European descent. Many of them have their own historical reasons to take a close interest in Russian aggression, authoritarianism, and international security issues. Working together helps us better explain to the American public why supporting Ukraine is in the interests not only of Ukrainians, but also of the U.S. and its allies.
We also work with business leaders. When influential businesspeople publicly support decisions that could weaken Ukraine's ability to defend itself, it is important for Americans to understand the consequences of such decisions, especially in bringing attention to the American businesses that have been targeted by Russian attacks in Ukraine since Feb. 24, 2022. We view public communication and peaceful protests near commercial facilities as one way to draw attention to the responsibility businesses have for their influence on societal processes.
Our task is not simply to express disagreement, but to convey our arguments to as broad an audience as possible and to translate public support for Ukraine into concrete policy decisions.
We see a basis for this work. According to the sociological studies on which we rely, the majority of Americans supports aid to Ukraine and views Russia as an existential threat to American interests. At the same time, this support cannot be taken for granted – it must be constantly reinforced by explaining to Americans what is at stake.
Strength lies in unity
The Ukrainian community in the U.S. is not homogeneous; among Ukrainian Americans, there are supporters of both Democrats and Republicans, representatives of different generations of immigrants, and people with diverse experiences and views on US domestic policy.
From the very beginning, the UCCA has been an organization that unites the community around shared national interests, rather than party affiliation. We have contacts with people who have worked in both Republican and Democratic administrations, and we collaborate with representatives of both parties. This allows us to convey the Ukrainian position to various political circles, regardless of who is in the White House or leading Congress.
The diversity of our community is not a weakness but a strength. It enables us to speak to different audiences in the language of their values and interests. For some, the main argument is the defense of democracy; for others, it is national security; and for still others, it is the need to prevent aggressive authoritarian regimes from changing international borders by force.
Ukrainians who arrived in the U.S. after the start of the full-scale invasion deserve special attention. The issue of their future and immigration status remains critical, and we are working with our partners in Congress and other government officials to advocate for their interests.
At the same time, their contribution to supporting Ukraine is already extremely significant. The Ukrainian community in America is raising funds, organizing humanitarian aid shipments, and assisting hospitals and the civilian population. Since the start of the full-scale war, tens and hundreds of millions of dollars in aid have been sent to Ukraine through various community initiatives and charitable projects.
Not everyone can attend a demonstration or speak out publicly against a particular political decision. But helping Ukraine takes many forms, and each one is important. Our goal is to create opportunities for everyone who wants to get involved, regardless of their background, political beliefs, or life circumstances.
One area of our work is direct humanitarian support for Ukraine. I recently joined the Ukraine Focus mission to deliver ambulances that were collected in Europe and transported to Ukraine. This time, there were about fifty vehicles intended for the needs of Ukraine's territorial defense forces and other units requiring medical transport.
Another important area is political advocacy. As early as 2000, the UCCA launched Ukrainian Days in Washington so that representatives of Ukrainian communities from across the country could meet with their congressmen and senators, representatives of research centers, diplomats, and other influential figures. Following Russia's aggression in 2014, we stepped up this work.
We also collaborate with other initiatives to strengthen U.S. support for Ukraine. Overall, our guiding principle is that the voice of the Ukrainian community must be heard consistently, not just when another crisis arises.
Ukraine's security is America's security
For decades, American leadership and cooperation with European allies have been key factors in the stability of the democratic world. If the U.S. distances itself from its partners in Europe or gives the impression that aggression can be rewarded with concessions, the consequences will be felt not only by Ukrainians. This will affect allies' confidence in American commitments, the ability to deter future conflicts, and the international system, in which the sovereignty of states should not depend on the strength of their neighbors.
We work earnestly to ensure that cooperation between the White House and Congress will pave the way for a more consistent policy toward Ukraine. It is important that our security issues not be turned into a tool for domestic political struggles, and that support for Ukraine remain a shared strategic interest of the U.S.
I often recall the words of American pastor Mark Burns, who, after visiting Ukraine and seeing things with his own eyes, said: "Ukraine is America First". These words are particularly telling in the context of the "America First" slogan frequently used by President Trump. Their meaning is that defending Ukraine does not conflict with American interests. On the contrary, Ukraine is part of the democratic world, and the outcome of this war will affect security, stability, and the future far beyond its borders.
That is why we will continue to explain to Americans that aid to Ukraine is not just a matter of solidarity, but an investment in international security and the protection of the principles of American democracy.
To the people in Ukraine, I want to say that we are constantly working for victory for Ukraine. Ukraine remains in our thoughts, in our humanitarian work, in our meetings with politicians, and in every effort to convince the American public that our struggle matters to the entire democratic world.
Having been to Ukraine several times since Russia's full-scale invasion, I, and my organisation, understand how difficult it is to live under constant rocket and drone attacks and how much depends on the support of our partners, so we will continue to work – in the humanitarian sphere, in political advocacy, and in building partnerships that help Ukraine endure.
I would like to thank Ukrainian Americans for their tireless work. Regardless of when they or their families arrived in the U.S., what political views they hold, or how they choose to help, their contribution is of great importance.
We must remain united around a common goal. We don't have to agree on every issue of the American domestic policy to understand that a free, democratic, and sovereign Ukraine is in the interests of both Ukraine and the U.S.
Our task is to continue our work, expand our circle of partners, find new ways to convey our position, and turn support into concrete actions. I am convinced that a strong, democratic, and sovereign Ukraine will remain an important strategic partner of the United States for infinity. And that is precisely what we are working toward.
Michael Sawkiw, President of the Ukrainian Congress Committee of America (UCCA) and Director of its Washington, DC bureau – the Ukrainian National Information Service (UNIS), Chair of the Ukrainian World Congress (UWC) Foreign Policy Council, and recipient of the Order of Merit II degree.

Russian attacks on three Ukrainian oblasts kill two people and injure 27
Two people have been killed and another 27 injured in Russian attacks on Donetsk, Kherson and Kharkiv oblasts on 23 October.
Source: Donetsk Oblast Military Administration; Kherson Oblast Military Administration; Kharkiv Oblast Military Administration
Details: Russian forces killed two people in Donetsk Oblast: one in Kramatorsk and one in Sloviansk. Another 18 people were injured: 14 in Kramatorsk and four in Sloviansk.
Six people were injured in Russian attacks on Kherson Oblast. Russian forces targeted critical and social infrastructure facilities as well as residential areas across the oblast. A high-rise residential building, a house and cars were damaged.
Three people were injured in Kharkiv Oblast: a 12-year-old girl in Kharkiv and two men in Cherkaski Tyshky.
Another four people were suffering from shock: three in Kharkiv, including a 13-year-old boy, and a woman in Blyzniuky.
Medics also treated a nine-year-old girl who had been injured in Izium on 22 October.
According to the Oblast Military Administration, Russian forces attacked Kharkiv and 15 other settlements in the oblast over the past day, using missiles, guided aerial bombs and drones, among other weapons.
Background: Russian forces attacked Ukraine with 126 Shahed and Gerbera attack drones, S-8000 Banderol/Dan-T drone- and air-launched cruise missiles and decoy UAVs on the night of 23-24 October. Strikes were recorded at 14 locations.

Türkiye’s innovation ecosystem grows with state support as active R&D centres top 1,300
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
05:46:22 UTC
14:46:22 KST

Türkiye’s innovation ecosystem grew significantly over the years, driven by state support, with the number of active research and development (R&D) centres reaching 1,365 and design centers totaling 348 by the end of September.
Data from the Turkish Ministry of Industry and Technology showed that R&D hubs employ nearly 94,000 workers nationwide, including nearly 57,700 with bachelor’s degrees, over 18,500 with master’s degrees, and over 2,100 with a doctorate or higher.
Türkiye’s academically well-equipped R&D workforce has completed more than 80,400 projects to date, with nearly 16,000 still underway.
The robust innovation hubs have generated almost 49,000 patents so far, with over 17,500 registered and about 31,300 awaiting examination results.
Türkiye’s R&D network spans the country and many sectors, from energy, agriculture, and healthcare to transportation, logistics, and aviation.
The machinery and equipment manufacturing sector led with 160 centres, followed by the auto supply industry with 136 and the software sector with 128, the data showed.
The drivers of R&D innovation also included the computer and communications technologies sector with 86 centres, chemicals with 82 hubs, textiles and electrical sectors with 77 facilities each, food and the defence industry (excluding weapons and ammunition) with 65 each, and the general manufacturing industry with 43 centres.
The facilities are spread nationwide, but Istanbul has the highest concentration of R&D hubs with 428 centres, Ankara with 168, Kocaeli with 137, Bursa with 134, Izmir with 105, Tekirdag with 54, Manisa with 34, Konya with 26, Sakarya with 25, and Antalya with 21.
Meanwhile, Türkiye’s 348 design centres employ 8,481 workers, 5,540 of them with bachelor’s degrees, 820 with master’s degrees, and 50 with doctorates or higher degrees.
While the design centres operate across a myriad of sectors, they are heavily focused on industrial and structural sectors, with the textile industry ranking first, boasting 54 centres, followed by engineering and architecture with 51, general manufacturing with 45, and machinery and equipment manufacturing with 43.
The design ecosystem also included 23 design centres for the auto supply industry, 17 for media and communications, 15 for the furniture sector, 12 each for construction and auto manufacturing, and eight for the defence sector.
Istanbul is home to most of the design centres, with 154, followed by the capital Ankara with 39, Bursa with 31, Izmir with 28, and Kocaeli and Tekirdag with 15 each, according to ministry data.

Japan's energy vulnerabilities exposed by Mideast crisis: white paper
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
13:41:16 CST
14:41:16 KST

TOKYO, Oct. 24 (Xinhua) -- Japan's vulnerability in energy supply and demand has once again come to the fore as tensions in the Middle East escalate, according to the Japanese government's energy white paper for fiscal 2025, released Friday.
The white paper said Japan has long relied on the Middle East for more than 90 percent of its crude oil imports. Following U.S. and Israeli military strikes on Iran in late February this year, shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, a key global energy transit route, was disrupted, creating uncertainty over supplies of crude oil and petroleum products.
The disruption also hindered the distribution of some petroleum-related products, including naphtha, the report said.
To secure domestic energy supplies, the government has released oil reserves and stepped up efforts to procure alternative supplies from regions outside the Middle East since March. These measures helped ensure crude oil supplies to Japan, according to the white paper.
However, concerns over the supply outlook prompted stockpiling of certain petroleum-related products, disrupting distribution and leading to uneven supplies across the country, it said.
The white paper noted that the energy crisis response mechanisms Japan had developed over decades following the oil crises of the 1970s are no longer adequate to address emerging risks to energy supplies.
The annual energy white paper is usually adopted by the cabinet around June each year, but its compilation was delayed this year until October to incorporate developments in the Middle East and the government's responses to the situation. ■

No single nation can unilaterally rewrite NPT: Iran UN envoy
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
05:24:34 UTC
14:24:34 KST

Addressing the UN General Assembly, Ambassador Gholamhossein Darzi pushed back against Western pressure, asserting that Article IV of the NPT (Non-Proliferation Treaty) guarantees all state parties the right to develop peaceful nuclear energy, including the full nuclear fuel cycle.
The following is the full text of the statement which is read:
Mr. President,
The Agency’s reporting must remain professional, objective, factual, and free from political influence. Its credibility depends on impartiality and technical integrity.
Nuclear energy is indispensable to development and energy security. Article IV of the NPT affirms the inalienable right of all States Parties to develop research, production, and use of nuclear energy for peaceful purposes, without discrimination and in conformity with Articles I and II. Yet certain States systematically demonize this right and weaponize proliferation concerns to pressure States into abandoning their national nuclear fuel cycles.
The United States, an NPT depositary, openly questions the very existence of States Parties’ right to pursue the full nuclear fuel cycle, including uranium enrichment. Denying States access to this essential technology while claiming to uphold their right to peaceful nuclear energy violates Article IV. No State can unilaterally rewrite the Treaty or impose its own political veto on the legitimate rights of other States Parties.
In response to Iran’s resolute defense of its inalienable rights under the NPT, the United States and the nuclear-armed Israeli regime launched two wars of aggression against Iran in 2025 and 2026, massively targeting its peaceful nuclear facilities under IAEA safeguards.
These aggressions caused immense destruction and killed thousands, including our martyred Leader, whose well-known fatwa rejects nuclear weapons and other weapons of mass destruction. They also violated international law, the UN Charter, the IAEA Statute, relevant IAEA General Conference resolutions, and Security Council resolution 487 (1981).
Neither the IAEA General Conference, the IAEA Board of Governors, nor the Director General has condemned these attacks. The Security Council has likewise failed to do so. The Director General has once again failed to condemn these attacks in his statements delivered today under this agenda item. Instead, pressure is directed against the victim while the aggressors escape accountability.
Certain Western delegations continue to invoke so-called proliferation concerns while refusing to condemn attacks against safeguarded peaceful nuclear facilities. This is not a consistent commitment to non-proliferation; it is the weaponization of non-proliferation for political purposes.
The hypocrisy of this approach is blatant. Iran, an NPT State Party since 1970, has consistently affirmed its commitment to its international obligations and diplomacy. Yet its peaceful nuclear program and safeguarded facilities have been subjected to political pressure and military attacks, while the Secretariat’s withholding of technical cooperation deprives Iran of the benefits of peaceful nuclear development that the Agency is mandated to promote. Meanwhile, the Israeli regime—the region’s sole possessor of nuclear weapons, with unsafeguarded nuclear facilities—continues to enjoy impunity. This selective application of non-proliferation standards exposes the political motives behind the pressure on Iran and undermines the credibility of the international non-proliferation regime.
These same delegations demand access for inspectors while military threats persist, disregarding the extraordinary circumstances created by aggression. Let us be clear: Iran has neither abandoned nor formally suspended its safeguards obligations. However, aggression has fundamentally altered the physical and security conditions for their implementation. The Agency’s own reports acknowledge that verification activities ceased and inspectors were withdrawn for safety reasons. Those same safety concerns cannot be ignored when their return is demanded.
The continued existence of safeguards obligations does not eliminate the need to assess whether verification can be performed safely and effectively. No country can reasonably be expected to provide access amid military operations and persistent threats without adequate safety guarantees. Responsibility for creating these circumstances lies with the aggressors, not their victim.
Iran will continue to cooperate with the Agency to the extent circumstances permit. However, such cooperation cannot come at the expense of the safety of its people, facilities, or IAEA inspectors.
Thank you.

Paris shuts museums as France braces for new nationwide protests with massive security deployment
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
05:22:01 UTC
14:22:01 KST

Major museums in Paris closed and authorities deployed a sizable police force for a round of new protests on Saturday across France, hoping to prevent a repeat of last week’s violent unrest that shocked the country.
Scenes of looting, burned-out cars and attacks on public buildings left the impression that the government had lost control, as groups of masked vandals targeted businesses in Paris and other city centres.
Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez said as many as 70,000 officers will be deployed nationwide, along with helicopters, armoured vehicles and water cannons.
A massive turnout is expected again after more than half a million took to the streets last week.
Museums are closed and shopkeepers are worried
Major museums including the Louvre, Orsay Museum, Picasso Museum and Grand Palais — where a major Cézanne exhibit is on display — are closed Saturday. Art Basel, one of the world’s most prestigious contemporary art fairs, opened to the public Friday, but only for the day, with the threat of unrest prompting organisers to cancel the weekend program.
Parisian shopkeepers have been barricading their stores all week. Near Place de la République in Paris, one of last weekend’s hot spots, a bank branch and other businesses were boarded up with wooden panels to deter potential looters.
Following the unrest, Paris police prefect Patrice Faure urged Parisian shopkeepers to hire security guards. He later clarified that protecting business owners and their establishments is the responsibility of the government.
Some 3,000 shops across France were damaged or looted last weekend.
Some protests have been banned
Protest marches are scheduled in Paris and Marseille, but some other rallies, including in Lyon, Nice and Montpellier, have been banned by local authorities. Cities outside Paris were hit hard by the unrest. In Limoges, a suspected arson nearly destroyed the 19th-century city hall.
Trade unions have criticised the bans, calling them violations of freedom of expression, which is protected by the constitution.
President Emmanuel Macron, a centrist, entered the crisis in the final stretches of his term, with his popularity at its lowest since he took office in 2017. He has said that the measures are needed to protect city centres, businesses and public buildings.
Saturday’s demonstration in the city of Orléans, about 110 kilometres (70 miles) south of Paris, will also be closely watched.
About 50 organisations have called for a protest against the far right on the sidelines of the two-day congress of Marine Le Pen’s nationalist, anti-immigration party ahead of next spring’s presidential election. Organisers include labour unions, left-wing parties, student and anti-racism groups.
Students and workers are angry
The demonstrations first erupted last month in a high school southeast of Paris over a lack of staff.
From there, class boycotts and demonstrations spread to other Paris suburbs and nationwide, including smaller towns. High school students have raised concerns about underfunded schools and staff shortages, particularly in lower-income neighbourhoods. Some also called for a reform of the university admissions system, seen by many as unfair.
With the government seemingly unable to respond to students’ demands, the movement has morphed into larger protests over soaring living costs, just months before the vote to choose Macron’s successor.
“The money is now concentrated in the hands of very few people," said Victoria Ambrosini, an art critic and art teacher at Saint-Denis University. “And it’s not possible anymore.”

More than a billion pounds was moved out of the defence housing budget during the Defence Investment Plan process, and the Secretary of State for Defence has told MPs he is not comfortable with the choice and will not pretend rephasing allows the department to deliver as much as before.
Wes Streeting was giving evidence to the Defence Committee alongside Jeremy Pocklington, the Permanent Secretary at the Ministry of Defence.
Ian Roome, the Liberal Democrat member for North Devon, asked whether a decision had recently been taken to move over a billion pounds from the defence housing budget. Streeting said: “My predecessor took that decision. The amount being spent on defence housing is unchanged, but I concede that the profile of that spend—back to Mr Twigg’s earlier question—is more backloaded than it would have been. That is not stopping us from making a big difference on defence housing. Is it as fast as we would all like to see? No. You cannot pretend that, by backloading, you are still able to deliver the same as you would have done earlier on. It will improve year on year, but a choice was made to focus on capability over housing at that point in the process.”
Roome told him that personnel are the best capability the armed forces have, said he has a large garrison in his constituency with poor housing in some areas, and that without personnel to operate it there is no capability.
Streeting said: “I absolutely take that on the chin. I think a lot about the responsibility that I personally, and we as the state, have to people who serve, their families and people who have served previously. When I see the condition of some of our defence housing, it is up there with some of my worst constituency casework. I expect a lot better for those families who make enormous sacrifices and experience a lot of disruption for what they do. I am not comfortable with that choice, and I am not going to add insult to injury by pretending that rephasing does not mean that we will not be able to do as much as we would otherwise have done on the previous phasing.”
He said: “There will be year-on-year improvement, and already, since coming in, we have brought 36,000 military homes back into public ownership, delivering significant upgrades. I am keen to see what more we can do to leverage in investment in that area, because I understand the choice, but I do not think any of us ought to be comfortable with it.”
Pocklington said: “It was a very difficult decision in the final stages of the defence investment plan that the Secretary of State’s predecessor had to take. I would emphasise that we are still getting on and delivering. We are going to refurbish 1,000 homes this year and move another 1,000 homes from void unavailable to void available. It is a technical change, but it will release more homes through the hard work of the Defence Infrastructure Organisation.”
The department bought back 36,000 service family homes from Annington Homes and has committed to a programme of repair and renewal across the estate. The condition of service family accommodation has been the subject of sustained complaint and featured in the work of the Armed Forces Commissioner.
Dan Jarvis held the defence post before Streeting and settled the Defence Investment Plan, which was published in June.

China Focus: China expands community-based care as population ages
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
12:51:03 CST
13:51:03 KST

The elderly learn opera at a community in Baohe District of Hefei, east China's Anhui Province, Oct. 9, 2026. (Xinhua/Guo Chen)
HEFEI, Oct. 24 (Xinhua) -- While his family set out for holiday adventures earlier this month, Wang Libing, 74, chose to stay behind as a persistent leg ailment made walking tough. But he was determined not to spend the holiday alone at home.
He checked into a care center, where he was looked after by caregivers and could socialize with other older residents in Xinyuan community in Hefei, capital of eastern Anhui Province.
"I fear loneliness more than anything else," Wang said. His children are busy with work and his wife sometimes goes back to her hometown to care for her mother.
Wang has used the center for short stays each year since 2017, enjoying the companionship and meals planned by professional dietitians.
Families can bring their elders to the center for a short-term stay when they are away for work or travel, said Feng Jinjin, Party chief of Xinyuan community.
Each eligible elderly resident is entitled to 15 days of free care per quarter and unused days can be accumulated for a stay of up to two months at a time, Feng said.
Xinyuan, a residential area of high-rise apartment buildings, has about 26,000 permanent residents. People aged 60 and over account for 30 percent of the population, including 352 aged 80 and above.
Wang's experience reflects efforts across China to meet the needs of an aging population through short-term community elderly care, health services and volunteer support.
Community service centers in Hefei provide a range of activities and basic health services. In the mornings, teachers from seniors' universities offer free classes, and medical workers conduct basic checks such as blood pressure and blood glucose measurements.
Community canteens serve nutritionally tailored meals at noon, with home delivery for those with limited mobility. Afternoons feature performances and sports activities.
"Our goal is to ensure that the elderly are looked after properly, have access to medical care, and can enjoy their later years," Feng said.
Two floors of the four-story Xinyuan community service center are dedicated to elderly care, and the center also offers 27 courses for elders, including dance, fine arts, table tennis and choir.
Communities in Hefei are also adopting simple ways to check on elderly people living alone.
At Binhu Shiji community, seniors switch on red balcony light bulbs between 7 p.m. and 9 p.m. and turn them off before bed. If a light is not switched on or off as scheduled, volunteers will come to check on their situation, said Lang Ping, a community official.
Similar arrangements in Taiyuan, capital of Shanxi Province, and Qinhuangdao in Hebei Province, both in northern China, use balcony lights or curtains as signals to help confirm residents are safe.
Volunteers also help elderly residents with daily chores. Ma Menglan, 86, lives alone in Xinyuan community, where Ye Qinghua, a 64-year-old community social worker, and other volunteers regularly visit to clean Ma's home and wash clothes.
"I retired not long ago and am in good health, so I wanted to do some volunteer work to help other much older people," Ye said.
Two years ago, Ye joined a community initiative pairing younger seniors with older residents who live alone.
The program helps ease pressure on community services. Xinyuan's service center has only about a dozen staff members and social workers, making it hard to meet growing demand, Feng said.
The community now has more than 10 small teams of social workers pairing with younger seniors to support community elderly care. Feng said the community hopes to attract more young people and students in the future.
Elsewhere in China, other cities are developing services tailored to local needs. In Ningbo, Zhejiang Province, in China's eastern coastal region, programs offer free help with medical appointments, medicine collection, health follow-ups, and household tasks. In Xi'an, capital of northwestern Shaanxi Province, retired residents with specialized skills volunteer as teachers for the elderly.
Researchers are also exploring ways to make residential areas safer for aging residents.
Li Lianjun, a research associate professor at the School of Public Policy and Management at the University of Science and Technology of China, is leading a study on fall-risk perception and prevention behavior among older adults. She hopes the findings will help improve age-friendly renovations.
"China has a huge elderly population with diverse care needs. This poses new challenges for grassroots public services while also testing the sophistication of grassroots governance," Li said.
Official data shows that China's population aged 60 and above exceeded 323 million by the end of 2025, accounting for about 23 percent of the country's total population.
Meeting those needs requires government support, professional services, and help from residents, volunteers, and researchers, which can make community-based care more targeted, diverse, and sustainable, Li said. ■
The elderly interact with an elderly care robot at a community in Baohe District of Hefei, east China's Anhui Province, Oct. 9, 2026. (Xinhua/Guo Chen)

====================================================================================================

Reading Xi's vision for global governance through metaphors
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
04:45:21 UTC
13:45:21 KST

The 2026 Global Governance Forum (Xiong'an) is set to open on Friday in the Xiong'an New Area, north China's Hebei Province, bringing into world focus a pressing question: How can countries work together to address shared challenges in an interconnected world amid growing protectionism and unilateralism?
In speeches and meetings on multiple occasions, Chinese President Xi Jinping has used vivid metaphors to articulate his vision for global governance. These metaphors offer insights into his approach to building a more just, equitable and inclusive global governance system.
IN SAME BOAT
"I was looking at the vast ocean when I boarded the ship, and it struck me that we are all indeed fellow passengers in the same boat," Xi said while addressing the 2018 APEC CEO Summit hosted at a unique setting -- onboard the giant cruise Pacific Explorer in Port Moresby, Papua New Guinea.
The metaphor embodies the essence of Xi's vision of building a community with a shared future for humanity, highlighting the interconnectedness of countries and the need for solidarity and cooperation in addressing common challenges.
Today, the interconnected world is grappling with four mounting deficits: a peace deficit that exacerbates geopolitical conflicts, a development deficit that widens the North-South divide, a security deficit that erodes mutual trust, and a governance deficit that undermines the effectiveness of multilateralism.
In 2019, at the China-France Global Governance Forum held in Paris, Xi proposed a four-pronged approach to addressing the four deficits. First and foremost, he called for fairness and reasonableness to address the governance deficit.
"It is advisable to uphold a vision of global governance featuring extensive consultation and joint contribution for shared benefits," Xi said, calling for actively advancing the democratization of global governance rules.
As the world has found itself in a new period of turbulence and transformation, global governance has come to a new crossroads. Against this backdrop, Xi put forward the Global Governance Initiative (GGI) at the Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO) summit in September 2025 in China's coastal city of Tianjin.
"I look forward to working with all countries for a more just and equitable global governance system and advancing toward a community with a shared future for humanity," Xi said, stressing sovereign equality and genuine multilateralism.
TRAFFIC LIGHTS
"A world without rules is like a crossroads without traffic lights, where chaos and disorder are all but guaranteed," Xi said at the 2026 BRICS Summit in New Delhi, India.
This metaphor highlights the importance of rules in maintaining the international order. While having rules in place matters, how they are made and who gets to make them matter even more. International rules must be written and upheld jointly by all countries based on the purposes and principles of the UN Charter, rather than dictated by those with the strongest muscles or the loudest voice, Xi once stressed.
He has also called for the purposes and principles of the UN Charter and other universally recognized basic norms of international relations to be observed comprehensively, fully and in their entirety.
"There should be no double standards, and the house rules of a few countries must not be imposed upon others," he said.
The GGI proposed by President Xi reflects the objective transformation of the world system and responds to the aspirations of most countries for a fairer and more representative system of global governance, said Rahmon Ulmasov, a professor at the Russian-Tajik (Slavonic) University.
MAKING THE PIE BIGGER
Xi has repeatedly used the metaphor of a pie to describe the gains of international cooperation. "We should make the pie of win-win cooperation bigger, and ensure that more development gains will be shared more fairly by people across the world," he said at the 23rd meeting of the Council of Heads of State of the Shanghai Cooperation Organization in 2023.
The pie metaphor reflects the people-centered and action-oriented vision of the GGI: making the gains of cooperation bigger while ensuring that they are shared more widely and fairly. When proposing the GGI, Xi emphasized the importance of "ensuring that the people of every nation are the actors in and beneficiaries of global governance."The SCO, the platform where Xi proposed the GGI, provides an example. Within the grouping, China has announced the establishment of cooperation platforms in energy, green industries and the digital economy, as well as centers for scientific and technological innovation, higher education, and vocational and technical education.
The expanding scope of cooperation shows how the "pie" can be made bigger in practice: by opening up new areas of cooperation, creating more opportunities for development and ensuring that the benefits reach more people.
Beyond making the pie bigger, Xi has also called for sharing the pie fairly to ensure justice and equity. For him, the ultimate purpose of better global governance is to promote common development and improve people's well-being across the globe.
At the G20 summit held in Brazil in 2024, Xi called for building a just world of common development, saying "prosperity and stability would not be possible in a world where the rich become richer while the poor are made poorer, and countries should make global development more inclusive, beneficial to all, and more resilient."
To build such a world, Xi said, there should be more bridges of cooperation, and less "small yard, high fences," so that more and more developing countries will be better off and achieve modernization.
Source: Xinhua

US lawmakers urge Pentagon to expand Starshield contract for Ukraine

US lawmakers urge Pentagon to expand Starshield contract for Ukraine
Members of the US Congress have called on Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth and the Pentagon to expand its contract under the Starshield programme and restore Ukraine's access to Starlink and Starshield satellite communications following recent disruptions.
Source: a letter from US lawmakers
Details: In a bipartisan, bicameral appeal, US lawmakers insist that services be restored without speed restrictions to ensure Ukraine has the technical capabilities it needs.
Quote: "Ukrainian forces depend on these services for command and control, intelligence sharing, battlefield communications, and the operation of unmanned systems. Any degradation in service, including reduced connection speeds, restricted geographic coverage, or interruptions in access, undermines Ukraine's military effectiveness and provides Russian forces with an operational advantage that will extend the conflict and put more civilians in harm's way."
Details: The lawmakers urged the US Department of Defense to maintain the coverage Ukraine needs to conduct legitimate military operations, including over Russian territory, and to ensure that the transition from the commercial Starlink service to the government-run Starshield programme takes place without any interruption to service.
"Decisions regarding service availability, coverage, and performance should not be left solely to the discretion of a private provider when they have direct consequences for Ukraine's ability to defend itself," the lawmakers added.
They also called on the Department of Defense to consider using its powers under the relevant provision of the Defense Production Act, which allows the federal government to require companies to prioritise government orders.
"The United States and Europe have made significant investments in Ukraine's defence because of how a Russian victory would put our security at risk. Those investments should not be undermined by preventable disruptions to the communications infrastructure on which Ukrainian forces depend," the lawmakers concluded.
Previously: President Volodymyr Zelenskyy confirmed on 23 October that speed restrictions for Starlink satellite communications terminals in Ukraine remain in force.
The New York Times reported that US senators had warned the White House they would withhold votes on nominees until President Donald Trump's administration ensured the restoration of the communications capabilities used by Ukrainian troops.
A bipartisan group of nearly 20 members of the US House of Representatives called on Trump to ask Elon Musk to give Ukraine access to Starlink systems to target missile launchers on Russian territory.
US Democratic Senator Chris Coons had previously contacted Elon Musk's SpaceX, asking the company to explain who had decided to restrict Starlink's operation in Ukraine and why.
Background:
- The Wall Street Journal reported that Elon Musk had ordered Starlink services to be slowed down. It is unclear to what extent Trump was involved in discussions about the slowdown.
- US Republican Senator Thom Tillis is seeking an investigation into the Pentagon's actions with regard to problems with Starlink satellite communications systems encountered by the Ukrainian Armed Forces.
- US House of Representatives member Joe Wilson and nearly two dozen of his colleagues prepared a letter calling for Ukraine to be permitted to use Starlink for strikes on launch sites within Russian territory.
- The Wall Street Journal, citing US and Ukrainian officials familiar with the matter, reported that Trump had called Musk and asked him to lift restrictions on the military version of Starlink in Ukraine.
- On the evening of 22 October, Trump said Musk had already lifted speed restrictions on the military version of Starlink in Ukraine but declined to say whether he had personally called him about the issue.
- Ukraine's Defence Ministry said it was recording disruptions to Starlink and Starshield services on the line of contact.

UN Day: How an exhibition in Astana tells stories of change
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
03:34:29 UTC
12:34:29 KST

UN Day: How an exhibition in Astana tells stories of change
Zeenat Muznabi was a child when her family fled conflict in Afghanistan. In Kazakhstan, she received an education and now helps raise funds for people in need. Her portrait features in the GLOCAL exhibition at Kazakhstan’s National Museum. It brings together photographs and stories of 30 people connected to UN-supported programs. Ahead of United Nations Day on October 24, Qazinform News Agency correspondent introduces several participants.
The name GLOCAL combines the words “global” and “local.” The exhibition shows how international goals become part of everyday life. For one person, that means the chance to learn a profession. For another, it means protecting women from violence or sharing family responsibilities differently.
Passing help on
In 2024, Zeenat graduated in Information Technology from Al-Farabi Kazakh National University. A government scholarship supported her studies. Kazakhstan provided it as part of its commitments at the Global Refugee Forum.
Today, Zeenat coordinates fundraising at the Kazakhstan Red Crescent. Its Direct Dialogue program helps provide regular humanitarian support. She trains staff, works with donors and partners, and keeps donation records.
“I had the chance to study, work and grow. Now I can help others support people in need.”
Another exhibition participant, Armin Talebi, followed a similar path. He also arrived in Kazakhstan from Afghanistan as a child. Two decades later, he is studying plastic and reconstructive surgery.
He wants to help people recover their health and return to everyday life. The DAFI scholarship program supports his education. It is backed by the Office of the UN High Commissioner for Refugees.
Armin has also contributed to the UN Youth Advisory Board and advocates for refugee inclusion.
His portrait carries the words “Together for Inclusion.” He explains that his profession helps him feel safe and part of society.
One button
For Aruzhan Mede, working on safety began with a specific problem. Women facing domestic violence needed a way to call for help quickly.
Her startup, AMAN, initially offered an emergency alert activated with one press of a button. The team later expanded the project. AMAN now uses artificial intelligence to identify potentially dangerous situations. The system works with security cameras in schools, workplaces and other public spaces.
Aruzhan trained through UN Women’s entrepreneurship program. She studied investment, sales and ways to enter new markets.
In 2026, she presented AMAN to international investors at GITEX AI EUROPE in Berlin. She now also helps other women turn their ideas into businesses.
“Every woman, every child, every person has the right to feel safe.”
These stories connect international programs with decisions people make every day.
Kazakhstan’s First Deputy Foreign Minister Yerzhan Ashikbayev discussed that connection at the exhibition’s opening.
“The theme of today’s exhibition underscores the importance of connecting this global agenda with national priorities and actions in our regions, cities, and rural communities,” he said.
Equality begins at home
In another portrait, Didar Smagulov holds a smiling child in his arms. He is a lawyer, head of the Adildik Zholy Public Association and father of three.
His story focuses on men’s participation in family life. As a United Nations Population Fund trainer, Didar works on responsible fatherhood. He helps civil society organizations promote shared household responsibilities and equal partnerships between spouses.
He follows the same principle in his own family: parents share responsibility equally. In the exhibition text, Didar connects this with children’s futures. What they see at home today will shape the families they build themselves.
For 17-year-old Konstantin Tsoy, equality also begins with someone close to him. He wants his younger sister to know her rights and freely choose her future.
At fourteen, Konstantin joined the Y-PEER youth network in Kyzylorda. The United Nations Population Fund supports the network. He now helps coordinate volunteers across 18 cities in Kazakhstan.
They teach their peers about reproductive health, rights and gender equality. For Konstantin, the network has become a community where young people support one another.
“Y-PEER showed me that being young, or coming from a small city, should never stop me from taking responsibility and changing society.”
At the opening, UN Resident Coordinator in Kazakhstan Sarangoo Radnaragchaa discussed growing inequality and other shared challenges.
“These challenges know no borders, they affect us all and they remind us of a simple truth, no country can address them alone,” she said.
For the exhibition’s participants, this shared work continues beyond the museum. Zeenat raises donations. Armin studies surgery. Aruzhan develops her safety system. Didar raises his children, while Konstantin works with his peers. Each of their stories is still unfolding.
Earlier, Qazinform News Agency reported that 63-year-old Danna from Kazakhstan and 17-year-old Venera from Kyrgyzstan. They help people in need, join environmental activities and encourage others to volunteer.

Former Port Adelaide AFL player Daniel Stewart dies at 37
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
03:29:23 UTC
12:29:23 KST

The Port Adelaide AFL club has said it will honour Daniel Stewart at the first home game of 2027 after the former Power forward's death at the age of 37.
Stewart, who played 36 games and kicked 31 goals for Port Adelaide between 2010 and 2013, died suddenly yesterday.
The tall key forward was drafted by the Power in the 2009 rookie draft and promoted to the senior list at the end of that season.
Originally from Victoria, Stewart was recruited from SANFL team North Adelaide after playing for the Eastern Ranges and AFL Queensland club Labrador.
His best AFL return came in the final round of 2010 at Docklands against Richmond, where Stewart kicked four goals in a 10-point win for the Power.
"On behalf of everyone at the Port Adelaide Football Club, I extend our deepest condolences to Daniel's family including his mum Donna, dad Byron, wife Laura, his two sons Bernie and Lando and his brother Leigh," Port Adelaide chief executive Matthew Richardson said in a statement.
"We also extend our thoughts to his friends, including his close friend and former teammate Matt Thomas, and to all those at North Adelaide and Labrador who knew him.
"Daniel was part of the Port Adelaide football family, and he always will be. A sudden passing like this is devastating and our thoughts are with everyone who loved him, and with the teammates, coaches and staff who shared the journey with him here at Alberton.
"The club will provide support to those affected by Daniel's passing, including his former teammates and the people who worked alongside him."
The club stated it would honour Stewart by wearing black armbands at their first home game at Adelaide Oval next season.

Last polls before Israel's election: Eisenkot ahead, both sides short of a majority

Updates
IDF Announces General Closure for West Bank Palestinians on Israel's Election Day
The Israeli military early on Sunday announced that the government had approved its recommendation to ban "the entry and exit of Palestinian workers" throughout the West Bank and to close all land crossings on Israel's Election Day, effectively imposing a general closure on the West Bank on Tuesday.
Additionally, the Israel Defense Forces said that Palestinian workers would not be permitted to enter Israeli settlements in the West Bank for work on Sunday and Monday ahead of the Election, except for "industrial zones and a limited number of other approved areas."
Netanyahu summons Police chief after the latter rebuffed Ben-Gvir's election readiness briefing
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu summoned Police Commissioner Danny Levy on Saturday to an unusual meeting on police readiness ahead of Election Day, after the police chief had refused to attend a meeting on the same subject with National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir on Thursday.
Last week, Ben-Gvir convened a meeting and summoned the Commissioner Levy alongside other senior officials. Senior law enforcement officials criticized the planned meeting and questioned its professional merit, citing in part Ben-Gvir's candidacy in the election and concerns that he would exploit the meeting to advance his own political goals.
"There is no need whatsoever for Ben-Gvir to be familiar with police preparations, and there is concern that he will use what he hears there for his political needs," a senior law enforcement official told Haaretz before the meeting.
Following Haaretz' report, Levy and other senior officials, including the head of the Investigations and Intelligence Department, announced that they would not attend the meeting. Ultimately, the heads of the Operations Directorate and the Police Operations Division did attend, with Levy authorizing them to provide only a brief overview.
Netanyahu fans the flames of war two days before Israel's election | Analysis
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu seized on Friday's deadly shooting attack, in which two Israeli soldiers were killed and three others wounded near Hebron in the West Bank, as if he had struck gold. Having, as of yet, failed to ignite the Iranian front ahead of Tuesday's election, he has no alternative but to make do with what he has.
Netanyahu is now trying to fan the flames in the West Bank and heighten the public's sense of a security emergency, while revealing more details of his grim vision for Israel under another four years of his leadership. He sees Israel becoming an isolated country, its economy increasingly cut off from the rest of the world and forced to make do with Iranian, North Korean or Russian-style schemes to somehow survive.
Private security firm to guard Eisenkot under Shin Bet supervision, Yashar party says
Opposition frontrunner Gadi Eisenkot will be guarded by a private security team starting Sunday, under the supervision and direction of the Shin Bet security service, his party, Yashar, announced.
In recent days, the Shin Bet instructed the leaders of all parties who have expressed concerns for their safety to contact a dedicated hotline and hire a security firm operating under the agency's guidance.
Unlike candidates who are sitting Knesset members or former prime ministers, Eisenkot has no state body responsible for his personal security.
Had he been a sitting lawmaker, he would have been protected by the Knesset Guard. As a former prime minister, he would have been under Shin Bet protection.
Democrats party leader Yair Golan is also not a sitting Knesset member and is not eligible for protection on those grounds. His status differs from Eisenkot's, however, because he is not a candidate for prime minister.
In August, the advisory committee on the protection of public figures recommended that the Shin Bet provide protection for Eisenkot. Later on in September, however, the agency announced that it would not do so.
'Necessary for the futures of our sons and daughters': Bereaved father of October 7 victim speaks at rally
Rabbi Elchanan Danino, whose son Uri was abducted and murdered in Hamas captivity, spoke in the rally held in Tel Aviv's Hostage Square.
"Three years and a bit after that bitter day, in which they kidnapped, killed, and burned our brothers and sisters," said Danino. "In the meantime, the government decided not to do the most important thing. Those at home must demand exactly what we are demanding - a commission of inquiry that will investigate everyone!"
"It will not bring our sons and daughters home, but it is necessary for the futures of our sons and daughters … and for the soldiers who are risking their lives for our existence here." As he spoke, calls of "shame!" were heard from the audience.
How did a key religious party lose its faithful in one of its most loyal strongholds?
Political posters on porches were once a fixture of election season in Israel, allowing voters in cities and towns across the country to signal their party allegiances to passersby. But in the lead-up to an election being cast as the most consequential in Israeli history, these once-ubiquitous displays of electoral loyalty are remarkably few and far between.
Netivot is a notable exception.
Located about 12 kilometers (7 miles) from the Gaza border, this western Negev town has long been a stronghold of Shas, the ultra-Orthodox Sephardic party. These days it is awash with election posters bearing the images of revered rabbis, though in almost all cases, and rather surprisingly, they are not endorsing Shas.
October 7 bereaved families rally for a state commission of inquiry three days before election
Thousands of Israelis are rallying nationwide against the government of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu On Saturday as the Knesset election is just three days away.
In Tel Aviv's Hostage Square, the October Council, an organization representing October 7 former hostages and bereaved families, is calling for the establishment of a state commission of inquiry into the Hamas attack on October 7, 2023, and the rally itself is named "For Their Sake and Ours." Alongside the bereaved families and former hostages, Israeli opposition leaders are expected to participate, and top Israeli artists will perform.
One of the exhibitions at the event shows a covered model of a Hamas tunnel at Hostage Square with 1,200 images of clocks set to 6:29, the time when the Hamas attack began, in memory of those killed.
"Three years later, there were more than 800 bereaved families," the description of the installation says. "What more needs to happen for us to wake up? We need to wake up to our lives - we need an official commission of inquiry."
Israel was built on hope. This election may be our last chance to save it | Opinion
Israel's national anthem, Hatikva, means "the hope." Israel is not just another country, but the culmination of a 2,000-year-old dream of national redemption. The rebirth of the Jewish people's ancestral homeland, just three years after the Holocaust, was a miraculous triumph of hope over all odds.
Today, that hope has been shattered and the elections on October 27 have become the most consequential in Israel's history.
Israel will decide what kind of country it wishes to be: a liberal democracy, or an increasingly illiberal one; a country that seeks peace with the Palestinians, or continues to glide toward annexation and a binational reality; a society of mutual solidarity, or warring tribes; and a country firmly anchored in the democratic West, or increasingly estranged from it.
By the next elections, demographic and political realities may have made it too late to reverse this.
As long as the mall stays open, Israelis can live with war crimes | Opinion
Not far from my neighborhood, between the main road and the mall, lies a park. The kind typical of the suburban development boom of the 2000s – flat, gaudy and full of unrealized pretensions. I sometimes wonder what this park is trying to say, though I suspect it was designed with Japan's lovely Zen gardens in mind.
Supposedly, the pathways take you on a kind of journey there. Supposedly, you can stop and rest at several points along the way – three pools reeking of chlorine, surrounded by makeshift fences, and a clumsy seating area made of supposedly ancient stones. Except there's never any shade along the paths, and no Zen shrine awaits at its end. Only the mall.
Two years ago, on my way to yet another protest on the asphalt expanse of Begin Road in Tel Aviv, I decided to conduct an experiment and went into the mall. It was my first visit since the war broke out, and I was astonished by what I found. The mall looked normal. It was full of people shopping as usual. Outside, in the public spaces of greater Tel Aviv's suburbs, some semblance of "routine" was ostensibly being maintained, but the streets were empty and under construction, and the walls shouted with slogans, names and faces of dead and abducted children. Outside, there wasn't a wall that didn't remind you of something, while the mall did everything it could to make you forget.

Iran has "increased efforts to target U.S. personnel," intel chief warns
