Iran has "increased efforts to target U.S. personnel," intel chief warns
Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton warned Friday that Iran has "substantially increased efforts to target U.S. personnel" abroad, with plots to kill Americans reaching "advanced stages" in the Middle East and other countries.
The warning, contained in an unclassified memo that was sent to Secretary of State Marco Rubio and obtained by CBS News, comes as the State Department adjusts staffing at diplomatic posts across the Middle East, and the U.S. military pares back its footprint in the region, amid concerns about direct threats from Iran and threats from the Iranian-backed Houthi movement in Yemen.
"The lethal plotting efforts by the Iranians against U.S. citizens have reached advanced stages in both the Middle East and certain other countries," Clayton wrote.
The memo, which was issued as the Trump administration weighs resuming military strikes against Iran, does not identify specific targets or countries where the alleged plots are underway, or indicate whether attacks may be imminent.
Clayton said the U.S. intelligence community is working to downgrade sensitive intelligence — received through various channels — so it can be shared more broadly with State Department personnel. CIA Director John Ratcliffe was copied on the memo.
Axios was first to report on the memo.
The warning follows a series of precautions at U.S. diplomatic facilities across the region. Earlier this week, the State Department ordered non-essential U.S. embassy personnel and their families to depart Saudi Arabia. Several other American embassies in the region adjusted their staffing under "restricted operations" status, which allows them to reduce the number of personnel without formally going on ordered departure, CBS News previously reported.
"When it comes to our staffing at embassies, we constantly evaluate new information about the security environment," a U.S. official told CBS News on Friday. "The threat of Houthi attacks and of Iranian terror plots targeting U.S. officials are informing our decisions on staffing adjustments for embassies on RO [Restricted Operations] Status in the region."
A U.S. official and a senior U.S. military official also told CBS News this week that the military has been quietly reducing its footprint at posts in the Middle East due to ongoing threats.
Houthi militants have stepped up drone and missile attacks against Saudi Arabia, targeting oil infrastructure and airports. One strike on Riyadh's King Khalid Airport earlier this month killed at least a dozen people, including a U.S. citizen, and injured hundreds more.
Last weekend, U.S. embassies in Saudi Arabia, Bahrain, Qatar, the United Arab Emirates and other countries warned Americans to exercise caution due to Houthi attacks.
Although the U.S. and Iran have refrained from striking each other in recent weeks, President Trump has not ruled out restarting hostilities after next month's midterm elections. Iran has also continued to take responsibility for attacks on oil tankers in the Strait of Hormuz.
At a campaign rally in Florida on Friday, Mr. Trump suggested the U.S. could launch another operation against Iran if Tehran failed to reach an agreement.
"We may do another little Epic Fury, or they'll agree," the president said, invoking the name of the U.S. military campaign launched in February.

Flavio Bolsonaro, son of former far-right president Jair Bolsonaro, won the first round of presidential elections with 47 percent of the vote over leftist Lula's 45 percent.
Following a first debate loaded with insults and practically empty of concrete policy proposals, the candidates on Friday questioned each other on Brazil's economy, infrastructure and regional development this time around.
Lula challenged his rival's plan to take a "chainsaw" to public spending in the style of Argentina's libertarian leader Javier Milei.
"I'll have the same job here (as Milei in Argentina) because you're leaving the country bankrupt," Bolsonaro retorted, adding: "Aren't you ashamed?"
Flavio Bolsonaro accused the president of allowing organised crime to expand, driving families into debt, and doing nothing to reduce the cost of living.
The right-wing candidate also reproached Lula for raising the minimum wage while keeping taxes high, mocking the finger the president lost in an accident as a metalworker when he was young.
"It's no use, Lula, giving with one hand and taking away with your nine fingers."
"I will not allow a militiaman to call me 'nine fingers,'" Lula replied, referring to allegations that his rival has ties to paramilitary groups in Rio de Janeiro.

Lula questioned the senator's experience, insisting that "he doesn't know Brazil."
His challenger doubled down on presenting himself as a capable candidate who represented change for the country.

This 150-million-year-old bird had dinosaur teeth and a strange secret
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
02:42:19 UTC
11:42:19 KST

This 150-million-year-old bird had dinosaur teeth and a strange secret
- Date:
- October 23, 2026
- Source:
- Chinese Academy of Sciences Headquarters
- Summary:
- A 150-million-year-old fossil discovered in China reveals a bizarre early bird with sharp teeth, a dinosaur-like claw, and a body built for life on the ground rather than flight. Scientists believe it represents the earliest known example of flight loss in birds, overturning assumptions about how these animals evolved.
- Share:
A remarkably preserved 150-million-year-old bird fossil discovered in China is challenging long-standing ideas about how birds evolved. Rather than developing increasingly sophisticated flight abilities, some of the earliest birds appear to have taken a very different evolutionary path, including losing the ability to fly altogether.
The newly identified species, Yuezhuornis yangyuanensis, lived during the Late Jurassic period (150-148 million years ago). Described in a study published in Nature, the crow-sized creature provides evidence that early bird evolution was much more complex than scientists once believed. Instead of evolving primarily to become better flyers, ancient birds were adapting to a variety of environments and ways of life, including those that favored living on the ground.
Researchers from the Institute of Vertebrate Paleontology and Paleoanthropology (IVPP) of the Chinese Academy of Sciences (CAS) and the Fujian Institute of Geological Sciences uncovered the fossil in the recently recognized Zhenghe Fauna of Fujian Province in southeastern China. According to their findings, Yuezhuornis represents the earliest known example of a bird lineage losing its ability to fly.
An Ancient Bird With Dinosaur Teeth and Claws
One of the most remarkable features of Yuezhuornis is its unusual combination of bird and dinosaur characteristics. Although it possessed skeletal features associated with birds, it also retained anatomical traits that would have been familiar among small predatory dinosaurs.
Its jaws contained closely spaced, serrated teeth resembling those of deinonychosaurs, a group of meat-eating dinosaurs that included agile predators related to birds. Such teeth are not normally associated with early birds.
Even more striking was its second toe, which could bend backward unusually far and carried a curved, sickle-shaped claw. This specialized feature is strongly associated with deinonychosaurs, including dromaeosaurids and troodontids, two groups of predatory dinosaurs.
"When we examined Yuezhuornis, we were struck by its extraordinary mix of features," said Dr. Min Wang, corresponding author of the study. "It possesses bird-like pelvic and hindlimb structures yet retains the specialized predatory foot and teeth of a small meat-eating dinosaur. It shows us that early bird evolution was far more complicated than we previously realized."
Where Does This Strange Jurassic Bird Fit in Evolution?
To understand how Yuezhuornis was related to other prehistoric birds and dinosaurs, scientists carried out detailed analyses of its evolutionary relationships. They used two approaches, maximum parsimony and Bayesian tip-dating, to compare anatomical characteristics and reconstruct the species' position on the evolutionary tree.
Maximum parsimony identifies evolutionary relationships that require the fewest changes in characteristics, while Bayesian tip-dating also incorporates statistical estimates of evolutionary history and information about when fossils lived.
Both methods produced consistent results, placing Yuezhuornis within Avialae, the evolutionary group that includes modern birds and their closest extinct relatives.
"The results consistently placed Yuezhuornis firmly within Avialae (the group containing modern birds and their closest extinct relatives), just crownward of Archaeopteryx and as a sister taxon to Zhengheornis," said Dr. Zhonghe Zhou, a co-author of the study.
This placement is particularly important because Archaeopteryx, which also lived roughly 150 million years ago, is among the most famous early bird relatives. The findings indicate that Yuezhuornis belonged to an early branch of bird evolution rather than simply being a small predatory dinosaur with bird-like characteristics.
Evidence That Some Early Birds Lost the Ability to Fly
The researchers also examined how Yuezhuornis might have lived. Using measurements of its skeletal proportions and statistical comparisons with other animals, they investigated whether its anatomy was better suited for flying or moving along the ground.
The results showed that its limb proportions closely resembled those of modern ground-dwelling birds and certain other prehistoric dinosaurs closely related to birds. This similarity suggests that Yuezhuornis spent its life on the ground and was likely unable to fly.
The findings point to an unexpected development in the history of birds. Rather than simply progressing toward stronger wings and more efficient flight, some early bird lineages appear to have moved in the opposite direction, adapting to lifestyles in which flying was no longer necessary.
This challenges the traditional assumption that the earliest stages of bird evolution were driven primarily by the demands of flight. Instead, birds were already exploring different ecological roles and developing a surprisingly wide range of body forms.
A 150-Million-Year-Old Discovery Rewrites Bird Evolution
The discovery of Yuezhuornis suggests that the evolution of birds was never a simple, one-directional process. Even during the Late Jurassic, when the earliest bird lineages were emerging, some species were developing adaptations that favored life on land rather than in the air.
Its unusual combination of bird-like anatomy, dinosaur-style predatory features, and apparent flightlessness provides a revealing glimpse into that evolutionary experimentation. The fossil shows that early birds were more anatomically and ecologically diverse than previously recognized.
It also underscores the scientific importance of the Zhenghe Fauna, a fossil assemblage that is helping researchers investigate a poorly understood period in bird evolution. As additional discoveries emerge from this region of China, scientists may gain an even clearer picture of the surprising evolutionary paths taken by the earliest birds.
Story Source:
Materials provided by Chinese Academy of Sciences Headquarters. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- Liming Xu, Min Wang, Ganmin Lin, Liping Dong, Ke Deng, Xing Xu, Honggang Du, Min Lin, Runsheng Chen, Zhonghe Zhou. Jurassic flightless bird reveals early ecological diversity of avialans. Nature, 2026; 658 (8136): 690 DOI: 10.1038/s41586-026-10972-z

Ukraine lost about $6 billion from port downtime in last three months
Unknown

MOSCOW, October 24. /TASS/. The loss of Ukraine’s foreign exchange earnings from the downtime of the ports of Greater Odessa, which has been going on for more than three months, amounted to about $6 billion, according to TASS calculations.
Commercial merchant ships continue to boycott the ports of Odessa, Chernomorsk, and Yuzhnoye; only vessels associated with the Ukrainian army enter them. Maritime trade is conducted through the Danube ports — Ukraine’s Izmail and Romania’s Constan·a, which together can potentially account for no more than a third of the exports that previously passed through the ports of Greater Odessa.
As a result, in September, Ukraine was able to export only 44% of the agricultural products planned for exports that month. Exports of metallurgical products ceased completely by the end of September. Together, these items accounted for about 65% of Ukraine’s exports and about $26 billion in foreign exchange earnings per year.
By using the railway network and the Danube ports for exports, Ukraine managed to partially reduce losses, but only slightly -- from about $70 million per day in August to about $60 million in September-October.
The idle time of Greater Odessa has been ongoing since July 22.

youtaro sakamoto’s kinetic thread column transforms human presence into shifting shadows
Unknown

youtaro sakamoto’s kinetic thread column transforms human presence into shifting shadows
a delicate column formed from fine threads moves in response to nearby visitors, casting constantly changing shadows.
prefer designboom on google
[FEATURED]
KINETIC THREAD COLUMN installation draws from SUDARE SCREENS
Created by Japanese artist, engineer, and researcher Youtaro Sakamoto, Schattenrequisit: Column is a kinetic installation formed from fine threads that explores the relationship between architectural permanence, human presence, and shifting shadow projections. Drawing conceptual inspiration from the light-filtering properties of sudare (traditional Japanese slatted screens), the project treats physical material and immaterial shadows as unified components of a single sculptural composition.
ANIMATING STATIC ARCHITECTURAL FORMS THROUGH HUMAN MOVEMENT
The installation takes the form of an architectural column constructed from closely spaced fine threads. Integrated millimeter-wave sensors detect the proximity of visitors, triggering a stepper motor developed through computational design and physical prototyping. In response to movement within the space, the motor slowly rotates and shifts the thread assembly, altering the overlap of the linear strands and continuously transforming the shadow silhouettes cast across surrounding walls and floors. By animating a typically static structural archetype, the installation by artist Youtaro Sakamoto mirrors the interaction between fixed urban infrastructure and transient human circulation.
project info:
name: Schattenrequisit: Column
artist: Youtaro Sakamoto | @youtarosakamoto
location: Hibiya OKUROJI, Tokyo, Japan
exhibition: DESIGNART TOKYO 2026
dates: October 30th – November 8th, 2026
photographer: Manabu Tanaka

Cattle prices hit 'a new gear' as rain tumbles down
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
02:06:02 UTC
11:06:02 KST

analysis
Cattle prices hit 'a new gear' this week as rain tumbled down
Cattle prices jumped this week as heavy rain fell across key production areas in Queensland and northern New South Wales.
Meat and Livestock Australia's (MLA) benchmark Eastern Young Cattle Indicator (EYCI) surged beyond 1,000 cents a kilogram, as restockers and backgrounders competed for numbers.
"The cattle market shifted to a new gear off the back of this rain," Stuart Bull, MLA's market information manager said.
"Some of these regions were in need of a good drink and this rain has really helped pushed prices, along with fewer cattle coming to market."
At Roma on Tuesday, some weaner steers from the Winton region sold for an incredible $7 a kilogram, which equated to more than $1,900 a head.
At Dubbo, the local saleyard report said restocker demand "sparked a market boom".
"Restocker demand was a stand-out, with young cattle selling up to an impressive 80 cents per kilo dearer [than last week]," the report said.
"Young steers reached a top of $7.40/kg, while young restocker heifers sold to $6.50/kg, showcasing the strength of competition and confidence among buyers looking to replenish their herds."
Loading...
Scott Loughnan, who runs a mixed farming operation west of Roma, had received more than 160 millimetres of rain when he spoke to ABC News.
"We'd organised to feed cattle all summer with forecasts of a super El Niño,"
he said.
"It was apparently never going to rain again, but this will definitely make it easier."
Mr Loughnan was in the middle of harvesting wheat, barley and chickpeas, and said for winter crops in the area, the rain was "not very good".
"I looked at some chickpeas this morning and they might not be much good, but I'm trying to look at the positives that this rain will grow us some grass and give us moisture for the next planting."
Record cow and heavy steers
Meanwhile, MLA's national processor cow indicator has cracked $4 a kilogram for the first time on record, and the national heavy steer indicator has also reached a new high of $4.77 a kilogram.
Global AgriTrends livestock analyst Simon Quilty said the supply of heavy steers was tight and processors were competing against feedlots to secure numbers.
"Once upon a time, feedlot operators wanted 450 kilogram to 500 kilogram steers, that was the preferred weight," he said.
"But that's now been lifted because of the lack of supply and they're taking 550 kilograms to almost 630 kilograms, creating an overlap [in demand] between processors and their needs for slaughter-ready cattle and the feedlotters who have extended the requirements of their cattle.
"So there's competition for numbers between the north and the south of Australia, plus processors versus feedlots [and] the net effect is this incredible demand for heavy steers that I think will continue."
Mr Quilty believes Australia's cattle industry is at the start of a herd rebuild and is forecasting cattle prices to increase next year.
He is forecasting heavy steer prices to rise by about 20 per cent to about $5.70/kg next year.

"These materials have been provided to appropriately-cleared senior staff on your team and we are available to brief you at your convenience. The memo emerged shortly after the State Department announced it is reducing staff at the US embassies in Jordan, Lebanon, Qatar and the United Arab Emirates.
The three officials said the threats from Iran and Yemen's Houthi militia are related to the staffing changes.
Houthi threat
The embassies involved are all under what is known as "restricted operations" status that has already reduced the size of their personnel footprints. The embassies will remain open.
However, unlike in Saudi Arabia, where nonessential US personnel and their families were ordered Wednesday to leave the country, staff in the other four countries are not compelled to depart.
In announcing the staffing drawdowns this week, the State Department pointed specifically to increased threats from Houthi militias and did not mention threats to US personnel directly from Iran.
US officials have adamantly denied they are tied to any potential new US and Israeli attacks on Iran.

Vedas
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
02:00:00 UTC
11:00:00 KST

The Vedas are the oldest surviving texts of any living religion. Their earliest hymns were composed around 1500 BCE – before Homer, before the Hebrew Bible, before Confucius – and they have been recited, essentially unchanged, ever since. For more than a thousand years they were not written down at all. Generations of priests memorised them syllable by syllable, with the accents, and developed elaborate cross-checking techniques to make sure that not a single sound was lost. When scholars finally compared manuscripts from opposite ends of India, they found the texts virtually identical. Nothing comparable exists anywhere else in the world.
But the Vedas are not a single book, and they are not what most people expect of a “scripture.” They contain no commandments, no founder, no creed, and very little that resembles a systematic doctrine. What they do contain is a journey: from hymns sung around a sacrificial fire to the first sustained philosophical questions about the nature of reality and the self. The whole of later Indian philosophy – including Buddhism and Jainism, which rejected the Vedas – can be read as a long argument with them.
What the word means
Veda comes from the Sanskrit root vid, “to know” – the same root as the Latin videre, “to see,” and the English wit and wisdom. The Vedas are, literally, “knowledge.” In Hindu tradition they are classified as shruti, “that which is heard,” as opposed to smriti, “that which is remembered.” Smriti texts – the epics, the law books, the Puranas – have human authors and can be revised. Shruti has no author. The Vedas are held to be apaurusheya, “not of human origin”: eternal truths that the ancient seers (rishis) did not compose but perceived, in states of heightened vision, and then put into words. For the orthodox schools of Hindu philosophy, accepting the authority of the Vedas is the single criterion that separates orthodoxy (astika) from heterodoxy (nastika).
This is worth pausing on, because it shapes how the texts were treated. If the Vedas are revealed knowledge, then every syllable matters, and the task of the tradition is not to improve them but to preserve and interpret them. That is why they survived.
Who composed them, and when
The Vedas were composed in Vedic Sanskrit by Indo-Aryan speaking peoples who settled in the north-west of the Indian subcontinent, in the region of the Punjab and the upper Ganges, during the second millennium BCE. Their society was pastoral and …

BERLIN, Oct. 23 (Xinhua) -- Borussia Monchengladbach ended their disastrous Bundesliga start with a 3-2 comeback victory at VfB Stuttgart on Friday, as Wael Mohya inspired the visitors to their first points of the season and helped avert an unwanted league record.

Stuttgart struck after just five minutes when Ermedin Demirovic fired from distance following Dzenan Pejcinovic's pass. Gladbach goalkeeper Moritz Nicolas reached the ball but could not prevent it from crossing the line.
The hosts initially controlled proceedings and threatened through Pejcinovic and Lorenz Assignon before Gladbach gradually found their rhythm.
Joe Scally equalised in the 38th minute, cleverly redirecting Zento Uno's effort into the net with his heel.
The visitors nearly completed the turnaround before halftime, but Stuttgart goalkeeper Dennis Seimen denied Florian Neuhaus before Mohya struck the crossbar.
Gladbach maintained their momentum after the restart and took the lead in the 51st minute. Mohya dribbled past two defenders before finding Shuto Machino, who drove the ball into the top corner.
Stuttgart coach Sebastian Hoeness responded with a triple substitution, introducing Deniz Undav, Jamie Leweling and Bilal El Khannouss, but the visitors extended their advantage in the 66th minute.
Seimen failed to gather Mohya's low effort, and although Ramon Hendriks cleared off the line, Scally recovered possession near the right post and lifted the ball back towards Mohya, who bundled it home from close range.
Demirovic reduced the deficit with a header from Leweling's cross in the 83rd minute, but Stuttgart could not find an equaliser despite late pressure.
"A lot of pressure has been lifted. The players have fully rewarded themselves today. We invested more in the game and showed greater passion," Gladbach sporting director Rouven Schroeder said. "The win is a relief for the entire club, but it can only be a starting point."
Despite the victory, Gladbach remain bottom with three points from seven matches, while Stuttgart sit 14th with six points after their fifth league defeat. ■

Former AFLW player and coach Lauren Arnell has slammed the standard of Collingwood, while emphasising the responsibility of coaches to "put on a show" to grow the game.

"Overall, it was not the best standard of AFLW football that we would expect to see at this point of season 11," Arnell said on ABC Radio.
"Ash Centra was one of the first to walk off the ground in tears right in front of us. Totally fair. I would probably be about the same level."
The pioneer of women's football and former captain of Carlton said while the AFLW continued to play 16 a side in venues open to conditions, unlike protected stadiums the MCG, Perth Stadium and Docklands in the men's game, if teams did not have high skill levels or offensive systems, they would not be able to put goals on the board.
"If you're Sam Wright, you've made some clear decisions where you want to play plus two behind the ball for a lot of the game. And my personal belief is that if you do that in AFLW, you're giving up score, and that's what we saw again tonight," Arnell said.
"And having coached against Collingwood in 2024, we beat them here at Alberton, and it was quite frustrating as a coach and someone who's been invested in women's sport and AFLW for a period of time, [as] you know that broadcast relies on high scoring.
"People who forever criticise AFLW as a sport, or a league, will always point to the lack of score and short quarters … and I'm a firm non-believer in heavy defensive systems for all of those reasons, not just because you can't score, but because we have a responsibility if you're coaching to grow the game and put on a show."
Last week, Collingwood CEO Craig Kelly fronted the AFLW playing group after media reports of player unrest and concerns with the operation of the women's program.
Kelly told News Corp that when AFLW was to be introduced in 2017, Collingwood put its hand up to be an inaugural club, but now he often wondered if the Magpies would have been better off waiting to enter the women's competition at a later date.
He conceded being a foundation AFLW club might have been a mistake, while ruling out any prospect of an independent review into the women's program, which other struggling clubs have done, such as Carlton in 2023, Richmond in 2025 and St Kilda following this season.
To Arnell, those remarks from Kelly screamed a lack of understanding between the executive and the playing cohort.
"That statement just immediately tells me you have never sat down with enough of your women's players and even asked them questions of their perspective and where they've come from," Arnell said.
"Like you've got no understanding of your playing group and potentially your coaching group."
Despite being one of the biggest sporting clubs in Victoria, Collingwood players are reported to feel behind local rivals in Melbourne, North Melbourne and Carlton, and are unhappy with multiple aspects of the program, including coaching, high performance and list management.
Collingwood is not alone down the bottom of the ladder, with St Kilda and Essendon also entering round 11 having won only one game this season.
"And I'll guarantee you, off the back of that, there's going to be a lot of movement in the trade period coming up in the next month and a half," Arnell said.
There is an expected player exodus from Collingwood at the season's end, with captain Ruby Schleicher already announcing she'll be leaving to head back to Western Australia. It is reported the West Coast Eagles offered her a four-year deal, while the Magpies' initial offer was a one-year contract extension, then upped to two.
On top of Schleicher, the high-profile players such as Tarni White, Brianna Davey, Sarah Rowe and Lauren Butler are all out of contract at season's end. Vice-captain Jordy Allen tried to exit last trade period for Brisbane but Collingwood blocked her attempts.
"I think the washout of this whole storyline will be well beyond Collingwood, and we're going to see evidence of it across the trade period coming in December, and it will be really clear which players feel like their club's not invested in the environment," Arnell said.

- Summary:
- Scientists discovered that the thick, sticky fluid surrounding glioblastoma tumors can make brain cancer cells smaller, more flexible, and better at invading surrounding tissue. Even more troubling, some of these changes persist after the cells leave the thick fluid, revealing a previously overlooked mechanism that could help this deadly cancer spread.
- Share:
Glioblastoma is among the most lethal forms of brain cancer, and scientists have uncovered a surprising factor that may help its cells become more invasive. The fluid surrounding the outer edges of these tumors is much thicker than the fluid near their centers, forcing cancer cells to encounter increasing resistance as they move into healthy brain tissue. Rather than simply slowing their movement, however, this environment appears to help the cells adapt in ways that make invasion easier.
To investigate this unexpected behavior, researchers created an innovative microfluidic chip that recreates the physical conditions encountered by glioblastoma cells. They found that spending extended periods in thick fluid caused the cells to become smaller, more flexible, and better able to squeeze through narrow openings. The discovery suggests that fluid viscosity does more than obstruct cancer cells. It can actively influence their behavior and potentially make them more aggressive.
How Thick Fluid Influences Brain Cancer Invasion
Cancer research has traditionally concentrated on chemical signals and the stiffness of the tissues surrounding tumors. Far less attention has been given to the viscosity of the fluid through which cancer cells travel.
In glioblastoma, this difference is particularly striking. Fluid at the tumor's advancing edge is approximately eight times more viscous than fluid in its dead tissue at the center. As cancer cells move outward, they must push through an increasingly resistant environment.
Studying this process has been difficult because conventional closed microfluidic devices cannot accurately reproduce these conditions. Their enclosed channels can limit access to oxygen and nutrients, while friction against the walls introduces additional forces that influence cell behavior. These limitations also make it challenging to observe how cancer cells respond to prolonged exposure to viscous fluid.
Researchers therefore needed a way to isolate the effects of fluid viscosity from other mechanical influences and determine whether extended exposure produces lasting changes in glioblastoma cells.
A New Device Reveals How Cancer Cells Adapt
Scientists from Chongqing General Hospital and Chongqing University in China developed a specialized open microfluidic platform to address these challenges. Their findings were published in Microsystems & Nanoengineering.
The device consists of a two-layer open microfluidic membrane equipped with a removable cap and an array of tiny pillars. This arrangement allows researchers to control precisely when cancer cells begin migrating while observing how their nuclei change shape as they move through confined spaces.
Unlike traditional enclosed systems, the platform also supports continuous cell culture for up to one month. This makes it possible to examine how prolonged mechanical stress changes the movement and invasive behavior of glioblastoma cells.
The researchers tested two human glioblastoma cell lines, U-251 and LN-229. Both were grown for a month in a thick fluid designed to reproduce conditions at the tumor's invasive outer edge (7.1 cP).
When the cells were subsequently examined using the chip, those that had adapted to the viscous environment traveled faster and covered greater distances than untreated control cells. This result was especially surprising because thicker fluid would ordinarily be expected to impede movement.
Brain Cancer Cells Become Smaller and More Flexible
Microscopic observations revealed how the adapted cells overcame this resistance. After prolonged exposure to the viscous fluid, they had become smaller and easier to deform, allowing them to maneuver through the narrow gaps between the device's microscopic pillars.
As the cells squeezed through these restricted passages, their nuclei underwent visible deformation. Researchers also observed an accumulation of YAP, a protein involved in sensing mechanical forces, inside the nuclei. This is a recognized sign that cells have activated pathways involved in responding to physical stress.
Although both glioblastoma cell lines developed similar changes in shape and movement, their underlying molecular responses were unexpectedly different.
U-251 cells underwent a form of mesenchymal-like reprogramming, activating genes associated with cancer invasion, including CD44, FN1, and MMP9. LN-229 cells, by contrast, became more flexible and mobile without showing substantial lasting changes in gene expression.
Further analysis using Western blotting showed that protein changes remained detectable even after cells were transferred back into fluid with normal viscosity. This indicated that at least some of the adaptations were persistent rather than simply short-lived responses to their surroundings.
Scientists Discover a Strange Kind of Cellular Memory
One of the most unexpected findings was that exposure to thick fluid appeared to leave a lasting imprint on glioblastoma cells.
The researchers had anticipated that viscosity would primarily function as a physical obstacle. Instead, their experiments showed that prolonged exposure could alter how cells behaved even after the original mechanical conditions were removed.
This phenomenon points to a form of mechanical memory, in which cells retain changes produced by earlier physical stress.
The open design of the new chip was essential for identifying this effect. By separating resistance from the fluid itself from the confinement imposed by channel walls, the researchers could investigate viscosity without the additional mechanical interference that complicates conventional experiments.
Observing changes in nuclear shape and migration patterns after weeks of exposure provided evidence that glioblastoma cells can adapt to their mechanical environment in lasting ways.
The contrasting molecular responses of the two cell lines were particularly revealing. Although both appeared to undergo similar physical transformations, only one showed extensive changes in its gene activity. This suggests that glioblastoma cells may acquire comparable invasive characteristics through different underlying biological processes.
A Potential New Approach to Studying Brain Cancer Treatments
Beyond uncovering an overlooked influence on glioblastoma invasion, the researchers believe their device could provide a valuable tool for investigating potential cancer therapies.
The open microfluidic platform fits into standard multi-well plates, allowing it to be incorporated into existing laboratory procedures for cell culture and imaging. Its accessible design also enables researchers to stain cells directly and observe them over long periods without the clogging problems that can occur in closed systems.
These features could make it useful for testing drugs that interfere with the cellular pathways responsible for detecting and responding to mechanical forces.
For glioblastoma, the results raise the possibility that highly viscous environments may favor cancer cells that are better adapted to invasion. Treatments targeting YAP signaling or the remodeling of the cytoskeleton, the internal framework that helps cells maintain and change their shape, could therefore be investigated under conditions that more closely resemble those inside tumors.
The technology may also prove useful for studying other cancers in which fluid viscosity varies across different regions. By examining how tumor cells respond to these mechanical conditions, researchers could gain a better understanding of why some cancers are particularly invasive and potentially identify patients whose tumors depend on mechanical adaptation to spread.
Although further research is needed to determine how these laboratory findings translate to tumors in patients, the discovery highlights an important and previously underexplored aspect of cancer biology: the physical environment surrounding tumor cells may actively shape their ability to invade healthy tissue.
Research Support and Funding

WA Greens senator Jordon Steele-John will not attend parliament next week
In short:
WA Greens senator Jordon Steele-John has confirmed he will not attend parliament when it resumes next week.
Senator Steele-John is facing allegations of inappropriate conduct towards women, which he has denied.
What's next?
An independent investigation commissioned by the WA Greens is expected to get underway imminently.
WA Greens senator Jordon Steele-John has reiterated he won't be attending parliament next week, after releasing and then deleting a copy of a letter detailing allegations of misconduct against him.
On Friday night the senator took to social media to publish the letter which is addressed to Greens leader David Shoebridge and signed by seven current and former Greens staff or party office bearers.
The writers, who are not named, state they have been made aware of "multiple allegations of serious misconduct" being made against Senator Steele-John "spanning almost a decade (2017-2025)".
"These allegations all concern his behaviour in the presence of women. We are aware of multiple women who have taken up roles or volunteered in the party, who because of these allegations, have been warned not to be alone with him."
The letter, dated October 13, goes on to state the accusations have come from both inside and outside the party, and urges Senator Shoebridge to commission an independent investigation into the allegations, and review and update gendered violence protocols.
Senator Steele-John has repeatedly and strenuously denied the allegations.
On Saturday the 32-year-old senator said a copy of the letter was sent to him by Chief Political Commentator for the Nine papers, James Massola, who then broke the story on October 15.
The senator said he had initially chosen to post the letter on his own social media accounts because he "did not want to be seen as hiding from it".
"I'm now not sure that was the right call and I've taken it down. I'm really sorry for any additional distress it caused," he said, and reiterated his absence from parliament next week.
The WA branch of the Greens has commissioned an independent investigation into the allegations.
'Growing chorus'
In the days after the allegations became public, Senator Shoebridge initially said he understood Senator Steele-John was taking leave from parliament.
But last Sunday the WA senator denied that was the case in a lengthy open letter, prompting the federal Greens leader to encourage his colleague to take leave.
"I think the community assumptions are that he step aside for the extent of this inquiry and I've communicated that to Jordon," Senator Shoebridge told ABC Radio National Breakfast on Thursday.
In a statement on Saturday, Senator Shoebridge reiterated his view that Senator Steele-John take leave.
"This is in no way a prejudgement of any of these matters," he said.
Senator Steele-John reflected in his post on Friday that there had been a "growing chorus" calling on him to not attend parliament next week, when senate estimates will take place.
"I have explored attending digitally but have been informed that would also be unacceptable," he said.
"The precedent has now been set: any MP can be kept out of parliament by allegations of allegations."

Inside the cyber flaw scramble that brought the AI threat to life
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
15:46:49 UTC
00:46:49 KST

Inside the cyber flaw scramble that brought the AI threat to life
Vulnerabilities in a programming language underpinning much of the web set off a hectic 72-hour rush among virtually every cybersecurity agency in the world.
The exposure was immense, with AI multiplying the risks — and yet time-tested global cybersecurity procedures appeared to be functioning. Then suddenly, it all broke down.
The decision by a cybersecurity company on Wednesday to prematurely release information about a flaw in the popular PHP computer programming language left much of the web exposed to hackers, triggering a panic that brought to life months of warnings of how the AI-powered era could cause widespread damage.
The flaws in PHP, discovered using AI tools through a months-long process coordinated by OpenAI, caused cyber agencies across Europe, the U.S., the U.K., Australia and Canada to post urgent warnings Wednesday. Numerous governments took websites offline as a precaution.
Advertisement
While no major hacking damage was immediately apparent, the way the incident unfolded over 72 hours showed how easily cybersecurity processes can break down and the outsized consequences of cyber risks in the AI era.
The man who set off the chain reaction with the early release — Chainguard’s CEO Dan Lorenc — quickly apologized in a LinkedIn post. But on Thursday, in an interview with POLITICO, Lorenc said he’d shared the information ahead of time because the flaw was already being exploited. Though others disputed that, Lorenc said he believed he’d seen enough evidence to invalidate an embargo set up to allow time to find a fix for the flaws.
While he disputed that his actions would have caused problems for other defenders, Lorenc conceded that the evidential threshold in these coordinated cyber defense systems is a “grey area.”
The revelation of the PHP flaw brings out into the open what cyber officials have been bracing for since the arrival of the most powerful tools of artificial intelligence, which not only can be used to discover vulnerabilities but also to exploit them at scale.
The cybersecurity world’s long-established protocols helped prevent disaster scenarios, in which hackers would have successfully exploited the vulnerabilities to take control of numerous websites and access their data. But now the scale and end-of-days potential of AI-driven cyber risks are visible for the world to see.
This “is what happens when AI turns up a flaw that’s been hiding for years,” said Eylam Milner, co-founder and chief technology officer at cybersecurity start-up Echo. The vulnerabilities, he added, are “about as serious as it gets for the web.”
Advertisement
Origin story
Understanding how this week’s emergency unfolded offers a glimpse at how companies and authorities are working to stave off attacks — and how much risk they face going forward.
The origins of the incident can be traced back as far as April when top frontier AI firm Anthropic unveiled Mythos, leading some in the cybersecurity world to worry that systems would quickly be overrun by advanced artificial intelligence, with potential for catastrophic events to ensue.
But while researchers did find more flaws in computer systems in the months after Anthropic and other AI firms like OpenAI released those models, they had little impact in the real world. Even the Hugging Face incident, a widely discussed hack that saw OpenAI's autonomous AI agents go rogue during an internal security evaluation, related more to the level of control AI companies exert over their models than their power to break into systems worldwide.
A figurine is pictured in front of the Anthropic logo in Paris on Feb. 13, 2026. | Joel Saget/AFP via Getty Images
That changed this week after researchers unveiled the vulnerability in PHP, a coding language estimated to be integrated into some 70% of the web.
The process by which information about flaws is released among cybersecurity officials and affiliated companies is crucial. Through a longstanding practice known as coordinated disclosure, researchers and companies that identify flaws can find a fix and share it confidentially with agencies and others before releasing to the public, meaning they don’t hand malicious hackers the gift of a hole without a fix.
In the case of the PHP flaw, that process worked well, but not perfectly. Information about the bugs started to circulate ahead of the planned release time. Then, according to the PHP Foundation, Chainguard “unilaterally broke the embargo,” which “disregarded weeks of work by many parties toward a coordinated disclosure.” PHP Foundation executive director Elizabeth Barron told POLITICO by email that while it was “disappointed” with Chainguard, it hopes to “rebuild trust with them in the future to ensure we can continue to collaborate effectively.”
Advertisement
After the leak— which meant information about the bugs was in the open before the fix was ready — confusion quickly ensued, with government bodies and private companies choosing to temporarily shut down their websites rather than risk potentially damaging breaches to their data and the sites themselves.
Early Thursday, Matthew Prince, the CEO of Cloudflare, an internet services company that is widely used by websites to block cyberattacks, giving it a high level of visibility over what hackers are doing, said in a post on X that it had seen “millions” of attempts to exploit the flaw.
Cloudflare saw thousands in the 10 hours before the flaw was publicly announced, then tens of thousands in the 45 minutes after the announcement, hundreds of thousands within two hours, and now millions, Prince said.
Amazon’s cloud division also said the flaw is “now being broadly exploited in the wild.”
One senior U.S. government cyber official said that federal authorities have been overwhelmed — and not just by PHP. The same day the world was racing to address PHP, they were also dealing with bugs in node.js, a widely used JavaScript framework, Fortinet, GitHub and Oracle.
“The fire department is fighting multiple fires at once,” the official said, adding: “The good news is they're all one-story structures on fire, which the fire department deals with all day, every day.”
Advertisement
Matthew Prince, CEO of Cloudflare, speaks during the Semafor World Economy conference in Washington, on April 17, 2026. | Mandel Ngan/AFP via Getty Images
More to come
Dauntingly, OpenAI said there’s more on the way. “These bugs are among several significant vulnerabilities we’ve already found and are working to fix, and we expect similar findings to increase sharply in the coming months,” the company said Wednesday in a statement.
Matthijs van Amelsfort, head of the Dutch cybersecurity agency, said in an interview that the job of keeping computer systems safe has been transformed by the advancement of AI. “As soon as the frontier models came out, that's exactly what we said, this will be the trend,” he said. “And actually that's happening now.”
Thomas Caspers, vice president of Germany’s cyber agency BSI, concurred: “We expect that [to be] happening more and more during the coming months.”
AI also ramps up the risks once the flaws are out in the open. Cyber agencies’ recommendation that organizations take their websites offline was “really a drastic measure,” Caspers said. “We wouldn't have done that a few years ago or so.” But because AI has made it quicker and easier to exploit flaws, “we had to do that,” he said.
At the same time, the use of advanced AI to detect the flaws may create a new level of protection against malicious hackers looking to take advantage of them. Caspers said that though his German agency has also seen attacks, it has not seen any successful use of the flaw by hackers.
“It seems a little bit more complicated than expected to exploit,” he said.
Advertisement
Despite the fact that AI offers a new way to discover flaws, the work involved in keeping systems protected is more quotidian, with cyber agencies urging organizations to install the fix shared by the PHP Foundation, in a process known as patching.
“There are three things that you have to do right now,” said van Amelsfort from the Dutch agency. “And that’s patch, patch, and patch.”

Being outside in high winds could make people "more vulnerable to injury," it said.
It advised residents to stay indoors "as much as possible."

Six Flags will add seat belts to some roller coasters after rider’s death
Emmett Lindner
- Six Flags will add seat belts to select roller coasters after Hassan Jihad Ibn Kariem, 42, died on Goliath at Six Flags Over Georgia. The ride is closed while state and police investigate.
- The company said independent engineers and inspectors are reviewing all rides. John Reilly said Six Flags will take action to “further strengthen” safety standards.
- Nitro and Raging Bull will also get seat belts. The move follows lawsuits over X2 at Six Flags Magic Mountain and wider scrutiny of ride safety.
AI generated
CHARLOTTE, North Carolina – Six Flags will add seat belts to select roller coasters across its parks, the company said on Oct 23, weeks after the death of a man who fell from a ride at one of its properties.
The announcement came as Six Flags contended with recent lawsuits over safety concerns.
John Reilly, president of Six Flags Entertainment, said in a statement on Oct 23 that the company’s parks hired independent engineers and inspectors to conduct safety reviews of all rides and attractions as the additional safety measures were put in place.
“We are committed to carefully evaluating their findings and taking appropriate action to further strengthen our standards and culture of safety,” Reilly said in the statement.
Earlier in October, Hassan Jihad Ibn Kariem, 42, was thrown from his seat and declared dead after riding Goliath at Six Flags Over Georgia in Austell, Georgia, the state’s tallest roller coaster. That ride is temporarily closed and will receive seat belts when it reopens.
Goliath was previously equipped with the commonly used lap-bar “clamshell” restraints, which swing down to lock above the riders’ laps.
The state authorities, as well as the Cobb County Police Department, are investigating the death, but there is no single federal agency responsible for enforcing safety standards for rides like Goliath, which had passed its most recent state inspection March 16.
The other attractions that will receive the safety additions are Nitro at Six Flags Great Adventure in Jackson, New Jersey, and Raging Bull at Six Flags Great America in Gurnee, Illinois, which is north of Chicago, a spokesperson for the company said in an e-mail on Oct 24.
Aside from Goliath, eight rides at five other parks are temporarily closed, Reilly said in his statement.
Ride safety at Six Flags parks has come under intense scrutiny over the past several weeks, even before Kariem’s death.
In September, three people sued the amusement park company and the ride’s manufacturer after suffering what they said were catastrophic brain injuries from riding the X2 coaster at Six Flags Magic Mountain in Southern California.
The lawsuits accuse Six Flags and a manufacturer of X2’s parts of operating a defectively designed ride and failing to adequately warn passengers about the risk of serious brain injuries.
That month, Six Flags Magic Mountain said the X2 would permanently close.
Before those lawsuits, Reilly said during an August call with analysts that the company incurred higher repair and maintenance expenses at certain parks as it reduced downtime, adding, “We will not compromise on safety.”
In its second-quarter financial filings, released in August, Six Flags reported that its net revenue was US$865 million (S$1.1 billion), a decrease of US$65 million from the same time in 2025. Attendance for the quarter was just above 13 million visits, a decrease from more than 14 million for the same period in 2025.
There are currently more than 220 coasters operating across all Six Flags parks, Reilly said on Oct 23.
“We will continue to communicate about our progress and hold ourselves accountable to our commitments to you,” he said. NYTIMES

CANBERRA, Oct. 24 (Xinhua) -- The Australian government on Saturday announced an additional 10 million Australian dollars (about 7 million U.S. dollars) in funding to upgrade an airport damaged by severe flooding in Queensland, the northeastern state of Australia.

The airport suffered significant flood damage during extreme weather events in late 2025 and early 2026.
The new commitment builds on 11.5 million Australian dollars previously provided jointly by the federal and Queensland governments for emergency repairs and flood resilience measures that allowed the airport to reopen.
Minister for Infrastructure, Transport, Regional Development and Local Government Catherine King said the additional funding would help ensure the airport continues to support essential services, including aeromedical transport and mining operations.
Cloncurry Airport serves as a key transport hub for the region's mining, agriculture and tourism industries, as well as fly-in, fly-out workers employed at nearby mines. ■

====================================================================================================

Reading Xi's vision for global governance through metaphors
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
04:45:21 UTC
13:45:21 KST

The 2026 Global Governance Forum (Xiong'an) is set to open on Friday in the Xiong'an New Area, north China's Hebei Province, bringing into world focus a pressing question: How can countries work together to address shared challenges in an interconnected world amid growing protectionism and unilateralism?
In speeches and meetings on multiple occasions, Chinese President Xi Jinping has used vivid metaphors to articulate his vision for global governance. These metaphors offer insights into his approach to building a more just, equitable and inclusive global governance system.
IN SAME BOAT
"I was looking at the vast ocean when I boarded the ship, and it struck me that we are all indeed fellow passengers in the same boat," Xi said while addressing the 2018 APEC CEO Summit hosted at a unique setting -- onboard the giant cruise Pacific Explorer in Port Moresby, Papua New Guinea.
The metaphor embodies the essence of Xi's vision of building a community with a shared future for humanity, highlighting the interconnectedness of countries and the need for solidarity and cooperation in addressing common challenges.
Today, the interconnected world is grappling with four mounting deficits: a peace deficit that exacerbates geopolitical conflicts, a development deficit that widens the North-South divide, a security deficit that erodes mutual trust, and a governance deficit that undermines the effectiveness of multilateralism.
In 2019, at the China-France Global Governance Forum held in Paris, Xi proposed a four-pronged approach to addressing the four deficits. First and foremost, he called for fairness and reasonableness to address the governance deficit.
"It is advisable to uphold a vision of global governance featuring extensive consultation and joint contribution for shared benefits," Xi said, calling for actively advancing the democratization of global governance rules.
As the world has found itself in a new period of turbulence and transformation, global governance has come to a new crossroads. Against this backdrop, Xi put forward the Global Governance Initiative (GGI) at the Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO) summit in September 2025 in China's coastal city of Tianjin.
"I look forward to working with all countries for a more just and equitable global governance system and advancing toward a community with a shared future for humanity," Xi said, stressing sovereign equality and genuine multilateralism.
TRAFFIC LIGHTS
"A world without rules is like a crossroads without traffic lights, where chaos and disorder are all but guaranteed," Xi said at the 2026 BRICS Summit in New Delhi, India.
This metaphor highlights the importance of rules in maintaining the international order. While having rules in place matters, how they are made and who gets to make them matter even more. International rules must be written and upheld jointly by all countries based on the purposes and principles of the UN Charter, rather than dictated by those with the strongest muscles or the loudest voice, Xi once stressed.
He has also called for the purposes and principles of the UN Charter and other universally recognized basic norms of international relations to be observed comprehensively, fully and in their entirety.
"There should be no double standards, and the house rules of a few countries must not be imposed upon others," he said.
The GGI proposed by President Xi reflects the objective transformation of the world system and responds to the aspirations of most countries for a fairer and more representative system of global governance, said Rahmon Ulmasov, a professor at the Russian-Tajik (Slavonic) University.
MAKING THE PIE BIGGER
Xi has repeatedly used the metaphor of a pie to describe the gains of international cooperation. "We should make the pie of win-win cooperation bigger, and ensure that more development gains will be shared more fairly by people across the world," he said at the 23rd meeting of the Council of Heads of State of the Shanghai Cooperation Organization in 2023.
The pie metaphor reflects the people-centered and action-oriented vision of the GGI: making the gains of cooperation bigger while ensuring that they are shared more widely and fairly. When proposing the GGI, Xi emphasized the importance of "ensuring that the people of every nation are the actors in and beneficiaries of global governance."The SCO, the platform where Xi proposed the GGI, provides an example. Within the grouping, China has announced the establishment of cooperation platforms in energy, green industries and the digital economy, as well as centers for scientific and technological innovation, higher education, and vocational and technical education.
The expanding scope of cooperation shows how the "pie" can be made bigger in practice: by opening up new areas of cooperation, creating more opportunities for development and ensuring that the benefits reach more people.
Beyond making the pie bigger, Xi has also called for sharing the pie fairly to ensure justice and equity. For him, the ultimate purpose of better global governance is to promote common development and improve people's well-being across the globe.
At the G20 summit held in Brazil in 2024, Xi called for building a just world of common development, saying "prosperity and stability would not be possible in a world where the rich become richer while the poor are made poorer, and countries should make global development more inclusive, beneficial to all, and more resilient."
To build such a world, Xi said, there should be more bridges of cooperation, and less "small yard, high fences," so that more and more developing countries will be better off and achieve modernization.
Source: Xinhua

Camille Cottin elevates French family drama 'Out of Love' as it opens in Israeli theaters - review
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
00:23:31 UTC
09:23:31 KST

Out of Love, directed by Nathan Ambrosioni, which opened in theaters throughout Israel on Thursday, is a well-made if somewhat bland French drama about a single woman forced through circumstances to care for her sister’s children.
It joins a long list of European movies that play briefly in theaters and tackle the kinds of issues that used to be a staple of American TV movies. Many people enjoy these relatable dramas, and this one features an element that nudges it a little above the usual standard for these films: the always watchable Camille Cottin in the lead.
She is one of France’s most popular actresses, and deservedly so. She is terrific in both comedy and drama, and she has real screen presence. When she’s there, you can’t take your eyes off of her.
Even if you don’t recognize her name, you have likely seen her in recent movies, such as Just an Illusion and In the Land of Arto, or the television series Call My Agent! and the recent movie based on it, where she played an intensely narcissistic character who nonetheless became a fan favorite. She also played Golda Meir’s secretary opposite Helen Mirren in the 2023 movie, Golda.
Jeanne, the character she portrays in Out of Love, is a tense, successful insurance claims adjuster who broke up with her longtime girlfriend because the girlfriend wanted children and she didn’t. So she isn’t exactly delighted when her younger sister, Suzanne (Juliette Armanet), after years of silence, shows up out of the blue with her two children (Manoa Varvet and Nina Birman), asks to stay over, and then leaves during the night.
Movie opens with a powerful scene
Jeanne has no idea where her sister is or why she has done this. The movie opens with what turns out to be one of its most effective scenes, told from the point of view of the children, who are waiting for their mother, who has gone into the store at a gas station and left them in the car.
They are anxious because she seems to them to have been gone a long time, and we soon learn how much her behavior has made them afraid in general lately.
At first Jeanne, understandably, thinks that her sister may be experiencing a momentary crisis and will soon return for the extremely sweet children.
But when she can’t get in touch with Suzanne after a day or so, she contacts the police, who say that they cannot do anything to find a woman who has left her children with a relative and gone away. If she will not care for them, the youngsters will be put into the foster care system and likely sent to different homes.
Scenes are well filmed, well acted
Jeanne reluctantly steps up, and the movie details her journey of trying to tap into her softer side to become a maternal figure to the children. She also copes with a troubled heritage from her very dysfunctional parents, which has harmed her sister deeply and which she has tried to push from her mind.
Each scene is well filmed and well acted. Thanks to Cottin’s performance, we are instantly in Jeanne’s head, and we feel for her. But it’s evident from the beginning that once she is called to take care of these children, it’s only a matter of time until she is transformed into the stable parental figure they need.
Although she has anxiety attacks and chain-smokes nervously, it’s clear that she has a core of inner strength, and the tone of the movie is generally upbeat. Her coworkers are understanding and helpful; even a police officer contacts her to apologize.
Out of Love presents a soothing universe where things fall into place in the end, perhaps a little more neatly than they do anywhere but in a TV-style movie.

Thousands rally in Tel Aviv against Netanyahu ahead of vote
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-25
00:10:00 UTC
09:10:00 KST

Thousands rally in Tel Aviv against Netanyahu ahead of vote
- Thousands rallied in Tel Aviv against Benjamin Netanyahu before Israel’s election, led by the October Council and families of Oct 7 victims and hostages demanding accountability.
- Polls showed no clear majority for either bloc, while opposition figures Gadi Eisenkot and Naftali Bennett drew support and vowed to challenge Netanyahu’s rule.
- The protest also pushed for an independent inquiry into the Oct 7 failures, as Netanyahu faced criticism over isolation, sanctions, and his talk of a possible alternate digital economy.
AI generated
TEL AVIV – Thousands gathered in Tel Aviv on Oct 24 for a large anti-government demonstration, three days ahead of a general election widely viewed as a referendum on Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.
The protest was organised by the October Council, a group founded by the families of victims and hostages taken by Palestinian militants on Oct 7, 2023, to demand accountability for the failure to prevent the Hamas attack that sparked the Gaza war.
According to Israeli media, the gathering saw the participation of the leaders of the four main opposition parties, including Gadi Eisenkot, the former military chief of staff who is neck and neck with Netanyahu and who received a warm reception from the crowd.
“Three days before the election, we will hold the culminating event marking three years of struggle to uncover the truth, demand accountability, and establish a state commission of inquiry,” the October Council wrote on X ahead of the rally.
The latest polls published before a gag period entered into force on the night of Oct 23 showed that neither bloc would obtain a majority of seats in Israel’s Parliament.
A poll published by public broadcaster KAN found that out of 120 seats in the Israeli Parliament, 52 would go to Eisenkot’s bloc and 50 to Netanyahu’s, with the rest going to non-aligned parties, including Arab ones.
An AFP reporter said thousands were marching from the central Rabin Square towards Hostages Square, a focal point for past anti-government protests to demand the release of those held captive in Gaza.
“Whoever has been leading us for the past four years (since Netanyahu’s government took office in late 2022) has done such a terrible job,” Hadas Feuershtein, 68, told AFP shortly before the start of the rally.
“Israel has never been in a situation as it is now,” she added.
Ahead of the rally, the October Council had alerted law enforcement of possible “provocations” from pro-government agitators.
The Israeli police said on the evening of Oct 24 that it “arrested a suspect for assaulting the security team of a public figure” in Tel Aviv, with the Israeli press identifying the target as former Prime Minister and opposition party leader Naftali Bennett.
The rally came after years of campaigning by Israeli civil society and opposition parties to establish an independent commission of inquiry on the security failures that led to the attack on Oct 7, 2023.
Netanyahu’s government has refused to establish such an independent body, the likes of which Israel has commonly set up in the past to investigate major state-level failings.
It has instead offered to create a “political” commission, half of whose members would be appointed by the ruling coalition and half by opposition lawmakers.
Opposition leaders, however, said they would boycott a commission appointed by politicians.
As the campaign draws to an end, Eisenkot and Bennett are expected to hold separate last meetings with voters in Tel Aviv on the evening of Oct 25.
No ‘bbCoin’
First-time voter Naama Bitterman, 18, said at the rally on Oct 24 that she was confident the anti-Netanyahu bloc she supports would have the upper hand in the vote and improve Israel’s international standing, tarnished by three years of war in Gaza, Lebanon and Iran and surging violence in the occupied West Bank.
“I think that if we win – and we are going to win – we can change how other people in the entire world see us,” she told AFP.
Britain and several other countries imposed sanctions targeting goods from Israeli settlements in the West Bank in response to a wave of settler attacks on Palestinians and settlement construction approved by Netanyahu’s right-wing government.
To circumvent Israel’s growing international isolation, Netanyahu suggested on Oct 23 that Israel may need to develop an alternate digital economy.
Netanyahu, who has previously called for Israel to become self-sufficient militarily, also said that multibillion-dollar weapons packages from key ally Washington “won’t keep coming”.
Opposition leaders on Oct 24 lambasted the premier’s suggestion.
Eisenkot sarcastically referred to the proposed parallel digital currency as “bbCoin”, using a common nickname for the premier, Bibi.
“Netanyahu says that if he is elected again, Israel will disconnect from the global economy. No online shopping, no investments in high-tech, no security. We must not let bbCoin destroy Israel,” he wrote on X.

Bulgaria votes for president in wake of deadly Black Sea drone strikes
SOFIA, Oct 25 - Bulgarians vote in presidential elections on Sunday as Russia's war in Ukraine spreads to the waters off Bulgaria's Black Sea coast.
Polls place acting President Iliana Iotova, 61, and ex-caretaker prime minister Andrey Gyurov, 50, as leaders in a race of 27 candidates.
While the presidency is largely ceremonial, Sunday's vote has taken on added significance after a series of drone attacks on merchant ships off Bulgaria's Black Sea coast that likely killed some two-dozen international seafarers.
The strikes, which sparked international condemnation and concerns about the growing reach of the war in Ukraine, prompted the government to seek allied assistance to bolster maritime security.
Bulgaria has stopped short of directly accusing Russia of carrying out the attacks, but Prime Minister Rumen Radev said their outcome "benefits the Russian Federation".
Both leading presidential candidates condemned the strikes, but they differ over the broader war.
Gyurov, who served as caretaker prime minister this year, is supported by pro-Western, reformist parties and has long expressed support for Ukraine. He signed a security cooperation agreement with Kyiv during his time as premier.
"I want Bulgaria to have a voice of its own in Europe. A reliable NATO ally that defends its interests through preparedness, strong diplomacy and a clear position," he said at a rally on Thursday.
Iotova, formerly vice president, became acting president in January after Radev resigned to enter the parliamentary race, which he won on what many political analysts considered a Kremlin-friendly ticket. Radev supports Iotova and they both call for a diplomatic end to the war.
A victory for Iotova would make her Bulgaria's first elected female president.
"My opponents argue that there must be a war of attrition." she told a rally on Thursday. "The truth is, we are all the ones who are most exhausted."
Polls by Alpha Research give Iotova 41% of the vote and Gyurov 28%. If no candidate wins a majority, a runoff vote will be held on November 1.
Voting starts at 7 a.m. (0500 GMT) and polls close at 8 p.m. REUTERS

New Delhi reiterated that Jammu and Kashmir remains an integral and inalienable part of India.
NEW DELHI: India tore into Pakistan at the United Nations for exploiting the international forum to spread propaganda while failing to protect its own citizens. New Delhi reiterated that Jammu and Kashmir remains an integral and inalienable part of India and demanded that Pakistan vacate all territories under its illegal occupation.Speaking at an interactive dialogue with the Special Rapporteur on Minority Issues at the UN General Assembly's Third Committee, India's First Secretary at the Permanent Mission to the UN, Raghoo Puri, called out Pakistan's conduct and said its representatives should focus on the welfare of their own people instead of taking directions from the military."Pakistan predictably misused the forum for propaganda. Jammu & Kashmir is an integral and inalienable part of India. Pakistan must vacate the territory under its illegal occupation," Puri said.He further said Pakistani representatives would do well to look inwards and address the concerns of their own citizens rather than act on military directives.
India slams Pakistan over minority rights
Puri underlined that protecting minority rights was primarily the sovereign responsibility of individual states, guided by the principle of sovereign equality.He said India's civilisational tradition of diversity was reflected in its constitutional safeguards for religious and linguistic minorities.
He also highlighted the substantial contributions made by minorities to India's national development, including at the highest levels of government and key institutions.
The latest confrontation followed India's strong rebuke to Pakistan at the UN on October 23 over its treatment of religious minorities. New Delhi accused Islamabad of failing to protect vulnerable communities while attempting to lecture India on religious freedom, burial rights and minority protections.During an interactive dialogue with the Special Rapporteur on Freedom of Religion or Belief, India's First Secretary at the UN mission, Bhavika Mangalanandan, challenged the report's approach to religious discrimination during the Covid-19 pandemic and its advocacy concerning funeral rights for terrorists.Mangalanandan argued that the report appeared to place disproportionate emphasis on discriminatory practices and shortcomings in countries in the Global South while overlooking similar tragedies in developed nations.
India asserts climate justice and judicial independence
Separately, India also defended its approach to climate change at the UN General Assembly, stressing the importance of equity, climate justice and sustainable development.Deputy secretary Barkha Tamrakar delivered India's statement before the Third Committee on the report of the Special Rapporteur on the independence of judges and lawyers, titled “An urgent and existential threat: the role of justice systems in addressing the climate crisis.”Tamrakar described climate change as a serious global challenge with consequences for development, livelihoods and human rights. She said India's response was guided by equity, climate justice, sustainable development and the principle of Common But Differentiated Responsibilities and Respective Capabilities (CBDR-RC).
She highlighted the Constitution, environmental legislation, the National Green Tribunal and an independent judiciary as key safeguards supporting environmental protection in India.Tamrakar also noted that the Supreme Court had recognised the fundamental rights to life and equality as essential protections against the adverse effects of climate change.On judicial independence, she pointed to transparent, institutionally supervised training programmes, including those conducted by the National Judicial Academy, as measures to strengthen impartiality and safeguard the independence of the judiciary.

PORT-AU-PRINCE, Oct 24 (Reuters) - Bodies believed to be those of four Salvadoran soldiers missing since an ambush by armed gangs in Haiti have been found outside the capital, Port-au-Prince, the New York Times reported on Saturday, citing two people close to the security mission.
The newspaper said the remains were recovered on Saturday and were badly burned, meaning autopsies would be needed to confirm their identities. It said the bodies were handed over at the international airport to a Salvadoran military team that had flown into Haiti on Friday.
The international security mission declined to comment. Reuters could not immediately confirm the report.
The four Salvadorans went missing on Sunday after they jumped from a burning armored vehicle that came under attack on the outskirts of Port-au-Prince while they were returning from a market to their base, Salvadoran officials said earlier this week. The ambush was the first major attack on the Gang Suppression Force, a United Nations-authorized multinational mission, since it began operations in Haiti this year.
President Nayib Bukele said on Wednesday that gangs were holding the four men and that El Salvador had launched a military operation to bring them back unharmed. Additional Salvadoran troops were later deployed to support search and security operations.
No group has publicly claimed responsibility for the attack. Local media have linked the ambush to gangs operating in the area, including powerful armed groups Chen Mechan and 400 Mawozo.
A year into its mandate, the GSF has about 2,000 troops on the ground, well below its authorized ceiling of 5,500. An earlier Kenyan-led security effort struggled with chronic shortages of money, equipment and personnel.
Haiti’s gangs have expanded sharply since the 2021 assassination of President Jovenel Moise, taking control of large parts of Port-au-Prince and displacing 1.4 million to 1.5 million people.

Yemen's Houthis renew warning against using Riyadh airport
Oct 25 - Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthis on Sunday renewed their warning against using Riyadh's King Khalid International Airport, hours after the airport announced it will designate two terminals for flights following a suspension earlier this month.
Houthi military spokesperson Yahya Saree said the airport remained a "military target" and operations targeting the airport will continue, warning all airlines, airport staffers and travellers against using it.
Late on Saturday, King Khalid Airport said Terminal 1 would be designated for domestic flights and Terminal 2 for international flights operated by national carriers starting Sunday.
Operations in the airport were halted on October 10, following an attack on the airport, claimed by the Houthis, that killed 13 people and wounded more than 300 others, the deadliest in the kingdom in more than a decade. The suspension of operations was extended two days later.
The Houthis have been firing ballistic missiles and drones at Saudi airports, ports and oil installations, turning US ally Saudi Arabia into a pressure point in the wider war.
Saudi Arabia has recently stepped up its military involvement in Yemen, launching strikes against the Houthis and backing a government counteroffensive after the Houthis seized strategic territory along the Red Sea coast last month. REUTERS

Massive Ukrainian drone attack hits shopping center in Russia's Belgorod Oblast, locals say
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
23:27:09 UTC
