Haredi Public's Moti Leitner: Israel’s future is our responsibility, too - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
17:47:26 UTC
02:47:26 KST

Nearly one in three Jewish children entering first grade in Israel attends a haredi (ultra-Orthodox) school. Some demographic projections suggest that by 2050, almost one in three Jewish Israelis could be haredi.
These figures carry a profound responsibility for our community. The education our children receive, the opportunities available to them, and their contribution to the country will help determine Israel’s future.
We are haredim. Torah learning and religious commitment are central to our lives. We know the challenges facing our community because we live within it. And we believe the responsibility for addressing them belongs to us.
For decades, haredi political leadership has concentrated on protecting Torah learning, religious identity, and communal independence. But the challenges of the coming decades demand a broader understanding of responsibility.
A community must prepare its children for the lives ahead, enable its families to achieve economic independence, and accept its share of responsibility for defending the country.
The future of haredi society and the future of Israel are inseparable. Across haredi society, families are already making choices that reflect this understanding.
Parents are seeking schools that combine serious Torah education with broader learning. Young men outside full-time Torah study are entering employment and military service. Women are seeking a greater voice in decisions affecting their communities and the country.
Nearly 19,000 haredi students were enrolled in higher education in 2024-2025, more than four times the number 15 years earlier. State-haredi schools are providing children with religious education alongside general studies.
These developments are taking place through families, educators, rabbis, and organizations working within haredi society.
The Haredi Public party has emerged from this constituency. Its slogan is simple: “Hapam lokchim achrayut.” This time, we take responsibility.
For us, that begins with education. Children deserve serious Torah learning alongside the knowledge and skills to earn a dignified livelihood, develop their abilities, and contribute to society.
It extends to military service. Those seriously devoting their lives to Torah learning should be able to continue learning. Those who are not seriously learning should share responsibility for defending Israel, within frameworks that respect their religious commitments.
Service is not merely a concession made to secure exemptions for others. The obligation arises because Israel is our country too.
Women already carry enormous responsibilities within haredi society. Their experience and abilities should also find expression in political leadership and in decisions affecting the country.
These commitments describe a haredi life in which religious identity and national responsibility belong together.
A lasting political voice
The Haredi Public is contesting the forthcoming election to give political representation to a constituency already pursuing a broader understanding of responsibility.
Representation in the Knesset would give that constituency a voice in decisions about education, employment, military service, and public policy. It would also give greater political standing to the people and institutions already working for change within haredi society.
The significance extends beyond our community. As the haredi population grows, its education, economic independence, and participation in national defense will increasingly affect Israel as a whole. Government policy matters, but lasting progress also requires people within haredi society who are prepared to take responsibility for these questions themselves.
We believe this undertaking should be understood across Israeli society. The responsibility for leading it belongs within haredi society, while its consequences concern the country we all share.
We have recently been approached about withdrawing from the election. We have no intention of doing so.
Our decision to enter politics reflects a commitment that extends beyond a single campaign. The people whose aspirations we represent are already building their lives around these responsibilities, and their political voice deserves to be heard.
We are here to stay. We are not going anywhere.
The question is no longer whether haredi society will shape Israel’s future. It will. The responsibility we are accepting is to help determine what kind of future that will be.

No Persian Gulf for old carriers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
17:47:11 UTC
02:47:11 KST

No Persian Gulf for old carriers
Top commander says American warships will never return as Strait of Hormuz becomes center of war
TEHRAN – The main confrontation between Iran and the United States in this war has been, and continues to be, in the Persian Gulf and the Strait of Hormuz, and senior Iranian commanders now say the era when American aircraft carriers cruised these waters with impunity is over for good.
In his strongest remarks to date on the naval war, Chief of the General Staff of the Armed Forces and Commander of the Central Khatam al-Anbiya Headquarters, Major General Ali Abdollahi, declared that the U.S. Navy has been rendered ineffective and will never be allowed back into the Persian Gulf.
Abdollahi said: The proud Armed Forces of Islamic Iran, with trust in Almighty God, have managed to render ineffective the U.S. Navy, which Trump and the leaders of that country regard as the pinnacle of American power and with which they threaten the region and the world, in such a way that it is no longer able to approach the seas surrounding the Persian Gulf and Iran’s territorial waters.
“The U.S. president must dream of his military and army once again entering the Persian Gulf. They will take this wish to the grave forever,” he added.
“We will under no circumstances and at no time allow American military vessels to enter the Persian Gulf,” he stressed.
From overthrow to reopening the Strait
His remarks, delivered as Washington and Tel Aviv openly speak of “finishing the job” and preparing a renewed offensive, underscore how far the war’s objectives have shifted. What began as an American-Israeli campaign to overthrow the Islamic Republic or force its surrender has now, after more than eight months of war, been reduced in practice to a struggle to reopen the Strait of Hormuz.
When the war began in June 2025 with surprise strikes in the middle of negotiations, and escalated again in February 2026 and June this year, U.S. President Donald Trump promised swift collapse in Tehran, destruction of Iran’s nuclear program, and an end to its missile and regional power. None of that happened.
Instead, Iran survived, retaliated with massive missile, drone and naval operations against American bases and Israeli targets, tightened its control over the Strait of Hormuz, and imposed an unprecedented energy and military cost on Washington. Moody’s estimates the war has already cost American consumers $265 billion this year, about $2,000 per household, half of it from higher energy prices.
Today, American officials no longer speak of imminent regime change in Tehran. They speak of restoring freedom of navigation, reopening the Strait, securing detained vessels, and preventing oil prices from climbing beyond $110 per barrel after mine incidents involving tankers. In other words, the superpower that came to bring Iran to its knees is now fighting to bring its own ships back through a waterway guarded by Iran.
Abdollahi directly mocked that reversal: Trump has repeatedly claimed that they have destroyed Iran’s nuclear facilities, but at the same time they keep repeating that Iran must not have nuclear weapons, and this blatant contradiction has no end.
“If you have destroyed everything, then what is the meaning of repeating these hallucinations? These remarks are utterly meaningless, contradictory and repetitive, and are consumed to deceive world public opinion and especially the American people,” he said.
“If you are sure that you have destroyed all of Iran’s military facilities and capabilities, then why do your rusted carriers, vessels and cowardly military forces not dare to approach the Strait of Hormuz and Iran’s maritime and land borders?” he asked.
Fifth Fleet no longer functional
That question now defines the military map of the region. Iranian officials say U.S. forces, after suffering painful blows from the guardians of the Strait, no longer come forward from the Arabian Sea, and whenever they have taken that risk, they have harmed themselves.
Leader of the Islamic Revolution Ayatollah Seyed Mojtaba Khamenei made the same point in his message of September 28, which Abdollahi’s statement echoed: These days [the enemy forces], because of the painful blows they have received from the guardians of the Strait of Hormuz, do not come forward from the Arabian Sea, and whenever they have risked this danger, they have inflicted damage upon themselves; and soon the Arabian Sea itself will rid itself of them.
Iranian commanders say this is not rhetoric but the result of sustained, heavy strikes on the very infrastructure that once sustained American dominance in the Persian Gulf.
According to Iranian military assessments, U.S. bases around the Persian Gulf — in Bahrain, Qatar, the United Arab Emirates, Kuwait and Iraq — have been repeatedly targeted since the start of the war and have suffered extensive damage. Above all, the U.S. Fifth Fleet headquarters in Bahrain, the command center of American naval power in the region for nearly three decades, has been rendered completely destroyed and unusable by Iran’s heavy missile and drone attacks.
For years, the Fifth Fleet, with its destroyers, coastal combat ships, minesweepers and logistics hub at Manama, was presented as the guarantor of American order. Iranian officials now say its piers are empty, its command facilities inoperable, and its remaining vessels forced to operate from far outside the Persian Gulf, beyond the reach of Iranian anti-ship missiles, speedboats, submarines, mines and coastal defense systems.
U.S. carriers that once docked in Bahrain and sailed routinely through Hormuz now remain in the northern Indian Ocean and the Arabian Sea. Resupply requires long detours. Insurance rates have soared. Even Washington’s allies on the southern shore of the Persian Gulf, who hosted U.S. forces in hope of protection, have found their ports and airfields turned into targets and have quietly asked Washington to reduce its visible presence.
No return to pre-war order
Abdollahi said Iran’s strategy is to deepen that quagmire: Undoubtedly, with the firm resolve of the brave and wise Leadership, the will of the risen and resistant people, the self-sacrificing Armed Forces and the officials of Islamic Iran, it has been decided to drown you day by day deeper into the quagmire you have built with your own hands — America and its illegitimate offspring, the Zionist regime, and your feeble and aggressive armies.
“With the help of Almighty God and divine victory, the strategy of a strong Iran is that the longer this confrontation lasts, the deeper you will be dragged into the swamp of death and decline, God willing,” he added.
Regional and even Western analysts now concede that the security architecture of the Persian Gulf will not return to what it was before the war. For thirty years, that architecture rested on a simple assumption: unchallenged American naval supremacy, an open strait under American escort, and regional states sheltering under the U.S. umbrella while Iran was contained.
That assumption has collapsed. Iran has demonstrated it can close or control the Strait at will, strike any base in a 2,000-kilometer radius, impose costs on global energy markets, and survive direct American-Israeli bombardment. Host states have learned that hosting U.S. strike assets invites Iranian retaliation. Shipping companies have learned that transit without Iranian consent is a military risk, not a routine insurance matter.
Tehran therefore rejects talk of a return to the status quo ante through a ceasefire that merely reopens the waterway for American warships. Iranian officials insist any durable arrangement must recognize Iran’s legitimate security rights, end aggression and sanctions, and exclude U.S. military vessels from the Persian Gulf altogether.
For Tehran, the message is both military and political: the Persian Gulf is no longer permissive waters for aging carriers, rusted destroyers and expeditionary fantasies. It is, in Iranian doctrine, the front line of national defense and the lever that turned an intended war of overthrow into a war of attrition Washington cannot win.

Israel must stop fighting itself and start winning the information war - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
17:46:36 UTC
02:46:36 KST

At a time when Israel needs every ounce of creativity, expertise, and influence it can mobilize, the government is wasting energy on internal political attacks instead of building the national effort needed to defend Israel against enemies working daily to delegitimize the world’s only Jewish state.
Israel is fighting on multiple fronts. Some are visible on the battlefield; others unfold on university campuses, in newsrooms, across social media and in foreign governments. Israel’s enemies understand that the battle for international opinion is no sideshow. It shapes Israel’s diplomatic room for manoeuvre, the legitimacy of its military actions and the willingness of allies to stand beside it.
Yet while adversaries invest in coordinated messaging, digital networks and international mobilization, Israel’s response remains fragmented. Talented people work in silos. Initiatives compete rather than cooperate. Resources are dispersed, responsibility is blurred, and too often the response begins only after the damage has been done.
This is more than an organizational failure. Why is so much energy spent defending a political monopoly and conducting smear campaigns when Israel needs a national strategy for the information battlefield?
Why have Israel’s extraordinary ingenuity, technological capability and human talent not been mobilized with equal urgency on the information front? Instead of welcoming expertise, innovation and independent voices, the political establishment appears determined to control who speaks for Israel, treating initiatives outside its orbit as competitors rather than allies.
The treatment of our party, People of Israel, illustrates the concern. When Israel should encourage every serious initiative capable of strengthening its international standing, defending political territory risks taking precedence over national security.
Israel needs credible voices able to reach audiences official representatives cannot; professionals who understand digital communication and media; entrepreneurs developing new tools; and partners in the Jewish world and beyond. Credibility depends on authenticity, which cannot be manufactured through political control.
Information war operates alongside the battlefield
One of the main reasons I joined Ofer Winter and the People of Israel party is that Winter is the only general I have met who understands that the information battlefield operates alongside the kinetic battlefield – and that both are matters of national security.
The answer is not simply to spend more money. Resources distributed across disconnected bodies can generate activity without results. Israel needs a unified national framework that turns existing capabilities into a coordinated strategic force.
The People of Israel party proposes establishing a National Command for Strategic Narrative and Public Diplomacy, led by Yoseph Haddad. It would coordinate government bodies, communications professionals, technology experts, independent organizations, and international partners, while respecting institutional responsibilities and operational security.
Its mission would go beyond responding to controversies. It would monitor emerging narratives, anticipate information crises, develop proactive campaigns, mobilize credible international voices, and assess whether communications influence understanding and behavior.
The Foreign Ministry, Government Press Office and IDF Spokesperson’s Unit would remain essential. But they should form part of a broader national capability, rather than carry the burden alone.
The command must be led by experienced professionals chosen for expertise, judgment and results – not political loyalty. Public diplomacy needs its own generals: people who understand international media, audience psychology, digital platforms and narrative warfare.
International opinion affects Israel’s diplomatic relationships and its leaders’ freedom of action. Hostile narratives can spread faster than official corrections. Jewish communities and Israel’s supporters are left answering allegations without timely information or coordinated support. Meanwhile, internal disputes consume energy that should be directed toward those undermining Israel abroad.
The irony is painful. Israel has world-leading capabilities in intelligence, cybersecurity, technology and crisis response. It knows how to identify threats, assemble expertise and act urgently when the stakes demand it. The challenge is to apply that seriousness to the information battlefield – and recognize that no political office can own all the talent required to succeed.
The government must decide what it wants to protect: its monopoly over the national message, or Israel’s ability to defend itself in the world.
Israel cannot afford to turn the defense of its international standing into another arena for domestic political competition. The country’s resources and ingenuity should be directed outwards: countering hostile propaganda, strengthening alliances and making Israel’s case to the world.
The government’s responsibility is not to monopolize Israel’s voice. It is to ensure Israel has the strongest possible voice. Until that distinction is understood, we will keep fighting over who controls the effort while our adversaries exploit the vacuum.
The information war will not wait for our politics to catch up.
The writer is an Israeli politician, diplomat, and former Jerusalem city council member and deputy mayor (2016–2024). She currently serves as Israel’s special envoy for trade and innovation at the Foreign Ministry. She is also a candidate for the 26th Knesset as part of the People of Israel list.

====================================================================================================

'Did we do well today?': This is what it takes to keep an independent restaurant open
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
17:45:00 UTC
02:45:00 KST

Grit, grind and the love of food: 48 hours in an independent restaurant
The work is relentless and the earnings unpredictable: So what keeps an independent restaurant owner in the game?
It's a Thursday morning and Bridget Raffal, co-owner of Claret Club, a restaurant and bar tucked into an old terrace on the edges of Sydney's CBD, is bracing for the worst.
One of the kitchen's two heat lamps has broken. Without it the venue's two chefs will struggle to keep food warm until a waiter can ferry their carefully prepared plates of risotto and quince and walnut clafoutis to customers.
"At first we thought it was just a broken bulb so we ordered one — a very expensive bulb," says Bridget, looking like she doesn't know whether to laugh or cry. "Now we think we have to replace it."
The bar's regular handyman, Christian, is on the phone and begins explaining Bridget's options. Her facial expression suggests none of them are great.
"I just want the best and cheapest," she says after she hangs up the call. "That's always what everything comes down to here — do we try for a quick fix or a long-term solution?"
Hospitality has never been an easy job, known for long hours, low margins and high personal risk. But in 2026 the industry is in extreme crisis, facing a tornado of unfavourable conditions. According to CreditorWatch, one in eight restaurants and cafes closed between July 2025 and July 2026, almost double the average of other sectors. Analysts blame inflation, cost-of-living pressures, skyrocketing costs and damaging policy decisions.
A generation ago, average net profit for a restaurant or cafe was around 10 per cent, says John Hart, national president of industry peak body Restaurant and Catering Australia (RCA). By the end of 2025, that had shrunk to 2.5 per cent. Now, with minimum wage increases and costs such as the recent policy shift that means restaurants must absorb card bank fees, profit has dwindled to almost nothing for many operators.
"Twenty or 30 years ago I warned this would be what I called a 'culinary Armageddon'," Hart says.
Rising food and wage costs are partly to blame, but Bridget and her partner and co-owner Harry Hunter say their biggest issue is cost-of-living pressures, which reduce customer attendance and spend.
"We run a tight ship," Bridget says. "We just need more people through the doors."
Independent venues, where the staff know your name and your drink order, where you can drop by for a meal and a chat after a long day at work, and where every inch of atmosphere is created by intuition and imagination, rather than AI — have never felt more important to the fabric of our cities and towns.
"'Commensality' — the idea of eating together to reinforce kinship links — is part of what brings a group together," says Teresa Davis, associate professor of marketing at the School of Business Analytics and Marketing and co-founder of the Australian Food, Society and Culture Network at the University of Sydney. "It builds and reinforces the social fabric."
Independent places like Claret Club do this particularly well. Their intimacy means customers connect not just with each other but with the people who bring the food and wine to the table.
Today, when the world swirls with uncertainty, upheaval and unrest, independent restaurants feel like a lifeline.
"The experiences of being able to hang out with your friends, being able to escape from whatever it is for a little bit … being around people that you don't know, being treated well — all of that feels more essential than it ever has to me before," New York Times food reporter Brett Anderson recently told The Daily podcast.
The ABC spent two days and nights at Claret Club, an independently run venue in Sydney's Darlinghurst, to witness exactly how much grit and grind it takes to stay open in today's crushing climate, and how much we stand to lose if places like it disappear altogether.
11:40am
The heat lamp issue has been set aside. Chefs Andy Buchanan and Fernando Vargas will have to make do with the remaining lamp for tonight's service, and the waiters and food runners will need to work twice as fast as usual.
Bridget and Harry have begun discussing marketing and social media. There's a wine event upstairs tonight, and another scheduled next week with tickets still available.
"Should I do a last-minute social media push on it?" Bridget wonders.
"I'll write an EDM on Sunday and send it out on Monday," offers Harry, fluent in the shorthand for Electronic Direct Mail, something few restaurateurs would have thought about a generation ago.
"I thought it would be nice if we could have Sunday off together?" Bridget suggests.
Sundays are the one day the couple tries to spend away from Claret Club and their other venue, the wine bar Where's Nick in Marrickville. They have a regular ritual of gathering with friends for a quiz at another wine bar, or cooking something special at home, music on and glass of wine in hand.
Harry shakes his head. "I have to be here for a photo shoot anyway so I may as well do it then." A small flutter of disappointment flickers over Bridget's face.
Bridget says she'll post about the Plat du Bar special the team changes every week: a single-plate dinner and glass of wine that can be eaten at the bar.
"They're a good boost for mid-week sales and they're also culturally important for us," she says. "Solo diners come in for it which we love. People are on their way home from work and instead of going home and standing in front of the fridge and eating a piece of cheese and feeling sad, this is our way to say, 'Come in, let us take care of you'."
But, she adds, "the marketing girl hasn't always been so diligent at remembering to make the posts."
Who is the marketing girl? "Ha! Me. I'm the marketing girl!"
The "marketing girl" has to work harder than ever to keep the customers coming through the door as people tighten their belts.
"If people weren't desperately struggling to pay their rent and mortgages they'd be able to afford to go out and support restaurants and our city would be more vibrant because of it," Bridget says.
There is also plenty of competition for the money people do have, particularly when hundreds of restaurants are accessible at people's fingertips from the sanctuary of a sofa at home. The food delivery industry — platforms like Uber Eats and DoorDash — is worth 1.8 billion according to IbisWorld data. DoorDash research shows nearly three-quarters of Australian consumers think of ordering delivery as "an act of self-care", something to comfort themselves after a big week or to celebrate a special occasion, which is exactly the role that a restaurant like Claret Club is trying to play.
Midday
A new problem. Bridget takes a call about a leak in the restaurant's roof. There's also a leak in the roof at Where's Nick. Both are the landlords' responsibility but it's still up to Bridget to coordinate the repairs. She calls her team at Where's Nick to ask if Claret Club can borrow their stand mixer.
"Our bread maker fell off the bench and getting it fixed is better than trying to get a new one," Bridget says.
1:00pm
Claret Club isn't open for lunch on Thursdays, but outside, Stanley Street is starting to get busy with the lunchtime trade. The white-tablecloth tables across the road at Bill and Toni's have a scattering of customers ordering red-sauce spaghetti and tiramisu. Junko, who runs the Japanese restaurant next door to Claret Club (they share a swag of festoon lights across their adjoining terraces) pops in to say hello. Christian the builder arrives, to nut out the heat lamp conundrum. Everyone greets him with hugs.
"It's a real little village here," Bridget says. "Bill and Toni's have sent people our way. The pub guys [The Lord Roberts, opposite] are great, the Bones Ramen guys are friends. There's a WhatsApp group where we all share information about the best plumber, the best ice supplier. Our ice maker broke and — thousands of dollars later — we still don't have an ice maker. So, we borrowed one from a neighbour."
That, she says, is one of the loveliest things about running a truly small, independent restaurant business. Everyone's hanging in there together.
Stanley Street has a long history of togetherness. It was one of Sydney's first true Italian precincts. Family-run Beppi's — famous for its hand-harvested mussels and veal saltimbocca — opened 70 years ago this year (and still stands today). If Beppi's was out of your price range, by the early 1970s you could head to Bill and Toni's, for huge plates of cheap spaghetti and cups of cordial.
Back then, Darlinghurst was a low socio-economic area, dominated by boarding houses. Today it's full of chic, renovated terraces, and residents with money to spend. The Claret Club team simply wish more of them would walk through their doors.
3:10pm
Harry gathers the team in the small alcove next to the kitchen for a blind wine tasting. It's something they do regularly, as he and Bridget want the team to be able to talk with customers about new bottles.
Everyone scribbles notes as they swill dolcettos and gamays, describing what they taste.
Claret Club has a strict policy about wine distributors trying to book themselves in for time with Bridget or Harry in the hopes of getting their wares onto the list.
"We do not take tasting appointments if you haven't been into the venue and spent money with us," Bridget says. "It's about taking the time to get to know us, and to think about how their wines will fit in. Emails are not a relationship."
3:50pm
Ten minutes until doors open, and Harry is still finishing the wine tasting. Someone presses play on tonight's playlist and a dramatic Italian version of Take My Breath Away from Top Gun fills the room.
"Harry loves a playlist," Bridget says. "We call this one 'Italian bangers'."
4:40pm
Guests have slowly begun arriving in the downstairs bar, but there are still plenty of spare seats.
6:00pm
An older couple steps inside. They stand at the entrance, looking slightly perplexed, and Bridget approaches right away. Her body language radiates warmth as she directs them to a table and points out the wine list scrawled on the mirror. She realises they are French, and switches to French herself so they feel even more comfortable.
It's impressive to witness how "on" a restaurant host needs to be, from the moment the first customer arrives until the last leaves. At every interaction Bridget's face is curious and interested, her body leans forward and every reply comes with smiles and wide-open arm gestures. It's easy to think a restaurant professional is merely passing on information about food and drink, but a good one makes you feel you're the best thing to have walked through the doors that night.
Bridget has hospitality in her bones.
"I grew up in a house that was totally centred on food and wine," she says. "The dinner table was where all the conversations happened. We never had a TV in the kitchen or anywhere near the dining table. Food was how we all came together."
She worked as a barista from the age of 16, then as both a chef and front-of-house, everywhere from France (hence her ability to speak French) to the Netherlands. In Amsterdam, Bridget's favourite moments were always spent around the dinner table with friends.
"You'd buy a bottle of three-euro Montepulciano from the supermarket and if it was a really special occasion, you'd splash out on a five-euro," she says, laughing. "The point was shopping for great food, having a glass of wine in your hand and making a meal with friends."
This, she says, is the sort of atmosphere she and Harry (who previously worked at Bentley Group and Dinner by Heston) wanted to recreate with their own venue.
"We wanted to run a place that reflects the values we care about, particularly treating our staff with respect, so they feel valued and protected. We couldn't do that if we worked for other people."
But autonomy can come with costs. Not only does endless worry over revenue and long hours make for stressful work, but it can be difficult for hospitality workers to take care of their physical and mental health. Bridget tries to make it to the gym three times a week to clear her head.
"We also try to do team beers maybe once a week, as a bit of a download and for connection," she says, but she steers clear of the heavy-drinking culture that is common to the industry. "I have a huge workload and focus is pretty important to me. I can't afford to be hungover."
7:50pm
The wine dinner upstairs is in full swing, and Matt Prokop and restaurant manager Utsav Shah are run off their feet to serve 22 guests. The missing heat lamp means they have to get the meals upstairs extra quickly before food goes cold. Downstairs is still quiet.
Bridget hides herself into a nook, just outside of the customers' line of sight, and tries to catch up on paperwork.
"I hate getting a laptop out during service — it's been drilled into me that you don't do that. But we are here for such long hours, if I don't do it now I'll never be able to do it."
Harry rushes past with wine bottles but pauses to drop a kiss on the top of Bridget's head. It's a small, private moment, one of the rare chances they have to connect in their long days.
9:04pm
The wine dinner guests have moved on to their main courses. Claret Club food has old-fashioned elegance to it: fish pies, rich with cream and potato. Beef rib braised in Barolo, served on polenta.
"It has a simplicity, and references to Elizabeth David," Bridget says, noting the iconic British cookbook author.
The wine dinner guests seem thrilled. Many remember Chef Andy from Melbourne's upscale Dinner By Heston (now closed), and several drop by to thank him for the meal.
This, says Bridget, is a big part of the reason they do what they do. "Our customers are often well-travelled and when they rave about our food we think, OK. This is it. What we're doing is working."
10:00pm
The kitchen team is beginning to wipe down benchtops and sweep the floors. Sommelier Matt had planned to knock off early but two customers appear at the door. He goes immediately to greet and seat them.
"We want to build a reputation for being open later at night, for being somewhere you can come at any time," Matt explains later.
"Our thing is, 'last guest out the door and we're done' — whatever time that is."
After being seated the two men change their minds. It seems they wanted more of a pub atmosphere than a wine bar where they're practically the only customers. Matt directs them to The Lord Roberts over the road.
"That's OK, we don't have to be for everyone," he says.
10:40pm
The chefs have left and Bridget has pulled the doors of the venue closed, but a few stragglers from the wine dinner are still hanging out at the bar. Harry and the remaining staff give their guests the same level of attention as when they first arrived: they're excitedly discussing the wines they drank and what they enjoyed.
11:40pm
The last guest has left, and Bridget pours a glass of Barolo for herself, and hands a beer to Harry. They drink as they bring in tables from outside and clear the linen from the tables inside.
"Are you ready to go home?" Harry asks Bridget.
"Yep, I think it's about time. That's a nice early finish," she says, "Twenty to midnight."
But then a friend and fellow hospo worker turns up at the door and suggests they all go for a drink. Matt brightens and everyone else agrees.
"You need a bit of time to decompress otherwise it's just this dystopian feeling of sleep, work, sleep, work," Matt says.
Together they head to a local bar.
Midnight
The team has ordered giant steins of lager. They share war stories about the night — who ordered what, who did or didn't like a dish.
There's no sense of hierarchy and everyone chats freely, with no indication that the owners are more important than the workers. A long day is a long day, for everyone involved.
"Did you see that guy who drank all his wines at the wine dinner, and then leant over and drank all of his neighbour's wines as well?" chuckles Matt.
Harry does a quick calculation about the wine dinner revenue.
"It was a lot of effort for not a lot of money. The tickets were under $200 for all those wines. So, we brought in about $3,000.
"Cozzie livs," he finishes with a sigh, ruing the cost of living in that distinctly Australian way.
Cozzie livs be damned. Matt and Harry agree that there's time for "just one more beer".
At 1:10am, they call it a night.
The restaurant landscape changes constantly, as it must if it hopes to survive.
It wasn't long ago that it was relatively rare to eat outside the home in Australia. Migrant communities in the mid-20th century ran small shops, trattorias and cafes, and by the 1980s restaurants of all kinds became more common, including American fast food.
Since COVID, the hospitality industry has arguably experienced more upheaval than ever before. Food ordered in-venue still makes up the largest revenue stream but data from point-of-sale software platform Lightspeed shows it's fallen from 31 per cent in 2024 to 20 per cent in 2025, as takeaway, delivery and catering take a larger share.
Younger demographics, with less money to spend, are looking for social interaction with a smaller price tag, such as relatively cheap frozen yoghurt and ice cream parlours.
Then there are the policy and societal problems that kneecap the sector: wage rises, capped migration, inflation and unfavourable tax pressures, which industry body the Australian Restaurant & Cafe Association (ARCA) says are causing carnage.
It suffered a recent blow: the Reserve Bank banned businesses from adding card surcharges to customers' bills. That cost is likely to be passed to customers as higher prices.
The last thing Bridget wants to do is make Claret Club less accessible, but she also knows they won't be able to absorb the costs.
Revenue challenges mean Bridget and Harry can't hire extra people to share the burdens they shoulder themselves.
"Our jobs are full-time hosts, reservations, operations, bookkeeping," says Bridget. "We write two wine lists, do HR for both venues. Combined it's around nine or 10 full-time jobs. We can't keep working like this. A good week for me is 60 or 65 hours. But it can easily be 90."
In Canberra, another restaurateur Louis Couttoupes was forced to close his independent venue, Onzieme, in May this year. Unlike at Claret Club, he says filling seats was never a problem.
"Because Canberra has such a big public service workforce ... people's incomes are more reliable and predictable," he says.
Instead, Onzieme was felled by the pressures of finding and retaining qualified staff, without them being poached by larger restaurant groups acting "as this vacuum cleaner for staff because they can offer more money", he says.
Those left in the pool tended to be wildly underqualified for the roles Louis needed to fill. "I got to the point where my lease was up and I looked ahead at the next five years and thought, 'I can't see this getting any better'."
So what happens to a city's soul if the only hospitality venues that remain are large groups, with focus-tested menus and cookie-cutter concepts? The sorts of places Bridget calls "Disneyland" restaurants?
For starters, there is likely to be far more homogenisation, as restaurants look to buy in "value-added" food products: items that are cheaper, easy to prepare, pre-packaged and exactly the same as those served by the restaurant next door.
"We've all seen the explosion in restaurants where everything is steak frites, seafood pasta," says RCA's John Hart. "We can all practically recite the menus."
Couttoupes offers a grim warning. The big groups will dominate, and the little guys will vanish altogether. "Small businesses are more connected to their staff, customers, suppliers and producers," he says. "If you lose them, then with it goes diversity, creativity and passion."
This idea of creativity, however, is where a venue like Claret Club may eventually eke out a small advantage.
Chef Andy still orders in beautiful red mullet, rather than easy-to-source, pre-cut barramundi or Murray cod. The restaurant's truffle supplier drives over the Blue Mountains with a haul especially for them.
Bridget uses her expert sommelier skills to buy and cellar bottles when they're young, which means she can hold onto them and sell them at a minimal mark-up compared to others who buy at peak price. This, says John Hart, is what diners will increasingly seek out as the "Disneyfication" of restaurants becomes more prominent.
"The ones that take ingredients and provide a dining experience that's something very special," he says, are the sorts of places we will yearn to go.
As long as the market conditions allow these independent restaurants to survive, that is.
Friday 10:30am
It's an earlier start today in anticipation of a busier Friday, and a lunchtime opening.
Harry and Matt are setting up, while sous chef Fernando is making bread with the stand mixer borrowed from Claret Club's sister venue.
11:35am
Bridget arrives looking fresh despite the 1am finish.
"Hi love," she says to Harry. Even though the couple live together, they've barely seen each other that morning.
"There's not a lot of opportunity in the week to have any connection," she says. "We make a point to remember to be nice to each other."
Marketing ideas are always churning in both Harry's and Bridget's brains.
Harry has an idea for an art-house cinema on the restaurant rooftop over summer.
Bridget looks pained. "I'm so in the weeds, Harry. When am I going to be able to think about that?"
Midday
Doors are open and a few office workers are having small meals on the sunny tables outside. But the venue is nowhere near full.
3:00pm
By mid-afternoon, Andy uses the time to test out new recipes, bringing a tuna and blood orange dish to Bridget and Harry for a taste test. The orange segments could be cut finer, but the flavour is spot-on. Bridget uses the spare moments to iron tablecloths.
4:22pm
Nervy about the number of guests, Bridget puts up an Instagram post advertising their $10 martini happy hour that began at 4pm.
Within 30 minutes a group of four — Bridget and Harry's friends who have an office nearby — have come in and ordered a round.
4:30pm
Chefs Andy and Fernando give themselves a coffee break. They crouch outside together in the little tin shed they built on their own — a minute's peace before what they hope will be a busy night.
4:50pm
But the hoped-for rush will have to wait. Andy comes back inside and finds Bridget.
"Hey Bridget. Do you want some good news?" he asks with a grimace.
"No. Don't tell me. What's broken?" says Bridget, her eyes widening.
"The pilot on the fryer has gone out."
Bridget momentarily closes her eyes. "We won't get anyone to fix it now. It's almost the weekend," she says.
The two discuss options. Not much can be done this close to dinner. One fryer is still working but just like the heat lamp, one will now be out of action.
They let the floor staff know to hold back on pushing menu items that need to be deep-fried.
Meanwhile, Bridget throws the problem into the Stanley Street WhatsApp group, and someone comes up with a repair contact right away.
"We can't have someone come here during service, and we can't afford the Sunday call-out fee, so it'll have to be Monday," she says.
"Hopefully we won't get stung with an 'urgent' loading."
5:18pm
Bridget checks the bookings for the night — just 34 covers in a venue that comfortably seats 60. Most are peripheral industry people — friends and colleagues they know — with a handful of first timers.
A couple comes in and orders glasses of wine.
"You're a very good addition to Stanley Street," the gentleman tells Bridget. "If you keep your heads above water you're going to do well."
Friends and family are an important part of Claret Club's customer base. It's also a big part of what makes the restaurant feel personal and welcoming. "Our whole business is built around relationships: we try to know everyone's name, if they've just had a baby and it's their first time out of the house," Bridget says.
Bridget likes to tell a story of how she does her banking at a branch in Marrickville, close to their other venue. One day her regular teller said she was planning to book Claret Club for dinner.
"When I saw her name on the bookings and when she showed up, that really meant a lot," Bridget says.
Just as often, strangers become friends. "We're a neighbourhood venue. We want the three generations, the kids, the place people think of for their special birthday every year."
In many ways this word of mouth is more effective than any marketing. "The old wisdom is everyone works really hard to capture new guests, and of course we do that," she says. "But if you work to get them back the returns are much higher."
10:00pm
The night has been busier than expected. But it's still quiet enough that Bridget has time to sit down and try Andy's red mullet with velouté.
10:37pm
Just four groups remain. Everyone is taking their time to finish a final few languid glasses of wine, while Bridget and Harry stop repeatedly at the groups to chat.
It's a long night yet again, but the team still look like they are in their element.
"We do it for the love of food and wine, really," Bridget says. "Connecting with people over those things is really fulfilling and restorative. Those little moments when people really get what we're doing and who we are — that's what makes it all worth it."
11:23pm
The team look tired, though they make plans for a couple of beers next door, like last night. For Bridget and Harry especially, Claret Club is more than just a workplace, it's the heart of their lives.
Bridget rests her head briefly on Harry's shoulder.
"The last thing we say before we go to sleep isn't 'I love you baby'," she says. "It's 'Did we do well today?'"

Nigeria's Tinubu launches re-election campaign as economic pain tests support
KADUNA, Oct 24 - President Bola Tinubu formally launched his campaign for a second term on Saturday in the northern city of Kaduna, where he sought to convince voters that painful economic reforms are beginning to pay off despite a lingering cost-of-living crisis.
Tinubu, 74, faces a contest ahead of a January 16 election that is likely to be dominated by the economy and security. His main challengers include former Vice President Atiku Abubakar and Peter Obi, who finished second and third respectively in 2023.
By midday, thousands of supporters of the president's All Progressives Congress party had filled much of the 10,000-capacity Ranchers Bees Stadium, with more arriving as the rally got underway.
"Thank you for this massive showing up. It is a promise. Come 2027, January 16, you must go out massively and elect me again," Tinubu told the crowd.
OPPOSITION CREATED PROBLEMS, SAYS TINUBU
Since taking office in 2023, Tinubu has scrapped fuel subsidies, devalued the naira and introduced other reforms credited with improving public finances, foreign reserves and investor sentiment. But the measures have also fuelled Nigeria's worst cost-of-living crisis in a generation.
Petrol prices rose to about 1,400 naira ($1.05) a litre in Lagos and Abuja in September and as much as 1,500 naira in parts of northern Nigeria, adding to pressure on household budgets.
Tinubu dismissed opposition complaints about hunger and poverty, arguing that his rivals created those problems.
"They created the hunger. They created the poverty. We are trying to eradicate it."
Phrank Shaibu, a spokesperson for the Atiku campaign, told Reuters the president was attempting to dodge responsibility.
"Mr President, blaming the opposition for hunger is either delusion or a staggering case of political amnesia," he said.
Security will provide another test. Nigeria continues to battle armed bandits and kidnappers in the northwest and a 17-year Islamist insurgency in the northeast, where militants have stepped up attacks on military positions.
Tinubu nevertheless enters the race with a formidable political machine. His camp says he has the backing of 32 of Nigeria's 36 state governors, potentially giving him an unprecedented organisational advantage, although past elections have shown governors cannot always deliver their states to presidential candidates.
His toughest electoral test could come in the north, where Atiku, a veteran northern politician with an established support base, will seek to erode the president's vote.
Tinubu has said he will not attend campaign rallies in all 36 states as he needs to remain focused on governing. The party's proposed timetable has him personally attending rallies in 12 states, culminating in a major closing rally in his home state of Lagos on January 9. REUTERS

alyona alyona underwent stomach-reduction surgery and explained why she decided to undergo the surgical procedure
Kyiv • UNN
The rapper underwent bariatric surgery after unsuccessful attempts to lose weight. She is currently recovering and aims to control her eating.
Ukrainian rapper alyona alyona underwent stomach-reduction surgery and spoke for the first time about how she is feeling after the procedure. The artist admitted that she is currently experiencing pain and is focused on recovery. She reported this on Instagram, UNN writes.
Details
According to the performer, after the surgery her main tasks are walking and lying down, as she is still going through the recovery period.
In a separate post, the rapper explained that she decided to undergo bariatric surgery after many years of trying to lose weight. Her decision was influenced by the experience of a childhood friend who, after undergoing the procedure, lost weight from 140 to 70 kilograms and has maintained the result for several years.
alyona alyona said that she had repeatedly tried to lose weight through exercise and other methods, including injections for weight loss. However, she was unable to achieve the desired result.
"I have shown my ways of losing weight with exercise and various things many times. I even shared how I injected myself and what those injections led to, and that they are not a panacea," the artist said.
The rapper admitted that she dreams of weighing 80 kilograms, but realizes that surgery will not automatically solve all her problems. She explained that because of her work schedule, acquired habits, and ADHD, it is difficult for her to devote her entire life to losing weight.
"In order for me to lose all the weight, I would have to give up my career and work and devote my entire life to losing weight," the performer explained.
According to alyona alyona, she views the surgery as a way to control her eating and avoid overeating. The artist also emphasized that this is her personal choice and that she is ready for possible criticism.
"For me, it is very important to work on myself, develop, change, and be an example. I am choosing this path. I do not care whether someone condemns me, devalues me, or refutes me — this is my path," the rapper concluded, thanking everyone who supports her during her recovery.

American are done paying for Trump’s family business
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
17:03:17 UTC
02:03:17 KST

American are done paying for Trump’s family business
TEHRAN — Donald Trump won the White House promising to “Make America Great Again,” then promised Americans a short, cheap war on Iran. They got a closed Strait of Hormuz, Brent crude above $116 a barrel, and gasoline past $5 a gallon in several states. He and his family got a windfall.
Nine days before the November 3 midterms, the distance between those two experiences has become the central fact of American politics.
In CNBC’s final pre-election survey, 36 percent of registered voters named government corruption among their top issues, ahead of food prices at 34 percent and gasoline at 23 percent.
Fox News found 60 percent of voters extremely concerned. People are reading their grocery receipts and the headlines as one story.
A war with a customer list
The campaign of aggression against Iran has already cost tens of billions of dollars, paid from the public purse. Some of it is landing with companies the president’s sons own or advise.
Powerus, which Eric Trump and Donald Trump Jr. are backing toward a stock listing, holds an Air Force contract worth up to $90 million for interceptors meant to counter Iranian drones.
Skeptics doubt the systems can stop Iran’s one-way attack drones, which have proved themselves in large numbers. Powerus is pitching them to Arab governments in the Persian Gulf anyway, the same clients Washington claims to be defending.
Trump Jr. also holds roughly $4 million in Unusual Machines, where he serves as an adviser. The “War” Department bought 3,500 drone motors and related parts from the company, and the Army has floated a follow-on order of 20,000.
Its shares jumped when his link became public. Rep. Jason Crow says firms tied to the sons have drawn about $3.7 billion in federal money this term.
The youngest Trump son, Barron, joined 1789 Capital days after the 2024 election. Among its holdings is Anduril, approved for a possible $2 billion interceptor sale to Kuwait.
Trump’s own portfolio includes Palantir, Lockheed Martin, General Dynamics and Northrop Grumman, whose revenues have swelled with U.S. military warmongering.
Richard Painter, who served as ethics lawyer in George W. Bush’s White House, told the Wall Street Journal that he sees no modern precedent. That is a notable benchmark, given the Bush administration’s own notorious record of foreign aggression and corporate enrichment.
Persian Gulf states, he says, are “under immense pressure to buy from Trump’s sons,” so the president will deliver what they want. It may be the first time, he adds, that a president’s family has made vast sums from a war launched without congressional authorization.
Arab monarchy money and a crypto pipeline
The Persian Gulf runs through the family’s earlier business too. In his upcoming book Princes and Thieves, Matthew Cole reports that Jared Kushner had access to at least two accounts tied to the UAE and Israel, together receiving about $2 billion, part of it Saudi-backed and moved through banks in Baku.
Dutch intelligence, which had penetrated his phone, helped trace the transfers. A third account, the report says, paid for an Israeli pledge to defend the Emirates against Iranian strikes.
Then came crypto. Days before the 2025 inauguration, an entity backed by Tahnoon bin Zayed, the UAE’s national security adviser, agreed to buy 49 percent of World Liberty Financial for $500 million.
An Abu Dhabi fund he chairs later bought $2 billion of the firm’s USD1 stablecoin. Months on, the administration eased AI chip exports to Emirati firms, including G42, which Tahnoon controls.
Trump also pardoned Binance founder Changpeng Zhao, whose company had paid $4.3 billion in fines, and accepted a $400 million jet from Qatar.
On October 22, a Circle shareholder sued in federal court, alleging violations of the Foreign Emoluments Clause.
Trump’s disclosures show $2.2 billion in earnings for his first year back, $1.4 billion of it from crypto, including about $636 million from a memecoin whose promoters advertised a dinner with him for its 185 biggest holders.
‘Slime, not crime’
Smaller scandals keep piling up. Ambassador to Greece Kimberly Guilfoyle resigned after the Wall Street Journal reported she asked a donor to cover a $100,000 credit card bill.
Adviser Corey Lewandowski faces a Justice Department inquiry. The New York Times says Alina Habba, Trump’s former lawyer, agreed to a $50 million deal with the family of a Venezuelan billionaire who later received a pardon.
Trump’s answer was to warn that dishonest allies “have to be prosecuted,” while his Justice Department charged a Virginia Democrat, state Sen. L. Louise Lucas.
Expect few convictions. Experts point to the Supreme Court: McDonnell in 2016 narrowed “official acts,” Snyder in 2024 excused gratuities paid after the fact, and Trump v. United States granted presidents sweeping immunity.
The Justice Department’s Public Integrity Section was effectively shut down in February 2025. What remains, some prosecutors say, is “slime, not crime,” despite overwhelming evidence of corruption that Americans across party lines can no longer ignore.
Nine days to judgment
Voters have noticed anyway. A Washington Post/ABC News/Ipsos poll found nearly two in three Americans think Trump is using the presidency to enrich himself, with most of the rise coming from Republicans and their leaners.
His approval sits at a record low of 33 percent, and Democrats have spent $182 million on corruption ads, more than the last four cycles combined, according to data from the firm AdImpact.
Vice President JD Vance calls the charge “laughable.” Trump’s pollster argues undecided voters will still choose on pocketbook issues. Perhaps. But $5 gasoline and a president’s sons selling drones are hard to pull apart.
The deeper question is what the money buys. In Matthew Cole’s account, Kushner held signing rights on an Emirati account while Abu Dhabi wanted the 2015 Iran nuclear deal (JCPOA) dead.
Trump quit the agreement in May 2018. Months after he left office, Saudi Arabia’s sovereign fund gave his firm $2 billion, despite a screening panel finding its due diligence “unsatisfactory in all aspects.”
Today, at least some of the transactions happen in plain sight: Emirati stablecoin purchases, chip exports, drone contracts, and more.

Trump says he may move White House press corps to new location
Trump’s remarks come amid a fractious moment between the US president and the journalists who cover him.
United States President Donald Trump has confirmed he could move the White House press corps to a different location, possibly away from the executive residence.
In a social media post on Friday, Trump described reports that he planned to remove the White House press briefing room in favour of restoring a historic swimming pool located underneath as “Fake News”.
“I NEVER even thought to do such a stupid thing!” he wrote in a Truth Social post.
Trump, however, indicated he may relocate dozens of reporters who cover the White House “to a less obnoxious location”.
The New York Times on Tuesday reported that Trump had pitched his former press secretary, Karoline Leavitt, on an idea to move journalists out of the White House’s storied James S. Brady Press Briefing Room. That proposal did not move forward during Leavitt’s tenure, which ended on August 27.
Trump’s remarks come amid a fractious moment between him and the journalists who cover him.
Last month, Trump banned journalists from three US-based media outlets – CNN, MS NOW and POLITICO – from the White House, a move that proponents of free speech said violated First Amendment protections.
A US federal judge ruled that the order was likely unconstitutional, forcing the White House to restore the journalists’ access. The Trump administration continues to fight the ruling.
Trump has also regularly chided and denigrated members of the media he claims cover him unfairly.
The latest incident was during an Oval Office event on Tuesday when Trump attacked The Independent’s White House Correspondent Andrew Feinberg.
“What’s wrong with you? Are you a sick person? I actually think there’s something wrong with you”, Trump said as Feinberg tried to ask a question. The moment was amplified by the White House on social media.
If Trump opts to proceed with changes to the White House press briefing room, it would be the latest in a long list of controversial projects he has ordered that would transform the property.
Since returning to power last year, the US president has demolished the White House East Wing to construct a new ballroom, installed concrete pavers over the lawn centred in the White House Rose Garden and built a helipad on the South Lawn.
The Times reported Trump told aides he wanted to bring back a West Wing indoor pool constructed in 1933 for use by President Franklin D Roosevelt, who suffered from polio and often swam, according to his presidential library, to ease soreness.
In the 1970s, former President Richard Nixon had a floor constructed above the pool to accommodate a briefing room for the growing White House press corps. The pool remains beneath the floor of the briefing room.
Leavitt confirmed during a Friday interview that Trump was “flirting” with the idea of restoring the pool.
“He just, maybe, wants to restore it to all of its glory”, Leavitt said during an appearance on HBO’s “Real Time with Bill Maher”. “I don’t know if he’ll do it.”
The White House did not immediately return Al Jazeera’s request for comment.

Ste Marie imbues Monos Vancouver office with "residential quality"

Unknown Publisher

Ste Marie imbues Monos Vancouver office with “residential quality”
Canadian interiors studio Ste Marie has designed the Vancouver headquarters of luggage brand Monos to emphasise simplicity and shift mood throughout the day.
Located in the city’s Mount Pleasant neighbourhood, the Monos office was created to reflect the brand’s development to date and provide space for continued growth.
Ste Marie was presented with an open-ended brief, allowing the studio to develop a “flexible framework” for a company that is “still exploring what it could become” and would allow its team to collaborate, experiment and host.
“Monos is a brand grounded in design, mindfulness, human connection, and we understood this as an opportunity to create a place where those values could be put into practice,” said Ste Marie.
“A place where their people could come together to work, create, exchange ideas, test new things, host events and gather as an extended community.”
The studio, which previously designed the interiors for a Monos store in Toronto, approached the workplace like a residential project and organised the spaces into three overlapping areas.
“Like an apartment, it accommodates everyday activity as naturally as moments of hosting,” said the studio. “The residential quality also supports Monos’ culture of openness.”
The first area features low, soft modular sofas for lounging and conversation, and enclosed banquettes below conical pendant lights that facilitate personal exchanges, small meetings or shared meals.
An elongated communal table at the centre of the open plan provides a flexible surface for meetings, product development, testing, dining and gathering.
Here, the custom millwork is arranged in perpendicular planes that form vertical supports and horizontal overhead light boxes.
At the back is a kitchen and tea room with solid-surface counters and handleless cabinets, continuing the minimalist schema that runs throughout.
“These areas can expand and contract as needed: a meeting can become a meal, a work surface can become a display, and a lounge can transform into an event space,” Ste Marie said.
The hardness of the polished concrete flooring and rift-cut timber millwork is offset by soft furnishings, natural-fibre rugs and sheer curtains.
Dimmable lighting enables the mood to shift from early morning focused work to more casual afternoon meetings and then evening events.
“The result is a workplace that feels considered but not overly designed, with the warmth and informality of a personal space and the flexibility of a creative studio,” said Ste Marie.
Ste Marie was founded by Craig Stanghetta and has developed a reputation for its cinematic hospitality spaces across North America.
Other recent projects by the studio include a trio of venues in Edmonton, a series of amenity spaces within a renovated 1960s tower in Chicago and a Vancouver restaurant influenced by Hong Kong’s “love motels”.

Operation al-Khalil exposes limits of Israeli aggression
Unknown

Operation al-Khalil exposes limits of Israeli aggression
TEHRAN – The resistance operation in al-Khalil (Hebron), which took place just days before the Israeli elections, was far more than an isolated security incident.
It raises fundamental questions about the limits of power within the Israeli regime’s security establishment and its ability to prevent armed resistance operations in the occupied West Bank.
Despite continued raids, tighter military restrictions, an expanding campaign of searches, arrests, detentions, and home demolitions, armed resistance remains ongoing. This exposes the gap between the ability to establish control on the ground and the ability to achieve lasting security.
The operation is significant because of its timing and the context in which it occurred. Raids by Israeli Occupation Forces (IOF) alongside settler terrorism on Palestinians, their land, and their property in the West Bank have been escalating, alongside threats to expand the aggression.
The question is not only what security consequences the resistance operation has produced, but what it reveals about the shortcomings of the regime’s approach in the West Bank. The IOF continues to pursue policies aimed at imposing new realities through aggression and the complete control daily life in the occupied territories.
The armed resistance operation in al-Khalil that killed and injured IOF troops cannot be understood separately from the conditions in the city and its surrounding areas, where IOF attacks on Palestinians continue and overlap with settler terrorism.
On September 24, homes and other structures were demolished in the area of Jinba near al-Khalil, displacing eight families comprising 55 Palestinians, including 32 children. Some were forced to seek shelter in caves.
On October 12 and 13, children and their vehicles were attacked with rocks and sticks as they made their way to school. On October 17, settlers attacked the village of Ma’in near al-Khalil, injuring three Palestinians, one of whom was shot with live ammunition. They also stole 380 sheep. On October 19, farmers were attacked while harvesting olives.
These incidents are also inseparable from the IOF restrictions imposed on Palestinians at the Ibrahimi Mosque in al-Khalil and the continued measures enforcing its division by time and space.
Palestinians face conditions in which Israel’s pressure extends beyond military operations into the details of everyday life and their ability to remain on their land, amid the ongoing threat of ethnic cleansing.
The al-Khalil operation raises questions about the occupation regime’s ability to prevent armed resistance, even under heightened alert and strict security measures. Military superiority, a heavy military occupation, and the capacity to carry out raids and arrests do not necessarily mean an ability to anticipate every operation or prevent it from taking place.
This is where the central contradiction emerges. The IOF can expand its raids and impose sweeping restrictions on Palestinians in the West Bank, but it cannot automatically turn this into lasting, guaranteed security. Controlling territory is not the same as being able to control every security or political development that occurs within it.
The fact that an armed resistance operation took place in al-Khalil at this particular moment exposes the IOF’s security failure to anticipate the operation, issue an early warning, and prevent it from happening. It also puts claims of comprehensive security control to a serious test and serves as a reminder that the regime’s security policy in the West Bank, however extensive, prolonged, or intensified, cannot eliminate the underlying factors sustaining the aggression against Palestinians.
This becomes even more significant given the Netanyahu government’s reliance on military force as its primary tool for establishing deterrence and reshaping the situation in the West Bank. As arrests and terror expand, the possibility of renewed confrontation remains strong. This is a natural consequence of any occupation.
The al-Khalil operation comes at a sensitive electoral moment for the Netanyahu coalition, which seeks to present its strategy of maintaining security control over the West Bank as proof of the success of its policies. An armed resistance operation occurring amid this rhetoric and strategy raises questions within the regime itself about the effectiveness of the approach and the Netanyahu government’s ability to deliver on its security promises.
Remarks by Netanyahu and Katz, about a large-scale offensive in the West Bank have been translated into expanded raids, sieges, mass arrests, demolition of homes and infrastructure, similar to the patterns seen in refugee camps across the northern West Bank. The rhetoric is reminiscent of similar aggression used during the Second Intifada in 2002 under Ariel Sharon.
The regime’s continued reliance on military force raises a fundamental question about the limits of this approach, which has failed to deliver security. Establishing security control does not guarantee safety or eliminate the causes of the conflict with the Palestinian people.
Nor can expanding the aggression guarantee complete security as long as the occupation, its policies, and its violations of Palestinian rights remain. The regime refuses to acknowledge these underlying factors and openly declares its intention to settle the conflict by force, presenting this outcome as inevitable.
Looking back, the occupation regime’s past experiences with the use of excessive force have failed to deliver the strategic outcomes.
In other words, force cannot settle a struggle over land. The strategic significance of the al-Khalil operation lies not simply in its immediate security impact, but also in what it reveals about the difficulty of turning IOF superiority into a definitive resolution amid the West Bank aggression.
The regime possesses overwhelming military power and an extensive, integrated security and military apparatus. It can impose realities on the ground and carry out its plans against Palestinians, but it cannot guarantee lasting security and stability.
From this perspective, many believe that the return of armed resistance operations amid the choices of occupation, settlement expansion, and ongoing aggression against Palestinians reinforces a crucial point: the issue goes beyond an isolated intelligence failure. The more pressure Palestinians face, the more likely such operations are to recur as a consequence of IOF policies and settler terrorism.
Armed resistance operations do not emerge in a vacuum. They arise in response to the occupation regime’s policies imposed on a people whose entire existence is under threat, even on their own land. Palestinian land is being seized and subjected to Judaization, while Palestinians face growing threats to their rights, presence, future, land, and holy sites.
With a large-scale IOF assault and forced displacement underway in al-Khalil, the West Bank faces the possibility of an escalation that could spiral out of control.
The regime’s real dilemma is not simply how to tighten its control over the West Bank, but its belief that control through force can bring the resistance to an end. Every military operation carried out by the IOF may alter certain realities on the ground, but it cannot erase Palestinians’ rights to their land or their other rights, nor can it extinguish their aspirations for freedom.
The regime’s military superiority does not, by any means, guarantee that the armed struggle can be brought to a definitive end as long as its political roots remain unresolved and resistance can rise again from the ashes.

EDITORIAL: Militarism, messaging, partnerships
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
16:43:43 UTC
01:43:43 KST

Two strands of a concerted misinformation campaign affecting Taiwan need to be resisted. The first is “US skepticism,” the idea that in the event of aggression against Taiwan by the Chinese People’s Liberation Army (PLA), Washington would be unlikely to intervene militarily. The second is “Japanese neo-militarism.”
Both originate from and serve the purposes of the Chinese Communist Party (CCP). The first is designed to shake the resolve of Taiwanese and the second to reduce obstacles to PLA aggression in the Taiwan Strait.
A US operational warfare guidance report released on Oct. 7 titled How the Army Fights describes how the US military intends to counterbalance its “pacing threat” — the PLA — by improving its warfighting infrastructure across the region. That is to be achieved by ensuring that forward deployments of weapons, equipment and supplies are present along the First Island Chain, enabling a rapid response to PLA actions.
This year’s Keen Sword military exercises, which started on Monday and run through Thursday, are operational practice runs by Japan and the US to protect Japan, including its Ryukyu Islands, with deployments on Okinawa, Miyako, Ishigaki and Yonaguni — only 110km from Taiwan — as well as on the main islands of Shikoku and Kyushu.
The addition of Indo-Pacific, Pacific and European nations — including France, Germany, the Netherlands, New Zealand, the Philippines, Australia and Canada — shows that other nations also see the benefit of the exercises.
The larger scale and wider participation at this year’s Keen Sword exercises demonstrate the evolving structure of the regional deterrence. They are the physical manifestation of the concepts laid out in the US’ operational warfare guidance report, just as they are the first trial run of Japan’s new Joint Operations Command, launched on March 24 last year to unify operational command of Japan’s ground, maritime and air self-defense forces.
The participation of the Philippines extends the scope of the exercises south along the First Island Chain, while the implications of the US report stretch north to South Korea, too, as the Chosun Daily reported in an article titled “US Army’s new guidance calls for full force against China in First Island Chain: New guidelines emphasize immediate action, impacting South Korea’s defense strategies.”
The article said that the new stance “necessitates changes to military assets on the Korean Peninsula, which hosts the second-largest US troop presence after Japan,” and quotes US Forces Korea Commander General Xavier Brunson as describing South Korea as a “fixed aircraft carrier between China and Japan.”
With these preparations in place, it is difficult to entertain any idea of “US skepticism.” The wide regional participation surely also quashes any suspicion of “Japanese neo-militarism,” yet the CCP continues to peddle this unfounded narrative to divert from its own blatant militaristic drive.
An article published in the English-language Chinese state media publication Global Times titled “Japan-US ‘Keen Sword’ pierces the ‘facade of peace,’” accuses Japan of “attempting to advance its maritime expansionist claims through military deployments and to exert pressure through force to secure control over the seas.”
The article said that “will send the wrong signal, exacerbate tensions in the Taiwan Straits [sic] and the East China Sea, and undermine regional peace and stability.”
The psychological projection of the CCP’s own intent is astonishing.
The article also contends that, during World War II, Japan “forged the Axis bloc with Germany and Italy; today, it leans on the Japan-US alliance alongside participating NATO nations,” attempting to tie Japan’s strategy with fascists, and to drive a wedge between the US and Japan.
For Taiwanese not to fall for this disinformation, they must first understand it for what it is. Then it is possible to discount it or push back against it.
However, more can be done.
Deterrence messaging is not just for Chinese President Xi Jinping (習近平) and the PLA’s military planners, it is for the Chinese public, too. Chinese must be made to understand the cost of aggression in the Taiwan Strait and that it can be avoided if their government draws back from its destabilizing militarism and agrees to come to the table with the elected representatives of Taiwan’s government, without preconditions, and with the understanding that it would need to compromise on its red lines.
The most troubling message coming out of Washington for Taipei is not any single statement but the cumulative effect of a series of signals suggesting that US President Donald Trump is rethinking Taiwan’s strategic value while viewing the US-China relationship through the lens of a transactional great-power bargain. The danger behind Trump’s new softness toward Beijing is a potential US-China bargain that undermines Taiwan’s core interests. During Chinese President Xi Jinping’s (習近平) recent state visit to Washington, Trump and Xi appeared to rewrite the history of World War II. In a Sept. 25 fact sheet on Xi’s visit, the White House said,
There was a moment, in 2015 or 2016, when Tulum was the coolest town on Earth. Every fashion magazine seemed to billboard the beach retreat on Mexico’s turquoise-water Caribbean coast as a mecca for global trendsetters. “Tulum style” came to describe a distinctive aesthetic — flowing fabrics, linen and crochet, neutral colors, bare feet, traditional craftsmanship — that blended rustic-chic, environmentalist and free-spirit ideals into the boho-luxe look of the moment. Skeptics counter that much of this manufacturing is mere final assembly — screwdriver work that adds little value. CDC warns storm raises the risk of some diseases
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
16:43:42 UTC
01:43:42 KST

Strong wind and heavy rain brought by Typhoon Champi increases the risk of some diseases, so people should take protective actions during cleanup activities, CDC Deputy Director-General and spokesman Lin Min-cheng (林明誠) said yesterday.
Wind and heavy rain can disrupt soil and sediment, stirring up pathogens and causing them to spread into the environment, increasing the risk of contracting diseases such as melioidosis, leptospirosis and tetanus, Lin said.
Melioidosis is an infectious disease caused by Burkholderia pseudomallei, bacteria found in tropical and subtropical soil and surface water, he said.
Photo: CNA
The bacteria can be transmitted through cuts or abrasions exposed to contaminated soil or water, breathing in dust or water droplets, or consuming contaminated water or food, especially during typhoons or flooding after typhoons, he said.
Leptospirosis is a bacterial infection caused by Leptospira bacteria, which spreads from infected animals to humans through wounds or mucous membranes coming into direct contact with contaminated water, soil or animal urine, as well as consuming contaminated water or food, he said.
Elderly people and people with chronic medical conditions, including diabetes and liver disease, have increased risk of severe melioidosis infection, which can cause pneumonia, sepsis or septic shock, Lin said.
People who frequently come into contact with wastewater, wildlife, aquaculture or livestock, as well as veterinarians and others who work with animals, and people who live or work in areas with severe rodent infestations are the main groups susceptible to leptospirosis, he said.
However, following a typhoon, torrential rain and flooding, the pathogens are easily flushed in large quantities onto the ground and into standing water, so people with open skin wounds who walk through water without proper protection are susceptible to the two diseases, he added.
Standing water after heavy rain is an ideal breeding ground for mosquitoes, increasing the risk of vector-borne infectious diseases such as dengue fever, Lin said, adding that people should also pay close attention to food hygiene after a typhoon to prevent gastrointestinal infections.
The CDC urges people to wear appropriate protective gear when cleaning and restoring their living environment after a typhoon or flooding, thoroughly clean and tidy the surroundings before and after a storm to eliminate mosquito breeding sites, do not consume water or food that has spoiled or been contaminated, and thoroughly clean and disinfect the home environment, he said.
Protective gear includes long waterproof boots, thick waterproof rubber gloves, medical masks, and protective eyewear or face shields, he said, adding that before cleaning up, people who have open wounds should dress and bandage them, and strictly avoid direct contact with contaminated water or mud.
The CDC recommends using bleach for environmental cleaning and disinfection, he said.
Wipe flood-affected surfaces with bleach diluted 1:100 with water, disinfect kitchenware and tableware with boiling water, or a solution of 40ml of bleach and 10 liters of water, then thoroughly rinse them with clean water before use, Lin said.
People should also wash their hands thoroughly with soap to eliminate pathogens, he said, adding that if they experience fever, headache, muscle soreness, diarrhea or jaundice after contact with floodwater, they should see a doctor immediately and inform the doctor about their exposure to floodwater.
