Brewers’ Misiorowski sets pitch record
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
16:43:41 UTC
01:43:41 KST

Jacob Misiorowski stepped on the mound for a World Series debut like no other.
“I had so much adrenaline built up,” he said.
He threw a pitch the likes of which had never been seen in the Fall Classic.
Photo: AP
The Miz broke the World Series velocity record with his very first delivery, a 103.5mph (166.6kph) fastball to the Tampa Bay Rays’ Yandy Diaz that was taken high out of the strike zone for a ball. He allowed one run over five innings to get his first postseason win as a starter, helping the Milwaukee Brewers to a 3-2 victory in Friday night’s opener.
“I don’t even know how to tell you how I felt,” the 24-year-old right-hander said a half-hour after the end of a crazy ninth inning, prolonged by a game-extending video review. “I still don’t know how I felt. I feel like I’m still trying to take everything in and understand what happened.”
Misiorowski gave up four hits and one walk, striking out a season-low three.
Aroldis Chapman of the Chicago Cubs had the previous mark for fastest Series pitch at 103.2mph in the ninth inning of Game 2 in 2016, an offering that resulted in a groundout to second by Cleveland’s Coco Crisp. The previous high by a Series starting pitcher since tracking began in 2008 was 101.1mph by the New York Mets’ Noah Syndergaard to Kansas City’s Ben Zobrist that was taken for a ball in the first inning of Game 3 in 2015.
Miz reached 100mph with 38 pitches, topping the previous Series high of 24 by Chapman in Game 5 of 2016. The most by a starting pitcher in the Series had been six by Tampa Bay’s Tyler Glasnow in the 2020 opener against the Los Angeles Dodgers.
Tampa Bay scored in the fourth when Jonathan Aranda walked, took third on Junior Caminero’s double over center fielder Garrett Mitchell and came around on Liam Hicks’ grounder to first baseman Jake Bauers.
Nearing the end of his first full major league season, Misiorowski has reached 100mph with 134 of 260 postseason pitches. However, his spin rate was down, a sign of a season in which he has pitched 188 innings — up from 141 1/3 innings last year. And he got just seven swings and misses, five on his fastball.
Tampa Bay batters fouled off 20 of his 78 pitches and tipped another.
During the regular season, Misiorowski reached 100mph with 1,115 pitches, including a high of 105.5mph to the Chicago Cubs’ Pete Crow-Armstrong on June 27.
“What we’re used to seeing in the regular season was Miz just mow through people and have two strikeouts an inning. That’s unrealistic,” Brewers manager Pat Murphy said. “This is the best team in the American League.”
Miz’s first pitch was so fast the scoreboard at American Family Field could not keep up, flashing 103.4mph— one-tenth of a mile less than it registered on MLB’s Statcast system.
“He’s such a special pitcher,” Rays manager Kevin Cash said. “I felt like for him to be out of the game at five innings, there’s a small win in that.”
Misiorowski threw fastballs on 10 of his first 12 pitches, then mixed in more offspeed stuff. In all he tossed 48 fastballs, 17 cutters, seven sliders and six curveballs.
Miz finished with 30 pitches at 101mph or higher, 11 of 102mph or more and three at over 103mph.
Warming up in the bullpen, he could not take in the introductions before Milwaukee’s first World Series game in 44 years. He thought about how far he had come, how he was at Double-A Biloxi two years ago.
“It was crazy,” he said. “It’s everything I dreamed of.”

Three arms programs facing delays: MND
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
16:43:37 UTC
01:43:37 KST

Three of Taiwan’s 24 US arms procurement programs are facing delays: the purchase of MK-48 heavyweight torpedoes, AGM-154C Joint Standoff Weapons and F-16V Block 70 jets, the Ministry of National Defense (MND) said in a report submitted to the Legislative Yuan.
Of the 24 ongoing procurement programs, 21 were progressing as scheduled, the report said.
The military planned to procure 24 MK-48 heavyweight submarine-launched torpedoes for combat use and four for training, at a total cost of NT$5.46 billion (US$167.96 million).
Photo: Hotli Simanjuntak, EPA
All the torpedoes were scheduled to be delivered by this year, but supply chain disruptions and the need to restart production lines had led to repeated delays.
The latest schedule calls for all the torpedoes to be delivered by 2028, the ministry said.
Taiwan also procured AGM-154C missiles under the F-16A/B performance upgrade program, known as the Feng Chan project, but the US had to restart production lines, source materials and resolve system integration issues as Taiwan had opted for the latest version of the missiles, it said.
The delays have pushed the completion of missile deliveries to 2028, it added.
The upgrades to Taiwan’s F-16A/B jets were completed in 2023, the ministry said.
Lastly, the procurement 66 F-16V Block 70 jets, for which NT$247.23 billion was allocated between 2020 and this year, is also delayed.
All 66 aircraft were scheduled to be delivered this year, but the relocation and restart of the production line, along with supply chain disruptions, have put the deliveries at risk, the ministry said.
The first two aircraft arrived at the air force’s Chihhang Base in Taitung on Oct. 2, and the remaining jets are to be flown to Taiwan in batches after preparations are completed, it said.
Other procurement programs have made progress, with all M1A2T tanks, Switchblade 300 drones and airborne operations parachute equipment scheduled under to be delivered this year, the ministry said
Deliveries of third-generation land-based communications systems, Stinger man-portable air defense systems, Harpoon coastal defense systems, MS-110 reconnaissance pods and MQ-9B drones are also expected to continue this year, the ministry added.
The third-generation land-based communications system program runs from 2020 to 2029, with more than NT$8.7 billion allocated. The procurement covers 154 communications nodes, 24 relay systems and eight network management centers.
Equipment is being delivered in batches, and the program is expected to be completed in 2029, it said.
The Patriot II system upgrade and Patriot III procurement program runs from 2007 to next year, with more than NT$179.1 billion allocated, the ministry said.
The procurement includes upgrades to three Patriot II missile system units, six Patriot III missile system units and 102 extended-range Patriot III missiles, it said.

Taiwan plans to build rare earths plant
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
16:43:37 UTC
01:43:37 KST

The Industrial Technology Research Institute (ITRI) plans to build a rare-earth demonstration plant that could meet half the nation’s needs by the end of 2030, as Chinese export controls heighten concerns over industrial supply chains, the institute president said.
In the planning stage, the facility aims to produce 500 tonnes of rare earths annually, ITRI president Chang Pei-zen (張培仁) said in a recent interview.
Construction is targeted for completion by the end of 2028, followed by work to refine production processes and reach the planned output.
Photo: Reuters
The ITRI intends to build the plant in an industrial park to facilitate its eventual transfer to a private company. Funding would need to be budgeted by the National Science and Technology Council, while commercial arrangements, including possible government price guarantees for investors, remain under discussion, Chang said.
Taiwan’s demand for rare earths is relatively small, but the materials are indispensable, he said, adding that the Ministry of Economic Affairs hopes to develop a domestic supply chain and expand production capacity to address concerns about export restrictions.
China’s controls have highlighted risks extending beyond the supply of raw materials to components used in industrial equipment.
Reuters on Thursday reported that Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co (TSMC, 台積電) was exploring alternatives to rare earth components in factory equipment to reduce the risk of disruptions at its advanced chip plants.
TSMC did not comment.
Rare earth magnets are used in motors that move parts in industrial machinery, including equipment in highly automated semiconductor factories, Reuters said.
Supply restrictions could affect manufacturers even when rare earths are not incorporated directly into their finished products.
The ITRI already operates an experimental rare earth production line, but its annual output is only about 5 tonnes, Chang said.
The proposed plant’s target would represent a 100-fold increase.
Equipment at ITRI’s headquarters in Hsinchu County handles rare earth separation and conversion into metals, while some equipment for making high-end magnets is at its Southern Region Campus in Tainan, Chang said.
Rare earth processing is technically challenging, as different elements have very similar properties, making them difficult to separate, he said.
Developing and fine-tuning the separation process can involve hundreds or even thousands of stages and requires substantial experience, Chang said.
The institute aims to refine its production processes by the end of 2030 as it works toward the annual output target. Alongside the technical work, further discussions will be needed on how to provide prospective private investors with sufficient assurances to participate, he said.

Formosa, Taiwan, weight of names
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
16:43:36 UTC
01:43:36 KST

Taiwan heads to the polls next month for local elections. Beneath the campaign ads lies a deeper question: What do we call this place and who gets to decide?
In the pages of the Oxford English Dictionary (OED), that question has been playing out across three centuries. The entries for “Formosa” and “Taiwan” chart an island’s journey from colonial fantasy to self-named reality.
Names are rarely neutral; they are the first act of possession. Nowhere is this more evident than in the OED, where the two entries serve as a linguistic seismograph for one of the world’s most enduring geopolitical fault lines. To read their historical quotations is to watch an island shed the skin of colonial romance and assume the complex, contested identity of a modern nation.
“Formosa” entered the English lexicon not as a place, but as a compliment. In the 1382 Wycliffite Bible, the term appears in the Latin phrase formosa mea (“my beautiful one”), a purely adjectival endearment. Centuries passed before the adjective hardened into a proper noun and when it finally did, it was through the ledger books of the empire.
By 1704, European trading manifests listed “sugar of Formosa” alongside “Japanese silver” and “China tea.” The West knew the island not as a society, but as a commodity. Even its natural endowments were inventoried for extraction: an 1889 entry priced Formosa camphor in the Hong Kong market, while a 1921 botanical report appraised the “crapy appearance” of Formosa oolong teas.
For 300 years, the island existed in the English language as a picturesque backdrop for trade, its indigenous inhabitants reduced to curiosities who made “a drink as strong and intoxicative as sack, out of rice.”
The lexicon shifted violently in the mid-20th century. After 1949, “Formosa” ceased to be a botanical footnote and became a Cold War battleground. The OED’s quotations from that era read like dispatches from the front lines of containment.
A 1950 Baltimore Sun article framed the island as “the last refuge of the Nationalists,” and a 1959 Economist piece tallied “United States aero-naval strength in the Formosa Strait.”
The name had become a geopolitical signifier, a synonym for the free world’s precarious foothold in Asia. Yet even as US admirals drew battle lines, the island’s own identity was quietly evolving.
The dictionary records the moment of transition with telling brevity. A 1972 entry in the Shooting Times carries the parenthetical “Taiwan to most, these days,” an author’s aside that the OED preserved, and one that quietly concedes the old colonial name was becoming an anachronism.
That was not merely a semantic shift; it was a reclamation. In that single parenthetical note, the dictionary captured the slow erosion of imperial nomenclature and the stubborn persistence of local identity.
The “Taiwan” entry, spanning 1958 to 2019, charts the emergence of a sovereign actor. Early citations still bear the scars of diplomatic isolation. A 1979 Time article lamented “disgruntlement and protest over derecognition,” but the quotations quickly pivoted to agency. Taiwan was no longer a refuge or a strait; it was a “silicon island,” an “Asian wunderkind” that “out-traded” its neighbors.
A 1976 Newsweek piece captured a peculiar moment of cultural victory, noting the embarrassment of US teams outslugged by Taiwan’s little league players, baseball being, after all, “as American as apple pie.” By 2000, the New York Times could describe a government committed to making Taiwan a “green silicon island,” a vision of technological sovereignty that would have been unintelligible to the camphor merchants of 1889.
Yet the OED also records the persistent friction of this self-naming. The newest source in its files is no longer a newspaper, but a tweet. A 2019 user observed: “If I were located in the U.S., I would likely be labeled a sinophobe because of my support for Taiwan,” proof that the name remains a political act, dangerous even in digital discourse.
The island’s identity is still negotiated in the space between Beijing’s sovereignty claims and Washington’s strategic ambiguity.
Even the word “Taiwanese” carries weight. In 1969, the Times noted that “63 percent of local government officials are natives of Taiwan,” a statistic that was then, and remains now, anything but neutral.
What the dictionary cannot resolve is the tension between the two names. “Formosa” carries the burden of the external gaze, colonial, romantic, reductive. It is the name given by sailors and merchants who saw beauty and profit, but not people. “Taiwan” is the name claimed by those who lived there, a word that encompasses baseball teams and semiconductor fabs, democratic protests and diplomatic slights.
The OED, in its admirable neutrality, simply records both. It offers no judgement on which name is correct, only evidence of how language bends under the pressure of history.
The dictionary, in the end, is not an arbiter of identity, but a mirror. It shows us that names are never merely descriptive; they are arguments dressed as labels. Formosa speaks of the colonial gaze; Taiwan speaks of a people’s insistence on being called by their own name. The dictionary’s record does not settle the matter. It merely acknowledges that Taiwan’s name, like its history, refuses to stand still.
For this nation, caught between history’s long shadow and the urgencies of the present, the argument is far from over.
Hugo Tseng has a doctorate in linguistics, and is a lexicographer and former chair of the Soochow University English Department.

====================================================================================================

The good guys notch a victory in the AI cybersecurity age
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
16:43:33 UTC
01:43:33 KST

The headlines were unremarkable. Researchers had found a way to weaponize two vulnerabilities in PHP, a programming language used for Web sites and apps, and companies were being urged on Wednesday to install a patch. A smattering of Web sites and services were taken offline while it was installed.
The US said it was looking into government systems and expediting mitigations. The media barely blinked.
However, like a thwarted terror attack, or the Year 2000 problem, the general feeling of a nothingburger can disguise the behind-the-scenes heroics that have — so far — averted catastrophe. That is the case here: an incident that should be considered the most significant victory for the good guys so far in the new artificial intelligence (AI)-cybersecurity age, a boon for the cybersecurity industry eager to prove it is more valuable than ever.
Illustration: Constance Chou
The vulnerabilities — named PHP2Shell — stood to affect about “70 percent of all Web sites in the world,” said Wiz, a cybersecurity firm owned by Google. These deep, underlying flaws, which had existed for more than a decade, allowed an attacker to execute code remotely — like handing a set of keys to an outsider to do and see almost anything it wanted.
“These findings rank among the most severe vulnerabilities discovered in PHP, and arguably in software history,” Wiz wrote.
An abundance of caution has gone global. Web sites belonging to several European governments and local authorities went offline. In the UK, the BBC took parts of its Web site down for maintenance. A US-based human resources company briefly went offline. Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi urged companies to apply the patch quickly. Yet so far, that was all this has amounted to: an abundance of caution.
PHP2Shell was discovered in August with the help of “frontier” AI models, the term given to the cutting edge of what was coming out of the leading labs, from OpenAI to Google. Wiz found the vulnerability in August. So, separately, did Calif, another cybersecurity firm, working with OpenAI as part of a coordinated effort called Patch the Planet, which was launched in the wake of fear around how AI could supercharge the capabilities of cybercriminals and rogue states.
To be clear, this was a far more complex task than simply asking the AI model to find a problem. Rather, this was a concert of model and human specialists, allowing what Wiz described as “an exceptionally complex chain of steps, at the edge of what human researchers could practically achieve.”
A single researcher in Wiz’s team handled in a week what would have taken a “world-class” team months, the firm said.
With the flaws discovered, the mitigation effort kicked in behind closed doors. The team that administers PHP — it is an open-source language — began developing its fix. Top Internet infrastructure firms such as Amazon Web Services and Cloudflare were notified.
The vulnerabilities (and the solution) were made public on Wednesday, with a patch released in the morning — a day ahead of schedule, because some details had been leaked. OpenAI put out a “skill” for its Codex platform that helps companies quickly determine which updates are needed.
Now that the exploit has been made public, hackers will be identifying those weak spots, too, and some have already done so.
Cloudflare chief technology officier Dane Knecht said the company had, before the patch was made available, seen “early attacks emerging” against its clients and was offering them stopgap measures until the weakness had been patched. These attacks are nothing compared with what might have happened had these vulnerabilities been discovered by bad actors first.
The incident underscores the growing importance of specialized cybersecurity firms in the AI age. It was only in February that the stocks of leading security companies such as Cloudflare and Crowdstrike took a bath over investor fears that AI lab Anthropic was going to steal their business. What nonsense that seems today, with the opposite proving true. The new paradigm of security threats has made cybersecurity expertise more valuable, so it is no surprise that Cloudflare shares rose about 7 percent on the news, up 76 percent since that February shock. Crowdstrike is up 146 percent in that time.
Of course, the AI firms are helping defend against a risk they helped create, but that cat is out of the bag now — the same technology that can discover new drugs or write complex code can be used to hack computers. The only course of action is to deal with it. This incident should provide encouragement. The takeaway is that a collaboration between security researchers and frontier AI labs gave the world a head start against a serious threat. These collaborative efforts must continue and be expanded.
We are not out of the woods yet. As ever in cybersecurity, the onus is still on security teams to act. However, these teams do so in full possession of the facts, with a patch ready to go, and in a state of relative calm thanks to trusted sources offering well-considered remedies. The fact that none of this made it to the front pages or nightly news bulletins counts as a battle won in what would be a never-ending war.
Dave Lee is Bloomberg Opinion’s US technology columnist. He was previously a correspondent for the Financial Times and BBC News. This column reflects the personal views of the author and does not necessarily reflect the opinion of the editorial board or Bloomberg LP and its owners.

Apple’s iPhone Duo hits stores with supply short, demand high
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
16:43:32 UTC
01:43:32 KST

Apple Inc quickly sold out of its limited in-store inventory for the new iPhone Duo, underscoring the strong demand for a foldable device that starts at nearly US$2,000.
The phone went on sale on Friday, bringing back the once-familiar sight of people lining up overnight to get their hands on it first. Marking the company’s most radical reinvention in the iPhone’s nearly two-decade history, the Duo is a major bet that Apple can establish itself in a category that is remained a niche so far.
Apple’s latest gadget packed stores from New York to Beijing and Singapore. The early turnout featured customers collecting their preorders, some trying their luck to secure limited inventory for walk-in purchases, and resellers hoping to flip the devices for a higher price.
Photo: Bloomberg
In Singapore, a few hundred people stood in line early Friday, including a family of seven from Myanmar who had camped out overnight.
“This is the first true innovation Apple have had in years,” said Peter Ingram, a chief technology officer visiting from London, who plans to buy it upon his return to the UK. “It is expensive. But I tried it out, played with it in the store. It’s incredible how it’s got no crease.”
In the US, Apple stores received about 50 to 200-plus Duo units per location, and they went fast. A store in Los Angeles had no units left for people who arrived after about 6:30am. The 256-gigabyte star white model, priced at US$1,999, was popular with shoppers.
Large crowds on launch day have mostly dissipated in the past few years after Apple, retailers and wireless carriers began maintaining enough inventory to fulfill most orders through home delivery or appointment-based store pickups. However, the company’s first foldable device arrived in much more limited supply.
Consumers placing new orders for the Duo on Apple’s Web site are being offered delivery at the end of January, though some have seen their shipping estimates move up to as soon as next month or December. The delays mark some of the lengthiest for a new Apple product in the company’s modern era.
Shoppers at the Domain Northside Apple Store in Austin were greeted by new chief executive officer John Ternus, who took the helm last month. At the Fifth Avenue location in New York, the line was already stretching multiple blocks at about 5am, three hours before doors opened to iPhone Duo customers. The launch there was marked by Apple’s senior vice president of marketing Greg Joswiak, and vice president of retail stores Vanessa Trigub.
At the Apple Store in Lawrence Township, New Jersey, about 64km outside Philadelphia, the 256 and 512-gigabyte configurations sold out within the first half hour, leaving the pricier 1 and 2-terabyte (TB) models.
Victor Osorio, a shopper at that location, said even though foldables are not new, “Apple always does something different and adds extra spice to it. I’m not nervous about the form factor but I am about the hinge. I don’t want it to get in the way but it looks OK so far.” Osorio arrived early with his partner, Victoria, who also purchased the Duo and said she was intrigued by the device’s multitasking capabilities.
At the same location, Naveed Abubacker said he trades in his iPhone every year. “Foldable technology has been around for a while and Apple is late to the gate but I’m ready for it,” he said. “If it doesn’t work out for me, I’ll return it.”
In China, Shanghai and Beijing saw a moderate turnout, with most Duo buyers already loyal Apple customers who said they were excited to try out the new design. Many had to register in advance to secure their unit.
“It will take some getting used to,” Andy Shen said at Apple’s Sanlitun store in Beijing. “I chose the Duo mainly because it opens up to a bigger screen to enable better experience with videos, though its other functions are not measuring up to earlier generations, like the camera.”
As one of the most expensive mainstream smartphones ever sold, the Duo had raised questions about just how much demand there would be. Most of the shoppers in Beijing and Singapore looked past the high price and focused on the promise of a truly new Apple product after many years of iterative updates.
The iPhone lineup is Apple’s largest moneymaker, generating about half of the company’s revenue. And the Duo is the biggest single design change in the device’s nearly history. Although the company was not first to market with a foldable phone, it looks to gain an edge with a more polished product built for Apple fans.
Rather than a repeat of the lackluster debut of the Vision Pro headset nearly three years ago, the Duo’s launch is shaping up to be a throwback to the iPhone introductions of old — when demand far outstripped supply. That is the case even with device prices reaching as high as US$3,199 for models with 2TB of storage.
Although the Duo’s cost sets a record for a mass-market smartphone, Apple’s competitors such as Samsung Electronics Co, Xiaomi Corp and Oppo have been raising prices as well. Shortages of memory chips and other components have made consumer electronics more expensive across the board.
The new phones from Apple are difficult to produce because of their advanced hinge and new display technology. They are also only built in a limited number of facilities in China. Apple expanded production in the past few years for its traditional iPhones, including to India, which has helped with supply.
Apple reports its quarterly earnings results on Nov. 2, but those would not include sales of the Duo because the period concluded at the end of last month. It would reflect early sales of iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max models, which debuted on Sept. 18.
Other new versions, such as the entry-level iPhone or the updated Air, would not go on sale until next year, Bloomberg News reported. That marks a change in the company’s usual release schedule, a move meant to help spread out revenue across the year.

====================================================================================================

WUFI calls for re-examination of Retrocession Day
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
16:43:31 UTC
01:43:31 KST

Oct. 25 should not only serve as a commemorative day for Chinese regimes, but also a day for Taiwanese to shatter the “two Chinas” lie and reaffirm their right to self-determination, the World United Formosans for Independence (WUFI) said yesterday.
On Oct. 25, 1945, the Republic of China (ROC) accepted Japan’s surrender in Taiwan and called the day “Taiwan Retrocession Day,” claiming that Taiwan was returned to China, it said.
On Oct. 25, 1971, the UN General Assembly passed Resolution 2785 which states that the People’s Republic of China (PRC) is the only legitimate representative of China at the UN, it said.
Photo: Screen grab from World United Formosans for Independence’s Facebook page
The two Chinese regimes use the events as basis for claims of sovereignty over Taiwan, WUFI said.
A military surrender and administrative takeover does not equate to a transfer of sovereignty, it said.
The San Francisco treaty, signed in 1951, states that the Japanese government renounces sovereignty over Taiwan and Penghu, but does not specify to whom that sovereignty was to be transferred, it said.
The Treaty of Peace between the Republic of China and Japan, commonly known as the Treaty of Taipei, signed in 1952, also contained no explicit clause transferring sovereignty over Taiwan to the ROC, WUFI said.
The Chinese Nationalist Party (KMT) government portrayed the post-World War II takeover as a “retrocession,” using Chinese nationalism to supplant the right of the Taiwanese to determine their own future, it said.
The 228 Incident, the White Terror era and the decades of martial law showed that being taken over by another regime did not equate to freedom for the people, it added.
UN Resolution 2758 addressed the issue of China’s representation at the UN, but it did not mention Taiwan, it said, adding that the resolution does not state that Taiwan is part of the PRC.
The European Parliament in 2024 passed a resolution stating that UN Resolution 2758 “takes no position on Taiwan” and does not have any bearing on Taiwan’s participation in the UN or other international organizations, it said.
The PRC has never governed Taiwan, yet it used its right to represent China to claim sovereignty over Taiwan and block the nation’s international participation, WUFI said.
The two Chinese regimes have competed over which one represents China, and share the belief that Taiwan belongs to China and that Taiwanese have no right to determine the nation’s future, it said.
That is a historical predicament Taiwan must overcome, it added.
Taiwan is neither territory that can be inherited as a byproduct of the two Chinese regimes’ struggle for representation nor property whose fate can be arbitrarily determined by either of them, it said.
Retrocession Day should be re-examined, WUFI said.
The organization called for the rejection of Beijing’s distortion of UN Resolution 2758, efforts to secure Taiwan’s right to participate internationally, and constitutional reform and normalization of the nation through peaceful, democratic means and self-determination.
Administrative takeover is not retrocession and representing China does not mean owning Taiwan, it said, adding that the nation’s future should be decided by Taiwanese.

There is no escaping tech tycoon villains (at the movies)
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
16:43:31 UTC
01:43:31 KST

There is a striking moment near the end of Musk, a new documentary by Oscar-winning filmmaker Alex Gibney, when the world’s richest man is asked why he considers it important to develop X into what he calls a global platform for collective consciousness.
“I guess ...” Elon Musk replies to his questioner, the billionaire Indian entrepreneur Nikhil Kamath, before his voice trails off. There is a pause of several seconds in which neither man says anything. Eventually, after a couple of false starts, Musk settles on: “To increase our understanding of the universe.”
The exchange — originally broadcast as part of Kamath’s People by WTF podcast in November last year — stands out because it follows more than three and a half hours of a film in which Musk is rarely short of words or solutions. We see his early successes during the dot-com boom, followed by his stewardship of Tesla Inc and SpaceX, the acquisition of Twitter and, ultimately, his alliance with US President Donald Trump.
Photo: AFP
At every step, Gibney depicts Musk as relentlessly accumulating money and power, shrugging off a string of controversies — business and personal — along the way. The section on the Department of Government Efficiency, the Trump administration initiative ostensibly created to identify and cut waste, is especially troubling to watch, particularly when it focuses on cuts to the US Agency for International Development and their impact on projects in Africa. However, when asked to articulate his deeper purpose, the tycoon is lost for words.
Musk represents a prominent example of a shift in contemporary cinema: While multibillionaire tech tycoons have made for convenient villains in the past, recent portrayals are more frequent and less ambivalent. Gibney, 72 — a prolific filmmaker who won the 2007 Academy Award for best documentary feature for Taxi to the Dark Side about abuse by US soldiers — paints a picture of ruthlessness, cynicism and a chronic lack of regulatory oversight. Musk is designed to leave the viewer feeling bleak about the world. As Gibney asks by way of a mission statement: “How could Musk assume so much power, and why had we given it to him?”
That question, to which there is no straightforward answer, speaks to a growing sense of public discomfort with the way superrich tech leaders and their companies have come to dominate the corporate, political and media landscape — as well as our personal lives. The release of Musk came just months after its subject became the world’s first trillionaire following SpaceX’s record-breaking initial public offering, an unheard-of level of wealth that is helping to fund Republican campaigns ahead of the Nov. 3 midterm elections. According to a Pew survey conducted last year, more than half of Americans have an unfavorable view of Musk, while two-thirds had a negative perception of Meta Platforms Inc chief executive officer Mark Zuckerberg.
Another version of Elon Musk appears in Artificial which screened at this month’s London Film Festival ahead of its release this winter. The film, directed by Luca Guadagnino, charts the early years of OpenAI, which Musk co-founded in 2015. Musk left the company in 2018 and has tried unsuccessfully to sue its present incarnation, allowing writer Simon Rich to make the film version played by Ike Barinholtz a form of comic relief — all facial tics and self-importance — rather than anything more sinister.
The role of tech tycoon villain instead goes to Andrew Garfield, who plays OpenAI CEO Sam Altman. The film portrays him as the ultra-ambitious and unscrupulous driving force behind the company that gave us ChatGPT, with the movie’s conscience represented by co-founder and chief scientist Ilya Sutskever (played by Yura Borisov — best known as the kind-hearted henchman in Anora).
Artificial goes on to tell the story of Altman and Sutskever’s eventual falling-out, with Altman fired and swiftly reinstated with the support of Microsoft Corp, OpenAI’s main investor. Garfield plays Altman as increasingly cold and manipulative, swatting aside any concerns about AI safety and the people who get in his way. “I didn’t invent teen suicide!” he yells at one fellow executive, when warned of ChatGPT’s darker potential.
Facebook founder Zuckerberg was the subject of David Fincher’s acclaimed 2010 movie The Social Network and it feels apt that writer Aaron Sorkin should return with a de facto sequel some 16 years later.
In the original movie, the action revolves around a litigation against Zuckerberg during Facebook’s early years. In this fall’s The Social Reckoning he is now well-established — and it is Wall Street Journal reporter Jeff Horwitz (Jeremy Allen White) and Facebook employee-turned-whistleblower Frances Haugen (Mikey Madison) who are out to get him.
The story shows how the duo worked together on Horwitz’s award-winning reporting on Facebook and its algorithm in 2021, with a particular focus on how users can become radicalized and pushed toward extremist groups.
The rather unsubtle point of The Social Reckoning is that Facebook and Zuckerberg are terrible, while journalists and whistleblowers are good. It was not as binary when Sorkin was writing The Social Network, where the Facebook founder could be seen as a misfit simply trying to get his own back on the alpha males and women he believed looked down on him.
Some might see Facebook as a product of the past, with the stakes around the technology developed by OpenAI and rival Anthropic PBC much higher. The drunk woman who delivers a racist diatribe at police officers at the start of The Social Reckoning — radicalized by Facebook, Haugen deduces — might seem trivial compared with the potential for AI to overpower humanity, as is threatened in Artificial.
The power of technology to turn people against each other, only for us all to be overpowered by robots, drives the fear coursing through all these films. “We’ll have to build a bunker,” Geoffrey Hinton (Mark Rylance), Sutskever’s early mentor, warns him early in Artificial. “And hide from the Terminator.”

Israel detains dozens of Palestinians in West Bank crackdown
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
16:32:55 UTC
01:32:55 KST

Breadcrumb
Israel detains dozens of Palestinians in crackdown on occupied West Bank
Around 70 Palestinians have been detained in less than 48 hours in a sweeping Israeli crackdown on the occupied West Bank, the Palestinian Prisoners’ Society said on Saturday.
The group said Israeli authorities are continuing their offensive across the West Bank, and that detentions have been on the rise since the start of the war on Gaza in October 2023.
The organisation also noted that a crackdown on Hebron, which started on Friday, has spread to other cities.
Arrests were recorded in various cities and towns, including Ramallah, Qalqilya, Jenin, Nablus, Jericho, Salfit, Tubas, Bethlehem, Tulkarem and occupied East Jerusalem.
Data compiled by the group shows that some of those detained have since been released; however, others are facing interrogations.
The data showed that many of those targeted in the crackdown were detainees who had previously been released, including some individuals who were freed as part of prisoner exchange deals.
Rights groups have decried the mass arrests as a systematic policy of persecution, and said the crackdown has extended to relatives and acquaintances of those who were formerly detained.
One of those who were targeted has been identified as Nael Barghouti. According to the official Palestinian Wafa news agency, Israeli forces raided his home in the town of Kobar, leaving his home partially destroyed and heavily vandalised.
The Palestinian Prisoners Society said that most of the detainees who were released said they were subjected to varying degrees of assault, including being blindfolded, shackled, and threatened.
The threats included being warned to not engage in any political activity.
Meanwhile, the rights group also noted that threatening leaflets were distributed across cities in the West Bank.
The development comes as hundreds of families were displaced from Hebron in the middle of the night following large-scale raids and the decision to place the city under lockdown amid a military operation.
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu vowed on Friday to collectively punish residents from a neighbourhood in Hebron, after an attack was carried out on an Israeli army checkpoint.
Palestinian prisoner groups have documented at least 26,000 arrests in the West Bank since the start of the war on Gaza, which does not include those detained in Gaza.

Babcock opens skills centre on Devonport waterfront
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
17:30:17 BST
01:30:17 KST

Babcock has opened a Skills Centre at Devonport Dockyard able to support fifteen hundred technical staff and apprentices a year, and has broken ground on an Integrated Logistics Hub at Sherford that will pull together more than thirty separate logistics sites, according to the company.
Luke Pollard, the Minister for Defence Readiness and Industry and the member for Plymouth Sutton and Devonport, formally opened the Skills Centre, which brings practical training onto the waterfront alongside the work it supports.
The logistics hub at Sherford falls within the Plymouth and South Devon Freeport, on an eighteen point eight acre site with room for a thirty thousand square metre facility. Babcock said it will increase operational capacity and resilience for submarine sustainment and deep maintenance at Devonport, supporting the dual-streaming of Astute class submarines and the transition to Dreadnought.
Pollard said: “Plymouth has always been at the heart of our national defence, and investments like this show how working with industry partners like Babcock can deliver both the skills our Armed Forces need, and the opportunities and growth this community deserves.
“The new Skills Centre will support those already in defence to learn new skills and grow their career and create new pathways for those entering defence for the first time, giving local people the chance to build a career they can be proud of.”
Neal Misell, chief executive of Babcock Nuclear, said: “Today demonstrates our long-term commitment to Plymouth and the wider region, developing the skills, capability and infrastructure needed to bolster the UK’s national defence resilience, while creating opportunities for economic growth and prosperity for future generations. Concluding the day at the new Babcock Capability Centre here in Plymouth city centre was a great chance to share our upcoming plans for the facility with regional partners which will see us relocate around 2000 colleagues into the heart of the city, bringing economic benefits and opportunities as we support the retention and creation of high value jobs into the future.”
Richard May, chief executive of the Plymouth and South Devon Freeport, said: “This is the Freeport doing what it does best – unlocking opportunities and turning plans into real investment. We’re delighted to be working with Babcock to bring this exciting project forward and build on the momentum we’ve created together. It’s a proud moment for everyone involved – and a great example of the defence dividend delivering real benefits for Plymouth and South Devon.”
Councillor Dan Thomas, leader of South Hams District Council, said: “This investment is part of the bigger picture for the South Hams. We promised to support a thriving local economy, create opportunities for good-quality jobs and build strong, resilient communities. By investing carefully and working with our partners, we are turning those promises into practical action that will benefit residents and businesses now and in the future.”

Ternopil region serviceman captured while seriously wounded returns home after four years in captivity
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
16:30:00 UTC
01:30:00 KST

Ternopil region serviceman captured while seriously wounded returns home after four years in captivity
His mother, Olha Chverenchuk, said this in a comment to an Ukrinform correspondent.
"My son took part in fierce fighting on the Lyman axis. That was where he was captured in September 2022. Andrii had a serious wound. He spent six months in hospital," the woman said.
According to Chverenchuk, the circumstances of her son's capture are recounted in the documentary "6th Company." In the film, his fellow servicemen explain that on September 25, two groups of ten men each set out to assault Lyman but fell into an ambush. Russian forces attacked the Ukrainian servicemen. Andrii was wounded and remained in an M113 armored personnel carrier with a fellow soldier. The two began fighting. They later received orders to withdraw into the forest so that artillery units could engage the enemy. Andrii and his wounded comrade, who used the call sign "Znakhаr" (Healer), were captured.
Andrii Chverenchuk is a chemist by education and holds a Candidate of Technical Sciences degree. When Russia launched its full-scale invasion, he was living and working in Kyiv. He joined the defense of Ukraine in the spring of 2022 and served with the 66th Mechanized Brigade.
"During the four years Andrii was in captivity, we wrote him many letters. We hoped they would support our son. Fortunately, he did receive one letter. Later, through the guys who were released from captivity, he sent us his thanks for writing to him. We also know that Andrii was initially held at the Sverdlovsk penal colony, then in Novosibirsk, and later transferred to Kamyshin, where things were the hardest," the serviceman's mother said.
She admitted that it was difficult to describe the emotions she felt when she heard her son's voice on the phone.
"I'm still euphoric. I still can't fully comprehend how happy I am," she said.
The woman said that prayer and faith in God had helped her endure four years of separation from her son and the uncertainty surrounding his fate.

In a statement, the Hebron municipality said the displaced families lived in the Deir Bahha and al-Jilda neighborhoods, which together are home to 500 families.
Israeli forces marked evacuated homes and distributed notices ordering the remaining families to leave without taking their vehicles, it added.

In a statement, the ministry described the threats as attempts to repeat the “Nakba” and carry out ethnic cleansing. It instructed Palestinian embassies and diplomatic missions to take urgent international action to press governments to adopt firm positions against Israeli practices.

The army imposed a closure on the city Friday after two Palestinians fired at an Israeli checkpoint. Both attackers and two Israeli soldiers were killed, while three other soldiers were wounded, according to Israeli figures.

Interior Minister Laurent Nunez had warned that authorities "will not tolerate any violence or any disturbance of public order."
French police had arrested 135 people nationwide and seized a variety of weapons, Interior Minister Laurent Nunez said, adding that, so far, "there has been no major incident".
Weapons confiscated included metal balls, lead pellets, fireworks, slingshots, steel balls, improvised weapons, a katana and airsoft weapons, he said.

Are Lebanese Shi'ites abandoning Hezbollah? Poll shows majority favor disarming group - analysis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
16:01:01 UTC
01:01:01 KST

Hezbollah may face growing criticism from within Lebanon's Shi’ite community, which has formed the backbone of its support for decades, according to a report from KAN on Saturday.
A recent survey of Shi’ites got attention in regional media. As reported by Israel's KAN public broadcaster and the Lebanese Kataeb.org website, the survey, whose results emerged in mid-October, suggested that many Shi'ites are increasingly questioning the terrorist group.
The main question is whether Hezbollah should keep its arsenal. People also questioned Hezbollah’s conduct in the wars with Israel. However, this did not necessarily mean that Hezbollah is losing its influence over the community.
Respondents said decisions regarding war and peace should be left to the Lebanese state
The survey, conducted by Statistics Lebanon in September among 800 Lebanese Shi'ites, found that 66.4% supported transferring Hezbollah's weapons to the Lebanese state. Another 29.6% preferred that the terrorist organization retain its weapons. The results were significant because Hezbollah has argued that its arsenal is essential for defending Lebanon against Israel.
Roi Kais at Israel’s KAN noted, “A new survey has revealed that about 66 percent of Lebanese Shi'ites support Hezbollah's transfer of weapons to the state, and more than 40 percent express anger and disappointment with its leadership. Amid growing criticism, the support networks and status the terrorist organization has given the sect still maintain its power - as long as no other entity fills the vacuum.”
Notably, Kataeb.org, the website of the Phalange Party (Kataeb Party), a political party in Lebanon, published details on the survey. The Christian Kataeb Party opposes Hezbollah. The website noted that 71.1% of respondents believed that decisions about war and peace should rest exclusively with the Lebanese state. Only 5.9% believed Hezbollah's leadership should have a greater role in determining Lebanon's future.
Only 16.5% of respondents had confidence in Hezbollah's ability to guarantee security
The survey also revealed considerable confidence in the Lebanese Armed Forces. Some 78.5% expressed trust in the army, while 51.1% identified it as the institution best suited to guarantee long-term security. Only 16.5% selected Hezbollah.
These findings raised questions about Hezbollah's traditional claim to represent the security interests of Lebanon's Shi'ites. They suggested that many within the community may prefer stronger state institutions, even if they continue to identify politically or socially with Hezbollah.
The survey also found that 67.4% believed Hezbollah had either failed to achieve its objectives in the war with Israel or had achieved only some of them. Another 42.1% expressed disappointment, anger or concern about Hezbollah's leadership and the consequences of the conflict. Nevertheless, 59.5% continued to express varying degrees of trust in Hezbollah, including 37.1% who reported a great deal of trust.
An earlier survey presented a very different picture. In a June 10 analysis published by Israel's Institute for National Security Studies (INSS), researchers Orna Mizrahi and Moran Levanoni cited a May 2026 survey by Lebanon's Information International in which 87.5% of Shiite respondents opposed disarming Hezbollah, while only 7.9% supported surrendering its weapons. More than 90% opposed ties with Israel.
The contrast with the September findings led to many questions. How can people hold such different views? Is it possible that some of the surveys are biased in their questions or agendas?
Mizrahi and Levanoni argued that Hezbollah's influence rests on its social and economic networks, political power, and the historical marginalization of Lebanon's Shi'ites.
They also noted that intimidation has discouraged opposition within the Shi’ite community. The researchers suggested that weakening Hezbollah's influence would require a stronger Lebanese army and Western and Gulf financial assistance to enable the state to replace Hezbollah's services.
This illustrated the complex relationship between Hezbollah and Lebanon's Shi'ites. Hezbollah is not just a terrorist group. It built networks of social services, financial institutions, and political influence to hedge its bets and take over the Lebanese state.
Now that it is so powerful, it is hard to uproot. Many people in Lebanon feared opposing Hezbollah over the years. For some Shi’ite families, it remains an important source of employment and assistance, even if they have to sacrifice their security due to the wars that Hezbollah has caused.
Lebanese fear Hezbollah-linked facilities could become Israeli targets
KAN highlighted an example from the southern Lebanese city of Tyre, where property owners reportedly opposed opening a branch of Hezbollah-linked financial institution Al-Qard Al-Hassan in their building. They feared the branch could become a target for Israeli strikes. The branches have been targeted in the past.
Hezbollah is attempting to regain support through reconstruction assistance. According to KAN, Hezbollah recently announced aid of up to $14,000 for eligible families in Beirut and its southern suburbs whose primary homes were destroyed, and up to $12,000 elsewhere.
The broader question is whether dissatisfaction will translate into political change. Hezbollah has suffered significant military and leadership losses since the war began, including the killing of Hassan Nasrallah in September 2024.
Yet its influence is rooted in decades of political and social organization. Lebanon did not jump at the opportunity to uproot the group in 2025. In March 2026, a new war broke out, leading to massive destruction of villages in southern Lebanon. Even today, Beirut moves at a snail’s pace.
The survey suggests that support for Hezbollah's terrorist role may be weakening even among its traditional constituency. However, unless the Lebanese state can provide security, reconstruction, and economic opportunities, the criticism won’t lead to major change.

Emotional struggles are linked to vulnerable narcissism but not grandiose narcissism, meta-analysis finds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
16:00:50 UTC
01:00:50 KST

A new statistical review of data from more than 12,000 adults suggests that difficulties with managing emotions are moderately linked to one specific form of narcissism, while showing virtually no connection to another. The research, published in Personality and Individual Differences, indicates that people with insecure and defensive narcissistic traits tend to struggle with emotional control, whereas those with more boastful, dominant narcissistic traits generally do not report these same struggles. These findings help clarify why past studies on narcissism and emotional health have produced conflicting results, and they may point to specific emotional skills that could be targeted in therapy.
In psychology, trait narcissism refers to a persistent pattern of personality characteristics centered on interpersonal antagonism, which includes feeling entitled, manipulating others, and lacking empathy. Rather than being a single uniform trait, narcissism is generally divided into two main subtypes: grandiose and vulnerable. Grandiose narcissism matches the common stereotype of a narcissist, featuring an outgoing, dominant, attention-seeking, and aggressively self-confident style. Vulnerable narcissism, while sharing the same core of entitlement and self-centeredness, looks very different on the surface, involving introversion, fragile self-esteem, deep feelings of inadequacy, and a heightened sensitivity to rejection.
Both forms of narcissism are associated with problems in relationships, including a lack of care for a partner’s distress, relationship dissatisfaction, and even intimate partner violence; a 2024 meta-analysis found that violence was more strongly tied to vulnerable narcissism (a correlation of 0.25) than to grandiose narcissism (0.11). Because personality traits themselves are deeply ingrained and difficult to change, psychologists often look for modifiable behaviors and skills that might help improve how narcissistic individuals function in daily life. One promising target is emotion dysregulation, which refers to difficulty understanding, managing, and responding to feelings in a healthy way that aligns with a person’s goals and social norms.
“Our broader interest in this area stems from wanting to understand the psychological factors that contribute to the interpersonal difficulties experienced by people with high levels of narcissism,” senior author Megan L. Willis, an associate professor in the School of Behavioural and Health Sciences and the Healthy Brain and Mind Research Centre at Australian Catholic University, told PsyPost. “I’m particularly interested in factors that may be modifiable – that is, things that we may be able to prevent or improve through psychological intervention.”
When psychologists study emotion dysregulation, they often look at several distinct areas where a person’s emotional control can break down. These areas include refusing to accept negative feelings, lacking awareness or clarity about what emotion is actually occurring, struggling to stay focused on tasks when upset, failing to control impulsive behaviors during distress, and lacking effective strategies to calm down. Studies linking narcissism to these emotional difficulties have produced confusing results, with some finding that narcissistic people had worse emotional control and others finding no link or even better emotional control.
Psychologists began to suspect that these contradictions happened because studies were measuring different subtypes of narcissism. For instance, a 2017 study of Chinese university students found that students with vulnerable narcissistic traits reported substantial trouble managing their emotions, while those with grandiose traits actually reported fewer emotional difficulties, which the authors linked to their higher self-esteem. Similarly, a 2020 study of undergraduates indicated that the defensive, self-protective side of narcissism was tied to poor emotion recognition and messy emotional reactions, whereas the assertive, self-promoting side was linked to better emotional management.
To make sense of the growing body of research, a 2024 systematic review summarized the existing literature and observed a consistent link between vulnerable narcissism and emotional struggles, alongside a lack of evidence connecting grandiose narcissism to those same struggles. However, that earlier review only summarized the studies qualitatively rather than mathematically combining their data, and it mixed psychiatric patients with the general public, which can weaken the correlations researchers observe. Willis, lead author Ria Tziliaskopoulos, and their colleagues at Australian Catholic University set out to conduct a full meta-analysis, a statistical technique that pools data from multiple studies to estimate the strength of the relationship between narcissism and emotion dysregulation in the general adult population.
“We wanted to establish the strength of the relationship between emotion dysregulation and narcissism in general, as well as determine whether this relationship differed between grandiose and vulnerable narcissism,” Willis explained.
The researchers searched five major academic databases through January 2026 to find studies written in English that measured both trait narcissism and emotion dysregulation in adults outside clinical settings. They excluded studies focusing on children or specialized groups like psychiatric patients or prison inmates, ensuring the results would reflect everyday adult populations. This screening process yielded 26 eligible studies from 25 reports, encompassing a combined total of 12,209 participants with average ages ranging from 18.7 to 62 years across countries including the United States, Italy, Turkey, China, Iran, and Brazil.
Because each included study used questionnaires to measure personality and emotional habits, the authors categorized the narcissism questionnaires into three groups: those measuring grandiose narcissism, those measuring vulnerable narcissism, and “combined” measures that blended both traits into a single score. For instance, the widely used Narcissistic Personality Inventory counted as a grandiose measure and the Hypersensitive Narcissism Scale as a vulnerable one, while the 2020 undergraduate study’s self-promoting “admiration” scale was counted as grandiose and its defensive “rivalry” scale as vulnerable.
Twenty-two of the 26 studies measured emotional difficulties using a standard questionnaire called the Difficulties in Emotion Regulation Scale, which scores both overall dysregulation and the six specific problem areas like impulse control and emotional awareness. The researchers extracted 80 individual statistical correlations from the 26 studies and used a method called robust variance estimation to account for the fact that several studies contributed multiple data points from the same group of people.
In statistical terms, a correlation ranges from -1 to 1, where 0 means no relationship, positive values mean two traits tend to rise together, and negative values mean one tends to fall as the other rises. By common convention, values of about 0.10 to 0.29 are considered weak, 0.30 to 0.49 moderate, and 0.50 or above strong. When the researchers pooled all 80 data points together without separating the narcissism subtypes, they found a weak positive correlation of 0.15 between overall narcissism and emotion dysregulation. This meant that across the entire dataset, higher levels of narcissism were only slightly associated with greater trouble managing emotions.
When the team broke the data down by narcissism subtype, a sharp divide emerged that helps explain why the overall correlation was so small. Vulnerable narcissism showed a moderate positive correlation of 0.37 with emotion dysregulation across 11 studies. In contrast, grandiose narcissism showed a correlation of 0.04 across 21 studies, a number so close to zero that it was not statistically significant.
“The relationship with vulnerable narcissism was moderate in size, which is quite a meaningful relationship in individual differences research,” Willis noted. “Narcissism reflects a cluster of personality traits, so we wouldn’t expect any single psychological factor to explain it. The size of the relationship suggests that difficulties regulating emotions are an important part of the psychological profile of people high in vulnerable narcissism.”
Measures that combined both forms of narcissism fell right in the middle, showing a weak positive correlation of 0.25 across five studies. Follow-up statistical comparisons confirmed that the link between vulnerable narcissism and emotional difficulties was substantially stronger than the link for grandiose narcissism. The authors also checked whether a few debatable coding choices drove the results. Dropping the grandiose scale of the Pathological Narcissism Inventory, which critics say overlaps too much with vulnerable traits, left grandiose narcissism at 0.03, and dropping the one study that counted the defensive “rivalry” scale as vulnerable narcissism left vulnerable narcissism at 0.37.
“The findings may help explain some of the interpersonal difficulties experienced by people high in vulnerable narcissism,” Willis said. “They tend to be hypersensitive to rejection and criticism, and our findings suggest they are also more likely to have difficulty regulating their emotions. When they feel rejected or criticized, they may struggle to manage the emotions that arise in these situations. This could contribute to hostile or aggressive responses, which can create conflict and damage their relationships with others.”
The researchers then examined the four or five studies that reported scores for each of the six domains of emotional difficulty, pooling all types of narcissism together. They found weak but statistically reliable correlations with three specific problem areas: limited access to effective emotion regulation strategies had a correlation of 0.21, trouble controlling impulses when upset had a correlation of 0.19, and refusing to accept negative emotions had a correlation of 0.18. Meanwhile, narcissism was not statistically linked to lacking emotional awareness (which had a slight negative correlation of -0.08), lacking emotional clarity (0.13), or struggling to focus on goal-directed behaviors when distressed (0.13). The link with emotional awareness was weaker than the link with every other domain.
The authors suggest this pattern means the emotional struggles tied to narcissism may be less about failing to notice feelings and more about how a person reacts once an unpleasant emotion arrives, such as struggling to accept the feeling, acting impulsively, or feeling there is no healthy way to calm down. Because these analyses drew on only a handful of studies and combined all forms of narcissism, they cannot show whether the pattern differs between grandiose and vulnerable traits. The authors note that these specific breakdowns could help explain why people high in narcissism may lash out, blame others, or withdraw during relationship conflicts.
These results align with a study covered by PsyPost in 2024, which also found that emotion dysregulation was tied to vulnerable rather than grandiose narcissism, although that earlier study tested psychiatric outpatients rather than the general adult samples analyzed in the new review.
The findings sit in partial tension with the 2020 study of undergraduates described earlier, which PsyPost covered in 2019, where the self-promoting side of grandiose narcissism was linked to fewer emotional difficulties and better emotional awareness. The meta-analysis included that study but counted its defensive rivalry scale as vulnerable narcissism, and across all the grandiose questionnaires combined, it found no link either way rather than a protective one.
The absence of a link for grandiose narcissism also contrasts with research covered by PsyPost earlier in 2026, which tied both grandiose and vulnerable traits to brain differences connected to hiding one’s feelings. That difference may reflect what was measured: the brain study looked at the specific habit of suppressing outward emotional expressions, while the meta-analysis assessed broader difficulties managing emotions.
As with all research, there are some caveats to keep in mind when interpreting these findings. Every study included in the meta-analysis relied on self-report questionnaires, which depend on participants being both honest and self-aware about their flaws. The authors point to a 2023 study that recorded facial muscle activity and found amplified emotional reactions to negative social evaluation among people with grandiose traits, suggesting questionnaires may miss some of their emotional responses.
“I also wouldn’t interpret the lack of a relationship with grandiose narcissism as definitive evidence that people high in grandiose narcissism don’t experience difficulties regulating their emotions,” Willis cautioned. “All of the studies relied on self-report measures, and people high in grandiose narcissism may be less likely to perceive or report difficulties with emotion regulation.”
All 26 studies also used cross-sectional designs, measuring personality and emotional habits at a single point in time. In addition, half of the studies (13 of 26) recruited only university students, and most were conducted in Western nations, meaning the findings may not apply equally to older adults or different cultural contexts.
“The main caveat is that all of the studies included in our meta-analysis were cross-sectional, so we can’t determine the direction of the relationship,” Willis said. “Difficulties regulating emotions may contribute to the development or maintenance of vulnerable narcissism, vulnerable narcissism may contribute to difficulties regulating emotions, or other factors may explain this relationship.”
One such shared factor the authors raise is early experience: vulnerable narcissism has been theorized to arise partly from childhood trauma or inconsistent parenting, which may also hinder the development of emotional skills. Results also varied widely from study to study, so the pooled correlations are best read as averages rather than as figures that apply equally to every group or questionnaire. Several statistical checks did suggest the findings were unlikely to be skewed by publication bias, the tendency for studies with positive results to be published more often.
Another limitation is that too few studies reported detailed breakdowns of the six emotional problem areas to allow the authors to test grandiose and vulnerable narcissism separately for each specific skill. The authors recommend that future studies routinely report data for all individual emotion regulation subscales alongside total scores, use longitudinal designs that follow people over time, and recruit more diverse samples across cultures and age groups. Even with these limitations, the authors suggest that therapies focused on emotion regulation, such as dialectical behavior therapy or schema therapy, may be worth testing for people high in vulnerable narcissism, though studies have yet to show whether such treatment improves their well-being or relationships.
Looking ahead, the research team is now examining the roots of these traits and how emotional habits take shape over time. In psychology, insecure attachment refers to relationship patterns characterized by anxiety or avoidance that often stem from inconsistent caregiving early in life.
“One of the things I’m particularly interested in now is understanding how vulnerable narcissism may develop,” Willis told PsyPost. “We’re currently testing models looking at the potential role of insecure attachment and difficulties identifying, understanding and regulating emotions. Ultimately, we want to identify potentially modifiable factors that could be targeted through prevention or intervention strategies.”
The study, “The relationship between narcissism and emotion dysregulation: A systematic review and meta-analysis,” was authored by Ria Tziliaskopoulos, Rose Ferguson, Wendy Song, and Megan L. Willis.

Myanmar: Conflict continues to rage across Rakhine State
Share
Statement24 October 2026
After intense and relentless shelling was heard from MSF’s base in Sittwe, Rakhine State, Myanmar, alongside exchanges of gunfire and the sound of aircraft overhead, our team in central Sittwe learned yesterday, 23 October, that at least two people were killed and 17 others injured in this latest escalation.
MSF understands that one of the shells exploded in downtown Sittwe, at a junction used by civilians to move around this increasingly restricted enclave, and that most of the casualties occurred there.
The injured were taken to Sittwe General Hospital for further treatment. This is the main referral hospital in Sittwe, and MSF has previously supported it by facilitating life-saving transfers for patients from other parts of the state where the specialised care they need is not available.
This latest escalation is not an isolated incident. People across Rakhine State continue to face deadly violence, whether through attacks on populated areas — such as the airstrikes in central Rakhine on 28 September, which killed at least 50 people — or as a result of being caught in the crossfire.
Civilians must be protected from conflict continuing to rage across Rakhine State.
Paul Brockmann, MSF Operations Manager for Myanmar
All warring parties must make every effort to protect civilians, in line with their obligations under international humanitarian law.
For more than 30 years, MSF has stood alongside communities in Rakhine State. While we are aware that some staff from other organisations have been evacuated, our team remains in Sittwe.
We reiterate our call for the protection of civilians — including medical staff and patients in need of care — and for all parties to facilitate the safe and unhindered delivery of humanitarian assistance to people living in a state torn apart by violence and deprivation.

Protector drone flight over Channel was not for Home Office
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
17:00:15 BST
01:00:15 KST

An RAF Protector RG-1 that flew over the English Channel on 14 October was operating in support of defence aims and not in support of the Home Office, according to an answer given in Parliament.
Ben Obese-Jecty, the Conservative member for Huntingdon, had asked for what reason the aircraft was tasked to support the Home Office in the Channel on that date.
Louise Sandher-Jones, the Minister for the Armed Forces, said: “The Ministry of Defence regularly and routinely monitors our waters to protect UK interests, contribute to domestic maritime security, and act as a deterrent against potentially malign activities.
“The deployment the hon. Member refers to was conducted in support of Defence aims, not in support of the Home Office.”
Protector RG-1 is the RAF’s version of the General Atomics MQ-9B SkyGuardian, and the United Kingdom has ordered sixteen of them to replace the MQ-9A Reaper fleet that was retired after two decades of operations over Afghanistan, Iraq and Syria. The aircraft has a wingspan of around twenty four metres, an endurance of more than thirty hours and a maximum altitude above forty thousand feet, and carries Brimstone 3 missiles and Paveway IV bombs alongside its electro-optical and infrared sensors and a maritime search radar.
The aircraft is built to a NATO airworthiness standard and fitted with a detect and avoid system, lightning protection and de-icing, and that certification allows it to fly in unsegregated British airspace alongside civil traffic without a reserved block of sky being set aside for it. The Reaper it replaced could not, and needed segregated airspace or a danger area for every domestic sortie. The fleet is based at RAF Waddington in Lincolnshire with 31 Squadron, and operations are flown from ground control stations on the station.
Surveillance of small boat crossings in the Channel has been contracted out by the Home Office to a commercial operator. The Portuguese company Tekever has operated its AR5 maritime surveillance aircraft over the Channel since 2020 under Home Office contracts, a framework worth up to £1 billion and renewed repeatedly since. The AR5 is a twin-engine fixed-wing aircraft that flies for more than twelve hours and carries maritime and synthetic aperture radars, day and night cameras and receivers for vessel identification and distress beacons.
Paul Webb, managing director of Tekever UK, has said of the work that “drones can identify humans in distress in a much faster way and help rescue teams.” The company has since sold the same system to the Portuguese government and has expanded into supplying uncrewed aircraft to Ukraine.

Text description provided by the architects. On a plot of land that rises thirteen meters (forty-three feet) from the street, "La Joya" House transforms the challenge of a steep slope into an architectural journey, revealing the landscape of San Agustinillo level by level.
The project emerged from a brief to develop three independent units: two small apartments intended primarily as rentals, and a larger residence for the owners' temporary stays. Instead of concentrating the program into a conventional volume, the steep topography offered an opportunity to fragment it and distribute it across different levels along the hillside. Consequently, each unit finds its own place within the site, maintaining privacy while enjoying a direct relationship with the sea.

North Korea improves ballistic missiles and mass-produces drones with Russian support – NYT
North Korea is continuing to upgrade its ballistic missiles and has launched the mass production of attack drones, largely thanks to its cooperation with Russia.
Source: The New York Times
Details: The Russians are sharing their developments with Pyongyang in exchange for soldiers, workers and weapons.
North Korea is modernising its armed forces and weapons with the help of Russia, having renewed military cooperation following the start of the full-scale Russian invasion of Ukraine.
In early October, Pyongyang tested a tactical ballistic missile that it claims is capable of carrying a nuclear payload. South Korea and Japan estimated it flew about 700 km (430 miles), while North Korea claimed a range of 1,000 km (621 miles).
"South Korea usually responds to North Korean missile tests with brief statements condemning them as provocative. But five days after the North's launch, it test-fired its own hypersonic ballistic missile for the first time, observed by President Lee Jae Myung, indicating that Seoul has grown increasingly uneasy over the rapid advancement of North Korea's missile technology," the NYT writes.
Specifically, Pyongyang has access to Russian deployment data and feedback. Anton Ponomarenko, an analyst, noted that this has allowed them to improve the accuracy and manoeuvrability of their weapons, making the threat to South Korea "more substantial".
Russia has also helped North Korea develop its own unmanned systems and their mass production.
"Pyongyang has learned from the conflict in Ukraine and the Middle East that inexpensive drones can overwhelm costly air defence systems. During a North Korean drill last month, a drone swarm attacked a target island, while cruise and ballistic missiles struck simultaneously from different directions. North Korea's evolving tactics will eventually force South Korea and its allies to redesign their air defences at exorbitant costs," the NYT explained.
Background:
- Bloomberg reported this September that Russia is involving North Korean citizens in the production of military drones, particularly at facilities in Alabuga, Tatarstan. Up to 25,000 North Koreans are believed to be working at Russian military plants.
- In addition, a North Korean missile forces unit, which could be equipped with 120 ballistic missiles and six launchers for strikes against Ukraine, has begun deploying in western Russia.
- Ukrainska Pravda previously reported that in August, Russia had asked North Korea to provide KN-30 ballistic missiles. In June 2026, North Korea announced the testing of a modernised 240mm multiple-launch rocket system, a tactical ballistic missile and a 155mm long-range artillery shell.

Ukraine’s military says Starlink satellite connection stable after recent restrictions
