Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
15:31:14 UTC
00:31:14 KST

Ukraine’s military has a “stable connection to Starlink”, the Ukrainian government said, 10 days after its ability to use the satellite communications system was suddenly restricted.
But hours after the announcement, SpaceX CEO Elon Musk, whose company owns Starlink, accused the Ukrainian military of violating the company’s terms. Neither Musk nor the US government, which operates Starshield using Starlink technology, took responsibility for imposing the curbs.
“Ukraine military violated Starlink terms of service and used it for offensive drone strikes to kill people. That loophole was closed last week,” Musk said in a social media post.
Serhiy Beskrestnov, a Ukrainian presidential adviser, said on the Telegram app that the country is “physically unable” to use Starlink for long- and medium-range attack drone operations.
Ukraine’s general staff and defence ministry did not immediately comment.
The Starlink satellite terminals, which are produced by Elon Musk’s SpaceX but managed by the US government, are a key component of Ukraine’s military operations. Sudden speed restrictions on the terminals, which capped operations at speeds of 160km/h (99mph), led to the failure of several Ukrainian combat missions earlier this month.
The military’s ability to intercept Russian attack drones was hampered and some Ukrainian operations to strike behind enemy frontlines were cancelled. Russia was able to launch ballistic missiles at Ukraine without any advance warning from the US.
The speed restrictions coincided with the announcement by Donald Trump of a US deal to buy Russian diesel, although the US president initially denied that his administration was behind the decision to cut intelligence sharing with Ukraine.
“I don’t know if it was anybody, but it wasn’t me, and I don’t think it was Elon,” Trump said, referring to Musk, SpaceX’s chief executive.
However, the US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, appeared to throw suspicion on Musk when he defended Trump last Wednesday. “The president has nothing to do with the decisions that are made by Starlink and Starshield and by Mr Musk,” Rubio said. “That’s a private company. The president doesn’t run that company and can’t direct that company to do anything.”
Musk was quick to blame the limits on Starshield on the Trump administration, writing on X last week that the systems were “owned and controlled by the US government”. “Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately Potus [president of the United States],” he wrote.
The US vice-president, JD Vance, backed Musk on Thursday, saying the billionaire “doesn’t want to get in the middle of what is a war between two state actors without the United States government effectively directing him on what to do”.
Ukraine’s president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, blamed both parties: “It was a message from [the] American government to limit the speed … And technically, SpaceX did it.”
There were no similar restrictions on Starshield terminals in EU countries and that they applied only to Ukraine, he added. “In other words, this is a planned operation.”
He said the decision would “bring a lot of human losses … of course people would die”.
Announcing the restoration of the system on Saturday in a diplomatic video address on the Telegram app, Zelenskyy expressed his gratitude to his US allies, including Trump and the US state department, for resolving the operational issue: “The most important development for today is that Starlink and Starshield have resumed operations at their pre-restriction speeds. The speeds are now at the level we need.”
The restoration began overnight. “By this morning, the speeds were already sufficient for operational use,” Zelenskyy said. “This is very important and significant for our frontline logistics and for defending Ukraine against jet-powered Shaheds.”
On Thursday, Trump had claimed the service was running again at full speed, but a European official speaking to the Associated Press denied the service was fully functioning.
When asked by reporters whether he would tell Musk to stop “messing around” with Ukraine’s access to Starlink on Friday, the US president said: “I’ve not spoken to him. I might have to … I’ve heard it was fixed. But if it’s not, I’ll speak to him … If there is a problem, I’ll get it straightened out.”
He then described Musk as a “very brilliant” and “very good” person.
Reuters contributed reporting

Israel brings talks with Lebanon to a standstill by refusing to withdraw from ‘pilot zones’
Talks between Lebanese and Israeli officials, hosted by the US in Tampa, Florida, this week, concluded without any breakthroughs, The New Arab reported on Thursday, citing its own sources.
The discussions were held at US Central Command headquarters, the Pentagon's Middle East operations arm. They come as Israel has continued its attacks on Lebanon this month, carrying out air strikes and home demolitions in the Nabatieh, Bint Jbeil, and Sidon districts.
The New Arab said it was told there was "intransigence in Israeli positions, while the Lebanese side is holding firm to its demands that steps must be reciprocal".
The Lebanese Armed Forces (LAF), largely funded by the US, has also rejected direct military-to-military coordination with the Israelis, instead preferring a third-party verification mechanism to be employed by the United Nations and allies such as France.
Israel has bombed Lebanon consistently since October 2023, after the Hamas-led attacks on southern Israel ignited the region.
A November 2024 ceasefire brokered by the former Biden administration did little to curb Israel's insistence that it was targeting Hezbollah leaders and weapons depots across the country, including in the capital, Beirut.
But it wasn't until this year that Israel significantly ramped up its military operations, mounted a ground invasion, and occupied long stretches of the south and east of Lebanon.
Since the US and Israel launched their joint war on Iran on 28 February, which prompted Hezbollah to launch attacks on Israel in defense of its ally, Israel has killed more than 4,300 Lebanese and displaced one million people in the country.
Lebanese officials have prioritized returning the displaced to their lands and demanded a timetable to do so from the Israelis, but there has been no movement on the issue since the US-sponsored framework was signed by the two sides in June.
Lebanon and Israel agreed to a trilateral framework with the Trump administration in Washington earlier this year, following five rounds of talks hosted by Secretary of State Marco Rubio.
The three countries held what was billed as a historic signing ceremony on 26 June.
Rubio said it was "the beginning of the beginning" in remarks to reporters at the time.
He later added the US would commit $100m in "humanitarian assistance in coordination with the UN" for affected communities, though he did not specify whether it was just for Lebanon or also for northern Israeli border towns.
Rubio said the LAF would be "reimbursed" by the Trump administration to the tune of $30m.
The framework led to the creation of the Military Coordination Group for Lebanon, which Washington would facilitate.
But the "pilot zones" that the Israelis pledged to withdraw from, in order to allow the LAF to take over, have not been expanded since July, with the Israelis claiming that the LAF have not had the capacity to disarm Hezbollah fighters.
Hezbollah is the key party to the conflict that was not represented in the talks.
It remains the country's most powerful military organization and far outmatches the LAF's capabilities. It was formed in the 1980s in response to the illegal Israeli occupation of Lebanon.
It has insisted that it cannot disarm while Israel remains a threat to Lebanon, and as Israeli officials normalize rhetoric about expanding Israel's borders to the north.

Denmark to Purchase New U.S.-Made Anthem Cruise Missiles
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
15:23:25 UTC
00:23:25 KST

Denmark will purchase Norwegian Joint Strike Missiles from Kongsberg to arm its F-35s, as well as new Anthem cruise missiles from the American company Covenant for launch from ground-based launchers. The Anthem was first publicly unveiled in early September.
The Danish Ministry of Defence announced the procurement.
According to the ministry, the goal of the procurement is to strengthen national and collective deterrence. These are weapons that NATO needs and that contribute to Denmark’s security.
The missiles are among various types of long-range, high-precision weapons that, thanks to advanced navigation technologies, can strike targets at great distances with high accuracy.
Covenant is an American defense company with an Israeli engineering and manufacturing base, founded in 2024 by Michael Kaufman and Ofir Dayan. Kaufman, an American-Israeli entrepreneur who previously worked with Peter Thiel, became the company’s CEO, while Dayan became the CTO. Covenant is headquartered in Washington, D.C., and operates a research and development and manufacturing complex covering approximately 3,000 m² in northern Israel.
Over the past two years, Covenant has raised more than $250 million in investments. Its investors include Andreessen Horowitz, Peter Thiel’s Founders Fund, Lux Capital, 8VC, Lightspeed, Altimeter, and the Israeli fund Aleph. The company has brought together more than 200 employees in the U.S., Germany, and Israel, including engineers with experience working at major defense corporations.
Covenant publicly unveiled its flagship product—the Anthem long-range cruise missile—only on September 9, 2026, after two years of development. At the time of the presentation, the company had already reported over 200 test flights of the missile and approximately $150 million in orders. Among its customers, the company named the U.S. Army and Navy, as well as international partners.
The Anthem is a ground-launched missile capable of carrying a payload weighing over 200 kg. It uses a solid-fuel rocket engine for launch. The developer has not publicly disclosed the exact flight range.
The missile is being developed with mass production and large-scale deployment in mind, alongside other long-range weapons such as the Tomahawk and JASSM-ER. According to Covenant’s management, once full-scale serial production begins, the target price for the Anthem will be several hundred thousand dollars.
To ensure mass production, Covenant has engaged three suppliers of solid-fuel rocket engines and has been working to bring on a fourth. The company has also signed long-term agreements for more than 4,000 rocket engines over the next two years. This approach is intended to reduce dependence on individual suppliers as production scales up.
The company is rolling out Anthem production in the U.S., Germany, and Israel. Once they reach full capacity, the facilities in Dallas and Saxony are expected to produce 5,000 missiles each per year, while the site in northern Israel will produce an additional 2,000.
The Joint Strike Missile (JSM) is a fifth-generation strike missile from Kongsberg, designed to overcome modern air defense systems.
It was developed based on the NSM naval missile. The air-launched variant, like the base version, is capable of engaging surface and ground targets, making it a versatile weapon.
The JSM’s stated range is 350 km. The warhead weighs 120 kg, and the missile’s total weight is 416 kg. It is 4 m long and has a diameter of 480 mm.
The missile can be stored in the internal bay of an F-35A fighter jet, preserving the aircraft’s low-observability characteristics.
The missile uses a high-precision navigation system that ensures a low-altitude flight profile. For terminal guidance, it employs a modern infrared seeker with imaging capability.

Democrats want to kill Trump’s diesel deal. Working Americans will pay the price
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
15:13:59 UTC
00:13:59 KST

Democrats want to kill Trump’s diesel deal. Working Americans will pay the price
With Americans struggling from soaring energy prices, and businesses across the country trying to keep their heads above water, the Democrats’ apparent priority is to threaten companies that might help ease the pressure.
According to an October 22 Washington Post report, Senate Democrats are preparing to investigate American companies involved in US President Donald Trump’s decision to ease sanctions on Russian diesel. The Senate Foreign Relations Committee has reportedly asked businesses to preserve relevant documents ahead of possible congressional investigations, should Democrats regain control of Congress in the November midterms.
For a party that claims to champion working Americans, this is a peculiar way of demonstrating its concern.
Diesel is the lifeblood of the American economy. It powers the trucks that carry food to supermarkets, the tractors that harvest crops, the machinery that builds homes and roads, and the locomotives that move freight across the vast country.
Yet the people who depend on it have too often been treated as an afterthought by the Washington establishment. They live and work in the industrial towns, farming communities and sprawling rural counties that coastal political elites dismiss as flyover country.
Just recall Hillary Clinton’s infamous 2016 description of millions of Trump supporters as a “basket of deplorables” – a perfect crystallization of the contempt that many ordinary Americans felt was directed at them by the Democrats.
A decade later, that perception is unlikely to be helped by the Democratic lawmakers’ threats to investigate businesses for participating in an arrangement intended to bring additional fuel to the market.
The timing makes those threats extra galling. America is facing an energy crunch aggravated by the Trump administration’s own military campaign against Iran. There is no reason to pretend otherwise. Yes, the president’s decisions helped disrupt global energy markets, and Americans are entitled to demand answers about their consequences.
But recognizing that responsibility does not mean opposing every subsequent attempt to alleviate the damage.
Trump’s decision to temporarily ease restrictions on Russian diesel represents an effort to increase available supplies at a time when the market desperately needs relief. It is a pragmatic response to an immediate economic problem, whatever one thinks of the circumstances that created it.
And now Democrats are determined to make that response costly for the companies willing to participate.
Congress has every right to examine whether the administration acted within its legal authority. But threatening private businesses with investigations for engaging in transactions authorized by the federal government is another matter entirely. If those companies comply with the law, why should they have to fear becoming targets of a future congressional majority?
The actual volume of Russian diesel involved is almost beside the point. Moscow initially pledged to release some 300,000 metric tons of diesel, with further shipments promised in the following months – a modest quantity compared to America’s enormous fuel consumption.
But that’s not what the markets will be reacting to. They react to expectations, regulatory certainty and the willingness of businesses to undertake transactions without fearing political retaliation. And now, even a lawful, government-authorized energy deal could expose companies to years of investigations simply because a different party took power.
Just imagine the chilling effect.
Today, the dispute concerns a relatively small quantity of fuel from one supplier. Tomorrow, the same approach could be applied to other commodities, trading partners or commercial arrangements that fall afoul of Washington’s shifting ideological priorities.
In effect, the Democrats want to hold American energy security hostage to domestic political warfare.
And for what? The ostensible objective is to keep pressuring Russia.
For years, Moscow has faced sweeping Western sanctions, restrictions on financial transactions and efforts to shut its energy exports out of international markets. None of this has forced Russia to accept any of the West’s demands.
Russia has shown it can adapt and endure economic pressure. While not entirely painless, sanctions have consistently failed to produce the political outcome their advocates have called and hoped for.
Meanwhile, Moscow has repeatedly signaled that it remains prepared to negotiate to reasonable counterparts that would take Russia’s own security concerns and national interests into account. Whether those positions are acceptable to Washington is a matter for diplomacy – and refusing to talk altogether is not diplomacy.
Trump is willing to acknowledge that Russia remains a major power with which the US must eventually find a workable relationship. It’s the baseline level of recognition of political reality one expects from the leader of a major world power.
What the Democrats are doing is the international-politics equivalent of pressing their hands to their ears and shouting ‘La La La’ at the top of their lungs.
The truck driver paying more at the pump, the farmer counting operating costs for the next season and the small-business owner watching expenses climb have little interest in Washington’s political theater. They want affordable fuel, predictable costs and a government that remembers whom it is supposed to serve.
Threatening investigations to discourage companies from helping supply the American market is not sending the message the Democrats seem to think it’s sending. It suggests that, to them, political obedience matters more than keeping the country running.
And ordinary Americans could once again be left paying the bill.
The statements, views and opinions expressed in this column are solely those of the author and do not necessarily represent those of RT.

By Murat Basoglu and Rania Abushamala
ISTANBUL (AA) - The US has warned its citizens against traveling to Iraq “for any reason,” citing security risks including “armed conflict, terrorism and kidnapping.”
The advisory, updated on Friday and published by the US Embassy in Iraq on Saturday, left the warning level and risk indicators unchanged.
“Do not travel to Iraq for any reason,” the State Department said, adding that the US government’s ability to provide emergency services to American citizens in Iraq was limited by security risks.
The advisory said Iran-backed Houthis had attacked Saudi Arabia, targeting civilian airports and critical infrastructure, causing civilian casualties and major travel disruptions.
It warned that hostilities “have the potential to escalate rapidly beyond that immediate area.”
The State Department said the Iraqi government “cannot guarantee the safety of U.S. citizens against sudden outbreaks of violence and armed conflict.”
US government personnel working in Iraq are subject to “strict security protocols,” and travel to the country requires “special authorization,” according to the advisory. Additional restrictions could be imposed as security conditions evolve.
The advisory also warned of “terrorism and kidnapping” risks, saying ISIS (Daesh) and Iran-aligned armed groups “encourage and conduct attacks against U.S. persons and interests in Iraq.”
It cited attacks involving improvised explosive devices, projectiles and drones in various parts of the country, including major cities.
“Targets of recent attacks have included hotels, universities, energy infrastructure, airports, and other locations perceived as affiliated with the United States, including diplomatic facilities,” according to the advisory.
On civil aviation, the State Department pointed to restrictions and warnings issued by the US Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) concerning flights in or near Iraqi airspace because of risks to aviation safety.
The updated advisory comes amid rising regional tensions and Western media reports of US-Israeli preparations for a large-scale attack on Iran, with the timing unclear as Israel’s Oct. 27 elections and the Nov. 3 US congressional midterm elections approach.

Report: Netanyahu told diplomats to back Argentina's call for Falklands talks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
15:08:39 UTC
00:08:39 KST

Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu instructed Israeli diplomats to support Argentina's call for negotiations over the future of the Falkland Islands and acknowledge Argentina's historical connection to the territory, The Telegraph reported Saturday, citing sources familiar with the matter.
The reported shift in Israel's position follows Britain's decision last month to impose sanctions on Israeli settlements in the West Bank. According to The Telegraph, the move reflects growing tensions between Jerusalem and London over Britain's policies toward Israel and the Palestinians.
The Falkland Islands, known in Argentina as the Malvinas, are a British territory in the South Atlantic, roughly 480 kilometers (about 300 miles) east of Argentina's coast. The dispute dates back centuries and culminated in 1982 when the two nations fought a war over the islands. Although Britain won, the Argentinians still claim the islands.
The diplomatic push comes as Israel seeks closer ties with right-leaning governments in South and Central America, while facing growing criticism from traditional European allies over the Gaza war and settler violence in the West Bank.
The change would not amount to formal Israeli recognition of Argentina's sovereignty claim over the islands, but has raised concerns in Britain that Israel could go further if London imposes additional sanctions on settlements, the newspaper reported.
However, an Israeli Embassy spokesman in London, Alex Gandler, denied that Netanyahu had issued such an instruction. Israel's Foreign Ministry also denied the report, saying: "The report is incorrect. There is no change in our position on the issue."
I categorically deny this allegation. No such directive exists.
Israel's Ambassador to the United Nations, Danny Danon, addressed the dispute at a UN session last week, calling for direct negotiations between Britain and Argentina. Sources cited by The Telegraph described his remarks as a significant departure from Israel's previous position, particularly because they acknowledged Argentina's historical connection to the islands.
Danon said Israel recognized the importance Argentina attached to the issue and its efforts to resolve it through diplomatic channels and in accordance with international law. He also called for direct, constructive and practical dialogue and said any progress should take into account relevant historical, legal and human considerations.
One source told The Telegraph that the wording of Danon's statement had been approved at the highest levels of the Israeli government. The source described the intervention as the first time Israel had become involved in the dispute.
The report linked the shift to Israel's close relationship with Argentine President Javier Milei, who has strongly supported Israel throughout the Hamas-led October 7, 2023, attack. Milei attended Israel's Independence Day celebrations this year, where he lit a ceremonial torch.
Israeli officials cited by The Telegraph also pointed to deteriorating relations with Britain, particularly over the sanctions and critical statements by British leaders. The newspaper reported that the Israeli position could further strain ties amid the dispute over Israel's West Bank policies.
Britain's decision to sanction settlements has brought bilateral relations to their lowest point in decades, following London's recognition of Palestinian statehood last year and its criticism of Israel's conduct in the war in Gaza.
The sanctions announced last month by British Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband expanded Britain's human rights sanctions framework to cover violations of international humanitarian law. The measures allow restrictions on individuals and entities involved in settlement construction, expansion and financing.
The new regulations took effect days before the October 19 deadline for bids on a construction tender in the E1 area of the West Bank, east of Jerusalem. Britain and other countries had warned contractors that participating in the tender could expose them to legal and reputational consequences. The planned construction between Jerusalem and the Ma'aleh Adumim settlement is opposed by Western governments because it could sever the territorial contiguity needed for a future Palestinian state.
Britain has also announced plans for a trade ban on settlements, joined by Canada and France. The British government has said the measure could take six to nine months to enter into force because of the legislative process required.
The measures followed Britain's adoption of the International Court of Justice's 2024 advisory opinion, which found Israel's continued presence in the occupied Palestinian territory unlawful. Separately, the Fourth Geneva Convention prohibits an occupying power from transferring parts of its civilian population into occupied territory.
In response to Britain's moves, Foreign Minister Gideon Sa'ar announced the closure of the British Consulate in Jerusalem. Seven British diplomats will continue to operate in the city under a reduced diplomatic presence.
At a UN Security Council meeting in February, Sa'ar had invoked the Falklands dispute while accusing Britain of hypocrisy over its opposition to Israeli settlements. Addressing then-British Foreign Secretary Yvette Cooper, he argued that Britain's position on Israeli residence in the West Bank contradicted international law and the Balfour Declaration.
"It is our country; it's not 13,000 kilometers from our country, like the Falkland Islands. The Argentinians call it the Malvinas Islands – a dispute you haven't solved with Argentina until today," Sa'ar said.
Despite the political tensions, Israeli government sources told The Telegraph that the two countries continued to cooperate closely on security and hoped to maintain the relationship.
Israel also has practical reasons to stop short of formally endorsing Argentina's claim. Intelligence cooperation with Britain gives Israel an additional channel into the Five Eyes intelligence-sharing alliance, while Israeli companies have commercial ties with British firms involved in the Sea Lion oilfield project near the Falklands.
Britain's Foreign Office has not commented on The Telegraph's report.

“Yesterday, we saw how dangerous their rhetoric is,” she said, calling on those who use racist language to stop doing so.
Tondelier said every life lost in France should be condemned equally, criticizing the alleged silence of some political figures following the shooting.
“I want to hear them commit to a realization and say they will stop these remarks because racism kills,” she said.
She also referred to the 12-year-old girl who was shot eight times, arguing that racist rhetoric could contribute to people being influenced by racist attitudes and lead to tragedies.
French President Emmanuel Macron described the shooting as a “racist terrorist attack” and called for action against all forms of racism.

Beyond Iran’s famous cities: villages that deserve a place on every traveler’s itinerary
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
15:08:09 UTC
00:08:09 KST

Beyond Iran’s famous cities: villages that deserve a place on every traveler’s itinerary
TEHRAN - Iran’s historical cities are renowned for their grand mosques, Persian gardens, traditional bazaars and Silk Road heritage. Yet beyond the familiar destinations of Isfahan, Shiraz and Yazd, to name a few, lies another side of the country: a landscape of mountain villages, ancient mud-brick settlements and rural communities whose traditions offer a different perspective on Iranian life.
Scattered across the country’s mountains, valleys and desert margins, these places reveal the diversity of Iran’s geography, architecture and cultural heritage. Some are easily reached on a day trip from a nearby city, while others require more time and effort to explore. Together, they offer travelers an opportunity to look beyond the country’s best-known attractions and discover the character of its rural regions.
Kandovan, life inside volcanic rock
In northwestern Iran, Kandovan stands out for its unusual architecture. Located near Tabriz, the village is known for its cone-shaped rock formations, in which generations of residents have carved homes and other living spaces.
Often compared with Cappadocia in central Turkey, Kandovan belongs to a small group of settlements where people have continued to inhabit rock-cut dwellings into modern times. Its distinctive landscape, shaped by volcanic activity and centuries of human adaptation, gives the village an appearance unlike that of most Iranian settlements.
Unlike archaeological cave sites preserved primarily as historical attractions, Kandovan remains a living community. Its homes illustrate how residents have adapted traditional building practices to the surrounding geology and climate.
The village is also one of the more accessible rural destinations for travelers visiting Tabriz, making it a convenient introduction to Iran’s countryside.
Palangan, a village climbing the Kordestan’s mountains
In Kordestan province, western Iran, Palangan is celebrated for its stepped architecture and dramatic mountain setting. Traditional houses rise above one another along the slopes, creating a compact settlement that appears to grow out of the surrounding terrain.
The village offers a glimpse into rural Kurdish life, including local food traditions and the close relationship between communities and their natural environment. Its river, mountain scenery and stone-built houses make it a popular destination for visitors from nearby areas.
Local restaurants serving river fish provide an opportunity to sample regional cuisine, while the surrounding hills offer a setting for walking and exploring.
Palangan is among several stepped villages found across the Kurdish mountain regions of western Iran. Although some rural settlements in the area remain relatively difficult to reach, Palangan can be visited from nearby urban centers, including Sanandaj, with onward travel arrangements.
Masuleh, where rooftops become streets
Further north, in Gilan province, Masuleh offers another striking example of architecture adapted to mountainous terrain. Its traditional houses are built along a steep slope, with the roof of one building often serving as a walkway or courtyard for the house above it.
The arrangement gives the village its distinctive stepped appearance and makes pedestrian movement an integral part of its architectural character.
Set amid the mist-covered mountains of northern Iran, Masuleh is known for its humid climate, lush surroundings and frequent clouds that drift through the settlement. Its popularity among domestic travelers means that its streets can become crowded, particularly during busy travel periods.
Nevertheless, walking trails leading into the surrounding mountains offer opportunities to escape the busiest areas and appreciate the landscape. Within the village, rooftops and narrow paths remain important spaces for everyday encounters, reflecting a strong sense of community.
Masuleh is therefore both a scenic destination and an example of how traditional settlements developed in response to steep terrain and local living conditions.
Gazor-Khan, gateway to the Alamut Valley
For travelers interested in history and mountain landscapes, Gazor-Khan in Qazvin province offers a combination of both. The village is best known as the gateway to the ruins of the UNESCO-listed Alamut Castle, a fortress associated with the Nizari Ismaili community, whose members became known in medieval sources as the Assassins.
Perched high above the Alamut Valley, the fortress occupied a strategic position and became an important center of the Nizari Ismaili state. Its history is closely associated with Hassan-i Sabbah, who established his base there in the late 11th century.
The Mongol campaign led by Hulagu Khan resulted in the fortress's capture and destruction in the 13th century. Although much of the original structure has disappeared, the remaining ruins and surrounding mountain scenery continue to attract visitors.
Beyond the historic site, Gazor-Khan is a quiet mountain village surrounded by orchards, including apple, apricot and cherry trees. In spring, flowering trees add color to the landscape, while hiking routes provide opportunities to explore the valley.
The journey requires more planning than a visit to villages close to major cities, but the combination of history, scenery and rural life makes it a rewarding destination.
Abyaneh, a living link to Iran’s past
Located near Kashan, at the foot of Mount Karkas, Abyaneh is among Iran’s best-known historic villages. Its red earthen buildings, wooden balconies, narrow lanes and traditional dress give it a distinctive appearance.
The settlement is often associated with Iran’s pre-Islamic past, although its long history spans multiple periods. Its architecture reflects the use of locally available materials, particularly the red soil that gives the buildings their characteristic color.
Abyaneh is also notable for the preservation of elements of local language and cultural traditions. Some older residents speak a distinctive local dialect, while traditional clothing remains an important part of the village’s cultural identity.
Men have traditionally worn dark coats and loose trousers, while women’s clothing is known for its colorful patterns and white headscarves. These customs provide a visible connection to regional traditions that have endured alongside broader changes in Iranian society.
Abyaneh’s popularity, however, has brought challenges. Visitors can fill its narrow streets, particularly during peak travel periods, and the village can sometimes feel more like an open-air heritage site than an ordinary rural community.
Nain, desert heritage beyond the main tourist routes
Between Yazd and Tehran, Nain offers a quieter encounter with Iran’s desert heritage. Although technically a small town rather than a village, it deserves attention for its historic architecture and relatively understated place on many travel itineraries.
The town is known for its historical Jameh Mosque, an old bazaar, traditional water reservoirs and the remains of Narenj Castle. Together, these structures reflect the architectural and engineering traditions that helped communities survive in Iran’s arid central regions.
Traditional water reservoirs, known as ab-anbars, were designed to store water for use during dry periods. Along with other water-management structures, they demonstrate the importance of adapting settlement patterns and architecture to scarce water resources.
Parts of Nain’s historic fabric have deteriorated, and some old buildings remain in poor condition. Yet the town’s less commercialized atmosphere can offer a different experience from more heavily visited heritage destinations.
Its contrast between historic quarters and newer neighborhoods also reveals how traditional settlements have evolved as residents adapt to contemporary life.
Kharanaq, traces of an ancient Silk Road settlement
Northeast of Yazd, Kharanaq is known for its abandoned mud-brick settlement and atmospheric ruins. The village developed along historic travel routes and is associated with the network of settlements that supported movement across central Iran.
Its old buildings, narrow alleys and earthen walls form a dense architectural landscape. Some structures are believed to date back many centuries, although the history of individual buildings varies.
Walking through the abandoned quarter offers a sense of how communities once organized their homes and passageways in a desert environment. From elevated points, visitors can see the settlement against a backdrop of surrounding mountains and open terrain.
The ruins are also vulnerable. Weathering, erosion and uncontrolled visitor access can accelerate the deterioration of fragile earthen structures. Exploring the area responsibly means avoiding unstable buildings, staying on established paths where possible and respecting any restricted areas.
Kharanaq can be combined with visits to Meybod and the Zoroastrian pilgrimage site of Chak Chak, making it a possible addition to a wider itinerary from Yazd.
Meybod, desert architecture and ingenious design
Meybod, another historical settlement near Yazd, offers a broader view of the architectural traditions of Iran’s central desert. Although it is a town rather than a village, its historic structures make it a worthwhile stop for travelers interested in the region’s cultural heritage.
One of its principal attractions is Narin Castle, a large earthen fortress whose origins extend back into antiquity. The town also preserves traditional water reservoirs and a historic pigeon house.
Pigeon houses were constructed to shelter birds and collect their droppings, which were used as agricultural fertilizer. Their design reflects the resourcefulness of communities that relied on locally available materials and developed practical solutions to meet everyday needs.
The pigeon house in Meybod is among the notable surviving examples of this building tradition in Iran.
Together, the castle, water-storage structures and pigeon house illustrate how architecture in the desert served practical purposes while also becoming part of the region’s distinctive cultural landscape.
Why Iran’s rural destinations matter
Exploring Iran’s villages and smaller historic settlements offers more than a change of scenery. These places reveal how people have adapted to different environments, from the volcanic formations of the northwest to the steep mountains of Kordestan and the water-scarce landscapes of the central plateau.
Their architecture reflects local responses to climate, geology and available resources. Their languages, clothing, food and customs also demonstrate the country’s regional and ethnic diversity.
For travelers whose itineraries focus on Iran’s famous cities, adding even one or two rural destinations can broaden their understanding of the country.

Security forces deploy as Milan braces for another day of protests
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
15:05:58 UTC
00:05:58 KST

Hundreds of Italian soldiers deployed as thousands protest in Milan
The Italian government sent hundreds of soldiers to the country’s fashion and financial hub ahead of anticipated unrest.
Milan, Italy – Thousands of protesters took to the streets across Italy to demonstrate against Giorgia Meloni’s right-wing government and the rising cost of living, a week after clashes with police and looting during demonstrations in Milan.
Protests were called in eight Italian cities on Saturday, including the fashion and finance capital, Milan, where the government deployed hundreds of soldiers.
As soldiers spread out and luxury boutiques were boarded up, two demonstrations marched through the streets of the northern city.
Around 50 people gathered spontaneously in Cordusio Square, heading towards the central Castle square and chanting, “We are all antifascists”.
Small groups joined the main demonstration along the way, swelling its ranks. Many of the protesters were young people.
At its peak, the protest drew around 10,000 people.
“I believe that the main obstacle to our future is our state,” Riccardo, a 17-year-old student from Milan who did not give his last name, told Al Jazeera.
“We are here because of the rising prices and because I believe that our government has no respect for its citizens,” another 17-year-old student from the province of Pavia added, without giving his name.
“There are four people in my family. My mother works in a factory, but my father is about to lose his job. It’s hard to make ends meet on just one salary,” he said.
For almost four hours, the protesters walked around the city centre, heading southeast while being watched by riot police. They finally stopped at 7:30pm local time (17:30GMT) in front of Milan Polytechnic University.
There were no security incidents in Milan, but protesters clashed with police in other cities, including Turin and Rome, Italy’s ANSA news agency reported.
Police said nine people were arrested in protests across Italy on Saturday, with a total of 371 briefly detained.
‘We distrust this government’
Saturday’s demonstrations followed an announcement online of a new round of protests by a newly formed group calling itself the ‘October 17 Movement’. It has been the main driver of demonstrations alongside student federations, grassroots trade unions and antiwar coalitions.
“Those who deny our future are truly violent,” the group said on Instagram. “We distrust this government because we see it as authoritarian.”
In response to last weekend’s looting, the government announced a series of new security measures, including the deployment of 500 soldiers to Milan on Saturday.
On Friday, police carried out raids and searches in several cities for people suspected of taking part in looting and rioting in last weekend’s protests, reported the Italian news agency Adnkronos. Another 150 raids were carried out on Saturday morning in the northern region of Lombardy.
On its Telegram channel, the October 17 Movement said many of those planning to demonstrate wanted to voice their dissent peacefully.
“We must be peaceful. If we give [the police] an excuse, they will charge against us,” a participant identified as E said on Thursday.
Others have stressed that there is no distinction between those who engage in violence and peaceful protesters. “It’s just us,” said a member identified as Q.
Protesters decided to keep the location of the demonstration secret until the last minute, with three meeting points announced on their social media accounts on Saturday afternoon.
Police confirmed to Al Jazeera that they had located and were questioning the administrator of the group’s Instagram page. According to the Italian daily Corriere della Sera, he is a 30-year-old Italian-Moroccan freelance journalist and researcher. He is currently under investigation on suspicion of “inciting crimes”.
Most of the arrested protesters were under 18.
Some joined the protests last weekend after being unexpectedly added to a Telegram group, Corriere della Sera reported.
“They said that they would raise chaos and we could take a lot of goods,” one of them said.
Lawyer Michele D’Agostino is defending two demonstrators, aged 21 and 15.
“[The youngest one] didn’t even know the reasons behind the protest; he had just seen it on TikTok and decided to check it out with a friend,” D’Agostino told Al Jazeera.
“He was not among the looters, but he did not realise the seriousness of what was happening,” he said.
The public prosecutor has blamed social media for misleading young people into taking part in what he described as “insurrectional acts”.
Justice Minister Carlo Nordio told Sky TG24 that there was a need to “expand the capacity of our youth detention facilities” in response to the mass arrests of under-18s.
“Looting is wrong, but I cannot understand why it makes more noise than what happens in southern Italy, where people are facing fuel shortages,” said a 17-year-old student, whose family is originally from Senegal and who joined the demonstration in Milan.
Earlier this week, truck drivers set up roadblocks in several regions of southern Italy to protest against soaring fuel prices, leaving many markets without supplies for days. On Thursday, the government sought to offer them some relief by granting tax breaks and establishing a special fund for farmers and fishermen.

Fire destroys Hitler’s ‘Eagle’s Nest’ mountain retreat
The Eagle’s Nest mountainous retreat built for Nazi dictator Adolf Hitler in the Bavarian Alps has been devastated by a blaze, the German police have said.
The former tea house for the leader of the Third Reich, which was constructed on the peak of the Obersalzberg in southern Germany in 1938, sits at an altitude of 1,834 meters (6,000 feet).
A fire alarm at the Eagle’s Nest went off on Friday evening, and it was completely engulfed in flames by the time emergency services arrived, the police said.
The high elevation complicated the work of some 200 fire fighters, who were only able to extinguish the blaze on Saturday morning, they added.
“It is damaged to a large extent. The house is unlikely to be saved,” a police spokesperson told Bild tabloid.
The police said that a suspect had been arrested in connection with the fire, but revealed no further details.
According to Bild, the detained person was a motorcyclist whom the officers encountered on their way to the burning retreat, but his involvement in the case currently remains unclear. Investigators believe arson caused the fire, the paper’s sources claimed.
Following reports of the blaze, the Bavarian authorities announced plans to rebuild the structure, Interior Minister Joachim Herrmann said.
“We will not allow ruins to remain there,” DPA quoted him as saying.
The Eagle’s Nest was one of the few historic building from Hitler’s era to avoid damage by bombing during the World War II. The retreat hosted a museum and a restaurant since the 1950s, becoming a popular tourist destination. It was preserved as “a cautionary reminder of the abysses of the inhumane Nazi dictatorship,” according to its website.

The Cinema of the South Festival will celebrate its 25th anniversary at the Sderot Cinematheque from November 1-5, with television premieres, Israeli and international films, filmmaker meetings, competitions, and music.
Founded by Sapir Academic College’s School of Audio and Visual Arts, the festival will highlight filmmakers from Sderot and the western Negev, including works exploring life in the three years since the October 7 Hamas-led massacres in Israel.

Israeli films, TV series that got our vote
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
14:37:13 UTC
23:37:13 KST

Given how central politics is to Israeli life and how passionate most Israelis are about it, you might think it would be a mainstay of Israeli entertainment, but except for a few feature films and series, it hasn’t been. Perhaps that is because when people go to the movies, they want to escape from the political discussions that roil everyday life here.
When it comes to the documentary realm, there are enough political films to fill an encyclopedia, and they vastly outnumber feature films and television shows that dramatize or poke fun at the political realm.
But as we head into what is arguably the most contentious election in Israeli history, here is a selective list of feature films and television series that show what Israelis have thought and felt about their political system at different points in the country’s history. Most are available on various streaming platforms, including the Israeli Film Archive (https://jfc.org.il/en).
Twelve movies to enjoy this week
1. Sallah Shabati (1964) – Legendary writer/director Ephraim Kishon dominated the early years of Israeli cinema, and his films always included some kind of dig at the political system, but his criticism was as funny as it was insightful. Sallah Shabati is a classic comedy about a new Mizrahi immigrant (Chaim Topol) navigating Israeli bureaucracy, and it includes the very funny election plotline in which rival parties try to secure his vote. He is in a quandary until he learns about the secret ballot, and then he promises each party representative his vote, in exchange for perks.
I first saw this movie in ulpan, and my teacher promised that if we learned enough to understand every reference in the movie, we would understand just about everything going on in Israel. This turned out to be true, and it’s remarkable how little has changed. It was also the first Israeli movie to be nominated for a Best Foreign Language Film Oscar. Arik Einstein appears in one of his early roles as a kibbutznik who falls in love with Sallah’s daughter.
2. The Big Dig/Blaumilch Canal (1969) – Another Kishon classic, this spoofs how an escaped psychiatric patient’s unauthorized digging upends Tel Aviv as politicians vying for votes in an upcoming municipal election try to take credit for this supposed urban improvement project.
3. The Fox in the Chicken Coop (1978) – A third Kishon film, this stars Shaike Ophir (after whom the Ophir Awards are named) as an aging political wheeler-dealer who visits a peaceful village and introduces political organizations, rivalries, and power struggles into the lives of its residents.
4. The Battle for the Committee (1986) – The battle for power in a tenants’ committee is the subject of this satire by Avi Cohen, starring the comedy trio HaGashash HaHiver.
5. Streets of Yesterday (1989) – Judd Ne’eman’s political thriller about the assassination of Israel’s foreign minister just as he is announcing peace negotiations with the Palestinians turned out to be sadly prescient after prime minister Yitzhak Rabin’s murder a few years later.
6. Time of Favor (2000) – Joseph Cedar’s debut feature is a thriller infused with political themes, as it tells the story of a love triangle set in the milieu of a yeshiva led by a radical West Bank rabbi, played by Assi Dayan, who tries to mobilize an army unit to carry out terrorist acts against Palestinians.
7. Rabin, the Last Day (2015) – Amos Gitai’s docudrama about Rabin’s assassination explores its theme through archival material and dramatized scenes surrounding the Shamgar Commission’s investigation.
8. The 90 Minute War (2016) – Eyal Halfon made a mockumentary proposing that the Israeli-Palestinian conflict be settled by a soccer match, which, in the film’s telling, looks like a pretty good idea.
9. Norman: The Moderate Rise and Tragic Fall of a New York Fixer (2016) – Another film by Cedar, this one told the story of a failed American-Jewish businessman (Richard Gere), who finds himself in a position to influence the Israeli prime minister (Lior Ashkenazi).
10. The Unorthodox (2018) – Eliran Malka’s dramedy is about the birth of the Shas party and portrays its founders as rather lovable.
11. Silent (2022) – Shemi Zarhin directed this movie about a television interviewer who confronts the rise of a candidate for prime minister who refuses to speak or reveal his positions.
12. Yes (2025) – A provocative political satire by Nadav Lapid, set after October 7, following a musician and his dancer wife who entertain Israel’s elite after the musician is assigned to create a new national anthem.
Television series to enjoy this week
On the small screen, most political satire has been confined to sketch comedy shows, such as Zehu Ze and Eretz Nehederet. But a few others exist, and most can be streamed as well.
1. "War Room" (2005) – Written and created by Yair Lapid, currently one of Israel’s leading politicians, about a fictional unit in the Prime Minister’s Office (PMO) coordinating national-security decisions, which many felt was inspired by "The West Wing."
2. "Polishuk" (2009-2014) – Sasson Gabai plays an unlikely government minister navigating advisers, rival politicians, scandals, and his own limitations in this political satire, created by Shmuel Hasfari.
3. "The Prime Minister’s Children" (2011-2012) – Created by Shahar Magen and Noa Rothman, the series features Rami Heuberger as the prime minister and follows how his family adjusts to power, public scrutiny, and life inside the official residence.
4. "Shadow Government" (aka "State Rules") (2018) – A political thriller about parliamentary aides whose relationships, ambitions, and intrigues shape what happens in the Knesset.
5. "Autonomies" (2018) – A dystopian drama that portrays an Israel divided between a secular state centered in Tel Aviv and an ultra-Orthodox autonomy centered in Jerusalem, that was created by Ori Elon and Yehonatan Indursky.
6. "Sweetie’s Party" (aka "Motek Bool Ba’emtza") (2021-2025) – Shmuel Hasfari returned to political comedy with this series about a broke former reality-show contestant and social media influencer who enters the Knesset and discovers the world of lobbying, political deals, manipulation, parliamentary power, and mostly, the money and perks that come with the job.

Mona Lisa off limits as Paris shuts museums over protest fears

14:37:07 UTC
23:37:07 KST

Demonstrators took to the streets of France on Saturday under the watch of 70,000 police officers, with unrest appearing markedly less severe than a week earlier despite scattered confrontations in several cities.
Tens of thousands of people marched peacefully through the French capital, according to police numbers, denouncing the high cost of living and accusing President Emmanuel Macron of cutting public services while failing to tackle rising inequality.
"Down with the state, the police and the fascists," some of the flag-waving crowds chanted.
Elsewhere, police fired tear gas at people in Clermont-Ferrand, Grenoble, Lille and Nice, where a water cannon was deployed after protesters refused orders to pull back.
In France's second and third cities, Marseille and Lyon, clashes broke out between hooded youths and police.
The government deployed 10,000 more police and gendarmes than on October 17, when nationwide protests descended into some of the worst unrest in France in years.
"We have to be ultra, ultra responsive," said Interior Minister Laurent Nunez, who has accused far-left groups and criminal gangs of fomenting violence.
Nunez told reporters that police had arrested 135 people nationwide by early afternoon, many following pre-emptive searches that he said had uncovered fireworks, ball bearings and other items that could be used as weapons.
Top tourist destinations shuttered
Much of central Paris took on the appearance of a city under lockdown, with shopkeepers boarding up storefronts, museums closing their doors and more than 20 metro stations shut.
Business groups urged retailers to remain closed after thousands of shops and businesses were damaged or looted across France last weekend.
"There are hardly any customers, so it's not really worth staying open," said Oskar, manager of a Kiton boutique in Paris.
Several of the capital's best-known cultural institutions, including the Louvre, the Musée d'Orsay and the Paris Opera, closed for the day as a precaution, leaving tourists frustrated.
"Everything's boarded up, and we're not quite sure where we should be," said Xavier Dolliole, a tourist from the US city of New Orleans.
The route for Paris' main demonstration was settled only after a legal battle triggered by a last-minute police order moving organizers away from the city center towards the southeastern fringes of the capital.
Police said the original route passed through areas with a high concentration of businesses similar to those targeted last weekend. Leftist politicians said the late change was aimed at causing confusion and keeping people away.
Hard-left leader Jean-Luc Mélenchon, who joined the Paris rally, hailed what he called a "magnificent mass display of collective discipline and self-restraint."
He said the protests would continue unless Macron addressed the social malaise in France, one of the world's richest nations but with a growing debt that has alarmed investors.
"Given the current situation, I think he will come to understand that this will happen again every week. There is still time for (Macron) to give in. After that, the only thing left to him will be the exit door," Melenchon told reporters.
Islamophobic shooting carried out in Paris
Many demonstrators have accused the government of overreacting, as soldiers were dispatched to patrol the Champs-Élysées, a grand boulevard lined with luxury shops and restaurants.
"We shed tears for shops, not for the people who are being impoverished all year round," said Clara Lebbadi, a 22-year-old arts student.
"My friend and I almost didn't come because we were scared, but we came precisely because it's important not to let repression win," she added.
The first authorized march on Saturday passed off peacefully in Orléans, around 120 km (75 miles) south of Paris, where demonstrators rallied against Marine Le Pen's far-right National Rally as it held a party congress in the city.
A shooting west of Paris on Friday heightened tensions. A gunman suspected of acting out of Islamophobic hatred killed one person and wounded four others, including a 12-year-old girl.
"We have come to tell the far right, face-to-face, that we are not afraid," said Bally Bagayoko, the mayor of Saint-Denis and a member of Melenchon's France Unbowed party.

Thousands protest in Turkey over journalists’ arrests, media shutdowns
ISTANBUL – Thousands rallied in Istanbul and Ankara on Oct 24 against what they described as growing pressure on journalists in Turkey, including arrests, media shutdowns and the appointment of state administrators.
“Enough. We can no longer breathe,” shouted marchers in the crowds, which were composed mainly of journalists, rights groups and opposition party representatives.
Press freedom has been increasingly constrained in Turkey since a failed coup attempt in 2016, with sweeping prosecutions and digital censorship.
But recent weeks have seen what rights advocates say is mounting pressure on independent journalism.
Eleven journalists have been jailed in the past two months and several media outlets shut down, according to the Turkish Journalists’ Union.
At least 3,000 people gathered on the Asian side of Istanbul, according to police.
They held up photos of jailed journalists, chanting: “We will not be silenced. Enough is enough!” and “We will not bow to pressure”.
Earlier in October, police raided Turkey’s most-watched news channel, Halk TV, halting broadcasts and installing a government-appointed administrator.
The move was the latest against media outlets seen as critical of President Recep Tayyip Erdogan and his government.
It followed the closure of the website and social media accounts belonging to leading digital news outlet T24 over what authorities described as “LGBT propaganda”.
“This gathering is not simply about standing up for journalists,” veteran journalist Zafer Arapkirli told AFP after the Istanbul protest.
“It is also about defending respect for society’s right to access information and news through journalists and independent media,” said the columnist for the BirGun daily.
Intimidation
For Arapkirli – who himself faces lawsuits – the more intense the pressure becomes, the stronger the response and the determination to stand against it must be.
“What the regime wants is to intimidate, silence and frighten society through such pressure – by arresting individual journalists, seizing media outlets, banning news coverage and blocking access to social media,” he said.
“We must show that we will not allow this to happen.
“We have done so up to now. I believe we are now moving towards demonstrating this determination on a much larger scale.”
In Ankara, at least 3,000 protesters gathered, according to a police count.
They shouted: “No to censorship” and “Freedom for jailed journalists”.
“Today’s protest was important both because it brought journalists together to make their voices heard and because it defended citizens’ right to access information,” Gokcer Tahincioglu, coordinator for the shutdown T24, told AFP in Ankara.
“Journalists are determined to get one message across: we want to practise journalism, and we want to be able to do so freely,” he said.
Praising the solidarity after the now shut T24, Tahincioglu said: “We want to regain the conditions necessary to report freely as soon as possible.” AFP

European Parliament Vice President ends hunger strike following Oleshky ceasefire announcement
The European Parliament Vice President Pina Picierno ended her hunger strike, meant to raise awareness for the humanitarian crisis in the Russian-occupied town of Oleshky, Kherson Oblast, following the announcement of a ceasefire agreement, Ukraine's human rights ombudsman Dmytro Lubinets said on Oct. 24.
Lubinets said he informed Picierno that a temporary local ceasefire in Oleshky had been agreed to allow humanitarian aid deliveries and the evacuation of the civilian population starting on Oct. 27. 
The agreement includes demining the road to the town, deliveries of food, water, medicine, and medical equipment, and the safe passage of civilians, he added. 
Some 2,000 civilians remain trapped in Oleshky, located just across the Dnipro River from Kherson, with Russian troops blocking humanitarian aid from entering, despite a critical shortage of food and medicine. 
Civilians attempting to flee via the mined roads in and out of the city are frequently targeted by drones.
Picierno announced the hunger strike on Oct. 20, demanding an immediate humanitarian truce in the occupied town. "It is time to act together, so that diplomacy delivers concrete results and no one is left to die in silence," she said. 
Her announcement came days after Pope Leo XIV called for a ceasefire following a phone call with Russian President Vladimir Putin on Oct. 16.
Ukraine will fulfill its part of the "extremely difficult" humanitarian operation, President Volodymyr Zelensky said in a video message on Oct. 24. "We hope that it will be possible to carry out this humanitarian operation — to unblock Oleshky," he added.
The temporary truce was facilitated by U.S. first lady Melania Trump, who spoke with both the Russian and Ukrainian sides.
"Non-military, civilian leaders from both countries will work together to visit Oleshky residents in their homes and determine the level of assistance they require," Melania Trump was quoted as saying in a press release.
"Residents who wish to evacuate will receive coordinated support and transportation to their preferred destination. I anticipate some will want to go to Russia, and some to Ukraine."

Protecting minorities: A test for Syria's new political order
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
14:22:24 UTC
23:22:24 KST

Breadcrumb
Protecting minorities: A test for Syria's new political order
Damascus - Almost two years on from the fall of Assad’s regime in 2024, continued violence targeting Syria’s ethnic minorities is placing the country’s post-war recovery under strain as the government struggles to manage persistent sectarian tensions.
Earlier this month, pro-government demonstrators gathered in Kurdish areas of Hasakeh and Raqqa, vandalising Kurdish symbols and calling for the government to take full control of the region.
This comes amid the ongoing integration of the Kurdish-led SDF into the Syrian state.
The unrest followed a series of mob attacks and acts of vandalism targeting Christian homes, vehicles and shops in Al-Suqaylabiyah, a predominantly Greek Orthodox town in Hama province.
These are not isolated incidents. Post-Assad Syria has seen “several minority communities that have feared systemic discrimination and unfair treatment - particularly the Kurdish, Druze and Alawite communities,” Caroline Rose, a senior director at the Soufan Center, tells The New Arab.
Al-Suqaylabiyah has already experienced a previous spate of mob violence over the past year, while Syria continues to witness sectarian killings on an almost daily basis.
The country’s post-war recovery was also blighted by a series of massacres targeting Syria’s Alawite and Druze minorities in 2025.
Syria’s decade-long civil war deepened sectarian hostility. Assad sought to frame the conflict as a sectarian war between Syria’s minority communities and Sunni “Islamists” and “terrorists”.
As the revolution progressed, opposition to Assad became increasingly Islamist and sectarian in nature. During the conflict, communities on all sides were targeted, with many villages and neighbourhoods suffering killings and displacement.
The collapse of the regime saw many displaced communities return to their destroyed homes, in many cases living alongside those they believed had destroyed them in the first place.
While the government has repeatedly moved to clamp down on outbreaks of violence, two years into Syria’s “transitional period”, it has struggled to address many of the underlying grievances that allow disputes to escalate into communal violence.
Rebuilding trust in the security services
It is this legacy of civil war grievances that allows disputes, often rooted in personal conflicts or criminal activity, to escalate into communal violence. The recent violence in Al-Suqaylabiyah began with a fight between two men, one of whom returned to his village to rally a mob.
Although Damascus has made efforts to deploy its security services to quell unrest, in many parts of Syria this does not necessarily create a greater sense of security among local communities.
“Local officials and security chiefs come mainly from the networks that toppled Assad, often recruited for their loyalty. Minority recruitment into the security forces remains limited,” explains Dr Nanar Hawach, an independent expert specialising in Syria, to The New Arab.
“The already few minority recruits mostly hold desk or traffic jobs, and the armed patrols in their areas are often drawn from elsewhere,” he adds.
“As a result, many ethnic minority residents hesitate to report threats to the officers who patrol their streets, who they may not trust.”
Over the past two years, although the government has made significant strides in filling the security vacuum that emerged after the collapse of the regime, the Interior Ministry remains understaffed according to analysts.
One way to address this, alongside the communal sense of distrust, would be to encourage the recruitment and active deployment of security personnel from minority backgrounds, particularly in areas where minorities make up a substantial proportion of the local population.
However, Gregory Waters, an independent researcher and senior fellow at the Atlantic Council, cautions against establishing a system of local communal policing on ethnic or religious lines which he believes in the long run may serve to “solidify sectarian divisions” by clearly demarcating that “this is a Christian town with Christian police, and that is a Sunni town with Sunni police”.
He argues that alongside more personnel, the local security services need to improve their coordination with local communities, in order to be quickly made aware of and pre-emptively halt sectarian mobilisations before they become violent.
However, analysts agree that establishing civil peace requires more than simply securitising the issue.
Achieving a sense of justice
Local disputes have long been common in many of these communities, although they have taken on a more sectarian character in post-Assad Syria because of grievances that emerged during the civil war.
“For many of those people returning home, seeing their hometowns destroyed has a very visceral impact,” says Waters.
He suggests that this sense of grievance manifests as anger stemming from the perception that “the people responsible were let off the hook”. Those affected perceive a lack of genuine transitional justice.
The Syrian government has begun the long and complicated process of trying those responsible for crimes committed during the civil war. In August, Bashar Al-Assad and several senior regime figures were sentenced to death in absentia.
Despite this, many lower-level figures have not yet been arrested. According to Waters, this gives aggrieved communities “an excuse to cause problems”, even when those targeted by retaliatory violence were not actually responsible for the original crimes.
However, many within minority communities are sensitive to perceived state overreach. Genuine arrests linked to transitional justice can also be misrepresented, with such actions “often get[ting] blown up and distorted through misinformation and fake news”, explains Waters.
The arrests “become construed as the government targeting ethnic minorities – which can aggravate these communities further”.
Waters suggests that building genuine civil peace requires more than simply imposing justice. Instead, he argues, there needs to be “a systemic whole-of-sector approach, that brings together local leadership, revolutionary figures, security chiefs, and most importantly, those who are causing the civil disturbances”.
Local governance and the economy
Governance disputes appear to be a driving force behind much of the recent violence in northeast Syria.
The integration of the SDF into the government is “sparking fears amongst Kurdish communities about the loss of Kurdish political autonomy, Kurdish language rights and security control in the region,” says Rose.
“These fears have been exacerbated by increasing fuel prices and the general cost of living, which have also contributed to public demonstrations.”
Meanwhile, Arab communities in the northeast are frustrated by the slow pace of integration. Reflecting long-standing grievances over what they perceive as corruption and discrimination under SDF rule, some want Damascus to take a more direct role in governing the region.
There is an economic dimension to this issue. The risk of violence erupting is heightened by the lack of real livelihoods for young men, and the sense that material support remains scant.
“You have unemployed young men, angry that their homes and workplaces are destroyed with nowhere else to channel their frustration,” says Waters. “These are the types that are sparking incidents.”
Alongside economics, part of the frustration is rooted in the sense that “communities have limited influence over how their areas are governed,” Hawach explains to The New Arab.
“Alongside security officials, local civilian leaders are often recruited from opposition networks. Minority candidates may be viewed with a degree of distrust, particularly Alawites, given their association with the former regime.”
Hawach suggests that the authorities could address these concerns by giving local communities more meaningful decision-making powers. He points to the Ismaili Council in the town of Salamiyah as a key example.
The Ismaili Council, which represents Syria’s Ismaili community, established contact with HTS before the fall of the regime and helped facilitate the city’s handover to advancing opposition forces.
Since then, the council has worked closely with local security chiefs and community leaders to ensure that occasional incidents of violence do not spiral into broader communal conflict.
“Syria could develop these local bodies with genuine authority over local services, public employment and disputes,” suggests Hawach.
Ultimately, ensuring civil peace in Syria will require the Syrian government to not only develop its security architecture but also address the grievances that cause local disputes to escalate.
Without meaningful accountability, economic development and greater local representation, efforts to restore stability risk leaving the underlying causes of communal tension unresolved.
Cian Ward is a journalist based in Damascus, covering conflict, migration, and humanitarian issues
Follow him on X: @CP__Ward

Thai authorities are continuing to step up enforcement against Israeli tourists, with a special committee on the island of Koh Phangan recommending the revocation of an Israeli woman's visa following complaints about her conduct toward hotel staff and tourists.
The "Special Committee for Reviewing the Behavior of Foreign Nationals on Koh Phangan" announced on Thursday that it had recommended revoking the visa of Einav Ashuel, a 33-year-old Israeli woman, after local police received complaints alleging "threatening and abusive behavior toward employees and tourists."
According to an official statement from the Koh Phangan district administration, two police complaints were filed against Ashuel.
Authorities allege that while visiting Than Sadet National Park and a hotel, she "used services without paying for them, shouted, cursed, insulted employees, and even threatened to physically harm staff members and tourists."
The recommendation followed a Thursday meeting chaired by Koh Phangan District Chief Paisit Thongcharoen, with local police commanders, immigration and tourist police representatives, and senior local officials in attendance.
Thai authorities have taken a strict approach to such incidents. Following the meeting, the committee recommended revoking Ashuel's visa and referred the case to immigration police for further action.
However, authorities have not confirmed whether her visa has been revoked or whether she has been deported.
Three Israelis previously deported from Thailand
Ashuel is not the first Israeli to face immigration enforcement measures on Thailand's popular tourist islands.
In late March, the same committee recommended revoking the visas of three Israelis who had displayed Chabad "Messiah" flags, distributed leaflets, and used WhatsApp groups to invite people to Passover activities on the nearby island of Koh Tao.
Thai authorities said at the time that the activities had raised concerns among residents, business owners, and tourists, and warned that they could disrupt public order.
The three Israelis were subsequently deported, according to a report published on a Chabad website.
In a separate case in September, Thai Prime Minister and Interior Minister Anutin Charnvirakul signed a deportation order against Israeli citizen Yaakov Ohayon after he was convicted of making threats during a dispute involving a zoo on the island of Koh Samui.
A court sentenced Ohayon to a suspended 15-day prison term and fined him 5,000 baht. A deportation order was later issued against the zoo's owner, a French citizen, over his conduct in the same dispute.
Thailand increases scrutiny of foreign tourists
Although Israeli nationals have repeatedly appeared in reports issued by Thai authorities, the stricter enforcement measures are not limited to Israelis.
In early April, the Koh Phangan district chief announced that authorities had revoked the visas of 13 foreign tourists in the preceding period due to inappropriate behavior.
He said inspections and monitoring would continue as part of efforts to protect the safety of residents and tourists.
The Israeli Embassy in Bangkok also issued a special warning to Israeli travelers in May after authorities in Phuket province stepped up enforcement of local laws.
In its advisory, the embassy said local officials had been instructed to impose stricter penalties on those who violate the law, including revoking visas in serious cases.
The embassy urged Israelis traveling to Thailand to comply with local laws and regulations to avoid legal or immigration consequences.
Responses from Ashuel and the Foreign Ministry regarding the allegations in the current case have not yet been received.

'We will get them': Haredi Public Party leader vows to help fill IDF manpower shortage

Haredi Public Party chairman Moti Leitner insisted that his party would cross the electoral threshold in the upcoming Knesset election despite pressure from Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and established haredi parties to withdraw from the race, telling 103FM on Friday morning that internal polling showed growing support.
Speaking to Ron Kofman and Prof. Aryeh Eldad, Leitner discussed his party's chances of entering the Knesset and explained why he believes a segment of the haredi community is seeking an alternative political home.
"We are setting out to win. We will cross the electoral threshold with full force. Our polls show us winning between two and three seats, and we are on an upward trajectory," Leitner said.
"I can see the momentum. It started at fractions of a percentage point, and we have already crossed 2%. We will see what the polls we conduct in the coming days show. We are here for those who have no political home."
Leitner also described his party's preparations for election day.
"Of course, we have invested significant resources and established a large, highly calibrated operation. We are fully focused on election day," he said.
Haredi voters reluctant to publicly support the party
Leitner acknowledged that his party's polls have struggled to accurately measure support among haredi voters, partly because some are reluctant to publicly identify with the party.
"Our pollsters are having difficulty sampling our voters. We are also seeing considerable growth outside the haredi community, particularly among the traditional public. But some voters are afraid to express their identification with the party and openly acknowledge it. Anyone who publicly identifies with it faces threats and violence and could pay a very heavy price."
"People are sending anonymous links, and it is hard to believe who is behind them," he added.
According to Leitner, the haredi community is not a monolithic bloc, and attitudes toward his party vary among its communities and rabbis.
"There is no chief of staff here," he said. "Haredi society is divided into many streams and diverse communities. Tens of thousands of haredim ask their rabbis a great many questions. Alongside the rabbis who support us, we see many rabbis who have not publicly announced their support for us but express that support to their students."
Leitner believes support for his party is much broader than its public visibility suggests.
"We feel that there are tens of thousands of haredim who are going to vote for us, who want to take responsibility for our future and the future of the country."
Haredi enlistment and responsibility for Israel's future
The issue of haredi enlistment in the IDF is central to the party's platform. Leitner seeks to distinguish between haredi men who are not studying Torah and yeshiva students, whom he believes should continue to receive exemptions from military service.
"Anyone who does not study Torah must take responsibility and enlist. We will encourage them and respect them."
At the same time, he argued that yeshiva students should remain exempt from military service.
"We believe that the Torah is the foundation of our existence and that it is what has protected us to this day. This is a debate we will not resolve," he said.
He emphasized the need to pursue practical solutions.
"In politics, the goal is to solve problems and move us forward. The IDF says it is short 12,000 combat soldiers? We will get them."
Leitner argued that greater haredi participation in civic and national security responsibilities serves the interests of both the haredi community and the country as a whole.
"The fundamental problem is one of values. We, as haredim, need to take responsibility for our lives, understand that the State of Israel is also ours, take responsibility for the country, participate in the economy and in security service, and be part of the Jewish story," Leitner declared.
"If we do not do this, we are putting both haredi society and the State of Israel at risk."
