flash forest scatters millions of seeds across canada’s wildfire-damaged landscapes
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
14:15:07 UTC
23:15:07 KST

flash forest scatters millions of seeds across canada’s wildfire-damaged landscapes
biodegradable capsules packed with native seeds and beneficial fungi help restore wildfire-damaged landscapes across northern quebec.
prefer designboom on google
[FEATURED]
flash forest plants for life after wildfires
Across the blackened forests of northern Quebec, drones fly above the remains of burned trees, launching small, seed-filled capsules into the earth. Each carries the beginnings of a new tree, packed with ingredients intended to help it grow in damaged soil. The system is developed by Canadian company Flash Forest, which is using aerial technology to replant landscapes devastated by wildfire, including remote areas that are difficult to reach on foot.
The work follows Quebec’s devastating 2023 wildfire season, when around 4.5 million hectares of forest burned across the province. Flash Forest has since expanded its planting operations across Canada. According to its latest impact report, the company planted 686,147 trees across five sites in 2025, covering 429 hectares of burned forest. The technology allows large areas to be seeded quickly while keeping heavy planting equipment off the forest floor.
tiny engineered pods give seeds a place to grow
At the center of Flash Forest’s operation is a biodegradable seed pod designed to support a young tree through its earliest stages of growth. Each capsule contains nutrients, moisture-retaining additives and mycorrhizal fungi, which can help developing roots absorb nutrients from the soil. Customized drones propel the pods directly into the ground, where the seeds can germinate without first spending years growing in a nursery.
The capsules are manufactured to consistent dimensions so they can pass through the drones’ automated feeding mechanisms. Their composition is developed around the needs of the seeds, with materials intended to retain moisture and support early growth. By sowing seeds directly into the landscape, the company also avoids the transplant shock that can affect nursery-grown saplings. Yet even with this engineered starting point, germination remains dependent on the conditions of each planting site.
collecting millions of seeds in northern quebec
Behind the automated planting process is a remarkable effort to gather seeds from the forests themselves. Flash Forest has been working with the Oujé-Bougoumou Cree First Nation to restore areas damaged by the 2023 wildfires, which destroyed wildlife habitats and affected traditional hunting grounds. When northern Quebec faced a shortage of native seeds, the team worked with local partners to collect jack pine cones directly from trees, traveling by snowmobile and climbing through forests in temperatures as low as -30°C.
The winter operation yielded approximately 8.5 million jack pine seeds, which were incorporated into planting pods within five months of collection. For Benny Blacksmith of the Oujé-Bougoumou Cree First Nation, the aerial process offers a way to restore habitats while avoiding further disturbance to the land. He describes the impact of the fires on wildlife, recalling how even small animals disappeared from affected areas, disrupting the food sources of larger species. The community hopes to see native trees such as white birch and black spruce return to the damaged landscape.
the longer process of rebuilding a forest
Flash Forest’s work continues after the drones have finished planting. The company surveys each site to assess existing vegetation before returning to monitor seedling growth. Experimental plots compare the performance of its engineered pods against untreated seeds and areas left to regenerate naturally. Some sites in Quebec have already experienced delayed germination following warmer temperatures and reduced rainfall, with further monitoring planned for fall 2026.
Wildfire is itself part of the natural cycle of boreal forests. Jack pine cones can open in response to heat, releasing seeds onto the exposed ground, although increasingly severe fires and changing climate conditions can interrupt this process. Flash Forest’s technology offers a way to introduce new seeds where that recovery is struggling. The drones can put them into the ground in a matter of seconds. Whether they establish themselves, and what kind of forest eventually grows around them, will become apparent over the years ahead.
project info:
project: Flash Forest automated reforestation
company: Flash Forest | @flashforest.ca
founders: Bryce Jones, Cameron Jones, Angelique Ahlstrom
location: Canada
founded: 2019
project partners: Oujé-Bougoumou Cree First Nation

NEW DELHI: The long-awaited 666-bed super speciality block at Dr Ram Manohar Lohia (RML) Hospital has secured fire safety clearance, bringing the Rs 482-crore facility a step closer to becoming operational and expanding access to specialised treatment at the Central government-run hospital.The 11-storey block will add 666 beds to the hospital’s existing capacity of 1,538, taking the total to 2,204. It will house 18 operation theatres, 99 intensive care unit (ICU) beds, 196 high dependency unit (HDU) beds and three catheterisation laboratories.
The facility will strengthen treatment in oncology, oncosurgery, hepatology, gastrointestinal surgery and liver transplantation. It will also have two linear accelerators for cancer treatment and a nuclear medicine department equipped with positron emission tomography (PET) scan facilities.The fire safety clearance removes a key hurdle to commissioning the facility, which is expected to expand the hospital’s capacity to handle complex cases and provide critical care. The timeline for making the block operational, however, has not been specified.The development comes as Union health minister JP Nadda reviewed healthcare services and infrastructure development at RML Hospital on Friday, emphasising patient-centric care and wider access to advanced medical facilities.Once operational, the new block is expected to significantly expand RML Hospital’s tertiary care capacity, catering to patients from Delhi and neighbouring states.

Do abstaining voters hold the key to Brazil’s 2026 presidential election?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
13:58:14 UTC
22:58:14 KST

Sao Paulo, Brazil – The first time she voted in a Brazilian presidential election, in 2014, Larissa Campelo voted for centre-right Senator Aecio Neves. Four years later, in the next presidential race, she supported a centre-left candidate, former Sao Paulo Mayor Fernando Haddad.
But ahead of what is expected to be one of Brazil’s tightest presidential run-offs ever, the 30-year-old mother of one has decided she has had enough with politics.
She is abstaining from the vote on Sunday, just as she did during the first round of the election on October 4.
Voting is compulsory for most Brazilian adults. But Campelo is part of a historically large chunk of the electorate sitting out this year's presidential race.
Some 33.4 million Brazilian adults did not show up to vote in the first round, resulting in a 21 percent abstention rate, the highest for a general election since 1998.
“It’s my form of protest. I don’t want to dirty my hands with these candidates,” said Campelo, who lives in the Sao Paulo city of Araraquara.
“This isn’t apathy. It’s because I don’t feel there’s anyone qualified enough to earn my vote.”
But appealing to abstaining voters like Campelo may prove to be a path to victory in Sunday's run-off.
A dead heat
The final vote features two presidential candidates well known in Brazil's political establishment.
The left-wing contender, Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva, is the incumbent president, seeking an unprecedented fourth, non-consecutive term in office.
His rival, Senator Flavio Bolsonaro, is a member of a far-right political dynasty, hoping to follow in the footsteps of his father, imprisoned former President Jair Bolsonaro.
In the first round of voting, Bolsonaro won 47 percent of votes cast, surpassing Lula’s 45 percent. Just 2.2 million ballots separated them, out of more than 158.7 million registered voters.
The final round is set to be even tighter. The research firm Quaest published a poll on Wednesday that showed the two candidates in a statistical deadlock.
Bolsonaro earned 50.5 percent of respondents' support, well within the margin of error for Lula's 49.5 percent.
But experts say polarisation within Brazilian politics has created a population of voters unwilling to cast a ballot for either Lula or Bolsonaro.
In the Quaest poll, 52 percent of respondents said they would never vote for Bolsonaro.
Some 47 percent said the same for Lula, although the pollster noted that the president’s rejection rate had fallen six points in a week, in a promising sign for the incumbent.
A polarised political climate
Joao Guilherme Bastos dos Santos, a director at the Democracy in Check Institute, an independent research nonprofit, explained that polarisation reinforces the public's disengagement with politics.
In a deeply divided political landscape, dos Santos pointed out that voter behaviour often changes.
Voters can become motivated by fear. In turn, they are more likely to vote in opposition to a candidate than in support of one.
"That creates profound exhaustion," dos Santos said. "The fighting seems to go nowhere."
Campelo, the mother in Sao Paulo, echoed that sense of exhaustion. Her decision to stay home during Sunday's election was motivated in part by her rejection of Brazil's deeply antagonistic political culture.
"Politics in Brazil has become like supporting a football team," she said. "Politicians do things wrong, and people keep defending them. It makes no sense."
The morning of her interview with Al Jazeera, Campelo said her husband's family broke into an argument over Lula on their WhatsApp group.
"People are adopting their own pet politicians," she quipped.
Who are the abstainers?
Abstaining voters like Campelo are a diverse group, according to experts. Their reasons for dodging the ballot box can vary dramatically.
Mayra Goulart, a political scientist at the Federal University of Rio de Janeiro, said that those who actively reject Lula and Bolsonaro may only be a minority of Brazil’s abstainers.
Many could be merely uninterested in politics. "Life is difficult enough that they don't have the headspace, time or resources to devote to politics," she explained.
Luciana Veiga, a political science professor at the Federal University of the State of Rio de Janeiro, also pointed out that Brazil’s abstainers are not merely a bloc of disillusioned voters waiting to be won over.
They may have practical considerations that prevent them from casting a ballot. “We cannot say that abstention is simply a political 'no' to voting," Veiga said.
Abstention, she noted, often occurs among people who move cities without transferring their voter registration, as well as those who have work or family care duties on election day.
There are also some voters in isolated areas who struggle to reach distant polling stations.
In addition, voting is optional for 16- and 17-year-olds, people aged 70 or older, and those who cannot read or write.
"Of Brazil's electorate of [158.7] million people, around 21 million are not legally required to vote," Veiga explained.
The penalty for failing to vote is often minor. Without justification for their absence, voters face a fine of up to 3.51 Brazilian reais — less than a dollar — and can have their registrations cancelled after three missed elections in a row.
Until these fines are paid, citizens are unable to obtain or renew passports and other ID documents, nor can they take part in the selection process for civil service jobs.
A final push for victory
With such a slim margin between the candidates, both campaigns are hoping to court the first-round abstainers ahead of Sunday’s showdown.
In the weeks since the first vote, Bolsonaro has promised new tax breaks to help boost the economy.
A central part of his platform is a pledge to address his father's legal predicament: Jair Bolsonaro is currently serving a 27-year prison sentence following his conviction over a coup plot.
Lula, meanwhile, has made reducing abstention a central part of his second-round push.
After round one, his campaign has highlighted Lula's work to end Brazil’s six-day workweek and unveiled proposals for free public transport on weekends and debt relief for small-scale entrepreneurs.
Goulart said that these measures "have much more of an effect on those who are uninterested in politics than on those who reject the candidates".
The first round, however, seemed to hand Bolsonaro an advantage. Not only did he secure the largest number of votes, but many of the candidates who were eliminated were his right-wing competitors.
Some experts predict that the nearly 8 percent who voted for those candidates will migrate to Bolsonaro's camp in the final round.
Bolsonaro also has historical precedent on his side. Brazil began holding direct elections for president in 1989, after its return to democracy.
Since that time, no candidate who trailed in the first round of voting has ever won in the second round.
But Goulart warns against treating precedent as destiny. “A historical observation is not a causal relationship," she said.
She also pointed out that voters may act in unpredictable ways. Wednesday's Quaest poll suggests those who backed eliminated candidates in the first round have not uniformly flocked to Bolsonaro.
While the senator has attracted 43 percent of that support, Quaest found that 37 percent were leaning towards Lula — a more balanced redistribution than initially expected.
Quaest's results also indicate Lula may have an advantage among voters who abstained in the first round or left their ballot blank.
Forty percent of those respondents supported Lula in the poll, compared with 36 percent for Bolsonaro.
While poll numbers do not guarantee results, even modest fluctuations in voter participation could be decisive in such a narrow race, according to experts.
Veiga, the political science professor, believes some of the most crucial statistics will be voter participation rates in regions where each candidate has a strong base.
Lula has a left-wing stronghold in the northeast, while Bolsonaro boasts strong backing in the south and southeast.
"Look at whether turnout falls in either candidate's bases," Veiga said. "Any small movement makes a difference."

Ukraine’s Ministry of Defense has confirmed that Starlink and Starshield satellite communication systems are once again operating at speeds exceeding 400 kilometers per hour, restoring connectivity critical to Ukrainian military operations, including drones, logistics, and battlefield communications.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.

We hope this humanitarian operation can be carried out – access to Oleshky can be unblocked, food and medicine can be brought in, and people can leave this combat zone,” Zelenskyy said in his video address Saturday.
“We have been negotiating this for some time and at various levels. Ukraine will do its part. We count on American mediation to work,” Zelenskyy stressed.
As previously reported, the White House announced on Friday that U.S. First Lady Melania Trump had secured truce between Russia and Ukraine, covering the town of Oleshky, to facilitate the delivery of humanitarian aid and prepare for the evacuation of civilians via a designated safe corridor. The local truce is set to take effect on October 29.
According to statements from the Russian side, the Russian Armed Forces, in connection with a humanitarian operation, are implementing a "ceasefire" in the area of Oleshky, on Kherson front, starting at 3:00 a.m. Kyiv time on October 27, and will "ensure the safe movement of a humanitarian convoy to Oleshky for the delivery of essential goods."
The General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine also announced that Ukraine is implementing a ceasefire in a specific area of the temporarily occupied town of Oleshky, in Kherson region, starting at 3:00 a.m. Kyiv time on Tuesday, October 27, to facilitate a humanitarian operation.
The General Staff noted that Ukrainian units have previously carried out multiple missions to deliver humanitarian supplies via drones to the residents of Oleshky and surrounding villages.
"We trust that humanitarian access for the sake of the people in Oleshky will be guaranteed," the statement reads.

Under the scheme, passengers can opt for insurance by paying a premium of 45 paise per passenger, offering coverage of up to ₹10 lakh in case of death or permanent total disability arising from a railway accident or untoward incident.
LUCKNOW: Indian Railways has decided to extend its Optional Travel Insurance Scheme (OTIS) to passengers booking reserved tickets through Passenger Reservation System (PRS) counters from October 27, in compliance with Supreme Court directions.In an order issued on Saturday, the Railway Board directed all zonal railways to make necessary arrangements for implementing the scheme at reservation counters.The decision follows the Supreme Court's October 6 order in the Union of India versus Radha Yadav case.Under the scheme, passengers can opt for insurance by paying a premium of 45 paise per passenger, offering coverage of up to Rs 10 lakh in case of death or permanent total disability arising from a railway accident or untoward incident.The policy also provides Rs 7.5 lakh for permanent partial disability, up to Rs 2 lakh towards hospitalisation expenses and Rs 10,000 for transportation of mortal remains.According to the Railway Board, insurance will remain optional, and reservation staff must inform passengers about its availability before booking.
Passengers opting for insurance must provide a mobile number and pay the premium through digital payment modes only.
The premium will be collected along with the ticket fare.Insurance policy details will be communicated to passengers through their registered mobile numbers.The Board clarified that the existing terms and conditions applicable to IRCTC e-ticket insurance will also apply to tickets purchased at reservation counters.Divisional railway managers and commercial officers have been directed to monitor implementation, while zonal railways must submit compliance reports confirming operational readiness.

Harmonized regulatory frameworks urged in Africa to advance pharmaceutical self-reliance
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
21:32:57 CST
22:32:57 KST

ADDIS ABABA, Oct. 24 (Xinhua) -- Industry experts and stakeholders on Friday called for concerted action to establish a robust ecosystem for bioequivalence testing to ensure locally manufactured generic medicines across Eastern and Southern Africa are safe, accessible, and scientifically proven.
The call was made during a regional workshop focused on developing a White Paper on bioequivalence testing and regulatory harmonization in Eastern and Southern Africa, held in Addis Ababa, the capital of Ethiopia. The five-day event, which ran from Oct. 19 to 23, highlighted the critical need for harmonized regulatory frameworks and expanded domestic testing capacity to eliminate costly reliance on overseas facilities.
Jointly organized by the Intergovernmental Authority on Development (IGAD), the Ethiopian government and the World Bank, the workshop brought together national regulators, pharmaceutical manufacturers, experts and researchers, as well as development partners to establish a comprehensive regional framework for bioequivalence testing.
Experts and policymakers at the gathering emphasized that relying on external testing facilities imposes significant economic burdens and causes regulatory approval delays for locally manufactured generic drugs. They stressed the urgent need to expand domestic testing capacity to support sustainable pharmaceutical growth across the region.
Addressing the workshop, Girum Hailu, a senior policy and partnership specialist at IGAD, highlighted several critical gaps affecting the sector, including limited regional bioequivalence testing facilities, heavy dependence on overseas testing, high study costs, and inconsistent regulatory requirements across borders.
To overcome these challenges, experts advocated for advancing regulatory harmonization aligned with international standards, implementing phased, risk-based compliance pathways for legacy products, and establishing shared regional testing capacity backed by strong oversight mechanisms to support local manufacturers.
Stakeholders also underscored the vital importance of making bioequivalence services more affordable and accessible to local pharmaceutical manufacturers, outlining priority investments and capacity-building measures for accredited centers across the region. ■

====================================================================================================

Investment security key to global gas market stability
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
13:15:57 UTC
22:15:57 KST

According to Iranian oil ministry's news service-SHANA, in an interview, Ali-Mohammad Mousavi, deputy oil minister for international affairs and trade and Iran’s representative at international energy forums, discussed the Moscow summit’s objectives, Iran’s agenda, the GECF’s role in global energy governance and opportunities for advancing Iran’s gas diplomacy.
Q: What are the circumstances surrounding the eighth GECF summit, and how do you assess its significance?
Mousavi: The eighth GECF summit is taking place at a critical juncture in the evolution of the international energy system and coincides with the forum’s 25th anniversary. In recent years, the global natural gas market has undergone significant changes driven by geopolitical, economic, technological and environmental factors.
Changes in international gas trade patterns, the expansion of liquefied natural gas (LNG) infrastructure, growing concerns over supply and demand security, intensifying competition for investment and rising energy needs in emerging economies have underscored the importance of dialogue and coordination among gas-producing and exporting countries.
Against this backdrop, the summit provides an opportunity for leaders to exchange views at the highest political level, assess long-term market trends and strengthen common approaches to strategic issues facing the natural gas industry.
The significance of the summit extends beyond reviewing market developments. It can also help reinforce the GECF’s position as an influential platform for international energy dialogue and for safeguarding the legitimate interests of gas-producing and exporting countries.
Q: What level of participation will Iran have at the Moscow summit, and what is planned for the Iranian delegation?
Mousavi: Iran was the principal proponent of establishing the GECF and is one of its founding members. As a country with some of the world’s largest proven natural gas reserves, Iran has consistently played an active and influential role in the forum’s activities.
At the eighth summit, Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian will lead a high-level delegation accompanied by Hamid Bovard, caretaker oil minister.
The president’s address to the summit, outlining Iran’s principled positions on international developments and the global energy market, as well as the country’s views on the future of gas cooperation, will be among the main events of the visit.
Before the leaders’ summit, the forum’s 28th ministerial meeting will bring together ministers and senior representatives of member countries. The meeting will review and approve the secretariat’s programs and finalize the documents to be presented to the summit.
The Iranian delegation also plans to hold bilateral meetings with senior officials from member and observer countries, particularly on energy cooperation. Discussions will explore opportunities to expand bilateral and multilateral ties in natural gas trade, investment, infrastructure development, technology transfer, technological cooperation and the use of shared capacities among member countries.
Q: What are Iran’s main priorities and positions at the eighth summit?
Mousavi: Iran’s positions can be outlined along two principal dimensions: political issues and strategic energy priorities.
On the political front, one of the Iranian delegation’s priorities will be to explain the dimensions of the military aggression by the United States and the Israeli regime against Iran and condemn actions targeting the country’s national sovereignty, territorial integrity and security.
In this context, the martyrdom of the Leader of the Islamic Revolution, military commanders and civilians, as well as events related to Minab and Lamerd, will be addressed in line with Iran’s official positions.
In the energy sector, our key priorities include protecting the collective interests of forum members, strengthening the role of natural gas in energy security, ensuring continued investment across the gas value chain, countering unilateral restrictive measures against producers, and expanding technical, commercial and investment cooperation.
We believe energy security is a balanced, multidimensional concept. Achieving it requires simultaneous attention to security of supply for consumers, security of demand for producers, investment security and the sustainability of energy trade flows.
Q: Given recent geopolitical developments, how do you view the relationship between political stability and security in the global gas market?
Mousavi: Because the natural gas industry is capital-intensive, involves long investment recovery periods and depends on extensive production, transmission, processing and export infrastructure, it requires political stability, investment security and predictable market conditions more than many other economic activities.
Any escalation in geopolitical tensions, threats to energy infrastructure, disruption of transportation routes or imposition of unilateral restrictions can affect project financing costs, investment risks and energy prices, ultimately undermining supply security in regional and global markets.
For this reason, we emphasize the need to prevent the politicization of energy trade and its use as an instrument in international relations. I believe the global gas market should develop on the basis of cooperation, mutual benefit, respect for contractual obligations and nondiscriminatory access to technology, equipment and financial resources.
Energy security is a shared responsibility among producers, consumers and countries through which energy is transported. None of these stakeholders can guarantee lasting energy security without taking the interests and concerns of the others into account.
Q: How do you assess the role of natural gas in the global energy mix in the years ahead?
Mousavi: Given its technical, economic and environmental characteristics, natural gas will remain an important pillar of global energy supply in the coming decades.
Compared with coal, natural gas emits less carbon dioxide when burned to produce the same amount of energy. If methane emissions across the supply chain are effectively managed, it can also help reduce greenhouse gas emissions.
In addition, the flexibility of gas-fired power plants allows them to support the integration of intermittent renewable energy sources, including solar and wind power.
Population growth, industrial development, urbanization and rising electricity demand in developing countries also provide considerable scope for natural gas to maintain its role in the global energy mix.
However, energy transition pathways differ from one country to another. Energy policies must reflect each country’s economic conditions, level of development, resource base and national priorities.
At the Oil Ministry, we believe the energy transition should be realistic, equitable and based on diversifying energy sources. It should not lead to unreasonable restrictions on investment in the natural gas industry.
Q: The GECF has emphasized the need for investment in the gas industry. Why is this important?
Mousavi: The sustainable development of the natural gas industry requires continuous, long-term investment across the entire value chain, from exploration and field development to processing, transmission, storage, exports and LNG infrastructure.
Because major gas projects generally require substantial financial resources and long periods for design, construction and operation, a stable and predictable investment environment is particularly important.
Reduced or delayed upstream investment can constrain supply capacity over the medium and long term, intensify price volatility and increase the vulnerability of the global gas market. Such an outcome would benefit neither producers nor consumers.
Accordingly, one of Iran’s key messages at the Moscow summit will be the need to strike a balance among energy security objectives, economic development and environmental considerations.
Producer countries must have fair access to financial resources, advanced technologies and consumer markets. Political barriers and unilateral restrictions should not obstruct the development of natural gas production and export capacity.
Q: What role does the GECF play in developments in the global gas market, and can it be considered an organization similar to OPEC?
Mousavi: The GECF is an intergovernmental organization with a consultative, analytical and cooperative mandate. It was established to strengthen engagement among natural gas-producing and exporting countries.
Unlike OPEC, the GECF does not have a mechanism for setting production quotas or directly managing natural gas supply volumes in the global market.
Structural differences between oil and gas markets, including the significant role of long-term contracts in gas trade, dedicated transmission infrastructure and the regional characteristics of gas markets, mean that cooperation within the forum operates differently.
Nevertheless, the GECF can play an effective role in strengthening natural gas’s position and defending producers’ shared interests by facilitating the exchange of views, experience and information; conducting specialized studies; providing long-term market outlooks; promoting technical cooperation; and coordinating members’ positions in international forums.
Strengthening the secretariat’s technical and research capabilities, expanding technological cooperation and increasing the forum’s participation in global energy discussions can further enhance its role in international energy governance.
Q: What capacity does Iran have to expand gas cooperation with other GECF members?
Mousavi: Thanks to its vast natural gas reserves, strategic geographical position, extensive gas transmission network, long experience in developing and operating gas fields, and technical and engineering capabilities, Iran has considerable potential to expand regional and international cooperation.
Iran’s geographical position, connecting energy-rich regions with consumer markets, offers opportunities to develop regional gas trade and transit cooperation.
Potential areas of cooperation with GECF members include expanding gas exports through pipelines and LNG, establishing swap and transit arrangements, cooperating in field development, participating in processing and infrastructure projects, and exchanging technical expertise.
Cooperation in reservoir management, improving recovery rates, reducing gas flaring, optimizing energy consumption, cutting methane emissions and developing technologies across the gas value chain could also become part of specialized engagement among member countries.
Realizing this potential will require political will among member countries, favorable economic, technical, contractual and investment conditions, and arrangements that ensure mutual benefits for all parties involved.
MNA

BRUSSELS, October 24. /TASS/. Shops in Brussels have taken extensive precautions ahead of a potential new wave of rioting this Saturday, boarding up their storefronts with wooden panels, a TASS correspondent reported.
Several major retailers and shopping arcades, including the flagship Apple store and numerous jewelry boutiques, have opted to suspend operations entirely.
In the capital’s luxury shopping districts along Avenue Louise, Boulevard de Waterloo, and in the Rue Neuve and Sablon areas, more than half of the storefronts have been covered with particleboard panels.
"Naturally, we hope that the police will be able to contain the unrest this time. But we have a grim history. Hopes aren't always realized," Antoine, the owner of a city center electronics store, told TASS.
According to him, the emergency installation of panels on a small shop featuring two glass display windows and a door costs owners between 1,500 and 2,000 euros. Although the panels are firmly screwed into the structural framework, such defensive measures "will only deter opportunistic rioters who aren't specifically targeting a particular store."
Last weekend, street unrest that began as student protests devolved into the looting of city center shops. This week, calls to "take to the streets for social justice on October 24" have once again circulated widely across Belgian social media. Shop owners are discussing online the possibility of legally using civilian or non-lethal weapons to defend against rioters. However, Belgian self-defense law justifies the use of force only to protect life and physical well-being, not property.
Brussels authorities have also undertaken extensive preparations. Reinforced police units are stationed at major intersections in the city center, and the number of patrols circulating throughout the city significantly exceeds that of an ordinary day.
By midday, the situation in the city remained calm. The areas around Brussels’ three main railway stations - North, South, and Central - where groups of protesters typically gather, are under heightened police surveillance, though the situation there remains peaceful for now.

- A small device that gently stimulates nerves through the ear could offer a new way to tackle stubborn high blood pressure. In a clinical trial of 63 patients already taking medication, the treatment proved safe, easy to use at home, and well tolerated. Although it did not significantly outperform a placebo overall, patients with more severe hypertension showed promising reductions in blood pressure.
- Share:
A small device that delivers gentle electrical pulses through the ear could offer a new approach to treating stubborn high blood pressure. In a clinical trial led by researchers at Queen Mary University of London, the technology proved safe, well tolerated, and practical for patients to use at home.
Although the treatment did not significantly lower blood pressure compared with a placebo device across all participants, researchers observed encouraging results in patients with more severe hypertension. The findings suggest that stimulating nerves in the ear could eventually help certain people whose blood pressure remains elevated despite taking medication.
The results come from the SCRATCH-HTN trial, published in Hypertension, a journal of the American Heart Association. Researchers emphasize that larger studies are needed to determine whether the approach can provide meaningful benefits and which patients might respond best.
How Ear Nerve Stimulation Could Lower Blood Pressure
The experimental treatment uses a technique called transcutaneous autonomic neuromodulation (tAN), which aims to influence the autonomic nervous system. This network of nerves automatically controls essential bodily functions, including heart rate, digestion, and blood pressure.
By delivering mild electrical signals to nerves in the ear, researchers hope to influence the body's natural mechanisms for regulating blood pressure without requiring an invasive procedure.
The handheld device, developed by Afferent Medical Solutions, uses two small clips positioned on the tragus, the small flap of cartilage located just in front of the ear canal. These clips deliver gentle electrical stimulation, allowing patients to administer the treatment themselves without visiting a clinic.
Clinical Trial Tests the Device in 63 Patients
The clinical trial, funded by the National Institute for Health and Care Research (NIHR), enrolled 63 people with uncontrolled hypertension. All participants were already taking at least one medication to lower their blood pressure, but their readings remained above recommended levels.
Researchers randomly divided the participants into two groups. One received active nerve stimulation, while the other used a sham device designed to serve as a comparison. This approach helped investigators assess whether the electrical stimulation produced benefits beyond those associated with using the device itself.
Participants used their assigned devices for 30 minutes daily during the first two weeks. For the following 10 weeks, they reduced their sessions to once per week.
The results showed that the treatment was safe and generally comfortable for participants. Most also followed the prescribed schedule, suggesting that the technology could be practical for regular use at home.
However, when researchers compared blood pressure changes across the entire study population, they found no statistically significant difference between patients receiving active stimulation and those using the sham device.
Promising Results in Patients With Severe Hypertension
Despite the lack of a significant overall benefit, the researchers identified a potentially important finding among participants who entered the trial with more severe hypertension.
A prespecified subgroup analysis, meaning the researchers had planned this comparison before examining the results, revealed a greater reduction in blood pressure among these patients when they received active nerve stimulation rather than the sham treatment.
This finding raises the possibility that the technique may work better for people with particularly difficult-to-control blood pressure. However, the trial was relatively small, and the subgroup results require confirmation in larger studies before any conclusions can be drawn about its effectiveness.
Dr. Ajay Gupta, Chief Investigator, Clinical Reader at Queen Mary University of London and Consultant Physician at Barts Health NHS Trust, said:
"This is an exciting, highly patient-acceptable technology that could ultimately provide a cheap, scalable solution for millions. Although the trial did not achieve significance across the broad unselected group, those with more severe hypertension exhibited a clear blood pressure reduction in the active group compared to sham.
"As the first and most thorough study of its kind, this points towards important new research directions that could help us understand whether non-invasive neuromodulation can benefit particular groups of patients with uncontrolled hypertension."
A Potential New Option for Hard-to-Control Blood Pressure
High blood pressure, also known as hypertension, is a major contributor to cardiovascular disease and increases the risk of heart attacks and strokes. It places additional strain on blood vessels and the heart, potentially causing serious damage over time.
Although medications help many patients manage their condition, a substantial number continue to have blood pressure readings above recommended targets even while receiving treatment.
This ongoing challenge has encouraged scientists to explore additional approaches that could complement existing therapies.
Ear nerve stimulation is one such possibility. Because the device is small, does not require surgery, and can be used at home, it could offer a convenient option if future research establishes that it reliably lowers blood pressure in certain patients.
For now, the findings represent an early step rather than proof of an effective new treatment. The researchers say larger clinical trials will be essential to confirm the encouraging results in patients with severe hypertension and identify which groups, if any, could benefit most from this approach.

Unknown Publisher

13:14:26 UTC
22:14:26 KST

Germany is negotiating a deal with Ukraine to purchase Bars jet-powered drones, a German official with knowledge of the matter told the Kyiv Independent on Oct. 24.
Berlin is discussing the deal with Kyiv as Germany plans to buy thousands of deep-strike weapons from European arms companies, as initially reported by Bloomberg on Oct. 23.
According to officials Bloomberg spoke with, Germany’s future strategic thinking involves using masses of cheap missiles to overwhelm enemy air defenses. Currently, Germany’s army only operates midrange Taurus cruise missiles, while the U.S. warned its allies to expect years-long delays for missile deliveries.
The Bars jet powered drone has a range of 1,000 kilometers and can reach speeds of up to 700 kilometers per hour. The manufacturer of the drones is not publicly known for security reasons.
The Ukrainian army launches around 2,000 of these drones per month, targeting Russian oil refineries, power plants, and substations, a representative of the company told Ukrainian media outlet NV in September.
Germany and Ukraine signed a deal to jointly produce Bars in July 2026 as part of the Build with Ukraine initiative. Under the first stage of the deal, Germany would finance the production of the drones, while all manufactured equipment would be sent to Ukraine’s Armed Forces.
Recently, President Volodymyr Zelensky said that Bars have proven to be one of the most effective interceptors against Russian jet-powered drones, as Moscow escalates attacks on Ukrainian cities, Ukrinform reported on Oct. 10.
Germany has emerged as the biggest foreign partner in Ukraine’s burgeoning defense tech sector. A September report from the Kyiv School of Economics Institute found that there were 36 joint ventures between Ukrainian and German firms, as Berlin prioritizes deep-strike technology and intelligence.

Dominican Republic becomes latest Latin American country to adopt IHRA antisemitism definition amid regional shift to the right
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
13:10:00 UTC
22:10:00 KST

On August 24, the Dominican government adopted the International Holocaust Remembrance Alliance (IHRA) working definition of antisemitism, infamous for equating opposition to Israeli apartheid and Zionist colonialism with antisemitism. President Luis Abinader made the announcement in Santo Domingo, while speaking at an event organized by the U.S. Zionist organization Combat Antisemitism Movement. Subsequently, a statement from the Dominican Foreign Ministry justified the decision by invoking a supposed official policy against hate and discrimination dating back to 1938 when, according to the text, “the Dominican State was the only one to offer asylum in Sosúa to a significant number of Jewish refugees fleeing the war crimes perpetrated by the Nazi regime”.
In 1938, the racist and genocidal Trujillo dictatorship was in power. Just as the Israeli regime pushes for the redefinition of antisemitism to shield itself, in Orwellian fashion, Abinader is rewriting the past to accommodate the neo-Trujilloist present.
It is not surprising that the Dominican government, led by Abinader, would uphold the Trujilloist legacy. This is a government that has denied the significance of slavery during the Spanish colonial period that preceded the formation of the Dominican state, that does not officially commemorate the genocide against Haitians in 1937, known as the Parsley Massacre, and that denies the existence of widespread racism in the Dominican Republic while keeping more than 200,000 Dominicans of Haitian descent stateless. President Abinader boasts of following the ideas of dictator Joaquín Balaguer, one of the Trujillo era’s main ideologues. Abinader follows in Trujillo’s footsteps regarding what Dominican racists dub “the Haitian problem,” as shown by his policy of mass deportations and the construction of a border wall—an aggiornamento of the Trujillo-era political program known as the “Dominicanization of the border.”
Today’s neo-Trujilloist regime, with its apartheid policies of racial mass deportations, denationalization and statelessness, is coherent in its support of the genocidal Israeli regime and in claiming the legacy of the dictatorship. This is the true significance of the Dominican endorsement of the IHRA definition through a statement that upholds the legacy of a totalitarian regime that extorted and killed Jewish refugees.
In the context of the ongoing genocide in Gaza, the Dominican government has signed agreements with Israel on issues such as water management and has acquired Israeli weapons. By adopting the IHRA’s working definition of antisemitism, Abinader now threatens to further erode the weak democratic rights that still exist in this Caribbean country by moving in the direction of weaponizing accusations of antisemitism to criminalize solidarity with Palestine.
Abinader’s total subordination to Trump is another key driver of his support for Israel. The Dominican government has aligned itself with the pro-Trump “Shield of the Americas” regional coalition and has made its airports available for U.S. military operations in the Caribbean and against Venezuela; it has even agreed to accept deportees from third countries arriving from the U.S.
The Dominican government’s alliance with Israel is part of this broader trend, and one of the clearest indicators of the region’s shift to the right is the intensification of ties with Israeli apartheid.
The IHRA definition and the regional shift to the right
Due to a combination of strong U.S. interference and the decline of center-left parties, elections over the past year have brought right-wing governments to power in Bolivia, Chile, Honduras, and Colombia. In the cases of Bolivia and Colombia, which had no diplomatic relations with Israel, these were immediately reestablished. In Chile and Honduras, where relations had been degraded by the withdrawal of ambassadors, there was a full diplomatic normalization.
The Venezuelan government’s capitulation to Trumpism, following the U.S. military attack on January 3, 2026, and the kidnapping of Nicolás Maduro, is also part of this regional shift to the right. Interim president Delcy Rodríguez reestablished diplomatic relations with Israel in August, following a campaign of “disaster diplomacy” by Netanyahu, who took advantage of the twin earthquakes in northern Venezuela that left more than 6,500 dead and tens of thousands injured. Relations had been broken since 2009.
In turn, the adoption of the IHRA’s definition of antisemitism has become an indicator of how closely Latin American regimes align with the objectives of Israeli foreign policy and their willingness to criminalize solidarity with Palestine. The definition in question was drafted in 2004 and adopted by the IHRA in 2016, after which it was promoted by Israeli foreign policy as part of its “new antisemitism” doctrine, which views opposition to Israel as the most significant form of antisemitism. Its text includes questioning the democratic character of the State of Israel among its examples of antisemitism. The definition was referenced in a Trump executive order in 2019 and in Latin America it has been adopted by right-wing governments in Argentina, Colombia, Costa Rica, Panama, Guatemala, and Uruguay before being adopted by the Dominican Republic.
Over the past two years in Argentina, legal proceedings have been initiated, using the IHRA definition, against Alejandro Bodart, Vanina Biasi, and Mariano Soria, leaders of the Left and Workers’ Front-Unity, a Trotskyist coalition that holds four seats in the National Congress. In Brazil, socialist leader Zé María of the PSTU and the Jewish journalist Breno Altman have been criminalized for criticizing the Israeli state and calling for Palestinian freedom “from the river to the sea.” Zé María was sentenced to two years in prison, Altman was fined, Bodart won an appeal that overturned his conviction, and the cases against Biasi and Soria remain open.
Kenneth Stern, the main drafter of the IHRA definition, who describes himself as a liberal Zionist, has criticized its use by right-wing Jewish sectors to limit freedom of expression and foster a McCarthyist environment, citing the case of Germany, where authorities have used it to label Jewish people as “anti-Semites” for opposing Israeli crimes in Gaza. Stern recommended the U.S. Senate in 2025 to not adopt the IHRA definition.
Dominican legal scholar Jaime Rodríguez has pointed out that, within the Dominican legislative framework, the Abinader administration’s endorsement of the IHRA definition is not yet legally binding, though he has warned of the risks of censorship and persecution that would result from moving forward with enshrining it into law. Democratic guarantees and freedoms in the country are already fragile, and the alliance with Israel has contributed to their weakening, as evidenced by the Dominican government’s use of the Israeli spyware Pegasus against journalists.
But the peril is an even greater one. There is a clear affinity between the Neo-Trujillista regime led by Abinader and the Zionist project, as Israel is viewed by the Dominican right as a blueprint for Dominican apartheid. Neonazi organizations regularly wield Israeli flags at racist marches against Haitians. Much like Trujillo in 1938, Abinader is unconcerned about antisemitism or discrimination more broadly, as the regime he leads is carrying out a brutal crackdown on Haitian migrants and Dominicans of Haitian descent, conducting a campaign of more than one million deportations over the past six years during which dozens of people have been killed and many more subjected to horrific violence. Normalizing genocide abroad is a way of normalizing apartheid and ethnic cleansing it at home.

Opposition supporters and students mobilised in the Albanian capital, with riot police using water cannons on large groups of protesters. Authorities said 2,500 police officers were deployed to the streets of Tirana.

In the latest of several clashes between police and protesters since mid-October, government buildings were attacked and dozens of demonstrators were detained. Authorities said that more than 300 protestors and police have been injured.
The protesters had heeded calls from organisers for students and others around Albania to attend the rally. Various groups, including university professors, artists and opposition parties, have announced their support or attendance.
Supporters of the opposition Democratic Party earlier gathered outside the prime minister's office for around an hour and a half, setting fire to pillows that Rama had placed there as a symbolic invitation to dialogue with students.
The demonstrators then headed towards the Ministry of Education, where a separate student protest took place.
For their part, high school and university students are demanding lower tuition fees, greater state investment in education and protesting corruption in the education system. Some have joined a broader anti-government movement calling for the resignation of the prime minister.
Prime minister Edi Rama issued a stern warning against violence, pledging a sustained response from the authorities.
"All those who glorify violence, all those who echo violence, and all those who perpetrate violence must understand that just as the urban terror was intense, concentrated, and prolonged, so too will the response from the state be prolonged and persistent," Rama said.
Anti-government protests refuse to die down
Anti-government protests started in May, sparked by a luxury hotel project linked to US President Donald Trump's family, which scientists said in July had already caused irreparable damage to a once pristine stretch of Albania's coast.
Anger over the resort development has morphed into a broader push against corruption, amid ongoing demands for Prime Minister Edi Rama to step down.
Rama has blamed "foreign actors" for the violence and accused both Russia and Iran of driving online misinformation.
The prime minister has also called for "dialogue".
The demonstrators have distanced themselves from any political party, and regularly carry signs accusing both Rama and longtime opposition leader Sali Berisha of corruption.
They chanted "Rama in prison" and "Berisha in prison" on Saturday, blaming the entire political class for the crisis.
The prime minister had earlier published photos of around 40 people, identified by their initials, whom he accused of violence, and renewed his call for the heads of dozens of public institutions to resign.

2 children killed, 3 civilians wounded in Houthi attacks in Yemen&#8217;s Taiz: Rights group
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
12:39:12 UTC
21:39:12 KST

Two children were killed, three civilians wounded and four people abducted in Houthi attacks in Yemen’s southwestern Taiz province over 24 hours, a rights group said Saturday, Anadolu reports.
In a statement, the Yemen Network for Rights and Freedoms said it had “documented 21 crimes and violations by the Houthis over the past 24 hours in Taiz governorate,” including the firing of around 213 projectiles at residential areas.
“Three civilians, including two women, sustained various injuries, while four other residents were abducted and taken to unknown locations,” the group said.
The network also accused the Houthis of continuing their siege and restrictions on civilian movement and the delivery of essential supplies.
It said the Houthis raided and looted three homes in the al-Hujariya area south of Taiz and damaged seven others, including two that were completely destroyed.
The rights group called on the international community to “take action to protect Taiz residents from repeated shelling and the siege,” warning that residents and health facilities were becoming less able to cope with the crisis.
The Houthis did not immediately comment on the allegations.
The developments come amid a military escalation that began in July, described as the most extensive since the relative calm following a truce launched in April 2022.
Since Oct. 5, Yemeni government forces have been conducting Operation Dawn of Yemen, which Presidential Leadership Council Chairman Rashad al-Alimi said aims to regain control of state institutions from the Houthis and recapture the capital, Sanaa.
Yemen has been engulfed in conflict since the Houthis seized Sanaa and several other provinces in 2014, prompting a Saudi-led coalition to intervene in March 2015 in support of the internationally recognized government.
The Houthis control much of northern and western Yemen, while government forces and their allies hold Aden and large parts of the country’s southern and eastern provinces.

The Hebron municipality estimated that 35 hectares (86 acres) had been destroyed or marked for destruction and about 1,500 people had been evicted from their homes by Saturday afternoon in the district of Ein Deir Baha. The whole city of 250,000 people was sealed off by checkpoints on every point of entry.
Videos sent by a Hebron resident showed a substantial area of devastation with every house over several blocks flattened in an urban area. One video showed soldiers marking Palestinian houses with a sprayed black cross, another showed a bulldozer tearing down a stone wall on a hillside and another showed a large residential building festooned with Israeli flags.
People said the building was the home of a prominent Hebron family that had been commandeered as a temporary military headquarters.
The large-scale demolitions follow an attack on Friday on an Israeli military checkpoint outside Hebron by two gunmen. After a 20-minute gunfight, two Israeli soldiers were killed, three injured and the two gunmen were also killed.
Israeli elections will take place in four days and the prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, and the extreme-right finance minister, Bezalel Smotrich, travelled to the site of the attack to promise an immediate and ferocious response.
Netanyahu said Israel would “act to destroy this place”. Smotrich who is standing for election in a smaller coalition party, had himself filmed wearing body armour in front of a Palestinian building being demolished. He said he had ordered “the immediate demolition of a wide row of illegal Arab structures adjacent to the attack site”.
Smotrich also called for “a comprehensive military campaign … exactly like in Gaza and Lebanon”. Ein Deir Baha, the focus of the demolitions, was alleged to be the home district of the two gunmen.
A spokesperson for the Hebron municipality said that about 300 families had been evicted. Some had taken refuge in the homes of friends and relatives, while the municipality said it had opened community halls and children’s play areas to shelter others.
A Palestinian news agency, Wafa, reported Israeli plans to displace a further 2,500 people. “We are being collectively punished for something we neither did nor supported,” a Hebron civil rights activist, Issa Amro, said. “Our suffering is being turned into political material for Israel’s elections, while innocent families pay the price.”
Amro said his sister’s family was one of the hundreds driven out of their homes.
“We are talking about hundreds of families who left their homes because of this, and they are not at all connected to what happened yesterday [Friday],” Amro said in a telephone interview. “It’s a very big area and we don’t know what’s going on, whether it is only election propaganda or if it’s a serious plan from decisions on what to do after the election.”
The Israeli army was approached for comment on the operations and on videos showing extensive devastation.

7 trapped after 16-storey building collapses in Kenya's Nairobi

Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
12:33:00 UTC
21:33:00 KST

Rescue teams were searching for seven people feared trapped after a 16-storey building under construction collapsed Friday in Kenya’s capital, Nairobi, Interior Minister Kipchumba Murkomen said.
Videos circulating online showed the building suddenly crumbling, sending massive clouds of dust into the air in Eastleigh, a densely populated area with a mix of residential and commercial buildings.
The structure was reduced to a heap of rubble as emergency crews rushed to the scene. Rescuers faced difficulties accessing the site, which was wedged between other high-rise buildings.
“Eleven shops on the ground floor and in the basement were occupied at the time of the collapse. Seven people have been reported missing,” Murkomen wrote in a post on X late Friday.
He said 66 of the 67 people working at the construction site had escaped unharmed, while one person was injured.
Earlier, police said they had rescued a woman from the rubble and could hear another person calling for help.
“The contractors and the engineers are supposed to ensure that the works are followed by professionals. But most are not,” Bibiye Mahmoud, president of the Institution of Engineering Technology of Kenya, told Agence France-Presse (AFP) at the scene.
“This is why we are seeing these catastrophes ... There is no accountability,” she added.
A report by Kenya’s National Building Inspectorate found that 87% of buildings audited nationwide last year failed to meet standards or lacked the required approvals.
“Our concern is to save lives,” Nairobi Gov. Johnson Sakaja told reporters, adding, “This building has no occupation certificate ... this has potentially cost lives.”
An occupation certificate is formal approval from the relevant authorities confirming that a building is safe and legally fit for occupancy.
John Ogallo, vice president of the Institution of Engineers of Kenya, who was also at the scene, said there had been warning signs before the collapse.
“People here are saying distresses were observed, like cracks,” he told reporters.
If a building is constructed with the wrong materials, “it becomes a time bomb,” he added.
Nairobi is experiencing a construction boom, with high-rise buildings springing up across the city, particularly in Eastleigh, known for its busy markets and large Somali community.
The number of buildings completed annually in Nairobi rose from 20,025 in 2022 to 25,090 last year, according to the country’s statistics bureau, as East Africa’s leading business hub attracts people from rural areas and neighboring countries.
Local media reported looting shortly after the collapse, which occurred around lunchtime.
AFP journalists saw police use tear gas to disperse crowds gathering near the site.
A report by the Kenya Institute for Public Policy Research and Analysis documented 86 building collapses in Nairobi between 2009 and 2019, resulting in an estimated 200 deaths.
Corruption has allowed contractors to cut corners and bypass building regulations.
Five people were killed when a six-storey building collapsed in a town on the outskirts of Nairobi in September 2022.
In April 2016, 49 people died when a six-storey apartment building collapsed in the northeastern part of the capital after days of heavy rain caused flooding and landslides.

The Strategic Outline Case for the Strategic Sealift Future programme, which will decide how Britain replaces the ships that move the Army’s heavy equipment, is intended to be completed before the end of this financial year, according to an answer given in Parliament.
Ben Obese-Jecty, the Conservative member for Huntingdon, had asked whether the case had been completed.
Luke Pollard, the Minister of State for Defence, said: “The Strategic Outline Case for the Strategic Sealift – Future programme is intended to be completed this financial year.”
A Strategic Outline Case is the first of the Treasury’s five case stages and sets out the need and the range of options before any procurement decision is taken. Ministers confirmed earlier this month that all four Point class roll-on roll-off sealift ships will receive extensive refits, work that keeps the existing capability available while the replacement programme is developed.
The Point class carry armoured vehicles, artillery and stores for deployments and exercises, and the fleet underpins Britain’s ability to move a division sized force by sea. The ships were built in Germany and South Korea and entered service from 2002 under a private finance arrangement, with the Ministry of Defence later buying the hulls outright.

Iran has developed a detailed plan to attack submarine telecommunications cables in the Persian Gulf in the event of renewed military strikes by the U.S. and Israel.
This was reported by Reuters, citing two high-ranking officials from Iranian security agencies who agreed to speak on condition of anonymity
Tehran also plans to hinder repairs to damaged lines in order to prolong communication disruptions as long as possible.
The agency’s sources did not disclose the methods to be used for the operations or the exact locations of the planned targets.
On October 21, the deputy head of the political department of the IRGC stated that seven major internet cables laid along the seabed of the Strait of Hormuz could become potential targets.
According to data from the United Nations International Telecommunication Union, approximately 99% of global internet traffic passes through undersea cables. At the same time, less than 1% of international network bandwidth passes through the Strait of Hormuz, so the global consequences of any damage would be limited.
For Gulf countries, however, simultaneous damage to several lines could cause slower internet connections and disruptions to financial transactions, e-commerce, and cloud services. The extent of the disruptions will depend on operators’ ability to reroute traffic via alternative routes.
Restoring communications amid hostilities may also be complicated by limited access for repair vessels to territorial waters, rising insurance costs, and the need to obtain special permits. This creates the risk of prolonged disruptions even after the attacks cease.
In addition to cable networks, Tehran is considering strikes against U.S. digital infrastructure in the region. Data centers and facilities related to artificial intelligence have previously been cited as potential targets.
Similar attacks have already occurred. In March 2026, Iranian strikes damaged two Amazon Web Services facilities in the UAE, as well as infrastructure near the company’s data center in Bahrain. At that time, the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps named American technology companies—Microsoft, Google, Apple, and Nvidia—among potential targets.
Iran expects that concerns over multibillion-dollar investments in the region’s technology infrastructure will prompt them to oppose a resumption of hostilities.
Earlier, Militarnyi reported that Iran is strengthening the protection of its nuclear facilities, rebuilding its military capabilities, and preparing the population for a possible escalation with the U.S. In particular, Mohsen Rezaei estimated the value of technology infrastructure linked to American companies in the Middle East at over $2 trillion and warned of the possibility of its destruction in the event of a new war.

Although the demonstrations have different demands, they reflect mounting political and economic tensions across Europe, with governments facing growing pressure over living standards, public spending and social policies.

U.S. air base in Japan to block Chinese BYD cars over data fears
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
12:05:31 UTC
21:05:31 KST

- Kadena Air Base will bar all BYD vehicles from Oct. 26, including private cars, taxis and delivery vans, Yonhap reported.
- The U.S. Air Force’s 18th Security Forces Squadron will turn back BYD vehicles at every gate with no exceptions.
Kadena Air Base in Okinawa will bar all vehicles made by Chinese electric carmaker BYD from entering the installation starting Oct. 26 over concerns that the cars could expose sensitive military information, Kangnam Times reported.
The ban covers privately owned cars as well as contractor vehicles, taxis, delivery vans and other commercial vehicles. The 18th Security Forces Squadron, which guards the base’s key facilities, will stop BYD vehicles at every gate and direct them to turn around, and the base does not plan to grant exceptions, according to the report.
Kadena is one of the U.S. Air Force’s largest bases in the Indo-Pacific and home to the 18th Wing, part of Fifth Air Force, which operates fighters, aerial refueling and surveillance aircraft from the island.
The concern centers on how modern electric vehicles work. Many use cameras and sensors to map their surroundings and rely on software and network connections that can send data to outside servers or allow remote access. Information gathered by a car driving through a base could reveal the layout of facilities and patterns of military activity.
A similar problem surfaced last month in Norway, where rental cars used by the Norwegian Armed Forces during Exercise Hovedstad near Oslo Airport from Sept. 14 to 18 recorded soldiers, their movements and the access codes they typed at military gates. At least two of the vehicles were Deepal models built by Chinese state-owned automaker Changan and supplied by Hertz Norge, which is indirectly owned by China’s Geely group, Norwegian business daily Dagens Næringsliv reported.
Other militaries have already restricted Chinese-made cars. Poland has barred Chinese-made vehicles from certain military facilities, citing the risk that onboard sensors and cameras could collect sensitive data, and the Israel Defense Forces has banned Chinese vehicles from its bases.
The U.S. military has tightened rules on Chinese technology at its installations for years. In 2018, the Pentagon ordered base exchanges worldwide to stop selling smartphones made by Huawei and ZTE over security concerns. In June 2026, the U.S. Department of War reportedly added BYD to its list of Chinese military companies operating in the United States, a list that does not by itself ban the use of a company’s products.
BYD has been expanding in Japan, launching models tailored to the Japanese market and opening more dealerships, particularly in regional areas where public transportation is limited.

Three Suspects Arrested in Slavi Binev Killing, Third Businessman Murder in Bulgaria in 3 Months
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
12:01:22 UTC
21:01:22 KST

Prices Keep Bulgaria’s Public Tension High Despite Gradual Decline
Bulgaria’s Public Tension Index edged down to 6.10 points in the third quarter of 2026 from 6.22 in the previous quarter, continuing its decline at a slower pace
Three men have been detained in connection with the fatal shooting of businessman and politician Slavi Binev at his home in Sofia’s Pavlovo district, with investigators suspecting an unresolved financial dispute rather than a contract killing, the Sofia Directorate of Internal Affairs (SDVR) said at a briefing.
The SDVR and emergency medical services confirmed that a report about the shooting was received at 10:28 a.m. An ambulance arrived within seven minutes, but paramedics could only establish that Binev had died. Police said the emergency call had been logged at 10:18 a.m., prompting teams to head immediately to the scene.
According to Acting Chief Secretary of the Ministry of Interior Lyubomir Nikolov, three men were at Binev’s residence and were believed to be regular visitors who had also been there the previous day. A witness reportedly heard a gunshot and then saw the men leaving by car.
Police located the vehicle as it was leaving Sofia and stopped it near the Trajan’s Gate tunnel at kilometer 54 of the highway, using a blocking maneuver that prevented the occupants from resisting arrest. Unconfirmed initial reports said the three men had been detained on the Trakia Motorway.
Nikolov said two of the suspects had Turkish names and Turkish citizenship, while the third held a Bulgarian identity card. All three were involved in construction and were developing two residential complexes in Sofia. Investigators have found no publicly documented business ties between them and Binev in the construction sector.
Two handguns were recovered. Police believe one was the weapon used in the killing and said it had been discarded shortly before the vehicle was stopped. The other was found in a small bag belonging to one of the passengers. Investigators also found a single spent shell casing at the scene, which they believe may have come from the discarded handgun. Binev was killed by a single bullet to the head.
The Ministry of Interior believes the suspected murder weapon was legally owned, as the detainees have valid firearms permits. The suspects are to be taken to the Sofia Directorate of Internal Affairs, where pretrial proceedings will be conducted.
Nikolov said the leading theory was that the killing stemmed from unresolved financial matters, although investigators considered it too early to reach a firm conclusion.
SDVR Director Chief Commissioner Nikolay Peltekov ruled out classifying the killing as a contract assassination at this stage, citing the longstanding relationship between Binev and the suspects and the apparent lack of planning to conceal their identities.
“I do not believe this act can be classified as a contract killing,” Peltekov said, adding that the men had known Binev for a long time and that the incident appeared to have erupted spontaneously.
Nikolov likewise said there were no eyewitnesses to the conversation that preceded the shooting, only people who had seen the suspects arrive and leave. Investigators have not officially established the precise circumstances of the killing.
The death of Binev is the latest in a series of high-profile killings involving Bulgarian businessmen. The report described it as the third public-style assassination of a major businessman in three months, following the killings of Iliyan Filipov and Vladimir Yankov.
Filipov, 53, was killed on September 30 on his own property. He co-founded PIMK, one of Bulgaria’s largest companies, which operates in international transportation, construction and rail freight through PIMK Rail. A consortium involving his company had recently won a public procurement contract worth nearly 44 million leva to reconstruct Hristo Botev Stadium. Filipov was also president of Botev Plovdiv football club.
The fatal shooting took place at around 1 a.m. According to forensic experts, the gunshot wound to the head indicated a contract killing. A key witness was Filipov’s 28-year-old pregnant girlfriend, who was the first to notice a masked, armed man on the staircase. Filipov confronted the intruder himself without calling the emergency number 112. Two days earlier, he had met former Plovdiv Mayor Zdravko Dimitrov, appearing calm and expressing no concern for his safety. Police detained a suspect on October 1, and the intentional homicide investigation remains ongoing.
Yankov, 56, ran a major business importing coffee, tea and vending machine equipment from Italy, with annual turnover exceeding 100 million leva. His business partners described him as a “disguised bird.” He avoided publicity and traveled without personal security, while maintaining a strong interest in blockchain technology and cryptocurrency investments.
On the night of July 27, Yankov had dinner at a restaurant in Sofia with a popular former gymnast before friends dropped him off near his home on Moskva Street in Bankya. Investigators said he was subjected to three hours of brutal violence, including torture and beatings, before being strangled. The perpetrators then poured flammable liquid into the house and set two separate fires to destroy biological evidence. The Sofia City Prosecutor’s Office is investigating the possibility that the killing was intended to steal a digital crypto wallet containing assets worth millions. Investigators are relying on nearby security camera footage, believing the perpetrators had studied Yankov’s habits in detail.
Binev, whose full name was Slavcho Penchev Binev, was born in Sofia on December 10, 1965. He was a taekwondo athlete, businessman and politician who won the title of absolute European champion at the 1992 championships in Celje, Slovenia. After his competitive career, he worked as an international referee, coach and sports administrator, holding senior positions including chairman of the Bulgarian Olympic Taekwondo Federation and vice president of the European Taekwondo Union.
During the 1990s and early 2000s, Binev developed business interests in security, construction and entertainment, managing popular nightlife venues in Sofia. His political career began in 2007, when he was elected to the European Parliament as a member of the Ataka party. He was reelected in 2009 and focused on economic and sports issues.
After splitting with Ataka’s leadership, Binev established his own political project and later joined the Patriotic Front coalition. He was elected to Bulgaria’s 43rd National Assembly in 2014 and initially became chairman of the Parliamentary Committee on Culture and Media. He resigned following protests and objections from the cultural sector, then took over the Committee on Children, Youth and Sports.
Binev was also a member of the initiative committee that nominated Iliana Yotova for president.
