The Danish labor market added 3,600 wage earners in August, according to a report published Wednesday morning by Danmarks Statistik, the national statistical authority of Denmark.
The increase follows a July that showed signs of a small slowdown.
The new numbers support the view held by financial group Nykredit that the Danish job market remains active.
Palle Sørensen, who serves as chief economist at Nykredit, noted that the trend is clear over a longer period.
“It is completely clear when you look at the development over a slightly longer horizon. In the past 12 months alone, there have been 29,638 more wage earners,” Sørensen said in a written comment.
He added that the job market matches the general economy.
“The development in the labor market matches well with the general economic development. Activity is increasing, and it is therefore not surprising that more people are entering employment,” Sørensen said.
There are multiple reasons for the increase in employed people.
One of the main reasons is foreign labor, according to Jesper Grunnet-Lauridsen. He works as chief analyst at 3F, Fagligt Fælles Forbund, which is the United Federation of Danish Workers and the largest trade union in Denmark.
“An important explanation is that more foreign employees have arrived, at the same time as more seniors are staying longer in the labor market,” Grunnet-Lauridsen said in a written comment.
He explained that these groups have helped employers find staff.
“This has made it possible for employment to continue to rise without companies having a correspondingly harder time finding employees,” Grunnet-Lauridsen said.
Neither Nykredit nor 3F expects the Danish labor market to slow down in the near future.
Sørensen said that recent experience shows that later retirement and foreign workers make the size of the total workforce more flexible.
“This is somewhat of an innovation compared to previously, where employment growth was often assumed to be temporary,” Sørensen said.
Energinet to prioritize addressing public service queries as power grid capacity runs short
Denmark’s power grid operator will answer hundreds of connection requests in November while big data centers face long delays.
Energinet, the Danish state-owned electricity transmission company, has now mapped out the capacity needs on the country’s strained electricity grid, the company said in a press release on Wednesday.
With this overview finished, the company will be able to answer applications from several hundred electricity consumers and power producers in November about whether they can connect to the grid.
“In a time of sharply rising demand for electricity, we unfortunately cannot give connection to everyone at the pace they desire,” said Soren Dupont Kristensen, the acting chief executive officer of Energinet.
“But there is room in the transmission grid to cover the electricity needs of ordinary households, smaller businesses, and critical societal functions such as healthcare, defense, and emergency preparedness, both now and in the years to come,” Kristensen said.
Customers will be sorted into four priority categories that were recently passed by a broad political majority as part of an emergency plan for the power network.
Projects placed in Category 1 and Category 2 will get their answers first. These two groups include critical public services, as well as green transition and electrification projects.
Category 3 includes energy storage systems, such as large battery facilities. Category 4 covers major electricity users, including data centers.
“We do not have all the results in place, but it looks difficult to give full grid access to projects in categories 3 and 4,” Kristensen said in Wednesday’s statement.
The political emergency plan was designed to let Energinet and local electricity companies choose who gets hooked up to the power lines. Under this plan, large data centers are pushed to the back of the line because the grid does not have room for huge new projects.
Energinet has faced heavy criticism for expanding the Danish electricity network too slowly. This criticism has come from several groups, including Rigsrevisionen, the National Audit Office of Denmark.
In March, the state company stopped connecting new projects. At that time, Energinet announced that no new connection contracts would be signed until the autumn.
In May, the company stated that very large connection projects could face waiting times of five to ten years. At that point, Energinet also admitted that demand for power had grown at an unexpectedly rapid speed.
Several business groups say it is good news that applicants will soon get answers, but they stress that Denmark still has a real shortage of space on its power grid.
This warning came from DI, Dansk Industri, the Confederation of Danish Industry, which is the main employers’ and business association in Denmark; Dansk Erhverv, the Danish Chamber of Commerce, an employers’ organization representing businesses; and Green Power Denmark, the business and trade group for the green energy sector.
Ulrich Bang, the deputy director for climate, energy, environment, and building at Dansk Erhverv, said the likely lack of space for Category 3 and Category 4 projects shows how serious the situation is.
“Denmark cannot build the industries, business community, and jobs of the future in a waiting room,” Bang said.
“Therefore, action must be taken now, and we look forward to dialogue with authorities and grid companies on how room can be made for more on the electricity grid in the very short term,” Bang said.
The payment company Nets has lost a court case against Konkurrencerådet, the Danish Competition Council, which serves as the public competition authority in Denmark.
The ruling was delivered Wednesday by Sø- og Handelsretten, the Danish Maritime and Commercial Court.
Nets had asked the court to set aside a decision made by the Competition Council. That decision concluded that Nets abused its dominant position in the market for payment solutions between the years 2012 and 2016.
The case involves the company Teller, which was a subsidiary under Nets during that period. Teller offered what were described as exclusivity discounts to a number of large customers. The competition authorities determined that this practice broke legal rules meant to secure free competition, and they made their official decision on the case back in 2018.
The legal process has taken several years. Alongside the civil lawsuit, police have also run an investigation into Nets. That investigation led to criminal charges against the company, with authorities seeking a fine. The criminal case was put on hold to wait for the result of the civil case, and it has not yet gone to trial.
The specific legal reasons behind the court decision are not yet known. In a brief summary published on its website, the Maritime and Commercial Court stated that the full ruling will be released within four weeks.
The court noted that the delay is needed because the text of the ruling may contain business secrets that cannot be made public.
Share of 21-year-olds living at home in Denmark nearly doubles since 2011
More young adults in Denmark are choosing to stay in their family homes, with the share of 21-year-olds living with their parents rising from 32 percent in 2011 to 57 percent in 2025.
The figures come from Statistics Denmark and are highlighted in a new study by Realdania, a Danish philanthropic association focused on the built environment.
Henrik Mahncke, Realdania’s head of analysis, says high housing prices could partly explain the trend. Another possible reason is that many young people enjoy living with their parents.
However, where young people grow up also influences when they move out.
In Albertslund, a municipality near Copenhagen, 61 percent of 21-year-olds still live at home. On the island of Læsø, the figure is just 14 percent.
According to Statistics Denmark, distance to educational institutions is an important factor. Young people who live farther from places of study are more likely to move out.
Cultural background also plays a role, with young people from non-Western backgrounds generally staying at home longer.
Housing availability and prices may also influence their decisions.
Mette Mechlenborg, a senior researcher at Aalborg University who studies housing, points to another explanation: the design of modern family homes.
Many young people grow up in spacious houses with separate areas for parents and children, giving them greater privacy and independence.
This can make staying at home more attractive than moving into a small, expensive room.
Realdania’s study also found no overall difference in quality of life between young adults living with their parents and those who have moved out.

Plans to tighten Denmark’s senior pension rules dropped after political opposition
The government has abandoned proposed changes to Denmark’s senior pension scheme after failing to secure support from parties behind the existing agreement.
Employment Minister Ane Halsboe-Jørgensen announced the decision Tuesday following a meeting with the parties involved.
The changes were part of the government’s proposed 2027 budget and were expected to save 200 million DKK in 2028, 500 million DKK in 2029 and 800 million DKK in 2030.
Under the proposal, applicants would have needed to prove that their ability to work was limited to 15 hours a week or less across all types of jobs, rather than just their most recent job.
This would have made qualifying for senior pension more difficult. In 2026, a single person receiving senior pension gets 22,053 DKK per month.
The scheme was introduced through a political agreement in 2019. Its signatories include the Danish People’s Party, the Social Democrats, the Socialist People’s Party, the Moderates and the Social Liberal Party.
Changes to the agreement require approval from all participating parties during the parliamentary term.
Several center-right parties opposed the proposal, while the Red-Green Alliance also rejected changes.
“We respect the agreements we have. It has not been my intention to terminate any agreement,” Halsboe-Jørgensen said.
“On the contrary. The fact that I called the colleagues from the other parties together today was precisely an expression of the fact that I actually wanted to discuss it with them, and that I respect that the agreement we have with each other gives all of them a veto right against changes in this area,” she added.
Dropping the proposal leaves a gap in the government’s budget plans.
Halsboe-Jørgensen said spending priorities would need to change but did not specify where the missing funds would come from.
Finance Minister Peter Hummelgaard will now have to address the shortfall during negotiations on the 2027 Finance Act.

About 14,000 higher education students living with their parents would lose their entire state education grant under the government’s proposed 2027 budget.
Another 8,000 students in the same group would receive lower payments, Research, Education and Digitalization Minister Christina Egelund of the Moderates said in a parliamentary response.
Denmark’s state education grant is commonly known as SU.
An estimated 31,800 higher education students living at home received SU in 2025.

Minister calls for talks after report finds major employment losses due to stress
Economic and Interior Affairs Minister Pia Olsen Dyhr will convene labor unions, employer organizations and other groups for talks on preventing work-related stress.
The first roundtable discussion will take place Friday following a new report from the Danish Economic Council’s independent economic advisers.
The report estimates that severe work-related stress reduces Denmark’s labor supply by between 16,000 and 39,000 people.
More than one in 10 people affected by severe stress do not return to employment, while more than one in three disability pension recipients receive the benefit after a stress reaction, according to the report.
“Stress makes us poorer,” Dyhr of the Socialist People’s Party said. “This applies both to the individual person who becomes ill with stress and their family, but it also matters for our society.”
Chief Economic Adviser Jakob Roland Munch said severe stress has long-lasting effects on people’s connection to the labor market.
However, the report found no evidence that the number of severe stress cases has increased during the past 15 to 20 years.
Dyhr said Denmark must place greater emphasis on preventing stress instead of responding only after people become ill.
The government’s proposed 2027 budget includes 50 million DKK for a prevention fund intended to help people remain healthy and employed.
Dyhr said the government wants stronger evidence about which preventive measures work before deciding how to prioritize future efforts.
The European Commission has made security the main focus of its new Arctic strategy as Russia and China expand their activity in the region.
The approach marks a significant shift from the European Union’s 2021 strategy, which concentrated primarily on international cooperation, climate and environmental protection.
“As Russia and China increase their presence and ambitions, the Arctic has become a frontline in the global power competition,” EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said.
The Commission fears the Arctic could become a major source of conflict with Russia after the war in Ukraine ends.
The strategy proposes expanding Europe’s icebreaker capacity and strengthening protection of northern maritime borders and critical undersea infrastructure.
The EU’s 27 countries collectively have about 10 icebreakers, compared with an estimated 40 operated by Russia.
The Commission also proposes creating a maritime security center to monitor activity in the Arctic.
A separate Arctic cable center would monitor, protect and repair undersea cables in the North Atlantic and Arctic. It could later track ships belonging to Russia’s so-called shadow fleet, which transports sanctioned oil and gas.
Western intelligence services also suspect that Russia has used shadow fleet vessels in hybrid attacks.
The strategy contains no spending figures and must now be discussed with EU governments.
Kallas said Arctic security was a European concern because Denmark, Sweden and Finland are Arctic countries and more than 500,000 EU citizens live in the region.
Record trout catch in Varde River follows restoration efforts
Anglers caught a record 1,400 large trout in Denmark’s Varde River during 2025, according to science news outlet Videnskab.dk.
Researchers have also found trout fry at more locations in the river system than at any point during the past 40 years.
“It is good to see that efforts to remove obstacles to fish movement are beginning to work in Varde Å,” said Bjarke Ibsen Dehli, a fish conservation adviser at DTU Aqua, the National Institute of Aquatic Resources.
However, he said Denmark remained far behind in restoring healthy, natural river systems.
Rivers have historically been straightened, widened and deepened to drain surrounding farmland. Stones and gravel were removed, despite fish such as trout and salmon relying on gravel for spawning.
Aquatic plants have also been removed, reducing places where fish can hide.
Sluices, dams, water mills, fish farms, bridges and pipes can block migrating fish. Fish gathered near such barriers may become easier prey for cormorants, herons, otters and seals.
DTU Aqua’s latest survey found healthy trout populations along 14 percent of the examined stretches of the Varde River system. That was up from five percent in 2016.
Associations can apply for funding to restore local waterways, including grants from DTU Aqua for spawning gravel and shelter stones.
Dehli encouraged residents to join local organizations working to improve rivers and streams.
Social Democrat warns foreign labor risks creating master-servant society
Social Democratic finance spokesperson Kaare Dybvad Bek has warned that Denmark risks developing a society divided between those providing low-paid services and those becoming dependent on them.
“What do we become as human beings if we slowly let low-paid Africans and Asians do everything that is not immediately manageable?” Dybvad Bek said Monday during a budget debate in the Folketing, Denmark’s parliament.
He questioned whether Danes lose practical skills and the ability to learn when they rely on foreign workers, delivery services such as Wolt and artificial intelligence for routine tasks.
Dybvad Bek referred to German philosopher Georg Hegel’s theory that a master becomes increasingly helpless as a servant performs more of the work.
He said individual consumers were not responsible for the development.
“It is up to us politicians to stop the flow of underpaid labor that forms the basis for these services,” he said.
Dybvad Bek argued that goods and services should be priced at a level that allows workers to earn a living wage.
He also warned that Denmark could create new parallel societies if foreign workers remain socially separated from the people they serve.
The comments came as Dybvad Bek presented a government proposal requiring employers to finance Danish lessons for workers from countries outside the European Union before they arrive.
He said companies should help pay for the integration of workers from whom they profit.

“Lego is an exceptional brand, regardless of how you measure it,” Brand Finance Chief Operating Officer Mike Rocha told Børsen.
Brand Finance calculates how much a company would hypothetically have to pay to license its brand if it did not own it.
The consultancy said Lego’s financial performance contributed to the increase in value.
Lego recorded revenue of 83.5 billion DKK in 2025, an increase of 12 percent from the previous year and the highest annual total in the company’s history.
Growth accelerated during the first half of 2026, when Lego’s revenue rose by 21 percent compared with the same period in 2025.
Lego declined to comment to Børsen on the Brand Finance report.

The feature will appear under the app’s “Wallet” menu in an update being gradually released from Tuesday, Vipps MobilePay said.
Users can add a passport-style photograph to the digital proof, which displays only their name, photo and age category.
Vipps MobilePay product manager Dennis Kvade said the need to confirm age and identity was increasing both online and in physical stores.
“It is not particularly practical to bring your passport on a night out,” he said, adding that existing age checks can also be vulnerable to fraud.
Supermarket chain Rema 1000 will accept MobilePay’s proof of age. Its employees will receive information about the feature.
However, the MobilePay document is not an official identification card and cannot replace a passport, health insurance card or driving licence.
It is intended for situations in stores and nightlife venues where young people must show they are old enough to purchase restricted products such as alcohol.
Individual businesses can decide whether to accept it, meaning users cannot assume it will be recognized everywhere.
Denmark’s Agency for Digital Government launched AltID earlier in 2026 as the country’s first official digital proof of age and identification app for both online and in-person use.

Between 10 and 12 pensioners occupied Rehabiliteringshøjskolen in Risskov on Tuesday and locked staff outside to protest its planned closure.

“The folk high school cannot raise the dead, but it can keep them alive,” read one sign displayed in a window.

Danish home sales fall 12 percent as higher rates slow market
Denmark’s housing market is showing signs of slowing after a strong start to 2026, according to transaction figures from property portal Boligsiden.
A total of 7,709 homes were sold in September, 12 percent fewer than in the same month last year.
Housing transactions during the first nine months of 2026 were three percent below the corresponding period in 2025.
Apartment sales have fallen most sharply. Eight percent fewer apartments have been sold nationwide this year, while Copenhagen has recorded a decline of 23 percent.
Brian Friis Helmer, personal finance economist at AL Sydbank, said rising mortgage rates could partly explain the slowdown.
Fixed-rate mortgages have recently fluctuated between four and five percent, compared with 3.5 percent at the beginning of the year.
Higher prices for gasoline, natural gas and electricity are also reducing the money households have available, he said.
However, strong employment and rising inflation-adjusted incomes continue to support the housing market.
Sales of houses and terraced homes are also below last year’s level. Holiday home sales, by contrast, have increased by 4.5 percent.
Boligsiden communications director Birgit Daetz said the increase indicates that many households remain financially secure because holiday homes are traditionally purchased during periods of economic strength.
Rising property values and the possibility of rental income may also make such purchases more affordable, she said.

What Does Bulgaria's President Actually Do?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
06:30:00 UTC
15:30:00 KST

Prices Keep Bulgaria’s Public Tension High Despite Gradual Decline
Bulgaria’s Public Tension Index edged down to 6.10 points in the third quarter of 2026 from 6.22 in the previous quarter, continuing its decline at a slower pace
On Sunday, Bulgarians will choose a head of state for a five-year term beginning in January 2027 and most of them will do it knowing that the person they elect will not run the country. Bulgaria is a parliamentary republic. The prime minister and the Council of Ministers set policy, parliament passes the laws, and the president has no right to propose legislation, no seat in the cabinet and no say over the budget beyond a veto that 121 of the 240 MPs can override.
That makes the office sound weaker than it is. The president is the one official every adult Bulgarian votes for directly, commands the armed forces, represents the country abroad, decides when an election is called and, at moments of political deadlock, picks the people who run the state while parliament cannot. Over the past five years of snap elections those moments became routine, and the presidency grew into one of the most consequential institutions in the country, which is exactly why parliament moved in 2023 to cut it back.
Bulgaria had no president for most of its modern history. From 1879 the head of state was a prince (knyaz), and from 1908 a tsar, until a referendum on September 8, 1946, abolished the monarchy and opened the way for the People's Republic. Under communism the role passed to a collective body, first the Presidium of the National Assembly and from 1971 the State Council, which Todor Zhivkov chaired until his removal in November 1989.
The modern presidency was born in the turbulence that followed. In April 1990 parliament made Petar Mladenov, Zhivkov's successor at the head of the State Council, the country's first president. He lasted three months, resigning in July after a recording surfaced in which he was heard telling colleagues during a December 1989 protest that it would be better if "the tanks came." The Grand National Assembly then elected dissident philosopher Zhelyu Zhelev in August 1990, and the constitution it adopted on July 12, 1991, turned the presidency into a directly elected office. Zhelev won the first popular vote in January 1992.
Since then the office has been held by Petar Stoyanov (1997–2002), Georgi Parvanov (2002–2012, the only president so far to serve two full terms), Rosen Plevneliev (2012–2017) and Rumen Radev (2017–2026). When Radev resigned in January 2026 to found Progressive Bulgaria and run for parliament, Vice President Iliana Yotova became the first woman and the first vice president to take over the office, serving out the remainder of his term. The presidency sits at 2 Dondukov Boulevard in central Sofia, which is why Bulgarians use the address as shorthand for the institution.
Further reading: Tanks, Mandates and Caretakers: The Story of Bulgaria’s Presidency Since 1990
The constitution sets four conditions. A candidate must be a Bulgarian citizen by birth, be at least 40 years old, meet the requirements for election to parliament and have lived in Bulgaria for the previous five years. The term is five years, and a president can be elected only twice, consecutively or not. Once in office, the president cannot sit in parliament, hold any other state, public or business post or serve in a party's leadership.
President and vice president are elected together on a single ticket. To win in the first round a ticket needs more than half the valid votes with turnout above 50 percent. If either condition is missed, the top two tickets go to a runoff a week later, where the higher vote wins regardless of turnout. No Bulgarian president has ever been elected in the first round, and with turnout this year expected below 40 percent, the November 1 runoff is all but certain.
The vice president has no independent powers of their own. The office exercises whatever authority the president delegates by decree, in practice the handling of pardons, citizenship and asylum, and steps in if the presidency falls vacant, completing the term. If both offices are empty at once, the Speaker of parliament acts as head of state until a new election, which must be held within two months.
The president's main tool against parliament is the right to return a law for reconsideration before signing it. The veto can be used only once per law, and the National Assembly overrides it by passing the text again with the votes of more than half of all MPs, 121 of 240, after which the president must promulgate it. Against a government with a stable majority, such as Progressive Bulgaria's 131 seats today, a veto delays a law and forces a public debate, but it rarely stops one.
The stronger instrument is the Constitutional Court. The president is one of the few institutions that can ask the court to strike down a law or to give a binding interpretation of the constitution, and also appoints four of its twelve judges. The president can also formally propose constitutional amendments, although parliament decides on them.
Most presidential decisions take the form of decrees, and most decrees must be countersigned by the prime minister or the relevant minister, which keeps the government in the loop on appointments, awards and similar acts. The exceptions are the ones that matter politically: scheduling elections, dissolving parliament, returning laws, handing out mandates to form a government and appointing a caretaker cabinet all happen on the president's signature alone.
Those mandates are where the office becomes central in a fragmented parliament. After an election the president hands the first mandate to form a cabinet to the largest parliamentary group and, if that fails, the second to the next largest. The third mandate goes to any group of the president's choosing, a real discretion that has decided governments in the past. If all three fail, the president dissolves parliament, schedules a snap election and appoints a caretaker government to run the country until a new parliament elects a cabinet. Bulgaria has had a dozen caretaker governments since 1990, seven of them in the last five years.
The president is supreme commander-in-chief of the armed forces and chairs the Consultative Council for National Security, which brings together the government, parliamentary leaders, the military and the security services. The council has no executive power, but convening it is a political signal. The president appoints and dismisses the senior military command and confers the highest ranks, though only on the government's proposal, and the constitution allows the head of state to declare war or martial law when parliament is not sitting, subject to its later approval.
Abroad, the president represents Bulgaria, receives the credentials of foreign ambassadors and, on the government's proposal, appoints and recalls Bulgaria's own heads of mission. Foreign policy itself belongs to the cabinet, and the president usually does not represent the country at European Council summits, where the prime minister sits.
The president also signs the decrees that appoint several of the state's most powerful officials once other bodies have chosen them, including the prosecutor general and the heads of the two supreme courts. The president may send a nomination back once, but a repeated proposal must be signed.
Some of the presidency's most sensitive work happens far from the headlines. The president grants, restores and revokes Bulgarian citizenship, grants asylum, pardons convicted criminals and can write off uncollectable debts to the state. By long tradition these powers are delegated by decree to the vice president. A presidential commission reviews the requests, but its members have been kept anonymous, and the motives behind individual pardons are not routinely published, which is why critics are now calling for the process to be opened up.
The president also awards state orders and decorations, renames towns and villages, schedules local elections and national referendums once parliament has approved them and addresses the nation on New Year's Eve.
While in office, the president and vice president cannot be detained or criminally prosecuted, and they bear no liability for acts performed in the course of their duties, with two exceptions. They can be removed for high treason or for violating the constitution. An impeachment motion needs the signatures of at least a quarter of MPs and must then be approved by more than two-thirds of the National Assembly, 161 votes, before the case goes to the Constitutional Court, which has one month to rule. If the court finds the president guilty, the mandate ends.
The bar is high enough that it has never been cleared. The nationalist Ataka party tried to start proceedings against Rosen Plevneliev in 2013 after he backed early elections during that year's protests, but it could not even gather the support to put the motion on the agenda. A president can otherwise leave office early only through death, a permanent illness that prevents the work, or resignation, which must be submitted before the Constitutional Court.
For most of the post-communist era the caretaker power was a formality, used briefly between elections. That changed after 2021, when Bulgaria entered a cycle of eight parliamentary elections in five years. Each failed parliament left Radev to appoint another caretaker cabinet, and the governments of Stefan Yanev and Galab Donev, both men ran the country for long stretches, signing off on energy contracts, defense decisions and the handling of the war in Ukraine without any parliamentary majority behind them. Critics argued that the president had effectively become the head of the executive.
Parliament answered on December 20, 2023, when GERB, We Continue the Change, Democratic Bulgaria and the Movement for Rights and Freedoms passed the sixth amendment to the 1991 constitution. Alongside a large judicial reform, it took away the president's free choice of caretaker prime minister. The president must now pick from a short list of officials: the Speaker of parliament, the governor or a deputy governor of the Bulgarian National Bank, the chair or a deputy chair of the National Audit Office, or the Ombudsman or a deputy. The list was quickly nicknamed the "house book," after the old apartment-building ledgers where residents were recorded.
The Constitutional Court struck down most of the 2023 package in July 2024, including the judicial changes, but split six to six on the caretaker provisions, so they survived. A second challenge brought by Radev and two groups of MPs failed in July 2025 for the same reason, when only six of the twelve judges, one short of the required seven, found the rules unconstitutional. The practical effect has been visible since. In 2024 Radev had to appoint Audit Office chair Dimitar Glavchev, a long-time GERB figure. In February 2026 Yotova said ten eligible officials had turned her down before Andrey Gyurov, then a suspended BNB deputy governor, accepted, and complained that the amendments had left the presidency without a real choice.
The politics have since turned upside down. Radev, now prime minister with a majority of his own, announced on August 24 that his government will propose restoring the president's free hand over caretaker cabinets, arguing that "when the President's hands are tied, the procedure almost came to a standstill." No text has been tabled yet. If the change goes through, it would hand back the power to the president.
This article is part of Novinite's editorial series on Bulgaria's October 25 presidential election. It was not commissioned or paid for by any candidate, party or initiative committee, and it does not endorse anyone.

United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher

07:00:43 BST

The Permanent Secretary at the Ministry of Defence was asked five times by a member of the Defence Committee whether the Defence Investment Plan settlement is backloaded, telling MPs at one point that he was not sure he understood the definition and finally that there was not more he could give the committee.
Jeremy Pocklington was giving evidence alongside Wes Streeting, the Secretary of State for Defence.
Derek Twigg, the Labour member for Widnes and Halewood, put it to Streeting that John Healey’s resignation letter had said the funding settlement was insufficient, and that the extra support was backloaded when the pressure of operations and the imperative to speed up readiness falls in the first two years.
Streeting said extra funding was won by Dan Jarvis during the Defence Investment Plan process and brought in the Permanent Secretary, who had been party to those discussions.
Twigg asked: “Is it backloaded or not?” Pocklington began: “Additional resource DEL was given to the Department between the time of John Healey’s resignation and Dan Jarvis settling the DIP.”
Twigg interrupted to say he wanted a straight answer for the committee and repeated the question. Pocklington said: “The overall departmental spending is on a rising profile, so by the end of this Parliament it will be 27% higher in real terms than at the start.”
The chair, Tan Dhesi, intervened twice to ask for an answer, and Pocklington said: “I am keen to help the Committee. I can read out what our spending totals are for each year.” Asked again, he said: “I am not sure I understand the definition.”
He then said: “We received additional support between the time between the time of John Healey’s resignation and Dan Jarvis that meant that the spending power of the Department has actually increased by £15 billion. It was a lower amount at the time that John Healey resigned. We do have additional support, including, in particular, additional support for RDEL for readiness.”
Asked a final time whether he agreed with the previous Secretary of State on the point, Pocklington said: “I think the settlement had changed. There is not more that I can give to the Committee.”
On the trajectory of spending, Streeting told the committee that defence spending was 2.3 per cent of national income when Labour came to office and will be 2.7 per cent in 2027-28, and that the Chancellor has said he will plug a £4.7 billion gap at the Budget with more to come at the spending review.
Twigg pressed him on whether there is any commitment to reach three per cent by 2030. Streeting said: “But we would not normally, and we do not normally, set out ahead of spending reviews what the control totals will be.”
Dhesi told him: “It seems palpable to many of us that we are not meeting the moment, and that is why there is a sense of exasperation.” He noted the committee had visited Denmark, which has gone from spending 1.3 per cent of national income on defence to 4.99 per cent within four years.
Streeting said: “And in those cases, Chair, look at the cost of borrowing in those countries. We are not comparing like with like.” He said the debt-to-GDP ratio is around a hundred per cent and that roughly one in every ten taxpayer pounds goes on servicing debt interest.

Russia senator says Western sanctions may remain in place forever

MOSCOW, October 24. /TASS/. Western countries may temporarily ease sanctions against Russia in their own interests, but they are unlikely to completely abandon them, Federation Council Vice Speaker Konstantin Kosachev said in an interview with TASS.
But Moscow should not worry, because it has proven its self-sufficiency.
"It can be assumed that we will live to see the moment when sanctions are lifted legally, but, in my view, their inclusion in US legislation and in the relevant directives of the European Union is, if not an eternal phenomenon, then at least an extremely long·term one, because lifting sanctions requires consensus — a convincing majority, in case of US Congress, or consensus, unanimity, in case of the European Union," the senator said.
According to Kosachev, temporary exceptions to the sanctions regime are possible thanks to the interests of the Western countries.
"My prediction is that the sanctions regime will be eased over time, because maintaining it at its current maximum level clearly runs counter to the interests of those who came up with and are using these sanctions," he explained.
However, the parliamentarian continued, the Westerners will certainly retain the ability to reinstate the sanctions at any time if "Russia behaves, in their view, in a way they do not like."
"I am convinced that this is not the issue we should be focusing on, because over these decades -- if we look at the period starting from 2008, when sanctions related to the Georgian issue first appeared -- we have proven that Russia cannot be isolated, that Russia cannot be broken even by the most severe sanctions, and that we are able to maintain our self·sufficiency and our ability to develop regardless of what is happening around us," the senator believes.
He added that the maintenance or lifting of anti-Russian sanctions in one form or another is "a headache for those who imposed these sanctions," not for Russia.
Sanctions and Russian diesel fuel
The White House is exempting Russian diesel fuel supplies to global markets from sanctions until April 7. On October 9, Russian President Vladimir Putin and US President Donald Trump discussed over the phone the supply of petroleum products. Later, the Russian president confirmed Moscow’s readiness to supply oil and oil products to the American and global markets. Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak previously told TASS that Russia is beginning to lift the ban on diesel fuel exports early and is ready to supply 100,000 tons of diesel in October, 500,000 tons in November, and 1 million tons in December, with the potential to increase this volume to 3 million tons per month.

This 150-million-year-old bird had dinosaur teeth and a strange secret
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
02:42:19 UTC
11:42:19 KST

This 150-million-year-old bird had dinosaur teeth and a strange secret
- Date:
- October 23, 2026
- Source:
- Chinese Academy of Sciences Headquarters
- Summary:
- A 150-million-year-old fossil discovered in China reveals a bizarre early bird with sharp teeth, a dinosaur-like claw, and a body built for life on the ground rather than flight. Scientists believe it represents the earliest known example of flight loss in birds, overturning assumptions about how these animals evolved.
- Share:
A remarkably preserved 150-million-year-old bird fossil discovered in China is challenging long-standing ideas about how birds evolved. Rather than developing increasingly sophisticated flight abilities, some of the earliest birds appear to have taken a very different evolutionary path, including losing the ability to fly altogether.
The newly identified species, Yuezhuornis yangyuanensis, lived during the Late Jurassic period (150-148 million years ago). Described in a study published in Nature, the crow-sized creature provides evidence that early bird evolution was much more complex than scientists once believed. Instead of evolving primarily to become better flyers, ancient birds were adapting to a variety of environments and ways of life, including those that favored living on the ground.
Researchers from the Institute of Vertebrate Paleontology and Paleoanthropology (IVPP) of the Chinese Academy of Sciences (CAS) and the Fujian Institute of Geological Sciences uncovered the fossil in the recently recognized Zhenghe Fauna of Fujian Province in southeastern China. According to their findings, Yuezhuornis represents the earliest known example of a bird lineage losing its ability to fly.
An Ancient Bird With Dinosaur Teeth and Claws
One of the most remarkable features of Yuezhuornis is its unusual combination of bird and dinosaur characteristics. Although it possessed skeletal features associated with birds, it also retained anatomical traits that would have been familiar among small predatory dinosaurs.
Its jaws contained closely spaced, serrated teeth resembling those of deinonychosaurs, a group of meat-eating dinosaurs that included agile predators related to birds. Such teeth are not normally associated with early birds.
Even more striking was its second toe, which could bend backward unusually far and carried a curved, sickle-shaped claw. This specialized feature is strongly associated with deinonychosaurs, including dromaeosaurids and troodontids, two groups of predatory dinosaurs.
"When we examined Yuezhuornis, we were struck by its extraordinary mix of features," said Dr. Min Wang, corresponding author of the study. "It possesses bird-like pelvic and hindlimb structures yet retains the specialized predatory foot and teeth of a small meat-eating dinosaur. It shows us that early bird evolution was far more complicated than we previously realized."
Where Does This Strange Jurassic Bird Fit in Evolution?
To understand how Yuezhuornis was related to other prehistoric birds and dinosaurs, scientists carried out detailed analyses of its evolutionary relationships. They used two approaches, maximum parsimony and Bayesian tip-dating, to compare anatomical characteristics and reconstruct the species' position on the evolutionary tree.
Maximum parsimony identifies evolutionary relationships that require the fewest changes in characteristics, while Bayesian tip-dating also incorporates statistical estimates of evolutionary history and information about when fossils lived.
Both methods produced consistent results, placing Yuezhuornis within Avialae, the evolutionary group that includes modern birds and their closest extinct relatives.
"The results consistently placed Yuezhuornis firmly within Avialae (the group containing modern birds and their closest extinct relatives), just crownward of Archaeopteryx and as a sister taxon to Zhengheornis," said Dr. Zhonghe Zhou, a co-author of the study.
This placement is particularly important because Archaeopteryx, which also lived roughly 150 million years ago, is among the most famous early bird relatives. The findings indicate that Yuezhuornis belonged to an early branch of bird evolution rather than simply being a small predatory dinosaur with bird-like characteristics.
Evidence That Some Early Birds Lost the Ability to Fly
The researchers also examined how Yuezhuornis might have lived. Using measurements of its skeletal proportions and statistical comparisons with other animals, they investigated whether its anatomy was better suited for flying or moving along the ground.
The results showed that its limb proportions closely resembled those of modern ground-dwelling birds and certain other prehistoric dinosaurs closely related to birds. This similarity suggests that Yuezhuornis spent its life on the ground and was likely unable to fly.
The findings point to an unexpected development in the history of birds. Rather than simply progressing toward stronger wings and more efficient flight, some early bird lineages appear to have moved in the opposite direction, adapting to lifestyles in which flying was no longer necessary.
This challenges the traditional assumption that the earliest stages of bird evolution were driven primarily by the demands of flight. Instead, birds were already exploring different ecological roles and developing a surprisingly wide range of body forms.
A 150-Million-Year-Old Discovery Rewrites Bird Evolution
The discovery of Yuezhuornis suggests that the evolution of birds was never a simple, one-directional process. Even during the Late Jurassic, when the earliest bird lineages were emerging, some species were developing adaptations that favored life on land rather than in the air.
Its unusual combination of bird-like anatomy, dinosaur-style predatory features, and apparent flightlessness provides a revealing glimpse into that evolutionary experimentation. The fossil shows that early birds were more anatomically and ecologically diverse than previously recognized.
It also underscores the scientific importance of the Zhenghe Fauna, a fossil assemblage that is helping researchers investigate a poorly understood period in bird evolution. As additional discoveries emerge from this region of China, scientists may gain an even clearer picture of the surprising evolutionary paths taken by the earliest birds.
Story Source:
Materials provided by Chinese Academy of Sciences Headquarters. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- Liming Xu, Min Wang, Ganmin Lin, Liping Dong, Ke Deng, Xing Xu, Honggang Du, Min Lin, Runsheng Chen, Zhonghe Zhou. Jurassic flightless bird reveals early ecological diversity of avialans. Nature, 2026; 658 (8136): 690 DOI: 10.1038/s41586-026-10972-z

Ukraine lost about $6 billion from port downtime in last three months
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
02:27:01 UTC
11:27:01 KST

MOSCOW, October 24. /TASS/. The loss of Ukraine’s foreign exchange earnings from the downtime of the ports of Greater Odessa, which has been going on for more than three months, amounted to about $6 billion, according to TASS calculations.
Commercial merchant ships continue to boycott the ports of Odessa, Chernomorsk, and Yuzhnoye; only vessels associated with the Ukrainian army enter them. Maritime trade is conducted through the Danube ports — Ukraine’s Izmail and Romania’s Constan·a, which together can potentially account for no more than a third of the exports that previously passed through the ports of Greater Odessa.
As a result, in September, Ukraine was able to export only 44% of the agricultural products planned for exports that month. Exports of metallurgical products ceased completely by the end of September. Together, these items accounted for about 65% of Ukraine’s exports and about $26 billion in foreign exchange earnings per year.
By using the railway network and the Danube ports for exports, Ukraine managed to partially reduce losses, but only slightly -- from about $70 million per day in August to about $60 million in September-October.
The idle time of Greater Odessa has been ongoing since July 22.

"Its core lies in the films and cinematic activities inside the screening venues," he told Xinhua.
Held in the Red Sea resort town of El Gouna from Oct. 15 to 23, the festival featured 77 films from around the world, alongside screenings, discussions and industry events.
CineGouna, the festival's industry and funding platform, also supports connections among film professionals and the development of projects at different stages, Mohsen said. ■

youtaro sakamoto’s kinetic thread column transforms human presence into shifting shadows
a delicate column formed from fine threads moves in response to nearby visitors, casting constantly changing shadows.
prefer designboom on google
[FEATURED]
KINETIC THREAD COLUMN installation draws from SUDARE SCREENS
Created by Japanese artist, engineer, and researcher Youtaro Sakamoto, Schattenrequisit: Column is a kinetic installation formed from fine threads that explores the relationship between architectural permanence, human presence, and shifting shadow projections. Drawing conceptual inspiration from the light-filtering properties of sudare (traditional Japanese slatted screens), the project treats physical material and immaterial shadows as unified components of a single sculptural composition.
ANIMATING STATIC ARCHITECTURAL FORMS THROUGH HUMAN MOVEMENT
The installation takes the form of an architectural column constructed from closely spaced fine threads. Integrated millimeter-wave sensors detect the proximity of visitors, triggering a stepper motor developed through computational design and physical prototyping. In response to movement within the space, the motor slowly rotates and shifts the thread assembly, altering the overlap of the linear strands and continuously transforming the shadow silhouettes cast across surrounding walls and floors. By animating a typically static structural archetype, the installation by artist Youtaro Sakamoto mirrors the interaction between fixed urban infrastructure and transient human circulation.

name: Schattenrequisit: Column
artist: Youtaro Sakamoto | @youtarosakamoto

WA Greens senator Jordon Steele-John will not attend parliament next week
In short:
WA Greens senator Jordon Steele-John has confirmed he will not attend parliament when it resumes next week.
Senator Steele-John is facing allegations of inappropriate conduct towards women, which he has denied.
What's next?
An independent investigation commissioned by the WA Greens is expected to get underway imminently.
WA Greens senator Jordon Steele-John has reiterated he won't be attending parliament next week, after releasing and then deleting a copy of a letter detailing allegations of misconduct against him.
On Friday night the senator took to social media to publish the letter which is addressed to Greens leader David Shoebridge and signed by seven current and former Greens staff or party office bearers.
The writers, who are not named, state they have been made aware of "multiple allegations of serious misconduct" being made against Senator Steele-John "spanning almost a decade (2017-2025)".
"These allegations all concern his behaviour in the presence of women. We are aware of multiple women who have taken up roles or volunteered in the party, who because of these allegations, have been warned not to be alone with him."
The letter, dated October 13, goes on to state the accusations have come from both inside and outside the party, and urges Senator Shoebridge to commission an independent investigation into the allegations, and review and update gendered violence protocols.
Senator Steele-John has repeatedly and strenuously denied the allegations.
On Saturday the 32-year-old senator said a copy of the letter was sent to him by Chief Political Commentator for the Nine papers, James Massola, who then broke the story on October 15.
The senator said he had initially chosen to post the letter on his own social media accounts because he "did not want to be seen as hiding from it".
"I'm now not sure that was the right call and I've taken it down. I'm really sorry for any additional distress it caused," he said, and reiterated his absence from parliament next week.
The WA branch of the Greens has commissioned an independent investigation into the allegations.
'Growing chorus'
In the days after the allegations became public, Senator Shoebridge initially said he understood Senator Steele-John was taking leave from parliament.
But last Sunday the WA senator denied that was the case in a lengthy open letter, prompting the federal Greens leader to encourage his colleague to take leave.
"I think the community assumptions are that he step aside for the extent of this inquiry and I've communicated that to Jordon," Senator Shoebridge told ABC Radio National Breakfast on Thursday.
In a statement on Saturday, Senator Shoebridge reiterated his view that Senator Steele-John take leave.
"This is in no way a prejudgement of any of these matters," he said.
Senator Steele-John reflected in his post on Friday that there had been a "growing chorus" calling on him to not attend parliament next week, when senate estimates will take place.
"I have explored attending digitally but have been informed that would also be unacceptable," he said.
"The precedent has now been set: any MP can be kept out of parliament by allegations of allegations."
